Just want to throw my positive review in the group so hopefully some day its rating will improve and more people will check this game out.
I understand the launch was really rough and its taken awhile for things to get patched, which is tragic and I have to wonder where the blame for that really lies but looking past all that this is an incredible sequel that improves and expands much upon the original.
The game runs fine for me, after tweaking some settings around its been a mostly smooth 60 at 1080.
My specs for ref. :
3770k @ 4.7ghz
nvidia 1070 - latest drivers
16gb 1600 ram
win 7
installed on ssd
As for the game itself though, I'm blown away by it. I just got around to playing the first game and after a heavy binge playthrough of that I jumped right into this and its an improvement in almost every way. The artstyle is refined and with the better graphics behind it the world is utterly captivating to take in. My first run through was with high chaos and there was a visual sickness and despair in the world, kind of felt like a Dark Souls game in that regard.
Combat has been expanded upon, sword charge attacks, human meatshields, better slide controls, more stylish takedown animations , 2 characters to choose from each with their own powers/bone charms/ weapon upgrades.
Level design is through the roof this time around, big city levels with civilians and non hostile/ hostile zones. A bunch of verticality and many buildings to explore you can spend so much time exploring each level and collecting all the loot/ upgrade materials. And a couple levels out of the game (wont give spoilers) have raised the bar so high not just for level design but technical achievement too. I can say without doubt a certain mission and its special item mechanic is the coolest thing I have seen in a game.
The story follows a similar thread to the original, nothing hyper complex or anything but it does raise some good morale questions and "who is really in the right here" type of thing. Also its presented so well which just goes back to the amazing art direction, the main villain really feels like some evil queen you would seen in a disney movie or something.
There are still some minor things that could use improvements , some of which were present in the first game as well but overall this is such a solid game. With depth and care put into it that you just dont see much these days. Also it is highly replayable between the high/ low chaos different characters and builds.
Probably my favorite game this year.
I hope you will give it a try and the tech issues arent too bad for you because you would really be missing out by not playing it.

All too often the mechanics are the same: run through a level hacking and slashing at anything that moves, racing to the next cutscene or grinding it out for the next big weapon,  barely paying attention, because you're steady mashing on that guick save button so you're golden no matter what happens... this game is not like that. Every enemy demands your full attention. And one slip up could cost you. There's no do overs - only consequences. Sure, you can often find a player or two willing to help you through a tight spot, or maybe they'll rip their way into your game and gank you for the fun of it. Sure it's going to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off at times, but it's a sweet madness, because every minute you know you earned everything you got.
This game is so much fun! I can't put it down. I will say that I often wish the online co-op experience wasn't always so transient. If you find someone you really enjoy playing with.. too bad, because once you're through the level you'll never see them again. It'd be nice if you had the option to stick around in someone's world as long as you wanted - or at least as long as you could survive for. But I guess it fits with the whole "you're on your own" vibe. Still... I want mmos to have combat like this. lol

An interesting jump from the original Dark Souls.  As an independent title, it stasds head and shoulders above the rest of the big budget games of the year, as a sequel to Dark Souls 1 it's easy to have some serious critiques from a design perspective.  I appreciate the move to create viability across all the weapon classes.  The major critique I have are the red phantoms in NG+, there was a shift and those phantoms don't have to play by the same rules the player do (a huge step backwards from DS1) and you legitimately get into unfun scenearios that you can't learn from and compensate for becasue what's happening is out of your control.  The design philospohy of "Fair but punishing" was what allowed me to fall in love with the Souls series to begin with, moving away from that philosophy grates on my nerves a ton. All my other critiques are for PVP and those wouldn't be objective critiscisms.
However, many paragrpahs following the previous would be singing this game's praises.  I absolutely adore it, being able to fly in the face of most AAA game developer tendencies and make a game that can act within itself and allow the world to justify the actions is fantastic, it's hard to create a game where you can observe it in a vacuum and justify the mechanics from a lore and world building perspective.  Fantastic job, I love this game.

Thimbleweed Park is a point and click adventure game that wants to stay in the past. Even if I grew with old MMucasFlem, ehem, LucasArts games, I feel I moved on from some of the ideosyncrancies games like this one.
For those you have not noticed that already, the game UI and art style evokes an era around 1990. You get a bottom side of the screen with both the verb list and the inventory. For those you did not live through that era, the developers even matched the verb list with the keyboard shortcuts. The story itself is also set in 1987, so it is hard not to think of nostalgia. Computers like the C64 are in the game.
The problem I see is regarding the innovations the developers tried for this game. One of them that you will notice is that almost every location spans over one screen. I get that you can now make every location stretch, unlike earlier games like Monkey Island, where pan movement of the camera was a truly first for a game like that. However, it makes traversal slower. Add to that that stretched locations do not add much to the game at all, with them being empty. Cemetery is especially aggravating. Developers added some tricks to make traversal faster - and even so I feel it is a little bit slow to my taste.
Another inguriating feature of the game is the multiple characters you take into control. This feature, when done correctly, does add something extra to the game. You shall expect actions that can only be done by a character, like the computer game designer being proficient with computers. There are a few situations where two characters need to do two separate things based on a timer, but that is all that it is. There is no direct interaction between characters except for transferring inventory items. Motivation of the different characters working together is non existant. One annoying feature of the game is that various characters do tell the same lines, just with different voice actors. There is an in-game joke that plays at the end of the game regarding that, although by that time I was alread past the annoyed phase.
As with any graphic adventure game, inventory and dialogue puzzles are the centre piece of the game elements. They are OK, nothing too stravagant or anything like that. I need to add that puzzles can only be solved in specific acts inside the game. You might already have all the components, but you cannot get past that hurdle until the dialog option opens. Apart from that, they are not too far fetched. That is, if you assume characters are telepathic or something.
The story is OK, although I do not particularly agree on how it is split.
I am sure that those that Kickstarted the game like things like appearing in the phone book. As a non backer, I have mixed feelings about that. I feel it pads the game with unnecessary and distracting info. The worst idea is that you more or less need to watch an early video at the Kickstarter page in order to know how to solve a puzzle.
I hope this review tells you which kind of game you are getting into. I was disconnected from the characters during most of the game, thus not really wanting to see what is next. If you have a lot of patience and endurance, feel free to apply.

It's hard to meet expectation. From waiting years as a backer to who created it, Ron Gilbert, Godfather of the point and click and now back in his realm. But if I'm honest, this game has smashed right through my expectations and risen above and beyond what I hoped for and imagined. It's like waiting years and years for a new record from your favorite band and somehow it's better then ever before, it's an entire album of new personal favorites.
The story shocked me in how cinematic it was written, so well orchestrated I found myself pondering what a movie would be like if made (id see the crap out of it). The humor was what I worried about, could it cut it with today's tastes. Another strong yes, I laughed out loud dozens of times from inside jokes to the adventure gamer to just great wit. Then there's the insult clown who's voice acting is tip top and who's lines are legitimately edgy here in 2017. It's not PC and I loved it.
The puzzles are magnificent. Put it this way- I got really stuck twice and in the end I was literally over thinking it both times. That's refreshing from a genre where more often than not you could rip hair out over-thinking and still not come to grips with what the game wanted. Not in this game. It's intuitive and I think I got held up or stuck when I treated it like adventure games past, only to realize I skipped an obvious or simple approach and find that was the solution.
The characters and story intertwined beautifully both as an epic journey and as a puzzle solving team. In fact the co-op use of the 5 unique characters made it hard to feel trapped, anytime progress was thwarted I'd switch characters, make progress with them and return to the other with a fresh mind set.
I'm sad it's over, the ending was hilarious, incredibly creative and actually a bit touching.
This has to be the greatest game in my favorite genre, ever. So here's to the team making more and meanwhile, enough time passing so i can play it again!
Compared to the standards that Monkey Island 2 has set, Thimbleweed Park is not a perfect game. However, even with its flaws it is still a highly recommended game for all point-and-click fans.

Ever since I played Resident Evil 3, I dreamt of a Resident Evil game with large open areas, that felt like an actual town instead of a bunch of corridors. The Evil Within 2 is the closest I've gotten to that so far.
The developers learned from their mistakes from the first game; the upgrade system is better, there's more weapon variety, more enemy variations, and Sebastian has become much more talkative (a little too talkative). But the most notable difference is the larger, more open areas in the sequel. I'll admit, at first I was worried that this would mean the game would feel more empty, but nearly every location in the larger maps has some loot or item that made exploration enjoyable. I never explored an area and said to myself "that was a waste of time." Speaking of wastes of time, thankfully, the base sprinting time is greatly improved from the first game, in order to deal with the size of the maps. There's tons of crafting supplies scattered around the maps, too, so while ammo may be scarce, you can always craft more.
You better like stealth if you're going to get this game, though. Compared to the first game, stealth has become extremely easy and overpowered, while combat has become much more difficult. Enemies approach much more quickly and have twitchy animations that can make them hard to hit, so you'll likely struggle if you prefer head-to-head combat. Even three normal enemies can be overwhelming. Meanwhile, enemies won't even bother to look if you crouch into a bush, or turn two corners, and a stealth kill is always easier than landing multiple headshots.
I do have a few minor complaints, though. Like the first game, for some reason you cannot change model or texture quality in the graphics options. I guess it has to do with their engine, but it seems like every PC game should have those options. There are also too many supplies; I finished the game with over 200 gunpowder, which is enough to craft 40 shotgun shells, or 200 assault rifle ammo. Also, invisible walls are everywhere, and in nonsensical places that are close to actual walls. Finally, the bosses aren't as interesting this time around. Only a couple have any fun gimmicks.
If you enjoyed the first game, you'll likely enjoy this one (unless you hate stealth).
If you haven't played the first game, I'd recommend you play it before this one. It's not mandatory for enjoying the main story, but you'll miss a lot of nods to the first game. But if you really want to jump into the sequel before playing the first, you'll still be jumping into a pretty good game.
I'd give this an 8.5/10.
: Having completed a second playthrough, I want to say that this game is decently replayable. A lot of games, especially horror games, these days have unskippable events and cutscenes that make second playthroughs boring, but The Evil Within 2 keeps it to a minimum.

Retro is a funny thing. When something is deliberately retro then it is seen as a feature. You can often see this with titles that use pixel-art intentionally to capture the nostalia of the early-80s gaming and many people love the game all the more for that fact. But when a game isn't trying to do that it looks and feels dated. That is Chaos Code.
When you look at the videos and such things are moving at such a blistering speed due to the skill of the players it all looks fantastic but when you sit down with the title and actually play it the jerky animations and lacklustre character resolution make it seem like you've loaded up an arcade title on MAME from the 90s. We're talking about graphics that are only a shade better than something like Marvel vs Capcom 2. The game's general presentation is also poor, it looks and feels rushed with spelling mistakes due to translation issues, menus that don't quite fit on the screen and stupid oversights like the inability to preview which color-switch you've selected from the character screen or the option to cancel your character choice and go back a step.  On the audio front the sound quality is... varied. Some of the voice samples sound like someone was far too close to the microphone, while others appear fine but with Ray his voice lines actually sound like they were being played back from a VHS tape from the 80s due to the audio quality. The music is hit and miss with some very fitting tunes but none are especially memorable.
But enough of the aesthethics, how does it play?
Frankly, the inputs are somewhat unforgiving. After playing many hours of SF4 you get to realise that Capcom give you very narrow windows of delay to complete specials simply to make the game more accessible. Looking back over the years you can see how this has developed because I remember days when I would struggle to perform Akuma's Shun Goku Satsu super move and now I can do it far more reliably in SF4. Chaos Code doesn't really do that as you soon discover that attempting many of the air-specials or air-super specials is very hit and miss. You can only really pull them off if you've chained them into a ground-special that will allow for an air-juggle since the animations give you a little more time to rotate the movement stick. In terms of the technical side, far too many characters play very similiar to each other and projectiles are very very common which really devalues the experience in my opinion since you spend much of your time trying to close the gap with the opponent if they are spamming them. The game leans heavily on specials as the varity of normals is simply not there. Many fighting games these days have different normals when moving forwards, jumping straight up, jumping forwards, crouching and standing still but Chaos Code generally has only normals for standing, couching and jumping. Some characters do have advancing normals but this is specific to them only. Some players may find that fine but frankly I'm not keen on leaning on specials to counter an opponents movement because there isn't a normal available due to a reduced repertoire that has become standardized in many other games from this genre.
On the plus side, the game has a wonderful sense of humor with many characters although this is not consistant across the all so its hard to really say if the developers were trying to be light-hearted with the tone of the game or not. It does suffer from a bit of an identity crisis as a result. The specials themselves are also very easy to remember due to many being half or quarter circles which is great of you like to vary which characters you use.
All in all, this is not something I can recommend though due to the negatives far out-weighing the positives. There are far better examples of 2D fighting games around that don't feel like you've booted up an arcade emulator and run a ROM from the 90s. As much as I love the concept of Chaos Code the way the game is presented is simply poor from both the visual and audio aspects; plus the underlying mechanics are not up the usual standard of quality you expect from the genre these days.
I was able to easily remap my buttons. No problem at all. And they even changed for the menu. Amazing, how far the fighting game technology has come!
This game contains a cyber ninja, goth lolita androids, a Lovecraft-themed magical girl, and a giant Italian chef who fights with restaurant tools. That's enough for me.

ARC System comes back with another great fighting game! And man, it is so much fun! With its easy-to-learn mechanics and smooth combos and graphics, we have to take a look at this game! Released in 2016 for PC and PS4, Chaos Code can easily be described as the simplest ARC System game, and we are going to figure out why.
Gameplay: This game is a 4 button fighter similar to SNK's King of Fighters series. It works in it's favor too, as it has the 2 punches and kicks. Of course, we also have specials, and like Street Fighter 3, pressing multiple punches or kicks will allow for an EX version doing more damage. Supers are also in and are self explanatory with level 3s. It is so fun and addicting on itself, but there is more: certain characters like the smol Rui allows you to do air combos. Speaking of characters, when you pick one, you are given 4 options, 2 new specials, and the other 2 are reversal counter moves. You are also given the option to choose run or a SF3 style dash jump. You can also do ARC styled super jumps, double jumps, and air dashes, but you cannot do multiple jump styles. Now of course, we get the usual modes, arcade, survival, online, and the ARC System staple: score attack.They mostly work well, and I do have some issues, but we will get there later.
Graphics: This game uses hand drawn anime graphics with some pixel style art. The combination works better than you may think. This causes a smooth gameplay style where you know what you are doing. I barely have any issues, if at all! Even at max graphics on my dirt powered computer, the game runs at a smooth 60FPS with no noticeable frame drops or slowdown. The stages present are also cool with a good variety, but they don't really have too much animation, but that is fine, it does not take down my enjoyment of the game.
Sound and Music: The game's OST is well made, but isn't really memorable. This is an issue with plenty of fighting games. Capcom are the main guys who make great fighting game OSTs, so they should be hired. The sounds themselves are not too bad, and they fit. Attacks sound great with some good voices, but one character does have a really annoying sound when hit.
Replayablility: Fighting games always do well here with the combos you can learn, character styles, and so much more. I won't go into detail here as I'll just repeat what I said in my Skullgirls review.
Extra notes: Here we go. The survival and score attack modes are broken. What I mean is that they do not follow your options, meaning you MUST only have one round and MUST have them at rising difficulty, and it rises fast and hard! It gets to BS levels of hard and definitely frustrating. Online mode, well, nobody plays online. No joke. It's impossible to find a game unless it's with a friend.
Final verdict: So many good things and only a few bad things. You can predict my final thoughts. Now, obviously, you might disagree with me, and that is fine, opinions. However, based on my experiences and playtime, I can say that I can give this game an 8/10 with a Rui doll. It is so good that you have to play it to know. If it was not for Maximilian Dood, I would have never heard of this game... maybe. But still, I thank him. Since the game is only about 20 bucks, you are not losing much, so I highly recommend it.
Also, Rui is just, so cute! I know I say that about a lot of female characters, especially in anime inspired games, but how can I resist?

long version
This game use delay based netcode. Having underwater matches when your ping is too big is to be expected. But this game netcode has some serious problems elsewhere: dealing with -unstable- ping. It will desyncs for very little ping variation, and in a good case it detects the desync and terminate the match. In a bad case, it will freeze the game and you will have to close the program and reopen it.
With this said, this game is still awesome.
The ost is brilliant, going from jazz funk "no forgiveness" by Mint Jam, classic music like "sonata for celia" by Kou, the more techno-ish funk "Rumble" by nekono, and the full blown out techno "Cut N' Run" by -45. Just for the number of different composers and how well some of them are (like Mint Jam), it's obvious how much care was put on the ost.
The gameplay have a mix of elements from different games that might please lot's of different people. It have airblock and the option after using a jump to do a doublejump or airdash (not both), that gives the spacing a ASW feel. Your 2D/cr.HK usually is the normal with more range but cant be canceled into special moves (that gives a street fighters 3 and onward feel). Jumping during a dash will trigger a super jump automatically and you can cancel special moves into supers by expending a extra bar (later kof's elements).
But there are lot's of original elements in the mix that gives the game it's own flavor. You can "customize" your character by choosing 2 between 2 extra special moves and 2 extra supers. And separate from that, you can choose between run style dash and step style dash. It might sounds like something from kof98umfe, but it's different. By choosing step dash, your walk speed don't increase, but your meter gain will. Also, it have a little of invul in the legs and you can cancel close normals into step dash, making it the way to go for tick throws. On the other side, the run have faster activation and recovery speed, so you can move more safely and microdash to convert into a combo from more situations.

Black Mesa is the rarest of things, a remake which actually works. I've followed the project since it was announced and the way they have meticulously gone about remaking every little detail about it is astonishing.
Black Mesa follows the basic setup of the original half life game, the maps are very similar and the sto9ry follows the same pattern. What they have also maanged to achieve is to add more to the game, taking out certain story elements which slow down the pace of the game and adding in more modern functionality. The NPC characters react and speak like half life: episode 2 characters, with graphics in the whole game being to the same level.
It should be noted that there are still gripes with the title. As a remake some of the voice acting is not spectacular, however this does not detract from how you play the game. Secondly is that the game is still in development - the final chapters are still to be released, which some people may find offputting.
All in all I can thoroughly recommend this game, I played it when it was originally free and then went out to support the dev's and bought it again. for me, this is now the modern definitive version of half life.

I wanted to give this game a positive review so goddamn bad. I enjoyed Just Cause 2 both on Playstation 3 and PC, and have over 500 hours total in that game.
When Just Cause 3 got announced, I was instantly hyped for this sequel for the oh so good Just Cause 2. However, the developers seem to think that a GTX 980 is minimum in a low end PC these days, so the framerates on my GTX 960 (the 2 GB edition by MSI) just cannot push this game beyond 40 frames per second. That is, if you forget about all the lag spikes that happen every 1 to 2 seconds.
The game itself is pretty well made. The wingsuit is a nice addition to move around the world quickly, and it works flawless in combination with the grappling hook. Speaking of the grappling hook, this thing has been completely redesigned. The keys to use it are no longer on the keyboard but mapped on you mouse so you can always use it quickly in any situation. You can now apply strength to the rope to pull stuff apart or to help you blow stuff up to gain more chaos points.
Chaos points don't seem to do anything anymore. They are just there because they were there in the previous games as well and it is probably still there for the sake of being. In Just Cause 2 you had to collect chaos points in order to progress in the game, however in Just Cause 3 that is no longer the case. New story missions unlock as soon as you have completed the previous ones, and most of the time you have done the stuff you have to in such mission before you start it, which doesn't add to the fun.
The game is gorgious and sure runs fine on a system using a high end quad/six core processor combined with 16 gigabytes of RAM and a GTX 980 or equivalent, but it seems that Avalanche Studios have forgotten about their 'cheapskate' community. For those that cannot afford a high end gaming system, pass on this game. The game runs horrible and there is little to no optimalisation, something we have seen different in Just Cause 2. That game runs on ultra on a potato, for that matter.
Rico has grown older and so have his powers. He is now capable of using multiple thethers at once, and can survive nearly every explosion if they are further than 3 feet (1 meter) away from him. This only adds to the fun. You truly feel like you are playing as some kind of reborn rebel that can save the world like any superhero can. Your arsenal has been expanded with some new interesting weapons (You can now fire mini nukes, ♥♥♥♥ yes!).
I do recommend this game to those who own a high end system, however, everything below a GTX 970 or R9 390 combined with a mid range processor will not pull this game at 60 at any settings. I have played this on my i5 4460, 8GB RAM, GTX 960 system and it doesn't matter which settings I use, I never reach a stable 60 frames per second and I have always suffered from major lag spikes. Adding to this that the last update, which had to fix some performance issues, only made the game run worse, this game is a total flop.
Man I had hoped this to be so ♥♥♥♥ing good.
[EDIT #1 May 19. 2016] I am changing this review to positive. Most gamebreaking bugs have been solved and the memory leak issue has been fixed. My relatively low-spec system can now run this game at 60 frames per second all the time on medium. It is still not as good as Just Cause 2, both story and gameplay wise, but it is now an enjoyable game.

The controls are tight and responsive, and the atmosphere the game creates is one of the tensest I've ever felt. The game may have an awkward HUD and weak weapons but they are what make it great. You have to survive and the game will make that a challenge for you. You must time your hit, ration your health, plan your attack, you must check every corner for enemies, you must choose your upgrades wisely, and you must survive everything the game throws at you.
All in all this game remains great and I whole heartedly thank the wonderful people and Night Dive Studios who have brought it back for future generations to enjoy and are working to bring back so many other classics like it.

This game is billed as a nostalgic throwback to the adventure games of the nineties, and it delivers on that a bit too much. I both enjoyed this game and was deeply annoyed with it the entire time I was playing.  I wish there was a third option between thumbs up and thumbs down.  Maybe a shrug.
The good:
-The puzzles! There are some really excellent puzzles in this game that require a bit of lateral thinking, but even when I was stuck the solution never felt unfair.  For the most part the game lets you figure out the solutions without too many hints, which is refreshing.
-Multiple playable characters.  The townsfolk react differently to different people, which is fun and adds an extra dimension to the puzzle solving.  It's also fairly easy to  move between different locations, so haiving the wrong person in the wrong screen isn't really a problem.
-The art and animations are really well done
The bad:
-The writing is a mixed bag.  The constant in-jokes and fourth wall breaking are really heavy handed - it's a steady stream of "nudge-nudge wink-wink" that gets to be obnoxious after an hour or so.  We get it.  We know who Ron Gilbert is, we know we're playing an adventure game (and if you don't, you aren't going to get the joke anyways).  I realise this is personal taste though and YMMV - if you love this sort of humour then you're in for a treat.
-The "plot twist" is telegraphed from a mile away and is pretty cliche - it also makes the mysteries you've been trying to solve up until that point irrelevant, and the ending feels rushed.
-The voice acting is wildly uneven.  I ended up turning it off and cranking up the text speed.
If you love old-school adventure games and have played every game in the LucasArts catalogue multiple times, you've probably already bought the game.  If you're newer to the genre I'd suggest starting elsewhere.

This might actually be one of my new favorite anime fighting games, and that's considering I've played Uniel, Blazblue, and Nitro+ and none of those really clicked with me entirely, but something about this game's flow and mechanics just feel solid. Super slick fighting game. Everything felt smooth as a fighting game fan. Really love the diverse cast of characters and the ways they each play!

Chaos Code is one hell of an underground game. The visuals feel very unattractive, the story and dialogues are exceptionally stupid, even among anime fighters. Voice acting is so damn cringeworthy that it becomes funny in the end. To top it all, there are typos all over the place - what the hell were the developers even doing? All in all, the first impression may be kinda unappealing. But what lies beneath the surface is a very enjoyable little fighting game.
There is a generous roster of characters with different playstyles and customizable moveset. Even though the visuals are ugly, the combat feels really smooth and responsive. The moves look cool and combos are satisfying. I fell in love with the stages, which are very often lively, colorful and funny. The background music is top-notch (really, Cthylla's stage BGM is just lovely) and the ending CGs are beautiful. There is also a lot of single-player content to enjoy, in case you don't have friends to play with or don't know about Discord.
While Chaos Code certainly isn't an A-tier fighting game (like GG, BB, Uniel and so on), I still think it would be a mistake to just dismiss it. I'm having a blast with the game at this moment and I think I will be coming for more in the near future.

For any major fans of something like Guilty Gear or Blazblue, I'd recommend you stay away from this one, but if you are just a nerd/major fan for anime fighters in general... there should be -something- here for you to enjoy. All that being said, I just cant bring myself to truly recommend this game. As stated, if you are fan of much faster combat in terms of fighting games, you might want to avoid this one, but if you are a major fan of any and all anime fighters you are sure to find something to enjoy with this.

The game trusts you to figure out things  on your own, and feels more immersive because of it. Example: at one point, you have to find a computer chip to access a certain area. Instead of "objective complete: found chip," you have to sprint to the storage area where electronics are located, reference the chip model number in your email, and find the correct model of chip before continuing. When you want to use a door keycode, you'll be checking your PDA for the code, and keeping your head on a swivel while you punch in the numbers, all while Shodan goads you like a glitchy/vindictive GlaDOS. Like the original Half-Life, there's something about the gameplay that's addicting and massively fun.
Btw, if  you're worried about "nostaliga goggles," I played this for the first time last year, and it still holds up.
One quick con, though: the game allows you to upgrade what you want, even if it leads to failure. Hacking and radiation resistance is highly recommended.

I7-6700
32GB Ram

Dishonored 2 had a rough start with its poor optimization giving people fps issues, though I did not experienced this in dishonored 2 as i got the game after many different patches were released, I have experieneced fps issues in other games so I know what it is like to have these sorts of problems.
I am running a MSI 390 gpu with a i5 6600k cpu and getting an average of 60-70 fps with it rarely dropping to around 50 fps (I was also testing my fps around the city parts on the map as this is where people are getting the most problems with their fps).
Gameplay is more fun then its ever been as we now have a second protagonist, Emily Kaldwin. She has a completely different set of skills and powers to use compared to corvo who we are still able to play as, him still having his norwal set of skills and powers from the first game. My favourite power of Emily's is the domino effect which grants the ability to link the fates of multiple characters together, and whatever you do to one character then affects the others in the same way. Another thing they have added other then abilitys is a new gadget called the 'Timepiece' which essently allows you to transtion between the past and present during during certain situations. This opens up a new way to solve puzzles throughout the world.
The story is essentially the same as the first though I have not finished this I think I know where the story is headed though I will not spoil anything, they have added back the chaos feature which decides the fate of the outcome of the game. Chaos can be effect by who you choose to kill or not kill, who you choose to side with and what route you take which might be stealthy or chaotic.
The visual aesthetics and art style in this game is amazing right down to the dark, plague ridden streets of Karnaca.
To sum it up this game has a attractive art style, fun gameplay and a fairly decent storyline.

Dark Souls 2 is basically Dark Souls 1 with less creative bosses and all around more stuff to kill. All around fun and awesome game. However, there are two major flaws with the game, one was poor design and the other was intentional bad design.
The poor design is the lack of dedicated servers. They are in the game, but only for duels and co-op. However, they aren't for invaders and invading. So, the classic problems from the first game with those laggers come back. This allows for people to have daggers with striking distances of spears. Also, the cross region setting isn't actual regions; it's just Japanese players or not.
The intentional bad design is Soul Memory. Instead of basing invading/jolly co-op with soul level like it did in Dark Souls 1, Dark Souls 2 uses Soul Memory, which is a total amount of souls your character has found. Even if you die, those souls were counted. This fixes the twink problem in the first Dark Souls, when players would have a lvl25 with max gear and invade noobies. This doesn't happen anymore; but it has a terrible cost. Now endgame builds are insane. In Dark Souls 1, the PVP lvl range for endgame was around 100~120; but for the sequel, there isn't any cap.
With the two negatives above mixed, you have situations in New Game+ and beyond where you encounter broken builds and laggers constantly via invading. There are ways to block invaders... But it also blocks co-op and the ability to be summoned by all the covenants.
I'd recommend making a new character after awhile, or duking it out with the invaders. Otherwise, the game is fine.

Where do I start.....
The single player is a standard affair, nice time killer and overall was fun.  I wouldn't call it the greatest single player experience in the world but it def was enjoyable.  Kevin Spacey does a great job, and the fact the a corporation can wield that much power doesnt seem that off base.
Now lets get to the heart and soul of the game which is its multiplayer component....
This review is of the multiplayer in its current state 4/18/15 after I have logged 289hrs of multiplayer time.  Right now the multiplayer is broken..... The patch that came out on 4/8 ruined the game for most players.   RIght now many players are experiencing hard disk errors and the game crashes to desktop almost upon load up.  I find myself having to log in 3/4 times just to sign in..... Once you are in multiplayer you're ok.... but not really.  Due to no dedicated servers you are once again at the mercy of P2P host connections which are spotty at best.  If you dont go into you're config files and change the default "max_ping "800" to a more reasonable number you will be playing people in Bangladesh.... Before the patch the game ran fairly well! I have a GTX970 and it smashes through 9/10 games on the market today.  HOWEVER, this game is a direct console port so you have fps lag in a lot of maps and overall lag from the P2P connection.  Sooooo you have to play the "find the best gfx setting" game to get the right balance.  Honestly SHG needs to get in and fix the maps and the fps lag, its inexcusable that a game thats been out 5+ months isnt running smooth on most cpu rigs.  I'm optimistic they will re-patch and fix these glaring errors because they're borderline game breaking right now.
The overall fun factor once the game is actually working is great!! The new mechanic of the exo suits are a nice change of pace from the standard fare of just rushing around on the ground.  Although you have an exo now you also have to keep your head on a swivel because attacks can come from all sides and at a super fast pace.  This is def the fastest COD I've played and I've played them all.  I love the guns!! The variety and the customization is one of this games strong points.  There def was some OP guns at launch and guns that needed a buff, but they have def patched the guns properly thus far.  The M14 still needs some love tho!!! The EM1 laser gun was horribly OP previously but has been rendered useless after this past patch.  The "pick 13" class setup should be used in all COD's going forward, it really allows you to mix and match ur classes up and is a welcome return from Black Ops 2.  Overall, the experience is a fun one and should be played if you love the franchise.  Its not a perfect game by any stretch but when its working right, its a blast!!
I would recommend this game to anyone who loves COD and is a FPS genre fan in general.  I do want to add that If you haven't played since launch I would wait till the patch fixes the current issues.  The game has a low player count due to these current issues so wait on ur purchase till they iron out the "kinks".

Considering netcode: It's OK. If I'm to compare it with other titles using Steamworks, I would rate this game as 6\10, GG REVELATOR 10\10. Overall, the more I play, the more I like this game :)

Review based partly on my many hours of experience with the "vanilla version" of Chaos Code on PS3.
One of the best fighting games out there that isn't from an established developer, and arguably a contender for the title of best non-Japanese fighting game. (FK Digital is based in Taiwan and Australia, although all the voice acting is in Japanese.) Chaos Code mixes attributes and mechanics from various Capcom, SNK and ArcSys fighters with a surprisingly appealing and memorable cast of characters, along with a well-animated visual style that's very much its own thing. While there isn't much backstory to the cast, and it's all buried within the arcade mode and website, you'll probably enjoy getting acquainted with a magical girl themed after the Cthulhu mythos, a wrestling chef who incoporates a huge variety of cooking tools and ingredients into his moveset, and a flamboyant crossdressing manga artist who has a completely different costume for almost every one of his attacks.
Despite a surface similarity to the KOF series, there really isn't another fighting game with a roster like this one, and none of the characters fall neatly into the usual archetypes of shoto, grappler, zoner, etc. Unusually for a fighting game, there is a dual emphasis on both traditional SF/KOF-style ground game footsies, and GG/BB-style, high-flying airdash antics. Thankfully, these elements are integrated together smoothly, and don't feel disjointed when they're used at the same time.
The combo system is quite deep, yet significantly easier to pick up than in KOF, GG or Blazblue, largely because of the intuitive "magic series" combos for normals and the generally forgiving input windows. (Unlike in other recent 2D fighters, there are no autocombos.) Because the original PS3 version infamously lacked any form of online play, I've almost never had the chance to play it with other human beings until now. But it seems to me that the roster is pretty balanced, aside from the super armor-heavy brawler Ray being perhaps a bit too cheesy.
The most original gameplay concept of Chaos Code is that before a match begins, every character can choose to equip two unique extra moves out of a pool of four, which includes both specials and supers. You can take both extra specials, both extra supers, or one of each into the fight if you want. A personalized move selection might help you to be able to pick up a character that you wouldn't otherwise be comfortable playing as, and allows for a lot of added variation in your playstyle. A Street Fighter III-style parry is also present, and is far easier to pull off than in that game, although it costs meter to use here.
Additions to New Sign of Catastrophe from the PS3 version include two completely new characters, a color edit mode (though you can only select from preset colors), an expanded gallery mode that unlocks with in-game currency, a KOF-style mission mode that should help to familiarize players with the different characters and mechanics, and most importantly, the long-awaited online mode.
My only real issue is the annoyingly long loading times I've been experiencing, which were almost as bad on PS3. In this case, though, it seems they're the result of my playing the game on my near-toaster level PC, and anyone with the specs to run modern AAA games should have no problem at all. I've also encountered some occasional sound glitches, though these could also be on my end. The online netcode itself is of decent quality, especially for the developer's first try. It probably can't be relied upon for opponents on the other end of the United States, or on other continents, but it should function fine when fighting anyone in your general area. I still highly recommend Chaos Code to any fan of 2D fighters, especially if you're looking for something off the beaten path that hasn't been over-played and over-analyzed to death.

This is a 15 years old game, and sadly one that didn age very well. Graphics are obviously bad for today's standards and wasnt its major trait even back then. What the game really do well, and thats one time can't take away from it, is the atmosphere.
You are some sort of super soldier in a groundbreaking space ship mission, but you were kinda sleeping prior to the events of the game, and wakeup right when things are completely out of control. The world you see around you looks really like Dead Space, in the sense that you are in a decaying space ship, everyone is dead, you are basicly alone and everything that is kinda alive wants to kill you. Also a lot like Dead Space, weapons, heals, ammo and better gear are highly scarce, so you have to play the game in the most conservative way possible, making every bullet count, or even spend some time of the adventure avoiding enemies or killing them with melee to save ammo... they can get this much scarce.
With another comparison, this game have a lot in common with Bioshock, not only the name, but many mechanics are present here, like upgrading your weapons and hacking stuff (HACK EVERYTHING! even that portable game console you get early on.LOL), and even spells, in system shock named Psionics. but unlike Bioshock, there are many other mechanics here, like your weapons getting worse with use and eventually breaking completely (consecutively maintenance and repairing), researching new strange artefacts to gain extra advantages or use new itens and a RPG like statistics and skills, basically leveling up.
The sounds, while in my opinion not of incredible quality, are remarkably well designed, adding greatly to the atmosphere you are inserted in, with enemies making disgusting sounds and being possibly heard from far away and several strange entity talking directly to you, including one human. these work to make you feel even more confused and helpless about whats is going on and make the whole experience much more scary and enjoyable, even if is by never letting you get confortable. And the music in my opinion should just get muted, because its breaks the immersion.
The atmosphere is finally completed by several audio logs scattered around which contain both the last words of some of the living, which gives you insight on how was things doing in the ship before you woke up and information both crucial to the progress on the game and some useful, but missable things, with that in mind searching for the audio logs is a must as it enhances greatly the atmosphere and the immersion of the game, Just like Doom 3, if you have ever played that.
There is also some cons to the game, but i think they are minor, for example, models are really ugly and they animations are quite stiff and unnatural, and AI can be really dumb some times,  like melee attacking enemies not attacking you, but instead keep forever running after you, even if you are "touching" each other, if you just keep moving in any direction that is not into them. In other hand, AI is good enough to actually hit you with ranged attacks, even if you are moving, by calculating where you will probably be and shooting ahead of your movement.
Also, while the game took me something like 12H to finish, the last 2 hours, the last areas and bosses were kinda underwhelming and felt a bit rushed and the ending was clearly a joke. But thats just 1/6 of the game, dont let it spoil the whole master piece that the other 10 hours are.
Overall the game delivers one of the best immersive, unsettling, and scary experiences i had with gaming, as well as a great and interesting story, and i played a lot of games. The sad part is that the game is really hard and unforgiving with the newcomer, it needs the player to settle down, read a lot to understand the game mechanichs and even then, think a lot to know what to do with them, just like any RPG, not a run and gun.
This game was insane for its time and still a very valuable experience today as it has influenced many modern day hits like Dead Space and Bioshock and helped create that whole new genre of game, the FPS/RPG hybrid, as well as the now popular survival horror. So as long as you dont care about its age and how bad it looks for today standards, that kind of experience cant really get much better.

This  game runs poorly on the PC. DISHONORED 2 uses the id Tech 5 Engine vs. the id Tech 6 Engine which powers the recent DOOM reboot. The sixth iteration uses/offers modern programmatic mechanisms such as asynchronous shaders and VULKAN (low level API akin to DirectX 12) to maximize frame rates. Despite the fact that a previous id game, RAGE, also used the fifth iteration, DISHONORED 2 runs extremely poorly on my Core i7 (IvyBridge) alongside an original nVidia GTX Titan GPU,  it struggled to reach/maintain 30 fps. That's not the worst of it though. The games exhibits lots of "rips" where polygons/textures meet with the effect being you see lots and LOTS of white pixels along these seams. The problem manifests itself to such a large degree that it is an acute eyesore/distraction. This problem seemed more common in the late 90's and early naughts (2000s) and it surprises me to see it in a modern title to this degree. And since the game has been out several months, it may never be patched to address this. In short, this is the broken record of a PC port of a AAA title being the 2nd class citizen ("Batman: Arkham Knight" anyone?). In the end, I wound up getting a Steam refund and simply bought the PS4 version. It runs fine on the PS4 Pro (frame rate) and free of all bleeding white pixels along seams -- no need to ruin DISHONORED 2's wonderful motif & artistic direction. If you have a PS4, go play that version instead... this game on the PC version simply isn't worth it.

Ravenfield originally started out as a test in the Unity engine for ragdolls. It slowly turned into a simple Unity project, and then a fully fledged game.
I've been testing Ravenfield since before the beta released, and it has been amazing watching this game grow. The game exploded in popularity on itch.io, and suddenly though all of the commotion there was a big community and YouTubers making videos on the game.
The reason I enjoy Ravenfield even though it's a singplayer game as much as I do is the weapons. The animations are solid. They feel like they pack a punch, and when you hit your target it feels satisfying. The AI you're up against is decent, but it does have its quirks. That's not to say that it's bad, they can be challenging. Silly little behaviours can happen, but often there's a chuckle or two involved. Overall, it's the combinations of weapons and AI that makes it enjoyable.
The vehicles are limited in this first release, but of course that's going to change. The vehicles alone are fun to use, even challenging. Some have taken issue with the controls, but that's nothing a quick rebind can't fix.
There's a limited number of maps in the game so far, but they're sufficient and well put together. Full support for mods is planned, including a map maker. I can't wait to see what kind of content the community cooks up.
Overall, the future for the community and this game seem very bright. I'm more than happy to be a part of it, and if the price doesn't seem justifiable at this point, don't be afraid to wait.

***SPOILER FREE REVIEW***
Although Alien: Isolation may not be the Holy Grail of the Alien Franchise as many had hoped, this game does very little wrong with its formula. It made a proper stealth action game out of the Alien property. Nearing the end especially, the game drags on. The suspense that took so long building doesn't really feel like it leads up to anything. It just keeps building until the game abruptly ends. I would recommend this title as a rental if you have a good few days to set aside. Other than that? Wait for a sale. The only thing worth playing in this game is the storyline. Unless you enjoy a timed cat and mouse session, the Survival Mode is pretty boring.
PROS:
- Captures the spirit of the original movie perfectly
- Builds suspense very well
- Avoids pandering to fans too much
- Realistic AI for the alien
- Genuinely surprising jump scares
- Impressive cinematics
- Good level design
CONS:
- A bit too long to maintain suspense
- Certain cinematic sequences like the escapades out in space detract from the anticipation
- Many mechanics are not explained well in the game, such as the Rewire Stations
- Technical Issues: The game itself runs at a variable framerate, but the sound anticipates a fixed 60 fps, which causes audio/video lag. This is most noticeable during cutscenes.
NOTES:
- Little to no replayability
- Took approximately 23 hours for a leisurely playthrough

Dark Souls II, for you uninitiated, is a dungeon crawler that pits you against a relentlessly hostile world, tasking you with navigating deathtrap environments populated by enemies fiendishly positioned to put you between as many rocks and hard places as possible. It sells itself on its difficulty, and to its credit it is a difficult game. It will kill you with rage-inducing frequency until you git gud.
The levels are visually varied and, for the most part, aesthetically pleasing. Moving away from Dark Souls' run-down brown and grey color pallete, Dark Souls II reflects the world's descent into decay in full color; Heide's Tower of Flame looks no less doomed to vanish completely beneath the waves for all its dazzling blues, and in this respect Dark Souls II has clearly surpassed its predecessor.
It's difficult to immerse yourself fully in the game's world, however, because the story is bad. That's really all there is to it. The design philosophy underlying Dark Souls series storytelling is immersion through sparcity: you are left to tell your own story, piecing together a narrative from the skeleton provided you by the game and the things you find and do while playing. In order for this to work, however, the game needs to provide a workable skeleton. Dark Souls did this. Dark Souls II does not.
Dark Souls starts off with a brief genesis myth, outlining the great powers that have shaped the world and naming major names that you should watch out for. It gives you the general problem afflicting the world: the Fire is dying, and the lands are overrun with undead. You are one such undead, locked away in the Undead Asylum because nobody knows what else to do with your kind. The game starts. Oscar of Astora breaks you out of the asylum and delivers to you a vague prophecy that promises that if you travel to Lordran and ring the Bell of Awakening you will discover the fate of the undead.
This is your motivation. Discovering the fate of the undead is relevant to you personally as one of the undead, and it could potentially solve one of the two major problems plaguing the world. You don't know what the Bell of Awakening is, yet, but you find out immediately after arriving in Lordran; there are actually two Bells, and you have to ring them both. You are given  sparse direction about how to do this, the game telling you only that one bell is in the Undead Parish and the other in Blighttown. You are left to find these places for yourself but you know it when you do find them, and this lets you know that you are on the right track. Once both bells are rung that narrative thread runs out, but you are given a new one, involving both the dying of the Fire and the fate of the undead and tying back in to the genesis myth from the introduction. You follow this second thread to the end of the game. The ending's meaning is not explicitly explained, but over the course of your journey you are given enough information to piece together what has happened and what the effects of your actions are.
Notice that for all it took two meaty paragraphs to type up, the story is actually bare-bones, even downright simple. This is how it should be. People talk a lot about the Souls series having complex and difficult lore--and it does--but the *plot*, the sequence of events that befall your character, is straightforward and easy to understand. The complexity lies in the backstory, the half-glimpses of other places and times that contribute to the world you move through but with which you do not directly interact. That's fine: you don't need to know anything about the politics of the Dragon School of Vinheim for the things your character does to make sense. The plot has to answer a single question for you: Why are you doing what you are doing?
Dark Souls II fails at this.
You are told that you are one of the undead, doomed to degenerate into a mindless Hollow, feeding on the souls of human beings. Once you had a life, with other people in another place, but the curse has taken that from you. In search of a cure you wander, drawn inexorably to the kingdom of Drangleic. You don't have a choice in the matter: Drangleic is a lure for the undead, calling them across space and time for unknown reasons, and you will eventually find yourself there. Two general problems, then, much like the first game: you are slowly Hollowing and need a cure, and Drangleic is vaguely ominous and possibly evil and while you're there you might as well find out why.
You wind up in Majula and run smack into the Emerald Herald. She's Ms. Exposition, or what passes for it in a Souls game, and she's here to do what the Crestfallen Warrior did: give you a goal to be on the lookout for, some vague hints as to where you'll find it, and send you off. You start talking to her, and she tells you about how to become the next monarch of Drangleic.
Wait, what? No, ma'am, I think you're confused. Drangleic is the secondary plot thread at the moment, it doesn't come to the forefront of the story until I've learned more about what's happened to it while trying to find a cure for the undead curse. You're not supposed to be talking about becoming the monarch and seeking the king until the second half of the game. But no, no more from her about curing the curse. Not that the curse is suddenly forgotten: every time she addresses you you're the "Bearer of the Curse" so it's always there, right in your face, and you wondering what in God's name happened to trying to cure it. Why am I running around killing the four Old Ones to take their souls? Are they going to help me cure the curse? No, they'll let me seek an audience with the King. Why do I want that? Not telling me? Oh, okay.
The hideous part is that this is completely explained in literally four lines of unused dialogue. "The curse is a part of life itself. No one will ever be rid of it. And so there is only one choice. To await a worthy monarch. A monarch who can shoulder your burden. Lest this land swallow you whole… As it has so many others." Those aren't the only last-minute omissions that damage the story, either. It's done in other places, always to the game's detriment. The effect is deeply unsatisfying and sours the rest of the game.
Corners have been inexplicably cut in other places as well. The pleasing-but-unspectacular graphics are a pale shadow of what we saw in the teasers, and the lighting engine and torch mechanics were almost completely stripped out. The rate at which equipment loses integrity was tied to either the frame count or the processor speed, leading to weapons and rings breaking twice as fast on the PC as on consoles: there is no fix for this as yet. Enemies are given absolutely bizarre tracking, massive bosses spinning on a dime to strike players standing behind them (look up a video of the Covetous Demon or the Rotten spinning like tops). Because of this, fights fall into a pattern of strike, dodge out of range, wait for the enemy to exhaust their pattern, repeat, turning them more into tests of patience than tests of skill.
Most damning is the broken multiplayer matchmaking system. Sorting by Soul Memory instead of Soul Level means that there is no incentive to ever stop leveling up. Character builds are a thing of the past: you will move towards the mathematically optimal monobuild, maximizing defense and offense with no tradeoffs or interesting quirks, or you will be curbstomped by other players who have. This is a game-breaking flaw. It also means that you can't stay and co-op on a single boss whose fight you particularly enjoy; you'll quickly move beyond the Soul Memory range.
All in all, it smacks of a cash-grab, laziness from a dev team who knew they were guaranteed sales based on the good name of previous releases. It is not what it could, or should, have been.
Do not reward this misbehavior. Do not buy this game.

Note: This Review is for Casual Mode
I remember when Thimbleweed Park was first announced several years ago, when all we had was a simple concept art of Agent Ray and Reyes. And now look at the masterpiece this game has become..
Thimbleweed Park is game that has two mysteries in one: figuring out a murder mystery and solving the mystery of the Pillow Factory Fire that occured before the events of the game.
Ron Gilbert and Gary Winnick have done an amazing job with immersing players into the decrepit and spooky town of Thimbleweed Park. Oftentimes, I find myself getting the chills looking at the run down buildings. The graphics fit the game perfectly.
The soundtrack of Thimbleweed Park is also memorable. I find myself humming the game's theme song. The sound effects like opening and closing doors, hearing footsteps, and even the ambient environment noises like the wind blowing in the distance, crickets chirping at night, or a fire hydrant splashing water really add to environment, further immersing players into this world.
What really drives Thimbleweed Park foward are the characters. Agent Reyes and Agent Ray share a unique relationship with each other. Neither one trusts the other, but they choose to work together. Delores is the perfect programmer/nerd girl with a passion for following her dreams. Ransome the Clown is obnoxious and full of sarcastic remarks. Franklin the Ghost is depressing, but also adds an entire layer of puzzle solving an already amazing adventure game.
The gameplay in Thimbleweed Park takes a step back from modern adventure games and lets you do all the work in figuring out what to do in your environment. Playing this game makes me realize just how much modern adventure games hold our hands and silo us down a typical path. One of the things that I love is being able to test and experiment around with different commands. This usually pays off in very interesting or unexpected results. I found myself stuck in the game multiple times only to do something weird and solve the puzzle! I feel like a lot of the puzzles in this game are either predictably logical, or they require you to think about it from a different perspective to figure out. I was never stuck for too long, and having that "Ah ha!" moment was always worth it. I was able to finish Casual Mode in 12 hours.
Perhaps one of the things that I enjoyed the most about Thimbleweed Park was the immersion itself. Never did I feel impatient on wanting to progress the plot further. Sometimes, I would just sit in the cafe and take in the welcoming environment. Other times, I would sit in the Edmund library and just peruse the tons of books that the game has to offer. There's just so much in this tiny world worth exploring, that I never felt bored expecting something more to do. Even as something as little as revisitng areas to look for collectable specks of dust. Yes! Specks of dust!
Gripes. There were a few things that did make Thimbleweed Park frustrating to play. Thankfully, there wasn't too much, but I do need to address them:
- Some characters in the game share task lists. This isn't a problem, but if you have multiple playable characters, it can be annoying having to make sure both characters meet up to give each other items. It immediately reminded me of Gilbert's The Cave game, where characters had to constantly backtrack to give each other items. The map item resolves problem pretty fast.
- At some points in the game, I found that the Part I was in prevented certain tasks from being completed. For example, Franklin's task list had goals that he needed to accomplish, but I had to wait until I was in a later part of the story to accomplish that specific task. Don't include the task in that part of the story until it's needed. It would have saved me a lot of time!
- I found it quite strange that playable characters couldn't communicate with each other. If Agent Reyes and Agent Rey are in the same room, why can't there be some conversation topics that they can share between themselves? Even if it doesn't necessarily pertain to the plot. Another example of this is when Agent Rey goes to the Edmund Mansion to speak to Delores, but Delores dismisses her. Agent Rey never has a future conversation with Delores. I know that these characters are all on their own storylines, but the only real cohesion between them was at the very end of the game. Maybe this was on purpose? Perhaps we are supposed to feel this disconnect between the characters, because they are all operating on selfish gains? And the very end of the game causes all of them to work together? I don't know. I can't really peg this as a gripe -- maybe I was just expecting something else.
Overall, Thimbleweed Park was a joy to play. Playing the game felt like I was binging a Netflix show. Ron Gilbert did a fantastic job grabbing players into this world and holding them tight in figuring out the mysteries. Even after finishing the game, I still find myself excited to go back and play the Hard Mode, ready to check out all the puzzles and different locations I missed from my first playthrough.
I highly reccomend this game to people that love adventure games; you are in for a welcoming and truly wonderful treat.

I have put in 20 hours into this game, 20 painful hours hoping that gameplay would improve. I have no idea what the dungeons are like but I can describe the grind involved with leveling up your character. Very very frustrating…
Let's start with the map system because your going to spend a lot of time looking at it to orientate yourself. You get a world map, town map and compass. The compass would work fine if your destinations where all in a staight line. Since you cannot fly you will be forced to navigate around the countless obstacles like towns, mountains, bridges, water, and the like without the aid of a mini map and to make things even more difficult to arrive at your destination, 50 percent of the time it will be dark…
The inventory provided with your character is extremely limited which really adds to the frustration of continually returning to a town to unload. You will spend a lot of time, running, walking and riding.
You are also required to learn all the trades and skills as a level up option which is confusing due to the limited storage space. So after you learn them all, you can only concentrate on one due to limited space. So what's the point of giving them all to you ???????
The fighting is slow and awkward with no real sense of when you're in danger until it's too late. You will have a very difficult time playing this game alone. I have better luck with the mouse and keyboard as it is not controller friendly on any level of this game.
The quests are found randomly by exploring with no real or believable indication that you're ready for this quest.The colours green, yellow orange and red next to the quest title are what you get….you'll get you’re a** kicked on yellow most of the time and some green are impossible alone and by the time you are strong enough to combat it alone the items and quest will be useless to you. Its just hard too hard to lvl up alone....

I wanted to give this game a positive review so goddamn bad. I enjoyed Just Cause 2 both on Playstation 3 and PC, and have over 500 hours total in that game.
When Just Cause 3 got announced, I was instantly hyped for this sequel for the oh so good Just Cause 2. However, the developers seem to think that a GTX 980 is minimum in a low end PC these days, so the framerates on my GTX 960 (the 2 GB edition by MSI) just cannot push this game beyond 40 frames per second. That is, if you forget about all the lag spikes that happen every 1 to 2 seconds.
The game itself is pretty well made. The wingsuit is a nice addition to move around the world quickly, and it works flawless in combination with the grappling hook. Speaking of the grappling hook, this thing has been completely redesigned. The keys to use it are no longer on the keyboard but mapped on you mouse so you can always use it quickly in any situation. You can now apply strength to the rope to pull stuff apart or to help you blow stuff up to gain more chaos points.
Chaos points don't seem to do anything anymore. They are just there because they were there in the previous games as well and it is probably still there for the sake of being. In Just Cause 2 you had to collect chaos points in order to progress in the game, however in Just Cause 3 that is no longer the case. New story missions unlock as soon as you have completed the previous ones, and most of the time you have done the stuff you have to in such mission before you start it, which doesn't add to the fun.
The game is gorgious and sure runs fine on a system using a high end quad/six core processor combined with 16 gigabytes of RAM and a GTX 980 or equivalent, but it seems that Avalanche Studios have forgotten about their 'cheapskate' community. For those that cannot afford a high end gaming system, pass on this game. The game runs horrible and there is little to no optimalisation, something we have seen different in Just Cause 2. That game runs on ultra on a potato, for that matter.
Rico has grown older and so have his powers. He is now capable of using multiple thethers at once, and can survive nearly every explosion if they are further than 3 feet (1 meter) away from him. This only adds to the fun. You truly feel like you are playing as some kind of reborn rebel that can save the world like any superhero can. Your arsenal has been expanded with some new interesting weapons (You can now fire mini nukes, ♥♥♥♥ yes!).
I do recommend this game to those who own a high end system, however, everything below a GTX 970 or R9 390 combined with a mid range processor will not pull this game at 60 at any settings. I have played this on my i5 4460, 8GB RAM, GTX 960 system and it doesn't matter which settings I use, I never reach a stable 60 frames per second and I have always suffered from major lag spikes. Adding to this that the last update, which had to fix some performance issues, only made the game run worse, this game is a total flop.
Man I had hoped this to be so ♥♥♥♥ing good.
[EDIT #1 May 19. 2016] I am changing this review to positive. Most gamebreaking bugs have been solved and the memory leak issue has been fixed. My relatively low-spec system can now run this game at 60 frames per second all the time on medium. It is still not as good as Just Cause 2, both story and gameplay wise, but it is now an enjoyable game.

This  game runs poorly on the PC. DISHONORED 2 uses the id Tech 5 Engine vs. the id Tech 6 Engine which powers the recent DOOM reboot. The sixth iteration uses/offers modern programmatic mechanisms such as asynchronous shaders and VULKAN (low level API akin to DirectX 12) to maximize frame rates. Despite the fact that a previous id game, RAGE, also used the fifth iteration, DISHONORED 2 runs extremely poorly on my Core i7 (IvyBridge) alongside an original nVidia GTX Titan GPU,  it struggled to reach/maintain 30 fps. That's not the worst of it though. The games exhibits lots of "rips" where polygons/textures meet with the effect being you see lots and LOTS of white pixels along these seams. The problem manifests itself to such a large degree that it is an acute eyesore/distraction. This problem seemed more common in the late 90's and early naughts (2000s) and it surprises me to see it in a modern title to this degree. And since the game has been out several months, it may never be patched to address this. In short, this is the broken record of a PC port of a AAA title being the 2nd class citizen ("Batman: Arkham Knight" anyone?). In the end, I wound up getting a Steam refund and simply bought the PS4 version. It runs fine on the PS4 Pro (frame rate) and free of all bleeding white pixels along seams -- no need to ruin DISHONORED 2's wonderful motif & artistic direction. If you have a PS4, go play that version instead... this game on the PC version simply isn't worth it.

This has been a little game I had under my radar for a while mainly because I like RPG Maker games and the business theme looks pretty interesting. Plus it had a similar art style to OFF and while OFF was okay, it’s art was pretty interesting. So is it good?
Story:
In a world where corporations run rampant, companies can bribe to get what they want. women are treated as mere plants that look pretty and the mere act of refusing a product is enough to land you in jail. In this world, you live as a simple drone until events happen that put you in an adventure that might change the world.
There isn’t much to characters here but there’s a decent story here. Not great but there’s a lot of little details like how normal all the corruption or that all the plants have female names. And while you get some party members, they don’t have anything to do with the story.
I admit this game is pretty dark and can it too close to reality with how corporations are trying to take over unchallenged, the game seem more like a black comedy. Most of the NPCs have puns for name, while there are parodies, they are pretty fun or cleaver and some of the situations you get into are just weird, like you might find a group of religious people and depending in what you say will comment suicide.
Gameplay:
The opening and first district give a good idea on what to expect from this game, like crates and bins might contain goods, what secret walls look like and that you have to look around and talk for your side quests even if most of them are optional bosses.
The combat is standard with a business theme with it with moves like throwing you suitcase and bribing enemies to lose. But I must say this is the games biggest problems. Yes, the enemies have a lot of colourful moves like one boss can attack you twice and decrease your defence, but your strategy will never change. In the first area, there’s a side quest where you can find a guy called Jerome and he’ll force himself into your party. The thing about him is that his staple attack has a good chance of causing paralysis to anyone and that includes bosses, Even the final boss is a joke and I fought some pretty easy final bosses during the years since you can just wail on him once he paralysis. and since he’s the only party member that uses magic, you can keep all the mp recover items for him. You even get another party member late in the game but he doesn’t add much other than another character to just attack with.
If there’s one thing that’s good about the combat is that it never drags. Even bosses can be bested in a few turns which is more than what can I say about OFF who’s boss fights just drag on.
Presentation:
One thing I don’t see in many RPG Maker games is that it opens with an actual cinematic. Sure it’s just a series of pictures but it suits the tone of the game. Sure most of the NPC’s have the same sprite and everything is grey and dull but that just suits the mood with all the suits being faceless drones of society and the depressing mood over the the world. There is one section we’re there is a lot of colour which was okay.
The enemies also have some pretty creative designs like the guards who are bipedal dogs with suits tied to their leashes or the Chef Justice boss who has two gavels the words “THE” and “LAW”. I think one of my favourite designs has got to be the dockworkers since they clearly have a design to be like monkeys.
The music is decent. Nothing memorable but it suits the mood of the game with the dull and simple trumpet(I think). There’s is one notable song for a boss which is just dinosaur over and over again before screaming about the real issue bout having real dinosaurs as co workers.
Verdict
While the combat isn’t the challenging, the creative and dark world just drew me in more than OFF has.
7/10
