King's Quest is related to a series of point-and-click games that started in the 1980's on systems like ATARI and even on DOS, which continued through the late 1990's with more updated 2D graphics and then abruptly ended. This version of King's Quest is a reboot of the series that puts in 5 chapters of gameplay which span across (or between) the time periods of the original series. Note that there is also a rather short Epilogue after Chapter 5, and it is missing from the Season Pass version of the game and is missing from Steam entirely.
Some people complain about this game over "canon" or lacking similarities to the original series, but I am not going to judge it that way because it's a rather different ballpark for this game in comparison to the original ones.
Further, I do
think that it is necessary to play the original series before this game.
So to get into it finally, I would say that I enjoyed King's Quest quite a lot, right from the beginning, though I feel like the development cycle for it sort of fell apart as more chapters were released. Chapter 1, which is actually free for people, is the longest and probably most fun chapter of the whole game, in my opinion. That is not to say that the rest of the game is bad by any means, but the remaining chapters get shorter and start limiting your locations, which was somewhat disappointing.
Nevertheless, the storyline and the characters kept my interest going and I still enjoyed what I reached by the end of the game.
The storyline focuses on King Graham in his old age, telling his previous adventures to his grandchildren. And honestly, the storyline is one of the key points to me, as the writing is pretty well-done even if events sort of shrink down as you go along. Each chapter focuses on Graham at a certain age, starting out as a teenager in Chapter 1 and growing older each chapter. One of the downsides with the progression is that the timeline really jumps quickly after Chapter 3, and thus severely limits what else can be done.
What you should expect in gameplay is semi-linear exploration, a lot of point-and-click elements of collecting items and choosing where to use them, and a lot of puzzle-solving and riddles. Take note that Chapter 1 has many quick-time events (QTE's) scattered around it, but those seem to disappear for the most part in the remainder of the game.
The game also has a large amount of dialogue with many fun characters, and you get to make some choices for how King Graham grows over time. As a word of precaution, however, and a criticism against the game, a lot of the decisions seem to follow the pattern of developers like Telltale nowadays. If you are not familiar with them, I will just say that many of your decisions do change later scenes in
ways, and also affect your grandchildren a bit, but
.
Again, as said earlier on, I definitely think that Chapter 1 is the best of the entire game, so some people might not like King's Quest as they continue playing. Chapter 1 simply allows a larger amount of places to navigate and more decisions to make, while the remaining chapters are more linear and don't give you much freedom. This is extremely true in Chapter 4, which I would say is the worst by far in terms of gameplay, where you end up going though about 20 puzzle rooms in a row.
Despite the issues above, the storyline still remains very interesting, and I loved nearly all of the characters and had fun with the exploration, hence that alone made it worth the time for me.

Pleasant enough, and maybe good for a rainy day, but somehow it feels a bit hollow, lifeless, and dull, despite some good technical polish.
My experience with the King's Quest franchise is limited to VI only, and although I loved the artwork (at the time), it too felt a little flat, compared to other adventure games of that era. Fast forward to now, and again I feel the same. I really appreciate the visuals, they have a nice style, the world is really well designed, and the animations are fluid and expressive. Sound, music and voice acting are good as well. But the story, characters, scenarios, puzzles, etc, all feel cliched, and surprisingly joyless.
I'm also not sure who the audience is. Since it's not a remake, more of an "inspired by," I can't see how it would appeal to fans of nostalgia. The tone is neither smart or self-aware enough to be satirical of its well-worn tropes, yet it's not imaginative enough to transcend the very genre its mired in. Adults might find it childish, and children might find it boring.
So, I feel bad giving it a negative rating, especially since I haven't played all the chapters, but that's the point: nothing compels me to want to do so. Maybe one day I'll revisit this game with a different perspective, but for now, though I genuinely appreciate the artistry on display, I can't recommend it.

Listen, do you want someone to hold you hand while you poopoo, and wipe your bum and hand you gold stars for your lack of accomplishments? Cause ♥♥♥♥ you if that's the case, and go play something else you filthy casual. This is hands down one of the best games you'll play, and it's not because it's hard, or because it has a feeling of  hardcore nostalgia, or because it's hard, it's the mechanics and how it feels so right in almost everyway.
First, this game, in my oppinion improves in all aspects over the first.
I will let this redditors' comments speak for my opinion as well in this matter.
Second, if you're going to play a game, and be invested, make it this one. Not everyone will feel rewarded by the punishment it serves, but it will definitely give you some sense of accomplishment that most games totally lack today.
For starters, every enemy you face falls under the same game rules you do. Weight; stamina, strength, dex, all these things are of significant importance to building your character the way you want to play. That's right,these stats actualy matter, and drastically change how your character behaves. And because enemies are just as strong as you, you have to fight with the intelligence of a human being, because your wit, is the only thing you have over them. And every enemy you encounter has a chance to drop their armor and weapons, allowing you access to their move sets and  attire, to become that fantasy fashion designer you always really never knew you wanted to be. That's flipping amazing if you ask me.
It's not all about collecting hundreds of awesome items (though those in fashion souls would argue, that's all it's about) that the game has to offer. It's not just that, NG+ and NG ++ (new game) have even more to offer than your first time through (if you make it through). It's not that PVP is can be extremely frustrating at times, AND at others extremely rewarding. This game is an amazing sequel to the original Rome: Total War.
Pros:
- CAMPAIGN MULTIPLAYER AT LAST! It works just like the single player campaign, except for when you go in to a battle. When you go in to a battle, the player that isn't part of the battle can assume control over the AI opponent.
- NAVAL BATTLES!
- A new system for leveling up your army, fleet, agents, generals, and admirals. By fighting or completing tasks they level up, which allows you to choose what kind of bonuses you want to give them.
- The graphical fidelity is stunning. I'm using a GTX 760 and only 6 gigs of ram, and I can play on maximum settings with four thousand soldiers on the battlefield.
- A very complex strategy game with lots of features. The tips at the top of the screen can almost give you a complete understanding of the game.
- Battles can be done with AI only in case you don't like that aspect of the game.
- Huge map
- Lots of factions
- Lots of gametime in one campaign
- You can play as lots of different factions in different scenarios
- Quick battles let you just play skirmishes between armies you set up
- The Provinces system adds a new mechanic where you can capture all the cities in a larger province, which lets you issue various edicts to the province for bonuses.
- The happiness of cities has been completely reworked to include lots of new features.
- Lots of small improvements over the Rome 1, including a more indepth political system, a new agent, new units, and various neat features here and there
Cons:
- You can NOT buy cities anymore. In Rome 1 you could purchase cities from AI for a lump sum of gold, giving you complete control over the city. Now you must gain "control" over that city by making them a military ally or a client state.
- This is an opinion, but I do not like how Rome is now one faction. You choose what house you want to be, each one giving different buffs/debuffs, then you assume control over all of Rome. The other houses will still fight for control of the senate. When you recruit a general or admiral, he comes from one of the houses. You can voluntarily choose to give all the political related bonuses to generals in your house, while ignoring the generals of the other houses.
- Another opinion, but I do not like how you are required to give a General or Admiral to an army/fleet. In Rome 1, a captain would be randomly assigned from a normal troop if you didn't have a General or Admiral. The captain would not be nearly as good as a Captain or General, but it felt less restricting when you could do that.
- No more family tree. It wasn't a crucial feature, but it was cool to see your generals come of age and to see your family progress. Now you simply recruit a general when you need one.
If you want incredibly realistic battles buy this game. The campaign may not be as realistic but are still very fun.

I feel the game is cheating on me. It is a very well made game in terms of graphics and all the stuff. Very nice. But why does the human enemies always search where I am hiding? The first time you meet them in this big hall with ballustrades on both sides. When you are entering the room they search downstairs when you get upstairs they just coincidentally search upstairs as well. And when I get further they follow me out of pure coincidence. And of course, not to mention they got these eagle eyes. Nice.
This is no stealth game like Metal Gear Solid where you can actually get away from your opponents by deploying stealth or outsmart them. You get by by reloading and pure chance. One time I wanted to lure them after me and ran back and fro in circles on the stairs in the lobby to have them chase me and then bypass them. They were like, looking, staring and then calling off the search: "Just my imagination." Then I frustratedly stopped, crouched and after some seconds they spotted me and started to shoot. Yea, right.
In this game your enemies always search near you, because the game knows where you are. And the Alien? Yea, I am on the edge of my seat. But why is it always rummaging near you, even if you sneaked into the next dozen of rooms unseen? And then in this comm section where alarms are blaring all over, androids are running all around and you are sneaking through the shadows, the Alien is always in the vents over your head. How? It smells me? Oh yes, my smell must be something wall-shattering and steel-piercing unique. Please just come down and simply relieve me of my smells, okay?  Oh, you do not come down? Why is that? Something menacing down here? No? So you just happen to be drooling in your vent right over my head now, right? Well, I call you a cheater, mate.
You know what I hate about horror movies? The stupidity. The opponents are cheating on you. They know things only the script writers know and you are expected to believe that. I hate that and I do not watch horror movies, because - besides the fear - they simply insult me. Never experienced that? You have. And we are on the same page now.
And now I bought this game where on this huge space station where you got stations and trains connecting the huge vastness of this thing, one single Alien always creeps through the vents right over my head. Never mind I just took a train somewhere else. Never mind I sneaked for miles and miles unseen. Never mind the architects probably did not design the vents for being some interconnecting fast-travel-network for aliens to keep lurking whereever you go. Never mind my chance I could even live all my life on this station and by pure chance would never meet this thing and we both grew old there and never knew of each other due to simple vastness. But here I am with an alien constantly over my head and I am to believe that, right? Really? I hate it. But I will continue playing the game and will beat it. And all the times the game places me in situations where the Alien cheated me to death again I will have this tired and annoyed look on my face and shrug it off. I think. Or I might just dump this game. Who knows.
Update: I had this great experience in the train station where the Alien was just on the other side of one of these solid columns and was stomping up and down and I was tiptoeing around this column to avoid contact and I was so sure I was gonna die, but somehow it stomped off for a moment and I was abe to dart into one open train there and escape. That was actually awesome in hind-sight, but absolutely terrifying in that moment, of course. But again, the game says the transfer system would be the fastest way to travel around the three towers of the station, but that cannot be true: The vents are obviously as fast, because the Alien was in the next station in short.
This goes as far that you are getting into the next area unseen, the door closes behind you, and you sneak into the next bureau and hide there in the locker just to relax a moment and what happens? After a moment the Alien stomps in, goes straight to the locker and says hello. So if it does smell you so well that it can follow you into ares without having seen you, then just so it should be able to pinpoint your very location right away, just like I experienced. But if that would be the case, the game would be pointless, so this was just coincidence, I guess. Btw when you got such heavy footing how on earth are you able to walk through vents which are only supposed to carry air?
Anyways, if you like getting fooled over and cheated on, all while wetting your pants, this is your game and the game is absoltely marvellous at that. And I have to add, that the graphics are really really great and the game mechanics as well. So the guys did make a good game there. They just shouldnt have let the Alien check the script now and then.

is a team singleplayer FPS by Johan Hassel, or SteelRaven7. The game consists of hectic, fast-paced red-against-blue warfare over a variety of maps, guns, and gamemodes. The game is praised for it's sandboxy feel, it's pick-up-and-play gameplay and for it's hectic battles.
The game works with two teams, Blue and Red (they are referred to as "Eagle" and "Raven" in game). The player chooses a map, a team, and the number of bots (of which there are no limit). The player may then change settings, such as make it night, disable vehicles, or swap the spawn points. The player then chooses 1 primary gun, 1 secondary gun, 1 team support item/throwable, and a rocket launcher, and deploys into the map.
:
-The developer has shown huge enthusiasm and good ideas for the game. A campaign is promised, along with the ability to make maps, more offical guns, modding and more offical maps. He also works very closely with his community, and has a Discord set up where he takes feedback and bug reports.
-There are 7+ guns to choose from (2 sniper rifles, one Designated Marksman Rifle, an AK, an Light Machine Gun, a pump-action shotgun, a pistol, a supressed pistol, and a Magnum) along with 3 rocket launchers, 2 throwables and 3 support items. The developer promises lots more.
-There are 6 vehicles, with more on the way:
Helicopter (comes with a turret controlled by a passenger, and missiles controlled by the driver)
Jeep (Four seats with a usable machine gun attached to one of the seats)
Plane (One seat that comes with a turret)
Quad (Two seats)
Tank (Two seats, one for driver who operates missle, and one for a passanger who operates a turret)
Dinghy (a sort of lifeboat with 5 seats, useful for ocean maps)
There is also a flak cannon for anti-aircraft, but it's not really a vehicle as it is stationary.
-There are four maps, each tailored for a unique gameplay:
Island: A small island, with a focus on fast-paced close-to-medium combat in the open.
Dustbowl: A large desert, with a focus on sniping and aviation (both helis and planes).
Temple: A temple of sorts with heavy snowfall (the only weather map so far), with a focus on close-to-medium combat in enclosed spaces.
Archipelago: A very small island and an aircraft carrier, with a heavy focus on planes, dogfighting, and close combat.
The developer says more will be made.
-There are 3 gamemodes (Point Match, Batallions and Spec Ops), which are easy to get the grasps of and are quite fun.
:
-The developer says updates will be out every 5 weeks, which can be too short for some people.
-The price doesn't line up with the game at the moment, although that might change.
-There are a lot of glitches within the game.
-Some maps can be quite frustrating to play.
-Batallions does not fit in with the game's pick-up-and-play style, and most (if not all) people require it to be explained in order to understand it.
-The game (for some) can get boring after an hour or so of gameplay, as there isn't much variety in the gamemodes, and there's only so much you can do with the guns.
-It is singleplayer-only, and the developer has no intention whatsoever of changing this in the forseeable future. This is what frustrates most people, as the game has a big opportunity for multiplayer.
-The AI aren't very smart when it comes to very close quarters (sometimes the enemy team walks right past you), and there is no way of commanding them as of yet.
Overall, I'd give the game 7.5/10. Points off for glitches and the AI. Singleplayer-only doesn't really concern me, but I'd hope to at least see co-op in the future.

- Sneaking is broken (understatement). As soon as you fire something (like an arrow) it punts you out of sneak mode. Even if you are in the pitch black and you try to hide, it's pretty impossible. Also, the advantages of sneaking on previous elder scrolls are pretty much gone on this one.
- The levels are shared with other players. Today I was fighing this NPC and as I was about to kill it, some random player comes in and kills it. I understand the MMO part of it, but I feel like some parts of the game should be solo+party ONLY (*cough* Destiny *cough*).
- An artifact of the previous point: If you are fighting through something (like a cave) and you have to go back, tough luck because ALL the NPCs respawned. Actually, they will respawn even if you are exactly on their spawn point.
- The game drops a lot. I noticed this went all of a sudden I could not run, or open doors, or pick up objects. After a while trying to figure out what was happening, I got punted from the game as asked for my login again. This is specially bad during missions, you need to do it all over again.
- Something I always found awesome in the TES games was that most things in the world are interactable. This game is the opposite. You cant interact with most things. For example, book cases, even though i can see they have things on them, the interaction is the same as opening a book. Silver goblets and other items of such, are not interactable.
- Most of the missions need to be done in one way only. So if I want to take the violent route, sometimes the game prevents me from attacking NPCs.
- Overal unpolished, unimpressive. The graphics are from oblivion era and everything looks a little clunky. The menus, the stories, the interaction...

I wanted to give this game a positive review so goddamn bad. I enjoyed Just Cause 2 both on Playstation 3 and PC, and have over 500 hours total in that game.
When Just Cause 3 got announced, I was instantly hyped for this sequel for the oh so good Just Cause 2. However, the developers seem to think that a GTX 980 is minimum in a low end PC these days, so the framerates on my GTX 960 (the 2 GB edition by MSI) just cannot push this game beyond 40 frames per second. That is, if you forget about all the lag spikes that happen every 1 to 2 seconds.
The game itself is pretty well made. The wingsuit is a nice addition to move around the world quickly, and it works flawless in combination with the grappling hook. Speaking of the grappling hook, this thing has been completely redesigned. The keys to use it are no longer on the keyboard but mapped on you mouse so you can always use it quickly in any situation. You can now apply strength to the rope to pull stuff apart or to help you blow stuff up to gain more chaos points.
Chaos points don't seem to do anything anymore. They are just there because they were there in the previous games as well and it is probably still there for the sake of being. In Just Cause 2 you had to collect chaos points in order to progress in the game, however in Just Cause 3 that is no longer the case. New story missions unlock as soon as you have completed the previous ones, and most of the time you have done the stuff you have to in such mission before you start it, which doesn't add to the fun.
The game is gorgious and sure runs fine on a system using a high end quad/six core processor combined with 16 gigabytes of RAM and a GTX 980 or equivalent, but it seems that Avalanche Studios have forgotten about their 'cheapskate' community. For those that cannot afford a high end gaming system, pass on this game. The game runs horrible and there is little to no optimalisation, something we have seen different in Just Cause 2. That game runs on ultra on a potato, for that matter.
Rico has grown older and so have his powers. He is now capable of using multiple thethers at once, and can survive nearly every explosion if they are further than 3 feet (1 meter) away from him. This only adds to the fun. You truly feel like you are playing as some kind of reborn rebel that can save the world like any superhero can. Your arsenal has been expanded with some new interesting weapons (You can now fire mini nukes, ♥♥♥♥ yes!).
I do recommend this game to those who own a high end system, however, everything below a GTX 970 or R9 390 combined with a mid range processor will not pull this game at 60 at any settings. I have played this on my i5 4460, 8GB RAM, GTX 960 system and it doesn't matter which settings I use, I never reach a stable 60 frames per second and I have always suffered from major lag spikes. Adding to this that the last update, which had to fix some performance issues, only made the game run worse, this game is a total flop.
Man I had hoped this to be so ♥♥♥♥ing good.
[EDIT #1 May 19. 2016] I am changing this review to positive. Most gamebreaking bugs have been solved and the memory leak issue has been fixed. My relatively low-spec system can now run this game at 60 frames per second all the time on medium. It is still not as good as Just Cause 2, both story and gameplay wise, but it is now an enjoyable game.

Dishonored 2 is the sequel to Arkane Studio’s 2012 magic stealth game. It kicks off 15 years after the events of the first game and avoiding spoilers some more bad stuff happens and once again you’ve got to sneak around figuring out how to beat your enemies.
The core gameplay is very much the same as in Dishonored. It’s a first person stealth game with a ton of exploration, a solid combat system as well as some very creative magic abilities to use. It’s the powers that really allow the game to shine since they’re integrated so well into the gameplay. You’ve got Blink which lets you warp across short distances making for some very creative entrances and exits from areas especially once you level it up a bit. Possession too is a lot of fun as you can control rats to get into tight spaces or at higher levels you can do the same to guards or dead bodies. It’s a lot of fun.
I guess the most unique factor within the Disonored games is the Chaos system. It’s kinda like the ranking systems from other stealth games but it gives more impact to how the game progresses and what ending you get. I was a bit disappointed with how Dishonored 2 handles this since the first game changes aspects of levels depending on if you killed people beforehand adding more guards or rats or weepers which can drastically change the difficulty of a level but in 2 it only really affects the ending from what I’ve seen.
You can also play as either Emily Kaldwin or Corvo Attano – the protagonist from the first game. They have different abilities and overall playstyles as well as some neat alternative interactions with characters throughout the game. I picked Corvo initially and beat the game with him just because I played as him in the first game and I’ve also played a bit with Emily too but not as much, while not drastically different their powers do affect the way you approach different situations and it’s a nice touch for replayability.
Arkane Studios have done a great job with the world building here too, tons of smaller stories about areas or characters you don’t even meet in the game. You can also pick up documents along the way which give you more insight into what’s going on in the world and it really helps make Karnaca and Dunwall more real.
The level design is some of the best I’ve seen in a long time.  There are so many alternative routes for different playstyles, going high chaos and killing everyone, going full ghost and never getting spotted, you can even opt to do a no powers playthrough and the levels cater for that as well. As I played through areas I found so many shortcuts and better ways of doing things I often reloaded levels so I could do things more efficiently and this further adds to the good replayability. I have a feeling this will become a mainstay of the speedrunning community because of the number of routes to take as well as powers like Blink opening up routes you probably shouldn’t be taking.
My initial playthrough took me 17 hours. This was fairly slow due to me repeating areas so I reckon 12-14 hours would be a usual playtime. There’s a lot of collectibles in every level from runes to maps and blueprints and collecting all these will substantially add to the game time. Then you’ve got a second playthrough as the other character and maybe even another few to see the chaos differences. There’s a ton of replayability and Dishonored 2 is a great value game because of it.
There are problems though. PC performance is pretty crap. I’m running an MSI 980Ti and a 4790k and I’m struggling to maintain 60FPS on medium settings at 1440p which shouldn’t be happening in a game that looks like this. It’s not a bad looking game, it actually has a cool art style which I like a lot but it’s not exactly Battlefield 1 which runs superbly. This is even after the performance patches that have come out. I didn’t experience any bugs though so that’s a good thing!
Overall Dishonored 2 is one of my favourite games of 2016. A worthy successor to Dishonored and one of the best designed games I’ve played in a long time. I don’t know why I skipped picking it up at launch because as soon as I started playing it a few weeks later I remember how good the first game was and I got sucked in straight away.

One of the most hallowed, respected and enormously influential computer games in history, System Shock 2 does without doubt deserve such an accolade, though it is not an undertaking for the fainthearted for a number of reasons.
Before outlining the frustrations which can be inherent playing this, firstly, let us extol its virtues.
The back-story of a spacecraft whose crew have all mysteriously been violently killed has intriguing depth and immersive appeal, especially important for a role-playing game. Giving the player choices of which particular skills to require before the game-proper actually begins, does indeed give one the feeling that you are forming the player character out of your own choices and decisions and this further increases one's emotional involvement.
As you slowly begin to explore the craft and pick up clues as to what has caused such havoc, the tension is palpable. From emails and voice recordings which you discover as you journey onwards, a sense of an actual place which was once full of living, breathing humans definitely starts to take shape. In addition to these manifold good points, the graphics themselves still look great even 15 years after the game was made.
However, there are more than a few droplets of vinegar mixed in with the Ambrosial honey.
Primarily, the main drawback, or perhaps a kinder word might be ;challenge', to System Shock 2 is the often bewildering complexity of elements at your player-characters disposal. In order to make intelligent progress, akin to how one might actually behave in such a real-life situation itself, the player has to juggle a veritable myriad of game-world stimuli. Emails, personal data assistants, logs on computers, notes and letters found on bodies, a constant stream of voice-messages in your character's earpiece, and much more of the detritus of exploring the seemingly dead spaceship, constantly seems to bombard the player until at times one can feel at a loss as to what to take note of and what to ignore. Perhaps this can be seen as part of the character's real-life predicament, but if the designers had taken the trouble to give more structure and order to the bombardment of information thrown at the player throughout it could have led to a less confusing and more enjoyable gaming experience.
On the other hand, maybe I'm just a bit slow at times, or too methodical and tidy in my own personal way of dealing with tasks so I do hold my hand up and offer that as an explanation to the above constructive criticism.
Even so, I have heard from several other sources of note, such as some seasoned gamers and highly respected gaming press, that System Shock 2 involved far too much traipsing back and forward through similar-looking corridors in search of a vital key or door-code or something of the like, without which further progress was not possible. Yet, for the gamer, completing these tasks became distinctly arduous, often extremely monotonous and frankly, unpleasantly exhausting. Elongating the play-time of a game in such a manner is frowned upon these days and for good reason.
However, these constructive criticisms are as nothing compared to the monumental depth, complexity, tension and intrigue of this computer game behemoth, which also includes one of the most legendary and infamous end-of-game bosses in the annals of video-gaming.
To play this game is not just to steep oneself in an immersive, tense and believablely frightening world, but it is to experience a piece of computer-gaming history.

Note: This Review is for Casual Mode
I remember when Thimbleweed Park was first announced several years ago, when all we had was a simple concept art of Agent Ray and Reyes. And now look at the masterpiece this game has become..
Thimbleweed Park is game that has two mysteries in one: figuring out a murder mystery and solving the mystery of the Pillow Factory Fire that occured before the events of the game.
Ron Gilbert and Gary Winnick have done an amazing job with immersing players into the decrepit and spooky town of Thimbleweed Park. Oftentimes, I find myself getting the chills looking at the run down buildings. The graphics fit the game perfectly.
The soundtrack of Thimbleweed Park is also memorable. I find myself humming the game's theme song. The sound effects like opening and closing doors, hearing footsteps, and even the ambient environment noises like the wind blowing in the distance, crickets chirping at night, or a fire hydrant splashing water really add to environment, further immersing players into this world.
What really drives Thimbleweed Park foward are the characters. Agent Reyes and Agent Ray share a unique relationship with each other. Neither one trusts the other, but they choose to work together. Delores is the perfect programmer/nerd girl with a passion for following her dreams. Ransome the Clown is obnoxious and full of sarcastic remarks. Franklin the Ghost is depressing, but also adds an entire layer of puzzle solving an already amazing adventure game.
The gameplay in Thimbleweed Park takes a step back from modern adventure games and lets you do all the work in figuring out what to do in your environment. Playing this game makes me realize just how much modern adventure games hold our hands and silo us down a typical path. One of the things that I love is being able to test and experiment around with different commands. This usually pays off in very interesting or unexpected results. I found myself stuck in the game multiple times only to do something weird and solve the puzzle! I feel like a lot of the puzzles in this game are either predictably logical, or they require you to think about it from a different perspective to figure out. I was never stuck for too long, and having that "Ah ha!" moment was always worth it. I was able to finish Casual Mode in 12 hours.
Perhaps one of the things that I enjoyed the most about Thimbleweed Park was the immersion itself. Never did I feel impatient on wanting to progress the plot further. Sometimes, I would just sit in the cafe and take in the welcoming environment. Other times, I would sit in the Edmund library and just peruse the tons of books that the game has to offer. There's just so much in this tiny world worth exploring, that I never felt bored expecting something more to do. Even as something as little as revisitng areas to look for collectable specks of dust. Yes! Specks of dust!
Gripes. There were a few things that did make Thimbleweed Park frustrating to play. Thankfully, there wasn't too much, but I do need to address them:
- Some characters in the game share task lists. This isn't a problem, but if you have multiple playable characters, it can be annoying having to make sure both characters meet up to give each other items. It immediately reminded me of Gilbert's The Cave game, where characters had to constantly backtrack to give each other items. The map item resolves problem pretty fast.
- At some points in the game, I found that the Part I was in prevented certain tasks from being completed. For example, Franklin's task list had goals that he needed to accomplish, but I had to wait until I was in a later part of the story to accomplish that specific task. Don't include the task in that part of the story until it's needed. It would have saved me a lot of time!
- I found it quite strange that playable characters couldn't communicate with each other. If Agent Reyes and Agent Rey are in the same room, why can't there be some conversation topics that they can share between themselves? Even if it doesn't necessarily pertain to the plot. Another example of this is when Agent Rey goes to the Edmund Mansion to speak to Delores, but Delores dismisses her. Agent Rey never has a future conversation with Delores. I know that these characters are all on their own storylines, but the only real cohesion between them was at the very end of the game. Maybe this was on purpose? Perhaps we are supposed to feel this disconnect between the characters, because they are all operating on selfish gains? And the very end of the game causes all of them to work together? I don't know. I can't really peg this as a gripe -- maybe I was just expecting something else.
Overall, Thimbleweed Park was a joy to play. Playing the game felt like I was binging a Netflix show. Ron Gilbert did a fantastic job grabbing players into this world and holding them tight in figuring out the mysteries. Even after finishing the game, I still find myself excited to go back and play the Hard Mode, ready to check out all the puzzles and different locations I missed from my first playthrough.
I highly reccomend this game to people that love adventure games; you are in for a welcoming and truly wonderful treat.

Thimbleweed Park marks the return of Ron Gilbert and Gary Winnick to classic "point and click" adventure games. It was funded on Kickstarter in 2014 and raised around $626,000, resulting in the game not only being funded but also reaching a number of stretch goals including voice acting and mobile ports.
I backed this game on Kickstarter and recieved a Steam key when the game launched.

The game takes place in 1987 in a small town called Thimbleweed Park. There, a body was found and two FBI agents - Angela Ray and Junior Agent Antonio Reyes - are dispatched to investigate the murder. However, not only does the Sheriff try to prevent them from solving the case, they also find out that some strange things are happening in Thimbleweed Park...
Thimbleweed Park features a style similar to the ones seen in older
MmucasFlemm games. But, instead of relying on "soft" edges like in Monkey Island 2, the art is crisp and detailed, utilizing an neat color palette across the various areas of the game. Some areas even make use of parallax scrolling, emulating "depth" where none exist.
The level of detail seen in the background art is quite fantastic. Many signs across town are actually legible, individual leaves are visible, fireflies are buzzing around, tufts of grass are moving in the wind, broken lights are flickering...the list goes on.
The characters are even more resemblant of Maniac Mansion than the backgrounds, mainly because their heads are larger than one would expect, allowing for neat facial expressions despite the technically "low" resolution of the character sprites. As a little extra, there's even some form of dynamic lighting being applied to the character sprites, making them seem more "in place" when walking past lights.
Overall, I can't find anything wrong with the visuals, although the big-headed characters might be off-putting to some people.
Honestly, I didn't have any expectations when it came to sound. In fact, I completely forgot that the game recieved voice acting, which was a nice surprise when I started playing.
The music fits the theme of the game very well, being reminiscent of film noir - dark, slow and moody.
Thimbleweed Park also utilizes quite a few ambient sounds, including but not limited to wind rustling, grills chirping, dogs barking and so on. None of it ever seemed out of place.
And while the voice actors overall do a great job, I'm not entirely satisfied with the audio quality. I assume it's deliberate, but the voice acting sounds like it's played back from a cassette tape - one that has been used quite a bit. The audio is not "slurring" but the heights aren't as crisp as they could/should be. Again, it might be deliberate but I'm not too fond of it.
The game is able to keep the tension while at the same time being pretty much littered with dry jokes that very much remind me of Gilberts and Winnicks previous works. It made me laugh out loud several times - now, that may seem like a pointless thing to mention but it's actually quite difficult for games to make me laugh.
Thimbleweed Park also drops quite a few references, not only about older LucasArts games but about adventure game tropes in general. It doesn't take itself too seriously which works very well.
I don't want to go into much detail in order to avoid spoilers, but the story might be the only somewhat polarizing part of this game. But I did find it very enjoyable.
People looking for a classic point and click adventure experience will enjoy this game. On "hard mode" (which is more like normal mode) the game requires you to think outside the box very often, but without relying on blatant moon logic. And there are loads of red herrings that you can pick up. You *will* get stuck on hard mode but you can do it. Try to not look up a walkthrough, okay?
Casual mode is a very nice addition. In that mode, roughly half of the puzzles in the game are pretty much skipped, allowing beginners to enjoy the story and get through the game without getting stuck too often. A great way to make the game more accessible without compromising the original experience.
A very good, super entertaining point and click adventure game that oozes charm and features a tremendous amount of puzzles, hilarious dialogue, diverse areas as well as likable and fun characters. The only drawbacks are (possibly deliberate) voice quality issues, some slightly unbalanced puzzles and a few questionable story decisions.

A statement about socialized health care and it's importance
A statement eco-shaming people for throwing out trash
A dissertation on how to make a game the 'right' way by eliminating deaths and dead ends.
Seriously, if this is what Ron Gilbert has to turn to in order to voice his political and social opinions then I'm simply not interested.  I LOVED his earlier games, but his motivations are just TOO heavy handed in the dialogue, and as others have mentioned, the sheer amount of fourth wall shenanigans wears thin fast, leaving you with an indie game that, were it not for Ron Gilbert and Gary Winnick's involvement, likely would be received much more poorly.
Half the dialogue seems to be trying to bank on earlier games he worked on with callback after callback, reference after reference, and frankly, it plays out as desperate rather than nostalgiac.
I just can't recommend a game with so much soapboxing and back-slapping in it.  An entertainment title is NOT the place for it.

Broforce is a 2D Run and Gun game where you are tasked with bringing freedom to the entire world. At least that is what they claim we are doing, as we blow enemy hideouts to smithereens and fly off into the sunset. To accomplish this we are given control of “Bros” which are all parody characters out of popular films such as Rambro, Bro Hard and Bronan the Brobarian. As you can no doubt tell, this is very much a tongue in cheek type of game. Broforce is centered around fast gameplay, epic guitar riffs and destruction above all else and has very little story to speak of. You and up to three friends can join in on the carnage via drop in, drop out online or local coop to deliver fiery freedom to terrorists. Starting off the game you will have the choice of either picking Campaign or Arcade Mode. They are mostly the same except campaign mode gives you an overworld while arcade is just back to back missions. Then you will be given the choice of normal and hard difficulty. It is suggested to start on normal since hard has faster rates of fire, more enemies and placements designed to annoy you.
At the start of each mission you are given a random Bro that you have unlocked and must make your way throughout the levels saving new Bros for extra lives. Bros all play differently from one another and each have special attacks. For example one bro may only have his fists and be able to send projectiles back at enemies, while another bro throws dynamite and is able to attract enemies via a cooked turkey with dynamite stuffed into it. There are also differences in speed, strength and range between them, so every Bro requires their own play-style, which makes the repetition in this game feel very minimal. To unlock more characters you have to a certain amount of Bros from their cages. The random nature in which you are given Bros is a double edged sword. On one hand you will not be able to rely on the character you are best at and only play as them throughout, but on the other hand some Bros are just not equipped for the task at hand, which will cause you to die until you are given a Bro more suited to the situation. You can retry a mission as many times as you like so it is a minor issue. Unless you are playing on IronBro mode, a permadeath mode that is unlocked later in the game and makes it so each Bro can live only once, once you lose all Bros it's game over.
To defend yourself you will have melee, ranged and special attacks. Melee and ranged can be used indefinitely while special attacks usage amount varies from character to character. Strangely enough you can only shoot horizontally, so any enemy above or below you is untouchable via weapon fire until they are on the same plane as you. That is unless you get clever with explosives or special attacks to kill them before they know what hit them. The problem with simply jumping below is that enemies have far greater range than most Bros do, so you have to get in rather close to shoot them. Since you die in a single hit that can be an unnecessarily risky move. This game does require a decent amount of foresight before going in guns blazing. You have to consider if there may be enemies hiding in the grass, if you can take out the enemies before they fire at you and shoot an explosive near you, or if it would simply be better if you punch through a wall and make your own path. There is a pleasant amount to consider before making your move and makes it all the more sweeter when you proudly stand alone in an environment torn apart by an intense battle. That is the perfect time to use the button dedicated to flexing your muscles.
Enemies have quite a bit of variety to them and range from dogs, suicide bombers and even supernatural enemies later on. They all have different means of attack and some are able to take a lot of damage. Terrorists have a certain room in which they will infinitely respawn until you destroy the ground under that door, causing them to all fall to their deaths. Sadly, AI is terrible in this game and enemies are very likely to be the cause of their own deaths. If you are spotted the enemy will just stand there and shoot at the direction he last saw you, over and over again until you kill him. The difficulty comes from the traps, enemy numbers and camera which you have no control over. Once you kill an enemy its corpse will provide cover to his friends behind it until you gib it with a few bullets, while enemy bullets can conveniently pass through the body. The camera is far too zoomed in, causing you to be killed by an enemy that was out of view or getting explosives dropped on your head that you had no way of knowing where there on occasions.
You will also face multiple vehicles like mechs, helicopters and trucks that spawn enemies from it. Out of all the vehicles you can only hijack the mechs by standing on it and pressing the melee button.  These deal some serious damage to everything it comes across, though its ability to move around is based on a very small fuel supply, so it won't last too long. Your main threats will be the crazy bosses in this game.  The amount of destruction they all cause is staggering and it is a joy to take these down. Some will not just die by shooting at it and will require some outside the box thinking. The overall amount of destruction you will see in this game is truly impressive. Nearly anything can be destroyed and the levels usually end up looking like the planet is imploding in on itself. The only things which can't be destroyed is the ground surrounding the American flag which is used as a respawn point. There is quite a bit of levels to play through on the campaign/arcade. It keeps getting crazier and crazier the further in you go until you are eventually fighting on American soil. What little dialogue there is, is delivered via text and adds nothing to the game. The only difference in campaign mode is the over-world I previously mentioned, where you can fly around and run into seagulls because why not, as well as be able to choose which levels to take on first at times.
To top it off this game supports custom maps via Steam workshop. These can also be played with friends and are just as enjoyable as the ones found in the main game. They can be downloaded right from in game and can also be saved so you can play them offline. These offer much more value to the game and are quite a few of them already. Great music is something Broforce also has, especially that final ending theme song. With its fast paced gameplay, considerable difference between Bros and various ways to tackle levels, it offers plenty of replay value even without the user made content. Its AI is unimpressive to say the least but there is a ton of fun to be had mowing them down in various ways. All levels are perfectly playable if you end up doing it solo and may even be preferable, so you know exactly what is going on, which can be pretty hard when you have three others blowing up the map. At the end of the day this is a great game that plays like a mix of Metal Slug and an extreme version of Dig Dug.  For those still unsure I highly recommend checking out the free game
to get a taste of what is on offer. Highly recommended to those that like the genre, want an action packed game or simply want a fun game to play with friends.

King's Quest is a good mix between an interactive movie and point click adventure. Gameplay differs a bit from episode to episode, it has some action episodes with QTEs early on, but the last two has less of that and more puzzles. Like any other interactive movie the game sometimes offers you a choice, which will impact the story. What I liked about this game is that some puzzles can be solved differently and story depends on how you will solve them. Graphics are amazing. Soundtrack is ok, it doesn't hurt your ears, but there's nothing worth remembering either. Voice acting is good, characters sound funny and charismatic. Plot is pretty simple, you play as King Graham, who's telling his grandkids about adventures he had when he was young. His stories span across many years, since day he became a king and to the day he became too old for that. It is interesting to see how characters and kingdom change through time.
Pros:
- Engaging story
- Amazing graphics
- Interesting puzzles
- Action sequences
- Choice affecting the story
Cons:
- Some puzzles aren't very intuitive and the game doesn't have a hint system to help you
- Bad pacing. In some episodes the story advances fast and there's lot of action. In others all you do is walk back and forth collecting items and solving puzzles.
If you're a fan of old point'n'click adventures then this game is for you. If you're looking for more relaxing experience, then you'd better get something from Telltale, 'cause this game has some really hard puzzles.

is a team singleplayer FPS by Johan Hassel, or SteelRaven7. The game consists of hectic, fast-paced red-against-blue warfare over a variety of maps, guns, and gamemodes. The game is praised for it's sandboxy feel, it's pick-up-and-play gameplay and for it's hectic battles.
The game works with two teams, Blue and Red (they are referred to as "Eagle" and "Raven" in game). The player chooses a map, a team, and the number of bots (of which there are no limit). The player may then change settings, such as make it night, disable vehicles, or swap the spawn points. The player then chooses 1 primary gun, 1 secondary gun, 1 team support item/throwable, and a rocket launcher, and deploys into the map.
:
-The developer has shown huge enthusiasm and good ideas for the game. A campaign is promised, along with the ability to make maps, more offical guns, modding and more offical maps. He also works very closely with his community, and has a Discord set up where he takes feedback and bug reports.
-There are 7+ guns to choose from (2 sniper rifles, one Designated Marksman Rifle, an AK, an Light Machine Gun, a pump-action shotgun, a pistol, a supressed pistol, and a Magnum) along with 3 rocket launchers, 2 throwables and 3 support items. The developer promises lots more.
-There are 6 vehicles, with more on the way:
Helicopter (comes with a turret controlled by a passenger, and missiles controlled by the driver)
Jeep (Four seats with a usable machine gun attached to one of the seats)
Plane (One seat that comes with a turret)
Quad (Two seats)
Tank (Two seats, one for driver who operates missle, and one for a passanger who operates a turret)
Dinghy (a sort of lifeboat with 5 seats, useful for ocean maps)
There is also a flak cannon for anti-aircraft, but it's not really a vehicle as it is stationary.
-There are four maps, each tailored for a unique gameplay:
Island: A small island, with a focus on fast-paced close-to-medium combat in the open.
Dustbowl: A large desert, with a focus on sniping and aviation (both helis and planes).
Temple: A temple of sorts with heavy snowfall (the only weather map so far), with a focus on close-to-medium combat in enclosed spaces.
Archipelago: A very small island and an aircraft carrier, with a heavy focus on planes, dogfighting, and close combat.
The developer says more will be made.
-There are 3 gamemodes (Point Match, Batallions and Spec Ops), which are easy to get the grasps of and are quite fun.
:
-The developer says updates will be out every 5 weeks, which can be too short for some people.
-The price doesn't line up with the game at the moment, although that might change.
-There are a lot of glitches within the game.
-Some maps can be quite frustrating to play.
-Batallions does not fit in with the game's pick-up-and-play style, and most (if not all) people require it to be explained in order to understand it.
-The game (for some) can get boring after an hour or so of gameplay, as there isn't much variety in the gamemodes, and there's only so much you can do with the guns.
-It is singleplayer-only, and the developer has no intention whatsoever of changing this in the forseeable future. This is what frustrates most people, as the game has a big opportunity for multiplayer.
-The AI aren't very smart when it comes to very close quarters (sometimes the enemy team walks right past you), and there is no way of commanding them as of yet.
Overall, I'd give the game 7.5/10. Points off for glitches and the AI. Singleplayer-only doesn't really concern me, but I'd hope to at least see co-op in the future.

This game is, as you'd expect, similar to Dishonored 1. Given that there are next to no games that do what Dishonored does these days, let alone with such quality, it has earned a recommendation a few times over. That's not to say it lacks flaws, however.
SPOILERS AHEAD FOR BOTH GAMES
As you probably know already, both Corvo and Emily are playable in this game. Corvo has the same skill tree he had in the previous game, though he has to start over because plot reasons. Emily has some major, if very few, differences in her powerset. The impression I get is that, where Corvo's skills promote scouting ahead and having a plan to kill or slip past everyone, Emily can wing it. I think she also has a higher skill ceiling. I still haven't found all the tricks Far Reach can do.
The plot, while fitting with the theme of the game, feels recycled. Not least because the main villain is pulled straight from the previous game's DLC. Even her nonlethal option is the same. A bunch of characters from the first game make an appearance in some way, it starts to feel like we're Forrest Gump, or Ezio Auditore. I think the writers were trying too hard to make the game familiar to fans of the first game.
And yet, there's no equivalent of the Hound Pits Pub. Your base of operations this time is a boat. There is nothing of value on that boat. No shop, barely any NPCs, and a couple of token sidequests that offer no reward as far as I've seen.
The plot also lacks the sense of high stakes the first game had. Objectively, they look about the same; you're framed for crimes of treason, and the villain takes over the empire, forcing you to become a fugitive to clear your name and take down the conspiracy which made this happen. But this time around, the game relies on you knowing at least some of what happened in the first game to understand what the stakes are. And even then, it doesn't become fully apparent how dire things are until the final mission, when you return to Dunwall and find streets full of corpses.
There's also no B-plot rat plague equivalent. Yes, there are bloodflies, but they're a native parasite thriving because of recent events, not a disaster tied to the plot.
The scenarios also feel samey. It's always "go to the bad guy's lair and kill them, or find a way to ruin them without killing them". Nothing more. The first game had you infiltrate a dinner party at which you had to figure out which of three masked women is your target. The closest thing in this game is figuring out which of two identical men is your target. You're told one of them is a smoker at start of the mission, and their dialogue makes it very obvious which is which.
One of the game's biggest mistakes, though it's not nearly as bad as it could have been, is mentioning the Outsider's origins, and even giving him a reason to be interested in the game's events. The Outsider is an appealing character because we know nothing about him and his motivations, so this was a step in the wrong direction.
In summary, this game is for people who like Dishonored. Which is good, as very few games are appealing in the way Dishonored is. But it has to lean on the formula of the first game to exist in the first place, lacking anything to set it apart. And even then, there are still some things the first game did better, particularly in regards to story.

VERY HIGHLY RECOMMENDED...provided you have a PC to handle this game + can tolerate random CTD's.
NOT RECOMMENDED yet...for those who have lower-end systems + those who don't want to deal with random CTD's.
Dishonored 2 is an absolute fantastic sequel to the original outstanding Dishonored game, often trumping it in almost every way with superb, clever + interesting level design (most are excellent, but The Time Manipulation + Clockwork levels are absolutely mind-blowing + incredible); outstanding gameplay; numerous ways to finish your objectives (stealth-style of action-style, with some choices along the way); fantastic graphics (and that's even when running the game at Medium settings).
I said "almost in every way" because...well, this game clearly has issues currently, unfrortunately. While the performance issues + technical issues might stop some cold with decent systems + from continuing to play the game until Arkane fixes some things, it certainly did not stop me.
Let's get the "bad" out the way here first. I was running the game at 1440p on my desktop PC with an i7 950 Bloomfield; 16 GB RAM DDR3; "4GB" 970; and W7 64-bit PC at Medium settings w/ V Sync Off - well, it took a bit to get this game running at anything worthwhile for me. With an in-game 60FPS cap, the game was rising + dropping like crazy, with framerates floating anytime from 30 frames to 60 feames at any moment; especially when out-doors. With an in-game 45 FPS cap, the game often hovered somewhere b/t 30FPS to 45FPS, which is certainly more acceptable than what it was doing with the 60FPS cap. On my gaming laptop equipped with an i7 4720HQ; 16 GB RAM DDR3; 4GB 960M - well, I had to run the game at Medium settings on 900p with V-Sync Off at Medium settings also with the 45FPS cap, just to try to keep the game somewhat stable.
While it's great that an actual PC game has a bunch of different FPS cap options in-game - which range from 30FPS, 45FPS, 60FPS + even above that for those with high-end monitors with awesome refresh-rates, BTW - and IMHO, more games should do this + have these kind of framerate-cap options - some gamers just might even want to use something like MSI Afterburner to lock the framerates down to something more specific and suitable for them, if necessary. While I was fine w/ the 45FPS cap, those with systems similar to mine might want to use Afterburner to set the cap to maybe 35FPS or even 40FPS, just to get the framerate stable even more so.
In terms of poor performance, this is very reminiscent of performance of another game, Batman: Arkham Knight. Though, at least Batman: AK didn't have random crashes, here + there - Dishonored 2 sometimes would have CTD's (Crashes To the Desktop) for who knows what random reason. B/c this is a stealth game (if you choose it to play that way, and you probably should at least try to) & you can save at anytime, most people likely are going to be Quick-saving & Regular-saving a lot anyways - but it's also going to be a great idea to do this anyways b/c of the technical issues this game has with random CTD's.
This game is running on the Void Engine, which is a very-heavily customized version of the highly unoptimized Id Tech 5 (which powered other games that had stiff reqauirements + technical issues upon release...such as RAGE; Wolfenstein: TNO + TOB; & The Evil Within). Dishonored 1 never-ever slouched on excellent art-design & this sequel here absolutely is no different - but the game's technical graphics + quality is outstanding here on this engine, provided you can actually get the game running + looking worthwhile to you. Tons of details, objects, and whatnot are loaded in this game-world, absolutely immersing the player into the fantastic game-world.
And what a game-world this is! With in-game Lore littered everywhere to find (whether it's in-game notes or audio-logs); an interesting plot with some twist + turns (especially early on & a lot later on); an absolutely great set-up; and making a fantastic villain take center stage here; and the option to be either Emily Kaldwin (who is now grown-up & about to take The Throne) or Corvo Attano (the assassin from the first game) - Dishonored 2 has plenty going for it. The world-building + the actual game-world is very easy to get immersed into, as every corner oozes with personality, details, information & intrigue.
After events from the first excellent game + its also excellent DLC's, Emily Kaldwin (who was a child in the first game) is about to take The Throne in Dunwall, with her father + protector (assassin Corvo Attano, from the first game) watching over her, by her side. Without spoiling things with specifics here, a certain person claims that he or she is an actual relative to the Kaldwins, takes The Throne by force & kicks Emily off the throne. From there, the player decides to either be Emily or Corvo (which each have their own special skills, BTW), leaves Dunwall & goes after those involved in this conspiracy to overthrow her. Also, not too far into the game, you will meet the Outsider & can even decide to accept his superpowers that he's offering you or reject them (and rejecting them will force you to play the game without them). It's up to the player on how to approach things, as the game's littered with options, both lethal & non-lethal for every mission.
Combat + stealth was great in the first and is even slicker + tweaked-up more so than the first - so if you enjoyed how combat played in that game, you'll be fine here & right at home. There are more options here, as you can even vault over walls + objects quickly & seemlessly & the player even can slide when running, making movement also more Kinetic and fluid than the first game. And yes, variations of the teleporting Superpower known as Blink are here from the first game, as Emily's can go further than Corvo's (it's called Far Reach) + Convo still has his Blink ability (specifically tailored for him) - which keeps the game's movement + combat for a stealth game at a much faster pace, keeping the stealth genre moving forward.
While the game's a fantastic stealth game if player that way, you can also approach it & dream up all kinds of combinations of attack from your Superpowers & make them come to life, which is very remisicant of Bioshock series. By finding Runes + Bone-Charms, you can also improve your Skills & enhance your in-game abilities, as well. Just keep in mind, playing Stealthy and not-killing will likely get you a better + happier ending than likely slaughtering everything in your path, even though playing with the Superpowers + chaining skills & attacks together is tons of fun!
When it's all said + done, after my first Playthrough as Emily Kaldwin, after experimenting here + there, dying quite a bit, reloading saves a lot, & exploring a good deal of the game-world that this game has to offer, taking around 23 hours or so, Dishonored 2 is finished. Despite the issues of performance + technical stabiilty from random CTD's, it could not stop me from playing the fantastic sequel to the orignal. In many ways, this is a much better Dishonored with much more meat to it, but technical + performance issues could stop some in their tracks from playing until Arkane fixes things up.  Provided one has a decent PC & can hopefully Blink their way past the assortment of technical + performance issues that this game unfortunately has, this is easily one of the best games released in 2016.

Gameplay is simple and addicting. You have few skills to use, but main fighting goes by simply walking into the enemies to cause damage. Developers did explain the reason for this in the Dev-room.

What with it being Halloween, I decided to write a lengthy review on the original game and also put down my thoughts on this sequel.  I'll try to keep this brief.
There are a few things here that are pretty much the same from EW.  The shooting, the stealth, the item/XP gathering.  It's all just as fun, which counts for a lot.
However, everything else is lesser.  It's less horrifying for starters.  The original game often reached Silent Hill levels in terms of being disturbing/grotesque.  Its also got far fewer enviroments (and I mean waaaaay fewer), fewer enemy types, less verticality, fewer surprises, far fewer mini-bosses/unique enemies, less variety in how levels play out or are explored, fewer puzzles, a lesser variety in pacing and fewer occasions to need the different weapons.
For example, the original game specifically had a whole bunch of situations where certain weapons were desperately needed.  Not so in this game; you can get by perfectly fine with the gun, harpoon and pistol, even on the survival setting.  In fact, you only get a sniper rifle halfway or-so through the game and a machine gun very late and ammo is very scarce for both but not in a good 'survival horror' type way.  In fact, it's entirely possible to miss the sniper rifle and flamethrower altogether.  Think about it this way.  If the game is made knowing you might not have these weapons, then how could they make varied situations/monsters that suit/require them?  They couldn't and they didn't.  I only used the sniper rifle once, on the end game boss.
I'd estimate that more than half the hours from this game come from two somewhat large and open areas.  They are both part of a run down town and are therefore almost identical.  They're slightly creepy in an RE2 kinda way.  It was fun to explore the first one but by the time I got to the second I was ready for something different.  I really cannot express the disparity between the two games in terms of variety, imagination, atmosphere and horror when it comes to the level design.
These same complaints about variety stretch to not just the enemies, but the situations that you'll be in when you fight them.  It's mostly corridor after corridor, room after room, street after street.  You're not gonna be dodging traps, moving in a cargo lift or avoiding a mini boss while you deal with ordinary creatues.  You're not gonna find yourself swimming from debris to debris, or timed gate to timed gate, while avoiding an invincible aquatic creature then climbing up a ladder into an abandoned office block, fighting a room full of enemies with more coming through the window before jumping back into the water to make a swim for it.  Yeah, that's a bit specific but I mention it to show just how much imagination the first game had in comparison.
The voice acting and script are better than EW.  The story is easier to follow and quite heartfelt at times.  I cared about what happened to the main characters.
My actual playtime was 20 hours, with the rest being me leaving the game on when not playing, so it's got a decent bit of content if you explore everything.  Mind you, I spent a lot of time making sure I killed everything I encountered for the XP (which I shouldn't have bothered with) and also ran back to the save points a lot so I imagine most people will complete the game at around the 15-17 hour mark.
I'm torn about whether to recommend it or not.  Wait for a sale would be my best advice.  I wish I had.  As you can tell, I was disappointed with it compared to the original but it's still one of the better survival horror games out there; it's not exactly a saturated genre after all.  I'm gonna just about fall into the 'recommend' category.  You can tell what bits I was disappointed by so if these things don't bother you then, of course, by all means go for it.  I hope you have a blast.

My review of The Evil Within 2:
Couple notes before we begin:
-The reason this review is so late is because I wanted to complete the game 3 times, once per difficulty, i'll be starting my classic mode run soon
- I've got near 100% completion, just missing some weapon upgrades and a few locker keys.
-I only own the PC version, cant comment on console look/performance.
Okay lets get started
I pre-ordered the evil within 2 a day before it came out. I loved the first game as it felt like the Silent Hill sequel we never got. It was the perfect blend of action and survival/psychological horror. The sequel had a lot to live up too. Lets start off with the games story.
Story:
TEW2 takes place 3 years after the events of the first game. This game brings a subplot from The Evil Within 1 to the forefront. You play as Sebastian Castellanos once again as he discovers his daughter, who he thought passed away in a fire, is still alive and is being used as an engine for a twisted machine that makes a virtual world. He must journey into the world of STEM to get her back. This time around the story is paced much better. One of my few issues with the first game was the lack of pacing. The story only got good and interesting within the final few chapters. Right from the opening chapters the story gripped me. The new voice actors are much more articulate and much more real this time allowing the player to get emotionally invested in the story. While its a shame the original voice actors didn't return for the games sequel there is no doubt in my mind that the new voice actors help pull the player into the world. It really sounds and feels like Sebastian wants to find his daughter. The story also is much more stable and easy to follow this time. While I wish that the story let the player figure stuff out on their own a bit more, adding a level of research needed to fully understand whats going on, theres no doubt the story being so easy to follow is a welcome addition for most fans.
Gameplay:
The core gameplay from the first game is still around. However, you can no longer upgrade weapons with the green gel found by killing enemies like in the first game. Now you must use the new crafting system. Sebastian can find supplies all over the world of Union. (The fictional town in STEM) which he can use at a crafting bench to create ammo/upgrade his weapons. At first i was scared the crafting system would be overbearing and forced on us, but it was a very welcome decision and the crafting helped me get out of some very sticky situations. When you're not near a work bench you can still craft ammo, however they will take more supplies to craft than at a work bench. The Evil Within 2 also features a semi'open world. The player will be treated to 3 main areas, the residential district, the business district, and the marrow. (the marrow being the one you can explore the least, as areas only open up as you progress through the story. ) I often found the areas requiring 2-3 hours to explore fully. They are filled with detail and events/loot. All of which help the player feel fully immersed in this world. I noticed a lot of reviews stating the game is more difficult this time around, but i defintely found the first game was much harder. Even on Nightmare mode I only found myself struggling at 2 or 3 parts. Its here where we find one of my biggst gripes with the game. The bosses. In the first game the bosses were plentiful and expertly designed. Reborn Laura, The Keeper, Heresy, Quell, Sentinel, Amalgam and Amalgam alpha were all amazing and memorable bossfights. In The Evil Within 2 we are treated to The Giggling Guardian, Obscura, Stefano, Harbinger, a short 30 second gauntlet of bosses from the first game, and the Matriarch. My problem with the bosses are that the guardian and harbinger have their fights, but then return almost immediately as regular enemies which just makes them feel like they weren't real bosses. The Obscura doesn't even have a real fight, just a part where you run away and a part where you have to distract it. Stefano is just a regular person with no creative design choices. The Matriarch is the only real bossfight. Obscura, Giggling guardian and Matriarch are the only bosses that have design that feels creative. This was such a huge let down as a fan of the original game.
Performance:
One of my gripes with the first game was the finnicky performance. Constant FPS drops, and texturing popping. This time around the texturing popping and constant FPS drops seemed to have been fixed. My rig has a GTX 960 and it ran the game fine on Ultra settings at around 30-45 FPS. However, the performance is not up to par. I dealt with constant crashes. Crashes aren't too much of a hassle until you play classic mode. The constant crashing can cause you to loose hours of gameplay for no reason. This was and will be frustrating (when i being my classic mode playthrough.) I hope this issue is fixed in a later patch. However, I must say that The Evil Within 2 is one of the most beautiful games to come out this year. It has stunning visuals. Some are big and bombastic while other visuals are just downright unsettling. (This is a good time to comment that the game is not as scary as the first either. It is rare that you'll be actually scared in this game. Fear was a constant feeling with the first.)
In conclusion, The Evil Within 2 is one of the best games to be released this year. This game is a must pick up for fans of the Resident Evil or Silent Hill franchise, or just survival horror fans in general. It provides an atmospheric and intense experience with a great story and fantastic/fun gameplay. If you're not a fan of survival horror titles I reccomend waiting for a sale and at least giving the game a try. While I do compare this game to the first one a lot in this review. It is important the game is also great as its own standalone thing. It was worth the full price to me, but everyone is different. I will be giving The Evil Within 2 a 8/10.

This game is delightful, fun, quirky, and plays out like a Disney movie! With an amazing cast of voice actors, beautiful rounded graphics, and a story that stays consistently interesting throughout the 5 chapters, this game is a winner in my book! There are bits of fast-paced action, but it's main thing is puzzles and riddles, which I personally enjoyed A LOT.
The one major downfall to this game was the fact that it doesn't give much direction. It sends you out to explore all on your own after the beginning where the main character, Graham, is narrating because he is telling the stories of his adventures to his granddaughter, Gwendolyn. Instead of keeping track of what you can/should be doing, you're left to adventure on, only having elderly Graham chime in when you find a new step to take. My problem with that was I ended up missing out on things I could've done and achievements because there were moments of unobvious choices to be made that weren't made apparent by direction. Some people might not find that as an issue, but I ended up consulting a walkthrough strictly for guidance so I don't miss anything again.
In the game, you pick what kind of king you want to be: Brave, Compassionate, or Wise. You get to make choices that affect the entire game, from the way Gwendolyn will behave due to the way you tell your stories, to the tapestries that hang, and even the way the townspeople will think of you. The couple in the potions shop are all about wisdom. The baker is about compassion. The blacksmith is about bravery.
Overall, GET THE GAME. It will make you laugh, gasp, and shout in relief. Just be sure to survey EVERYTHING so you don't miss anything!

Thimbleweed Park is a masterpiece of puzzle design. Many people think the adventure genre covers any game that combines a story with any old kinds of puzzles, but I have never believed that. A true adventure game entails puzzle-solving through deductive reasoning from the premises provided by the story and gameworld. This game does exactly that, only that, and brilliantly. Every puzzle is organic and can be solved by following the story and thoroughly exploring the gameworld. Here there are no non-contextual puzzles, no minigames, no moon logic.
The story is also terrific, so long as you take to heart this line from the game's description: "In a town like Thimbleweed Park, a dead body is the least of your problems." Not every detail gets wrapped up into a little box with a bow on top. If you need that kind of complete closure, then you might conclude, illegitimately, that the story is flawed. It is not. The story is something anyone with the ability to embrace nonconformity will truly relish.
The only "negative" I noticed is that getting to the main menu requires an odd key-combo rather than ESC, but, you know, see above re: nonconformity. ;-)

Thimbleweed Park is a love letter towards players from the golden age of adventure games back in the day. Highly recommended for gamers who used to play the Lucasfilm games in the eighties and early nineties or those who are discovering these old games with retro gaming. Lots of references (maybe too much) to those games as well.
Maybe a bit less recommended to those gamers who want everything quick and easy  (although I did not try out the easy mode myself yet). I do not want to go into spoilers, but one good thing for example is that by switching to multiple characters you can keep things going without getting stuck into one place for long.
Great retro style graphics which can probably run on older machines too, audio is okay, characters maybe not so lovable, plot may be better (although some silly things may be intentional), but puzzles are great. And overall a great achievement.
Conclusion: I certainly hope this is the start of a comeback for more adventure games. A must have!
