The year was 1999 when I first played this game. I had never and have never played the original System Shock but that never put me off. I'd seen and heard good things so I was eager to try it out. And try it out I did! So, what did I think?
It blew my F**KING mind! So complex and way ahead of its time. The first FPS I had played with an inventory system, audio logs and options to upgrade your statistics. It was very different to other shooters I had played. This was in a whole new league. Graphically it looked really good with music that complemented the eerie feel of the game. Speaking of eerie, this game is scary. The voices of the enemies is creepy and I'm not even going to mention the psychic monkeys, lest I break into a fit of pure terror. Combat is good though you must maintain your weapons if you don't want them to break. Melee combat feels slow and clunky.
The story... ah the story. From beginning to end the narrative manages to hold your attention and takes you on a great adventure, exploring every nook and cranny of your environment. The 'female' antagonist is one of the best ever portrayed in a video game.
A truly fantastic game back in 1999 and a great game now in 2015. I still wait in hope of a System Shock III.

I waited so hard for Black Mesa and when they finally released the Mod in 2012 I was blown away by how great the Remake has been made.
As an old Half-Life Fan I recognized most of the areas right away but some have been changed or replaced for a more realistic design and the level of detail is just incredible! Now Black Mesa feels much more like the research facility it always wanted to be.
But do you need the Retail version of BM when you can have the mod for free? I'd say yes!
The retail has a more balanced difficulty (now you don't need a full MP5 mag to kill one Marine), better graphics and it runs more smoothly.
The also extended some of the levels and you can choose how you want to play the game. You can switch to "always run" and then Black Mesa feels even more like Half-Life. Without it, it's a bit slower and more like Half-Life 2.
There are not many games where I say you have to play them, but Black Mesa is one of them and it's on my personal list of best games of all time and getting on that list is hard.

Oh Black Mesa... The Labratory that became the Home and begining of one of Gamings most prestigous Series' (Half-Life)
To be Honest I never really played the First Game. I touched a few Hours in Half-life: source But mainly I had played Half-life 2 and its short but meaningful expansions. I adored them... The level design, the Character profiles, The Back story which you didn't need to know, but was an achievement to grapse if you did. I Enjoyed all of that... But i had still never played where it all began.
One Christmas, When winter had come and Steam at bestowed on the Store some mightly sales I came across Black Mesa. At The time i hadnt really seen anything on it, Saw some trailers for the mod and few youtubers playing through it all, but i never really watched them for some some unknown reason. I knew it was essentially a Remastered version of the original Half-Life which brought it into a modified Source Engine. Since I was Sub-Counciously wanting to discover how one of my Favourite Games began I thought why not... It's on Sale! So i brought it. However packed with big releases like Fallout 4 (Which I was quite hyped for, but did eventually die out on me) I put it to rest in my Steam library; Installed but Un-Played.
Around 6-7 Months after Purchase I was bored, Nothing really to do during the Summer. I was in a Sci-fy mood but could never think of what to play for a good amount of time. After staring at my Library for god knows how long, I Noticed Black Mesa sitting there Still untouched.
Any reasonable Gamer would have thought "Well... might as well give it a go" And so Give it a go i did...........
... And let me tell you, was I a Happy Man after that.
Black-Mesa truly deserves some Kudos for what it has Acomplished. The Level design is Amazing, it keeps that Classic Valve Feel with an Ultimatly Expanded Feel while still keeping it with in the boundaries of what the Labratory was orginally designed to appear as.
The Voice Acting is spot on. Same with the Sounds and weapon design. AI Pathfinding has very lttile problems all though Larger Entities do have trouble navigating around certain Dynamic and Static props and the Assassin Units do have trouble tracking and maintaining suppression when in groups from the Rare Ocassion.
The Soundtrack is another point of mine... It's brilliant, It hits in with sceanrios brilliantly and you'll often hear people comment about how the made them feel when Doing X or they feel like a Y when they hear it.
I also enjoy the Backgrounds of how the world around you is constantly shifting after every Chapter, especialy when you Reach the surface.
Overall I only expereinced minor problems such as getting lost with how to proceed and about a single crash about half-way through the Game. I have not yet experience Multiplayer yet since the base game resembles that of the orginal Half-Life I imagine that it will be very similar to the orginal Multiplayer. Although at this time there is no Zen Chapters, The game itself is fantastic and a fitting Call for past Half-life fans or some who have not touched apon the orginal Game.

VERY HIGHLY RECOMMENDED...provided you have a PC to handle this game + can tolerate random CTD's.
NOT RECOMMENDED yet...for those who have lower-end systems + those who don't want to deal with random CTD's.
Dishonored 2 is an absolute fantastic sequel to the original outstanding Dishonored game, often trumping it in almost every way with superb, clever + interesting level design (most are excellent, but The Time Manipulation + Clockwork levels are absolutely mind-blowing + incredible); outstanding gameplay; numerous ways to finish your objectives (stealth-style of action-style, with some choices along the way); fantastic graphics (and that's even when running the game at Medium settings).
I said "almost in every way" because...well, this game clearly has issues currently, unfrortunately. While the performance issues + technical issues might stop some cold with decent systems + from continuing to play the game until Arkane fixes some things, it certainly did not stop me.
Let's get the "bad" out the way here first. I was running the game at 1440p on my desktop PC with an i7 950 Bloomfield; 16 GB RAM DDR3; "4GB" 970; and W7 64-bit PC at Medium settings w/ V Sync Off - well, it took a bit to get this game running at anything worthwhile for me. With an in-game 60FPS cap, the game was rising + dropping like crazy, with framerates floating anytime from 30 frames to 60 feames at any moment; especially when out-doors. With an in-game 45 FPS cap, the game often hovered somewhere b/t 30FPS to 45FPS, which is certainly more acceptable than what it was doing with the 60FPS cap. On my gaming laptop equipped with an i7 4720HQ; 16 GB RAM DDR3; 4GB 960M - well, I had to run the game at Medium settings on 900p with V-Sync Off at Medium settings also with the 45FPS cap, just to try to keep the game somewhat stable.
While it's great that an actual PC game has a bunch of different FPS cap options in-game - which range from 30FPS, 45FPS, 60FPS + even above that for those with high-end monitors with awesome refresh-rates, BTW - and IMHO, more games should do this + have these kind of framerate-cap options - some gamers just might even want to use something like MSI Afterburner to lock the framerates down to something more specific and suitable for them, if necessary. While I was fine w/ the 45FPS cap, those with systems similar to mine might want to use Afterburner to set the cap to maybe 35FPS or even 40FPS, just to get the framerate stable even more so.
In terms of poor performance, this is very reminiscent of performance of another game, Batman: Arkham Knight. Though, at least Batman: AK didn't have random crashes, here + there - Dishonored 2 sometimes would have CTD's (Crashes To the Desktop) for who knows what random reason. B/c this is a stealth game (if you choose it to play that way, and you probably should at least try to) & you can save at anytime, most people likely are going to be Quick-saving & Regular-saving a lot anyways - but it's also going to be a great idea to do this anyways b/c of the technical issues this game has with random CTD's.
This game is running on the Void Engine, which is a very-heavily customized version of the highly unoptimized Id Tech 5 (which powered other games that had stiff reqauirements + technical issues upon release...such as RAGE; Wolfenstein: TNO + TOB; & The Evil Within). Dishonored 1 never-ever slouched on excellent art-design & this sequel here absolutely is no different - but the game's technical graphics + quality is outstanding here on this engine, provided you can actually get the game running + looking worthwhile to you. Tons of details, objects, and whatnot are loaded in this game-world, absolutely immersing the player into the fantastic game-world.
And what a game-world this is! With in-game Lore littered everywhere to find (whether it's in-game notes or audio-logs); an interesting plot with some twist + turns (especially early on & a lot later on); an absolutely great set-up; and making a fantastic villain take center stage here; and the option to be either Emily Kaldwin (who is now grown-up & about to take The Throne) or Corvo Attano (the assassin from the first game) - Dishonored 2 has plenty going for it. The world-building + the actual game-world is very easy to get immersed into, as every corner oozes with personality, details, information & intrigue.
After events from the first excellent game + its also excellent DLC's, Emily Kaldwin (who was a child in the first game) is about to take The Throne in Dunwall, with her father + protector (assassin Corvo Attano, from the first game) watching over her, by her side. Without spoiling things with specifics here, a certain person claims that he or she is an actual relative to the Kaldwins, takes The Throne by force & kicks Emily off the throne. From there, the player decides to either be Emily or Corvo (which each have their own special skills, BTW), leaves Dunwall & goes after those involved in this conspiracy to overthrow her. Also, not too far into the game, you will meet the Outsider & can even decide to accept his superpowers that he's offering you or reject them (and rejecting them will force you to play the game without them). It's up to the player on how to approach things, as the game's littered with options, both lethal & non-lethal for every mission.
Combat + stealth was great in the first and is even slicker + tweaked-up more so than the first - so if you enjoyed how combat played in that game, you'll be fine here & right at home. There are more options here, as you can even vault over walls + objects quickly & seemlessly & the player even can slide when running, making movement also more Kinetic and fluid than the first game. And yes, variations of the teleporting Superpower known as Blink are here from the first game, as Emily's can go further than Corvo's (it's called Far Reach) + Convo still has his Blink ability (specifically tailored for him) - which keeps the game's movement + combat for a stealth game at a much faster pace, keeping the stealth genre moving forward.
While the game's a fantastic stealth game if player that way, you can also approach it & dream up all kinds of combinations of attack from your Superpowers & make them come to life, which is very remisicant of Bioshock series. By finding Runes + Bone-Charms, you can also improve your Skills & enhance your in-game abilities, as well. Just keep in mind, playing Stealthy and not-killing will likely get you a better + happier ending than likely slaughtering everything in your path, even though playing with the Superpowers + chaining skills & attacks together is tons of fun!
When it's all said + done, after my first Playthrough as Emily Kaldwin, after experimenting here + there, dying quite a bit, reloading saves a lot, & exploring a good deal of the game-world that this game has to offer, taking around 23 hours or so, Dishonored 2 is finished. Despite the issues of performance + technical stabiilty from random CTD's, it could not stop me from playing the fantastic sequel to the orignal. In many ways, this is a much better Dishonored with much more meat to it, but technical + performance issues could stop some in their tracks from playing until Arkane fixes things up.  Provided one has a decent PC & can hopefully Blink their way past the assortment of technical + performance issues that this game unfortunately has, this is easily one of the best games released in 2016.

Tight, improved combat with the new powers, weapons, and non-lethal weapons. The Heart had great voice-acting as always but other characters not so much. Level design: Some of the levels strayed from the typical Dishonored levels (i.e small zone with many buildings to explore before moving to the next one) to differing effects. One of the earliest levels is primarily set on a small island where you explore
which felt dragged out. Due to the enclosed nature of the area as well as some parts locked away due to story reasons, the level didn't feel as open to exploration as other levels. Other levels however, had some of the best design I've seen in a long time. A particular example being "A Crack In The Slab"
. "The Clockwork Mansion" had a unique level design in a different way, its use of
leant itself to a constantly changing level that I haven't seen in any AAA games.
Gameplay: Arkane doubles down on their implementation of powers that are fun to use. Emily's powers were fairly interesting with the key exception being Mesmerize which is a fairly simple power that does not lend itself to much creativity, even with the upgrades which are just numerical changes. Corvo's powers are just as fun as the last game and just like the last game, Wind Blast is a boring power.
New types of bolts and the stun mine allows for more fun for non-lethal plays. Unlike the last game, non-lethal was almost as reliable as lethal. The creation of air-assassination (non-lethal style) and non-lethal takedowns during combat that does not involve sleep darts allows for a player for enjoy the brutal violence while still getting the good ending. Lethal however, is still , superior for combat by design. Players will still have it easier during combat and assassinations when using lethal due to faster animations.
Voice acting: The main characters' voice acting, the Heart's, and Delilah had phenomenal voice acting. The voices all fit the characters with lines that change to fit different playstyles. Playing low chaos will create a more merciful, empathethic main character while high chaos will create a vengeful, violent character. The Heart's voice is enchanting as always with its ghostly whispers. Delilah's voice fit with her character from moments of anger to her talking to her followers. Other characters however, often had, while not terrible, not great voice acting. It would not detract much from the game and is barely noticable but it is there.
Enemy detection: This one deserves its own category. I played on hard mode so I expected rather unforgiving detection but it was strange. There were a few times where I was right next to the enemy at 10 O'clock (12 O'clock is straight ahead) but they did not detect me. Another time, I was hidden behind an object and was not detected yet in the next playthrough, in the same position, the I was detected. Most of the time however, the detection was fine.
Performance problems: Everyone already knows about these so I won't go into much detail. I had occasional stutters and black screens after loading but after a few seconds they went away. It might not be the same for yours but that's why Valve allowed for refunds before 2hrs.

SMITE is one of the best MOBAs out there in my opinion, mostly because of the immense amount of variety in all of the god's abilities, looks, and overall feel, but from other features like the third person camera angles that makes it more action-packed compared to other MOBAs,the fact that the gods come from various religions, countries, and mythology, resulting in more variety, and the large community of over 10 million players, meaning it won't be that hard to find a match.
I play SMITE on Xbox One and on PC, and find that the experience and players are great, there is virtually NO noticeable server lag, and that the visuals are outstanding. In case your wondering, no, the store doesn't allow players to just get over-powered abilities with in-game currency purchased with real money, it simply allows players to buy skins and different gods faster.
I find that the different god classes have different pros and cons, meaning there will be more teamwork, and the addition of the surrender vote and the removal of a leave game option is a great idea, and is very under-rated in games. However, I find that sometimes when I'm frustrated while playing a game of SMITE, the players that aren't having a bad experience vote not to surrender, resulting in some players not having a good experience.
This game, like all others, does have cons. Most games last at least 20 minutes, so if you're a busy person, you may want to stay away from this addicting game. Also, there aren't many game modes, and although the Game of the Day feature is smart, it seems like close to zero thought was put into these daily game modes.
Overall this game is a great Free-to-play game and gets a 9.2 in my book, only because of the reasons above. The gameplay and graphics are fast and steady, and they're always adding new gods. with over 70 gods and counting, I can't wait to see where this game goes.

I had a love/hate relationship with the first Evil Within, being frustrated by technical problems, clunky controls and some weirdly boring parts of the game. I am happy to report, that the second installment fixes a lot of the issues I had with the first one, although it isn't without fault.
The plot takes place 3 years after The Evil Within and lets us again play as detective Castellanos. After loosing his wife and child, he drowns his sorrows with alcohol and it is clear that he can't cope with whats happened in the first game. The game picks up when Kidman from the first game suddenly appears to tell him that his daughter is still alive, inside the STEM from the first game and that only he can save her.
I don't want to go into more detail than that, but the story is one of the most surprisingly good things about the game. Since the whole mystery around Moebius and STEM has been explained in the first game (including DLCs), they focused on our main character and him dealing with his past, which is an excellent idea. In the course of the game you'll realize, that the story is not so much about the task at hand, but about his character arc, being forced to confront his fears and sorrows, instead of running away and drowning in booze. The pace of the story is great and the directing in the cutscenes is in some parts almost arthouse-cinema-esque with camera angles and tracking shots being used as metaphors.
Sadly, the facial animations of the characters can't keep up with the detailed emotions they are ment to display. Uncanny Valley at it's worst, which really is a shame.
You are thrown again into the virtual dreamworld of STEM, while it mainly portrays a quaint american neighbourhood for you to freely explore. Intervened with the small open world of the town are smaller, more linear areas, which you enter to complete certain tasks. All in all, the atmoshpere is chilling and some of the more linear parts of the game can be truly frightening. What all areas have in common, is an excellent design, that really transpires the kind of feeling the developers want to invoke in the player and sets a great atmoshpere. While I really liked the open world parts of the game from a gameplay perspective,  I still felt that it hurt the creepy Horror atmosphere just a bit. Still, some parts of the game are truly frightening, especially some of the boss enemies you'll encounter are downright disgustingly horrible to look at and will increase your heart rate just by looking at them. I would have wished for more variety when it comes to enemies, since most of the time you just shoot dozens of the zombie-like creatures, but still, the ones they have designed work well.
When it comes to gameplay The Evil Within 2 is, for the most part, a normal survival Horror Game. You wander around, search every nook and cranny for rare ammunition or crafting parts and encounter enemies along the way, that you have to dispose of. Like in the first game, you often have the option to choose how you want to go about killing the disgusting monsters you'll find along the way. Go in guns blazing, popping heads like a sharpshooter, or sneak around, lure enemies away from each other and stealthily dispose of them, one by one. Both approaches work really well. Shooting enemies feels very responsive thanks to excellent controls, great feedback for hits and superb weapon handling. Stealth also works as intended, although the enemies are kind of braindead, so it's somewhat easy to trick them.
Crucial for a survival horror game is the difficulty: It can't be too easy or the whole concept of survival horror falls flat on it's a*se and the games becomes a shooting gallery. After trying out different settings, I found the balancing to be nothing short of perfect. The lowest difficulty is really easy, if you just want to run through and shoot everything, the normal one gives a bit of challenge and the hardest challenge that you can use from the get go is the one I used for my first playthrough. It forced me to reaaaally manage my ressources, encouraged me to engage enemies stealthily and I had a constant fear of running out of ammo which at some points in the game really happened. It was tough, never unfair and gave me a great feeling of accomplishment after beating it.
As stated before, the controls are damn good. Aiming, shooting, running, everything feels tight, responsive and very direct. Top notch work on this one. The only complaint I have is the fiddly cover system. I would have liked for them to implement an automatic system like the last of us has, but after getting used to it, it feels fine. Hooray for a good port.
The presentation overall is innovative, interesting and excellent. The lighting creates spectacular atmospheric setpieces, while the artists behind the game came up with some mind-bending visuals to flesh out their characters and worlds via envoirenmental storytelling. Effects like dust, smoke and gunfire also look superb, while the animations of enemies are fluid.
The only downfall visually are the sometimes dreadful NPCs in the ingame cutscenes. Their mimic capabilities aren't really that developed which in combination with waxy skin and their dead gaze makes them look like puppets trying to convey emotions. It just doesn't work as well as other games have shown, which is a damn shame. Still, while you are playing, visually the game is appealing and sometimes downright bizarre in it's artdesign.
The sound ist excellent as well. Gunshots are powerful while the enemies emit distinct and sometimes goosebump-inducing noises which will terrify the player to the bone. The music keeps itself restraint in the background to just create atmosphere, which is a good thing, but kicks in with stress-inducing terror, as soon a new nightmare jumps at you. Some pieces of the soundtrack, especially towards the end are beautiful orchestral pieces, and elevate the game to another level.

This is a point and click adventure that feels just like a classic LucasArts game. Which is no surprise of course, since the project is headed by Ron Gilbert, the Monkey Island and Maniac Mansion creator.
What surprised me the most is that even though I didn't find the game very funny, it didn't hurt my experience at all! It's instead quite charming and has more than a few heart warming moments. The puzzles are just the right level of difficulty on Hard for seasoned adventure gamers. And for newcomers there is a Casual mode that makes things less frustrating. Another thing that surprised me is that this is not a small adventure game, it's really long but I never got bored! I replayed Monkey Island 1 & 2 recently and none of them are longer than ten hours. Here I finished in at about 25 hours (exploring mostly everything) and even with a walkthrough I don't think I would have finished it in under 15 hours. There is lots of dialogue too good to skip through and there are many beautiful locations to explore.
Something that did annoy me in the beginning is the constant fourth wall breaking. Characters make many comments about being in a game, that you don't have to save often like in Sierra adventures and so on. The longer I played, the more I liked these things though.
Overall I really recommend this game. The old adventure game magic is here in spades.

Where to begin!?!?
This, in my opinion, is the greatest sci-fi game ever made. Not the biggest, nor the best, nor the one with the best graphics (the enemy models were considered poor even back when it was released, but you can update them now via a community mod).
The main character (nicknamed 'Goggles' by the community, due to his eyewear) can be upgraded in many ways. There are three main areas of expertise: Weapons, Tech (hacking etc.), and Psionic (magic, basically). On top of that, you can also upgrade your personal stats, like Strength etc.
Sadly, this is one of those games where there is a 'right' and 'wrong' way to level up. I will add, though, that it's hard to make your character completely useless. But not upgrading certain skills can make it VERY tough at the end of the game, similar to the Vampire: The Masquerade videogame.
So why do I think it's the greatest?
All the parts come together to create something greater than themselves.
Because, for me personally, they've nailed the atmosphere - and nothing else gets in the way. It's that simple.
For instance, Deus Ex: Human Revolution does a lot of the same stuff, gameplay wise. But I HATE the 'hacking' in that game with a wrath, which is why I will never reply it, ever. the hacking 'gets in the way'. I also can't stand the story or any of the characters.
There's only a very few cutscenes - and only the intro and end cutscenes remove control from the character. The rest of the story is told along the way, and the audio logs can fill in the blanks - or be ignored. Compare that to, say, the recent Fallout entries, which remove player agency far too often for me to be able to truly enjoy them. Oh, I LOVE them, don't get me wrong. But I don't need to deal with that at all here, because it never 'gets in the way'.
I can rebind keys effectively (I did not pay for a gaming mouse so that the extra buttons can be ignored, thanks), so that doesn't 'get in the way'.
the music isn't overly annoying (even if it should have been replaced with mood tracks and ambient sounds), so that doesn't 'get in the way'.
I don't need to install another Steam-like shopfront in order to play a game I bought on Steam (I AM LOOKING DIRECTLY AT YOU, GHOST OF GAMES FOR WINDOWS LIVE), so that doesn't 'get in the way'.
I don't need to install an inventory mod, because the inventory makes sense to me and doesn't 'get in the way'.
And while she's showing her age (well, the game is), SHODAN remains one of my favourite villains in any medium, ever. While her insults can be intrusive on a personal (to the character, not the player) level, they don't 'get in the way' of me enjoying the game.
In fact, the only thing that really 'gets in the way' for me when I play this game is...
...yep, you guessed it: Real Life.

"You should study Aerospacial Engineering", they said. "You will see the space!" they said. "You will find what happened to your mother", they said. But they never said that some kind of ugly, black beast will be pursuing you to devour your body... That's what this game is all about: Survival at its best, using improbable means to craft impossible tools in order to ultimately survive to the 'Alien', a creature which sole purpose is hunt down any creature in this galaxy.
WARNING: Playing this game in Nightmare is not suitable for impatient people or the light hearted. It is a true survival experience where You won't have anything with you, except maybe your cunning and stealth for salvaging items and hiding in impossible places in order to evade the Alien or other enemies that proved to have an excellent AI.
Let me start off from the Campaign. It is perfect. As an Alien saga true fan (meaning I just love 'Alien' and its sequel, 'Aliens'; and I just like 'Alien3' and 'Alien: Resurrection'), I can say that this game's Campaign is just awesome. Is a real 'Pre-Sequel' to 'Aliens' and a perfect candidate for 'Alien 1.5'. The way it developes, unfolding every single detail of the plot in a subtle way, making You search for lore around the Sevastopol Space Station while hearing those uncomfortable noises on the vents... You know a game has a great plot when You have the urge of exploring every single corner of every level in order to get answers to 'Why is that thing here', despite being chased by a killing machine that was genetically engineered to kill. I won't spoil any details of this plot but, again, 'wow'.
Sadly, it doesn't have any Multiplayer mode, but it could have been awesome if Isolation had some kind of Co-Op survival, kind of mixing 'Evolve' with this game's crafting mechanics.
As of Gameplay, this is not a 'Shooter'. Sure, You have weapons that might prove quite useful against a few foes (and not every weapon is as efective as other with a particular enemy), but the 90% of the game os about playing 'Hide and Seek' with quite inteligent NPCs (You'll die if You lose, by the way ;P). You can also craft a variety of homemade devices in order to Distract, to Damage or, sometimes, to Kill those who stand between You and your objective. You will feel like a real engineer, because Amanda Ripley will have to find virtually any single type of object in order to craft those devices.
As I just said before, AI is sublimely designed, making it react as the creature it is made for. The Humans will hide and shoot, but the Alien... It will chase You to the very last spot in the Sevastopol. It doesn't matter where you hide, it will find you... Moreover, all of the Station can be free-roamed in order to find Audio registers and Nostromo logs, and even salvage more materials and open closed doors You were previously not able to open.
In addition, Graphics are just awesome. Characters are detailed to the level you can see the sweat drops running along their face. The design of the Sevastopol is truly amazing too, because it uses all that big, chunky analogic technology seen in the movies. No LED screens, no Laser Beams... just phosphore displays, classic light bulbs and flashlights, back to the old days.
All of those elements, combined with the high quality Sound Effects this game offers, are more than enough to recreate that dark, claustrophobic atmosphere that the movies have and all of those previous Alien titles struggled to reproduce. After a few hours playing, You will feel paranoid, crouching while thinking about some kind of 'voice' or 'conduit sound', or even footsteps.
In Conclussion, Alien: Isolation is a must buy, a masterpiece. A true survival, scavenging and frightening experience that any Alien fan must own.

A fun adventure series with a great story and good puzzles that nicely pays homage to the classic Sierra series. First episode  is free and is the best of the five (though others are generally good too) - so check it out!

One thing I dislike about episodic games is the down time between episodes. Sometimes it is agonizing to wait for the next part of the story to come out because the episode you just played ended on such a cliffhanger and you won't find out until the next release, which could be months. For this reason, I tend to purchase episodic games when everything is released.
King's Quest approaches this model differently and it is refreshing. Rather than creating a major overarching story throughout the season, each episode focuses on one adventure at a certain period of time in King Graham's longstanding career as an adventurer. Yes, there is a cohesive narrative throughout the season, but it takes a backseat and lets Graham's story of the episode take center stage. Releasing these stories as episodes actually works, because there is a satisfying conclusion at the end, and you're not clamouring to find out what happens next.
Episodic games are like weekly TV serials, where you have to wait for the next episode to continue the story. King's Quest is more like a cinematic saga, where each movie is satisfying on its own.

Dark Souls II. Wow. What a game! The sequel to the original Dark Souls brings back the franchise with a punch. It's an amazing game with amazing features, small and big. I would highly recommend the game if you enjoy adventure, awesome landscapes, and impending death.

If you are looking for a casual adventure game, turn back now this is not the way. However, if you are looking for a challenging adventure game, with seemingly impassable obstacles and clever traps designed to kill your character again and again, this is the game for you.
In addition to the challenge and the feeling of victory which progressing through the game gives you, the game's story and mechanics work well for those who are observant. Certain bosses, and obstacles can be made easier for those who explore and observe their surroundings. Also unlike many other adventure games, Dark Souls 2 does not directly point you where you needed to go, but instead provides directions in contextual clues, like dialogues, in a way which helps immerse the player into the story and world.
To summarize, Dark Souls 2 is a difficult adventure game which will not only provide difficult challenges to overcome, but will also provide interesting features to discover which will help you as to pass through the game.

Broforce is a 2D Run and Gun game where you are tasked with bringing freedom to the entire world. At least that is what they claim we are doing, as we blow enemy hideouts to smithereens and fly off into the sunset. To accomplish this we are given control of “Bros” which are all parody characters out of popular films such as Rambro, Bro Hard and Bronan the Brobarian. As you can no doubt tell, this is very much a tongue in cheek type of game. Broforce is centered around fast gameplay, epic guitar riffs and destruction above all else and has very little story to speak of. You and up to three friends can join in on the carnage via drop in, drop out online or local coop to deliver fiery freedom to terrorists. Starting off the game you will have the choice of either picking Campaign or Arcade Mode. They are mostly the same except campaign mode gives you an overworld while arcade is just back to back missions. Then you will be given the choice of normal and hard difficulty. It is suggested to start on normal since hard has faster rates of fire, more enemies and placements designed to annoy you.
At the start of each mission you are given a random Bro that you have unlocked and must make your way throughout the levels saving new Bros for extra lives. Bros all play differently from one another and each have special attacks. For example one bro may only have his fists and be able to send projectiles back at enemies, while another bro throws dynamite and is able to attract enemies via a cooked turkey with dynamite stuffed into it. There are also differences in speed, strength and range between them, so every Bro requires their own play-style, which makes the repetition in this game feel very minimal. To unlock more characters you have to a certain amount of Bros from their cages. The random nature in which you are given Bros is a double edged sword. On one hand you will not be able to rely on the character you are best at and only play as them throughout, but on the other hand some Bros are just not equipped for the task at hand, which will cause you to die until you are given a Bro more suited to the situation. You can retry a mission as many times as you like so it is a minor issue. Unless you are playing on IronBro mode, a permadeath mode that is unlocked later in the game and makes it so each Bro can live only once, once you lose all Bros it's game over.
To defend yourself you will have melee, ranged and special attacks. Melee and ranged can be used indefinitely while special attacks usage amount varies from character to character. Strangely enough you can only shoot horizontally, so any enemy above or below you is untouchable via weapon fire until they are on the same plane as you. That is unless you get clever with explosives or special attacks to kill them before they know what hit them. The problem with simply jumping below is that enemies have far greater range than most Bros do, so you have to get in rather close to shoot them. Since you die in a single hit that can be an unnecessarily risky move. This game does require a decent amount of foresight before going in guns blazing. You have to consider if there may be enemies hiding in the grass, if you can take out the enemies before they fire at you and shoot an explosive near you, or if it would simply be better if you punch through a wall and make your own path. There is a pleasant amount to consider before making your move and makes it all the more sweeter when you proudly stand alone in an environment torn apart by an intense battle. That is the perfect time to use the button dedicated to flexing your muscles.
Enemies have quite a bit of variety to them and range from dogs, suicide bombers and even supernatural enemies later on. They all have different means of attack and some are able to take a lot of damage. Terrorists have a certain room in which they will infinitely respawn until you destroy the ground under that door, causing them to all fall to their deaths. Sadly, AI is terrible in this game and enemies are very likely to be the cause of their own deaths. If you are spotted the enemy will just stand there and shoot at the direction he last saw you, over and over again until you kill him. The difficulty comes from the traps, enemy numbers and camera which you have no control over. Once you kill an enemy its corpse will provide cover to his friends behind it until you gib it with a few bullets, while enemy bullets can conveniently pass through the body. The camera is far too zoomed in, causing you to be killed by an enemy that was out of view or getting explosives dropped on your head that you had no way of knowing where there on occasions.
You will also face multiple vehicles like mechs, helicopters and trucks that spawn enemies from it. Out of all the vehicles you can only hijack the mechs by standing on it and pressing the melee button.  These deal some serious damage to everything it comes across, though its ability to move around is based on a very small fuel supply, so it won't last too long. Your main threats will be the crazy bosses in this game.  The amount of destruction they all cause is staggering and it is a joy to take these down. Some will not just die by shooting at it and will require some outside the box thinking. The overall amount of destruction you will see in this game is truly impressive. Nearly anything can be destroyed and the levels usually end up looking like the planet is imploding in on itself. The only things which can't be destroyed is the ground surrounding the American flag which is used as a respawn point. There is quite a bit of levels to play through on the campaign/arcade. It keeps getting crazier and crazier the further in you go until you are eventually fighting on American soil. What little dialogue there is, is delivered via text and adds nothing to the game. The only difference in campaign mode is the over-world I previously mentioned, where you can fly around and run into seagulls because why not, as well as be able to choose which levels to take on first at times.
To top it off this game supports custom maps via Steam workshop. These can also be played with friends and are just as enjoyable as the ones found in the main game. They can be downloaded right from in game and can also be saved so you can play them offline. These offer much more value to the game and are quite a few of them already. Great music is something Broforce also has, especially that final ending theme song. With its fast paced gameplay, considerable difference between Bros and various ways to tackle levels, it offers plenty of replay value even without the user made content. Its AI is unimpressive to say the least but there is a ton of fun to be had mowing them down in various ways. All levels are perfectly playable if you end up doing it solo and may even be preferable, so you know exactly what is going on, which can be pretty hard when you have three others blowing up the map. At the end of the day this is a great game that plays like a mix of Metal Slug and an extreme version of Dig Dug.  For those still unsure I highly recommend checking out the free game
to get a taste of what is on offer. Highly recommended to those that like the genre, want an action packed game or simply want a fun game to play with friends.

I think I would have given this a thumbs up under a lot of conditions. If it was less popular for example, I would be moved to have a bit of pity for creators who have obviously put in some effort and simply lacked creativity or talent in some regard. Or if it wasn't in a genre I've played so much of and have so much to compare it to, RPG maker games that seek to subvert classic RPG style storytelling. Or maybe if it had, as a comedy game, made me smile even once during the entirety of the four hours I gave it. Alas, none of those conditions are in effect.
is just... not good.
As a turn-based RPG it is a mediocrely designed, adds nothing new to the formula, random enemy grind where your first character does damage, your second character stuns the single member enemy parties you fight for 90% of the game, and you never bother with anything else because this combination kills everything in a slow and sure manner. Until you get a third character much too late in the game, at which point you can just keep spamming confirm to attack for every fight.
As a story, this game is nothing but a vehicle for memes and pen15 jokes. If I had to explain to someone what lowest common denominator humor looked like, this game would be it. I suppose it grows some cliché anti-corporation popcorn and dead braincell plot towards the end, but that's all largely inconsequential in comparison to the game having a room full of popular Youtubers drawn as monsters, which I think is supposed to be funny? But there's no joke. It's literally just Youtubers with mildly stupid names based on their online personas. Because that in itself is funny right?

This review was written the day the game was released, and may have some edits as updates come out.
TL;DR: The game is great, but lacks the much vaunted content that we were excited for, and at $15 it's a little pricy for just matches.
The detailed review:
This game is a single-player only military FPS. You may think that makes it boring. It's not. The game is FANTASTIC. To be fair, it's a little overpriced at $15, but that's on release date, perhaps that number will go down as the game goes along.
So pros and cons?
Pros:
Relaxing yet not TOO relaxing gameplay.
Fairly decent AI for an indie game made by one person.
Guns are fun to play around with.
Controls are good.
Vehicles are pretty neat. It's fun to hop in the machinegun port of a tank right next to the enemy flag and blast everyone away.
For a singleplayer game, can be decently challenging.
Cons:
Fairly limited gameplay as of now, but it was JUST released, so that will change soon.
I was disappointed that the mod system isn't even released yet, but that's to be expected. However, the dev didn't even release the much spoken of campaign mode. Come on man, AT LEAST get that ready.
To be honest, the game doesn't feel...ready for even early access release. I got that feeling from another game that had DISASTROUS updates, Castle Story (which I also reviewed). Hopefully, this game won't go down that path.
I LOVED the free Beta on itch.io, and was hopeful for this game, but it really has been a little...disappointing on release.
STILL, this game is fun, even as is, and I have no regrets forking over $12 to get it. I'm excited to see what the dev will do as the game progresses.
Should you buy it? If you want a fun, single-player FPS game experience, sure, but maybe wait for the much vaunted content to come out before you dole out $15 for this game. That's a little pricy.

As a nostalgia-loving old-school Lucas Arts adventure fan, I was really hyped for Thimbleweed Park – and it didn't disappoint.
The game bursts with millions of nostalgic hints and references to Maniac Mansion, other Lucas Arts games and adventure games in general.
The characters are all likeable (in their own way) and perfectly written, voiced and designed. The story is ingenious and left me speechless. It feels like Ron Gilbert put all he had on his mind for the last 25 years in this game, not implying he's out of fuel now.
The only weak spot I found with Thimbleweed Park is that it's too easy. I played on hard mode (of course), and never really got stuck with any puzzle for too long. I guess that isn't necessarily a bad thing, but I often found myself thinking that certain puzzles were just too straightforward and could have included one or two more steps to solve them.
But apart from the low difficulty level (which didn't bother me too much) it was a hell of a ride to nostalgia..weed.. Park. ... No, wait, that sounds stupid, let me try that ag

Likeable main characters! Really important. Especially after #GG (what is that? I have no idea). An what is really an achievement? Likeable DIVERSE main characters! Without feeling artificial or forced. I COULD'NT BELIEVE IT A FIRST! They did it! Generally: Likeable characters with most of the time understandable, interesting, reasonable backgrounds and motives. Without being just stereotypes or trends. Or even if it happens and something seems a little bit stereotype'ish or trend'ish, even then it's likeable. Example: At the beginning of the Delores stroy. When Delores looks at her poster of Ada, and says that Ada is her role model, I was a bit like 'Uh, oh, here comes the SJW train... *chooo*" [Even if there is nothing wrong or untrue or unbelievable about the facts, I dunno why, but I had this thought. It's about something in the past I guess.] Oh, how wrong I was! Delores turned out to be probably the character I liked most in the end. While I liked all of them. I love Mexicans!
Great writing! [see above] Writing is funny, honest, sometimes self ironic, sometimes meta. I'm not too good in writing about writing. So, in general: writing is top notch!
80s!! 80s music! (ok, one short radio song..., but still!) 80s games! Chapter names always with "THE..." at the beginng like in 'Stranger Things'. Eventually even an upside-down world thingy! (like in 'Stranger Things'!) Story takes places in the 1980s! Like in 'Stranger Things'! I love it!
TRUE SCUMM'esque interface! With Retro options even! You can look at all the things! You can try to combine all the things! Sometimes it gives a funny hidden joke. However one tiny minor criticism: It behaves and feels and plays like with the classics and they really delivered it! But it is not as 100% consistent as with the LucasArts adventures. I at first was disappointed that I couldn't look at other person. In the olden times the main character then would tell me what he or she thinks or feels or discovers about another character. Like "Look at Willie"; "This man looks like he had seen better times." Example. This is sadly *not* implemented. (NO, I DIDN'T READ THE RPS ARTICLE BEFORE!) Secondly I was a bit disappointed that my main characters could not talk to each other. It is a bit strange at the beginning or first half of the game when one main character is missing for short/some time and comes back and the other main character doesn't react in any way. However this is just nit-picking and some healthy scepticism I developed about recent Kickstarter adventures games. *cough* 2+ million $ *cough*. Ha! With more time into the game and finally having finished it on normal/hard mode, they really did a great job here. It definitely is a classic graphic adventure game! It definitely feels and play like a SCUMM game! Yes!
99% Great German translation by Boris "Doc Bobo" Schneider-Johne! I played my first playthrough with all Retro options, no voice, and German texts. Just like the first time I played Monkey Island when I was 8-10 yrs old or so.  It felt like the good old days! Some minor tiny mistakes I found like sometimes "das", where it has to be "dass", or missing comma etc. But I'm no grammar nazi. No, I'm really not. (NO!) Translation is great, witty and funny. However very small mistakes or 1-2 missing letters at end of words however stretch through the entire game. Really tiny and only if you look closely. When you think about that Boris did the whole translation for just 1 (one) USD, this translation is his best and gets a 11/10 from me!
If you use no hints you can get 15-20 hours out of this game! I needed 22 hours. But I wanted to see everything, every line. Still haven't.

Clever good puzzles, with great difficulty.

Gameplay:
Pretty great. If you have an RPG itch, this game will scratch it. No non-optional random encounters--you fight monsters right on the screen. Otherwise, it is very reminiscent of a typical JRPG, with levels, monsters, equipments and four skills/special attacks. It was a bit annoying having to go through dungeons twice to get the stuff there was no way to get to because you didn't have the requisite skill unlocked though. And the first skill is a bit broken--it can be used through pretty much the entire game to kill everything. The last skill hits for more and is AoE but it has a cooldown so once again you fall back on the first skill. Getting all the best equipment from one dungeon also makes the next one trivial.
But all in all, this does a good job of scratching the RPG itch and even if it is a bit unbalanced, it was still fun. 8/10.
Music:
A bit repetitive because of the limited selection but it definitely outshines the graphics. Surprisingly well done score for a free game, I'll probably be downloading at least one track. 9/10
Translation:
Understandable but horrible. Translator doesn't know what tenses are or what the difference between singular and plural are. A bunch of places have "is" substituted for "are." Better than google translate would probably do but still a ways to go. 3/10
Graphics:
Pretty much exactly as one would expect from an F2P generic JRPG. Some sprites are pretty well drawn but I wish they were a bit less blocky. Also the fullscreen mode has some kind of bug where the floor shimmers in a weird way. 8/10
Story:
Pretty uninspired and generic. Not much here, this game is more about gameplay and music than the story. It does get pretty emotional but never gets suspensful. 7/10
Overall:
Overall, I'd recommend this game. Took me 9.5 hours to beat it completely but those hours were fun for the most part (except as noted above). I'd definitely play a sequel to this game if there will ever be one.

King's Quest is based on a series of adventure games by the same name. As an adventure game, the primary mechanics involve you (the player) moving a character through a series of levels collecting items to use in solving puzzles. It also does involve some quick-time events. In general mistakes are not overly harsh and gameplay is casual. If you're looking for action then this isn't the game for you.
If you've played the originals, then you likely will go into the game expecting a particular style of play; and, will likely be dissapointed. This may be considered a bad thing; however, I do appreciate the attempt to take an older series and revive it for a new, younger generation of gamers. If developers aren't free to make these attempts then we risk losing much of the classic games that came from the 80s and 90s and the stories they told. With any such attempt, there is risk involved; and, for die hard fans who grew up on the originals, there is much to complain about. However, for the sake of seeing these tales live on in newer audiences, and to encourage them to even play the originals, I would ask anyone picking up this game to view it for what it is, and to not let your expectations ruin what is an excellent game.
With all that said here is a general break down of some of the more important elements of any game:
Narrative - Not to spoil anything I'll simply say the story telling is what really makes this game for me. I've played through it multiple times simply to listen to the tale it tells. With fantastic choices in voice actors, many from well know movie classics, they really do a marvelous job of immersing the player in the story. The tale itself is delightfully charming, with puns galore (as the series is known for), along with many heartfelt moments, and a touching conclusion.
Gameplay - Simple, even for an adventure game. There are a number of excellent puzzles though that I very much enjoyed figuring out. As for quick-time events you either love-em or hate-em, but they at least help add some suspense at key story momments. My only real criticism here would be that I personally would enjoy even more puzzles, especially since some of the chapters can be a bit light on them. Speaking of chapters, the game is episodic. You can play the first chapter for free which is arguably the best chapter, so if you're even mildly interested I would highly recommend you give it a try. The chapters vary in length and some are more engaging than others. The game starts with allowing the player to chose between multiple "paths" which will affect certain story outcomes. However, as the game goes on there are fewer alternative options with the final chapter being very linear. Some may criticize this; however, if you follow the narrative it is a clear design choice and I believe it works well. The game very obviously pokes fun at many gaming tropes including its own linearity. The only truly bad chapter for me was the Epilogue as I felt the fifth chapter summed up the tale well and left the future to your imagination. Whereas, the epilogue was a bit of a let down being very short with little in the way of interesting narrative or puzzle solving. So if you buy it, get the season pass and skip the full collection to avoid the epilogue, or at least don't play it.
Soundtrack - A good soundtack helps any game greatly, and King's Quest does not disapoint. Reviving old 8-bit themes from the original series with full orchestral backing pulls you into the thrill of the adventure. If only they offered a download of the soudtrack as a DLC... There are some tracks I could listen to for hours.
Performance - Of course, it's not good to get a game if it won't run on your machine, and sad to say this is probably the most lacking area of King's Quest. When I first got the game I played it on what I would call a low-tier laptop, but it did have a decent i5 CPU and a dedicate GPU. It would play most games fine but this one had horrendous FPS and was unplayable. So, I switched to a better laptop that I would call an affordable mid-tier, still with i5 but a better GPU and more memory. It was then playable, but only on the lowest video settings and would still experience lag at certain points. Since then I have upgraded to a mid-tier gaming desktop with i7 CPU, a GTX 1060 GPU, and 16GB of memory and it runs fantastic on max settings. So, if you're going to play on something with lower specs than that I would advise some caution. Aside from general performance I've experienced no major bugs, or glitches and certainly no crashes or anything game breaking.
Conclusion:
King's Quest is a fantastic revival of a classic series, and there are far too few adventure games on the market these days (at least not many good ones). This one is a definite keeper and worth trying, if not buying for the listed price. If that's too much it has solid discounts during Steam sales. The game can be completed in around 20 hours or less (depending on your play style). As mentioned above, feel free to skip the epilogue chapter, but get the rest to complete the main story line even if some of the chapters aren't as good as others. If you've played the original series, my only advice is to at least give it a try, and take it for what it is without any preconcieved notions...you might be surprised. At the very least it has brought the name of King's Quest to the current generation. In many ways I like to think of the narrative as the fond retelling of the originals as though you were telling them to your own grandchild, details may have been left out and key plot points confused; but, I feel the essence of the classics is still there. Overall, I would highly recommend this game to anyone.

I am torn on whether to recommend
.  It was a famously good game at the time of its release in 1999.  It laid much of the foundation for the BioShock games.  Its malevolent AI, SHODAN, is a clear inspiration for GLaDOS.  It blends RPG and FPS elements in a way that was unequalled at the time, and would remain so until the release of
a year later.
All that being said, however
does not carry its age well.  Much of what it did so well at the time has since been eclipsed by more recent titles, which makes its flaws more evident.  The most notable way in which time has betrayed
lies in the graphics.  The game's abandoned-spaceship setting was eerie and atmospheric at the time, but now seems only boxy and retro, as it prompts instant comparisons to the similarly-set
series, against which the older graphics can't measure up.  Since it no longer meets, or even approaches the current standard for "realism" in a video-game environment, it loses the immersiveness necessary to make the horror aspects of the game compelling.  Similarly, what was a slick and functional UI system in 1999 feels rather clunky and clumsy in 2015.  Other issues, which were noted, but seemed less significant at the time, become more prominent now that the brilliance of the game has been dulled by our elevated expectations.
For the video-game afficionado, I'd recommend buying this game purely for the historical significance of it.  Unfortunately, the tarnish of age means that, if you haven't experienced it before, it's now not truly possible to experience playing
the way it felt to play it at the time.  But you can still appreciate it as an artifact.

Many RPG Maker games fall squarely into the territory of Sturgeon's Law, this is one of the few that somehow doesn't fall in it. I say this game
doesn't fall into Sturgeon's Law territory if only because while I was charmed by the story, humor, and gameplay, the game has quite a few spelling and grammar errors. I'm honestly not sure if the poor spelling/grammar is a case of laziness, or English not being the developers' primary language.
It's definitely one of the weirder games I've played on Steam, and I'm not just talking about the art style. The humor of the game reminds me of Earthbound, with nods and winks not just limited to its subject matter seen in the title of the game, but also Internet, popular culture, and political humor as well.
Gameplay is traditional turn-based combat, reminscent of older Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest titles. One of the characters you can recruit has a traditional HP/MP (or Fuel, in this case) bar, the other characters have a TP bar that only charges during combat. Most battles will end before you can ever gain enough TP to utilize TP-based skills, which may give the impression of the game being too easy.
The game isn't very long to begin with (I finished at 4 hours on my first time), so if you're looking for a good, short-ish RPG to play and don't mind the occasional spelling/grammar errors, there are worse ways to spend a dollar.

If you grew up in the '70s, '80s or '90s, Broforce is your game.  If you love old action movies and stars, Broforce is your game. If you love old side scrolling games with lots of guns and explosions, Broforce is your game.  If you don't mind a challenge and like a game that doesn't take itself too seriously, Broforce is your game.
Basically, Broforce is an homage to old action movies and action stars.  Going back to the '60s (James Bond) and all the way to the early 2000s, (Kill Bill, Planet Terror.)  Mostly, it's got a lot of “old” gold action stars like Arnold Schwarzenegger, Silvester Stallone, Wesley Snipes, Mr. T, Chuck Norris, etc. in parodies of their various roles.  The plot is a lot like a lot of those old action films:  bad guys are doing bad things and have taken good guys hostage and are threatening the world.  Your bros are sent in to kill the bad guys, save the good guys, save the world.  Basic action film stuff.
The graphics are done in wonderful '80s style pixel art.  The level design is pretty clever and varies.  Also, the game has random elements.  Placement of enemy types, explosive barrels, ammo drops and other things can vary from one play through to another in a single level.  Those aren't the only random things.  Which bros you are using are also chosen randomly, cycling through the ones you've unlocked as you die or as you save your allies.  These random elements add a huge replay value to the game as you may have different enemies and bros to contend with in the same level.
The play is very cool, side scrolling with lots of action, shooting and explosions.  The game is ultra violent.  Enemies (and bros) can be shot, stabbed, cut in half, shredded, exploded, decapitated, and crushed.  Blood, (pixels, of course) body parts, bones, etc. can scatter everywhere.  Though, the game isn't always fair.  In fact, it can be quite unfair at times.  The difficulty doesn't ramp up very quickly, but it does ramp up as you play.  When you get into the double digit Campaign levels, those boss fights can be quite tough.  Also, the game can sometimes give you “cheap” deaths.  But, it's all in good fun.  If you take it too seriously, you probably won't enjoy the game.  My hat's off to anybody who can get the “There Can Bro Only One” achievement.  ;)
So, that's about all I can say about this wonderful gem of a game.  I find it extremely enjoyable, if unfair and downright frustrating at times.  But, I like a challenge.

After playing "The Evil Within" 3 years back I always expected a sequel to be in the works considering that the first game ended abruptly with some open questions in mind. Come 2017, and "The Evil Within 2" came which was much better than the first and improved upon each and everything in terms of gameplay and story and also providing new players a fresh and exciting experience.
The protagonist of this game, Detective Sebastian Castellanos sets out to find his lost daughter, Lily who apparently was killed in a fire accident in their house. As he delves deeper into the story, he finds a big conspiracy involved and it ties up with some of the original's game story in a great way. I have to say that the story of the first game was a little confusing and all over the place but in this game they actually explain the plot very well through notes and cutscenes and makes us care for the characters and their situations.
While the first game was famous for its spooky victorian horror settings like an abandoned village, a haunted asylum, cemeteries and creepy mausoleums and dungeons, the second game goes for a more modern look with towns and buildings while occassionally showing us some medieval surroundings. Its a great contrast with the original and makes it stand out as a different game environmentally. Also, the game is less scary and disturbing than the original and goes for more of the psychological aspects. The villains were shown in great detail and the game explains their motifs for their behaviour very well. One of the best things which I loved about this game was the character of Sebastian, the protagonist and how he as become much more developed and third dimensional than in the first game. He is one of my favourite video game characters as I was able to connect to him much more and i would love to see him again.
The enemies in this game are for the most part like the first part but with more variety in terms of movement and sensing ability. Also, there are some intense boss fights and the difficulty is much ramped up. This time the game is more open world in nature and you can do side missions which give you special items and also search for supplies and upgrades for your arsenal while choosing to engage the enemies strategically . Its a great improvement from the first game which was linear in nature and you will often be underpowered against many enemies in the game especially if you are playing on one of the higher difficulties like "Survival" or "Nightmare" which is the recommended settings for this game. The rewards for completing side missions, killing enemies and exploring items and finding new weapons are great in this game giving players the incentive to search everywhere making the game more lengthy. As for upgrades you can upgrade weapons and craft ammunition for them by finding weapon parts and your abilities via green gel like in the first game. Also, a side note that not all levels in this game are open world in nature and the later levels go back to the linear formula but its still enjoyable nonetheless.
The game definitely gives the vibes of survival horror as ammo is always scarce and your weapons don't do much damage till they are upgraded to their maximum level with some combat skills. You can choose to play the game through stealh or combat or a mixture of both adding to variety in gameplay. Its more enjoyable and fun to play than the first game.
Performance wise I experienced 2 crashes on my Nvidia card and the game had some micro stuttering exclusive to Nvidia cards only which I was able to solve by tweaking settings in the Nvidia inspector by help on the steam forums. Apart from that the game is extremely well optimized and ran at solid 60 FPS.
I would recommend this game for all of you who loved the first game and are looking for a more intense survival horror experience. This a must buy for Halloween and in the heart of all the horror, bloodshed and scares lies an emotional and touching story which will move you in a good way.

Eternal Senia is a single-player, ARPG that is free to play; developed and published by Holy Priest, available on PC through Steam. Holy Priest states that the inspiration for the game came from Ragnarok Online and also the belief that gaming should be an enjoyable and relaxing experience. Now, I personally have never played Ragnarok Online but I loved the art style and feel of the game. I will say right off the bat that the effort put into the game was definitely felt and greatly appreciated.
You play as the heroine, Senia, who was saved and adopted by Magaleta, a priestess, at a young age after her village was attacked by demons. Senia wishes to one day be able to fight alongside and eventually be able to protect Magaleta, but of course Magaleta opposes against this for safety concerns. One day, Magaleta says her goodbye before heading out only to not return for several nights. Senia eventually learns that Magaleta had gone to the Tower of Eternity, which is rumored to be able to grant a person’s wish – should they prove worthy. Despite Magaleta’s warnings, Senia had been practicing swordsmanship in secrecy and heads to the Tower of Eternity to bring her sister back.
The game’s controls are very simplistic, using arrows to both move and attack by walking into enemies to initiate an auto-attack and later on gaining skills which can be activated via hotkeys Q,W,E, or R. There is a type of currency that is obtained through monster kills that is used to level up your skills, which are separate from character levels so you have a level of customization to your play-style. Additionally, some attacks are even used cleverly to assist in solving puzzles or uncovering secrets (hint hint) and it is rather satisfying in later levels. I did try to play with a controller but found it to be much more responsive on keyboard.
The gameplay is very smooth, screen-by-screen progression. Simple controls allows the player to strategize on the fly and go at the pace they want. There is optional mini-bosses and bonus objectives which yields some great rewards that really helps speed up the progression. If you want a challenge (or just plain lazy), you can skip these bonuses for some harder fights. There are also appropriately named “bonus rooms” where it’s basically a grinding area for leveling and collecting crafting materials. I ended up doing all these until I crafted the best set of equipment possible for each area because why not?
Additionally, you are also given the choice before each boss fight to select the difficulty. Now, one complaint I have is that once you beat a level, you cannot go back. There were several places I wish to revisit but am unable to do so since I never created multiple save files and don’t really have the time to play through it again…so the lesson here is to make multiple saves if you really enjoy a particular area unless you don’t mind replaying from the start.
The music is absolutely fantastically charming. It immediately got my attention at the title screen and only continued to impress me throughout. Soundtracks are one of the biggest things I look for in games because I find it really helps with immersion.
Now, sense of progression and character development is also pretty important. Overall, the game definitely does a great job at progression, giving you an option of difficulty in various ways (grinding “bonus rooms” and choosing boss difficulty) and the pace of the story assists with the character development as well. You are definitely overpowered in the tutorial (for obvious reasons) but then start from square one once you arrive at the first stage. I’m not ashamed to say that I actually died my first time through in this room, only to come back later and slaughter everything in one hit while I searched for hidden treasures (I still have no idea how to get that treasure chest that’s separated by water).
Admittedly, it felt really drawn out towards the end. There is a stage where the perspective and art-style changes which was quite a nice surprise, until I found out you were supposed to collect all these different orbs and just figure out which one goes on which pedestal to continue. This repeats quite a few times where I think honestly just twice would have been enough. Artistically, this section was great; mechanically, too drawn out and unnecessary. I did not get any sense of accomplishment by figuring out the “puzzle” not only once, but (I think) four times. Too much filler without any pay out. Then immediately after that you proceed through long corridors filled with enemies that just eventually turns into a slaughterhouse if you completed all the crafting.
The story is cliche, but was told in such a way that kept me engaged and gave me serious feels at the end. Gameplay and controls were very simple, making it very smooth and natural to progress through the game (completed in about 5 hours) and visually pleasing with great music! The boss fights were very satisfying, each one bringing something new to the table. The mini-bosses gave great rewards that didn’t make you overpowered for the next area and the optional bonus bosses actually made me feel good about figuring out their mechanics after a few deaths and then being able to consistently farm them for the next few minutes. If you have some spare time for a quick game, you can easily clear this in 4-5 hours and enjoy the feels at the end.

While at first glance this game just looks like a quirky game with a unique artstyle created in RPG Maker, its underlying message about corprate corruption and money in general is quite powerful. You go through the game as The Guy, (or whatever you named him I guess), on a quest to take out the C.E.O.s  of each district, fighting hobos, loan sharks, and some very out there creatures along the way. There are a ton of little side things that you can also do that really bring out this games personality, and give some replay value if you missed out along the way. The gameplay isn't too much to talk about, (again, this is an rpg maker game), and unfortunatly, there is almost no difficulty. However, it's made very clear that this game is more about the expirience itself rather than mechanics, similar to OFF, another RPG maker game, which is clearly an inspiration here. I would give this game a 7/10. I enjoyed this games humor and story from begining to end, however I do have a few complaints. First of all, as previously mentioned, this game is a cakewalk. Even if you ignore the final party member and just take Gerome, you will still most likely be fine. And while these are mostly just nitpicks, I found that the sprites really ruin the astetic of the rest of the game, and i think they should have been made in the same sketchy style everything else was done in. Lastly, and probably least importantly, overworld objects have weird detection and you can usually clip through them when walking. Other then that, i still think this is a great game. And at one dollar are you really risking anything? I would recomend Suits: A Business RPG to anyone who enjoys story driven RPGs, or just weirder ones in general.

I'm wasn't really a big RPG player a year ago, but ever since I played Suits, my view on RPGs have changed quite drastically! The game revolves around a business guy, just like everyone else, in a world taken over by the government. In my opinion, the standing point of this game is the references. Whether it's resolving actual world politics to fighting popular YouTubers, Suits loves to throw out things kids and adults can recognize.
Gameplay-wise, it's from an angled bird's eye view, so you can move in all directions, and combat is just like any other RPG. However, the most interesting part of the gameplay is interacting with the characters. Just explore the environment, really. You're bound to find weird, creepy, offensive, and laughable characters to either fight to do tasks for. Discovering all the crazy types of people that populate Suits, is it's best trait overall.
I really enjoyed this game. The combat is simple and easy to learn, but fighting Egoraptor in a skyscraper or delivering abortion pills from the left building to the right building are only two of the many experiences Suits had to offer.

Suits: A Business RPG is a bad game with an interesting personality. The game itself is bland. What makes Suits a fun game is the nonsensical humor within. I bought this game for ¥98 thinking it's just another poorly-made RPG that you see getting riffed on YouTube. My expectations were pleasantly surpassed.
The graphics are deliberately♥♥♥♥♥ All the characters and objects look like a 5th grader's doodles on a notebook. It's obvious that no effort was made, literally, when everything is a scribble. The music is like outsider music, but not as bad as Crazy Bus or Dontrel Dolphin.
All of it works well with the game.  The boring and uninspired art makes you feel like you're at some desk job with no clear description of what you do. It works with the drab and boring plot. It feel...businesslike.
It's an RPG Maker game. You fight, chat, and move. Combat is very simple and repetitive. I really don't have to use many special attacks to defeat the enemies, even for bosses. It feels more like doing work than playing a game.
The plot is simple. You are a new hire. Suddenly, the CEO gets threatened by you and tries to kill you. Because of so many side quests, I often forget what I'm supposed to do. But the gameplay is so simple, and the area is laid out is such a linear path that I can still progress.
I have to say, I don't see many games where everything is intentionally bad. You can tell the developer didn't even try to make a game. Why would they, when everything is already made for you via RPG Maker? Instead, most of the work was spent on side quests, containing bizarre and non sequitur jokes. I would call this an unique outsider game.
Despite all the sloppiness and half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥job this game is, it's still amusing. The humor is good and I'm always given something unexpected. It's lowbrow and juvenile humor, but it's delivered at the right time in a bland and boring game. It's ¥98 worth of fun, and it delivers on that.
Suits is a weird game at the least. Is awful and stupid, but in no way is it boring. The humor is great. It's a bag of odd jokes that's tied up by a flimsy game. Is it worth the dollar? Absolutely! You have to try it to get a feel of just how the humor works so well. Good doing business with you.
