I got this game in early access, loved it, and completed it each time the developers did an update. I like to play it slowly and thoughtfully, which makes the inevitably-emerging chaos more fun. This game reminds me of the best bits of Bio Menace the way I play it, then polished up to be even more fun - that's praise from me.
I enjoyed the new Aliens levels, vaguely reminiscent of Turrican 2 on my Amiga. I enjoyed the Hell levels less. The aesthetics were great, but deaths are so common and chaotic that it disrupts my slow and careful playstyle, and makes me adopt a more pannicky one which I don't enjoy so much. It often meant I only got through the level when the characters cycled back to one with the skills to get me through easily, which became grind more than fun.
The cycling of characters brings me to my one real irritation with the game: every time you rescue someone you become that character. Often I am having fun with one of the Bros, but rescue someone because I can't bear to leave a Bro behind (plus it is an extra life, and you'll need them in later stages), but then I'm forced to take on the new Bro immediately. Which doesn't really make sense: where does the first Bro go? They don't reappear when the rescued character dies. And often the rescued one is one that I don't enjoy playing so much.
Again and again I wished that I had one of these as an option in the settings:
- An option where you could rescue people but still stick with same character until you died (and only then switch to the rescued bro).
- An option to have the same character for the whole level - rescues just become extra lives, but each one is the same character.
Either of those would add a lot of fun for me. Maybe an option to choose the character, so you could use it as a way of practising, especially with characters you aren't very familiar with, or so you can create your own film (e.g. John McClane in a city level with high towers - Yippee Ki Yay MF). Note that I'm talking about options, not forcing anyone to play this way. But it would fit my playstyle well, and see me playing the game even more.
My final comment would be that in any game where you unlock features by playing, PLEASE include an option to unlock everything at once in the menu. It's an option, no-one's forced to use it, just like with cheat codes. The reason is that I usually play a game, complete it, then uninstall it. After completing it once I don't feel like playing it all the way through again immediately with a new weapon/character/costume. It might be a couple of years before I feel like playing it again. Of course, I install it and don't have access to the new options - I've got to play through again exactly as I did before. If not a menu option then at least give a code to unlock all features, or let us know what file to back up, so that if I reinstall a few years later I can unlock the new feature and have a playthrough with them. Having to repeat things rapidly becomes a chore.
So: Broforce is a very good game. If it had options to let the player have more control over how they played it, I'd then say it was a perfect mix of satire, personalisation, chaos and variety.

Alien: Isolation is set on the space station Sevastopol 15 years after the events of the film Alien. You play as Amanda Ripley, daughter of Ellen Ripley, the protagonist of the aforementioned film. A search party is sent out to the Sevastopol with Amanda on board after word gets out that the flight recorder from the Nostromo (her mother’s ship) has been located aboard. On their approach to the space station, Amanda is separated from her crew and you must investigate the Sevastopol on your lonesome in an effort to both finish your mission and find your team.
The Sevastopol Station is rich with atmosphere and based heavily on the design of the first Alien movie. The crippled station will lurch and rumble, suffering through collisions and system malfunctions. Aesthetics from the movie are preserved with a retro sci-fi design and padded walls. You may walk down a corridor, enveloped by flashing lights and klaxon alarms, only to react at the faintest sound or shadow. Or you may admire the reflections on the floor before receiving a telltale blip from your motion tracker. The atmosphere is perfect for the Alien threat and the retro design is a refreshing change from the sterile modern approach to sci-fi. The chunky keyboards, phone receivers, distorted CRT monitors, and blinking coloured lights should look dated, but it has quite the opposite effect. This is a tactile, practical, and convincing science-fiction world, with machines and environments that are functional and utilitarian, rather than overtly futuristic. You almost feel like you can reach out and touch it. As a result, in terms of consistency, vision, and thoughtful design, it’s the most visually striking game world since Deus Ex: Human Revolution.
But a sci-fi corridor, no matter how pretty it is, isn’t much without something horrifying to chase you down it. So it’s a good thing that Isolation is the first game—and it’s amazing it’s taken this long—to make H.R. Giger’s alien every bit as formidable and intimidating as it is in the films. In Alien, Ripley asks Ash how they can kill the creature that burst from Kane’s chest aboard the Nostromo, and he replies, gravely, “You can’t.” This, unlike the dumb drones you blasted your way through in Colonial Marines, is also true of Sevastopol’s alien. It’s a merciless, unstoppable force. “A perfect organism.” You can shoot it, but it’ll just get angry and pounce at you. You can burn it, but that’ll only scare it away for a few seconds. Isolation’s magic lies in the fact that you have to outsmart its single alien rather than kill it. This turns what could have easily been yet another FPS with xenomorphs into a thrilling, drawn-out game of cat-and-mouse with the scariest cat imaginable. It’s a deft blend of stealth and survival horror that, thanks to dynamic AI and clever, systemic design, is much more than the sum of its parts.
You'll know when the alien is near. As you creep through the station, you hear it above and below you, behind the walls, under the floor. You're relatively safe when it's hidden away like this, but you never know what vent, crack, or hole in the ceiling it'll suddenly emerge from. It arrives with a beastly hiss—a sound that becomes your cue to hide or run. Then you hear the pounding of its footsteps as it wanders the corridors, hunting for its prey. It's a massive, heavy thing that towers over Ripley, and if it sees her it lunges with a shriek, killing her instantly in a grisly, cinematic death sequence.
The alien is an almost constant threat, but there are other dangers on Sevastopol. Malfunctioning androids called Working Joes wander the station, brutally killing any humans they come across. Their rubbery, emotionless faces and glowing eyes are genuinely unnerving, and sneaking through groups of them is as nerve-racking as facing the alien. Get too close and they'll grab you, draining your health until you manage to break free. You can kill them, but they take a lot of resources to bring down, making stealth the best option. They're a lot slower than the alien, but every bit as deadly. Then there are other survivors. You'll run into them less often than the alien and the synthetics, and they're a lot easier to kill, but they usually work in groups. They won't shoot on sight, and will give you a few seconds to back away if you wander into their territory, but it doesn't take much to send them into a frenzy of gunfire. Luckily, if they shoot at you, the noise will attract the alien and it'll kill them all. This is often the best way to get past human enemies: provoke them, then wait for the bloodbath.
Whichever enemy you're up against, sneaking is always the key to survival. You'll pick up a shotgun, a revolver, and a few other weapons as you progress through the station, but they're more of a curse than a blessing. For one, they're only really effective against humans. It takes a dozen headshots with the revolver to drop a Working Joe, and the alien is essentially bulletproof. But the biggest problem is that, the instant you fire any weapon, the alien will come rushing to your location and slaughter you. The motion tracker, a series staple, will give you a rough idea of where enemies are, but they'll be drawn to its bleeps if you're too close.
The good news is that Sevastopol isn't short of places to hide. There are lockers and cabinets to cower in, vents to escape through, and desks to crouch under. You'll spend much of the game creeping silently and methodically between objectives. This might sound dull on paper, but the presence of the alien makes almost every moment exhilaratingly tense. Encounters with the alien are not scripted. Its behaviour is unpredictable, and the impressive, reactive AI creates the illusion that it's an intelligent creature. You really feel like you're being hunted as it moves from room to room, tracking your movements, sniffing you out. But as smart as it is, there are ways to exploit and confuse it. You can easily throw a noisemaker at a group of humans, and the alien will come out of hiding and slaughter them all, clearing your path for you once it leaves. Ripley had a strangely intimate relationship with the aliens she faces in the films, and I felt the same thing happening to me in Isolation.
But now for the weak link. The story is disappointing, retelling a familiar yarn we've already heard countless times in the Alien universe: sinister corporations, murderous androids, rogue AI, and others I can't talk about because of spoilers. The good thing about this is that it lets you relive classic Alien moments and experience them from a more visceral perspective. The bad is that it feels derivative, never taking the opportunity to make its own mark on the mythology. Really, though, the story is just a means of getting you from place to place, and in that sense it doesn't matter that it's lightweight. It's ultimately the journey and the moment-to-moment experiences that define the game, not the overall narrative.
It's ridiculous that it took the developers of a historical RTS to finally create an authentic Alien game, but The Creative Assembly have managed it. They've succeeded where countless others have failed by treating Giger's monster with the reverence it deserves: as something to be feared and respected, not faced head-on with a pulse rifle. Isolation is a taut, confident, and electrifying horror game that perfectly captures the essence of Ridley Scott's legendary film.

Alien: Isolation follows Amanda Ripley (daughter of Ellen Ripley from the movies) as she goes with a Weyland-Yutani team to recover the flight recorder of the Nostromo. The game's atmosphere and attention to detail is pretty darn good. You'll feel like you're back in the original Alien movie from 1979.
Ok, so about the game!
Fun game, but very, very stressful. This is a stealth game with some gunplay action. You are greatly rewarded for stealth as there are some whole sections you can avoid the Alien if you can keep yourself and your enemies quiet. The moment gunfire erupts.. the Alien comes to play! :)
You have 3 main enemies, the Alien, where almost all attacks are 1 shot kills (sometimes you can fight it off with the flamethrower and take 50% max life damage), humans who spot you easily and are in turn easy to kill, and then the androids whom of which can be devilish hard to kill because they're so tough, especially the ones in weather suits, but otherwise are slow to chase and spot you.
Once you learn the basic behaviors of these 3 enemies, it's pretty easy to move quickly through the game using distractions and your motion tracker to avoid most combat. The game does a good job of changing up the formula by giving you missions only against androids/humans/alien, etc. There's even a breath of fresh air near the middle of the game (no spoilers!).
Unfortunately I have my own criticisms of the game. While I'm not a big fan of jump scares, there were some spots where the Alien placement was pure bogus, the kind where even while playing correctly (stealth and what not), the Alien just pops down from a vent in front of you and gets you- not a big deal after the flamethrower, but before then, you're ET chow. Many of the distraction items are kinda underwhelming, like the smoke grenade, flashbang, and molotov - even the noisemaker wasn't effective in a lot of cases. And lastly, you'll get weird weapon bugs and see models floating in the air, on occasion not a biggie.
Bottom line: After playing through this ~18 hour journey, focusing solely on the campaign, and ignoring most collectables, I would have to say this was a good game. If you are an Alien fan and you want an actual quality experience (NOT Colonial Marines) then this is a must buy- I caught it on a 50% off sale @ $24.99.
Just be warned, it's an Aliens game with an Aliens ending. ........And after playing through Amanda's struggle... this sadened me, greatly.... but it's about the journey, not the destination, I suppose.

With over 100 hours now registered on Hurtworld, I feel I've experienced enough to be able to give a fully fledged review.
Hurtworld is an early-access survival game that, as stated in the description is extremely punishing in vanilla. Many servers usually increase the amount of items you get from killing animals, mining, etc. to decrease the level of punishment, which allows players (including myself) who don't enjoy grinding to get into (in my opinion) the 'fun stuff'.
While some of the community is saltier than the Dead Sea
Polskis
the other half are great people, allowing you to enjoy a mixture of teamwork and heavy combat between those two kids who always kill on sight (with winning against the w*nkers being extremely satisfying). I have also enjoyed many a tense moment too where , and I'm being hunted through a ruined town and needed to escape without being spotted - seriously fun.
Hurtworld is best enjoyed while playing with friends, though, and in my opinion this makes up around 50% of the experience: building an awesome base together, driving out into the red desert or the snowy regions & fighting off players trying to take the stuff you have mined and taken from the radtowns, and much more.
As I said earlier, about half of the Hurtworld community is very salty. Unfortunately this ruins the experience for some, especially those who can't defend themselves on their own against end-game players who just camp you and KoS. I have to admit that I stopped playing Hurtworld for a long while until two mates persuaded me to jump back into the game with them.
The vulnerability of the lone player is no doubt enjoyed by some more hardcore players, however for a more casual player like me it was literally a game breaker. Keep this in mind if you don't know too many people on Steam.
Keep in mind that this is also an early-access game. Not all of the features of the end-game have been done yet, and though they look awesome the lack of them does limit the gameplay to some extent. Seeing as combat is a major part of Hurtworld, the limited variety of weapons, especially guns, is painful. Until ItemV2 comes out (bringing with it the ability to add attachments and customise weapons) this is even more limited. While this of course won't be the case forever, it is at least at the time of writing this review.
Hurtworld is, at the end of the day, a fantastic game. It is great fun for hardcore players, and is great for casual ones as well if you have a few mates who get the game as well.
It has phenomenal potential, and by the time it comes out of early-access it well be very well fleshed-out. I'm always on the edge of my seat waiting to see what the devs will come out with next.
However, if you play casually and don't have many friends on steam who'd be interested in playing this, then I wouldn't recommend it to you. If you're the sort of person who despises games that aren't fully fleshed out as well, then I'd recommend you wait to pull the trigger until Hurtworld comes out of early-access.
If either of those two things don't apply to you though, I highly recommend you buy Hurtworld. While I can't say it doesn't have its flaws, there can never be a perfect game.

Solid follow-up to The Evil Within. The new hub-based level design is interesting and gives the game an almost Silent Hill-ish feel. Stealth has a much a greater presence than in the first game (and is in some cases pretty overpowered) but resource management is still a core mechanic. Rewarding kills by giving you gel (i.e. XP) might seem to undermine the whole "survival horror" aspect (since enemies can represent something to farm rather than fear) but it offers a compelling choice: do I risk losing ammo/health in order to gain XP/crafting parts? On Nightmare difficulty, this is often a question you have to ask yourself (at least in the early game). Figuring out the most efficient ways to dispatch enemies is interesting and encourages you to learn the nuances of the gameplay systems. Core gameplay is largely the same as in the previous game, though the match mechanic was sadly removed. Enemies are generally much more mobile than before, though you can still outrun most and leave their aggro radius with relative ease. As a whole, TEW2 feels far more consistent than the first game, which offered a significantly different experience between the first and second halves.
If you didn't enjoy the first game, it's hard to say whether you'd like this one. There are certainly improvements in some areas. Controls are generally more responsive, with shorter startups and recoveries for all of your actions. The hub-based levels encourage more exploration. The stealth mechanics are more fleshed out. The story is conveyed in a more intuitive manner. There are no more cheap instant kill surprises either. However, there's still some jank. The game likes to hijack the camera whenever you get grappled or perform a takedown, which can result in crazy camera swings when the camera eventually tries to look where you're looking. Also, although you can break out of certain actions by moving or attacking, you can't break out by interacting. This means you'll break open a crate with a melee attack, but won't be able to immediately grab the stuff inside unless you move first. It's not a big issue but definitely feels like sloppy oversight. Also, hit reactions aren't entirely consistent. When you shoot someone in the leg, they might stumble or fall or they might just ignore the hit entirely and keep running at you. This can be frustrating in the early game when you don't have the damage output to compensate for the RNG. Finally, the characters and enemy designs aren't quite as memorable as in the first game. Most of the enemies are basically the rage zombies from 28 Days Later. The unique enemies are much more interesting but aren't very common.
As someone who enjoyed the first half of TEW, I enjoyed all of TEW2. It's not perfect, by any means, but it succeeds in creating an open-ended survival horror experience.

I'd like to recommend the game, but it has a LOT of usability issues that make playing the game a chore, and in it's current state it is diffucult for me to recommend it. Maybe if the devs spend enough time fixing these issues it's playable and I can change this review.
The devs really have spent too much time reminiscing about what was so good about the good old days, and too little learning about how modern point & clicks have evolved.
Here's my long list of complaints, some of them bigger, some of them smaller, but the sheer number of them is the most worrying thing. Mostly they are usability issues, things making the game more clumsy and annoying to play, but there are a few issues with the game writing, voice acting, etc. as well.
Roughly in order of most to least annoying:
---
It feels like the game regularly fights against you, you know what you should be doing, but the game just refuses to acknowledge you're even trying the right thing. Then it turns out some really uninteresting detail to the player is the key to progressing.
Seriously, this is bad. The *ESC* key does not open the menu. Ctrl+O does. This has to be a bad, sick joke. Right? Ha ha, april fools is gone. Fix this. Now.
The game depends on you retrying the same thing multiple times - INCREDIBLY bad adventure game design.
You have to open each and every drawer separately, to the point where you just repeatedly hear "Nothing." and go on autopilot, and fail to notice that some of them actually had contents in them.
All machines supposedly have a speech interface (you can TALK to them), except the only one you really want to use. It doesn't seem to be possible to use the machine until you need it, even though you can find it, and only after you need it can you activate it using the USE verb.
The game seems to make jokes about pixel hunting by having "specks of dust" littered around, and then uses pixel hunting as an actual necessary mechanic.
At one point you have to go through *10* identical scenes in order to find the one with the thing you need. There is no reason given for this, or any hint as to where you might find your thing, or even a reason for you to go searching, you just have to do it to progress.
Most of the time the characters are not dumb enough to e.g. require you to USE stairs, you just walk to them, but there is *ONE* exception where the game requires you to use the USE verb at the bottom of the stairs to climb them. You aren't even required to activate the verb to get back down. These are not the first stairs you encounter.
There are regularly sound volume issues, some sounds are very loud, sometimes they play really quiet.
There are multiple long winded scenes that seem to have been made just to waste your time. Long sections of manual walking with exactly NOTHING to interact with or anything to see. It's like the devs just had a brainstorming session about how to waste the most player's time.
The game backseat games itself with "I should really be ..." -timed dialog lines, worst of all it's done when the player is not stuck. Quickly becomes incredibly irritating.
Characters regularly interrupt each other and themselves with timed dialog lines. You try to click on something and the text + speech gets cancelled by something you really don't care at all about.
The default action for interacting with items is often intuitively "wrong", not what you'd expect or want to do.
You have to remember various things people say or you read to pick the correct choice in dialog trees, OR you might even have to just guess them (codes, model numbers, teen slang, ...).
The journal (notebook) system is confusing - different people's notebooks have mostly identical content, but some of it is different so you always have to check what everyone wrote in their notebook, and sometimes the UI controls for them are different. Things not being said or done appear only in the notebook.
Sometimes there are timed animations, e.g. a few moments after exiting an elevator the doors close. During this animation the game stops responding to your controls and even hides the cursor.
Interactable things regularly get hidden behind foreground graphics, there can literally be a door behind a giant pillar blocking your view.
Verbs sometimes just deactivate if you don't use them quickly enough.
The area edges are poorly highlighted on the cursor, easy to miss the highlight completely when moving the cursor slightly past the edge.
The characters regularly walk the wrong way and have other odd path finding issues when you're just walking on a straight line. They often complain "I can't reach that" when trying to click on an exit.
The game is made in a retro style, which is cool, but in many parts they've made it "worse than retro". E.g. even back in the early 90s the point & click games with lots of verbs had keyboard shortcuts to activate them so it wouldn't be so clumsy, Thimbleweed Park does not. You have to click on the verb every time you want to do something, which is really annoying to an adventure game veteran like myself for whom pressing P for pickup is in the backbone.
With text + voice enabled, the dialog often continues unexpectedly - you first see a few words, and when you hear the guy finishing on that you click on the next thing but he surprisingly had more things to say. More text fits on screen, so it could've been there, or they could have a "..." indicator or something for when they are going to continue.
Text in dialog mode doesn't wrap when it reaches the edge of the screen, but scrolls horizontally when you hover over it. I'd of course want to see all of the text at once.
Some of the few keyboard shortcuts the game does have stop working if you have caps-lock on, even the one on the "."-key.
It seems the writing sometimes contradicts itself, e.g. a guy mentions 3 machines, and then speaks of "the 4 machines", or a salesperson asking for a "2 character code" for a part, and then you find a 3 character code for a part of that type.
A good modern point & click should have an easy key to highlight all interactable items on screen.
Scroll-wheel doesn't work for browsing through the inventory.
Sometimes the voice actors read the text you click on in dialog mode, other times they don't. It's inconsistent.
One of your characters (an agent) keeps telling everyone to not leave town for no reason, which seems odd.
The voice acting seems clumsy at times, and the voice directing is off - often the voice acting just doesn't seem to fit the intent of the lines.
The GIVE -verb does not recognize every person as a possible target.

I'm writing this review as someone who has no nostalgia for the game. I never played it back in the day, but finally played it today.
It's... good. In fact, I could see if I was playing the game back then, I would have considered the game amazing. Unfortuantely, being used to modern games, there are a lot of things that make this game feel extremely dated. There's 0 auto-saving. Which means when after 45min of playing the game, when I died, I went back to the beginning. I understand, auto-saving wasn't really a thing back then. I can't blame the developers for that. However, it is something to take heavily into consideration when playing this game. SAVE OFTEN.
I liked the game's set up and tutorial. It made you connect more with the character by choosing what branch of the military they joined and what missions they went on while at the same time choosing stats. It is a unique and interesting approach even today.
The controls are extremely dated, so I highly recommend you customize them first chance you get.
Other than the dated aspects, the game is great. Highly recommended. I probably won't play more just because losing 45min of progress was a huge bummer and I have a ton of other games to beat anyway.
If you didn't play System Shock 2 when it was released, then avoid it. Just replay Half-life again.

It is improved in almost all its sectors, making it a better game than its predecessor.
Gameplay: The multiple ways in which you can approach any mission(you can finish the mission by assasinating your target, but you can also finish it by letting him live), the old good mechanics of the first Dishonored with the addition of some new ones, the character abilities which is the greatest element this game has, all these things will keep you from being bored. Emily's abilities are really awesome.
Level Design: I was impressed from the way every area was designed, giving the player a big variety of options on how he will reach his target(OMG that "Clockwork Mansion" mission...!!!). Many thumbs up for the designers.
Art Direction: From some nice paintings and decorations in the "rich" areas of Karnaca, to some destroyed and abandoned places, the art direction is one of the best i have ever seen in a game. I really liked this "classic" style of Dishonored 2.
Soundtrack: In contrast to the original Dishonored, this one has great soundtrack(main theme, ending theme etc.). I didn't expect to get impressed.
Story: After the main happening at the beginning of the game, I believe the story was a little expected, but it's an ok story.
Graphics: The poorest part of this game, as its predecessor, but also improved due to the new engine it uses. Personally, I didn't care so much about the graphics neither the poor optimization, which has some improvements since the game release(I noticed some framedrops, but nothing that could ruin my experience).
The first Dishonored was the best stealth game i have ever played, but now I believe that Dishonored 2 "took the throne" ^_^

So on the whole Dishonored 2 is a cool and fun game to play.  If we take a standpoint of looking at the GAME only.  However this has to be the most technical messed up game I have ever dealt with.  Took me 2 hours to figure out how to get it to start.  The problem was that this game does not seem to get along with the NVIDIA control panel.  It would go through the loading screen and give me a black screen.  If any of you are having this problem here is the steps to delete the Nvidia configuration for the game.
Delete "dishonored2Config.cfg" located in C:\Users\<user>\Saved Games\Arkane Studios\dishonored2\base (by default).  Relaunching the game after doing this should reset all settings back to default.
I would recommend this game after they fix all the technical bugs.  It is not worth the money at the moment.  But when they fix it I will give this game a thumbs up.

This game has a really cool and refreshing combat system. The block mechanic means you dont just cast a spell that will block for you and your team and automatically blocks incoming abilities, instead you have to click your mouse button and predict or react to mobs abilities or auto attack animations. Honestly, the game did a lot correctly in the sense that there was a trinity, there were leaderboards, cool visuals etc.
Now, Why do I not reccomend this? So to begin with I didn't play much of the game but that was the issue - I was bored. The start of the game was interesting because I had a new combat system to play with and a tonne of things to get my head around. But then once I hit around level 9-10 I just kept seeing the same thing over and over again. The stairways to dungeons were the same, the bridges used the same design, the mobs were the same and there was an awkward leap between questing levels meaning I was either breezing through mobs or getting my butt handed to me meaning I had to grind on mobs that don't give much exp.
I just found myself bored by level 10 and that really isn't a good sign. It was feeling grindy already and that is meant to happen around level cap and due to the flexibility of each character, there is no real incentive to create new characters like in other mmo's.
To be fair, I didn't play through on different characters but I predict that they would feel very repetitive. Every class/race can acess all the weapons - which is OK. BUT. There are no different skills - THEY ARE EXACTLY THE SAME as if you were to play it on a nightblade or a sorcerer or a Dragon knight.. This is really disappointing to see. I have played about 1000 hours of gw2 and what I loved about that game is there was a lot of variety. If you picked up a greatsword on a Mesmer it would have different skills and in this case a completely different range than if I was to use a greatsword on a warrior. This is an awesome feature as it kept the game fresh. I was so disappointed that ESO didn't include this. I understand what they were going for but they really ruined that for me.
In summary, feel free to try out the game, the beginning is awesome for sure but if you have had MMO experience then I really don't see how you would hit lvl 50 or VR16 and maybe even make some alts, because its just a lot of the same content which is a massive shame. There is some awesome nostalgia from Skyrim - not as much as we would hope but it is there.
Hope this helps you make a decision. I realise I stated pros and cons but maybe it will make up your mind. If it were me, I wouldn't listen to some review on steam and I would want to try it for myself but this is just me giving my piece of mind.

Remember those old days of huddling in the dark, jumping at every sound, and hoping that you won't be seen? Well, for all those old-school survival horror fans, this is the game for you. This is an Alien game actually done right by making you feel like you're in one of the movies. The creators of this game wanted to recreate the same experience that Ridley Scott did and they succeeded.
There aren't many games now that gives you that sense of vulnerability, but with Isolation, instead of running in with guns blazing, you're more likely to be hiding under a table, listening to the increasing pitch of the motion sensor.  Nowhere is safe and you have to be wary of your surroundings. Go under a vent and you'll get ambushed. Hide in a locker for too long and the Alien will hear your stifled breathing. Even when you wander through a vent, you might find yourself face-to-face with an unexpected visitor.
Yes, the Alien is relatively smart, though it sometimes lingers for too long. But unlike other AI, it gradually starts to learn from your behavior. So while a noise maker might distract it a few times, eventually it's going to try to find the source of the sound. If doors are opened and objects are moved, it's going to notice it.
While the constant button-pressing from opening doors and restarting systems does get tedious, overall, this is a immersing, terrifying experience that finally stays true to the original Alien movies.

Wow. This is a triumph in gaming. The reviewer who reviewed this from IGN doesn’t know his♥♥♥♥♥♥from his elbows. What an amazing game. Well, I say game. It’s not so much as a game as an experience. This is the Alien Experience and the true sequel to Ridley Scotts original vision. This game is a masterpiece in gaming history. It won’t be for everyone’s tastes, sure. This is the classic vintage; a glass of red wine, a tipple of single malt whiskey with a dash of tepid water served on chilled amazeballs.
For any fans of Ridley Scott’s first film this will allow you to live the nightmare … and it’s freakin awesome. It’s like playing a new Alien movie with a great plot, great actors, creepy henchmen, and an absolutely fantastic lead villain, oh and not to forget an absolutely wonderful little voice performance from the most awesome Sigourney Weaver. With just a moment she adds a touch of class to an already brilliant piece of Art.
Graphically stunning, the visual design was beautiful right from the very opening moments of inhabiting Ripley’s body. The lighting, the smoke effects, all the little attentions to detail thrust me right into Servastopol. It’s like wandering the sets of the original movie and it ran like a dream on my machine. I rarely find games that will run at top graphics and run well. This had no trouble at all. The optimization was spot on.
The opening Act was nothing short of Oscar worthy. By the end of it I had Ripley cowering in a corner and I had a smile on my face so big it hurt. I was terrified and loving it. The music just kept building and building and I found myself wanting to shout at that little f*&(#$ to stop toying with me and come get me. That experience alone was worth the price tag for the game. The rest was just icing on the cake. People have complained about the length. Fools. This game just keeps giving. And don’t be put off by one of the earlier levels. The designers switch it up during the game; they just give you a taste of the rough stuff early on to keep you on your toes throughout the rest of the ordeal, though I will admit, there was a point during this level where I thought to myself, ‘if it is like this for the rest of the game this won’t be a fun experience.’ Take heart, this is just a tough level.
And one cannot even begin to praise this game without first giving a nod and a tip of the hat to the sound design which is nothing short of spectacular. If Oscars were given to games the sound design for this game would most definitely win and be praised for years to come. Listening to that little f*&$%$ crawling around in the vents above you fills you with all the right emotions. The sound of the dying station creaking and moaning submerses you into the game world. The soundtrack immerses you into the world and builds at times in such a wonderful way it makes your heart thump all the louder.
The AI of the alien is excellent. During my time on Sevastopol I really felt like I was being hunted. Watching that creature from the shadows filled me with dread as it actually appeared to be trying to seek me out. I often felt like it knew I was there or, at least, that I had recently been there not long before. And sometimes I even felt like it was trying to trick me to come out of hiding just by the way it acted. I was hid under a table at one time and waited quite some time before plucking up the courage to head for the door, just mere meters from my position. At one point I watched on my sensor as the Alien raced off through the vents at great speed. I was about to come out when the little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ came racing right back and dropped from a nearby vent with a hiss.
As with any form of art opinions will differ. This will not be everyone’s cup of tea. But for those of you who love computer games for what they can do, what boundaries they can push, like the wonderful Half Life in its glory days. This is one of those games that will be remembered and not just for the amazing visuals, Oscar worthy sound design or even the most worthy AI of the exomorph hunting you, but also for the way it weaves the story. Telling story can be hard in games, especially first person shooters. This does it superbly. The link to the original movie is perfect for sucking you right into the universe. It is not a complicated story. It is simple and all it needs to be to experience the horror Ripley experiences on her journey to Savastopol. And what a journey it is.
There are so many little touches that I would love to share about the game but that would just serve to spoil. All I would say is, don’t read spoilers or how-to’s, and don’t watch play-throughs or walkthroughs. Go in knowing as little as possible. Throughout my play-through I was often pleasantly surprised at the twists this game took and the places it dared to tread through the Ripley Scott classic. I often found myself guessing seconds before and saying “Nooooooooo,” as I realized the horror the game was placing me in next.  But each time that smile would return as I would relish the beautiful sci-fi horror of it all. 10 out of freakin’ 10!!!

Alien fans, you will be in heaven... Well, actually stuck in a space station with humans (how boring), synthetic androids (bloody hard to kill) and your one and unique little black pet with his/her double extendable set of teeth and a very sharp and pointy tail.

During your journey, you will be able to collect items like scraps, ethanol, sensors etc. With it you will be able to craft well needed objects like Molotov, Pipe bomb, Noise maker, Medipack and others.

Very competent sequel that improves the foundations of the first game but somehow looses some of its gritty gothic moments and memorable villains. So the sequel to one of the most underrated survival horror games and one of my favorites came out of nowhere, The Evil Within 2. Is it as good or even better than the first underrated gem from Resident Evil mastermind Shinji Mikami ? Well... yes and no...
The first game was very hard and low key which means it wasnt aimed much at casual gamers but more for the serious survival horror fans out there. Plagued with technical issues and brutal, unforgiving difficulty. I look at you chapter 6 on Akumu xD it was a game that you either loved or completely hated. As a longtime fan of the original Resident Evil from 1996 and a fan of Shinji Mikamis work and games I can say that it was an underrated game and I was pleasently surprised to find out that they will release a sequel to it this year.
So after putting around 30 hrs into The Evil Within 2 I can tell that its a good entry and solid sequel but it lost its charm from the original. All the awesome gameplay mechanics like burning bodies with matches or bypassing deadly needle bombs are gone. The bosses are fun but not even nearly as memorable and difficult as in the Original. Same as with the antagonists, they come out of nowhere and there is no awesome Boxhead enemy that follows you around. They tried to tack in some weird Laura type creature thing that stalks you around but it felt also out of place.
Where the sequel shines thou is its story and of course gameplay. The story this time around is very personal and the last chapters convey the raw emotions Sebastian goes through pretty well. When you finally finish this game you will feel like you have overcome a true nightmare very similar to the first game but with more closure.
So in the end this game turned out to be a pretty well done sequel to its original masterpiece and I hope there will be a third entry to explain some loose ends this game leaves open. Final score 8 green gel bottles out of 10 :D

The game is difficult and easy for the wrong reasons, overall it is too easy. The gameplay mechanics are rather clunky and the game itself comes off as a sloppy, lazy mess.
The difficult aspects of the game are due to clunky character controls and overall gameplay mechanics. For example, when the main character is struck by an enemy, you are unable to control them until they recover. However, the character stands idle for a bit of time at the end of the recovery, leaving you vulnerable to a second hit. This can lead to moments where you're hit repeatedly, unable to control your character.
The easy aspects of the game come from the amount of stuff, especially healing items, you're able to find in the game world. This makes the game boring, as you're never in a dire situation, save for when you're hit repeatedly, as noted above. About halfway through the game, I found that most of my deaths were a result of seeing how poorly I can play and still stay alive.
Here are some of the reasons why I find this game to be mediocre and sloppy -
- The levels are poorly designed. A big part of the game is searching for extra items, gel, etc.. However, these levels are revisited at times and magically refill with more items. This forces you to search through the entire area/map a second time, which is just a lazy way to drag the game out.
- When you die, weapon selections are lost and you'll automatically start using the default weapon again. Why?
- Sometimes commands overlap. For example, pressing 'B' with a particular item equipped causes 2 actions to be done. This doesn't affect gameplay all that much, it just demonstrates the shortsightedness of the gameplay.
- Enemies clip into walls and teleport.
- Your character gets stuck on objects; your character can mount certain objects which sometimes causes them to get stuck. Sometimes your character can get out of it, other times you can't and the game has to be restarted.
- When certain enemies are (visibly) staggered, they cannot take damage (but this is not conveyed to you), leading to wasted time and resources.
- The game already looks 2-3 years old. I'm pretty sure The Evil Within 1 looked better.
- The developers tried really hard to elimnate loading screens, but this leads to awkward interludes where you walk around until the next level is ready which, again, wastes time.
- Light on the horror, heavy on the action. Not really a bad thing, just misaligned expectations.
- Granted, it's like a B 'horror' movie, but the cut scenes are too long and the voice acting is pretty subpar. The main character always has the same line, "what the hell?"
- and more.
The game isn't all bad. The gunplay is okay and the game doesn't take itself too seriously, which is refreshing at times. None of the aspects I noted above are game-breaking, just things you notice as you play and wonder why/how they made it into the final package. I went into this game with low expectations and was still disappointed.
The Evil Within 2 is not worth the $60 price tag, wait for it to go on sale. Or just buy Resident Evil 7 instead.

88/100 (8.5/10 seemed too low...and 9/10 seemed too high..so this felt just right)
I was never a Survival Horror type of player...but the Resident Evil series was a balance I liked (especially the first and second) so when I found out Evil Within 1 was directed by the same guy that made the first one...I felt I had to play it...And was very happy I did.
Now as for the second one compared to first one (without ruining story):
I felt the first one was longer (at times maybe a bit dragged out but looking back I had a blast).  Story wise...you play a detective and in the first one you really are trying to investigate whats going on...so that added to the interest of the story and lore...part 2 i felt was too spelled out for you which I felt was a shame..It felt dumbed down...and I found out the director of part 2 wasnt the same as part one so maybe that explained alot.  The trailers gave away alot of the cutscenes and enemies you would face even very late in the game and I did not like that level of spoilers...So I recommend not watching them at all before going in.
Stealth mechanics improved ALOTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTT from part 1...part one was super clunky and very difficulty to be stealthy...part 2 you can stealth kill almost everything with ease esp after upgrading some key Stealth abiltiies.
In terms of scariness...I found this game no where near as jumpy or freaky as part one...And I have no idea why people say its scary :s part one you had some intense chapters followed by chapters where it felt more like a break...here the environments probably more scary as the graphics and ambiance is far more improved as well as the sounds of some of the creatures...but overall i didnt really jump alot or was too stressed playing part 2. ..also the variety of enemies is far less as well as the number of bosses which is a shame I think..and is why i felt it lost points from being a perfect game...It felt very watered down...
The Puzzles in the game also dumbed down alot...no difficulty at alllllll...very stale... I am noticing this trend of dumbing down alot of games for the masses which is a shame really.
The crafting and upgrade system of the game is vastly improved and a welcome addition...I like having 2 separate resources to upgrade my character and weps rather than the same for both...and the crafting means I can manage what I want to make rather than get too much of 1 thing.  I am not sure if I miss the "Matches" from part 1...it was a unique item to the game and also made using dead bodies as a great trap to lure some zombies to then toss it to burn all...some hated it..some liked it I guess...I just found it to be different.
Graphics are amazing I felt overall...played on max settings and was very happy...some of the gestures with other NPCs needs a bit of work  (the eyes as well as body language) but overall great.
Final Thoughts:
The story was TOO straight forward...there was no big mystery or massive surprises...alot of things were hinted at before getting to the point you were SUPPOSED to be surprised; especially when compared to part one where you felt "WTH IS GOING ON?!" and had to really look at all the files and put the pieces together to get the bigger picture (which goes back to the dumbing down of games I mentioned early) and that was part of the fun of discovery as well as, again..you ARE playing a detective! the creators should not forget that!...But I still enjoyed it alot and would recommend...I love the theme of this survival horror the most...the idea of going into the mind of a serial killer or someone crazy and the sort of nightmarish things you can find...since its the mind there are no rules for creative restriction so as the creators of this game they can go all without restrictions.
TLDR
They improved the game ALOT in terms of game mechanics from part one...and the graphics are much better (as it should be since its 2017)  But the story was too straight forward and in many regards...boring sadly ; ; The jump scares were very few...The environment and sounds of creatures kept me on the edge...but nothing came to push me over.  But I still recommend..it is a great sequel to part one none the less and I had alot of fun playing it.

After finishing The Evil Within 2 I was exhausted, like I’d been through an ordeal. Thinking back on my 20 hours with it, I had. The Evil Within 2 is an ambitious, genuinely tense, and at times brutally difficult experience, but one that left me exhilarated. Like the original before it, The Evil Within 2 may not know how to deliver convincing dialogue or maintain a consistent tone, but it does know that the mark of pure survival horror is to leave you feeling like you only just survived, time after time after time.
Developer Tango Gameworks has done a good job at a cleaner set-up this time around by sending protagonist Sebastian Castellanos to rescue his thought-dead daughter from The Evil Within’s version of the Matrix, called STEM - adding some vital emotional stakes that were lacking in the original. Sebastian himself, on the other hand, is somehow even more dull three years later. Despite having gone through all this once before, he still regularly quips mundanities at the weirdness of it all. Pedestrian lines like “What the hell?” and “Ugh, who comes up with this stuff?” break the horror spell, and most of the time I just wanted him to shut up and let the creepy world around him speak for itself.
The wider cast doesn’t fare much better. Aside from one interesting character you meet later on, they are merely serviceable archetypes there to push the plot forward (the psychologist’s running gag is that she is a psychologist). The awkward dialogue can occasionally lend a certain B-movie charm, but it feels like a missed opportunity to not let them have a little fun in such an eccentric setting.
This is still The Evil Within, though, and its world remains delightfully malleable and weird: mirrors take you to safehouses! Burning paintings make barbed wire disappear! A cat gives you green gel so you can upgrade your abilities! There’s a shooting range in the world through the mirror run by a nurse! The sense that the world could change the rules at any moment keeps things interesting, despite, or perhaps because of, its inherent ridiculousness.
The Evil Within 2’s story travels an unusual road, as its first half is tonally very different from its second. Sebastian begins his journey preoccupied with a deranged murderer inside STEM, which is a meandering mystery punctuated by a weak boss fight (an easily dodged primary attack made this one genuinely boring) that made me miss the non-stop climactic encounters and big moments of the original. Its second half, on the other hand, travels at a breakneck pace and is deadeye focused on the broader task at hand and its personal implications for Sebastian. The latter’s strength and surety made me wonder what the first half was even there for, and left me feeling like The Evil Within 2 was telling two completely distinct stories, one much stronger than the other.
I would never accuse it of being inconsistent in its mood, however. At every turn Tango has done a great deal with lighting, and dimly lit corridors feel claustrophobic, creating a sense of inevitability; of course there’s something waiting for you around the corner! Oddly shaped shadows become crouching monsters while swathes of darkness promise either loot or death. I jumped for no reason more than once.
It’s a much bigger mini-sandbox this time around, too, and you have more freedom in exploring it. Union  - aka “Anytown, USA” - is a sprawling post-apocalyptic mess of diners, picket fences, and a main street that ends at a gaping Silent Hill-esque chasm, its other half lost to the atmosphere. Though not every building can be entered or clambered up onto, there are a welcome number of nooks and crannies that offer unique enemy encounters, side quests, and loot that feel organically baked into the world.
Once I stumbled upon a lost agent who’d found himself surrounded by enemies, and after I saved him he gave me a further two quests that took me to the far reaches of Union’s underground tunnel system. Another time I was checking out what I thought was an innocuous diner before its interior changed with the click of a jukebox track and I was suddenly being chased by a screaming ghoul. I loved the promise that such discoveries could be around any or every corner.
In every instance, exploration in The Evil Within 2 is worth it, and in the case of scavenging for loot it’s absolutely vital. Green gel (used for upgrading Sebastian’s health, athleticism, recovery and combat prowess), gunpowder, and weapon parts (used for crafting ammo and upgrading your arsenal) are scarce but necessary to stay alive, so I was frequently putting Sebastian in ridiculous amounts of danger just to find enough weapon parts to add another bullet chamber to my handgun. Blindly sprinting towards a glimmering light in the distance as the sound of enemies roaring at my heels with The Evil Within 2’s excellent score pounding in my ears was a rush each time.
If you’re caught by a mob, particularly early on before you’ve upgraded your arsenal, you’ll die more often than not. Like The Evil Within before it, enemies in The Evil Within 2 are plentiful, relentless, and delightfully gross in their attacks. The Lost are its familiar raging shamblers, but there are also monsters that vomit acid onto your face for a one-hit kill if you get too close (as I did often), monsters with burlap-sack masks who wield flamethrowers, and various composite bosses that are seemingly results of a brainstorming meeting where someone said “What if we mixed X with Y?” Though these don’t quite match the creative lunacy of those in the original - The Keeper remains the series’ highlight -  there are still some brilliant encounters here. An early boss is made out of body parts held together by a backbone and a buzzsaw, while a later one is part camera.
While deranged, these monsters will still chase you if they spot you, and if they lose you they’ll search the area for a while, so it’s important to keep moving. More, they’re quite erratic in their movements, so sneak kills aren’t always the best option if you’re not close to your target. I got right behind a flamethrowing Harbringer after five minutes of stalking him before he suddenly turned around, immediately spewing flame into my face. Their credibly unpredictable behaviour made every encounter a tense one.
You don’t always have to fight. Like its predecessor, The Evil Within 2 allows for a stealthy approach, and it’s slightly more feasible this time around thanks to a bigger playground and a new stealth upgrade path that allows you to increase the ‘quietness’ of your footsteps or pace while crouching. Though I found shooting enemies in the head was a more accessible option on the whole, stealth was still a viable option depending on the circumstance.
In classic survival-horror style, much of the exhilaration in The Evil Within 2 comes from being spotted and having to suddenly launch into a fight, making do with whatever sparse resources you have at hand. I was frequently forced to experiment with the lesser-used weapons in my arsenal, such as the crossbow and its variety of creative bolts, and found myself delighted as a freeze bolt stopped a rampaging lunatic in his tracks before his head was shattered by my shotgun. Other times it was a case of absolutely needing to land every single headshot with my handgun while desperately searching for respawning ammo in the near vicinity before landing that final, crunchy blow.
The Evil Within 2 gives you more options to play your way in a much bigger survival-horror playground than the original. Although a disjointed plot and weak protagonist make it slow to get started, being pursued through an intriguingly bizarre world by plentiful and disturbing monsters kept my palms sweaty and my heart in my throat thanks to a strict adherence to the most important survival horror rule: you should always be on the back foot.

This games deserves a good word. Quickly:
- Graphics : Perfect, crisp and atmospheric.
- Sound Design: Again, as a horror game they nailed it. In fact, enemies' sounds are way scarier than their appearance. Music on point.
- Voice acting/ animation cinematics: Lip syncing is off and in some cases downright cringy. But it holds up and doesn't break immersion.
- Story: Good and cohesive. Not Witcher 3 in terms of world-building, dialogue and detail, but it is MUCH MUCH better than the ♥♥♥♥fest mess that was previous game. It is still somewhat of a ....reach in terms of realism.
- Level Design: Amazingly, the story isn't quite as linear as last time. There are optional hidden bosses, weapons, upgrades and story segments for those willing to invest the time and effort. In return, these nougats flesh out the story.
- Pace: Perfect. You start slow, build up, climax, climax and climax. Starting from chapter 8 all the way to chapter 16 it is one adrenaline rush after the other.
IF you can, then buy this game. I was genuinely suprised by this game since its predecessor failed - in my opinion - miserably.

The Story - The story is disjointed, makes little sense, is intertwined in a nonsensical way, and is ultimately uninteresting. There is no real connection between the characters, nothing that really drives them at least (except for a ghost and his daughter), yet they are all working towards the same goal through you. Some of this is explained at the end, but by the time you reach the end, you will no longer be interested in the story at all. Throughout the game I kept asking myself why I was playing this. What is the point? What is the goal of the game? You only find out what the point is in the last five minutes of gameplay making the entirety of the game rely on a feeling of nostalgia and a hope that, somehow, Ron Gilbert MUST have come up with something better than this and, perhaps, if you keep digging deeper you will find it.
In other adventure games you would at least have a sense of what the goal was, of what you were trying to achieve. For example, Guybrush Threepwood wants to become a pirate and later rescue Elaine; Indiana Jones wants to stop the Nazis from getting to Atlantis; Bernard, Hoagie and Loraine want to stop Purple Tentacle from taking over the world; Even Dave and the other two tuna heads want to rescue Sandy in Maniac Mansion. Thimbleweed Park, however, has no drive.
Furthermore, the ending is extremely disappointing. There is no resolution and is exclusively meta.
The Characters - The characters are flat. They have two-dimensional motivations. One of them is entirely propelled by expletives. There is no endearing character, no relatable one.
I don't know... I'll leave it here. I'm kind of tired of spending time thinking about this game. I don't recommend it, it has been an interesting but disappointing 14 hours.

Before I begin my review I'd like to add some context - Just Cause 2 was one of the first games I've played when I got my own pc back in 2011. It was a very enjoyable open world game that defined the current generation of sandbox games. So when Just Cause 3 was announced last year, I was genuinely hyped. Even though these days you can't get hyped about a game without worrying about how it'll perform on launch day, I didn't care, because Just Cause 2 was a very optimized game and Square Enix has a decent record of games with good optimization.
That being said, I was getting ever and ever more doubtful, how the pre-release coverage of the game showed so little as opposed to other AAA titles, how no one was talking about the map, performance or anything. Hell the biggest feature of this franchise, the map, was shown only a week eariler before release. And when it did release, I couldn't play the game because of the horrible optimization. That being said, after a few patches and buying more RAM, I finally got to play it. Now on to the review.
The graphics in this game speaks for itself. You can see farmlands, sunflower fields and scattered villages for miles. The spires of big bases have a very significant apperance of Di Ravello's oppresive regime. Beautiful sea beaches merge with coves and scattered cliffsides. At night the cities and bases light up and provide a beacon for it be discovered.
This game is a treat for the ear as much as the eye - guns sound powerful, sports cars sound ferociously fast and explosions give that great sound of satisfaction that you may not find in any other game.
Now on to the part which I found most controversial. The map of Just Cause 3 seems much more lackluster compared to JC2. There aren't any more landmark locations like the Mile High Club, the Radar Dish, or the Radio Tower. Instead there's just a lot of villages and bases. Sure they look unique from each other, but it's a step back from JC2. Also half of the biggest island is literally walled off and abandoned, where in a similar way in JC2 there were  a lot more villages, bases etc. Roads look like masking tapes put on the floor, the highways have no hoardings above them, there are no dividers and the biggest city - citate di ravello, is as lack luster as it can get.
The gameplay is a bit cumbersome. Auto aiming is gone, so expect a lot missed shots. The health meter is gone, though now it's the same as not getting health pack like in JC2. The minimap is gone, so you won't know where are the enemies and you won't notice the remaining chaos objects without pausing the game and looking up on the map.
Sure they changed the driving model, cars tend not to swivel out of control, but bikes on the other hand will behave realistically and just won't go straight. I wish  the Sleeping Dog's driving model was implemented here.
The biggest change this game offers is the wingsuit and in the sky fortress dlc, it turns into a ♥♥♥♥ing jetpack. Though it's quite fun. It is only one step forward from the last game.
Just Cause 3 behaves similarly to Just Cause 2,the map has been stripped to just bases and cities. As if the developers played a lot of Far Cry 3 and added it's wingsuit and nothing much else. There is much more accesibility, and the game is still jolly good fun. I'd recommend buying now. Because once this goes on sale, it'll just be another $5 game that you'll never play , another entry in your untouched game library.
Avanlanche needs to hire some writers and work on more compelling quests, but the core gameplay is still fun.

Hell of a game! Great step up from the previous in several ways.
PROS:
- Story and Characters: Boiled down, it's a typical "viva la revolucion", destroy the oppressive regime story, but they did a fantastic job with it. The story missions are entertaining as hell. More distinctly than the previous game, the characters are much better defined and far more interesting.
- Navigation: Holy damn, the wingsuit is fantastic. That, combined with your parachute, fast travel, and vehicles everywhere, getting around is a breeze and loads of fun.
- Weaponry: Easy choice here, it's chaos on a massive scale, and it's balls-to-the-wall fun with tons of options.
- Scenery: Medici is a beautiful place. Even on only "high" settings, it's a well-designed place with towns that feel alive and countryside perfectly populated to feel realistic.
CONS:
- Performance: As is everyone else's complaints, I've noticed it also. Even scaling down to "high" settings, there are occassional dips in FPS, especially with destruction.
- Bugs: There are a few bugs with weaponry and planes, one in particular that prevents campaign completion (heat seeking doesn't working in "Rico and the Rose").
- Police Stations: Claiming most is fine, usually simple. But the "destroy X PLUS cause chaos" leads to a few terribly stupid situations where you're waiting for reinforcements one by one to kill enough crap to conquer it. Dumb mechanic.
- Vehicles: Most are useless, honestly. Motorcycles especially drive like absolute garbage. Most cars/boats don't get much use, you just end up find the most useful tanks/fighters/combat boats and using those. Fun for collecting and messing around, at best.
Honestly, given its scope, there's not too much about the gameplay I have complaints about. It's unadulterated chaos in a beautiful open world. Definitely recommend it.

A great stealth sequel to a fantastic stealth game, offering a range of different approaches and playstyles, depending on how you like to play. The narrative is paper-thin (almost disappointingly so), but the environmental storytelling and incidental writing in books and letters you find are as strong as ever. Don't expect a riveting plot or particularly engaging characters and what you'll find are some incredibly inventive and vast levels that are fun to explore and play around in.
I would wholeheartedly recommend turning off the Objective and Heart markers from the HUD options as soon as you start the game. They are not necessary (and should you feel frustrated not knowing which direction your target is at, you can always click them on briefly to get an idea) and turning them off gives you a much more tense, Thief-like, exploration focused experience as you have to actually scout the environment and seek out your objectives. It's very rewarding. I also feel like the people saying the game is short only ran directly to their objective markers without looking at anything else, essentially missing a whole bunch of narrative and upgrades. My first playthrough clocked in at 31 hours, and I wasn't even deliberately going for a 100% for everything, but finding the runes, Outsider shrines and reading everything just got so engaging, I certainly didn't feel it was short.
Apparently some people were having performance issues with the game, so maybe read up on some of that before buying full price, there's also been a few patches since release so not all complaints are timely anymore. I did not have problems, so I also can't side with the people screaming the game is a ripoff for being broken.
I feel like the first Dishonored is still my favourite of the two, but this is a vast, rewarding follow-up, with new abilities and some absolutely fantastic setpieces and locations that are a marvel to behold and sneak through. The Clockwork Mansion is easily one of the coolest levels I've experienced in a game in years. If you enjoyed the first game, D2 is "more of the same" and I enjoyed it a whole lot.

This game has a really cool and refreshing combat system. The block mechanic means you dont just cast a spell that will block for you and your team and automatically blocks incoming abilities, instead you have to click your mouse button and predict or react to mobs abilities or auto attack animations. Honestly, the game did a lot correctly in the sense that there was a trinity, there were leaderboards, cool visuals etc.
Now, Why do I not reccomend this? So to begin with I didn't play much of the game but that was the issue - I was bored. The start of the game was interesting because I had a new combat system to play with and a tonne of things to get my head around. But then once I hit around level 9-10 I just kept seeing the same thing over and over again. The stairways to dungeons were the same, the bridges used the same design, the mobs were the same and there was an awkward leap between questing levels meaning I was either breezing through mobs or getting my butt handed to me meaning I had to grind on mobs that don't give much exp.
I just found myself bored by level 10 and that really isn't a good sign. It was feeling grindy already and that is meant to happen around level cap and due to the flexibility of each character, there is no real incentive to create new characters like in other mmo's.
To be fair, I didn't play through on different characters but I predict that they would feel very repetitive. Every class/race can acess all the weapons - which is OK. BUT. There are no different skills - THEY ARE EXACTLY THE SAME as if you were to play it on a nightblade or a sorcerer or a Dragon knight.. This is really disappointing to see. I have played about 1000 hours of gw2 and what I loved about that game is there was a lot of variety. If you picked up a greatsword on a Mesmer it would have different skills and in this case a completely different range than if I was to use a greatsword on a warrior. This is an awesome feature as it kept the game fresh. I was so disappointed that ESO didn't include this. I understand what they were going for but they really ruined that for me.
In summary, feel free to try out the game, the beginning is awesome for sure but if you have had MMO experience then I really don't see how you would hit lvl 50 or VR16 and maybe even make some alts, because its just a lot of the same content which is a massive shame. There is some awesome nostalgia from Skyrim - not as much as we would hope but it is there.
Hope this helps you make a decision. I realise I stated pros and cons but maybe it will make up your mind. If it were me, I wouldn't listen to some review on steam and I would want to try it for myself but this is just me giving my piece of mind.

I waited until this game was part of a Humble Bundle and waited even longer to play it.  I thought it would just be capitalizing on the popularity of Telltale Games (TWD, GoT, Batman, etc) and copy that format, but it is completely different.

The story is a clever and touching narrative that progresses through the chapters showing the aging of King Graham and the maturation of his family.  It hearkens back to the original series in inventive ways, and you can tell deals with the developers' own experiences with making the games and likely growing through various life stages while creating the classic series.

The puzzles are great.  Unlike recent Telltale games, you actually have to think about these.  However, they aren't too hard and every time something has happened that makes me a little frustrated, the game redeems itself by reaching new levels of creativity and characterization.

The references to the original games are placed into the story and puzzles with just the right mix of new and old, so you never feel like you are playing an old game.  Instead, you are constantly connected to the history behind the original series in a perfectly balanced way.  This has really pulled me back into the lore.  I was enjoying the new chapters so much that it prompted to me stop playing and actually watch some walkthroughs of KQ 1-5 on Youtube!

In case my picture didn't tip you off, I like this game. Like, alot. However, there are some VERY important criticisms that you might want to know before  playing:
-The game is difficult, and while it is usually pretty fair, there are some very, VERY unfair sections. [PSI reavers and the radiation water in the BotM come to mind]
-Weapons are really unbalanced. Any first time player is essentially forced to use Standard weapons, since all the other weapon classes have one really good weapon and two really crap weapons, with the excetion of Energy's EMP rifle [Also, kudos to Looking Glass for creating the Stasis Field Generator, the most useless weapon since the Giant's Knife]
-The annelid worms. These parasitic buggers are the worst thing... Ever. They serve no real in game purpose other than to annoy and irritate. They can be killed in one hit with any non energy weapon, but you can't use melee against them because they're too small, they never stop moving, and the hand-to-hand collision detection is bugger all. So, you end up wasting about 50 bullets worth of ammo on these pests, and in game that's THIS heavy on resource management, you might as well start tossing your med hypos into the never-ending vacuum of space.
However, the Pros outweigh the cons greatly. Specifically...
-The atmosphere. Put on headphones. Turn off the lights. Play for 5 hours straight. I can't even properly describe it.
-The depth. Games like Bioshock and Human Revolution are massively fun, but they tend to be more action games than they are RPG's. Make no mistake; System Shock is an RPG, and a fine example at that. Easily my favorite feature is how it handles exerience, not as a well to be drawn from, but as a resource to be handled wisely. You HAVE to specialize and think long term when picking skills.
-SHODAN.
So, should you play this game? Well, if you like RPG's, and you haven't, then you're kind of obligated to. So do it. NOW>

I bought this with my allowance soon after it was first released. I was 11 years old. It terrified me. I loved it.
And I still love it. I've played through it a few times, and it just gets better every time. It isn't for everyone (there are spots that can be flat-out aggravating). But, if you enjoy an immersive and (dare I say it?) realistic (there, I said it) sci-fi experience, this game is just great. This game is rather intense, and probably not for the casual gamer.
This game was the inspiration from BioShock, and it has many of the same elements. But, BioShock kinda dumbs it down a bit to make it more forgiving for the casual gamer. The thing about this game that I love the most (and provides the element of "realism" that I mentioned before) is that everything is in real time.
Let me emphasize: EVERYTHING you do in the game takes place in real time. Wanna hack a security terminal? Watch out for the hybrid coming around the corner with his shotgun. Wanna hack that turret so that it will help you? Better finish before security comes back up; otherwise, prepare to eat lead.
On the subject of "not dumbing it down," don't expect to generally have a good supply of ammo. That wrench is going to be a close personal friend of yours (if you survive, you puny insect). But don't worry, there are times when you have a bit of ammo. Unfortunately, on this ship, the most common reason to have a good supply of ammo is that your pistol is broken. And, given the limited inventory space, it doesn't generally pay to carry extras around.
But don't worry. When you are feeling down, then SHODAN will give you some uplifting words ("You are a remarkable example of a pathetic species").
Let me sum up: The game is great. Lots of replay value. The game is full of in-depth details. But, you have been warned. Keep your life-alert button handy ("you insignificant speck").

I'm always apprehensive about reviewing classics. Anyone familiar with the game will already have their mind made up on it, and it's often hard to convince those who aren't to try it. I haven't played System Shock 2 since its release ages ago, and I'm happy to report that it holds up surprisingly well for newcomers and veterans alike. Not for the whole game, sadly, but for enough of it.
System Shock 2 is one of the originators of the FPS/RPG genre, which spun out Deus Ex, Vampire, Bioshock, and all manner of dense shooters. You play a hacker stashed aboard the USS Von Braun, mankind's first faster-than-light starship. It becomes immediately apparent that issues have arisen during the voyage, and it's up to you to hopefully make things right. You do this by scavenging weapons and gadgets, hacking devices, upgrading your skills, researching the odd artifacts you come across, and killing lots of really, really freaky monsters. There's an enormous range of activities involved in growing your character, and a little of everything is required to keep up with the surprisingly varied enemies you encounter.
The story is among the best the FPS genre has ever seen, detailing the final hours of the Von Braun's crew and leading you through every nook and cranny of the enormous ship. A competent minimap and extensive log of the audio files you find through the game help keep you on track as you progress through the ruined decks. Unfortunately, the game starts to come apart after you leave the Von Braun. The open maps and fully-realized levels give way to isolated setpieces and cramped, confusing halls filled with monsters. It's very clear the back end of the game was rushed, and it suffers terribly for it. Abuse of the quicksave system is a must near the end, which sadly drains a lot of the tension from the game.
It really cannot be overstated how good the atmosphere is either, which makes its collapse near the end all the more tragic. The sound design is incredible, with unsettling cues popping up at all the right times. Well, except for the music which you should mute immediately, unless you have an irrational love for 90s programmer techno. Even the graphics hold up, with the bold colors and boxy designs masking the incredibly low-res textures. You'll feel like an idiot the first time a chunky-looking enemy makes you jump, but your heart will be pounding too much to care.
It very much is a classic for a reason, and the precipitous drop in quality near the end still can't sully the first 8 or so hours. It's a long, long game, with plenty of secrets and scares to keep you engaged. If you've never played System Shock 2 I guarantee you're in for a treat, and if you haven't replayed it recently I can still promise the same.
