I probably won’t be saying much of what has already been said about this game, but in my opinion System Shock 2 is one of the most pivotal games to hit the market.  System Shock 2 arguably created a type of genre that has been and is still being mimicked/used to this day in the gaming market; and that genre is what I call the FPS/RPG survival hybrid; you see this ‘inventory and upgrade’ based system in many of today’s games for both survival and shooter style games alike.  System Shock 2, although somewhat antiquated for today’s standards was very groundbreaking for its time (this could be said about both SS1 and 2), but without saying more repetitive rhetoric that’s already been said I will get down to the pro/con list in this game that I think is appropriate:
Pros:
-Groundbreaking FPS/RPG hybrid that works very well even to today’s standards.
-Very immersive atmosphere (it really does feel like your there).
-Fluid and extremely customizable and varied control scheme system (you can even save your control scheme setup!).
-Varied options in terms of playstyle and choice of weaponry.
-Various interesting choices and options that actually make you THINK in which a lot of modern games today even lack.
-Small options and features that only add to the immersion such as weapon customization and maintenance, hacking games, inventory management perks and sub-perks, and a currency system for hacking and the purchasing of items via ‘value-rep/vending machines’ (you can even add markers on the mini map and name them as well as add markers in the level in real-time).
-Occurrences in the game that were some of the first of their kind (‘meeting shodan’ for example).
-A game engine that seems to have stood the test of time (with the recent (and even old) updates to the game it runs extremely fluid on pretty much all modern systems).
-Fun and satisfying combat.
-The game creates an overall feeling of fear and tension that was done well.
-Interesting and diverse enemies to fight against.
-Very high replay value.
Cons:
-Some of the options available for upgrade/purchase can be redundant and useless (although every option does have its uses depending on playstyle and skill level of the player).
-Some minor bugs/exploits.
-cyber interface and control scheme can be somewhat complicated for new players.
Overall I consider System Shock 2 to be one of my few personal all-time favorite games and I place it high on my list.  I feel that if you enjoy FPS games and like deep immersion you really should consider giving this game a try.
My rating breakdown:
-.1 some redundant upgrade and weapon choices dependent somewhat upon playstyle
-.1 minor bugs/exploits
(10-.2 = 9.8)
Final rating of 9.8/10

If you grew up in the '70s, '80s or '90s, Broforce is your game.  If you love old action movies and stars, Broforce is your game. If you love old side scrolling games with lots of guns and explosions, Broforce is your game.  If you don't mind a challenge and like a game that doesn't take itself too seriously, Broforce is your game.
Basically, Broforce is an homage to old action movies and action stars.  Going back to the '60s (James Bond) and all the way to the early 2000s, (Kill Bill, Planet Terror.)  Mostly, it's got a lot of “old” gold action stars like Arnold Schwarzenegger, Silvester Stallone, Wesley Snipes, Mr. T, Chuck Norris, etc. in parodies of their various roles.  The plot is a lot like a lot of those old action films:  bad guys are doing bad things and have taken good guys hostage and are threatening the world.  Your bros are sent in to kill the bad guys, save the good guys, save the world.  Basic action film stuff.
The graphics are done in wonderful '80s style pixel art.  The level design is pretty clever and varies.  Also, the game has random elements.  Placement of enemy types, explosive barrels, ammo drops and other things can vary from one play through to another in a single level.  Those aren't the only random things.  Which bros you are using are also chosen randomly, cycling through the ones you've unlocked as you die or as you save your allies.  These random elements add a huge replay value to the game as you may have different enemies and bros to contend with in the same level.
The play is very cool, side scrolling with lots of action, shooting and explosions.  The game is ultra violent.  Enemies (and bros) can be shot, stabbed, cut in half, shredded, exploded, decapitated, and crushed.  Blood, (pixels, of course) body parts, bones, etc. can scatter everywhere.  Though, the game isn't always fair.  In fact, it can be quite unfair at times.  The difficulty doesn't ramp up very quickly, but it does ramp up as you play.  When you get into the double digit Campaign levels, those boss fights can be quite tough.  Also, the game can sometimes give you “cheap” deaths.  But, it's all in good fun.  If you take it too seriously, you probably won't enjoy the game.  My hat's off to anybody who can get the “There Can Bro Only One” achievement.  ;)
So, that's about all I can say about this wonderful gem of a game.  I find it extremely enjoyable, if unfair and downright frustrating at times.  But, I like a challenge.

Remember those old days of huddling in the dark, jumping at every sound, and hoping that you won't be seen? Well, for all those old-school survival horror fans, this is the game for you. This is an Alien game actually done right by making you feel like you're in one of the movies. The creators of this game wanted to recreate the same experience that Ridley Scott did and they succeeded.
There aren't many games now that gives you that sense of vulnerability, but with Isolation, instead of running in with guns blazing, you're more likely to be hiding under a table, listening to the increasing pitch of the motion sensor.  Nowhere is safe and you have to be wary of your surroundings. Go under a vent and you'll get ambushed. Hide in a locker for too long and the Alien will hear your stifled breathing. Even when you wander through a vent, you might find yourself face-to-face with an unexpected visitor.
Yes, the Alien is relatively smart, though it sometimes lingers for too long. But unlike other AI, it gradually starts to learn from your behavior. So while a noise maker might distract it a few times, eventually it's going to try to find the source of the sound. If doors are opened and objects are moved, it's going to notice it.
While the constant button-pressing from opening doors and restarting systems does get tedious, overall, this is a immersing, terrifying experience that finally stays true to the original Alien movies.

Wow. This is a triumph in gaming. The reviewer who reviewed this from IGN doesn’t know his♥♥♥♥♥♥from his elbows. What an amazing game. Well, I say game. It’s not so much as a game as an experience. This is the Alien Experience and the true sequel to Ridley Scotts original vision. This game is a masterpiece in gaming history. It won’t be for everyone’s tastes, sure. This is the classic vintage; a glass of red wine, a tipple of single malt whiskey with a dash of tepid water served on chilled amazeballs.
For any fans of Ridley Scott’s first film this will allow you to live the nightmare … and it’s freakin awesome. It’s like playing a new Alien movie with a great plot, great actors, creepy henchmen, and an absolutely fantastic lead villain, oh and not to forget an absolutely wonderful little voice performance from the most awesome Sigourney Weaver. With just a moment she adds a touch of class to an already brilliant piece of Art.
Graphically stunning, the visual design was beautiful right from the very opening moments of inhabiting Ripley’s body. The lighting, the smoke effects, all the little attentions to detail thrust me right into Servastopol. It’s like wandering the sets of the original movie and it ran like a dream on my machine. I rarely find games that will run at top graphics and run well. This had no trouble at all. The optimization was spot on.
The opening Act was nothing short of Oscar worthy. By the end of it I had Ripley cowering in a corner and I had a smile on my face so big it hurt. I was terrified and loving it. The music just kept building and building and I found myself wanting to shout at that little f*&(#$ to stop toying with me and come get me. That experience alone was worth the price tag for the game. The rest was just icing on the cake. People have complained about the length. Fools. This game just keeps giving. And don’t be put off by one of the earlier levels. The designers switch it up during the game; they just give you a taste of the rough stuff early on to keep you on your toes throughout the rest of the ordeal, though I will admit, there was a point during this level where I thought to myself, ‘if it is like this for the rest of the game this won’t be a fun experience.’ Take heart, this is just a tough level.
And one cannot even begin to praise this game without first giving a nod and a tip of the hat to the sound design which is nothing short of spectacular. If Oscars were given to games the sound design for this game would most definitely win and be praised for years to come. Listening to that little f*&$%$ crawling around in the vents above you fills you with all the right emotions. The sound of the dying station creaking and moaning submerses you into the game world. The soundtrack immerses you into the world and builds at times in such a wonderful way it makes your heart thump all the louder.
The AI of the alien is excellent. During my time on Sevastopol I really felt like I was being hunted. Watching that creature from the shadows filled me with dread as it actually appeared to be trying to seek me out. I often felt like it knew I was there or, at least, that I had recently been there not long before. And sometimes I even felt like it was trying to trick me to come out of hiding just by the way it acted. I was hid under a table at one time and waited quite some time before plucking up the courage to head for the door, just mere meters from my position. At one point I watched on my sensor as the Alien raced off through the vents at great speed. I was about to come out when the little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ came racing right back and dropped from a nearby vent with a hiss.
As with any form of art opinions will differ. This will not be everyone’s cup of tea. But for those of you who love computer games for what they can do, what boundaries they can push, like the wonderful Half Life in its glory days. This is one of those games that will be remembered and not just for the amazing visuals, Oscar worthy sound design or even the most worthy AI of the exomorph hunting you, but also for the way it weaves the story. Telling story can be hard in games, especially first person shooters. This does it superbly. The link to the original movie is perfect for sucking you right into the universe. It is not a complicated story. It is simple and all it needs to be to experience the horror Ripley experiences on her journey to Savastopol. And what a journey it is.
There are so many little touches that I would love to share about the game but that would just serve to spoil. All I would say is, don’t read spoilers or how-to’s, and don’t watch play-throughs or walkthroughs. Go in knowing as little as possible. Throughout my play-through I was often pleasantly surprised at the twists this game took and the places it dared to tread through the Ripley Scott classic. I often found myself guessing seconds before and saying “Nooooooooo,” as I realized the horror the game was placing me in next.  But each time that smile would return as I would relish the beautiful sci-fi horror of it all. 10 out of freakin’ 10!!!

Alien: Isolation
~~~~~~~~~~~~
Alien fans, you will be in heaven... Well, actually stuck in a space station with humans (how boring), synthetic androids (bloody hard to kill) and your one and unique little black pet with his/her double extendable set of teeth and a very sharp and pointy tail.
This game is seriously creepy from the start and really true to the Alien movie franchise, especially the first one. I personally like the 1980 monitors on the space station.
You play Amanda Ripley and your quest is to find out what happened to your mother. You will end up on a station call Sevastopol, where your trouble will begin.
Essentially, this is more a stealth type of game rather than action (shooting) and make sure you know where you can hide. You will eventually find a gun but the ammunitions do not come in abundance, so really look after them. During your journey, you will be able to collect items like scraps, ethanol, sensors etc. With it you will be able to craft well needed objects like Molotov, Pipe bomb, Noise maker, Medipack and others.
Great graphics, splendid audio which empower the fabulous and scary atmosphere. The hairs on my back stood up more than once.
Positives:

-	Great Graphics
-	Great Audio
-	True to the Alien movie franchise
-	Runs Smoothly
-	Achievements
-	Story and Survival Mode

A little late for this review, but it has been on my to-do list!
Being a massive fan of the movie series ever since I was a kid, I had high hopes for this game. It is poised to fill the gap between the "Alien" and "Aliens" movie releases. I won't go into a scene-by-scene walk-through for the entire game, nor any spoilers, but I think it adequately fulfills what it set out to do through theatrics. What it didn't do though, is provide long-term "enjoyable" gameplay. When I say gameplay I mean things like "how predictable is this going to be" and "how many repetitive actions do I have to perform as the player in order to do something simple". Suspense = good. Pushing a few buttons and then clicking a bunch to pull a lever = bleh. That doesn't make me feel like I am really there.
By the middle (or what I thought should have been the midpoint) of the game I really wanted some closure. I just wanted to see the ending credits! A lot of FedExing random items around maps and avoiding an oddly scripted Alien (that is invulnerable by the way) for 20 hours can get a little taxing. I depleted my entire arsenal multiple times just trying to scratch the alien. Nope - still shiny!
Overall, I'd recommend this game to anyone with the warning that it's not for everyone. Treat it as a puzzle that requires you to play in order to understand the story.

I really wanted to like this game. The visual style, atmosphere, sound design, and faithfulness to the orgininal film are all amazing. Chunky, unreliable gizmos clunk and whirr and play silly chiptunes while displaying their manufacturer's logos. The Alien looks perfect, makes appropriately creepy sounds, and has convincing animations.
Unfortunately you can't create a good game on style alone. At some point in this game's development, its creators decided that dying repeatedly in the most frustrating and random of ways equates to "scary". Repeating the same areas again and again until the Alien happens to thump off to the right instead of the left, giving you that crucial few seconds to enter a door code or cut it open with a torch simply isn't fun.
As someone who has put many hundreds of hours into the first three Thief games (the ones that count), Achieved the highest ratings in the last few Hitman games, played successfully through Deus Ex: HR and Dishonored in stealth playstyles on high difficulty settings, and even who makes his Skyrim and Fallout-type characters stealth-based, I can assert that it is not the vulnerable-protagonist stealth gameplay of Alien: Isolation that is stumping me.
Saying that the Alien's behaviour is unpredictable and "natural" may sound like fun, but what it amounts to is repeatedly rolling dice until you get a lucky roll and can move to the next savepoint. The Alien, completely at random as far as I can tell, magically gains the ability to see through hiding places, changes direction without warning, and drops out of holes in the ceiling, sometimes in areas where the player cannot take any action to save himself. Sometimes it does these things, and sometimes you get lucky. If you enjoy reloading saves until you get lucky, then by all means this is the game for you.
To me, it isn't scary at all. It's just frustrating. I got enough of Evil Otto back in the 80's.
Edit: Having put a few more hours into this game in the hopes that it would improve, it doesn't, really. It does become slightly less frustrating, as they give you more options for dealing with the Alien (namely, a flamethrower), but it remains repetitive and far, far too long. Literally nothing works on the first try, and apparently being a space engineer is a comedy of errors, where in order to flip switch A, you have to climb down into a dark scary corridor to flip switch B. But wait, you can't power up switch B because there are 3 circuit breakers that need flipping first-- and so on.
Additionally, a lot of the tension is artificial, generated by the loud soundtrack and overpowering ambient noises (which frequently overpower the dialogue completely. I've missed several bits of story because I simply couldn't hear what was being said over the music or rumbling elevator or hissing steam, or whatever obnoxious overpowering noise. My sound settings are default; I shouldn't have to adjust relative music/speech/environment volume to make the game useable.)
I will finish the game just for the sake of having done so, but it is feeling more and more like a chore. It still isn't scary like Silent Hill or the Shalebridge Cradle in Thief 3. Its jump scares are cheap and it fails at generating a sense of dread, unlike some of the X labs in STALKER games, where you are reluctant to keep moving forward because of the creepy atmosphere and fear of the unknown.
Buy it when it goes down to 14.99 USD or something, if you're curious about the design and atmosphere. Otherwise, just pass on it.

You know, I never expected The Evil Within to come back. I had never played the first one myself, but the videos told you all you needed about it: it was like a broken Resident Evil trying to go back to it's horror roots, with none of the classic characters we all knew and loved.
Given all of that I would NEVER expect a good franchise to be made out of this. Back then I honestly thought this was either gonna be a weak one-shot attempt at creating a new series, or one more franchise that constantly disappoints us.
But they really did it, they pulled it off. The gameplay feels fluid, horror parts can legitimately give you a scare, the graphics are fine and the story is actually great. They even nailed the character development. Sure there were one or two characters that simply didn't have enough screen time to develop more, but they all had the potential to be likeable. The end of the character arc of each friendly character was well-done and impactful, I still wonder what really happened to Sykes.
And the main villains, oh-hoo, let me tell you about that. Each and every villain were a blast to watch, from their maneurisms to their goals, interests and final boss fights. Although I'll say the first major villain, Stefano, simply takes the cake for me. His power was so creative and his strong character traits let him really shine through the start of the game, as you slowly find out more about this phase-shifting murderer that's cut loose in STEM.
The environment also is quite a highlight to this game. While not a complete open world experience, it has fairly large areas in which you can miss events or items that may help you along the story, and honestly just the small stories you can find in houses, or hidden events and/or areas just make it that much more worthwhile to explore it all.
STEM itself is a great choice for the game. Given it's not a real location and is in fact a world created by merging the consciousness of a good number of humans together, you can expect the worst kinds of nightmares to emerge. Or in fact, you can't expect anything. The possibilities of different enemies, be it a giant white blob monster, a "grim reaper" ghost or a sawblade wielding monstruosity, create a far more threatening atmosphere, as you can't fully predict what you'll face next. And hell, even the normal "zombie" enemies are handled well. Their constant hyperactivity, looking at both sides while walking and overall uncertain move pattern, while will get old near the end of the game and experienced players will be able to remember the patterns, give a good challenge to any player that tries to either sneak-kill them or sneak past them.
Overall, this was the game I never knew I wanted so much. This game not only nails being the third person Resident Evil that Capcom never managed to make (instead switching to a first person shooter) but being amongst the best zombie survival games ever made, and that's without it even trying to be that.
9/10 for me. The performance problems a lot of people are complaining about simply haven't affected at all, the game ran smoothly through my entire playtime.

Quick review:
If you enjoy survival horror - action, this is a great game.  Get it.  It's similar to Resident Evil 4 but has a more interesting plot.  It's similar to The Evil Within 1 (obviously), but fixes a great deal of the annoyances of the first.
Pros:
* Story is a lot of fun.  It has a great mix of thrilling and bizarre with a lot of horror elements.
* Enemy designs are well done.
* Controls and camera angles are mostly good. In the first game, there were a lot of issues with this.  These aren't fully fixed but a great deal of the issues from the first are gone.
* Upgrade system is pretty well done.   They give you quite a bit of upgrade material so go ahead and upgrade!
* Game length is quite decent - I'd estimate 15-25 hours.   25 if you're being super completionist.  I logged 19 hours, I missed some things, but I got a good deal of the story things.
* I enjoyed the graphics and they had very cool looking environments.
* Difficulty level was good; it was difficult enough to be challenging and thrilling but not challenging enough to be frustrating.
Cons:
* Stealth can be quite frustrating.  It feels like 75% of the time, they'll turn around right when you're about to perform a stealth kill.  It's also really annoying trying to sneak up behind someone who's just walking normally and finding out you can't cuz they walk faster than you can "sneak" (esp if you don't get upgrades).
* Bugs. The game is a bit buggy.  I apparently went a few places where I wasn't supposed to yet and the areas were bugged.  Like a workbench was unusable and items there were missing.  I left did something else and came back and it fixed itself.  Another point a fuse box had a symbol indicating you could interact, but I couldn't.  There was a point where I called a character to meet me.  It faded out and the character was next to me, but I STILL was talking on the walkie talkie.  After the conversation was over, I stayed on the walkie talkie and couldn't do anything except "press to skip".  I skipped and it fixed itself.
* My most hated boss from Evil Within returns for a cameo in Evil Within 2.  And she's again my least favorite boss.  Laura, for those who are curious.  Basically she auto-kills you if she catches you and you have to try to coax her in a certain area and have her stay there when you flip a switch.  (She's chasing you so it's really annoying).
* Technically the story has some pretty big flaws in it, but if you ignore them, it's a ton of fun.
* A few times they end a cut scene with guys charging at you and it's really hard to avoid getting hit.  I didn't like those.  It rarely happens though.
Some advice for people who decide to play:
Essential skills: Ambush in the Stealth tree (if you hide and a guy comes over you get the option to stealth kill).  Bottle Break also in Stealth (escape grabs as long as you have a bottle).  Second Chance in Health (basically health injections and health kits act like fairies in Zelda- if you die, you don't die, you instead use one of them).
Useful skills: Increasing Stamina and stamina recovery, sneaking speed.
Everything else is nice but you can pick and choose those at your leisure.

TL;DR: good for players new to the MOBA scene, Decent community, Great for partying with friends. Highly recommend.
Camera angle: I won't go to far into other that is unique to Smite, and that it definatly takes away the multitasking of searching the map while controling your character.
Gameplay:
Very streamlined now with the new patch with Season 3. Gods have limited but useful customization with items purchased during play to build them to your play style. Gameplay is similar to league and dota, though map variations (6 maps with respective game modes) introduces variety. Adding to that the 72 Gods to choose from, its pretty good MOBA with some variety to sink your teeth into.
I will add however that Gods go through free rotation just like in LOL and that you can either earn enough favor to buy more or pay actual money for Gods, skins, etc. You do get 4 gods free starting out, however it will take some time and experimentation to know a gods strengths and weaknesses.
Community:
Oh this is an interesting one. You might read a lot of comments praising the Smite community as a paradise. The caveat here is that Smite is a paradise when compared to LOL's community which is known to be infamously bad. Smite is new when compared to its competitors but has gained a sizable player base over the years. That said there are still some players who will harrass others during and even after games. Reporting such players do little if anything, and it really comes down to whether Hi Rez studios can find better alternatives for highlighting abusive players.
Be warned; while the community is pretty great at the best of times, as the game gets bigger and the competitive side grows, expect more toxicisity.

Before I begin my review I'd like to add some context - Just Cause 2 was one of the first games I've played when I got my own pc back in 2011. It was a very enjoyable open world game that defined the current generation of sandbox games. So when Just Cause 3 was announced last year, I was genuinely hyped. Even though these days you can't get hyped about a game without worrying about how it'll perform on launch day, I didn't care, because Just Cause 2 was a very optimized game and Square Enix has a decent record of games with good optimization.
That being said, I was getting ever and ever more doubtful, how the pre-release coverage of the game showed so little as opposed to other AAA titles, how no one was talking about the map, performance or anything. Hell the biggest feature of this franchise, the map, was shown only a week eariler before release. And when it did release, I couldn't play the game because of the horrible optimization. That being said, after a few patches and buying more RAM, I finally got to play it. Now on to the review.
The graphics in this game speaks for itself. You can see farmlands, sunflower fields and scattered villages for miles. The spires of big bases have a very significant apperance of Di Ravello's oppresive regime. Beautiful sea beaches merge with coves and scattered cliffsides. At night the cities and bases light up and provide a beacon for it be discovered.
This game is a treat for the ear as much as the eye - guns sound powerful, sports cars sound ferociously fast and explosions give that great sound of satisfaction that you may not find in any other game.
Now on to the part which I found most controversial. The map of Just Cause 3 seems much more lackluster compared to JC2. There aren't any more landmark locations like the Mile High Club, the Radar Dish, or the Radio Tower. Instead there's just a lot of villages and bases. Sure they look unique from each other, but it's a step back from JC2. Also half of the biggest island is literally walled off and abandoned, where in a similar way in JC2 there were  a lot more villages, bases etc. Roads look like masking tapes put on the floor, the highways have no hoardings above them, there are no dividers and the biggest city - citate di ravello, is as lack luster as it can get.
The gameplay is a bit cumbersome. Auto aiming is gone, so expect a lot missed shots. The health meter is gone, though now it's the same as not getting health pack like in JC2. The minimap is gone, so you won't know where are the enemies and you won't notice the remaining chaos objects without pausing the game and looking up on the map.
Sure they changed the driving model, cars tend not to swivel out of control, but bikes on the other hand will behave realistically and just won't go straight. I wish  the Sleeping Dog's driving model was implemented here.
The biggest change this game offers is the wingsuit and in the sky fortress dlc, it turns into a ♥♥♥♥ing jetpack. Though it's quite fun. It is only one step forward from the last game.

Hell of a game! Great step up from the previous in several ways.
PROS:
- Story and Characters: Boiled down, it's a typical "viva la revolucion", destroy the oppressive regime story, but they did a fantastic job with it. The story missions are entertaining as hell. More distinctly than the previous game, the characters are much better defined and far more interesting.
- Navigation: Holy damn, the wingsuit is fantastic. That, combined with your parachute, fast travel, and vehicles everywhere, getting around is a breeze and loads of fun.
- Weaponry: Easy choice here, it's chaos on a massive scale, and it's balls-to-the-wall fun with tons of options.
- Scenery: Medici is a beautiful place. Even on only "high" settings, it's a well-designed place with towns that feel alive and countryside perfectly populated to feel realistic.
CONS:
- Performance: As is everyone else's complaints, I've noticed it also. Even scaling down to "high" settings, there are occassional dips in FPS, especially with destruction.
- Bugs: There are a few bugs with weaponry and planes, one in particular that prevents campaign completion (heat seeking doesn't working in "Rico and the Rose").
- Police Stations: Claiming most is fine, usually simple. But the "destroy X PLUS cause chaos" leads to a few terribly stupid situations where you're waiting for reinforcements one by one to kill enough crap to conquer it. Dumb mechanic.
- Vehicles: Most are useless, honestly. Motorcycles especially drive like absolute garbage. Most cars/boats don't get much use, you just end up find the most useful tanks/fighters/combat boats and using those. Fun for collecting and messing around, at best.
Honestly, given its scope, there's not too much about the gameplay I have complaints about. It's unadulterated chaos in a beautiful open world. Definitely recommend it.

I personally was rather disappointed by the game, even after just a few minutes. It's been a very long time since I played the classic LucasArts like Monkey Island, Indiana Jones, Day of the Tentacle etc... But what I've kept from these after all these years was the humor, the atmosphere, the consistency of the story. In TWP I've only smiled a few times, was rarely really pleasantly surprised at a situation, rarely thought that one puzzle or another was actually wicked. There's a lot of foul language that IMHO shouldn't have been used ("crap" and &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;, for instance, aren't words I expect to be hearing, and the *beep*ing for the even fouler phrases doesn't really help). The characters are rather bland -- it's actually really disappointing that, even though you can control up to 5 characters, in most cases most of them react exactly the same way to similar situations, have the same conversation lines, etc. Makes you wonder why they give you this many, also because the stories behind each character (and the role they play in the game) are rather weak and feel unfinished. I've fallen in love with Guybrush Threepwood, or even with the hamster in DotT, but none of the characters in TWP have given me that feeling. Honestly, the best moments in this game were when stumbling across one of the ((too?) many) references to one of the olden games, and the memories these brought back ("I'm selling these fine leather jackets" :-D must've missed the three-headed monkey though!). But there's nothing of the sort I will remember from TWP. After more than two years of hope that I would relive the emotions that kept awake up for hours so many years ago, I'm feeling very empty and dissatisfied.
Oh, and actually making me *die* (yup, with a big fat "Game over" across the screen) after telling me that dying is not possible in this game, and having me play again through several loooooong hours (because, well, no auto-save...), was *not* a fun idea.

Alright, here's the essay I accidentally wrote:
I was really looking forward to this, and my playthrough just revealed so much untapped potential. It felt very flat in some ways, like my interactions with NPCs seemed to be lacking depth. I went in with high expectations, but I also went in wanting to love this game with every fibre of my being. I watched the process of it being made and just knew it was going to be something special. And it is. It's definitely unusual.
But like others have said, I felt the ending was a cop-out. Maybe that's in the tradition of similar mystery/sci-fi/x-files-esque media? Just like Twin Peaks, really.
Honestly, I almost wish you had been able to choose one character at the beginning and then stick with them. Or at least talk to the others. I wanted to see Delores interact with the agents, Ransom, etc., which never really happened.
Thinking about it, I just wish the game would developed the conspiracies a little better. I know there are only so many avenues you can take with a plot like this, but by the end it hardly seemed like Ray and Reyes, the original characters from the Kickstarter, mattered at all by the end. It almost seemed like two games spliced together. One with the agents, and one with Dolores where the agents are just vessels to move items around and help with puzzles. (Sorry, Reyes. I still love you.)
Either way, I would play it again. I really hope it makes enough money for them to produce more and better games. The talent is there! Also, I wouldn't mind seeing Dolores again. She was a lovely character.

Basically, this game is a lot of fun until you die a lot or “beat” it a few times. If you are in that group that will dedicate time, you can certainly beat the “dollar an hour” value of the game. If you don’t have a great PC, good internet, and the time for it, I don’t recommend this game.
Graphics: Very pretty shell shading. Not extremely friendly on low end computers.
Audio: Well built. No complaints.
Controls: Other than desync with server, no complaints.
Gameplay: Not friendly. Everything wants to and will kill you. Quite grindy as well.
Replayability: Decent, but still grindy. Death often means you HAVE to replay.
The graphics for the game are quite nice. Just the character alone looks so good that it makes me want to continue playing the game. I have very little complaints about anything appearance wise, not counting the mechanics of the game. The animations are smooth and precise. The game appeared to have no jumping or ‘jittery’ effects while playing.
Again, I have nothing to complain about the audio. Vehicles could be refined a bit, but other than that, everything sounds correct and in place. If you closed your eyes and walked around, you would be able to tell what you’re walking on. If you randomly punched things, you would know what it was. You may even be able to navigate the map if you were blind and had a high quality headset (although I don’t recommend it).
The controls are solid and feel accurate. The buttons are mapped in a sensible way that lets you play without having to look down at the keyboard every 15 seconds to see what button you’re trying to push. The only complaint about controls I have is when playing on a server with high latency.
A bad connection to the server obviously can cause problems, but in some instances, it causes great problems. For example, I was playing on a server that had a less than great ping. I picked up my spear after throwing it and tried to stab a deeralope to death. (Yes, I’m calling it a deeralope.) After picking up the spear, to my client, I was ready to stab. When I went to stab it, the server was out of sync and thought I wanted to throw it. The spear disappeared from my hands and appeared far away in a bush and I froze to death because I couldn’t kill the creature attacking me to stop and build a fire.
Minecraft is a popular game that a lot of people can reference to. Imagine Minecraft with good graphics, you only stay above ground, you’re playing on uber hardcore mode, there’s monsters wanting to kill you all day and night, and food is a lot harder to get. On top of that, crafting supplies is a lot grinder and it’s extremely easy to freeze to death or die from heatstroke. Starter equipment will only take you 30 minutes or so to build up. A simple hut to not freeze to death is also fairly easy. Everything past the starter level equipment is hell. Getting killed is not uncommon, and when it happens, you are often sent back to the start with nothing but the tools you had. If you manage to build up enough equipment to survive well, you’ll likely have to spend hours hunting for more materials to build better equipment. On top of doing all of this work, most servers have a bi-weekly reset. This means everything on the server is wiped and everyone starts from scratch. This is good for people who enjoy building up and grinding to the best equipment and who do well, but if you expect to get to the top of the world by playing this game more relaxed over several weeks or months, sorry for crushing your dreams.
The game is quite replayable if you’re okay with the grind and can survive well. Building bases in new locations, encountering new friends or enemies, getting into small raids or huge fights… Even taking on the wilderness itself can be mysterious and different every time you try. Knowing the entire game is played on multiplayer servers online (there is no single player mode), you will often come across real players. These players may obviously try to help you, take you as a slave, or even kill you on sight. This large human element adds a lot of unpredictability and random encounters to gameplay keeping it very interesting… unless you just get shot and are forced to start the game over every time.
The servers feel very first-come first-served when it comes to controlling the server. The environment and player elements are completely brutal. I was dying for half an hour straight, barely holding on by sacrificing what supplies I had to keep me and a friend going. Just about the time we were both going to kick the bucket, an unknown individual pulled up with an ATV. I had my bow out and my friend had his pistol. We were both prepared to shoot. The guy on the ATV simply wished us a good day and drove off. Confused, my friend and I continued moving. A few moment later, the guy with ATV was riding passenger in a buggy and the driver ran us off the road, did a few loops, and ran both of us over.
That was the last time I played Hurtworld. I didn’t rage, I just didn’t want to grind up again. I can see playing for a bit every night or every other night on a server, but if you don’t really play this game hardcore, you’re not going to get to the top. The graphics are great, I wish my laptop could run it well (had to use my desktop to play). The reason the servers reset is because the game gets boring when you get to the top and people should have opportunities to start fresh with the long term players too. At the same time, dying repeatedly and being forced to nearly start over every time isn’t that much fun either. Basically, this game is a lot of fun until you die a lot or “beat” it a few times. If you are in that group that will dedicate time, you can certainly beat the “dollar an hour” value of the game. If you don’t have a great PC, good internet, and the time for it, I don’t recommend this game.

I really wanted to like this game. The visual style, atmosphere, sound design, and faithfulness to the orgininal film are all amazing. Chunky, unreliable gizmos clunk and whirr and play silly chiptunes while displaying their manufacturer's logos. The Alien looks perfect, makes appropriately creepy sounds, and has convincing animations.
Unfortunately you can't create a good game on style alone. At some point in this game's development, its creators decided that dying repeatedly in the most frustrating and random of ways equates to "scary". Repeating the same areas again and again until the Alien happens to thump off to the right instead of the left, giving you that crucial few seconds to enter a door code or cut it open with a torch simply isn't fun.
As someone who has put many hundreds of hours into the first three Thief games (the ones that count), Achieved the highest ratings in the last few Hitman games, played successfully through Deus Ex: HR and Dishonored in stealth playstyles on high difficulty settings, and even who makes his Skyrim and Fallout-type characters stealth-based, I can assert that it is not the vulnerable-protagonist stealth gameplay of Alien: Isolation that is stumping me.
Saying that the Alien's behaviour is unpredictable and "natural" may sound like fun, but what it amounts to is repeatedly rolling dice until you get a lucky roll and can move to the next savepoint. The Alien, completely at random as far as I can tell, magically gains the ability to see through hiding places, changes direction without warning, and drops out of holes in the ceiling, sometimes in areas where the player cannot take any action to save himself. Sometimes it does these things, and sometimes you get lucky. If you enjoy reloading saves until you get lucky, then by all means this is the game for you.
To me, it isn't scary at all. It's just frustrating. I got enough of Evil Otto back in the 80's.
Edit: Having put a few more hours into this game in the hopes that it would improve, it doesn't, really. It does become slightly less frustrating, as they give you more options for dealing with the Alien (namely, a flamethrower), but it remains repetitive and far, far too long. Literally nothing works on the first try, and apparently being a space engineer is a comedy of errors, where in order to flip switch A, you have to climb down into a dark scary corridor to flip switch B. But wait, you can't power up switch B because there are 3 circuit breakers that need flipping first-- and so on.
Additionally, a lot of the tension is artificial, generated by the loud soundtrack and overpowering ambient noises (which frequently overpower the dialogue completely. I've missed several bits of story because I simply couldn't hear what was being said over the music or rumbling elevator or hissing steam, or whatever obnoxious overpowering noise. My sound settings are default; I shouldn't have to adjust relative music/speech/environment volume to make the game useable.)
I will finish the game just for the sake of having done so, but it is feeling more and more like a chore. It still isn't scary like Silent Hill or the Shalebridge Cradle in Thief 3. Its jump scares are cheap and it fails at generating a sense of dread, unlike some of the X labs in STALKER games, where you are reluctant to keep moving forward because of the creepy atmosphere and fear of the unknown.
Buy it when it goes down to 14.99 USD or something, if you're curious about the design and atmosphere. Otherwise, just pass on it.

You know, I never expected The Evil Within to come back. I had never played the first one myself, but the videos told you all you needed about it: it was like a broken Resident Evil trying to go back to it's horror roots, with none of the classic characters we all knew and loved.
Given all of that I would NEVER expect a good franchise to be made out of this. Back then I honestly thought this was either gonna be a weak one-shot attempt at creating a new series, or one more franchise that constantly disappoints us.
But they really did it, they pulled it off. The gameplay feels fluid, horror parts can legitimately give you a scare, the graphics are fine and the story is actually great. They even nailed the character development. Sure there were one or two characters that simply didn't have enough screen time to develop more, but they all had the potential to be likeable. The end of the character arc of each friendly character was well-done and impactful, I still wonder what really happened to Sykes.
And the main villains, oh-hoo, let me tell you about that. Each and every villain were a blast to watch, from their maneurisms to their goals, interests and final boss fights. Although I'll say the first major villain, Stefano, simply takes the cake for me. His power was so creative and his strong character traits let him really shine through the start of the game, as you slowly find out more about this phase-shifting murderer that's cut loose in STEM.
The environment also is quite a highlight to this game. While not a complete open world experience, it has fairly large areas in which you can miss events or items that may help you along the story, and honestly just the small stories you can find in houses, or hidden events and/or areas just make it that much more worthwhile to explore it all.
STEM itself is a great choice for the game. Given it's not a real location and is in fact a world created by merging the consciousness of a good number of humans together, you can expect the worst kinds of nightmares to emerge. Or in fact, you can't expect anything. The possibilities of different enemies, be it a giant white blob monster, a "grim reaper" ghost or a sawblade wielding monstruosity, create a far more threatening atmosphere, as you can't fully predict what you'll face next. And hell, even the normal "zombie" enemies are handled well. Their constant hyperactivity, looking at both sides while walking and overall uncertain move pattern, while will get old near the end of the game and experienced players will be able to remember the patterns, give a good challenge to any player that tries to either sneak-kill them or sneak past them.
Overall, this was the game I never knew I wanted so much. This game not only nails being the third person Resident Evil that Capcom never managed to make (instead switching to a first person shooter) but being amongst the best zombie survival games ever made, and that's without it even trying to be that.
9/10 for me. The performance problems a lot of people are complaining about simply haven't affected at all, the game ran smoothly through my entire playtime.

Quick review:
If you enjoy survival horror - action, this is a great game.  Get it.  It's similar to Resident Evil 4 but has a more interesting plot.  It's similar to The Evil Within 1 (obviously), but fixes a great deal of the annoyances of the first.
Pros:
* Story is a lot of fun.  It has a great mix of thrilling and bizarre with a lot of horror elements.
* Enemy designs are well done.
* Controls and camera angles are mostly good. In the first game, there were a lot of issues with this.  These aren't fully fixed but a great deal of the issues from the first are gone.
* Upgrade system is pretty well done.   They give you quite a bit of upgrade material so go ahead and upgrade!
* Game length is quite decent - I'd estimate 15-25 hours.   25 if you're being super completionist.  I logged 19 hours, I missed some things, but I got a good deal of the story things.
* I enjoyed the graphics and they had very cool looking environments.
* Difficulty level was good; it was difficult enough to be challenging and thrilling but not challenging enough to be frustrating.
Cons:
* Stealth can be quite frustrating.  It feels like 75% of the time, they'll turn around right when you're about to perform a stealth kill.  It's also really annoying trying to sneak up behind someone who's just walking normally and finding out you can't cuz they walk faster than you can "sneak" (esp if you don't get upgrades).
* Bugs. The game is a bit buggy.  I apparently went a few places where I wasn't supposed to yet and the areas were bugged.  Like a workbench was unusable and items there were missing.  I left did something else and came back and it fixed itself.  Another point a fuse box had a symbol indicating you could interact, but I couldn't.  There was a point where I called a character to meet me.  It faded out and the character was next to me, but I STILL was talking on the walkie talkie.  After the conversation was over, I stayed on the walkie talkie and couldn't do anything except "press to skip".  I skipped and it fixed itself.
* My most hated boss from Evil Within returns for a cameo in Evil Within 2.  And she's again my least favorite boss.  Laura, for those who are curious.  Basically she auto-kills you if she catches you and you have to try to coax her in a certain area and have her stay there when you flip a switch.  (She's chasing you so it's really annoying).
* Technically the story has some pretty big flaws in it, but if you ignore them, it's a ton of fun.
* A few times they end a cut scene with guys charging at you and it's really hard to avoid getting hit.  I didn't like those.  It rarely happens though.
Some advice for people who decide to play:
Essential skills: Ambush in the Stealth tree (if you hide and a guy comes over you get the option to stealth kill).  Bottle Break also in Stealth (escape grabs as long as you have a bottle).  Second Chance in Health (basically health injections and health kits act like fairies in Zelda- if you die, you don't die, you instead use one of them).
Useful skills: Increasing Stamina and stamina recovery, sneaking speed.
Everything else is nice but you can pick and choose those at your leisure.

First, The positive!
I'd never really played much of the original series of king's quest games, but have always been into the adventure style games (some point and click, some not) and so when I saw this game on steam I figured it was worth a try. And boy was it!
From the very first chapter it is quite easy to see how much care, attention and even love has been poured into this game, and altogether it helps to suck you in to the story. This is especially good considering that not everyone will have played the previous games and so it does a very good job of not excluding you if you aren't aware what came before. That being said, there are plenty of throwbacks that remind you of puzzles, characters and plot points that were in previous games and as a newby to the series it did quite well at explaining these without breaking the feeling of the story.
The art style is reminiscent of some of the telltale games that I have previously played (namely a mix of The Walking Dead and Game of Thrones) and whilst it is cartoony, it is also quite beautiful. The developer's have really made a huge effort to give the characters some gravitas too by selecting voice actor's that are of good calibur such as Christopher Lloyd, Wallace Shawn and Tom Kenny in particular, all of which make the characters come to life.
The story is masterfully done and each chapter tells a story that would have fit between some of the previous games. This means that whilst it refer's to some event's that have previously taken place, you don't necessarily have to have experienced them yourself as it does quite a good job of explaining thoise things to you. The ending, even though rather obvious to me personally, was also very well written and did a good job of tapping into your emotions due to the depth of the characters that you had experienced throughout the game.
The puzzles are all quite well thought out too and there are a good mix of easy ones to get you going in each chapter, followed by a few that will likely require a bit of time and logic to progress. Also there seems to be several ways to complete some of them which I thought was a nice touch considering that it would offer you some variation on a second and possibly third playthrough. This can range from allying with one particular npc or another, solving a puzzle iwith either logic, strength or skill, and to what you buy and what exactly that will do to the ctiry on your current playthrough.
Now for the bad,
After completing the game I decided that it was so good that I would look to see if there were plans for a sequel, although instead of finding this info (it doesn't look like there will ever be one) I found something a little more sinister. It seems that the developers (The Odd Gentlemen - TOG) had previously created a kickstarter project in order to fund a game for the IP Homestuck through the publicher What Pumpkin (WP). They successfully obtained the funds required for the game, but during development TOG also obtained the rights for King's Quest and subsequently ceased their development of Hiveswap so that they could concentrate on Kings Quest. This meant that the funds they had obtained from the kickstarter project (or a portion there of) were then used to create King's Quest instead of the game for which they were intended. Personally, I see this as a very shady business practice that is borderline theft, and from the research I have done it does seem that I am not alone in that view. This obviously leaves me somewhat conflicted about the game and certainly about the developers TOG.
So would I recommend buying this game?
This is indeed a bit of a tough one from the moral side of things, as I do not think what TOG did was right by any stretch of the imagination but the game itself is a considerably good one. After playing through the game and seeing the love and dedication that has been poured into it, I would say that yes I would recommend buying the game SO LONG AS it is on sale for a very low price or you can obtain it from someone who maybe even is a key reseller (which I really wouldn't use on any other circumstance). This is basically because I think that King's Quest is a very well made game that deserves the time of anyone who likes puzzle games, but ethically I would not recommend paying full price to a company that would effectively steal people's money through a bogus kickstarter project. I can say that I really did enjoy every minute of the game and will play it again in the future, but I honestly do not want to ever purchase a TOG product ever again after what I have discovered about the company. If the company had have acted ethically I would say that the game is worth anything up to £20/$25 but as they didn't seem to, I wouldn't recommend paying any more than £5/$8.
It's worth noting that What Pumpkin has also now continued development on the Hiveswap game, but obviously it is several years after it was originally planned due to the actions of TOG. So the people waiting for it will get a happy ending, eventually!

This older-syle of game (with verbs you use on/with items) tend to be tricker for me but I haven't encountered any "bad video game logic" moments yet.  I didn't have any real expectations going into this game but it is a very likely candidate for my top games of the year.

This is a complicated game to review.  I did enjoy it.  It was more than long enough to justify the price.  It definitely felt like a good balance of oldschool mechanics and modern (superior) adventure game conventions.  Not particularly atmospheric in terms of graphics or music, but it more than gets the job done.  The characters were more interesting than I expected.
But there are problems here, particularly with the ending.  The ending breaks the fourth wall more dramatically than anything I can recall having seen before.  That's more or less fine, but it completely takes the place of a proper ending, which the game then, simply, lacks.  This is frustrating because, to make it that far, you have to really keep the goals and objectives of all five characters in mind and play to resolve them.  As a (somewhat spoiler-y) example,
That occurs halfway through the game, and, just in case you happened to find at least that bit satisfying, the game eventually makes it clear that all you were really doing there was
Further, it's possible (if not extremely likely) that you'll simply complete the game with the character who's most obviously making progress first, which will then cause the game to end without any resolution for the other four characters at all.  This seems fine at first -- the ending isn't entirely unpleasant -- but it sneaks up on you later.  "Wait.  There was no ending, really.  It's like they just tried to ship the game on time by not making one, and just repurposed what was originally intended to be an easter egg to stand in for one."
Aside from that, there are things that the game does well.  It makes very good use of the "multiple characters" puzzle mechanic (even if it frequently does so despite there being NO WAY these characters could even be aware enough of each other's problems to work together in the first place).  It's often goofily funny, which, coming from me, is high praise indeed, because my sense of humor usually has different preferences.  Puzzle logic is thoroughly sensible, even in cases where the puzzles themselves are kinda not.  Making progress after being stuck for a bit feels really rewarding.
All in all, a good experience.  You will likely want to go back and play it again because you're annoyed with it -- an odd, mixed statement of praise, but praise nonetheless.

Alien : Isolation... Where do I start with this one? I should preface this review with a disclaimer. I played the entire game in virtual reality via the Oculus Rift DK2. My review will be based on that experience. Playing on a monitor is sure to be a different feeling and I do plan to replay the entire game that way. When I do I will add to the bottom of the review what I thought of playing it that way.
In the 90s there was a virtual reality arcade in the mall where I worked at a movie theater. It was the Virtuality machines that ran a game called Dactyl Nightmare. By VR standards, or any standard really, this game was pretty awful. I loved it however because I'd never experienced anything like it. I told myself the minute Sega and Nintendo bring this technology home I was getting it. Years went by. Nintendo gave us the horrific Virtual Boy. We gave it back. There was nothing “virtual” about it. VR didn't happen. The technology just wasn't there. Years rolled and I forgot about it. Fast forward to about   2013 or so and all of a sudden I hear about a new company called Oculus. This time VR is going to happen they say. I'll believe it when I see it. I saw it. I now believe it. But there's still no “killer app” for VR. Even Oculus themselves bemoan that fact and say they can't wait until that happens. They're excited to see what it will be.
It's already here. And what's even more fitting is that after all the years it was Sega that brought it home. Alien Isolation is absolutely VR's killer app by a mile. Everything about this game is amazing in the Rift. The developers at Creative Assembly have hit a major home run with this game. Never will you have experienced anything in the Rift like this. I found myself thinking about this game. Dreaming about it. Always wanting to hurry up and get back home so I could put the headset back on and disappear into Seegson's run down and destroyed Sevastopol space station. I wasn't just playing a video game. I was actually there. I have “3-D memories” for lack of a better way to describe this. Whenever I think of this game I remember being in that place. I have dreams of being on a space station and being terrified for my life. I have dreams of walking in space and looking out at a blazing star and a huge gas giant. I was on Sevastopol. No other game can do this. Our future will be filled with these experiences but right now Alien is the one that does it.
The game was clearly created by people who are huge fans of the first Alien movie. You can see it everywhere. The detail is astounding. The sounds are all from the movie. The doors, computer terminals and every little beep and sound you can think of. If you've seen Alien you will recognize it all. The space ship you start out on is Weyland-Yutani through and through. It's unmistakable. These people left no little detail undone. We've always wished someone would finally make a proper Alien game and now it has finally happened. Some have called this game a love letter to all the Alien fans and that about sums it up. Creative Assembly did their homework. No Alien game ever made could hope to touch this. Thank you Sega for standing behind this and distributing a very risky game with a AAA backed development. This could have been a disaster. I can't really see any major studio taking a gamble on a game like this. But Sega did and for that I'm ecstatic.
The Alien truly is scary in VR and the AI of this thing is totally unpredictable. There are cues you will learn. Did it hiss? It probably saw you. Sneak away and hide somewhere else. Did it scream? You're f*@ked. Run! The tools you can craft are quite useful at diverting it's attention and even getting it to get rid of other humans who are in your way. I never tired of the cat and mouse game with the alien. It was always incredibly intense and led to wild events that I will always remember as some of my greatest gaming moments. Flying down a hallway screaming with this thing tearing behind you while it keeps stopping to kill the random other human you just ran past... scary and pulse pounding. Hiding under beds while it stomps around the room screaming and smacking things around and looking under stuff trying to find you... wow. In VR you won't forget these moments. There are times in the game where you are prompted to hold your breath. In real life you will already be doing that.
The game is not without it's flaws. And the only flaws I can find are related to the VR implementation which Creative Assembly didn't actually finish. They aren't deal breakers but I really do wish CA would go back and finish the VR support and make the game perfect because it's just so close.
1. Using computers in the game causes the computer screen to fly up into your face. On a monitor this is nice I'm sure. In VR this is wildly painful. You have to close one eye or you will get insane eye strain trying to view the screen up that close. This is also a problem, though to a slightly lesser degree, when cutting open doors with the torch.
2. The headset does not stay horizontally centered and will occasionally require you to re-center it. It's not a major problem. It's easy to do. Just tap both shoulder buttons on the controller at the same time and it re-centers. Still, it would be nice if I didn't need to do that at all.
3.  Judder. The game does judder a bit in places with wide open areas. Most of the time though the game ran perfectly smooth which shocked me with how awesome the graphics are and having to run it in stereo 3-D at 75fps. But it actually worked really really good! Just wish it worked that way all the time. I think we can chalk this up to video card technology not quite being good enough for VR yet though and not really something Creative Assembly did wrong. I use a Geforce GTX 980 but even that isn't really good enough for the type of VR experiences we all hope to be able to have. Nvidia needs to step it up.
That's really all I can say bad about the game. Some people complained about “wooden acting” but I don't know what game they played. The acting was great in this game. I have no complaints there. Others complained that it was too long. The game is longer than you think it will be. There are many times where you are convinced you're at the end but then you realize you aren't. I love the game so much I was always happy to realize it wasn't actually over. I will agree that it pulls the pacing down a bit but this isn't a movie. This is an event that is happening to you. You are there. It isn't about pacing. It's just about getting through this horror on this space station and were this real life no one would say “Wow. That was crazy. I can't believe that happened to me. The pacing was a little slow though.” I think the reviewers for websites that complained about length mostly did so because they need to hurry and get through the game to get the review out as soon as possible and it was probably aggravating to them that the game didn't end in 10 or 15 hours. I finished it in 30 hours and I wish it were longer.
This is clearly the 2014 game of the year and easily one of the greatest gaming experiences of my life. I'll never forget the terror of standing at a save station, inserting the card (complete with original Alien sounds!) and thinking 'Hurry! Hurry! Hurry! Save!' and hearing a hiss. You think to yourself, “Was that a pipe? Oh no... it's behind me isn't it?” And then you hear the squishy gut stabbing sound of it's tail running you through as you look down and watch it happen.
They even managed to make saving the game a panic inducing gameplay mechanic.
10/10

This game is one of the best games i've ever played for many reasons. Not only does it have amazing realistic graphics, but the gameplay is richer than most games. I usually am not into horror games but this one realed me in due to the fact that I really enjoyed the movie. I was very impressed with the way the game turned out because most remakes of movies or books or shows aren't so amazing. The ability to craft things and interact with the world around you gives the game a survival feel, whether you're playing Campaign or survival mode. Another thing about the gameplay I found impressive was the mobility and control you have over your movements. You can choose to slightly peek over ledges, hide in small areas, hold your breath, and even your focus changes when you look at an item up close. This sort of additions into gameplay are small but do make a difference, it brings you closer to real life and makes the game feel more immersive, which is very important in horror and survival games. The ability to craft new items as you progress gives you a feeling of progression and the game changes as you go through it, you can go from shooting things w/ a revolver to disabling androids with EMPs and blowing up people with pipe bombs. But, even after all those great aspects of the game, the story was interesting and exciting. Ripley was a great main character, and behaved very realisitically to the situations that she was presented in, escaping homocidal white bald robots, almost getting smashed by multiple large objects in the game (such as elevators or reckage), and hiding from the Alien. The story itself was interesting and rich with twists and obstacles, but the most memorable thing was for sure Ripley. Finally, when you go on a space walk (which happens a few times in the game) and go outside and see the planet you are orbiting, the station itself, and even the sun, you can get a true understanding about how unbelievably great the graphics are in the game. Overall, I give the game a 10/10, there was not a single issue with the game I could find and I enjoyed every second of playing it, it did exactly and much more than any horror survival should do, scare you and encourage you to survive. Get this game, you will not regret it.

A glorious homage to the original Alien film, capturing the look and sound perfectly and gradually introducing motifs from the original soundtrack throughout the game. Almost embarrassingly thrilling to discover voice-notes recorded by the original cast later in the game too. It completely immerses you in the Alien/Nostromo universe. Where it falls down for me is in mechanics - there seem to be very limited options for tackling the various adversaries you'll encounter, and while that fits in with the overall concept of the game and its vulnerable, human protagonist, it means that gameplay itself can become a faintly tedious creep-hide-creep-hide experience. Perhaps I approached it in the wrong way, expecting to be able to tackle an area with a combination of stealth and action - this game is not as flexible as say, Dishonored. Having said that, it does deliver in the tension department - hiding in a locker, drawing back and holding your breath (in game, and in real life!) when the Alien is right outside the door is just one example.
I've just finished the main story, have yet to try the other game modes and the DLC (a bit annoyed that the Season Pass doesn't include all of it, unlike Season Passes I've bought for other games), so will be going back to it, but I think I'm unlikely to replay the original game right through again.  Even having said all this, the best Alien game I've ever played (and I go all the way back to 'Aliens' on the ZX Spectrum!).
Should mention the game seemed rather crash-prone on my normally reliable system, seems to have settled down after a recent large update but for a time it was impossible to get it to even get past the loading video without crashing to the desktop, but the following day it would work again.

This is definitely my choice for the game of 2014. Instead of rehashing the typical action-based shooter style game that Gearbox spectacularly failed at when producing Aliens: Colonial Marines, Alien: Isolation primarily focuses on stealth mechanics to project its sense of suspenseful horror and it just simply excels at it. Not that stealth games are new and coming by any stretch of the imagination but it certainly is specifically for the Alien franchise and it's refreshingly different by AAA standards.
Speaking of AAA standards, the production value of this game is nothing less than stellar and the developers' attention to detail in building the 1979's vision for what the future looks is ubiquitous and just down-right awesome. The props in the environments are filled with CRTs, Commodore-64 looking keyboards and analog-tape driven tech (ie. cassette tapes). The horror element comes and goes particularly when frustration sets in due to the difficult nature of the game but it still sometimes finds itself now and then, which is okay with me since the horror element almost always goes away after the first few levels of any horror game.
If you're a fan of horror, stealth, the Alien franchise or all of the above (as I am), then you're probably going to really enjoy this game. As noted before, this game is very HARD and I'd advise Normal or Easy (or Novice =P) difficulty if you're not very good at stealth games. However, its difficulty and other problems are very minor issues to me and I'm very glad they did not compromise for the sake of mere broad appeal. Kudos to Creative Assembly who somehow managed to produce this awesome game despite a lengthy history of RTS games. It's the best game in the Alien franchise I've played since Aliens vs. Predator (1999) and I definitely highly recommend it.
And you should definitely only play this in the dark and with the audio turned up!

Black Mesa is a remake of the 1998 classic Half-Life, made by fans, for fans, and it shows in every facet of the game. From the beautiful art to the faithful-yet-original voice acting, to the just-updated-enough gameplay, everything in Black Mesa not only shows off what makes Half-Life a special series of games, but why we need more games like it.
As it's currently in Early Access with the final few chapters of the game scheduled to come out summer 2017, completionists might want to wait until the game is fully finished, but anyone who wants to experience the bulk of the game now should definetly pick it up.
Also, for those creative types, Black Mesa has workshop support and comes with a set-up copy of Hammer Editor for all your level design needs.

With a release that could be compared to PTSD, Rome II has evolved into a truly great game.
There's a variety in the vanilla version, and a plethora of workshop content to keep you sated.
We'll look at Pros/Cons
Pros -
- Each culture has it's own preferred variant of warfare - Barbarians benefit more from a blitz strategy, while with the Greeks you'll find yourself wanting atleast a single 20-stack (A term for a full army) before you're able to deal with the many contenders around you.
- Semi-competent AI can keep you on your toes until you learn the mechanics of the game, and even then it can still surprise you, with few playthroughs of the Grand Campaign being quite the same (What comes to mind is the one time I managed to sign a Non-Aggression pact with the Seleucids as Egypt without ever being at war, something I've yet to replicate.)
- Romans aren't the Godsbane they were in Rome 1. I cannot stress how much better it is that Rome doesn't steamroll everything that flinches, though depending on your culture and when you encounter them, it can be easier/harder. (Most nations will need a ranged heavy army, especially Barbarians.)
- Civil Wars and other political shennanigans. This is a mechanic that for some reason irritates people, I find it absolutely fun. It adds a new level of management to your nation, and drives home the point that the larger your empire is, the harder it is to maintain.
- A fixed negotiation system. Any player of early Rome II will appreciate this, as it frustrated the game for a non-aggressive player.
- Unit positions matter. If you face your pikemen on the spade tip of your formation, they'll be much more effective than they would on a flank. Even what direction you face your unit matters, especially in defence/formation movement.
- Ability to use real world tactics/strategies to your heart's content. It may seem like you can do this in most Strategy games, but the ability to do so in Rome II truly shines. Charging the enemy's ranged backfield with a flanking force of calvary will cause your enemy's melee front to shift confusedly, as the AI attempts to divert troops. You'll find yourself actually using your shock calvary's charge multiple times, as opposed to leaving them bogged down in melee.
- (Somewhat) unique city designs - Cities like Alexandria look and feel different than Carthago or Athens, with the fully upgraded versions possessing an absolutely (in my opinion) stunning view, Carthago's harbor being a shining example.
Cons -
- Somewhat repetitive town/city design (Exceptions being major/named cities, IE Rome, Alexandria, Carthago.) Means you'll often find yourself using the same repetitive flanking manuvers while taking small unwalled, lightly defended settlements, and when the AI has a large enough army it generally will sally forth, taking much of the fun out of smaller urban fighting. I sometimes spend more time in the deployment phase than I do in the actual battle, trying to make a challenging approach to the settlement.
- DLC  - Everyone loves DLC. Everyone hates horribly overpriced DLC. That said, is it horribly overpriced? No. It is overpriced, but not at a WH40k Dawn of War II level. (Though it might be getting there.) Most DLC looks like it should've just been lumped into one 5-9 dollar package, and I've abstained from Pirate and Raiders and Daughters of Mars at the time of this review due to lack of interest, though Pirates and Raiders might soon join my collection.
- Multiplayer - I don't even try to play the game on multiplayer, my first day of it ended in frustration, it simply feels like you're being... Rushed. I don't like that from my Strategy games. Rushing is for Barbarians. (excuse the pun, Iceni players).
- Somewhat challenging to begin - I never even finished the tutorials, finding them not very helpful and participating in them up to the last mission simply for the story. My real education in how to play the game came at the reigns of the Egyptians, which I warmly reccomend to any starting player, they start in a powerful position with very little threat until (generally) turn 5.
- Unit clumping is OP. - Get a line of Pikemen. Put hoplites in front of the pikemen, but make the pikes stick further than the hoplites are positioned. Congratulations, you now have a melee line that is unlikely to ever break as long as it has missile support, primarily for killing off enemy javilinmen/slingers/archers. Unfortunately, clumping ranged units causes them not to attack. You've been warned.
- Skirmishers in skirmish mode. I understand, they run faster, they're ranged. I get that. But when 3 units of slingers can rout 12+ units of infantry just by outrunning turning around, and running as soon as they get close... I want to say it makes logical sense. I really do. But I just can't see it being believeable from unmounted units. Skirmish mode also has a wonderful ability to -ruin- your defensive line if you don't turn it off.
- Sieges. While the AI is undoubtedly better, and my performance on the sieges no longer consists of using slowmo or lagging to the point that I'm in slowmo, I've yet to actually put effort into holding a siege. There's never been a situation where my siege ladders didn't cut it. I dunno, I'd like to actually have encouragement to use other siege weapons.
Overall rating - 8/10
Reccomended?
Yes.
DLC reccomended?
There's really no reason for anything other than the campaign packs in my opinion, maybe the Greek Cultures if you're into leaning that way, and maybe if they're on sale.
Either way there are mods to unlock every subfaction that isn't unlocked by DLC already, and unit expansion mods to help beef up their rosters.
The only DLCs I actually find myself playing consistently are the Greek Cultures and the Augustus Imperator pack (Emperor Edition), and Hannibal at the Gates (Syracuse ftw).
Would play for another 700 + hours.
