When I started playing this game, I felt a little conflicted about it since the atmosphere didn't feel anything like the first game, and I wasn't sure about the more open world aspect. However, I started to think about this game's atmosphere in a similar way to the difference in atmosphere in the Alien movies, and I started to enjoy this game much more. The first Alien movie has a more dreadful atmosphere and tone than Aliens, which makes both of those movies kind of their own thing. I enjoyed the first TEW despite it's flaws, since I thought it had nice atmosphere and was fun to play. Don't me wrong, the gameplay mechanics in TEW2 are quite similar to the first, but there are many improvements to the first and that's probably why I enjoyed this game as much as I did. I actually found this game really hard to put down at points and I would end up playing it for 3 hours at a time. I played this game on nightmare difficulty, since I was told the survival difficulty wasn't really all that difficult, so keep that in mind as I write this review.
Gameplay Pros:
What I really like is that this game makes the combat feel like you're trying to survive, making use of the enviroment around you. Stealth is actually functional this time around, and you'll probably want to invest your green gel points into it first, since supplies are kind of scarce early on in the game, making you want to keep actual combat to a minimum. What makes encounters with enemies so fun is that each encounter requires a bit more thought than just trying to get in a good headshot. You can use the foliage to hide, kick over barrels to make puddles of gasoline, which you can shoot and set on fire. It's a blast to play.
Gameplay Cons:
The aiming feels a little worse than the first game, and it's partly due to the fact that almost all enemies are faster than the ones in the first game, but the actual aiming itself feels a little awkward, but maybe this is intentional. One thing I do miss from the first game is the match dropping mechanic, which is replaced by a stomp mechanic, but it's just not the same.
Visual Pros:
Some of the interiors of this game look really good, and I especially like the enviroments that you see when you face the first villain, Stefano. Those areas are thick with atmosphere and have really neat looking lighting.
Visual Cons:
Unfortunately, for every interesting looking location, there's a bland and kind of weak looking enviroment. The open areas of Union don't look all that great in my opinion. While this game's graphics are objectively improved over the first, this game lacks the stylistic flair that the first game had, which almost makes me prefer the first games visuals. The game's frame rate also didn't run at a solid 60 fps for me, so it's probably not very optimized, just to warn you.
Audio Pros:
There's a great cover of a Duran Duran song that you probably heard in this game's first trailer, and it still sounds great in here. The audio does a great job at helping the player keep alert of enemies around them. As I can tell each enemy apart off screen by their distinctive sounds that you learn while playing the game. The sound I heard would sometimes dictate how I would act in a certain scenario, which is pretty cool.
Audio Cons:
The voice actors have been replaced since the first game and they're not that great. Sebastian's voice sometimes doesn't seem to really fit.
Story Pros:
The story is cheesy good fun, and managed to keep me engaged towards the very end. Mentioning the end, this game's ending is quite satisfying, much more so than many other games. Overall it's quite entertaining.
Story Cons:
The dialogue can be quite cheesy, which I see more as a pro for me, since I kind of enjoy unintentionally funny dialogue, but I'll list it as a con anyways. I laughed when Sebastian would say lines like "ENOUGH OF YOUR ART SCHOOL ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥T!".
Overall, this game is a lot of fun, and I think you should give it a try if you like third person combat/exploration games at all. I can understand getting this game on sale, but it honestly has a good amount of content for a single player only game. You'll probably finish it in around 15-20 hours if you don't rush your playthrough. I'm already replaying it and it's still a blast to play. I've only stopped playing to play Wolfenstein 2, but I'll most likely come back to this game at some point before this year ends. Good game.

Disclaimer: I played this game on nightmare difficulty so I'm not sure if everything I say applies for other difficulties.
Very enjoyable game. For me it's big step forward from The Evil Within. Game now offers combination of open world and linear gameplay which in my opinion works really well. Exploration is very interesting and yields many rewards from ammo to ammo pouches and better weapons. Side missions are interesting - though there isn't that many of them. Sometimes you can actually get confused if you are working on a side or main mission since they are all very well done with cutscenes and they are not repetitive. There are many types of weapons in game and they further divide into sub-types where you can choose between different types of hundguns and shotguns - all of these have different playstyle advanteges and disadvanteges.
Although there are many weapons in game I found myself mainly using handgun and when I ran out of ammo I switched to crossbow or shotgun. I almost never used any other weapons in-game mainly because ammo for them is super difficult to find and in case of sniper rifle more expensive to craft. So in the end I was only crafting Harpoon bolts and handgun ammo.
This brings me to crafting. Crafting in this game is really interesting. You can craft ammo, bolts for your crosbow or medical supplies. I myself had only one problem and that was crossbow bolts need too much gunpowder to craft (the only bolt that doesn't need gunpowder is Harpoon). So in the end I was mainly crafting pistol ammo since I had all damage upgrades and I could drop enemies with 2-3 hits to their head.
There is also new skill tree which allows you to unlock new skills with green goo. I personally recomend going for stealth at the start since many enemies can tank so much damage before they drop and it's easier to stealth kill them.
The game is really well optimised. I managed to go all the way up with my old GTX960 2gbs.
Overall I enjoyed the game and I recomend it to everyone. My only two problems:
1) The game got a bit frustrating in about half way through, where ammo was so scarce I was constantly stuck with about 3 bullets to pistol and 1-2 buckshots for my shotty. The game does a great job with giving you ammo during boss fights, though.
2) Hit registration felt really bad when enemies got too close.
For me it's solid 8/10.

TL;DR: good for players new to the MOBA scene, Decent community, Great for partying with friends. Highly recommend.
Camera angle: I won't go to far into other that is unique to Smite, and that it definatly takes away the multitasking of searching the map while controling your character.
Gameplay:
Very streamlined now with the new patch with Season 3. Gods have limited but useful customization with items purchased during play to build them to your play style. Gameplay is similar to league and dota, though map variations (6 maps with respective game modes) introduces variety. Adding to that the 72 Gods to choose from, its pretty good MOBA with some variety to sink your teeth into.
I will add however that Gods go through free rotation just like in LOL and that you can either earn enough favor to buy more or pay actual money for Gods, skins, etc. You do get 4 gods free starting out, however it will take some time and experimentation to know a gods strengths and weaknesses.
Community:
Oh this is an interesting one. You might read a lot of comments praising the Smite community as a paradise. The caveat here is that Smite is a paradise when compared to LOL's community which is known to be infamously bad. Smite is new when compared to its competitors but has gained a sizable player base over the years. That said there are still some players who will harrass others during and even after games. Reporting such players do little if anything, and it really comes down to whether Hi Rez studios can find better alternatives for highlighting abusive players.
Be warned; while the community is pretty great at the best of times, as the game gets bigger and the competitive side grows, expect more toxicisity.

Always playing as Corvo so the gameplay is very similar to Dishonored 1 which is just fine by me. I really do not need (and probably do not want) total control/combat overhaul in every new game of the series (prime example of things going worse and worse being Dragon Age series).
Compared to Dishonored 1 the story setting seems less omnious (the original game world, if memory doesn´t fail me, was a bit darker with the rat plague and all). I kind of liked that setting slitghly better.
Another difference - I would say there were more interesting NPCs in Dishonored 1, let´s call them secondary characters. I especially remember the witch. I believe/remember you interacted with these NPCs much more. I might by wrong, but I know I won´t remember any secondary NPC from this game 6 months on, non of them is really memorable in any way.
Dishonored 2 seems more fair compared to Dishonored 1 because there are very few unexpected one hit death situations, you can basically remember them all after the first playthrough. I like that, one hit deaths are cheap. ;-)
People are reporting issues with controls, especially mouse I think. I have to say I´m glad I have 5000 DPI gaming mouse, because the game is playable just fine if I set mouse sensitivity in-game to max and mouse also to max 5000 DPI. Anything less (for example 3000 DPI) and mouse cursor moves way way too slowly, basically it would made the game close to unplayable. But as I said, with my 5000 DPI optical gaming mouse, it works fine.
Overall I´m very satisfied with the game. Storyline/lore is okay (I would rate it as slightly worse than Dishonored 1), gameplay is very similar yet I believe more fair, maps are fun to fight through and explore (for example in newest Tomb Rider I had difficulty motivating myself to explore whole areas, actually after first few maps I just gave up and ran through to finish the story and never look back). NCPs are again slightly less interesting compared to Dishonored 1 but still okay. Graphics improved (cannot play the game fully maxed on Gigabytes OC 980ti but close to it), music and sounds are fine.
Will be interesting to see where will the series go next. They created some nice options in the lore, if you were actually paying attention to the lore (I´m reading every book I find in every playthrough ;-)).

This is a wonderful love letter to the LucasArts adventure games of old.  Sam and Max holds a spot in my gaming heart.  Monkey Island will always be my favorite.  Maniac Mansion was an obsession.  Thimbleweed Park rests alongside those games, feeling like a warm cozy blanket of nostalgia.
This game is how I remember adventure gaming to be, even though there are afew more modern design elements that make this a more technically impressive package.  In a nutshell, this is a tightly crafted point and click adventure game, with multiple characters and an engrossing plot-a-boo.  There are tons of nods to the genre, to LucasArts games in particular and a metric ton of easter eggs and ties to Ron Gilbert's own games.
I cannot recommend this game enough if you are a fan of Maniac Mansion, Monkey Island or any of the LucasArts adventure game-a-renos.

This game is one of the best games i've ever played for many reasons. Not only does it have amazing realistic graphics, but the gameplay is richer than most games. I usually am not into horror games but this one realed me in due to the fact that I really enjoyed the movie. I was very impressed with the way the game turned out because most remakes of movies or books or shows aren't so amazing. The ability to craft things and interact with the world around you gives the game a survival feel, whether you're playing Campaign or survival mode. Another thing about the gameplay I found impressive was the mobility and control you have over your movements. You can choose to slightly peek over ledges, hide in small areas, hold your breath, and even your focus changes when you look at an item up close. This sort of additions into gameplay are small but do make a difference, it brings you closer to real life and makes the game feel more immersive, which is very important in horror and survival games. The ability to craft new items as you progress gives you a feeling of progression and the game changes as you go through it, you can go from shooting things w/ a revolver to disabling androids with EMPs and blowing up people with pipe bombs. But, even after all those great aspects of the game, the story was interesting and exciting. Ripley was a great main character, and behaved very realisitically to the situations that she was presented in, escaping homocidal white bald robots, almost getting smashed by multiple large objects in the game (such as elevators or reckage), and hiding from the Alien. The story itself was interesting and rich with twists and obstacles, but the most memorable thing was for sure Ripley. Finally, when you go on a space walk (which happens a few times in the game) and go outside and see the planet you are orbiting, the station itself, and even the sun, you can get a true understanding about how unbelievably great the graphics are in the game. Overall, I give the game a 10/10, there was not a single issue with the game I could find and I enjoyed every second of playing it, it did exactly and much more than any horror survival should do, scare you and encourage you to survive. Get this game, you will not regret it.

A glorious homage to the original Alien film, capturing the look and sound perfectly and gradually introducing motifs from the original soundtrack throughout the game. Almost embarrassingly thrilling to discover voice-notes recorded by the original cast later in the game too. It completely immerses you in the Alien/Nostromo universe. Where it falls down for me is in mechanics - there seem to be very limited options for tackling the various adversaries you'll encounter, and while that fits in with the overall concept of the game and its vulnerable, human protagonist, it means that gameplay itself can become a faintly tedious creep-hide-creep-hide experience. Perhaps I approached it in the wrong way, expecting to be able to tackle an area with a combination of stealth and action - this game is not as flexible as say, Dishonored. Having said that, it does deliver in the tension department - hiding in a locker, drawing back and holding your breath (in game, and in real life!) when the Alien is right outside the door is just one example.
I've just finished the main story, have yet to try the other game modes and the DLC (a bit annoyed that the Season Pass doesn't include all of it, unlike Season Passes I've bought for other games), so will be going back to it, but I think I'm unlikely to replay the original game right through again.  Even having said all this, the best Alien game I've ever played (and I go all the way back to 'Aliens' on the ZX Spectrum!).
Should mention the game seemed rather crash-prone on my normally reliable system, seems to have settled down after a recent large update but for a time it was impossible to get it to even get past the loading video without crashing to the desktop, but the following day it would work again.

This is definitely my choice for the game of 2014. Instead of rehashing the typical action-based shooter style game that Gearbox spectacularly failed at when producing Aliens: Colonial Marines, Alien: Isolation primarily focuses on stealth mechanics to project its sense of suspenseful horror and it just simply excels at it. Not that stealth games are new and coming by any stretch of the imagination but it certainly is specifically for the Alien franchise and it's refreshingly different by AAA standards.
Speaking of AAA standards, the production value of this game is nothing less than stellar and the developers' attention to detail in building the 1979's vision for what the future looks is ubiquitous and just down-right awesome. The props in the environments are filled with CRTs, Commodore-64 looking keyboards and analog-tape driven tech (ie. cassette tapes). The horror element comes and goes particularly when frustration sets in due to the difficult nature of the game but it still sometimes finds itself now and then, which is okay with me since the horror element almost always goes away after the first few levels of any horror game.
If you're a fan of horror, stealth, the Alien franchise or all of the above (as I am), then you're probably going to really enjoy this game. As noted before, this game is very HARD and I'd advise Normal or Easy (or Novice =P) difficulty if you're not very good at stealth games. However, its difficulty and other problems are very minor issues to me and I'm very glad they did not compromise for the sake of mere broad appeal. Kudos to Creative Assembly who somehow managed to produce this awesome game despite a lengthy history of RTS games. It's the best game in the Alien franchise I've played since Aliens vs. Predator (1999) and I definitely highly recommend it.
And you should definitely only play this in the dark and with the audio turned up!

I picked it up for $1.25 on sale. I'd heard it was the spiritual predecesor to Bioshock, which I hadn't played, but was expecting an 'old and flawed' game.
Colour me impressed.
I didn't even realy notice the dated graphics, the atmosphere was keeping me so engrossed. After my first session I installed a large modpack and went back into the game with modern graphics and improved gameplay, and the game was made that much better. The choices, the gameplay, the atmosphere... it all struck a chord. The huge twist halfway through the game was one I genuinely never saw coming, and one you sould aim to not spoil for yourself if you intend to play the game. The three 'classes' are three completely seperate playstyles, and each has their own ideas and possiblites.
The ship you explore feels brilliantly realized, a world I could see pepole living in. The tapes you find around the place only add the the eiree atmosphere, and the enemies have sent me into some genuine panics as I hid in the bathroom on three health, praying that the enemy I could hear stumbling around wouldn't find me. It came into the bathroom, moaning about how I did not belong, and as it went into the shower I came out of stall i'd been hiding in and hit it over the head with a wrench. It was one of the most heart-pounding moments of my life, and it sticks in my head to this day.
So how does it stack uo today? Install a modpack and the graphics are sent back to passable standards, and the gameplay, although sightly clunky, fits well with the theme of the game. The plot, while linear like most 'shock games, is still good today. The atmosphere is amazing, one of the few games which has made me feel extreme triumph, terror and loneliness in the space of one playsession.
Buy it. Play it. Enjoy it.
I know I did.

This is my first ever Steam review and It's for one of the best games ever. I've had tried getting into other MOBA games but simply coudn't. I gave Smite a chance because of the unique Gods theme and the playing camera angle and I'm glad I did. The game environment is absolutely chilling and addicting. All those gods and the powers make you wanna play it 24/7. Definately recommeded!

The MOBA for people who don't like MOBAS; A title rich in depth and strategy (albeit less so than its predecessors) with a unique action bend that renders the experience more approachable. all emcompassed within an instantly attractive theme (who wouldn't want to kick♥♥♥♥♥as an ancient diety?)
The game is, graphics wise, attractive and stylish, though a bit samey and muted when it comes to effects.  Character textures are distinct and immediately identifiable while also looking impressive enough to warrant the occasional skin purchase here and there.  Animations are usually smooth, crisp and appealing to the eye, though some characters do move and jump in notably odd ways.  Character abilities are usually downplayed in order to avoid cluttering the screen in combat; a necessary sacrifice given the limited perspective of the game, but a sacrifice still.  The art style tends to oversexualize the female characters, so do make sure to adjust your outrage accordingly.
Sound quality and voice work are overall well done, but do not stand out on their own.  Character VAs do a fine job of making every god sound distinct.  Character abilities are unique enough in sound to identify when something has been used.  The music of the game doesn't quite have the oomph of the old League war drums or the somberness of the DOTA world music, and does repeats itself a bit too often, but is not offensive.
The 3rd person perspective shakes up the MOBA genre in a variety of interesting ways.  The locked camera behind your character gives you a limited perception of what's going on around you, particularly during team fights.  Skill shots become a much more daunting task given you likely telegraph your attack by adjusting your facing.  These two elements alone emphasize a more chaotic style of combat during big team fights or even small ganks.  This in turn makes the game feel more casual and approachable.
In the game's attempts to break away from the traditional MOBA, it does make some missteps that will dampen the overall experience.  Many Gods feel samey in the mechanics of their abilities, likely due to the need to keep abilities simple for action purposes.  Far too many Gods have an ultimate that renders them immune to CC.  Items are simple and provide only passive benefits, with two exceptions being the active general abilities you purchase which will be dictated to you via a strictish meta, based on the role you enjoy.  The decision to put so much emphasis on voice commands (as typing in a game like this one would be too restrictive) burdens newer players with memorizing unintuitive key combinations to communicate with their team.
The game also falls prey to standard MOBA problems.  The meta is strong and stifling, and you will eventually see the same comps over and over again, changing only with the shifting patterns of the patches.  The community will get toxic at times, and will sabotage your games in their infantile rage.  While considerably more approachable than League or DOTA, the game is very much a MOBA with its learning curve.  The auto-buy and auto-level features are not enough to compete with those who spend time learning the mechanics.  If you're not willing to invest yourself into character builds, counters, jungle routes, ganking strategies, laning strategies, teamfight strategies and proper objective control, your gameplay will soon be soured and soured frequently by those who are willing.
While Free to Play, a $30.00 buy in (The all gods pack) will effectively give you everything you need to compete at whatever level you desire, with further purchases serving only cosmetic goals.  You can earn gods the slow way by playing, but the emphasis is on slow as the free currency does not travel very far.
If you like the teamwork emphasis of MOBA games, but hate their slow, plodding pace, this game will be a good match for you, considerably moreso if you convince your friends to buy in with you.  The game is also exceptional as a gateway to MOBA gaming, as many of the skills in this game transition well into League and DOTA, but it's also a fine stand alone title that's great for those with an hour to kill each day or those seeking competitive ranked gameplay.

I have finished the game once and now I´m trying to finish it again without dying once (just had third attempt fail).
Always playing as Corvo so the gameplay is very similar to Dishonored 1 which is just fine by me. I really do not need (and probably do not want) total control/combat overhaul in every new game of the series (prime example of things going worse and worse being Dragon Age series).
Compared to Dishonored 1 the story setting seems less omnious (the original game world, if memory doesn´t fail me, was a bit darker with the rat plague and all). I kind of liked that setting slitghly better.
Another difference - I would say there were more interesting NPCs in Dishonored 1, let´s call them secondary characters. I especially remember the witch. I believe/remember you interacted with these NPCs much more. I might by wrong, but I know I won´t remember any secondary NPC from this game 6 months on, non of them is really memorable in any way.
Dishonored 2 seems more fair compared to Dishonored 1 because there are very few unexpected one hit death situations, you can basically remember them all after the first playthrough. I like that, one hit deaths are cheap. ;-)
People are reporting issues with controls, especially mouse I think. I have to say I´m glad I have 5000 DPI gaming mouse, because the game is playable just fine if I set mouse sensitivity in-game to max and mouse also to max 5000 DPI. Anything less (for example 3000 DPI) and mouse cursor moves way way too slowly, basically it would made the game close to unplayable. But as I said, with my 5000 DPI optical gaming mouse, it works fine.
Overall I´m very satisfied with the game. Storyline/lore is okay (I would rate it as slightly worse than Dishonored 1), gameplay is very similar yet I believe more fair, maps are fun to fight through and explore (for example in newest Tomb Rider I had difficulty motivating myself to explore whole areas, actually after first few maps I just gave up and ran through to finish the story and never look back). NCPs are again slightly less interesting compared to Dishonored 1 but still okay. Graphics improved (cannot play the game fully maxed on Gigabytes OC 980ti but close to it), music and sounds are fine.
Will be interesting to see where will the series go next. They created some nice options in the lore, if you were actually paying attention to the lore (I´m reading every book I find in every playthrough ;-)).

Have you ever discovered a game at the right time to clear your cynicism with a genre?
As someone absolutely tired of the formulaic and predictable format of modern adventure games dominated by TellTale that rely more on brand recognition than innovating the genre or gameplay, I was surprised to find King’s Quest not only improves on the genre but is without a doubt my favorite storytelling-focused game. In many ways of how it’s handled, I prefer King’s Quest as a game over my favorite adventure game, Grim Fandango.
The biggest distinction that should inform whether you would enjoy King’s Quest is to state that it’s a modern adventure game, not a game like Shadowgate that adheres strictly to the ways of old. Even if you hate/love the older format, I believe KQ can still be enjoyed by anyone curious enough to try something different and diligent enough to listen to all the dad-level puns.
Adventure games at their best rely less on the strength of its writing but how the thematic usage of puzzles work with the storytelling, not against it. This quality in KQ is something I have yet to see handled more appropriately than any other game, even when I despise another Game of Wits; I enjoy knowing that King Graham and I are both puzzled, happy and punning all on the same page.
Similar to my review of HITMAN Season 1, I think it’s valuable to break down the episodes individually with this review serving as an overview of what to expect, which is namely the storytelling, the extent of choices, and the usage of puzzles to compliment the narrative.
Based on the first few trailers, you might get the impression that this game is not meant for older audiences when it is really in vein of a Dreamworks’ production by having comedy for both younger and older audiences while also not dumbing down the storytelling for the younger audiences. Underneath the charming appearances is a story that covers the legacy of King’s Graham’s beginnings, midlife crises, highlights, and the future of his kingdom that will appeal to the fans who fell in love with the franchise to see their favorite characters being developed while also expressing that nostalgia to new audiences in a gripping story without previous knowledge of the series. Even when the plot becomes darker, KQ does not shy away from the situation or hide away the consequences; KQ handles the story as a great young-fiction piece by treating the entire audience as adults.
With that being said as well as the obvious TellTale comparison, I imagine many expect a rant about how the extent of your choices are rather meaningless to the overall narrative and how that ruins the interactive experience. However, in spite of how the plot is tightly structured to work around your choices, I believe KQ is more upfront and respectful of the limitations of your choices in a way that will still make them mean something. Instead of the façade of a corner message telling you, “X will remember this,” choices may have gradual and immediate effects like in Chapter 2, or the game may subvert the expectations of your choices like in Chapter 3, or they may incorporate whatever choice you have within limitations of King Graham’s character to make sense. Similar to how Lee is handled in The Walking Dead, a linear storyline is not to the detriment of these games if the choices do not cheat you out of a choice later but offer you various ways to handle a situation and keep you guessing.
Along with the variety of choices is variety of the types of puzzles that changes with every episode to keep the experience from getting stale with some reoccurring challenges. I think this aspect has garnered a lot of mixed opinions as many fans expected more of the first episode which is as true to adventure game genre as possible in all the positive ways. Each chapter afterwards is more linear than the first, but the amount of options and consequences is still diverse as the puzzles shape themselves to suit the story in each episode. Variety is something the game does so well to be almost a fault to some.
What keeps it fresh and inconsistent is the thematic consistency of these puzzles that verges on Metal Gear Solid 2 with so much careful attention to detail. In Chapter 2, you’re dealing with a story about Graham’s hardships of being a king in making decision making, so the episode is a meta-game puzzle of making choices and consequences to save as many people as possible. In Chapter 3, you’re dealing with a double “first-love” at sight puzzle that uses questionnaires, opportunities to favor one, the other or both, or moments alone to build attachment similar to the set-up for Atlus’s Catherine. In Chapter 4, you’re dealing with the value of familial relationships when lines are divided and people don’t see eye-to-eye, so the puzzles all involve drawing lines and conforming perspectives to reach the goal. In the last Chapter, similar to the introduction, you see the adventure game at its absolute worst with “Moon meet Logic” puzzles and absurd leaps in logic as it deals with the aging King Graham on one more adventure.
It’s only when the puzzles deviate from the narrative into familiar obstacles like the Duel of Wits that the game ever feels like it has padding, but for the most part almost all the puzzles suit the narrative and give the player some tangible means to engage and shape the story. The frequency of these latter puzzles is so small that they don’t detract on how the gameplay benefits from the puzzles, not inhibited by them.
Since an adventure game is a game and a story meshed with puzzles all in one, I feel like any other concerns I have overall comes down to the quality of the writing and who it appeals to as well as any narrative issues I found.
As someone who loves a good dad-joke or cringe-worthy jokes that border on self-punishment, I found the writing to be charming and effective at disarming the player when something drastic happens. To some this quality might be annoying rather than appealing, and the tone-shifts can be so sudden they could be a flaw rather than a benefit to the overall experience. There are clever puns, implied quips and other forms of humor to interest others to not overstay its welcome.
The only negative quality of KQ’s story I don’t feel was flawless was how inconsistent those tone changes are in each chapter as well as oddly placed lines, especially toward the end with an epilogue that is best saved for the following day and not immediately after Chapter 5 as it doesn’t add any new types of puzzles nor anything for a climax to the story. Its ending is open-ended enough that I felt satisfied with the story as a whole.
Overall, most of the plot-threads are addressed, and out of all characters I felt only one would be unfamiliar to people not familiar with the KQ legacy. The greatest thing about KQ as it doesn’t steal the place of its legacy as many reboots rewrite themselves by the name as KQ is a nostalgic celebration for the many adventures of this game and the years of adventures of King Graham that players have cherished in revisiting the lands of Daventry for one more adventure.

This is definitely my choice for the game of 2014. Instead of rehashing the typical action-based shooter style game that Gearbox spectacularly failed at when producing Aliens: Colonial Marines, Alien: Isolation primarily focuses on stealth mechanics to project its sense of suspenseful horror and it just simply excels at it. Not that stealth games are new and coming by any stretch of the imagination but it certainly is specifically for the Alien franchise and it's refreshingly different by AAA standards.
Speaking of AAA standards, the production value of this game is nothing less than stellar and the developers' attention to detail in building the 1979's vision for what the future looks is ubiquitous and just down-right awesome. The props in the environments are filled with CRTs, Commodore-64 looking keyboards and analog-tape driven tech (ie. cassette tapes). The horror element comes and goes particularly when frustration sets in due to the difficult nature of the game but it still sometimes finds itself now and then, which is okay with me since the horror element almost always goes away after the first few levels of any horror game.
If you're a fan of horror, stealth, the Alien franchise or all of the above (as I am), then you're probably going to really enjoy this game. As noted before, this game is very HARD and I'd advise Normal or Easy (or Novice =P) difficulty if you're not very good at stealth games. However, its difficulty and other problems are very minor issues to me and I'm very glad they did not compromise for the sake of mere broad appeal. Kudos to Creative Assembly who somehow managed to produce this awesome game despite a lengthy history of RTS games. It's the best game in the Alien franchise I've played since Aliens vs. Predator (1999) and I definitely highly recommend it.
And you should definitely only play this in the dark and with the audio turned up!

I've played the game for almost 2 hours and feel I have enough insight to offer a formed opinion.
Firstly it's an excellent game in it's own right, and a brilliant adventure game and supports the genre nicely. For £14.99 I would say it's worth the money (Unless I finish within the next hour). I went straight into hard mode and I would suggest this for anyone who has played through a point and click adventure game. Two hours in and I am finding the puzzles a little on the easy side so far. However, the team behind the gamedo usually have a good dificulty curve and without giving any spoilers the way the game is designed I can see how it will (hopefully) become much more difficult.
If you are new to adventure gaming, I would suggest playing Day of the Tentacle / Monkey Island first and here's why
Cons:
- The games biggest downfall so far, it sells itself as not being a walking simulator, and i'm afraid so far that's how it can feel. I'm ploughing through puzzles but scenes such as the cemetary are stupidly long- winded and drawn out. Although you can double- click to run it does make my have to take a deep breath to continue playing it. Compared with Tentacle which is set in one area with scenes quickly accessible. I would worry that new comers might get bored of all the walking.
- As mentioned, so far the puzzles haven't been as challenging as i'd hoped (so far!)
- A minor gripe, a couple of the characters really grate on you after a while, you'll know who I mean when you play.
- So far I haven't actually found it too funny.
Pros:
- Great voice acting
- Amazing visuals (mimics classic PaC's of the 80's/90's
- Brilliant story which draws you in
- HUGE scenes and levels which as mentioned above is both good and bad
- Puzzles although simple so far, make sense and are smart. There's none of this 'Take the apple and mix it with the hair of a badger to make a stuffed toy' nonsense (not a real puzzle)
The pro's outweigh the cons for me, and you can tell straight away that a lot of love has gone into making the game. It's not easy to square up against monkey island or tentacle and this game manages it, falling short in only a couple of minor areas.
I would recommend to anyone - 9/10

This game, while potentially quite fun, definitely has its share of ups and downs.
Pros:
+ Excellent animations
+ Fine multiplayer
+ It's free
+ Fine dev support
+ Various weapons, both melee and ranged (from bows to firearms to explosives)
+ Various types of enemies (running, walking, child, crawling)
+ Good voice acting
+ Suspense. It can be quite satisfying to run to a rescue helicopter or truck among hordes of zombies, as you will be left behind if you're too slow, and the grabby mitts of those darned zed aren't helping matters!
Cons:
- Singleplayer. It is almost impossible to get through but a few maps on singleplayer, as enemy spawn rates, nigh on endless (and sometimes stupid) objectives, and lack of weapons/ammo make it extremely hard to survive on your own. This is a problem for those who don't really want to deal with multiplayer.
- Variety. There isn't really a whole lot of change between maps. Sure, it's a change of scenery and objectives, but it's rather easy for everything to blend together into a boring mass of "go here, blow this up, call for help, etc."
- AI spawning. I don't like clearing an area, going into a building for five seconds, and returning to find it swamped with zombies again. It's frustrating, and unrealistic.
- Excessive complication. Sometimes I wonder if the devs are trying to discourage players from even attempting singleplayer. The objectives for many of the maps are very numerous, complicated, and, as I said, sometimes stupid. A group of survivors in this scenario realistically isn't going to rush back and forth across the map to collect pieces of a microphone so they can call for help. Wouldn't it be easier to just leave?
Final Verdict:
To anyone thinking of downloading this game, I give a cautious recommendation. It's very free, so you don't have too much to lose, but know that this game most certainly is not for everyone, and you might get bored of it rather quickly. However, it CAN be very enjoyable to play a match with good players on muliplayer (rare an occurrance as this is), and enabling cheats can be quite satisfying, especially after losing a dozen times at the same part in a map where the undead just can't seem to stop popping up out of nowhere. Give it a try, I think you'd like it, if only for a while.

Really nails the limited ammo and scarce resources aspects of survival horror, horror games these days just don't have the balls to say "that's all you get!". Albeit it's frusterateing, but it's also puts you on edge in terms of horror.
You can play as a soldier (warrior), mechanic (rogue) or a psion (mage) and all suffer from limited resources, the wrench is a godsend for saveing ammo and Psi, but it's also a dagerous weapon since hybrids can take out a third of your life in one hit. True you can allocate your upgrade points evenly across the board, and doing so to a degree is a nessecity for your survival. but the master of none delema is readily aparent. Know how in bioshock you can buy a medkit or some ammo with your abudance of cash? In this game it could easily cost you a third of your nanites for just 6 rounds of regular handgun ammo! and that's makeing the assumption you've been meticuelous in scrougeing for all the nanites you could find.
Only gripes are that the item management hud is clunky and unwieldy, the tutorial is a bit long winded before you get to the meat of the game, and (so far) i've yet to see any sort of item recycleing station that you can dump useless inventory junk into for resources.

I just completed my first playthrough and this has been an incredibly rewarding and chilling experience. The people speaking of atmosphere aren't kidding. The game is genuinely unsettling, and the sound design is on point. There will be times where you're posted up in a corner because you're low on health and you heard a spider scuttling somewhere. Each enemy has a very distinctive audio signature that you come to acknowlege pretty quickly as your survival depends on it.
If you're a newer gamer and you're giving this a try, you need to be patient. It truly isn't going to hurt to do some basic research on skills before you dive in. The skill allocation can be particularly unforgiving depending on the difficulty that you play on given the rarity of upgrade modules. Also there are points in the story where you can be roadblocked, if not flat out stopped by a mis-allocation of points. Most notably the Research and Hacking skills. There are ways to offset this from the use of temporary buffs, and single use items found in the environment. However it seems possible to be locked into a restart.
In conclusion this game is worth a play if you're into the sci-fi genre, or are coming from Bioshock, such as myself. However, this game is NOT Bioshock. There is no hand holding, and it will throw you to the curb quickly.
PROS
-Amazing sound design
-Incredibly gripping narrative
-immersive atmosphere
-high replayability
CONS
-very frustrating platforming
-some environmental hazards feel cheap
-no indication of plot point skills needed until it's too late.

I am a huge fan of the old King's Quest games so I was ecstatic to come across this installment. The graphics were lovely and the perspective from which the story was told was rather unique. However, those positives (& nostalgia) aside, this game should not be put into the realm of KQ whatsoever. The riddles are overly simply and far too linear. This game requires no thinking or cleverness, simply walk in any given direction and the solution will make itself clear be it through narration or on-screen prompts. It just seems like the creator's of this game took the best parts of KQ and threw them in the garbage.

It's extremely hard to review King's Quest. It is by no means perfect, as some chapters are tedious and there have been really weird choices made by Sierra (for example, not including the Epilogue as DLC with the Season Pass, really?).
But, and this is a big one: I'm finding it very hard to find a modern adventure game that comes near this. Because when King's Quest reaches its high points, it soars. It's at times emotional, with exceptional dialogue and voice acting, but also a lot of times laugh-out-load funny (or should I say punny?) and just plain fun to play.
All in all I would definitely recommend this game. Even the low points (mostly chapter 2 and 4) have enough going for them for you to justify playing the entire game. A lovely experience, with a very beautiful story, solid gameplay and beautiful artwork.

This game has been described as a collection of vignettes, and that's basically all it is. But that's all it wants and all it needs to be, in my opinion. Mr. Burton combines simple visuals with evocative soundscapes to create a beautiful sense of place-without-place; ordinary objects and settings are made fantastic while somehow still maintaining a quiet mundanity.
Poetics aside, it feels like a set of art installations, or perhaps the portfolio of a particularly daring set designer, so if those are things which appeal to you, I would definitely recommend this, On the other hand, it's very short (you can complete it under an hour), and has minimal interactivity (you can rotate the "islands" and click on highlighted points), so anyone looking for something a bit more meaty and/or requiring more input should look somewhere else. Personally, I found the length to be a non-issue: you don't walk into a musuem and time how long you look at the paintings for to decide their value. In any case, I get the feeling that if there were more vignettes, it would have drowned out what felt special about those first few.
The only downside is probably the price; some might balk at spending that amount on something less than an hour long. But it costs only a little more than a pint would, and I think it's definitely worth more than that. If the price is only dealbreaker for you, the sale discounts are pretty steep so you could pick it up then!

The past few years have not been great when it comes to Alien games. Aliens versus Predator (2010) was alright but disappointing and Aliens: Colonial Marines... Well, we all know how Gearbox ♥♥♥♥ed that up. So along comes Aliens: Isolation, another Alien game published by Sega. I tried to keep my hopes down to avoid another disappointment but it just looked so good. And it is. It really, really is.
First of all, it's a excellent survival horror game. The gameplay is difficult and an encounter with an enemy (especially with the Alien) can be absolutely deadly. The game does not hold your hand. It's up to you to try to survive. You'll have to sneak around or distract the enemies and if you're brave enough you may even try to attack one, but in a lot of cases that will end with you being dead. The game doesn't rely on jumpscares but instead lets you feel terror and tension. Knowing that something out there is hunting for you, but you don't know where.
Then there's the amount of detail and love for the first Alien film that went into this game. This is a game made by fans for fans. If you've ever watched the film and wondered what you would do in that situation, here's your chance. There are no Colonial Marines to save you here. You're on your own. If you haven't seen the movies I'd really advise you to watch Alien (1979). I'd also watch the director's cut of Aliens (1986) so you know a bit more about the character you're playing in the game. Keep in mind that the game is set between these movies.
You'll encounter some hostile humans and androids throughout the game but what it's really about is the Alien of course. And they did an excellent job. The Alien AI is absolutely amazing. Not only does it relentlessly hunt for you, it also adapts to your strategies while doing it. For example, throwing a flare to distract it is a nice trick but eventually it won't fall for it anymore. And making a quick run towards the exit? Hah! Forget it. Once the creature catches you, it's game over. And it will catch you. Many times.
The graphics and sound design are superb aswell. There's some excellent lighting in this game and carefully listening to where the Alien is going could be the difference between life and death. Then there's the music, some of it new, some from the movie, that really adds to the atmosphere.
But the game is not perfect. While I'm glad that the campaign is lengthy (you get a lot of bang for your buck), I thought it was a bit too long. There are also a lot of moments with a lot of backtracking and there are many situations where you encounter a door that is locked and you have to go all the way to the other side of the map to restore power, or something along those lines. Then there's the flame thrower and the molotov cocktails. While you can't kill the Alien, you can use these to scare it away for a short while. This made the creature a little less scary in my opinion, although it does give you some time to breath.
All in all I think this is an excellent game. Something you really have to pick up if you're an Alien fan or just like a good scary survival horror game. And something a lot of other (horror) developers should take note of. Worth every penny.

Essentially; it's a massive cat and mouse game that takes place on a space ship. You are the mouse; but instead of a cat, it's an Alien. Stealth is key, there are occasions where you want to run, but doing so will alert the alien to where you are. You are given some items later in the game that can make the Alien retreat temporarily, but you are not given too many supplies so the feeling of dread remains as it drops back down 20 seconds later to look for you.
The only downsides to the game are the type of objectives you have to complete. You will find yourself backtracking alot, mostly just to restart a generator or enter a code to open a door. For example, to open this door you need to open it using a computer, to do that you have to turn on the power etc. This keeps you on your toes, just as you think you are getting somewhere you find your exit is blocked and an alternate route back the way you came has been highlighted on the map. This is not a game breaker, I just feel it is used a bit too much.
In conclusion, the use of lighting (or lack there of), great use of sound and the unpredictable A.I of the Alien makes this a incredibly tense, but overall a worthwhile experience.
8/10

I've played my first horror game as a kid back in 2001 and it was Alien versus Predator 2 franchise crossbreed. Its marine campaign gave me some nightmares, and at first to cope with paralyzing fear I had to retort to playing in a well lit room and muting the speakers. Maybe it wasn't that great of a game by today's standards, but for me it was the first exposure to genuine fear that went beyond boundaries of movies, a fear that stems from direct involvement and responsibility for character's survival. He wasn't gonna rescue himself while overcoming all the horrors in his way to then merrily drift away on a space shuttle into the pitch black darkness of space. You were that character, and you had to face those horrors yourself. Now this here is the first really good game based around pristine Alien universe/franchise, probably the best Alien game we’ll ever get, and the first horror game in 13 years that made me relive the same raw fear as if it was the first time.
For England based developer Creative Assembly (most famous for their Total War RTS/TBS hybrid strategy series) Alien: Isolation is the first experience in survival horror genre, and for their first try they did pretty damn well. A lot of work went into recreating aesthetics of the first Alien movie, the retrofuturistic vision from the 80’s and presentation of the Alien itself as superior, pure, primal, deadly being. The goal was to make the Alien scary again – a hard job considering his iconic status and instant recognition in pop culture – and they have actually managed to pull it off. The Alien is fast, has heightened senses, and most important, he is intelligent. Thanks to sophisticated AI behavior he’s not simply walking along the waypoints of a manual route, occasionally popping up for a scripted event (although there is a handful share of scripted events involving him). The Alien has his own little mind, and God knows what is happening in there. You may think he will walk past you, and then he will suddenly turn 180 degrees, catching you off guard. He may corner you in a room, and play cat and mouse with you for minutes, aware that you’re in there, to then walk past the locker you’re shaking in and rip the door off to pull you out. Even after you learn how not to give away your position - among other things he hears you running, your motion tracker bleeps in close proximity, doors and ventilation shafts opening and closing - and think you’re safe to roam Sevastopol unless you make any sounds and walk slowly, the Alien can still surprise you by coming down the vents just because he decided to breathe some fresh air. You never feel truly safe with this thing crawling around in the vents, making all kinds of muted sounds that echo around, and as revealed via motion tracker, following you.
Speaking of sound design, it’s the best and most immersive sounding game I’ve ever played. The air of Sevastopol station is virtually vibrating with all the mechanical sounds that make you paranoid because they are too similar to Alien moving around or too loud for you to pinpoint if he’s close or just came down from the vents, the electronics make all those silly bleeping and crackling noises, the automated lights in a room you just walked into turn on with a crystal clear clicking and humming, your boots produce distinct footsteps and squeak on the shiny floor every now and then. In addition, navigating by sound in this game often proves vital for your survival. By carefully listening to the sounds the Alien produces you can pretty much make out at what pace he moves, in what direction and how disturbed he is.
The music. Oh, the music! They pretty much based the whole score around that classic instantly recognizable sound of original Alien movie score by Jerry Goldsmith. Very nostalgic. The interiors, too, look like they were taken right from the set of 70-80’s science fiction movie, true to their origin. Beautiful visuals (sans badly implemented anti-aliasing) complement it all, down to the skull silhouette inside Alien’s head, delivering a movie-like quality picture.
All the praising aside, there are some flaws with the game that I'd like to point out:
But overall it’s a beautifully crafted game true to its roots in every sense, thoroughly entertaining from start to finish.
9/10
P.S.: Just do yourself a favor and play it on hardest difficulty (not Nightmare mode though, which is sort of a challenge for seasoned players with many features such as map and HUD turned off). After I finished the game I just had to look up people’s reactions when they had to sneak by the Alien, and many times I saw their experience get hurt by low difficulty they picked, when the Alien didn’t see them when he obviously should have, didn't react to them moving nearby, to sounds and visual cues such as flamethrower's ignition flame or a light on noisemaker. Better, smarter, tougher Alien on Hard difficulty is “the way it’s meant to be played”, encouraged even by developers as definitive one.

Edit: Word choice.

4/5: A good game that mechanically is better than DS1, but design/lore wise is much weaker. If you like the genre just buy it.
It is kind of like L4D1 vs L4D2 for me.
L4D1 had a very clear focus on the coop campaigns, you could tell because of the finely tuned levels balanced around slowly moving forwards at all times- and the weird multiplayer scoring mechanics. Much like Dark Souls 1 and its clear focus on a coherent world and strong NPCs, with some odd balance in gameplay(pyromancy/dark).
L4D2 had an almost singular focus on versus mode: the scoring system was much better, the new infected types were focused on making sure that there was no slow movement, but movement was done in fast bursts. The levels and events were also designed around this new focus, and it left the coop campaign section lacking(except hard rain-note how it forces you to stop and hole up more often, as well as pick movement paths much more carefully). But versus was much more interesting than l4d1 and I was fine playing that for a long long time.
Dark Souls 2: it seems to be built around consensual pvp and coop. It is so incredibly easy to do consensual pvp in DS2- beat 1/3 of the game and you can do it all you want, in a few different settings(I do count the rat covenant as consensual pvp, probably doors of pharros as well because they are small optional areas). With the rings for helping summon your friends, along with the soul memory mechanic and no infinite invasion items, you can summon friends for anything anytime with nearly no reprecussions(especially once you learn how to abuse the life rings). One of the biggest plusses for me was the relative balance of most of the mechanics: no longer is mage an unstoppable juggernaut from halfway through the game, or pyromancy a nearly costless source of power. Everything had a price and many of the weapons were pretty cool to use in pvp and pve, as well as reworked poison and a distinct lack of high end shields from early game.I was amazed that they replaced the backstab-centric combat correctly, where now I could whittle down the opponent without having to resort to only having 2 hits matter.
What has suffered in dark souls 2? World design- its been talked about before. Coupling their desire to gate out power(when do you get the primary seller for magic/cleric/dark?) with the super linear and non optional design- they have made it so that I never want to do the optional areas because they don't contain any lore I really feel like uncovering(ash lake), any interesting areas I feel like going to(ash lake!) or even any items I want to have(great ash lake barrier!). Add to this their desire to take out those nasty low level invaders(most of which people wanted gone were just straight up hackers) by again cutting non consensual invasion pvp.
------
I think DS2 is a mechanically superior game that lacked the amazing invasion pvp and world building that made DS1 great. I should be having more fun in pvp due to the plethora of weapons and builds and whatnot- except my character build does not seem unique or even a trade off, because when everyone is level 170 you can have 4 stats at 40. So unless you want some sort of hex dual wield falchion build, you can always have high weight capacity and hp.
I am a huge fan of the non consensual invasions- it was the price of going human in DS1 and while it might be weird this time around(so how about that there blue protection covenant, thats probably a good price for blocking invasions) it is a sorely missed feature that has really cut down on replay value for me.
------

Coming from someone who absolutely loved the first game, I personally had a blast with this one as well. Most aspects of the first are improved here, however, it is admittedly quite different and is more "accessible" for casuals.
The story of the Evil Within 2 is much more streamlined than the first game. Many people such as myself really enjoyed the psychological horror aspect of the first. You were frequently thrown around with bits of information being fed to you from time to time, and it was up to you to piece it all together. This certainly outraged casual gamers as they claimed the story made no sense whatsoever, but we know better. The simplicity of the story in the sequel isn't the worst offense and suits the objective of the game well, but don't expect a mind-splitting story like the first. Here nothing is left to ponder about; no questions about why or how expect a few.
The gamplay has been very much improved in the Evil Within 2. Everything feels much smoother, and also flows better. Stealth actually works well, even if the enemy AI isn't super sophisticated which can lead to some exploitation. Then again, how often isn't stealth used in games to exploit enemy AI. stealth is also necessary throughout most of the game (mostly applying to Nightmare difficulty, which is how the game should be played), whereas in the first stealth became virtually useless after the first few chapters. Enemies in the Evil Within 2 are faster than the first, heightening the need for precision shots and efficient evasive movement. Open, large maps allow the player to approach goals from whichever way they want. Fans of the first may miss the smaller, claustrophobic, linear level design but most of the time that kind of design served mostly for aesthetic appeal rather than enemy engagement.
Sebastian is no longer just a husk in the Evil Within 2. This time around he actually has character, leading to him being more expressive. I definitely found the lifeless Sebastian from before to be near unlikable. It wouldn't have been even remotely disturbing if Sebastian had died. This time around he certainly says more than just "What the..." every hour or so, although his catchphrase is still frequent. The driving factor for his character's development comes not only from his rescue mission to save a loved one, but also in his quest for redemption. I would liken Sebastian to Ash from the Evil Dead movies. Ash in the Evil Dead was a dull character, but in the Evil Dead 2 he goes from being a coward to a scared but eccentric survivor. In the end I found myself actually rooting for Sebastian. After playing with Sebastian for so long I absolutely wanted to see him to succeed.
In regards to the overall horror factor of the games, the first did it better. One of the best things of the original game was the sadistic, disturbing images. Entering an interior was a beautiful transition that instantly dimmed your lighting and turn the darkened space into an eerie, tense event. Enemies designs were unique and terrifying. The basic enemies were tortured, mutilated bodies, whereas the basic enemies in the sequel look like zombies with bubbles across their bodies. Additionally, the basic enemies came in different types, but the sequel relies more on special enemy types for diversity. The only enemies you're likely the admire in the sequel are the bosses. Union City in the Evil Within 2 is typical small American town that slowly breaks up and becomes chaotic as the story progresses. It doesn't even compare to the terror of the level design from its predecessor.
All things considered, the Evil Within 2 is a worthy successor, even if it's not the truest sequel it could and perhaps should have been. But if you love the Evil Within then I highly recommend buying this game to continue the experience and to support it. I seriously doubt that you won't enjoy the new game.

This game, while potentially quite fun, definitely has its share of ups and downs.
Pros:
+ Excellent animations
+ Fine multiplayer
+ It's free
+ Fine dev support
+ Various weapons, both melee and ranged (from bows to firearms to explosives)
+ Various types of enemies (running, walking, child, crawling)
+ Good voice acting
+ Suspense. It can be quite satisfying to run to a rescue helicopter or truck among hordes of zombies, as you will be left behind if you're too slow, and the grabby mitts of those darned zed aren't helping matters!
Cons:
- Singleplayer. It is almost impossible to get through but a few maps on singleplayer, as enemy spawn rates, nigh on endless (and sometimes stupid) objectives, and lack of weapons/ammo make it extremely hard to survive on your own. This is a problem for those who don't really want to deal with multiplayer.
- Variety. There isn't really a whole lot of change between maps. Sure, it's a change of scenery and objectives, but it's rather easy for everything to blend together into a boring mass of "go here, blow this up, call for help, etc."
- AI spawning. I don't like clearing an area, going into a building for five seconds, and returning to find it swamped with zombies again. It's frustrating, and unrealistic.
- Excessive complication. Sometimes I wonder if the devs are trying to discourage players from even attempting singleplayer. The objectives for many of the maps are very numerous, complicated, and, as I said, sometimes stupid. A group of survivors in this scenario realistically isn't going to rush back and forth across the map to collect pieces of a microphone so they can call for help. Wouldn't it be easier to just leave?
Final Verdict:
To anyone thinking of downloading this game, I give a cautious recommendation. It's very free, so you don't have too much to lose, but know that this game most certainly is not for everyone, and you might get bored of it rather quickly. However, it CAN be very enjoyable to play a match with good players on muliplayer (rare an occurrance as this is), and enabling cheats can be quite satisfying, especially after losing a dozen times at the same part in a map where the undead just can't seem to stop popping up out of nowhere. Give it a try, I think you'd like it, if only for a while.

Man...I grew up on Sierra games. Out of the Kings Quest series, KQ5 was the first one I played but definitely not the last. Anyway, this game brought all of those childhood memories back full swing, with references to puzzles and stories I remember from over 25 years ago. From a nostalgic perspective, this game is perfect. Nothing short of it. Someone who doesn't know the series might argue, but I think anyone who grew up loving this series like I did will enjoy it. Ken and Roberta Williams will always be the pioneers of gaming as we know it, but the Odd Gentlemen really does a great job paying tribute. Buy this game if you're thinking about. Especially if your memories are similar to mine.

This game really was a surprise for me. I must admit i've never played any King's quest game, this was my first and the journey of King Graham was a blast.
Game consists of five chapters and epilogue. It was released in an episodic format. When the game was complete i bought it on sale. The regular price of 40€ is too much for a short game.
First chapter starts as Graham telling about his adventures to Gwendolyn - his granddaughter. You start the game as the young Graham who wants to take part in a tourney and become a king. At the very start you see the quality of the game, graphics are beautiful and while gameplay is modernized it has that classic point&click vibe. You're running around collecting things then figuring out how and when to use them. First chapter is the longest one, it should take around 5-6 hours to complete. When i finished the first chapter i thought "this is one of the best adventure games i've played". It was amazing, i loved every character, every dialogue, every puzzle and every achievement. About achievements, they're pretty fun in this game, you should try and get them all.
Ok on to the second chapter. It's much shorter, around two hour mark and plays completely different. I'm not gonna spoil anything so i'll just say it's all about decisions. I loved this chapter too, again everything about it just shines.
The third one. Again surprise - it plays differently, yay! Graham is older now, more matured but still alone and the quest is to find a queen for you. Story is very good again but it lacked actual gameplay. Climbing is not very fun and there were only few puzzles. One was annoying though (i hate music puzzles). It felt even shorter then the second one.
Fourth one. I liked this the least. Graham is even older and he travels to the ice castle with his family. The problem with this chapter is that it basically consists of very similar puzzles. There are many rooms, you solve the puzzle in one room and go through the door into the next room where another puzzle awaits. And that's it. Story on the other hand is amazing again.
The last one and the saddest one. It could make you cry. Graham is old and his memory is fading out. You revisit the locations from the first chapter, pick up items, solve the puzzles, everything is back as it supposed to be in such a game. It was a pleasant chapter, loved it to the end. But couldn't figure out the last puzzle, so i used a walkthrough.
Finally epilogue. Probably to leave people happy after the sad fifth chapter. Nothing to tell other than it's funny and involves couple of classic "find the item, find the use for it" puzzles.
Graphics are very nice looking. I love cell shading. I like they took this approach, the game will still look good after 10 years. Performance was nice, didn't encounter any problems. Didn't notice any bugs or glitches.
Voice acting and music is of the highest quality.
I'd say it's a must for every adventure fan. Even if you're not one of them you may like it anyway. Puzzles are not too hard and not too simple, story is funny and sad, it makes you go through all the emotions.

Greetings, I hereby provide the following reasons.
Performance issues:-
Not everyone owns a super computer. I study abroad, my laptop only runs on an 860M. Outdated in today's technological standards. However, capable in performing extra on games such as DAI, Revelations 2, Battlefield 4, Hardline. You'd think that since you're able to play all these graphic intense games, Advanced warfare should probably be a walk in a park. Well, think again. 60 FPS is almost non-exsistent, we're in 2015 for ♥♥♥♥s sake.
Because advanced warfare isn't the most optimised games out there for the PC, running the game for long extensive hours could possibly wear out your hardware at an exponential rate. Updating your drivers could help, but I can hardly call that a fix.
Gaming content:-
The idea of the new supply drop system is by far, the most unique thing about Advanced Warfare. Though some may consider it a just system, i'd like to think otherwise. Most elite weapons that I have used, and by now, I have almost all, have been unbalanced, overpowered, and unfair to the other players who do not own the elite variant. For starters, weapon variants like MOST other games out there should only boost your tactical advantage by a small percentage instead of a huge margin. Players on the battlefield without the elites will feel short and at a total disadvantage during a standard one on one gunfight.
Based on statistics, that a supply drop will only be granted upon first kill/death after every 45 minutes of ingame time. You're looking at a 15% chance on getting an Elite weapon OR cosmetic from each box, let alone random boosters and reinforcements. Because of this, Sledgehammer games have recently pushed out an additional way in obtaining these wonderful Elites from something called the "Advanced Supply Drops". Priced at $1.99 (1), $5.99 (3), $9.99 (5), $19.99 (10). But don't wonder like a blind fly into their twisted web of deception, in doing so, you'd only fall short as a victim of modern day internet microtransactions. The game as it is, already priced at $59.99, and an additional $56.95 for the season pass, and yet you get additional virtual items such as these as if it was never enough to begin with. This has to be the most expensive "Call of Duty" ever in the history of the franchise.
Downloadable content for this game is restricted to only a few game modes. Ridiculous, considering the amount you spend. New weapons that were once unavailable, now premium for season pass and DLC holders. They show absolutely no balancing whatsover. Insignificant amount of cons overweighed by advantages that come with the DLC weapons. So long as you spend $15, you'd almost guarantee yourself plenty of extra kills on the battlefield.
I already have the season pass but jesus, they still advertise it all over my app and steam every single day. How many ♥♥♥♥in times do you want one to purchase your DLC? :|
Lack of players:-
From an outstanding number of 35K players when it first released in November 2014, to a pitiful 8K peak based off statistics gathered in the past 30 days. Never in the history of online shooters, have I experienced that many people going inactive in the course of 6 months. I have clocked in 800++ hours and have had 15 days of in-map time, and sadly, I have seen friends come and go in the snap of a finger. Unfortunately, games on most modes stop after 0:00 (UTC), making it a ghost game. You're in luck if you manage to join 1 or 2 full 6v6 games but usually on common modes such as Mosh pit, Team deathmatch, and Search and Destroy. You can kiss goodbye to the rest of the other modes. They are redundant at this point.
The quality of players are despicable. Commonly 12-25 yr olds thinking that the world owes them something. I've never seen a chatbox this amusing before in any shooter, let alone mmorpgs or anything that's online based and interactive with others. Call of Duty, in my conclusion, is mainly targeted for casual players. The moment you whip out dodgy skills and rack up the scoreboard, you've entitled yourself to the achievement of being the worlds most infamous video-game hacker in the history of mankind. That's just how the mindset has developed itself overtime.
2015 = No dedicated servers.
VERDICT: Did this call of duty manage to bring the franchise to it's former glory? To the days of Modern Warfare and Modern Warfare 2? Sorry, but not quite there yet.

Tense, atmospheric and true to the feel of the 1st Alien movie.

Essentially; it's a massive cat and mouse game that takes place on a space ship. You are the mouse; but instead of a cat, it's an Alien. Stealth is key, there are occasions where you want to run, but doing so will alert the alien to where you are. You are given some items later in the game that can make the Alien retreat temporarily, but you are not given too many supplies so the feeling of dread remains as it drops back down 20 seconds later to look for you.
The only downsides to the game are the type of objectives you have to complete. You will find yourself backtracking alot, mostly just to restart a generator or enter a code to open a door. For example, to open this door you need to open it using a computer, to do that you have to turn on the power etc. This keeps you on your toes, just as you think you are getting somewhere you find your exit is blocked and an alternate route back the way you came has been highlighted on the map. This is not a game breaker, I just feel it is used a bit too much.
In conclusion, the use of lighting (or lack there of), great use of sound and the unpredictable A.I of the Alien makes this a incredibly tense, but overall a worthwhile experience.

I've played my first horror game as a kid back in 2001 and it was Alien versus Predator 2 franchise crossbreed. Its marine campaign gave me some nightmares, and at first to cope with paralyzing fear I had to retort to playing in a well lit room and muting the speakers. Maybe it wasn't that great of a game by today's standards, but for me it was the first exposure to genuine fear that went beyond boundaries of movies, a fear that stems from direct involvement and responsibility for character's survival. He wasn't gonna rescue himself while overcoming all the horrors in his way to then merrily drift away on a space shuttle into the pitch black darkness of space. You were that character, and you had to face those horrors yourself. Now this here is the first really good game based around pristine Alien universe/franchise, probably the best Alien game we’ll ever get, and the first horror game in 13 years that made me relive the same raw fear as if it was the first time.
For England based developer Creative Assembly (most famous for their Total War RTS/TBS hybrid strategy series) Alien: Isolation is the first experience in survival horror genre, and for their first try they did pretty damn well. A lot of work went into recreating aesthetics of the first Alien movie, the retrofuturistic vision from the 80’s and presentation of the Alien itself as superior, pure, primal, deadly being. The goal was to make the Alien scary again – a hard job considering his iconic status and instant recognition in pop culture – and they have actually managed to pull it off. The Alien is fast, has heightened senses, and most important, he is intelligent. Thanks to sophisticated AI behavior he’s not simply walking along the waypoints of a manual route, occasionally popping up for a scripted event (although there is a handful share of scripted events involving him). The Alien has his own little mind, and God knows what is happening in there. You may think he will walk past you, and then he will suddenly turn 180 degrees, catching you off guard. He may corner you in a room, and play cat and mouse with you for minutes, aware that you’re in there, to then walk past the locker you’re shaking in and rip the door off to pull you out. Even after you learn how not to give away your position - among other things he hears you running, your motion tracker bleeps in close proximity, doors and ventilation shafts opening and closing - and think you’re safe to roam Sevastopol unless you make any sounds and walk slowly, the Alien can still surprise you by coming down the vents just because he decided to breathe some fresh air. You never feel truly safe with this thing crawling around in the vents, making all kinds of muted sounds that echo around, and as revealed via motion tracker, following you.
Speaking of sound design, it’s the best and most immersive sounding game I’ve ever played. The air of Sevastopol station is virtually vibrating with all the mechanical sounds that make you paranoid because they are too similar to Alien moving around or too loud for you to pinpoint if he’s close or just came down from the vents, the electronics make all those silly bleeping and crackling noises, the automated lights in a room you just walked into turn on with a crystal clear clicking and humming, your boots produce distinct footsteps and squeak on the shiny floor every now and then. In addition, navigating by sound in this game often proves vital for your survival. By carefully listening to the sounds the Alien produces you can pretty much make out at what pace he moves, in what direction and how disturbed he is.
The music. Oh, the music! They pretty much based the whole score around that classic instantly recognizable sound of original Alien movie score by Jerry Goldsmith. Very nostalgic. The interiors, too, look like they were taken right from the set of 70-80’s science fiction movie, true to their origin. All the praising aside, there are some flaws with the game that I'd like to point out:

This thing will not tolerate you running around, and trampling around its toes. This go's for everyone else on the station. The alien is hunting whatever is finds, not just you. You can use this to your advantage.
Coming into contact with the Xenomorph is instant death, and a trip back to the loading screen. Dont let it see you.
Story is pretty good. The absurd attention to detail in terms of the references to the Alien franchise as a whole is insane. Creative Assembly have crafted a loveletter to the Alien community who appriciate this attention to detail. I'd average the normal players playthrough would be around 20 hours long, and this is without dying a huge amount. This game will go on, and on, and on.
Unlike some other horror games which Isolation seems to have taken tips from, such as Outlast and Amnesia; there is quite a lot of combat in this game. The main enemys that you will face, apart from the constant threat of the Alien, are Automaton androids called 'Working Joes'. Most of them are hostile and will attempt to blow you away if they see you.
Combat starts off great. As most of the time you will not be able to fight the things set against you, and will be forced to hide. Half way through the game you will be given certain weapons that can keep the Alien at bay, if not kill it untirely.
Working Joe's can be killed early, but most weapons are ineffective. Joe's will soak up bullets, blows, and just about anything. Kinda like the Terminator.
