You've probably heard it by now, but System Shock 2 can basically be described best as "RPG BioShock set in space". But considering SS2 was first it basically means BioShock is "FPS System Shock 2 set under the sea". But I digress.
SS2 takes place on the Von Braun, a spaceship that's surrounded by the darkness of space. After training for four years (or four minutes in our lives) you wake up on the Von Braun. If that's not enough to feel claustrophobic, early on you also find out something mysteriously and equally terrifying had happened on the ship on your absence. Guided by another survivor you start from the bottom of the ship and you work yourself to the top to uncover the ship's secrets. No marks, no hints, you're mostly on your own and there's little to no holdings hands (as it should be). Gameplay wise it holds up great, the combat is deep, the pacing is good, and there may be some dated animations here and there, but nothing too serious. Combat can be experienced as a little less flexible than BioShock for example, but that's because you're "stuck" with your current build, due to the skill points you invested in it, which means you can't drastically change your play style in SS2, which was possible in BioShock. But on the other hand, it means the replay value is higher in SS2.
This is the first time I played this 16 year old game and I'd definitely recommend this for other people who like a good RPG dripping with atmosphere that doesn't hold your hands, like most of the games nowadays.
+ An isolated feeling, claustrophobic, drips with atmosphere.
+ Main antagonist is very sinister and interesting, good story.
+ Optional audio logs you can find add to the atmosphere.
+ Expansive gameplay with lots of options to suit your play style.
+ Little to no holding hands. There are no markers of any sorts.
-/+ - No subtitles. Which isn't a big problem, even for non-native English speakers like me, but sometimes there's a lot of background noise in-game which makes it a little hard to hear. But there's a log system that you can use to reread most of the dialogues and diaries.
- Some (not all) songs are way too "bombastic' and sound somewhat out of place, they don't have that feeling of isolation and claustrophobia to begin with.
- Some enemies, at least at first, spawn very quickly, which can lead to some frustration. Especially in the beginning when you're not exactly full on Medical and Psi hypos.
- The final boss battle ends on a ridiculous and downright out-of-place note that may leave you with somewhat of a sour taste in your mouth.
The final cut scene after that is good though.

It took me a few hours to get used to the new wingsuit (particularly when doing the challenges) but that's the only downside to this amazing game. JC3 ROCKS!
According to Steam, I got 83 hours of play out of the main game, which is excellent value for money and a whole heap of fun.
This game is a big improvement over Just Cause 2 in every respect. Perhaps one of the biggest things is that Rico is no longer an anti-hero with a dubious mission. This time he's clearly on the side of good, and the people he's helping are good guys too (and not lunatics and criminals as in JC2). And it's made clear that his targets belong exclusively to the  corrupt government and military. At one point, early in the game, Rico is given explicit permission to destroy national assets on the grounds that the rebels will rebuild anything they have to once the people are back in control. I'd say the developers really listened to the player community this time.
Every aspect of the game has improved (with the single exception of flying planes - using only a keyboard - which still sucks most of the time, although those with gamepads and joysticks may have an easier time).
- The helicopters are better and there are more of them to try.
- The weapons are much better than before (and they actually hit what you're aiming at now).
- The resupply drops are faster, less intrusive, and way more fun.
- The collectibles include recordings of the dictators' diary which provides a better understanding of the villian.
- The wingsuit really changes the speed and excitement value of the game once you get the hang of it.
- The missions make sense, and even the repetative missions yield rewards that make them fun to play.
I can't wait for the DLC to come out so I can take to the skies again.

Hi-Rez Studios’ free-to-play Smite occupies an interesting space in a genre that’s going to see a deluge of new titles in 2014. Most multiplayer online battle arena (MOBA) titles feature top-down, isometric action, but Smite gives players the chance to play in third-person with a first-person shooter feel. Even auto-attacks are skillshots, making combat feel different from other MOBAs. Smite also features significant mode variety, allowing players to compete in unique deathmatches or themed games.
Smite puts you in the role of an ancient god; the character pool currently draws upon Greek, Norse, Chinese, Mayan, and more, allowing Hi-Rez a nearly infinite pool of flavorful characters with appropriate abilities. Thanatos can sense death and has a skillset focused on assassination, paired with an ultimate ability that allows him to execute a weakened player in a single, long-range dive. Zeus comes with all the powers you’d expect a thunder god to have, and Poseidon has the signature ability to “release the Kraken,” doing heavy AOE damage. The colorful cast of characters is interesting, and each god and goddess feels unique in terms of skillsets and style.
Smite’s third-person design changes things significantly from the top-down isometric MOBA paradigm. Every attack requires skill, so you can’t just rely on auto-attack to do your work. Everything from the basic slash of an axe or magic from a stave needs to be carefully timed and aimed in order to land. The range of each move is generally shown after a skill has been highlighted, and then you direct it to land in a specific area. Smite presents a huge change from games that often have “click-aimed” skills and abilities, and each character has specific nuances to master.
Smite features a classic competitive mode that mirrors the structure of the go-to MOBA map: creeps spawn in three lanes and are assisted by players pushing, ganking, and team-fighting to the opposing base. Smite also has an all-random, all-middle mode that is becoming more popular in MOBA titles. While the standard mode is certainly the go-to for competitive league play and balance, Smite’s Arena and custom modes make it stand out from competitors

This is my first MMO, and I was hesitant to purchase it because I had seen many friends play popular MMO's before and did not like what I saw. I've been an avid elder scrolls fan since Morrowind for Xbox, and was excited to hear about this release. Some friends play the beta and didn't recommend it. But it went on sale for Christmas last year and I had enough funds in my steam wallet so I said why not?! So glad I did! It's not really what I expected from an MMO (which was mostly negative before) and it's not quite the same as most of the other elder scrolls games preceding it (although a fresh approach was definitely nice!) you know the layout I'm talking about: run around, help rando's find their lost kitty, help other rando's assassinate their cheating spouse, accomplish side quests for factions that may or may not be more fun than the main quest which you never know if it will end up being very underwhelming and/or tedious, but at least feeling like the money spent on the game had been worth it...
TESO has definitely been all those things and , I feel, totally worth it. It has all those elements quintessentially elder scrolls with that odd [to me] MMO gameplay style that lends something fresh to the elder scrolls experience.
Sometimes other players can be of noxious and even downright rude, but my experience has been that the overwhelming majority of them are helpful or just leave you alone to do your thing in Tamriel, and there are countless guilds to join up with, meet new friends who love the elder scrolls series as much as you do, or or for you to teach them how!
I definitely recommend this amalgamation of MMO and elder scrolls to anyone looking to experience the series for the first time and for seasoned older scrolls fans alike. I won't pretend it's perfect, and there are plenty of things I wish it had that it doesn't, but at the end of the day this exists for entertainment and when I'm asked if I am not entertained, I must say I absolutely am, every time I log on!

4/5: A good game that mechanically is better than DS1, but design/lore wise is much weaker. If you like the genre just buy it.
It is kind of like L4D1 vs L4D2 for me.
L4D1 had a very clear focus on the coop campaigns, you could tell because of the finely tuned levels balanced around slowly moving forwards at all times- and the weird multiplayer scoring mechanics. Much like Dark Souls 1 and its clear focus on a coherent world and strong NPCs, with some odd balance in gameplay(pyromancy/dark).
L4D2 had an almost singular focus on versus mode: the scoring system was much better, the new infected types were focused on making sure that there was no slow movement, but movement was done in fast bursts. The levels and events were also designed around this new focus, and it left the coop campaign section lacking(except hard rain-note how it forces you to stop and hole up more often, as well as pick movement paths much more carefully). But versus was much more interesting than l4d1 and I was fine playing that for a long long time.
Dark Souls 2: it seems to be built around consensual pvp and coop. It is so incredibly easy to do consensual pvp in DS2- beat 1/3 of the game and you can do it all you want, in a few different settings(I do count the rat covenant as consensual pvp, probably doors of pharros as well because they are small optional areas). With the rings for helping summon your friends, along with the soul memory mechanic and no infinite invasion items, you can summon friends for anything anytime with nearly no reprecussions(especially once you learn how to abuse the life rings). One of the biggest plusses for me was the relative balance of most of the mechanics: no longer is mage an unstoppable juggernaut from halfway through the game, or pyromancy a nearly costless source of power. Everything had a price and many of the weapons were pretty cool to use in pvp and pve, as well as reworked poison and a distinct lack of high end shields from early game.I was amazed that they replaced the backstab-centric combat correctly, where now I could whittle down the opponent without having to resort to only having 2 hits matter.
What has suffered in dark souls 2? World design- its been talked about before. Coupling their desire to gate out power(when do you get the primary seller for magic/cleric/dark?) with the super linear and non optional design- they have made it so that I never want to do the optional areas because they don't contain any lore I really feel like uncovering(ash lake), any interesting areas I feel like going to(ash lake!) or even any items I want to have(great ash lake barrier!). Add to this their desire to take out those nasty low level invaders(most of which people wanted gone were just straight up hackers) by again cutting non consensual invasion pvp.
------
I think DS2 is a mechanically superior game that lacked the amazing invasion pvp and world building that made DS1 great. I should be having more fun in pvp due to the plethora of weapons and builds and whatnot- except my character build does not seem unique or even a trade off, because when everyone is level 170 you can have 4 stats at 40. So unless you want some sort of hex dual wield falchion build, you can always have high weight capacity and hp.
I am a huge fan of the non consensual invasions- it was the price of going human in DS1 and while it might be weird this time around(so how about that there blue protection covenant, thats probably a good price for blocking invasions) it is a sorely missed feature that has really cut down on replay value for me.
------

This game is really changed in a very positive way, that makes the game "breathe" more, and gives more insight in the Black Mesa facility. Combined with the subtitles making it possible to squeeze more out of the Half-Life story, which already, is pretty complicated to the uninvited to understand.
A very solid and satisfying remake of Half-Life.

If you have played the orginal or are new to Half-Life, I would still recommend you start your enjoyment right here!

The game has certainly improved since the first title in the series by adding new powers. For first time the ability to play through the perspective has Corvo's Daughter Emily Kaldwin. This is a nice feature but sadly I did not see much reason to replay through the game as another character because there are only few abilities that are tailored to either Corvo or Emily that you can use together in New Game+. Also one very 'BIG IMPROVEMENT' of where you can go to the Stats menu and check to see if you have killed anyone or have been spotted making it easier to do achievement runs. Another useful feature/limitation is you can choose to use supernatural powers or not and the game will block you off so you don't have access supernatural features taking away the stress of accidentally using a power in a no powers playthrough.
Voice, Sound and Music
Voice acting was preformed well but nothing mind blowing. Sounds from supernatural powers where well engineered and make you feel like you are in the supernatural void and you about to sneak up behind this guy and blow his brains out. Music was great and fits the style of the universe one soundtrack I really enjoyed was 'Sand of Serkonos' that is featured at the end of the game.
Graphics
Graphics definitely a step up visually and hardware wise from the original Dishonored. Graphicly the game looks amazing but not so amazing on the wallet if you mainly want to play in a constant 60fps you may want to consider an upgrade from the recommended 1060 I reviewed this game on 1060 holding 6gb VRAM I could run the game with a constant 80fps inside low lit areas but but a drop to 48 - 50 fps in out door areas on Very High Preset.

Months after release, I thought enough updates would have passed and made the game how it should have been at launch. Ha, no. I have an i5 processor, GTX 970 (which is actually the card recommended for the best experience on this game) and 8GB of RAM, and yet I can't run this game at the settings I should be able to without getting the worst framerate I've ever had to experience. At launch, I was able to fiddle around and make it work reasonably well, but come on. This game is months old and I still can't play it without nerfing the settings. And even when the settings were lowered it wasn't perfect.
As a result, I can't judge this game for it's merits. The unplayable choppy framerate (which gets worse with the more action) has left such a bad taste in my mouth that I can't look at the good points of this game without being annoyed. I've looked up fixes, made sure all my drivers are up to date, but I can no longer be bothered to look for ways to fix something that SHOULD NOT NEED FIXING. I'm not going to re-install my drivers or go into the game's files or whatever, 99% of other games don't require me to do this and I'm certainly not going to start now with this one.
Just Cause 3 will sit in my library, Steam will download it's updates automatically, and I will wait and see. And the longer it takes Avalanche to get it together, the more likely I won't buy anything they make in the future.

This is my first MMO, and I was hesitant to purchase it because I had seen many friends play popular MMO's before and did not like what I saw. I've been an avid elder scrolls fan since Morrowind for Xbox, and was excited to hear about this release. Some friends play the beta and didn't recommend it. But it went on sale for Christmas last year and I had enough funds in my steam wallet so I said why not?! So glad I did! It's not really what I expected from an MMO (which was mostly negative before) and it's not quite the same as most of the other elder scrolls games preceding it (although a fresh approach was definitely nice!) you know the layout I'm talking about: run around, help rando's find their lost kitty, help other rando's assassinate their cheating spouse, accomplish side quests for factions that may or may not be more fun than the main quest which you never know if it will end up being very underwhelming and/or tedious, but at least feeling like the money spent on the game had been worth it...
TESO has definitely been all those things and , I feel, totally worth it. It has all those elements quintessentially elder scrolls with that odd [to me] MMO gameplay style that lends something fresh to the elder scrolls experience.
Sometimes other players can be of noxious and even downright rude, but my experience has been that the overwhelming majority of them are helpful or just leave you alone to do your thing in Tamriel, and there are countless guilds to join up with, meet new friends who love the elder scrolls series as much as you do, or or for you to teach them how!
I definitely recommend this amalgamation of MMO and elder scrolls to anyone looking to experience the series for the first time and for seasoned older scrolls fans alike. I won't pretend it's perfect, and there are plenty of things I wish it had that it doesn't, but at the end of the day this exists for entertainment and when I'm asked if I am not entertained, I must say I absolutely am, every time I log on!
I dont usualy like MMO's but this one is different, and actually fun.

The first half of the campaign was by far one of the best COD campaigns that have came out, but then it goes to complete crap during the second half. The story itself was acutually good and has pretty good hidden messages regarding the dangers of PMCs and the diplomacy of the U.S, but these are locked away in Intel which 90 percent of players don't get to see. The second half of the campaign was absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in terms of the story. It just gets bad real fast. If you gonna get the game just for the campaign, wait until it's under 20 bucks.
EXO Zombies is by far better than Black Ops 2 zombies but it doesn't even come close Black Ops 1 and World at War zombie modes. There has only been one map that has came out so I can't criticize it that much.
Multi-Player- It has a lot of potential on PC but at it's current state, it's not good. This is mainly because this game is dead and has a small playerbase now. Finding matches for other game modes such as Search and Destroy is nearly impossible. PC gets updates weeks later and even then it can take 1 step forward and two steps back. This game is badly ported for multiplayer, there is constant stuttering in some maps and still hasn't been fixed. None of these issues exist in the console versions of the game.
Sadly, like I stated before, this multiplayer has loads of potential on PC, since it feels like a completly different game from the previous titles and even the console versions of this game. This game is extremly fast paced and players with good aim are the ones who dominate. For once, there is a skill gap in a Call of Duty game on PC. The game has lots of customization so it keeps you busy, without it being a complete grind-fest. As well killstreaks aren't that powerful and it requires lots of kills for it to unlock, which I like since the acutual combat remains to be gun to gun.
I'll go for to say that this is the best COD multiplayer since Modern Warfare 2/COD4, but not on PC. If you want to get this game for the multiplayer, get it on consoles. The dead playerbase and the bad port makes the console versions the better option.

Wow.
Got this a while back for a  buck, and decided to give it a shot while waiting for something else to download and install. Worth it. It was a great little 45 minute trip, which was the perfect amout of time for the installation.
There's no running, no jumping, just a little circling and a little clicking. It is very short, there's no replay value, no challenge, and no skill required at all. In fact, there are a lot of people who wouldn't even call this a "game." I can't call that negitive, though. It's a series of brief interactive experiences. It's like being able to play with some wierd kenetic sculpture installation at a virtual modern art museum. Use headphones. It's not like you're going to hunt down the soundtrack and pop those tunes on at the gym, oh hells no. It's just that the ambient sound design really enhances the feelings of immersion and disorientation.
You'll probably only ever play it once, but it worth it the next time you need to wait for something else to install.
Also, for the first and (most likely only) time you play it, if you happen to have access to a quality dispensary, I highly recommended making a quick stop there, first.
EDIT: I hadn't read any other reviews before writing this, and I just read a bunch right after I posted. The one thing that comes up, over and over (besides "not a game") is reviewers comparing it to an art exibit, or a series of sculptures, it's not just me after all. When you get a bunch of unconnected people say the same thing about something, that's pretty telling about what your experience would be like, as well. If that sounds even just a little appealing to, you should check it out.

Absolutely incredible.
Dark Souls 2 takes a step closer to perfecting the metagame concept. FromSoftware has continued to plug away at the idea that a game can have multiple levels of deepness and the lack of hand holding, the discovery aspect, the demand that the player must persevere in order to not only complete the game - but to enjoy it - connects completely to our own journey in the real world. Happiness is not given to us, it is something that we yearn, something that must be attained through effort and perseverance and in many, many cases by overcoming incredible odds. The founders of the United States enumerated man's rights as life and liberty - and the PURSUIT of happiness, not its attainment. Happiness isn't granted, it is earned.
That's the meta in the Souls universe and Dark Souls 2 is the best manifestation of this concept to date. You arrive in Drangleic as the equivalent of a newborn, you know nothing, you are given nothing but the bare essentials. Everything from this point on you must earn - through trial and error, through exploration, through failure and perseverance and through hard work. Even as you push forward against seemingly overwhelming odds, invaders and allies in the form of other players may attack or defend you. You may join alliances in the form of covenants, you may invade others as an agent of their doom or choose to lend them a helping hand. The key is that you must work at everything, even the  deep and often troubling story isn't given to you - just as in the narrative of your own life - you must create it from the bits and pieces that you discover on the journey and put it together as you move along.
Despite the 'warnings' about Dark Souls 2's level of difficulty - I would recommend the game to all players. It is an allegory for life, it is an excellent teaching tool for tweens and teens, and it hammers home the lesson that happiness and accomplishment are not guaranteed, they are earned.

This game is phenominal.
It is a successor to the old Lucasarts style point-n-click adventure games -- Monkey Island and Manic Mansion most notably, but also things like the Sam and Max games. It doesn't entirely trade off the back of nostalgia, and there is enough new stuff here, and enough understanding of how to properly execute the old stuff, that there is plenty of value added.
There are a few places where the game is a little rough around the edges and there are a few things I could nitpick (like, the menu resolution should really be the same as the game resolution) but that is to be expected with such a small development team. Make no mistake, this game is however a masterpeice of the point-n-click genre and easily stands alongside the greats.
I really feel like this game needs to be the first in a series, because it feels like a game that is just breaking the ice on something. I know a custom engine was built for the game, and I really hope the team use it in the future to produce more games. I'd be really interested to see what kind of gameplay mechanics and puzzles they can come up with from this starting point.
Highly reccomended.

Put simply, this game was ahead of it's time. It's Imersive, thrilling, original and it is an RPG/FPS game. I am still waiting for a new game to come out which ticks all the boxes like this game does. Been waiting litterally years!
The graphics are not the best today, but it is well worth playing at least once. Even now I still occasionally play co-op with a friend which also adds a different dimention to the gameplay. However I would suggest playing on your own first to understand what it is like helplessly being on your own while scrambling to survive, doing what another survivor is telling you via radio communication.
While you might feel like you are getting stronger receiving upgrading modules, the games difficulty progressivly gets harder and more challenging a long with the different and creepy kinds of enemys you face. The story is quite rich and each recording picked up adds a peice to the puzzle, all while painting a deeper picture of the environment you are in.
The RPG elements means you can customise your characters abilities:
-Physically (strength, agility, etc).
-Technically (hacking/repair/research/modifiying weapons).
-Weapons (the more invested allows for better use and abilities to use more advanced weapons in that field).
-Psionically (use a psi amp to attack enemys and substituting your lack in other areas with temporary boosts and abilities).
While you may start out in any given field, you can branch out based on your personal play style.
The music is quite awesome for its time and again different to many games out there. The scenery and environment is involved and at times interacted with.
As a whole the game pushed many boundaries and is very different. Chances are you will get something out of this game regardless of who you are.

With this being my first MMORPG, I was a little hesitant.  I love the Elder Scrolls series, I've simply shied away from online gaming because I don't play at "that level".  I will say this game has opened me up.  It scales nicely to the level you are at, and the playing style you choose.  Plus, there are always other people in game that are always willing to help.  I can be working on one quest, another player is at the same point, we group together and complete it.  One recommendation I would make is to join an established guild.  Not one of the guilds that requires you to spend your in-game resources to be a member, I think that is ridiculous.  I am part of a couple of guilds that cost me nothing, and they are successful guilds.  These guilds are key, I have found, to being successful.  They also make the game more enjoyable and you can get a lot of great advice from those that are more experienced.  So I would say the community is excellent.  As far as graphics are concerned, ramp yours up to whatever your machine can handle.  I have mine set to ultra with no problems and the game is beautiful, runs smooth.  I recommend turning the grass off, it's not needed.  As far as the internet connection, I live in an area where we have caps on our internet.  Downloading ate up a lot during the monthly cycle, after that, it barely scratches it.  So from someone that has always dispised online gaming, this game rocks, and I definitely recommend it.  If you played Oblivion and Skyrim and you loved them, you will love this.

This game is a must-play for anyone who enjoyed the film.  The set-design is amazing and immersive.  From the get-go you are dropped into the world of 'Alien' with it's retro-futuristic tech and sensibilities.  The world is consistent with that of the films but still feels plausible and very real.  It adds to the broader story in a way that many of the later films and games in the franchise failed to.

If you are looking for a scary game, you won't find one scarier.  Seriously.
If you are looking for an *enjoyable* game, I'm not so sure.  There are two ways you can approach this game.  Immersion is what I prefer.  I like to put myself into the game so deeply, I forget I'm playing.  If you're the same way, this game is NOT for you.  No matter how careful you are, how calculating, you will die.  Repeatedly.  There is no amount of luck that will get you alive through more than a mission or two.  It makes immersion absolutely terrifying.
The second approach is to use the game against itself.  Not sure where you need to go in the level?  Just sprint around to explore.  You'll die.  Repeatedly.  However, you'll get useful data for when you actually try to get through for real.  It takes the terror and sting out of being killed, but it pulls you out of the story.
I tried both approaches, but found that the game was honestly either too scary or not enjoyable.  I'm not sure, at this point, if I'm going to actually finish the game.
All that being said, it's an absolutely AMAZING game.  Top shelf.  The xenomorph is impeccably recreated and it's behavior is programmed with extreme malice.  It's GOOD at finding and killing you.  It's patrols are random.  You never know where it's gone or when it will be back.  I've snuck around a level, found my  key card, and opened the door to the next section, only to have the blasted thing standing on the other side of the door.  Scream.  Die.
There are awesome emergent moments, too.  Having a group of hostile humans blunder into the Alien and giving you the time to rush through to your goal is both realistic and amazing.  I've never been so happy to hear people screaming in fear and pain.  These moments make some of the dying you'll do worthwhile.
In the end, if you know what you're getting into and it sounds good, this game will be hugely worthwhile.  If  you play games mostly to relax, there is nothing about this game that is relaxing.  You are never given a moment where you can take a deep breath and let the tension go.  Death is quick, common, and waiting around every corner.  If following a trail of crumbs consisting of nuggets of story and some emergent cool moments through a valley of death sounds interesting, go ahead and buy this game.  Just don't tell me I didn't warn you.

Islands is not so much a "game" as an interactive sensory experience. Each level starts out as a simple model of a man-made island - one of the many mundane structures we float between every day in modern life: A bus stop, a bank of ATMs, a baggage carousel; each rendered in ethereal monochrome. And through simple touch and exploration these objects transform and evolve in beautiful and unexpected ways. I found it to be a relaxing, dream-like experience. I even found it helped me get to sleep at night. It's a very short game, but definitely recommended.
As others have mentioned, it's not really a game; more of a simulated sculpture. It makes for a nice wind-down activity between gaming and going to bed.

I'm really bummed to give this game a thumbs-down, because I like the artist so much and was really looking forward to this release. Leaving those expectations aside, Islands underachives on pretty much all levels.
The gameplay is boring and repetitive. It's a bit Homer Simpsons-esque... click on the glowing thing, watch the object go up, click it again, thing goes down. Do this a few times, and then you finish the scene. I could easily see how a little creativity would make "unlocking" the different phases of each scene much more interesting.
The islands are also pretty dull, with only a few exceptions. The overall setting and aesthetic of the game could best be described as "mildly interesting".
Sound design is OK, but I don't understand why headphones were necessary. The game only seldom makes use of stereo panning, and the atmospheric sounds aren't soft enough so that regular speakers couldn't do them justice.
Finally, the entire game is really short, about an hour tops. I know, I know... this sounds too much like "the food was terrible, and the portions are so small!" Perhaps this is the only saving grace of the game.
Overall, Islands has some creative potential but falls flat. IMHO, the author would be better off stripping it down to a non-interactive demo (as in, demoscene-type demo), or adding complexity to make it a more interesting puzzle game, like "The Witness". I realize that this game is meant to be more of an atmospheric experience than a conventional game, but frankly I did not enjoy it in either context.
Cool little interactive vignettes. The asthetic is really pretty and the sound design is nice. A nice short experience. Don't be disappointed if you don't like opaque arty fartsy stuff.

If you are looking for a nice relaxing experience and a short break from your everyday life, you're in the right place (or more exactly the right "non-places" huh). It won't change your life but it's a great side step from our way to watch our surroundings. In this fresh perspective all you have to do is click from time to time and witness the blooming of those Islands.
The ambience sticks with our brain for some time but the lack of interactivity only reveals a deeper game (/ experience/ whatever piece of art it could grow into) is welcome.

I really dig this in terms of the graphical style and colour. It is an Art piece at the end of the day, rather than a game, and interaction is pretty limited, but I'd actually love to see someone build a game around this sort of aesthetic.
Very beautiful. Very strange.

ISLANDS: Non-Places isn't a game. It's an interactive sensory journey. It appears to be an artistic expression of surreal and absurd interactions, however, beneath the surface there is a feeling of collective moral guilt, as themes of humanity influence the natural world. Transportation, entertainment, consumerism, economy, communication, habitation and overcrowding even the response to natural disaster is averted by human ingenuity. Defeating nature in every aspect makes for progression without concern. But when we reach out beyond our egotistical bubble, how will the universe respond?
Relax playing it. Smooth graphic and nice design!

Eerily surreal yet beautiful, Islands: Non-Places transforms everyday settings and environments into intriguing puzzles of unfolding layers. It's strengths lie with its visual aesthetic (it was even nominated for the Nuovo Award at the 2017 IGF). Don't expect a long point-and-click adventure. There is no "traditional" protagonist or storyline. It's less than an hour long, but perhaps as long as it needs to be as an artistic exercise in interactivity.

Dark Souls 2 is a game designed for dedicated. If you have no intention on making an effort and you want a cheap thrill, then Dark Souls 2 is not the game for you. Dark Souls 2 is based around the idea of learning from mistakes. Typically, if you make a mistake in this game, you die. If you get lucky, you may make it out barely alive, but these moments are few and far between. Instead of raging and throwing your controller out the window (Don't use the keyboard for this game unless you want it to be more difficult), learn from the errors of your way.
As the wise Rafiki once said, "The past can hurt. But from the way I see it, you can either run from it, or... learn from it. "
Do the later, or you'll spend the entire game running. Learn from how you died, and adapt or develop your tactics. For example, some big armoured guys aren't afraid of being stabbed, but they don't like getting hit with blunt objects so much. Also, don't be afraid to restart the game 6 hours in or so. Once you know the gist of what to do, start again and optimise your charecter for your style. It makes the rest of your playthrough so much more managable.
Dark Souls isn't about pulling unfair moves and watching you die without remorse. It's about you forcing you to learn to adapt and overcome challenges put before you.

King’s Quest is probably not the best adventure game out there, but it is still entertaining enough to deserve an up, and I will recommend it to anyone that want a more comedy based adventure game.
First of all, I think King’s Quest should have focused solely on the comedy all throughout. It is ever present in every chapter, but at the same time it includes some side stories that are needlessly sad for this kind of story, especially with the design of the characters and creatures supporting comedy and silliness over drama and emotional stories.
Given the character design I had expected heavy elements to be handled with some more dark/silly comedy, kind of like in the adventure game “The Book of Unwritten Tales”, where death himself is depressed because no one dies in a point and click adventure game, so when he finally gets to kill someone, he has to get a smoke after because it just felt that good… Or in Corpse Bride, with a skeleton running after a woman saying he enjoys women with meat on their bones, or a guy feeling great about being dead because he finally isn't being bossed around by his employeer. Just over the top silliness.
King’s Quest however…
Luckily the game isn’t filled with so much mean spirited “comedy”, and most of the jokes are just harmless and innocent, and even if they don’t make me laugh they make me feel happy because they are cute. Filled with facepalm worthy puns, that are mostly funny when other characters react to them, and over excitement.
The overall story is nice enough. Being told as flashbacks of an old king, recounting his old adventures to his granddaughter, occasionally cutting to the current situation around the castle. But it can at times be… A bit lacking. Because you only get chapters of the king’s life, it feels like there are many adventures missing, especially between the fourth and fifth chapter. The chapters are amusing enough on their own, don’t get me wrong. But there are stories and histories the characters develop between each other through the time that is skipped over, that you just have to guess. The ending is also a bit predictable, but given that it is more meant to be a simple adventure game in a comedy fashion that isn’t really a problem.
The first chapter is without a doubt the best one, as it is the one that is just pure comedy adventure fun. And it doesn’t really have any really bad elements, other than it is the only chapter where I couldn’t skip cutscenes for some reason when going back to achievement hunt. The others had some questionable decisions, but were overall nice experiences.
The character designs fit well with the comedy aspect, overexaggerated bodies and movements. And a lot of the puzzles are fun little challenges. Almost all of the characters are likeable. The problem being that almost all villains, except the main villain, are likeable too, so you end up feeling sorry for them, giving their stories are tragic not a result of negative choices/traits. At least I felt sorry for them.
All in all, it is a game with a lot of charm, despite its inclusions of elements that it isn’t able to turn funny, and isn’t serious enough to deserve including.

Time has not been nice to System Shock 2. I played for a few hours with a friend. A mistake I guess, but I probably wouldn't have had the patience playing solo even for that long. I played using NeutralX2's Mod Pack (better visuals).
Audio was pretty basic, albeit monkey screams echoing and hybrids telling you how sorry they are had more of a comical effect rather than a scary one. If only all the remade textures had worked, visually I wouldn't have much to complain considering the age. Everything is just a fistful of polygons, but stuff is at least recognizable most of the time.
The controls feel sluggish at times. It's hard to describe what it is, everything just feels numb. The wrench, the few weapons I could try, climbing ladders, running, jumping - the last two were perhaps just a problem in the co-op network code, but they were quite horrible. I watched some speedrun videos, and things looked a bit different. The players were flying through the corridors, but that's not what the average player is going to encounter.
I usually dislike the strictly linear nature of modern games. Here things seemed the opposite: you have to go back and forth all the time. The only joy we got from that was when we got lost all the time and laughed about it. The transitions themselves weren't really fun, especially when enemies spawn randomly to the rooms you just cleared. I get it, it's meant to give you this feel that the place is living were you there or not, but it's hard to suspend my disbelief when another service bot just spawned right from nowhere just to annoy the player. In an old school FPS game you are encouraged to explore the non-linear maps, but it's rarely enforced. Here, you reach X just to realize everything was in vain (scripted events), and you have to go back to Y first, and then return to X. It felt mainly tedious.
The mechanics will take some time to get into. Nowadays I'm not that patient a player as I used to be, and quirks and small things that as a kid might have seemed cool, felt unnecessary and complex in a bad way. E.g, I figure the weapons breaking only after a few shots is to to discourage the player to shoot'em up through everything, but when you have several skills and items to tackle the problem, it just feels dumb. There are psi skills, software upgrades, implants, but they usually seemed to be just buffs like "+5 % health" or something. Things seem very deep, but in the end aren't really, as basically you are shooting stuff either with a psi-amp or weapons, so why not just drop the other. Arguably variability like this adds replay value, and probably you can micromanage yourself a nice "build", but for a casual player, it's not entertaining or interesting. It's more like statistics and numbers than tactical choices. There's also currency you can use to buy stuff from vending machines, you can hack the machines to get discounts etc. Ultimately, it's all again just micromanaging, and the unpolished GUI isn't helping a bit.
The atmosphere is what everyone mentions as great. The game might have been scary fifteen years ago, but it isn't nowadays. Things felt a bit comical. I don't like survival horror, so it wasn't a good base to begin with, but it was hard for me to imagine suspense here. The audio and visuals have much to do with that, but with the clunky and heavy mechanics it felt hard to get immersed in the world.
What makes all this funny is how much I loved BioShock 1 and 2. All the mechanics - psi-skills, hackable vending machines, respawning enemies, audio logs, running back and forth - were there. But most of the time, interface and playability was smooth, there still was a lot of variety for weapon/psi combos. BioShock got things right. I have respect for SS2 in pioneering things, but the truth is, it just isn't enjoyable anymore.
On a side note, as some have already mentioned: the Linux version is actually wrapped with Wine, and there is no multiplayer option by default. You have to do some manual work to get it there, and even then you probably encounter some network issues as I did. Eventually I just played using Windows. It might be worth your time to install OpenAL in Windows to get echo effects - it's included in the Linux/Wine version by default, but not in Windows, but I read that you can get it to work.
In conclusion, if you want to check out a relic that introduced some new mechanics to the world, do try SS2. You might actually enjoy it. For casual gamers, you're probably a decade late for this ride.

As some of you might already now this  game is considered a classic and a milestone in the history of video games. But time can be brutal especially for games whom rely so heavily on graphics and the ergonomy of gameplay. So the question of the day is:  has system shock 2 hold up to time? and more importantly should you give it a shock? ( haha boring pun).
Anyway before I begin my review I must tell you I didn't play it back in the day so I am not blinded by nostalgia.
so lets begin the review shall we?
Pros:
+ The story ( spoiler free)
you are a nameless soldier that has just awakened from your slubber in a starship named the Vaun Braun trillions of light years away from Earth. As you start exploring the ship you understand something as gone terribly terribly wrong and with the guidance of a surviving crue membre it's up to you to save the day ( if ever it can be saved). And let me tell you that if the story sounds pretty generic I can assure you it become far more intricat and intresting as you slowly discover what happened. Most of the story comes in the formes of audio logs which helps you understand what the Van Braun used to be like and why it turned out the way it did. So to enjoy the story to it's full extent you will have to  find and listen to the logs. Never the less the story is fairly entertaining and hold up well to today's standards.
+ A range of play styles
Do you like to shoot you way trough ennemies only stopping to check there corpse for ammo?  or would you rather blast them away with scifi wizard powers? or would you hack trough the terminal to gain the upper hand? or maybe you would  love  to charge  enemies  with a old wrench screaming "Geronimo" to you screen? ( no?  That's just me? Well that's embarrasing...).
And now what if I told you System Shock 2 offered you any of these play styles. Great isn't it but you will have to choose which one because there are not enough upgrades to master everything. On the plus side it offers a great replay value for those willing to start all over again.
+ The ambiance
Rarely have I felt so emerdged in a game. I have lost count on how many times I bounced of my seat when a grunt sneaked up on me. And that is just the tip of the iceberg the Vaun Brun is a gem of design each area feels unique and believable. But the greatest accomplishement of the game is that overaching feeling of dread and doom you will feel as you dwelve deeper into the ship.
+ The sound
The music in this game is amazing. It is  gloomy and oppressif when your exploring this god forsaken ship and become catchy and pushing when you get into a fight. This means the ost never gets dull and really reflect what is happening on screen.

Mixed:
+- The graphics
The game came out in 1999 and at that time it would have blown my mind. But nowadays people expect HD, hyper realistic graphics and there is none of that even the mods ( which are great by the way) only offer a slight enhancement. I understand that this section is unfair to the game, as it came out 14 years ago but I feel the need to compt the graphics as a mixed opinion because  there are time when the npcs just came across as cheesy ( mainly there faces's) and it impeded my gaming experience. The environnements on the other hand still look and feel great and the robots still hold up to an extent. But at the end of the day if you can overlook the bulky npcs you will not mind the graphics.
Cons:
- The gameplay
Yet an other sign of the game's age the interface is abnoxious and you will have a lot of things to handle ( foods, weapons, different types of ammo, guns that break as you use them, medikits that heal you heath over time and not in a instant ect) this at times can feel overwhelming  specialy if your are in a middle of a gun fight even you magic wizard power need to be "reloaded". Speaking of reloads, there are not automatic you will have to press R to trigger the action. it might seem nitpicking but trust me it become nerve wreaking when you were one bullet short of defeting your foe and you die  because you didn't to press R but continued to press the trigger button instead.

- Backtracking
Let's get this straight nobody like to backtract to previous areas just to activate a code or to find some item you could have picked up before hand. It feels contrived and boring specialy because nothing new is added to those areas except maybe a "surpise" ennemy that pops out of nowhere for the hell of it.
- Some unfairness
the game may be unfair at certain points specially if you use up your last ressources ( ammo power medkits) and a tough fight is a head. Some might say that managing your ressource is  part of the game and to a certain extent they are right. but when you have used  up everything to get passed a hard point just to move on to a harder task you will feel as if the game had suddenly became impossible.
Conclusion:
To conclude System Shock 2 as aged pretty well giving the circumstances. The ambiance remains astonishing and it's story will drive you all the way trough. This game is according to me an experience that is worth the frustration and the unfairness so yeah you should give it a shock ( sorry I couldn't help myself) .

One-liner: "This is Amnesia in space"
This is as close as you'll ever get to the atmosphere of the original Alien movie. It even has two DLC's that give you a couple of missions with the original cast. The alien is creepy as hell and completely unpredictable. It's really, really well-done. Hiding under a desk, looking at the tail of the alien twirl around just beside you. Yup, bring clean underpants.
The gameplay is sort of a mix of a puzzle game and a strategy game, trying to figure out where the alien is, and whether you can make that next corner without running into it. At least the alien missions are.
Which brings me to the cons of the game. There are androids and humans, and they are annoying. Missions with androids - don't like them. Second con is that the game is probably double the length as it should be. Yes, I'm complaining about the length of a game. I wouldn't normally do this, if it was justified. But in this case it's just 6-8 hours of filler missions where all you're doing is dodging androids and bringing the power back on (again and again and again).
But it doesn't take away from the brilliant alien gameplay, which is, fortunately, located in the first half of the game (and in the end, but less interesting there).
Its a fun, scary game. Unlike other games, in this game you are very underpowered, and have to resort to sneakiness to avoid dying. Its a fun game, and requires some time to getting used to.

Finally a horror game that relies less on jump-scares and more on building a creepy atmosphere. Alien: Isolation is a love letter to Ridley Scott`s original Alien movie with meticulous attention to detail in the art-style and sound design. When played with a good headset you can pinpoint every sound around you, and more importantly sounds from the vents above you...
Sevastopol station is a huge space station floating around a gas giant. It reminds me of the Nostromo in many ways, which of course is intended, and everything from the dark hallways to the living quarters reminds me of Alien. In Alien: Isolation, just like the movie, quarantine procedures are not the crew`s strong suit, and combined with a corrupt megacorporation in control of the station, this of course leads to unwanted visitors on the station.
The Alien is an intimidating foe, and one of the more memorable monsters in movie history. It is recreated in a great way in Alien: Isolation, and every wrong step can be your last. Untill you get a flamethrower (with ammo in short supply) you are pretty much helpless and have to resort to hiding whenever you spot the Alien. The pacing in the game is also excellent, and even when it`s a long time since you have met anything that wants to hurt you, you never feel safe.
The graphics, in addition to the already mentioned sound-design, is great. Technically impressive and very well optimized on the PC. Lighting and shadows create an eerie and awesome atmosphere. IMO one of the best games of 2014.

By the time I'd finished the second mission of the game, I'd decided I was going to write a review of it.  Having completed it, here I go.  But, what to write about?  Many other reviewers have written about the graphics, sound and gameplay mechanics; so I think I'll write about how this game made me
.
Long after we forget about the mechanics or the graphic settings of a game, what stays with us the emotional memory of that game; I mean, this is why fanboys still weep for Morrowind, and why I've played Neverwinter Nights through countless times over the years!  Numerous other examples lead me to think it's a truly important factor, worthy of review.
So, what did this game make me feel?
.  Sheer, unmitigated terror.  Let me say,
I was in a shop somewhere the other day, and something beeped like the motion detector in the game, and I almost sh!t myself!  I also now have an irrational fear of a
creature that I have not been afraid of for over a quarter of a century!! (Yes, I'm old, I know).  It's important to note that I'm not talking about jump scares (yes, there are jump scares in the game, most of them are unexpected, and not one of them feels cliched or out of place).  I'm talking about the terror that comes from being in a life-or-death hunt, where all the odds are stacked against you, and all you can do is try to survive...
From the opening logos on, this game has been designed to recapture the atmosphere of its iconic progenitor, Alien.
Everything in game replicates the production design of that movie down to the smallest detail:  the odd juxtaposition of interstellar travel technology with late 70's crappy computers; the banal-combined-with-hi-tech decor; and other elements that I won't mention (spoilers).  The intended result is successfully achieved:
.  At no time did I doubt that I was in the Alien "Universe".
And, Sevastopol Station is the nightmarish rendering of that universe gone wrong.  As you travel through the station, you see the believable consequences of a calamity befallen group of people trying to survive when nothing works, and everything else is falling apart.  Desperate executives, terrified citizens, and malfuntioning androids, are juxtaposed with advertising posters and recordings of what Seegeson's dream was, and just how far it has fallen.  All this adds a layer of sadness that, in my opinion, adds to the believability of the unviverse.
The graphics and score add to the atmosphere of terror.  A shadow floating past a porthole had me jumping in fear, and when I looked, it was a piece of wreckage floating past, with the backdrop of the remainder of the station and the gas giant it orbits reminding me of just how small and insignificant I was.  In other parts, smoke, darkness, and beautifully rendered lense flair again add depth by making it hard to see what's ahead, increasing inherent fear.  Also, here, I have to mention one of my favourte features - the ability to change focus when holding the motion detector:  you can look at the detector, or everything else, but not both, and when you look at one, the other goes out of focus!  This can be scary as all hell!!!
The score seems to be based off the original Alien score, and in most instances, it adds to the tension with it's unnerving high-pitched strings that build to a crescendo as an object of hostility comes hunting for you.  Occassionally, it can be distracting, as it can drown out the sound of movement and the detector when a very dramatic piece plays, but this only became an issue for me once in the game.
Seven paragraphs in and you're going "this guy hasn't even talked about the Alien."  Ok, here we go.  The Alien is both unreal and terrible, and it is important to note that I use those words in a Lovecraftian context:  hiding in a locker, watching this "thing" move around and attack people while actively hunting me, had me thinking "this thing should not be!"  The creature is truly a thing of nightmare.  And when it hunts you, you know fear.  The first time it came for me, the events, music, and my experience as an avid fan of the series told me what was going to happen, and what to expect, and yet, when its head first appeared through a billowing cloud of steam, I had a moment of true terror.
.  I turned and ran like a little girl.  The Alien has heightened senses and an unmitigated savagery that make it a fearsome opponent, and many times, when I was hiding, I found
holding my breath until it passed, becasue if it gets you, it's all over, red rover.
This is a survival game, and it's best not to forget that, because if you do, you're dead.  If you decide to go all Duke Nuke-em, and charge in with guns blazing, you're dead.  If you get impatient and go "F#ck it, I'm going through, and I'll fight my way out if I have to," you're dead.  You
die in this game.  A lot.  Save points are strategically placed to make achieving the next one feel deeply rewarding, and also to reward smart gameplay.  Because, that's the only way to survive.  Stay low, quiet, and out of everyone, and everything's way.  You have to know when to run, when to hide, and when to make an aggressive assualt.  You have to pick your moments, otherwise, you're dead.
I had a rush of blood to the head when I got the flamethrower; I was like, "That's it! No more hiding for me!  It's time to give this Alien what-for, and make it run and hide!"  And I did.  And then I ran out of fuel.  And then I died.  While there's enough material floating around to craft the items that help you survive (some of which are truly indispensable),  you can't carry a lot of them, and more importantly, there's never enough ammo.  Even if you have enough ammo, it's not enough.  I played through on the recommended setting of hard, so I don't know if the easier setting gives you more ammo or not, but the (intended, in my opinion) effect of this was to create a feeling of helplessness:  I felt like I was powerless in the face of things far beyond my control, and all I could do was hide and try to survive.  Which, I believe, was the intended intention of the game! ;)
A quick comment on negatives:  I really only found two.  There is a part of the game where you will find two items you need, just lying in a spot for no particular reason.  They're there because you need them.  It stuck out to me as the only reality breaking moment in an otherwise seamless creation.  The other is the human AI; while the Alien and android AI's are both superb, the human AI fluctuates between hyper alert and bad.  I mean, laughably bad.  They'll spot you if you peep around a corner more than twice, but give up once you break line of sight.  Then they stand around mouthing idiotic comments like the guards in Thief.  Some of the comments are almost identical to comments in that game!  In one part, I was pressed up against a wall and the human walks past me, all the while looking right at me, but doesn't see me!  It made me want to have the Alien come and kill them!!
In summary, Creative Assembly should be proud of themselves for this near flawless masterpiece of gaming they've created, and I firmly believe they've set a new standard for FPS/Survival/Horror games, especially in terms of graphics, sound, atmosphere, and gameplay.  A game that plays out like a movie with total immersion, and psychological investment, is one that is worthy of both replaying, and having some fond, yet terrifying emotional memories!
9.5/10

Oh boy, what can I say that others haven't?  Well, I'll just give my personal impressions from a long standing ALIEN(s) fan.
If you are a fan of ALIEN, the original Dan O'Bannon / Ridley Scott horror film, then this is the game for you.  But it also may not be the game for you.  How can I say that?  Well, I'm one of those original ALIEN fans, but I'm not much of a survival horror gamer or even a fan of the horror genre at all.
Well this game dumps you right into the horror genre full force.  I wasn't prepared.  Oh mommy I wasn't prepared.  Having never played a survival horror game previously, I thought to myself "How bad can it be?".  It's THAT bad.  I would finish a mission and have to take a break for fear of my blood pressure causing an aneurism.
I'm guessing for those of you used to games like Amnesia and Silent Hill, Resident Evil and The Evil Within, then this kind of gameplay is old hat for you.  But me?  I pretty much play everything BUT survival horror.  From dozens of FPS, Strategy games, to RPG's, but never the horror games.
I spent hours hiding in lockers and storage cabinets terrified to get out of them.  Even with full knowledge that I had saved my game a hundred yards away, the Alien wasn't showing on the tracker, had gone into the air vents, and I hadn't really accomplished anything yet except for getting in the storage locker.
So what I'm trying to say here, is that if you love the ALIEN movie, but aren't really a survival horror gamer, then you may be better off watching the dozens of playthroughs on YouTube instead.
I ended up cranking the difficulty setting down to Easy by Mission 5, and let me assure you that ALIEN Isolation in Easy mode is hard mode in other games.  I attempted Hard mode at first, but found I was taking hours to get through even a single mission, and I honestly wanted to get out of a locker without dying and on with the story.
The story.  Ok, this is what drew me to the game in the first place.  The chance to see what Amanda Ripley was doing in the 57 year interim between ALIEN and ALIENS?  Hell, I thought they said illegal Alien and signed the ♥♥♥♥ up.  I love the premise of the story, and I really loved the entire setting of Sevastopol.  Finding the flight recorder and... well, I don't want to drop spoilers here, but the story is just great.  Really great.  This game could easily have been the next installment in the ALIEN franchise; and a worthy one unlike the utter crap that were ALIEN3 and ALIEN: Resurrection.
Graphics:  I played this game on a triple monitor setup with a GTX 670 Gigabyte video card.  I never experienced any lag or stuttering whatsoever.  There was a quite a bit of screen tearing, but I only noticed it during the less tense mooments when I wasn't being eaten.
Overall, the graphics are downright beautiful.  The lighting was perfect for the setting, the attention to detail in regards to the ALIEN franchise was top notch.  The San Cristobal medical facility mission was one of the best lit game levels I've seen in any game.
A couple things were overdone... did there really need to be a drinking chicken head toy on every dining table in the game?  I swear no one on the station owned a garbage can as trash was just everywhere and not in an "the Alien trashed this room" kind of way, but natural dirtyness.
A couple things made no practical sense whatsoever like the reactor core scene where it's simultaneously pouring water everywhere combined with electrical discharges all around you... Yeah, Ripley would have been flash fried within seconds of being there.  But it looked cool and it was a nice change of pace.
Sounds:  Top notch.  Easily one of the best audio experiences I've had in a video game.  Maybe ever.  MIssion 14 with the sound cranked up?  This is easily the mission where I decided I probably won't do a second playthrough of the game.  I found myself sneaking through this level whispering "Never again!" to myself.  Absolutely terrifying thanks to the great sound effects.
Also, a caveat:  If you are more of a fan of the ALIENS film and the original ALIEN film, then this game may not be for you.  There's no Pulse Rifles, grenade launchers or Gyro Arm mounted machine guns.  You do get couple weapons later on, but they have extemely limited ammo and are largely innefective.
*POSSIBLE SPOILER*
You do get a flamethrower that will chase the Alien off and make him run into the air vents.  What I discovered very quickly is that this makes the Alien come back with more frequency.  The Alien will typically spend quite a bit of time in the air vents walking around, but if you flame it and it runs into the air vents, then you've got about 30-45 seconds before he gets♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and comes right back.
If you must use the flamethrower, then vacate the immediate area quickly afterwards.  Don't stand around reading life stories on the terminals, just get out.
Once you get the flamethrower, DO NOT forget your roots.  Hiding in storage lockers still works and won't have him rampaging around the level looking for the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that just set him on fire.  I used it more like a last resort.  Ok, I'm cornered, nowhere to hide and he's RIGHT THERE.  Time to send him running and then GTFO.
*SPOILER END*
Now on to the things I didn't like.
Lets start off with the ending.  I'm not gonna spoil it here, but seriously F U SEGA.  What the crap is this ending?  No closure, no resolution, no tying up loose ends.  Just *BLAM* the game is now over.  It's absolutely the worst ending of a great game that I have ever experienced, but then again, I liked how ME3 ended so I'm not sure what that says about me.
Also, the legth of the game was a bit ridiculous.  The last two hours felt very contrived.  Hey lets keep having disaster after disaster to add more pointless game time.  Personally I would have ended it much sooner... like say on the Ambulance shuttle.  I'd have flown straight to the Torrens on that thing and thrown up dueces at Sevastopol.  Peace ♥♥♥♥♥es!  I'm out!
I know this has been said before in other reviews, but good grief the back-tracking was excessive.  I counted in one mission alone I had to go back and forth across the entire map seven times to get a single door open.  The entire map from one end to the other.  Ok, find a keycard, go to the other side of the level and open a safe, go to the other side of the level and start a generator, go back to the other side of the level and push a button, go back again and.... ect.
It wasn't just one level either.  Quite a few levels weren't all that big really, but were made to feel bigger by having to re-cross the same territory a few times.  For the sequels I suggest bigger levels, less linearity, give us a few things to do on that level and let us decide what to do first and how to do it.
My last con is this:  For the love of all that's good, let us quick save any damn where we please.  There's nothing more soul crushing that getting right to the elevator that you need, you haven't saved in 20 minutes of game play and you get ambushed from the ceiling.  If I'm hiding in a locker and I'm not sure I'm gonna make it to the next room, then let me save there.
Maybe have a hardcore mode where players can only save at save points for those to like to replay entire sections of the game repeatedly, but for those of us along for the story let us quick save on easy mode.

It's a free game, you get what you pay for it. Hit detection on moving targets is none existant, zombies have acquired mystal phasing abilities that allow them to pass through eachother and sometimes even strike or grab you through a fence, and as is the case in most games that feature stamina systems, it assumes you're an obese older gentleman with asthma. Animations are also laughably terrible, particularly on the players who shuffle about as if they have a load in their diaper, and all in all it's a terrible looking game.
But game play wise, besides the affore mentioned hit detection and stamina, it's decent and manages to create a stressful scenario as you have to dodge past dozens of zombies to get to the next objective, or fight off a giant horde trying to break into your "safe" house, while worrying about ammo and medical supplies running out, and whether or not someone on your team is infected and is out of pills.
Weapon models aren't terrible, however anything with a scope is essentially useless as the typical engagement ranges are at arm's length, especially the sniper rifles as the use of their scopes black out your peripherial vision entirely, and for some reason the MAC 10 that uses .45 ACP does significantly less damage than the M1911 which uses the same ammo. Otherwise most weapons only take one or two shots to down a zombie, so long as you're aiming for head shots, which you will need to if you want surive.
All in all it's a medocre game saved by the fact that it's entirely free to play, there's no freemium or hidden transactions here, and to that end it's a fine time waster if you get burned out on the other games in your library or just want to get a go at some real survival horror. The horror being the dated graphics and engine.

There is too much that is wrong with this game and I've found that contradicting something the Creative Assembly has said gets you insta-hate from their fanboys which is a constant on the forums or blocked entirely from saying anything constructive about the game at all. With a mix of bad customer service, bare-faced lying to their customers and combined with a broken game, this Total War game isn't worth your attention unless it's on sale for a very low price.

Maybe the engine limitations won’t be so annoying to those who prefer newer styles of adventure games (especially of the 3D variety) to the older point and click ones, but as a Sierra and KQ fan I gotta say that I’m sorely disappointed by the direction the devs chose for the game engine.

The first chapter is worth playing, as it's pretty much the only chapter that is true to the old Sierra adventure point/click games.  But I wouldn't pay for the whole collection, just play the first chapter for free.  The other chapters get progressively worse and worse.  It's kind of like when you try to start a new hobby, start off strong, but then you completely forget about it a month later.  That's kind of how the Odd Gentlemen have treated this old gem, started with a strong chapter representative of what made the old games great, but with each successive chapter it appears they remember less and less of what made the old adventure games great.  The biggest chapter is the first one, the rest are puny by comparison.  If you want to know the story presented in the later chapters, just watch playthroughs on youtube or read about it on wikis.

(Disclaimer: I've spent much more time in SyS 2 but outside of Steam).
Beforehand: I'm as far into the game that I just have to share my thoughts with you. I started with the vanilla version but I spent most of the time with a modded version (community patch, various texture and graphical mods). So my experience is mostly based on a patched up SyS 2.
As many others, I knew Bioshock before I've heard of SyS 2. I was aware that Bioshock was heavily influenced by Sys 2, the one can be seen as the spiritual successor or the other way round SyS 2 as the predecessor.
Some say that SyS 2 is the better game and I was sceptical about that because of the game's age and Bioshock's quality. Well, it's a matter of taste and I won't debate it here.
(Let's finally start with the review at this point.) However what SyS 2 delivers is downright beautiful. I actually turned the new NPC models (mod) off because the original ones with high poly scare the pie out of me.
This refers to my first point: -Atmosphere- The setting presented is executed in a brilliant way. Music (ambient one, not the DnB/Techno - at least for my taste) and surrounding are intertwined beautifully. Additionaly the mechanics and gameplay add to the hostile feeling and environment because you're constantly short on supplies. You are worried about every next step. This again meets with the urge to explore. The game does it right, because not only you want to explore, you also have to because of the supply shortage. And you don't feel forced to as well as you will get rewarded for your curiosity without making the game predictable.
I forgot to mention the customization which goes far deeper than in e.g. Bioshock. Your character can be developed in innumerous ways - not only in terms of common classes. In sum classes and specialization are very "fluid". Everything makes sense in-game - it isn't just there, so you can do it but it's thought through. The way this game makes you making choices is just hard to be matched.
-Realism- Some people classify this game as a "sim fpsrpg" and that for a reason. E.g. every weapon wears off. You can maintain, repair and modify objects. Certain weapons work on certain enemies etc. You have to know and can research your enemies weaknesses. It boils down to stats eventually but also on how you approach every single situation. Gunplay (if focused by your way of playing) itself isn't very satisfying but it serves its purpose.
-AI- Well the AI has aged but it has implemented the stages of awareness you might know of the Thief titles - being suspicious, alerted, etc. It may be clunky but pathfinding works good and it strangely fits the game. It is bone-hard to beat anyway, and the AI makes it even scarier.
Some final words: Of course the game has faced enough criticism as well for being clunky and overly complex but I guess the community patches have brought some extra balance and smoothed out the rough edges (graphically and figuratevly speaking). And the mod manager let's you turn mods on and off (!) in a matter of seconds which is a big advantage compared to dumb copy and paste of modded directories. Simply put, the (modding) community is great - also thanks to Looking Glass Studios.
Ad Backtracking criticism: I don't consider this as a problem. As aforementioned - it makes sense and is part of the realism. Furthermore it adds to reduce linearity so often seen in games and it rewards players who can memorise stuff.
Final words: SyS 2 reminds you of what a game can be and what a game can and should do right. I recommend it to everyone and plead for some patience of those who feel e.g. overwhelmed at first.
Yours,
B.

I loved Monkey Island when I was young, and this game gave me all the same great feelings when playing Monkey Island. The setting is great, the graphic is wonderful, the characters are well made, the humor is hilarious, and it has a very special atmosphere just like Monkey Island had. It has a great retro look and feel, but when you look more closely it is clear it is modernized quite a bit too, but not in a way that takes away the wonderful style of the old games. It has an old style, but does not in any way feel outdated!
I wondered if I liked is so much just because I am nostalgic, but my son (turning 10 soon) that has never played Monkey Island, loved it too. He was a bit skeptic to play a game with pixel graphic, but as soon as we started playing he was sold! This is a great game, and the genre is not in any way getting old!

The great:
- Finally, a true point and click game after 20 years
- It's huge
- The art and mood are fantastic
- They struck the right balance between retro pixel art, and using modern rendering (the parallaxing is awesome)
- The story is great (so far, I'm in chapter 3)
- It's genuinely funny
- 4 hours in, I completed only about 20% of the game (if the achievements are any indication), without walkthrough obviously
The pretty bad to downright inexcusable from the creator of the genre:
- Many points of the game refer to, or give you puzzle solutions for, things you haven't discovered yet. This sometimes is really confusing (from the very beginning - the very first action you can do, refers to an item in your inventory that wasn't even introduced if you didn't click on it)
- The default right-mouse click action on objects is most of the times useless/downright annoying. So you're forced to pick a verb and then click the object, for things that have an obvious action (which is most objects). A number of objects are packed close together and have small hitboxes, so this is even more aggravating when you have to pick a verb and then slightly miss the object, even on a 30" screen. Can't imagine what it will be like on a tablet.
- The dolores intro/flashback scene. It brought the game to a standstill and it was my least favorite puzzles so far.
- While the game world is huge, it feels pretty empty. Most things in scenes cannot be clicked on; even just to give some humorous text (even generic, if VO cost was a concern). Coming from just playing the DOTT remake where almost everything responds to the player, this was a big letdown.
- It references maniac mansion and other LucasArts games WAY too much. Wink wink lampshading is fine, but there is way too much of it.
- It is WAY too easy so far. Not the good kind of easy; the bad kind of easy where puzzle solutions are spoiled, or are super obvious. Probably the result of too much playtesting/panicking (note: I am playing in hard mode; I can't even imagine what easy would be like..)
- The music in some parts of the game is really annoying
- I'm not sure what the point of the multiple characters is, so far. 3 chapters in, only one puzzle action required using more than one character, and it was super obvious / automatically done by the game. Everything else in the game is literally the characters saying the very same thing when you do the same action on an object.
Overall, this game is such a rare treat that I highly recommend buying it right away and trying to sip it (rather than swallow ti whole) so you can really enjoy it. A lot of things are disappointing considering who made it, but since this is such a rare entry in the genre, that makes up for the flaws, I think.

I would approach this game more in the sense of paying to view a short minimally-interactive film or experimental art piece moreso than a traditional "game."
I picked the game up at a significantly discounted price, but I did enjoy what I saw of the experience. It is a very conceptual game you may find on mobile / web platforms ala ZenBound, and the gameplay here is rotation of environments  (or objects... an entire lounge which has an impressive flooding sequence, or a fridge which spews its contents into a light pattern you have to click on...) you are completely restricted to rotating objects and clicking on parts of them, meters, lights, etc... to trigger the next animation / level change / cutscene into happening. There is no story, instead you are observing ambient scenes with surreal effects. The game did begin to wear thin about halfway through its levels, as I found it to begin to feel a bit tedious/repetitive, but I really enjoyed the first 5 episodes or levels / scenes that I watched, the flooding lounge area being my favorite of what I saw.
That being said, its replay value is quite low and its initial presentation is fairly abstract with very minimalistic gameplay (no story, "rotating and click") which may turn off some of its appeal. What I have played of it is well-done and immersive.
