When Tango and Bethesda first revealed that Evil Within 2 would have open-world elements, I was among the group that worried this could lead to a dull, unfocused game bogged down by side activities and fetch quests. Thankfully, this turned out to not be the case - Evil Within 2 is, for the most part, an engaging, if somewhat standard, follow-up to the original game.
You once again play as now former police officer Sebastian Castellanos, who is recruited by Juli Kidman to re-enter the STEM machine and search for his missing daughter Lily within the disintegrating simulation of a town called Union. Finding and saving Lily involves shooting, stabbing, or sneaking your way past hundreds of monsters just like the enemies in the first Evil Within. You're given a greater variety of weapons this time around, and crafting and skills are expanded to allow for a wider variety of play styles, but the core mechanics remain essentially the same. You can try to remain out of sight of the enemies as much as possible to conserve ammo, but the open combat is enjoyable and robust in execution. Well-designed audio and video feedback makes weapons feel meaty and the enemies react convincingly to your presence, jumping in and out of your path and dodging your aim so that headshots take a degree of skill to execute. Most combat areas in the game also provide a variety of options for using the environment to take out enemies, such as flammable oil slicks or puddles you can shoot with a shock bolt.
Much like in the first Evil Within, you can collect brain gel from enemies and use it to upgrade Sebastian's health and skills. Evil Within 2 also introduces weapon upgrades and ammo crafting, which can be done in a safehouse at a workbench, or on the fly, though the latter uses more resources. I was initially worried that the crafting would be intrusive and too similar to an RPG, but in reality it's very straightforward and doesn't suck up too much of your time. The game doesn't have universal ammo, but you can craft the same resources into a variety of different kinds of ammo, which is helpful if you are trying to stick to particular playstyle. However, I can imagine that survival horror purists may not like that particular feature.
Survival horror fans may also have mixed feelings about the game's resource management and difficulty. At least on the "survival" difficulty, which is the middle of three that can be selected for a first playthrough, resources and ammo are relatively abundant and I only felt the crunch of low ammo reserves a couple times during the game. You can't just shoot at everything willy-nilly, but with a little exploration you shouldn't be finding yourself constantly running out of ammo on casual or survival difficulty.
This has the side effect of making survival much easier than it was in the first Evil Within. In fact, survival in EW2 feels about as easy as Casual in EW1 (if not easier). Those seeking the high level of challenge that the first game offered will need to start their first playthrough on nightmare difficulty.
Though Evil Within 2's combat remains quite similar to the first game, it makes significant changes with regards to pacing and level design. The first Evil Within was mostly linear, but featured a few marginally open environments that could be traversed in a variety of ways, such as the mansion near the midway point of the game. By contract, Evil Within 2 features two large, open hub areas, which you have to traverse between story missions and which also feature a few side missions and activities.
Thankfully, the game does not fall into the trap of becoming a boring open world game, though it does start off on the worst possible foot in this regard. After a fairly lengthy (and boring) opening scripted sequence, you are dumped into the first hub area and given a task to explore the area collecting readings with your magic plot-assistance communicator. This mission reminded me strongly of the boring sort of "walk here and watch a cutscene" missions that you find in Ubisoft-style open world games, and it made me worried that Evil Within 2 was going to devolve into a series of boring fetch quests. However, once you get through this initial slog, the pacing improves and the game becomes more combat-heavy.  You can continue to explore the hub areas for supplies and complete the small number of side missions, but after the introduction the majority of the game takes place within well-designed semi-linear levels. Of the 15 hours I spent on my first playthrough, I'd guess that only 3 or 4 were spent exploring the hub areas - the rest was story missions.
Speaking of the story, the one told in EW2 is much more straightforward and easy to understand than EW1's story. This both a blessing and a curse - those who found EW1's story confusing will be happy to know that EW2's story is understandable from start to finish. Unlike in the first game, Sebastian knows exactly what's going on from the beginning, and the game's ending wraps up the plot neatly, rather than leaving threads hanging like the end of EW1.
However, I felt that the confusing plot of EW1 actually contributed to the overall nightmarish aesthetic of the game. At the beginning of that game, Sebastian doesn't understand what's happening to him, and the constant shifting of setting and perspective reminds me of the experience of having a nightmare. Additionally, every environment Sebastian encounters in EW1 is uniquely unsettling, so you never become too comfortable with your surroundings. By contrast, EW2's straightforward plot and abundance of familiar safe areas results in a game that doesn't produce the same level of constant tension. EW2 still possesses a compelling horror aesthetic, but it fails to perfectly replicate the original's unsettling atmosphere.
On the other hand, Evil Within 2's plot delves more deeply into Sebastian's tragic backstory, and though many elements are very tropish, the story turned out to be more moving than I expected, and the loss of one particular character near the end of the game hit me harder than I was anticipating from a game about shooting zombies in the head.
Technically, Evil Within 2 is in so-so shape as of the date of this review (October 26th, 2017, two weeks after launch). While I'm able to get acceptable performance (70-100 fps at 1080p/max settings) on my Ryzen 7 1700 and GTX 1080, it's clear from others' reviews that the game doesn't scale very well for lower-end or even midrange graphics cards, and lowering graphics settings doesn't improve performance by much. For example, changing settings from highest to lowest on my PC gained me only about 15 fps. Also, GPU utilization is too low - only about 70% on my GPU at 1080p - and the issue persists even at 4K resolution, indicating that it's not being caused by a CPU bottleneck. Lastly, some users (including professional tech sites like Digital Foundry) have reported persisting stuttering that can't be solved by adjusting settings. I have not experienced these myself, but you should be aware of it because it's a well-known issue.
Bethesda claims there is a patch incoming "soon" that will hopefully rectify some of these issues, but until then, be aware that you may experience some of these issues if you pick up the game in its current state.
On the plus side, Evil Within 2 does feature an FOV slider, and it's much easier to control with a mouse and keyboard compared to the first game, where keyboard controls were an awkward mess. You can bind weapons and items to the number keys so you aren't forced to use the radial menu. Additionally, crouching is set to a toggle by default rather than hold, so this game won't kill your pinky the way the first game did.
Performance issues aside, this is a solid horror/stealth/action game with a compelling story that's worth picking up for fans of the genre, but by no means essential.

A series of surreal interactive landscapes - not really a game.
This game doesn't so much have a narrative as a series of interlocking puzzle landscapes. It's pretty enough for an indie title, although I'm halfway through in under an hour. Replayability is also not really a thing; there seems to be no difference in results based on how you interact with the landscapes. It succeeds as an experimental and atmospheric experience, but not so much as a game in itself. It went on sale for $1, although I'd say an apt price tag would be $2.99, reminiscent of packs of screen savers sold for early Windows versions.

A group of chirping eggs exit their bus, that disappears underground in a moment. They gather in the light of the bus stop, ready to be hatched I assume. Later some palm trees ride an escalator up to their automated watering spot. Meanwhile what looks like an office lobby is gradually consumed by flood water.
All these scenes - and more - are spinnable and slightly interactive, with light cues pointing to the things to be clicked.
Yes, it's not a game per se, but rather interesting set of ten interactive art installations with nice atmosphere. I call it walking simulator without walking. You should try it if you're into this kind of leftfield experimental stuff.
It's cheap and you can complete it in about 45 minutes.

This is not a game, so if you're looking for puzzles to solve, look somewhere else.
This is more like watching a virtual art exhibit; interaction is minimal (click where it's blinking or little more than that). It's a series of surreal environments where strange things happen as you click around, and I mean strange in a good, oniric way. Sounds and visuals merge beautifully into a mesmerizing experience.
As with all works of art, it's a very personal experience, so there's no way to know if you'll like it until you try it. My suggestion is, do try it, especially now that its price tag is 99 cents. Even if it's only to help out someone who's trying to do something different, and god knows if we need people like that.

Let's get the negatives out of the way:
- Bad performance, constant stuttering on i7 4790K GTX 970. Texture pop-in from the first game was not fixed.
- Incredibly buggy throughout entire playthrough (Try climbing on and off of a car)
- Meh story. The first game's story was incomprehensible, but this time the story is boring with bland writing, laughable voice-acting and mostly cookie-cutter premise.
- Some upgrades outright break the game, such as the stealth-kills from around corners, and the upgraded Gas Bolts.
- The match mechanic is gone. This means when you discover dead bodies that are obviously enemies waiting to activate, you have no choice but to use up ammunition
- The aiming is still f***ed, like the first game. Point-blank shots will often miss, ESPECIALLY with the shotgun. If you've played either game, you know what I'm talking about.
- Enemy AI is shockingly bad. Bushes are incomprehensible to enemies of the game
- This is subjective, but I'm not a fan of how cleaned-up the game looks atheistically compared to the first game, which was much more grimy and moody, which fit the tone more.
- Seb and Kidman's VA's are different. Blaaah
Now, you've read all of this and you notice I still recommend this game. Why is that?
+ There is a legitimate fun factor to this game. I love Resident Evil and Dead Space, and Evil Within 2 manages to capture that feeling just as well as the first game. When the combat works, it can be incredibly satisfying.
+ While aforementioned skills will break the game, there is an undeniable thrill to using them. Completely destroying an mob encounter with 1 gas bolt + 5 instakills is very enjoyable
+ The last couple of hours of the game are worth the trouble and are great treats for fans of the series
+ Some great enemy designs and a great, albeit easy final boss
+ Great end game rewards
+The design of the game is much more open than the first game. Rather than strictly point A to point B style of gameplay, Evil Within 2 is practically open world at some points, This was upsetting at first but this structure encourages exploration very well and I grew to love it
+ Plenty of great quality-of-life tweaks to gameplay compared to tew1
+ Argueably as scary or scarier than the first game. Surprisingly tense at times but I'm a huge ♥♥♥♥♥ don't @ me
---
TLDR
6/10
Evil Within 2 is rife with technical flaws and is not very original, but if you're in it for gameplay, you'll be happy to know its more of the same. If any part of the story of the first game appealed to you, you're in for a disappointment with this one

No More Room In Hell (NMRIH) is a nice game. It's kind of a diet-Day Z or H1Z1 (*shudder*). It's basis is great, a team zombie survival with a free-choice-non-gunslinging-actual-survival feel.
Gameplay:
Satisfying, a first person perspective with an *awesome* feel when you bash heads in with a sledgehammer. It's also great in the fact that the "survival" factor actually exists with bullets being semi-scarce but not so scarce that it's a huge burden to carry around firearms. Your team necessarily has a better chance of survival if you stick together and hunker down in a certain area. What you will quickly find is multiple expert players setting up bases and going on supply "runs" to gather ammo and other weapons for the group. The main focus of the game is to either get to a certain point or to defend/secure several areas, all whilst trying to defend yourself from the undead horde.
Display:
Realistic, smooth, the only complaint is about the zombies movement but, it's negligible.
Pros:
The game has several maps, each with it's own unique style and missions. My favorite map is Northway. With the ability to secure just one area and defend, or to play strategically and manage all of them, NMRIH should be a nice game to add to any library.
Cons:
With NMRIH's diet-DZ aspect, one should expect the player type known as "hoarders." to come. As usual some players do hoard important things like bandages, pills, and ammuniton.
Overall Grade: A-
NMRIH is a definite pickup for anyone looking to play a zombie-survival game without wasting hours on stocking up supplies or finding a good place to store said supplies without people stealing them. The timed, gamemode style of NMRIH adds a unique and refreshing aspect to a new and upcoming genre.

What's that? A SERIOUS review? Well, semi serious, at any rate.
WHAT IS IT?!
Broforce is a Run and Gun type shooter with a major coat of American Patriotism. For those of the NES era, think Contra. For everyone else, it's a 2D game where you run, jump, and blow up everything in sight from terrorists to Aliens (Yes, THOSE Aliens, I think Ridley Scott's gonna sue somebody!) and even Satan himself. Yes, not even the Devil can escape Freedom.
What makes Broforce so unique among its bretheren are the titular Bros themselves. All of them are clearly inspired by some of the 80s, 90s, and even 2000's greatest action movies, and have their own unique playstyle. What makes things chaotic is your Bro is completely random whenever you get an extra life or respawn. This means the game is chaotic moment to moment madness in the best possible way.
The game's worlds are nearly 100% destructable, which gives some very interesting options for proceeding through them. Be sneaky and dig tunnels past enemy fortifications! Blow up said fortifications all around your foes! Collapse ceilings to squish enemies! Climb up and over with your wall jumping skills! It's pretty much all up to you.
The game supports 1 to 4 players, has a level editor, custom campaigns, and pretty much ensures you'll always have a reason to keep playing. It's the most American action game ever, and y'know what, even if you hate America, you gotta love this game for trying. And being one of the most fun action experiences you can have on Steam today.

Amusing. If you are thorough, you can find all secrets in one playthrough of about 5 hours.
I was disappointed that Suits: A Business RPG wasn't a satire on corporate America. I was expecting a fuller commentary on United States capitalism. Instead, Suits treats the corporation, capitalism, the judiciary, the bank, and infrastructure as ways to present a curious story. The fact that the main character graduates from business school is only relevant to the plot in that he is on the way to becoming the CEO (who is not really a CEO).
Despite my mistake in expectation, Suits is quirky with some great allegorical content; certain parts of this game will definitely make you raise an eyebrow.

It is a simple RPG where you'll play as a new employee in a bizarre, gigantic corporation in an equally bizarre world. Inside its surreal atmosphere and surreal enemies (a stapler as tutorial boss, seriously?) you will find satirical--and also random--quotes and images about corporation, capitalism, the internet, modern life, etc.
The art style and the music go very well together in delivering the dark surreal atmosphere. The story, while might not be  entirely easy to follow (this is a bizarre and surreal world, anyways) is rich with message, though mostly subtle and open for interpretation.
The gameplay is also simple. The battles don't require much strategizing, which may not please hardcore RPG gamers. Even so, the bizarre enemy designs will not disappoint--where else can you fight lost ties, coffee mugs, loan sharks (yes, they are literally sharks), and Bustin Jieber?
In short, Suits: A Business RPG is quite a unique piece of art worth your time and money.

Quirky and fun game with some challenge (not too easy, not too hard). This game definetly uses comedy to make subtle political and economic statements about society but it's more for comedy/storyline than statement's sake. Unique pencil like grey/black/white graphics add to the dreary megacorpiration industrial setting and atmosphere. All in all good fun for a shorter length game (I estimate 7 days if you take your time and get all achievements based on the progress I've made so far).
With certainty, I can assure you that one would not regret spending a dollar on purchasing this game for it's comical lore and parody of political schemes.
If you like memes, sandwiches, and wearing a suit, then this game is for you. If you don't you'll be sent to the factory fields. I'm sorry, it's just business.

TL;DR: If you hate constant internet culture jokes and references, this game is probably not for you. Otherwise, pretty good.
Suits is a short RPG maker game heavily inspired by OFF. As one can see by the other reviews, the game's main selling point is its dark humor and the references it makes. The game refuses to take itself seriously all the way to the very end, and that can actually hurt the game's story at some points, even though the plot itself is pretty simple.
The artstyle and the music are very unique and go along pretty well, strengthening the game's unsettling atmosphere.
The gameplay is alright, but could use some improvement. There's a ton of secrets and optional events to find in every single area, which gives Suits some replay factor, but the battles are a bit too simplistic. Even though each character feels very different from the other two, the entire game can be beaten by using the same combination of 2-3 commands, only stopping every now and then to heal your party, but thankfully the game ends before this can become too repetitive.
With all that said, though, this is definitely one of the most unique and interesting RPG maker games on Steam, and definitely worth every cent. I really hope to see a sequel in the future.

This free portion of the game was better than most games I've paid full price for. The graphics are done like an animated film; and a very well-done film at that. The scenery is amazing and every scene or "room" is beautifully detailed with hand-drawn trees, flowers, logs, stones, buildings, rivers, etc. Each environment has been lovingly created and populated with all kinds of animated people, birds, butterflies, squirrels, frogs, etc that move around and react to your presence.
The characters are all, well....full of character. As they talk they move about with emotion and use hand gestures, different postures, and facial expressions. They do such things like kick the air when they describe how they kicked a bandit, then point to their throat as they explain how they kicked them in the neck. The voiceovers are all equally superb; the kind of stuff you would encounter in a Disney movie. In fact, I have found at least a few celebrity voices as in Christopher Lloyd (Back to the Future), Wallace Shawn (There's even a Princess Bride easter egg in the game), Zelda Williams (Robin William's daughter), and Tom Kenny (Spongebob Squarepants).
The humor present in the dialogue is cheeky and funny and full of delightful puns. It is true to all of the original King's Quest games or any other Sierra game like Space Quest and Quest for Glory. There is humor for both children and adults, but never in a way that is inappropriate or offensive. It doesn't stay on the rightful path enough to be boring or childish either. Feel free to screw up on purpose to see funny cutscenes and commentary as the game reloads right where you were if you die or mess up too badly.
The amount of work that went into the script and dialogue is evident. You can repeat the same action or interact with the same objects or people numerous times and get different voiceovers and results. Some of the results can be very funny and/or lead to Steam achievements. Actually, feel free to experiment in the game as nothing is punished. In fact you are frequently rewarded for curiosity and stupid choices.
If you have ever played the original Kings Quest or any other point-and-click Sierra game then you will definitely enjoy this game. It is a well-contructed throwback that clearly is the finished work of a labor of love. The game manages to preserve the point-and-click charm while simultaneously ridding itself of many of the frustrating aspects of that genre. While at first it may seem like you are missing the different action choices (use,drop,take,talk,run,walk,look,etc), it quickly becomes evident that combining all of those actions into the space bar doesn't detract from the game at all. Quite the contrary, as it adds a fluidity and ease to the game that serves only to improve the experience. It is all of the charm of old, only with modern graphics and a much-improved interface.
The best part is the first chapter (which is large and contains hours of play) is free. Try it out, what do you have to lose?
TL:DR - This marvelous game plays out like a modern point-and-click game of old, sans all of the negative aspects of that genre. The free chapter contains hours of playtime and will have you scrambling to buy the rest.

The series' unique blend of fairytale tropes, folk stories and children's fiction, combined with Sierra's signature witty narrative, memorable characters and state-of-the-art graphics made King's Quest - from early move-and-types to later point-and-clicks and even AGD Interactive remakes - one of the core adventure series I can safely say I grew up with, right next to all the "golden era" Sierra and Lucasarts titles. I imagine most of '80s gamer kids were just as hyped as I was, when a reboot (of sorts) was announced, endorsed by Sierra Online.
Spoilers ahead.
The first chapter was a hoot. The environments were perfectly crafted, the characters well written, the animations properly cartoonish, voice acting was just splendid, and the story was your typical KQ run: a contest that's rigged and needs more rigging, a townful of inhabitants to help out, cute forest animals to befriend (or not), a bridge trolls' guild on strike, a shady merchant's cart driven by goats-turned-unicorns, some seriously out-of-the-box thinking, and utterly ridiculous puns delivered by the elderly Graham, narrating the whole thing - just what you'd expect from a fairytale game.
Then came episode two. Goblins in love with stories and playing them out - all right, that's cool. Throw in a changeling theme with some characters possibly having unforeseen depth - great, bring it on. Now add some survival drama with you having to decide whom of your fellow prisoners to feed or cure, or they'll grow weaker until they starve or collapse from sickness - and you only have a few days to break out of the prison, time is ticking. And there's no manual save or load feature, so your decisions are final. Wait, what the hell? I thought I was playing a fun, fairytale-themed game, what's with this PG-15 content? I certainly felt disappointed with this chapter. A promising story was overshadowed by unnecessarily serious gameplay mechanics, violating every rule of un-failable, experimentable, infinitely explorable, tongue-in-cheek adventure. From a King's Quest game I expect surreal entertainment by characters' wacky antics, not trauma by motion-captured animation and impeccable voice acting of likable townspeople moaning and weakly struggling to rise off their beds because I chose to eat and gain strength to pull a lever, instead of feeding them, for chrissakes. Sure, there are some pretty dark fairytales out there, hell, most of Andersen's and Grimms' classics were often just morbid, but their serious undertones were administered either as warnings, or as unavoidable consequences of non-controllable protagonists. Here, we're seeing nice people's realistic suffering because of the items the player chose to click on other items, not even realizing (yet) the gravity of the choice. It's not like there wasn't ever a death theme in classic adventure games - hey, people got killed left and right, but that was either a dark-humoured form of slapstick comedy, or it was the player who got maimed and dismembered in a hundred different ways and we were happily restoring a saved game, often intentionally trying stupid things, just to watch the hero burn. If I wanted hard consequences and see the game punish me with killing off people I grew to like because of something stupid I did, I'd play The Witcher, The Walking Dead, The Last of Us, or This War of Mine, or even Life is Strange. Strike one, KQ.
Episode Three went back to the fairytale roots, this time playing with love tropes, such as "girl in the tower", "true love breaks curses", in quite clever ways. The musical score was spun around variations of the King's Quest 5 theme song, hitting all the right nostalgia notes - all in all, the King's-Questiness is back. The downside is that it's rather short, and there's not a lot to do, really - there's about 3 or 4 items to use on 3 or 4 objects or persons, and that's it, the rest is all cutscenes, dialogue, and some arcade climbing.
Episode Four… isn't an adventure game anymore. It's a puzzle game, and all built atop a basic walk-from-start-to-end scheme, just with more and more obstacles added. There's some witty dialogue between Graham the Dad and Alexander the Misunderstood Emo Teenager, but the gameplay is just boring puzzle-solving. Theme-wise there's an obvious Snow Queen vibe going on, but the climax makes little sense, as all the typical reunion and curse-breaking tropes are underexplored. All in all, I'd just played a one big "escape room" puzzle episode in which some fun one-liners were thrown and then there was a lackluster ending, roll credits.
Finally, there's Episode Five. The bedridden King Graham is about to die, his mind is going and we're now playing an adventure consisting of him frantically trying - and failing - to remember first some minor details, then the main story itself. We're playing a story being told, and partially reinvented, to a family gathered around a dying, old man by his granddaughter, because her grandpa's too delirious to narrate his story himself. It's not a "piece a broken mind together" story, either - gramps is not getting better. And he's not some random "old dude", he's the very guy we've seen become a king and raise a family. We've experienced his adventure, romance, starvation, now let's experience dementia and death. Fun, isn't it? Oh, and his granddaughter gets to be queen, because... why exactly? All we know is that she was more into adventure (apparently the most important family motto), so her gramps liked her more. There seems to be a chapter missing here, explaining why exactly is she a worthy successor, with a quest of her own, choices and so on, otherwise neither of the children is shown as fit to be a king/queen. The grand moral of the story ends up ambiguous: all we can see is an old man trying to pass his adventuring hat to a worthy heir, but actually passes the crown instead, even though it's clearly established that the two headpieces represented conflicting goals.
Season pass owners got a special "Epilogue" bonus chapter, but in case you were worried the developers held back a "true ending" - don't worry. It's a 10-minute-long micro-adventure, adding no real value to the story, but at least trying to lighten the mood again after the funereal tone of the last episode.
All in all - I'm forced to give this one a thumbs-down. Two fun, adventure-filled episodes against one boring puzzler and two total downers, that's not how I like my King's Quest served. The Odd Gentlemen, please don't touch any more classics, thank you.

After years (almost decades) of immersing myself in dark and mature story rich titles like Mass Effect, Dragon Age, Metal Gear, etc., Kings' Quest filled a gap I didn't know was missing with grin inducing jokes, heartwarming stories, and silly albeit well thought out characters that I thoroughly enjoyed. The animation of certain objects are a bit stiff at times, but it conrols perfectly. The puzzles are varied from one moment to the next and never get dull. You never what challenges the next moment will present to you-- it's no mere 'find this, put that there' type of adventure game, but there is plenty of that still. There might be a few stumpers along the way, but looking up a walkthrough to me defeats the rewarding moments when you figure it out.
Interestingly, King's Quest isn't strictly linear, as there are choices to make, side quests that may have consequences later on, and sometimes quests that are just there you make you laugh, giving this unique game some replay value just to see how the story changes. I don't play a lot of adventure games-- the last one I attempted was Amnesia, but King's Quest got me looking at the genre once again.

King's Quest. Sierra's classic point-and-click adventure game returns with a new coat of paint, and an annoying save system
Pros
- The entire first chapter is free to play, and includes 17 achievements for you to collect. For the other four chapters, It's $24.99, unless you want the Epilouge, in which case you'll have to get the $29.99 version, still not too bad of a pricing, in my opinion
- Old Graham / Narrator is voiced by Christopher Lloyd, Doctor Brown from Back to the Future. Merchant of Miracles is voiced by Tom Kenny, Spongebob. Manny is voiced by Wallace Shawn, Vizzini (Inconceivable) from The Princess Bride. and Whisper is voiced by Richard White, Gaston from Beauty and the Beast
- Game breaks the fourth wall
- Game makes puns
- Game is easy to run, as long as you're not playing on a calculator, and still manages to look well made and well thought out
- Game has a well pased story with twists and turns and plenty of things to explore in the fully, fleshed out kingdom of Daventry and beyond
Cons
- Game can be somewhat linear at times, and most of the puzzles make more sense than a Sierra game should allow
- Game can be considerablly short, unless you're going for all of the achievements and get stuck on chapter four a lot like I did
- Game might use the 'fourth wall breaks' a little too often and break the immersion
- Game has a difficult to navigate save system. You can't just load up a certain section of the game, if you want to get to a certain point in a certain chapter you'll have to play through that entire chapter to get to whatever point you want. Plus the game will often quicksave, and because of this, if something happens that you didnt want to happen and the game quicksaves, you'll have to play through that chapter to that part all over again. This is probably my biggest problem with the game, I wanted to get all of the achievements for the game, mostly because most of the achievements were'nt too much of a hassle to get, I had to remake save files constantly, just so I could replay a part to get them. I dont know why Sierra couldnt have just used the original Kings Quest save system
King's Quest first chapter is free, so go play it.

**First let me point out that the steam log of my hours doesnt relate to my actual hours, since finding the performance increase from launching the eso.exe directly, i have put in another 800hrs.**
What we have here is a deep, mesmerising world full of oppurtunity and multiple choices for direction. This is as good an RPG as any geek could dream for. Zenimax has realised that Skyrim was too small, and have expanded the Elder Scrolls Universe to include almost every area Lore has refered to.
Your range of classes and races, and the multitude of mix n match options to get what you want, is just wonderful. Stealthy thief that kills at range but can disappear instantly when attacked up close? Tick. Combat Medic who can stand in the middle of the fray and absorb damage like a tank? Tick. Standard melee DPS hair streaming wildly swinging a broadsword gashing wild random death amongst her enemies? Tick.
I started this game with trepidation, as the first area is horribly bland and dull in colour, but that is part of the storyline. The second you move to the following areas, things get more "Skyrimmy". The attention to detail, and the tiny little hidden and special things are tremendously abundant. So much so, that you don't notice initially the copy paste standard dungeon layout we have seen throughout the series. There are a number of unique dungeon layouts, but about 6 are re-used, and honestly, you have to be on the lookout to notice this. They have REALLY taken the time to decorate and give a unique feal to every area.
I spend a large amount of my time wandering around just looking at things. My child tells me to go outside as there are real life things to see outside the house, and well, this is better. Deep in the darkness of an eerie mine, sneaking behind some dishevelled mishappen creatures, green slimy ooze dribbling out of its mouth, i stumble across a skeleton hidden in a corner away from the evil, a hastily scribbled note to his loved one lies next to him bemoaning his state and "why did I ever leave you my love, the riches promised down here could never compare to the treasure in your heart". *flutter*
Little conversations amongst random NPCs all over the show adds to the atmosphere and interacting with non quest NPCs is possible, either for a little detail, or comic relief. The talking Skeleton in the Thieves Refuge in Morhould is one of my favourites. Humour is superb and prolific throughout this game, much of it just silly silliness and the rest some good solidly laid out humour, most of the side quests are funny in one way or another, wheres the main questline retains a rather serious undertone. Some good balancing there!
Voice actors such as John Cleese and that wonderful human from Underworld Bill Nighy along with Kate Beckinsale as well as Michael Gambon and Peter Stormare are just a portion of the MARVELOUS talent and a hint at the storyline you are about to experience. This is all just mesmerising and truly immersive.
I stumbled across a petrified completely naked and rather hungover Nord in Deshaan, musclebound as he was, he was in dread fear of his wife and "the witches who stole my clothes! (hic)", further conversation with the wife reveals this is a common occourence, and when i went to fetch his axe, a family heirloom, things got a bit crazy, for there indeed was a witch! Why his clothes disappeared is anybodies guess, but the tongue lashing he was recieving as I rode away on my Horse with the gold his wife had given me was quite inspiring to never get thot frunk. Again...
I yearned for Cyrodiil though! And initially i went as far as galloping across two maps to enter The Rift and visit Riften, one of my favourite areas in Skyrim and of course where i was hoping the thieves guild would be! Upon arrival the instant death my level 8 toon recieved was a bit shocking, turns out areas are designed to feed you along per level, and the rift is about 2/3rds in! So what now! Well, upon hitting level 10, I was invited to join in a bloody campaign. TO WAR! And Cyrodiil!
Basically, with the 900+ hours I have under the belt, I havent finished more that 1/5th of the main questline, as upon entering Cyrodiil, the PvP section and Alliance War area, I discovered it impossible to leave....
This battle arena is the entirety of the old TESO IV :Oblivion map. One huge battlezone. Each of the three factions has a section of the map that contains their Home Keeps, and two Elder Scrolls. You spend your days protecting your own, setting up ambushes for incoming maruaders or going deep behind enemy lines to steal resources or gank unsuspecting stragglers.
The intensity of your Squad of 24 slowly and surely getting into position to Siege an unsuspecting Keep, the sudden call for SIEGES UP!!! Trebuchettes rising out of the ground to begin hurling immense flaming balls of rock at the enemies defenses, hurtling overhead these messages of doom explode upon the enemy sundering man, stone and beast alike. They do not take this lightly! INCOMING!!! Oil and rotten meat is getting hurled over the walls at our troops! But its not too late! A breach! 4 of my brethren can take it no longer, the battle lust fills them and they revert into their natural werewolf form! The attack resumes as the enemy try to push us back, we storm through the breach into the inner courtyard, the call is for a battering Ram on the main gate, fiery burning oil is splatteting all around us but our Combat Medics are prepared, purging us of this new death they stand steadfast in the middle of the fray.

The ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I'm totally comign back to get him.

ISLANDS is a strange little surrealist piece by Carl Burton, who's art i've followed for a while. You will notice I said "piece" and not "game" because ISLANDS can't really be called a game - it's an interactive art exhibit. Bought it on sale for less than a pack of gum so I can't complain about the price.
You click the lights, something animates, you wait for the next set of lights, repeat. If you came for a game, you will be dissapointed. There is no wandering through the scene, nothing really to explore or discover. Everyone complaining about it not having enough "game" for them obviously didn't watch the trailer, look at the screenshots or read about it. It's blatently not a game, nor is it trying to be. It's a set of nice little animations which takes less than an hour to go through.
The scenes are nice, surreal, otherworldly - all things I can get behind. But by the last of the 10(ish?) different scenes (pieces? stages?) I was getting quite bored. I'm not sure exactly what the whole thing was trying to say, maybe that's just me, but I really feel that the whole thing could have been done in a different way, with more exploration of each scene.
So I found it wasn't really for me, but if you catch it on sale and have 45-60mins to kill then it's maybe worth a look. (Steam really needs a "mixed" or "neutral" feedback option).

+ Creative

- (Arguably) too short for the price
This is exactly what it looks like: a game where you look at things, poke them, and then watch what happens. It's linear, with each small vignette playing out a set narrative and then disappearing. Sometimes the game really worked for me; the dev has a great imagination, and the liminal spaces on display (parking lots, ATMs, fountains) are explored in delightful ways that blend the mechanical with the organic.
One downside is that the environments feel fixed. You can't look up or down, just rotate the scenery. Your impact on each scene is quite limited; it isn't always clear whether your clicking is the reason you've moved on to the next "stage" of a level or if it's just timed. I used my laptop's touchscreen, which was definitely more immersive than just clicking around, but interaction still felt constained at times and the objects weren't that responsive to touch. The game is missing that tactile feeling you get from similar games like Windosill or Metamorphabet, where you can click, drag, and relocate almost anything onscreen.
The sound design is also an issue. Almost everything makes some sort of electronic noise, but the developer seems to have overlooked the fact that the sounds of alarms, telephones and sirens were deliberately designed to be as grating as possible. The racket can disturb the zen feeling the game is going for―at times I rushed through a level just to get the damn ringing to stop.
I don't think the hour or so of gameplay will be worth the price for most people, but if it's on sale then people who enjoy surreal, casual art games should take a look.

I'm going to make this review short. Evil Within 2 was an excellent game and I had alot of fun playing it. There aren't that many good sequals to games these days, but this game is one of the few that is actually good. The game's graphics are also very beautiful, so you better have a good pc if you want to run the game at its best. I look forward to seeing how the DLC will turn out.

Evil Within 2 does afew things better than the firest, but overall, isn't an improvement.  The story is told in a more linear fasion, making it easier to understand.  There are more supporting characters, although not many more, and they actually have an impact on the story.   The hub world setup of the early game gives you initial freedom to explore in any direction, and ignore the main plot completely for hours if you wish.
This is where the improvements give way to an incredibly medocre horror experience though.  The environments are painfully mundane throughout the entire game.  The facade of the 'everytown USA' you're thrown into to eventually gives way, gently mind you, to dusty concrete warehouse type enviornments.. and maybe an occasional sewer.  It's really that boring.  The walls don't bleed.. nothing jumps out at you (this game actually dosen't have a single jump scare)  It's so minimalist I think they simply forgot to go back and add the 'horror' when they were done programing afew of the steaIth boxes from The Last of Us.  I can't remember a single time the game thrust me into a combat situation where I couldn't just use stealth to avoid all combat, aside from the 4? boss fights.  There was a distinct lack of varied enemy types.  Where the first game would introduce a new enemy type, and an environment that gave it a huge advantage over you, the second simply sprinkled the 5 or 6 different types around as the game progressed, saving the 'harder' enemies for spawning at the earliest parts of the main story.. leaving nothing but reskined basic enemies for the majority of the mid and late game.   I can think of two parts in the game where I was actually forced to fight enemies who knew where I was despite what I did, and they were fun.  It felt like whoever directed the majority of this game didn't really understand what made the first one fun to play.   Stealthing around and conserving ammo is great, but without combat heavy portions of the game to burn up that ammo you're saving,  you simply end up with a ton of useless, boring ammo.  And that's what happened to me with minimal effort on the survivalist setting, because this game simply does not want to get in your face like the first one did.
I'm still in shock at just how boring this game was.  I remember thinking the first one was way over the top with its ridiculously bloody environments and (I thought) almost useless steatlh system in the late game.  But ♥♥♥♥, I was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.  That's what actually made it fun.. the ridiculous amounts of gore and the excessive use of combat boxes.  Oh, and the clausterphobic boss fights.  There were alot of those.. I kind of forgot to mention how fun those were on the harder modes.  Being shoved into a tiny cage with a scarey♥♥♥♥♥boss over and over never really got old.  Doesn't happen even once in the second game.   Come to think of it, I didn't loose a single boss fight.. probably because I had nearly max ammo for all of my most upgraded 'boss' weapons, everytime.  I wish this was even a slight exaggeration.
Ok, I'm rambling, but one more thing.  One of the green gel upgrades in this game actually gives you bullet time slow motion when you're aiming your weapon.  This literally breaks the game.  You can't miss after you aquire this skill.  If you can't miss, there's no difficulty.  I mean, ♥♥♥♥, I I think I messed up stealthing maybe 10 or so times in the entire game (I'm really patient) but after I had that skill, I didn't even need stealth.  You can just use the pistol to kill everything easy as hell.  I really dont' know what they were thinking when they added a cheat mode to a game that despirately needs difficulty.  The combat actually suffers from the fact you're hardly ever forced to participate in it.  It's ripped directly from the first game, so mabye they just decided that this one would have 'good stealth' since the first one didn't after a certain point.  Way to ♥♥♥♥ it up in the opposite direction.
Anyway, TLDR ratings
6/10 gameplay - Just like the First one but you can be a ninja
4/10 story - Told well, but boring, with an ending that wastes a lot of potential
1/10 Atmosphere/Horror - This game doesn't try to be scary.  I'm not sure if they were even going for a horror game.  If just having monsters in your game made it a horror game, almost every game would be in that genre.  A complete failure.
If you liked playing the first Evil Within, you might enjoy playing through the stealth DLC that is Evil Within 2.  I'd recommend waiting for a discount though, since as a huge fan of what the first game did well, I can't recommend this one as a sequel.

One-liner: "This is Amnesia in space"
This is as close as you'll ever get to the atmosphere of the original Alien movie. It even has two DLC's that give you a couple of missions with the original cast. The alien is creepy as hell and completely unpredictable. It's really, really well-done. Hiding under a desk, looking at the tail of the alien twirl around just beside you. Yup, bring clean underpants.
The gameplay is sort of a mix of a puzzle game and a strategy game, trying to figure out where the alien is, and whether you can make that next corner without running into it. At least the alien missions are.
Which brings me to the cons of the game. There are androids and humans, and they are annoying. Missions with androids - don't like them. Second con is that the game is probably double the length as it should be. Yes, I'm complaining about the length of a game. I wouldn't normally do this, if it was justified. But in this case it's just 6-8 hours of filler missions where all you're doing is dodging androids and bringing the power back on (again and again and again).
But it doesn't take away from the brilliant alien gameplay, which is, fortunately, located in the first half of the game (and in the end, but less interesting there).
Its a fun, scary game. Unlike other games, in this game you are very underpowered, and have to resort to sneakiness to avoid dying. Its a fun game, and requires some time to getting used to.

Finally a horror game that relies less on jump-scares and more on building a creepy atmosphere. Alien: Isolation is a love letter to Ridley Scott`s original Alien movie with meticulous attention to detail in the art-style and sound design. When played with a good headset you can pinpoint every sound around you, and more importantly sounds from the vents above you...
Sevastopol station is a huge space station floating around a gas giant. It reminds me of the Nostromo in many ways, which of course is intended, and everything from the dark hallways to the living quarters reminds me of Alien. In Alien: Isolation, just like the movie, quarantine procedures are not the crew`s strong suit, and combined with a corrupt megacorporation in control of the station, this of course leads to unwanted visitors on the station.
The Alien is an intimidating foe, and one of the more memorable monsters in movie history. It is recreated in a great way in Alien: Isolation, and every wrong step can be your last. Untill you get a flamethrower (with ammo in short supply) you are pretty much helpless and have to resort to hiding whenever you spot the Alien. The pacing in the game is also excellent, and even when it`s a long time since you have met anything that wants to hurt you, you never feel safe.
The graphics, in addition to the already mentioned sound-design, is great. Technically impressive and very well optimized on the PC. Lighting and shadows create an eerie and awesome atmosphere. IMO one of the best games of 2014.

By the time I'd finished the second mission of the game, I'd decided I was going to write a review of it.  Having completed it, here I go.  But, what to write about?  Many other reviewers have written about the graphics, sound and gameplay mechanics; so I think I'll write about how this game made me
.
Long after we forget about the mechanics or the graphic settings of a game, what stays with us the emotional memory of that game; I mean, this is why fanboys still weep for Morrowind, and why I've played Neverwinter Nights through countless times over the years!  Numerous other examples lead me to think it's a truly important factor, worthy of review.
So, what did this game make me feel?
.  Sheer, unmitigated terror.  Let me say,
I was in a shop somewhere the other day, and something beeped like the motion detector in the game, and I almost sh!t myself!  I also now have an irrational fear of a
creature that I have not been afraid of for over a quarter of a century!! (Yes, I'm old, I know).  It's important to note that I'm not talking about jump scares (yes, there are jump scares in the game, most of them are unexpected, and not one of them feels cliched or out of place).  I'm talking about the terror that comes from being in a life-or-death hunt, where all the odds are stacked against you, and all you can do is try to survive...
From the opening logos on, this game has been designed to recapture the atmosphere of its iconic progenitor, Alien.
Everything in game replicates the production design of that movie down to the smallest detail:  the odd juxtaposition of interstellar travel technology with late 70's crappy computers; the banal-combined-with-hi-tech decor; and other elements that I won't mention (spoilers).  The intended result is successfully achieved:
.  At no time did I doubt that I was in the Alien "Universe".
And, Sevastopol Station is the nightmarish rendering of that universe gone wrong.  As you travel through the station, you see the believable consequences of a calamity befallen group of people trying to survive when nothing works, and everything else is falling apart.  Desperate executives, terrified citizens, and malfuntioning androids, are juxtaposed with advertising posters and recordings of what Seegeson's dream was, and just how far it has fallen.  All this adds a layer of sadness that, in my opinion, adds to the believability of the unviverse.
The graphics and score add to the atmosphere of terror.  A shadow floating past a porthole had me jumping in fear, and when I looked, it was a piece of wreckage floating past, with the backdrop of the remainder of the station and the gas giant it orbits reminding me of just how small and insignificant I was.  In other parts, smoke, darkness, and beautifully rendered lense flair again add depth by making it hard to see what's ahead, increasing inherent fear.  Also, here, I have to mention one of my favourte features - the ability to change focus when holding the motion detector:  you can look at the detector, or everything else, but not both, and when you look at one, the other goes out of focus!  This can be scary as all hell!!!
The score seems to be based off the original Alien score, and in most instances, it adds to the tension with it's unnerving high-pitched strings that build to a crescendo as an object of hostility comes hunting for you.  Occassionally, it can be distracting, as it can drown out the sound of movement and the detector when a very dramatic piece plays, but this only became an issue for me once in the game.
Seven paragraphs in and you're going "this guy hasn't even talked about the Alien."  Ok, here we go.  The Alien is both unreal and terrible, and it is important to note that I use those words in a Lovecraftian context:  hiding in a locker, watching this "thing" move around and attack people while actively hunting me, had me thinking "this thing should not be!"  The creature is truly a thing of nightmare.  And when it hunts you, you know fear.  The first time it came for me, the events, music, and my experience as an avid fan of the series told me what was going to happen, and what to expect, and yet, when its head first appeared through a billowing cloud of steam, I had a moment of true terror.
.  I turned and ran like a little girl.  The Alien has heightened senses and an unmitigated savagery that make it a fearsome opponent, and many times, when I was hiding, I found
holding my breath until it passed, becasue if it gets you, it's all over, red rover.
This is a survival game, and it's best not to forget that, because if you do, you're dead.  If you decide to go all Duke Nuke-em, and charge in with guns blazing, you're dead.  If you get impatient and go "F#ck it, I'm going through, and I'll fight my way out if I have to," you're dead.  You
die in this game.  A lot.  Save points are strategically placed to make achieving the next one feel deeply rewarding, and also to reward smart gameplay.  Because, that's the only way to survive.  Stay low, quiet, and out of everyone, and everything's way.  You have to know when to run, when to hide, and when to make an aggressive assualt.  You have to pick your moments, otherwise, you're dead.
I had a rush of blood to the head when I got the flamethrower; I was like, "That's it! No more hiding for me!  It's time to give this Alien what-for, and make it run and hide!"  And I did.  And then I ran out of fuel.  And then I died.  While there's enough material floating around to craft the items that help you survive (some of which are truly indispensable),  you can't carry a lot of them, and more importantly, there's never enough ammo.  Even if you have enough ammo, it's not enough.  I played through on the recommended setting of hard, so I don't know if the easier setting gives you more ammo or not, but the (intended, in my opinion) effect of this was to create a feeling of helplessness:  I felt like I was powerless in the face of things far beyond my control, and all I could do was hide and try to survive.  Which, I believe, was the intended intention of the game! ;)
A quick comment on negatives:  I really only found two.  There is a part of the game where you will find two items you need, just lying in a spot for no particular reason.  They're there because you need them.  It stuck out to me as the only reality breaking moment in an otherwise seamless creation.  The other is the human AI; while the Alien and android AI's are both superb, the human AI fluctuates between hyper alert and bad.  I mean, laughably bad.  They'll spot you if you peep around a corner more than twice, but give up once you break line of sight.  Then they stand around mouthing idiotic comments like the guards in Thief.  Some of the comments are almost identical to comments in that game!  In one part, I was pressed up against a wall and the human walks past me, all the while looking right at me, but doesn't see me!  It made me want to have the Alien come and kill them!!
In summary, Creative Assembly should be proud of themselves for this near flawless masterpiece of gaming they've created, and I firmly believe they've set a new standard for FPS/Survival/Horror games, especially in terms of graphics, sound, atmosphere, and gameplay.  A game that plays out like a movie with total immersion, and psychological investment, is one that is worthy of both replaying, and having some fond, yet terrifying emotional memories!
9.5/10

Oh boy, what can I say that others haven't?  Well, I'll just give my personal impressions from a long standing ALIEN(s) fan.
If you are a fan of ALIEN, the original Dan O'Bannon / Ridley Scott horror film, then this is the game for you.  But it also may not be the game for you.  How can I say that?  Well, I'm one of those original ALIEN fans, but I'm not much of a survival horror gamer or even a fan of the horror genre at all.
Well this game dumps you right into the horror genre full force.  I wasn't prepared.  Oh mommy I wasn't prepared.  Having never played a survival horror game previously, I thought to myself "How bad can it be?".  It's THAT bad.  I would finish a mission and have to take a break for fear of my blood pressure causing an aneurism.
I'm guessing for those of you used to games like Amnesia and Silent Hill, Resident Evil and The Evil Within, then this kind of gameplay is old hat for you.  But me?  I pretty much play everything BUT survival horror.  From dozens of FPS, Strategy games, to RPG's, but never the horror games.
I spent hours hiding in lockers and storage cabinets terrified to get out of them.  Even with full knowledge that I had saved my game a hundred yards away, the Alien wasn't showing on the tracker, had gone into the air vents, and I hadn't really accomplished anything yet except for getting in the storage locker.
So what I'm trying to say here, is that if you love the ALIEN movie, but aren't really a survival horror gamer, then you may be better off watching the dozens of playthroughs on YouTube instead.
I ended up cranking the difficulty setting down to Easy by Mission 5, and let me assure you that ALIEN Isolation in Easy mode is hard mode in other games.  I attempted Hard mode at first, but found I was taking hours to get through even a single mission, and I honestly wanted to get out of a locker without dying and on with the story.
The story.  Ok, this is what drew me to the game in the first place.  The chance to see what Amanda Ripley was doing in the 57 year interim between ALIEN and ALIENS?  Hell, I thought they said illegal Alien and signed the ♥♥♥♥ up.  I love the premise of the story, and I really loved the entire setting of Sevastopol.  Finding the flight recorder and... well, I don't want to drop spoilers here, but the story is just great.  Really great.  This game could easily have been the next installment in the ALIEN franchise; and a worthy one unlike the utter crap that were ALIEN3 and ALIEN: Resurrection.
Graphics:  I played this game on a triple monitor setup with a GTX 670 Gigabyte video card.  I never experienced any lag or stuttering whatsoever.  There was a quite a bit of screen tearing, but I only noticed it during the less tense mooments when I wasn't being eaten.
Overall, the graphics are downright beautiful.  The lighting was perfect for the setting, the attention to detail in regards to the ALIEN franchise was top notch.  The San Cristobal medical facility mission was one of the best lit game levels I've seen in any game.
A couple things were overdone... did there really need to be a drinking chicken head toy on every dining table in the game?  I swear no one on the station owned a garbage can as trash was just everywhere and not in an "the Alien trashed this room" kind of way, but natural dirtyness.
A couple things made no practical sense whatsoever like the reactor core scene where it's simultaneously pouring water everywhere combined with electrical discharges all around you... Yeah, Ripley would have been flash fried within seconds of being there.  But it looked cool and it was a nice change of pace.
Sounds:  Top notch.  Easily one of the best audio experiences I've had in a video game.  Maybe ever.  MIssion 14 with the sound cranked up?  This is easily the mission where I decided I probably won't do a second playthrough of the game.  I found myself sneaking through this level whispering "Never again!" to myself.  Absolutely terrifying thanks to the great sound effects.
Also, a caveat:  If you are more of a fan of the ALIENS film and the original ALIEN film, then this game may not be for you.  There's no Pulse Rifles, grenade launchers or Gyro Arm mounted machine guns.  You do get couple weapons later on, but they have extemely limited ammo and are largely innefective.
*POSSIBLE SPOILER*
You do get a flamethrower that will chase the Alien off and make him run into the air vents.  What I discovered very quickly is that this makes the Alien come back with more frequency.  The Alien will typically spend quite a bit of time in the air vents walking around, but if you flame it and it runs into the air vents, then you've got about 30-45 seconds before he gets♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and comes right back.
If you must use the flamethrower, then vacate the immediate area quickly afterwards.  Don't stand around reading life stories on the terminals, just get out.
Once you get the flamethrower, DO NOT forget your roots.  Hiding in storage lockers still works and won't have him rampaging around the level looking for the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that just set him on fire.  I used it more like a last resort.  Ok, I'm cornered, nowhere to hide and he's RIGHT THERE.  Time to send him running and then GTFO.
*SPOILER END*
Now on to the things I didn't like.
Lets start off with the ending.  I'm not gonna spoil it here, but seriously F U SEGA.  What the crap is this ending?  No closure, no resolution, no tying up loose ends.  Just *BLAM* the game is now over.  It's absolutely the worst ending of a great game that I have ever experienced, but then again, I liked how ME3 ended so I'm not sure what that says about me.
Also, the legth of the game was a bit ridiculous.  The last two hours felt very contrived.  Hey lets keep having disaster after disaster to add more pointless game time.  Personally I would have ended it much sooner... like say on the Ambulance shuttle.  I'd have flown straight to the Torrens on that thing and thrown up dueces at Sevastopol.  Peace ♥♥♥♥♥es!  I'm out!
I know this has been said before in other reviews, but good grief the back-tracking was excessive.  I counted in one mission alone I had to go back and forth across the entire map seven times to get a single door open.  The entire map from one end to the other.  Ok, find a keycard, go to the other side of the level and open a safe, go to the other side of the level and start a generator, go back to the other side of the level and push a button, go back again and.... ect.
It wasn't just one level either.  Quite a few levels weren't all that big really, but were made to feel bigger by having to re-cross the same territory a few times.  For the sequels I suggest bigger levels, less linearity, give us a few things to do on that level and let us decide what to do first and how to do it.
My last con is this:  For the love of all that's good, let us quick save any damn where we please.  There's nothing more soul crushing that getting right to the elevator that you need, you haven't saved in 20 minutes of game play and you get ambushed from the ceiling.  If I'm hiding in a locker and I'm not sure I'm gonna make it to the next room, then let me save there.
Maybe have a hardcore mode where players can only save at save points for those to like to replay entire sections of the game repeatedly, but for those of us along for the story let us quick save on easy mode.

Thimbleweed Park seriously feels like a lost Lucasarts classic. The tone, the writing, the graphics, the atmosphere, everything is spot on. Yet at the same time the game doesn't feel old. Gary Winnick, Ron Gilbert and their team have improved upon the formula with small quality of life improvements and general streamlining.
The puzzle difficulty is spot on: you'll be able to think of logical solutions to most puzzles reasonably quickly, and the times when you can't, there's almost always something else you can be doing and moving the story along somewhere else.
The game is simply a joy to play, and the story goes in some very unexpected directions. Don't miss out on Thimbleweed Park: I have a feeling it'll be recognized as a classic adventure game in years to come.

Basically I loved this, and already miss it.

I remember first playing Left 4 Dead 2, it was quite fun for the first 3 hours. Now Left 4 Dead walks in the shadow of this amazing stand alone mod for Half-Life 2. How the devs have managed to do so is not a surprise, i mean, Left 4 Dead is just shoot zombies with ammo that seems to pop out your butt and hack 'em to peaces with melee weapons.
As much I want to tell you how good this game is, i have to run though the bad stuff... lets get that over with, shall we? Firstly the zombies, they're near perfect... but i feel their walking motion could be better, also they only recently added crawling zombies? I thought those should've been first biuld type things. Secondly escape helicopters, they all good and well when the blades move I really am nit-picking here but I kinda have to with this game.
Now to the good part! Graphics are quite good and seem consistant, they may not be the prettiest graphics but they are better then others. The sounds the zombies make really do sound like zombies, things sound like they're meant to, some games can't even get that right. The soundtrack is amazing as well, very fitting for the kind of game this is, you will have to turn it down if you want to hear people though. Lets not forget about map designs, they are well made and hard to exploit.
Ammo and guns are rare, except 9mm and pistols, so ammo consumtion quickly becomes a problem leaving melee weapon to dominate. Inventory also becomes a problem, two handed guns and melee weapons take up lot of space leaving little room for anything else like ammo. Zombies are also quite troublesome because there are many and have a furthur melee range then you. Runners, Military, Children and Crawlers add diversity and challange to such an already exquisite game. If theres one important lesson in this game its that you should sick with your team, becuase when three Runners and a Child are after you youll be glad they have guns as well.
This game is so great for a mod, it's still fun even after 3 hours. what more its free, game devs need to step it up if a free game is better then Left 4 Dead.

this game seems so appealing, and it has so much promise. at first it makes you feel like a total badass, giving you powers and cool abilities to beat up bad guys and punch satan in the the throat. the game feels like so much fun at first, with clever level designs and cool bosses and vehicles and different characters from movies we've long loved. but after playing for a bit, you start to unlock characters that aren't so good, are severly limited in their ability, which would be cool except you never choose when to use those characters, you just seem to keep having to play as them, whether you want to or not.
this game is built on randomness and chance and unfortunately the randomness is rarely on your side, you often find yourself saying "well that was unfair", "how could i have seen that coming" "the level didn't play out like that last time, what changed". usually things changing on you is a good thing, but not in this game. everything acts unpredictably and you are never really given much chance to adapt. yeah sure, the game conveys mechanics fine, and those mechanics play out predictably on their own, but paired together the levels soon start to feel like rube goldberg machines with the main intent to kill you. and to top it off, you have to play through them without knowing which character you'll be playing. the game forces you to switch characters with the promise of extra lives. yeah, you CAN pass off the extra lives, but then, when you die, and you WILL die, then you have to start the level over. so you take the extra life, and pray you get someone cool, but 7/10 times you get someone who is absolutely useless in the given situation.
a similar mechanic in Binding of Isaac (a procedral roguelike shooter) shows you the abilities before you pick them up. you can still get flawed powers and unpredictable synergies, but you still know what you're getting yourself into, you can see the power before you take it, and if you are aware of it's potential, either avoid it, or take it at your peril.
broforce feels like it has zero respect for the player, or maybe too much... it has unreasonable expectations of the player to exceed, when it knows damn well that the results are not controlled. you'll find yourself dying by a falling block, or a falling enemie, or a gunshot that you didn't see and why didn't you see it? because the screen is COVERED in mayham. cool on paper, but in terms of game design is just awful and frustrating.
also, a note, if you are considering this game for multplayer, the online is buggy and laggy and adds to the unpredictable nature of the game, making the game even more frustrating, but i will say, online multiplayer is still nice, considering the local co-op craze right now.

Evil Within 2 is a half-baked joke. It is the Resident Evil 5 of Resident Evil or the Silent Hill 5 of Silent Hill or the Metal Gear Solid 4 of Metal Gear Solid. It looks and sounds like EW but everything that made EW good is gone. It is just a mediocre game riding on the coat tails of a much better original title.
There are multiple aspects of this game that fail. The presentation, open world, and the AI are key offenders. In Evil Within 1 the game was constantly throwing enemies that you barely understood at you and only through trial and error did you survive. In fact, the hardest part of EW 1 was the tutorial with the Chain Saw guy. Or Laura for example wasn't introduced in a cut scene. She just appeared and chances are she killed you. It was terrifying. That is the theme of the first game. Terrifying encounters with no preparation or build up. It made you paranoid but that is what built up the fear and kept you on your toes. Every section of the game was stressful because you knew something would appear that you may or may not have enough ammo for. As a result, there were plenty of challenging moments. It was survival horror at its core.
The new game has none of this although on some rare occasions it may get close. Most of the time you will find yourself farming for resources in unnecessary open areas or exploiting the stupid AI by "pulling" them MMO style towards a bush where the enemy will immediately forget you are there and start to backtrack to their zoned area. Of course while they are in the process of backtracking you can easily backstab them and just repeat the process. In the open areas all enemies have a maximum distance where they will chase you and then they will forget you ever existed.Just backstab once the enemy forgets. It’s stupidly easy and you will find yourself doing this most of the time BTW throughout 75% of the game. I was playing the game on the hardest difficulty the entire time...
Gone are hiding under beds or inside closets. Also gone are matches. While maybe story-wise it doesn't make sense to have matches, it was a great mechanic for taking down many enemies at once to save precious ammo. Gone are all of the awesome levers and environmental methods for killing enemies. In EW 2 there are some environmental hazards in the form of oil barrels and fire hydrants but the levers that activated traps are all gone or incredibly sparse.  Expect to find yourself pulling enemies, backstabbing, and farming for gel most of the time.
Ironically the parts of the game that feel the most like the original is when you are forced into linear claustrophobic levels. And maybe for a few moments you will be reminded of the first game.
The other problem with EW 2 is the story. It's too linear. Gone is the vague Japanese style of storytelling for a more linear and bland story. What I enjoyed most about the original EW was the disorientating nature of STEM. In UNION things are a little too orderly.
I don't recommend this game because it's not going to give you the same thrill as EW 1. I had a bad feeling when I first learned that Mikami wasn't directing it and even more of a bad feeling when I saw the gameplay.
EW 2 should not have been a game clarifying the vague nature of the first game but one that adds even more layers of complexity and questions that the first one raises. For a game that exists inside a dream world, EW 2 does exactly what people don't want. Answer every question people don’t actually need answers too.

This falls into the exact same catagory as Rust Arc and countless other games that require resource gathering up the butt to progress anywhere in the tech tree. You NEED friends and you NEED to suck up to someone who is already advanced in the game, otherwise someone with a rifle is going to shoot you once in the head from across a valley and you're going to lose 2 hours of work because the resources you were gathering were on the other side of the map from your base.

This requires constant stops along the way to warm up by a bright stationary fire with your wooden bows, meanwhile everyone who makes that enviroment their permanent home has rifles and the clothing necessary to move freely and stealthily, and they want what little resources you have gathered. I bought this game because the showcasing of vehicles implied it would be easier to progress around the map, but of course this is only true for those who can gather said resources and puts another weapon in their hands against newer groups.

Alien Isolation has been called the game the Alien franchise and fans always deserved, I couldn't agree more.
This game serves as the true sequel to Ridley Scott's original film by creating an atmosphere uncannily similar to the film. After years of focusing on the action of the Alien sequels we finally have an Alien game that perfectly recreates the feeling of terror produced by the film. When creating this game particular attention was payed to the designs of props, items, environments and characters to create a low-fi sci-fi feel. The game takes the 1970's view of the future and retroactively shapes the world in this style.
The story follows Amanda Ripley, the daughter of Ellen Ripley who travels to Sevastapol, a space station holding the flight recorder from the Nostromo. The plot is engaging and interesting. The game has a Bioshock esque world and feel of a civilisation in ruins. The plot takes interesting twists and unexpected turns that keep things very entertaining, try and avoid any detail about the story because going in blind will make your experience all the better.
The graphics and the visuals are fantastic. The environments are incredibly detailed and in combination with the dynamic shadows the game looks amazing. Every single frame of gameplay is beautiful. The animations are also perfect both on Amanda and the Alien, giving an amazingly realistic sense of weight and speed to both. However one problem is the facial animations of the characters. They are somewhat unexpressive and the lip syncing is plain awful. This problem can make it harder to take character interaction seriously and should really have been improved but in the grand scheme of things it doesn't distract from the rest of the game. On the other hand this game has the best full body awareness I have ever seen. The camera tracks Ripley's head perfectly, this may sound restrictive but really it just creates an excellent sense of immersion that makes the fear all the more real. Also, Ripley's hand shakes in fear when she holds her revolver expressing her emotions in a subtle way that the player really has to notice for themselves. When looking out of windows at space and the surrounding space station distance is portrayed incredibly well. Stars can be beautiful but when taking the distances into perspective the feeling of isolation and vulnerability is powerful, nothing makes you feel more helpless in this game than looking out at the stars. It's like they say, in space no one can hear you scream.
I have never played a game with better sound design than this. If you are going to play this game make sure you are using headphones or surround sound because it will make the game so much better. Directionality and distinction of sound becomes a core gameplay element. All interactive props have a distinct sound that you can use to locate them. The Alien also makes different noises based on being in or out of vents as well as for hopping in and out of them. All of these sounds are perfectly produced and greatly help to immerse you in the world. You begin to process the level on an auditory level as well as a visual one. The music is also perfect reinforcing the atmosphere of each scene perfectly. The voice acting is also superb especially from Amanda Ripley.
The gameplay is hugely enjoyable, that is if you enjoy being in a state of constant fear. The mechanics are deep while remaining intelligent. The crafting system is implemented in a way that really allows variations on play styles in a way that most games brag about but do not deliver. It fits perfectly and is never overlooked. This game respects the intelligence of the player. The gameplay is challenging and the player is never spoon fed especially on harder difficulties.
All these elements add to the atmosphere which is the main focus of this game. It maintains a constant feeling of dread, there is not a moment when you won't worry about where the Alien is.
In my opinion this game is a must buy. This is my favourite game of 2014 and I would highly recommend it. But if you are going to buy it be sure to watch the movie first.

I've played a ton of different survival horror/horror games over the years. Included among them are the likes of Resident Evil, Silent Hill, Fatal Frame, The Last Of Us, Dead Space, Clocktower, etc. and I can honestly say no other game has actually caused as much fear and tension as this game. There is something about Alien: Isolation that makes you feel like you're constantly being stalked even in the bits where you aren't. That's where this game prevails, the tension that it builds is uncanny. I feel that's why it succeeds where so many other horror games fail, it understands that gore is not terrifying. It's the unknown that is terrifying, the ambience.
I can only say that if you play this game, which I highly recommend you do, that you take breaks after a few hours of play. This game stressed me out so much that I had bloodshot eyes after one gaming session and while I was laying down attempting to sleep I was hyper alert to all sounds around me. All things considered though this is more than a game, it's a visceral experience that any fan of the Alien series and survival horror games in general should experience.
Does the Alien franchise great justice! Would recommend to all.
