Okay, here's the thing.  I absolutely LOVED the first chapter of this game!  The characters were charming.  The puzzles were fun.  And the story was interesting.  I bought this game as a gift for two people based on the first chapter alone!  Unfortunately, each chapter lost a bit more charm and creativity with each release.
The second chapter was tedious.  The third was a bit better, but you don't really get to interact with the charming characters in the first and second chapters.  The fourth chapter was an absolute CHORE to get through.  It wasn't true to the King's Quest puzzles, but on par with mundane jumping puzzles.  I even solved the final "escape room" puzzle in 10 seconds but was forced to finish the rest of the room in order to activate the door.
And the last chapter was downright depressing.  And honestly, I had to look-up online what the last chapter was because I completely forgot what it was about.
It's a shame, because I know a lot of work was put into this game, but it seemed like story and puzzle-wise, the effort, severely dropped-off after the first chapter.  I don't know if the developers lost creative talent staff, or if their ingenuity rain dry, but it was a shame that the game lost a lot of its pleasant qualities and momentum with each subsequent chapter.

Chapter 1 - Oddly begins with an action sequence, but otherwise the biggest and best chapter.

This is a MOBA for people who don't like MOBAs. I've never liked Dota 2 or LoL, but Smite hooked me instantly. Not only are all of the characters really cool with unique mechanics, but the game modes have so much replay value. Don't like tower objectives? Play Arena. Want to play 5v5 in one lane with random gods? Play Assault. Joust has one lane, Seige has two, and Conquest has three. You'll find yourself skipping around game modes and gods constantly, which prevents you from getting bored.
The game is also very beginner-friendly, with suggested item builds (3 suggested "core" items, 3 suggested offensive items, and 3 suggested defensive items), so you don't have to search through every item in the game when you know nothing. Last-hitting on creeps and enemy gods is still there, but you get partial gold for every kill your team gets so it's harder to fall behind when you're still learning.
I bought the $30 all-gods-included-forever add-on and never looked back. Compared to some other MOBAs, this game is a great value for what you get. I would 100% recommend this game to lovers of MOBAs and action RPGs in general. I'll be playing this for a long time.

It's a real learning curve game that if you play one match and do bad in and stop playing forever because of that then you're really just punishing yourself. I'm not a MOBA player,i've tried League of Legends out after a long time of playing Smite and as much as I liked it I still preferred/came back to Smite. It's a game that i'd recommend you watch gameplay or read some guides on playing before you do because if you go in without knowing how to play you will get murdered. I know a lot of people who complain because of the skins/chests you can buy in game with real money and who actually hate the game because of them but they're just for vanity,they don't actually affect your characters stats or anything like that. I've spent a LOT of money on this game (I own basically every skin thats available to buy and most that aren't anymore,only missing some exclusive skins to the leagues players which i didn't play at the time) and I don't regret it at all, you can buy voice packs too which change the ingame commands to your characters voices and some of them alone are worth it for the funny♥♥♥♥♥♥that they say. Theres 6 game modes at the time of this review, Arena,Conquest,Joust,Siege,Clash and MOTD. Arena is the most beginner friendly, a straight up team deathmatch style,Conquest is the main MOBA three lanes,towers,phoenix(the last defence before the titan) and the titan (kill him to win),Joust is one lane with jungles on the sides and towers,phoenix and titan, Siege is probably the least popular game mode, two lanes large middle jungle,towers,phoenix titan but in this a large Juggernaut arrives to help you destroy towers, Clash,the newest game mode at the time of this review is meant to be the "beginner friendly" mode that shows players how to play the main Conquest, It has two lanes,towers,phoenix and titans but also the jungle camps that conquest has minus one or two,its more of a joust mixed with arena. And MOTD which is match of the day which is usually just random game modes with special settings (more starting gold,infinite mana etc.)
Theres 72 gods and goddesses in the game at the time of this review,all from 8 (right now) Pantheons, Norse,Chinese,Egyptian,Greek,Roman,Hindu,Mayan and the newest one Japanese.
Each play somewhat differently from the others,but are all part of a role ADC,Mage,Tank,Warrior,Assassin.
There's the more competitive scene then,Ranked. These are League's where you play Conquest or Joust 1v1 and soon coming in is Joust 3v3 and you rank up through the ranks from Bronze to Platinum and Masters.
All around the game is a great game with lots of stuff to do like levelling up your account,or getting masteries on gods which lets you get gold,legendary and diamond skins for the god/goddess.(You get worshippers which is basically exp every time you play a match with a god/goddess.)
I do highly suggest watching gameplay and learning to play/build gods before you start playing the game and if possible play with a friend or friends because the game is 100 times more fun with people.

EDIT #1
Apparently, there are keyboard shortcuts for the verbs after all, but, unlike the ones found in the original Lucas Arts adventure games, they are not very intutitive. If in most LA quests they were just the first letters of the verbs: O - open, W - walk, U - use, and so on, in Thimbleweed Park it's Q, W, E, A, S, D, Z, X, C. WIth Q mapping to "open". There is some sense int that - as the 3x3 square of keys on the keyboard can be directly translated into the verbs displayed on the UI. Still, the original system was more user-friendly. I remember just pressing what seemed to make sense and it did what I expecte it to do. In this game I found out about the shortcuts only after finishing the whole game and writing this review.

As much as I absolutely love this game, I'm going to try not to circlejerk about it, because it truly isn't for everyone. For one, it's damned frustrating and very difficult and takes quite a bit of patience, even on its easier difficulties, so if you're one to easily get put on tilt, this game isn't for you. Also, if you're obsessive over graphics, this game is not for you, because while there are add-ons that improve the graphics, the game still doesn't look nearly as good as modern games, with the one exception maybe being the corridor lighting, which still look fairly good today. System Shock 2 is an incredibly tense and scary experience; the game literally plays with your paranoia, with enemies that you can hear from far away and constant enemy respawn, you will never really feel safe. Unlike other select survival horror titles, the classic System Shock 2 can scare while still having excellent gameplay; it was one of the first titles (if not the first) to effectively merge the first person shooter and rpg genres. Additionally, it has open-world style level design that feels claustrophobic and fresh to this day and for days to come.
Though most would agree that the majority of System Shock 2 is excellent, everybody who has played the full game will know what I am talking about when I say that the end bosses (which I won't spoil) are terrible. The unanimous consensus is generally that the ending is downright awful too; even people who enjoyed the ending (myself included) would tell you that it's only enjoyable because of how terrible and cheap it is.
That being said, what are you waiting for? Go play System Shock 2, but only if you plan on playing it in its entirety, from start to finish.

Suits: A Business RPG is one of those video games I'd recommend to anyone who thinks all indie games are just gimmicky, cash grabs with minimum effort put into them.
A lot of attention went into this game, from the NPCs to the turn based fighting system; I can't find a fault with this game. The turn based fighting system is actually very fairly balanced, and never did I find myself thinking the game was too difficult or too easy. Even the black and white, doodlish style that might turn people off works in the game's favor. It perfectly reflects the bland, mass produced dystopia of a monopoly controlled world where even human life is treated as nothing more than capital gain or loss. It also has a very neat, brilliant ending I dare not spoil. These were some of my highlights.
Simply put, it's a fun game. Some reviews assert the game only mocks one topic and bashes it into the ground, but there is so much more to the humor than that.
I feel as long as you don't take anything too seriously and appreciate straightforward humor you'll enjoy the game for what it is.

Just as a summary, I wholeheartedly recommend this game to pretty much anybody old enough/mature enough to handle it, even my girlfriend is a little scaredy cat and she ended up loving sitting by my side and helping me finish this masterpiece.
So let's go through the checklist
Gameplay: This game has improved pretty much all mechanics and controls from the first game, first of all expanding to a much more sandbox approach, which actually makes things a lot more enjoyable. They've redesigned everything to make it far more accessible for the average user playing with a gamepad, and the keyboard gives you hugely expanded accessibility in terms of additional options ( more weapon slots, excellent mouse accuracy and good button placement on keyboard)
The stealth mechanics are also massively improved, enemies react a little more "Game-like" in terms of predictability and pattern recognition, this time around you definitely have a stealth option for the vast majority of the game.
Shooting mechanics are pretty nicely improved, with a huge array of weapons to select from, with a variety of the pistol weapon type.
Enemies broadcast their attacks which gives you the opportunity to play skillfully, but at the same time, your restricted field of view can mean you are unaware of enemies on the other side of you, this forces the player to constantly be checking their surroundings, and to place themselves strategically in all firefight situations.
8/10
Graphics: The environmental scenes can be bland, but at the same time beautiful, with a small variety in the colour pallette, but excellent attention to detail, and a wide variety in assets. Textures are at a pretty high bit-rate overall, but this game shines specifically with animations; enemies move in a horrifying way, which adds to the terror and makes things a little more frantic.
8/10
Sound: Just phenomenal, just as the first game. This game presents insanely thematic music, that really just couldn't set the tone any better if it tried, enemies make unique and terrifying noises, voice acting is the only thing that didn't quite hit in this game, for some reason the protagonist just didn't really hit the right tone in about half the scenes, which is a real shame, some of the secondary voices (Myra in particular) are excellent.
Replayability: This game takes a leaf out of the classic survival horror games like Resident Evil and Silent Hill, with tons of replayability options, New Game +, additional weapons, new costumes, additional difficulty settings and lots of achievements to hunt the second time around.
This is my game of the year so far for 2017, thoroughly recommended

this game seems so appealing, and it has so much promise. at first it makes you feel like a total badass, giving you powers and cool abilities to beat up bad guys and punch satan in the the throat. the game feels like so much fun at first, with clever level designs and cool bosses and vehicles and different characters from movies we've long loved. but after playing for a bit, you start to unlock characters that aren't so good, are severly limited in their ability, which would be cool except you never choose when to use those characters, you just seem to keep having to play as them, whether you want to or not.
this game is built on randomness and chance and unfortunately the randomness is rarely on your side, you often find yourself saying "well that was unfair", "how could i have seen that coming" "the level didn't play out like that last time, what changed". usually things changing on you is a good thing, but not in this game. everything acts unpredictably and you are never really given much chance to adapt. yeah sure, the game conveys mechanics fine, and those mechanics play out predictably on their own, but paired together the levels soon start to feel like rube goldberg machines with the main intent to kill you. and to top it off, you have to play through them without knowing which character you'll be playing. the game forces you to switch characters with the promise of extra lives. yeah, you CAN pass off the extra lives, but then, when you die, and you WILL die, then you have to start the level over. so you take the extra life, and pray you get someone cool, but 7/10 times you get someone who is absolutely useless in the given situation.
a similar mechanic in Binding of Isaac (a procedral roguelike shooter) shows you the abilities before you pick them up. you can still get flawed powers and unpredictable synergies, but you still know what you're getting yourself into, you can see the power before you take it, and if you are aware of it's potential, either avoid it, or take it at your peril.
broforce feels like it has zero respect for the player, or maybe too much... it has unreasonable expectations of the player to exceed, when it knows damn well that the results are not controlled. you'll find yourself dying by a falling block, or a falling enemie, or a gunshot that you didn't see and why didn't you see it? because the screen is COVERED in mayham. cool on paper, but in terms of game design is just awful and frustrating.
also, a note, if you are considering this game for multplayer, the online is buggy and laggy and adds to the unpredictable nature of the game, making the game even more frustrating, but i will say, online multiplayer is still nice, considering the local co-op craze right now.
i don't think i would ever recommend this game, i don't think it can be fixed with a patch, because the inherent core of the game is what is in question. the game would have to be completely redesigned and changed before i would recommend it, and as unfair as that is to this game, that is what it would take to make me play it again.

Finished the game at exactly 25 hours, but it was a jam-packed 25 hours.
The ending was terrible, but other than that, this game is great! Bioshock was good, but System Shock 2, despite being 8 years earlier, is so much better. It's short enough to play a second time, and you might want to, as the story keeps you on your toes and there are at least 4 different experiences of the gameplay to have, since you have total control over your character's stats and proficiencies... and they matter!
Some people complain about difficulty, but I've found it pretty reasonable even on hard, just expect that you WILL die... save often as there's not really an auto-quicksave, and try to conserve your ammo. It's not like Resident Evil in terms of ammo scarcity, the game is pretty generous in resources, but you don't want to run out all the same. This game for me is on the border between recommended and not recommended. If I had NOT recommended it, I probably would have praised it. However, as you can see I DID recommend it, therefore I am going to pull it down somewhat. It is a very good game, the detail in 'manual battle mode' is amazing, especially if you zoom in to the units. However, I hardly ever used 'manual battle mode', because there is little motivation to do so, and it takes so long. More than 90% of the time I just 'auto-resolved' the battles, as it is much quicker. Therefore I spent over 90% of the time on the 'campaign map', which becomes boring after a while. I conquered half of the known world, (overwhelmingly with 'auto-resolve') and after a while the game becomes very boring and repetitive. Once you've learned how to stabilize 'public order' in newly conquered settlements you've pretty much got the game. The process go like this, conquer new settlements, baby-sit newly conquered settlements with 'military presence' and by building 'public order' improving buildings, and once 'public order' is stabilized, stop baby-sitting and move your armies on to conquer new settlements, and start the whole process again. There is more to it, like 'food surplus' and 'income', but basically it gets very repetitive. Like I have said, I have conquered half the known world, and I just can't be bothered to conquer anymore, so I have basically stopped playing the game. Do you get your money’s worth out of the game? Probably, but not all of it. It is a complicated game, don't get me wrong, it's not simple, however, it just gets very boring and repetitive, and there is no reward for conquering new regions/provinces. Now that I have pulled the game down, I would say that I would probably recommend it, as you get some of your money's worth. I would say I still prefer RTS games like Age of Empires, and I am still not a fan of turn-based games, however, as far as turn-based games go, this is a good one.

Ok, since the Emperor Edition came out, I have to re-review this game. Because, boy, the EE changed everything.
The Total War saga is clearly one of the greatest installations in real-time battles realism and offers a great turn-based non-combat gameplay. You'll always get goosebumps when you'll find yourself commanding an army of 6000+ men against another 6000+ men's army. If you've played this game before, and quitted after finding it full of bugs and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ AI, it's time to get back to Rome II and play it, since several patches made it a much more enjoyable experience, with new (and completely reworked) building chains, units' abilities and, more importantly, game-changing politics (civil wars are now avoidable, if you run your empire correctly), and a working siege AI. Truly, the Emperor Edition has changed every single aspect of the game.
Overall, this game started buggy, with bad politics' administration and broken AI; now, it is worthy of bearing the name Rome, as the righteous successor of Rome: Total War.

Black Mesa is a love letter to Valve and the Half Life series. The sheer amount of dedication that went into this project over the years, before it was even considered for a commercial release was inspirational to other mod developers such as myself. When it was announced that a more polished version of the game would be available for purchase on Steam, there was no question that the developers had earned it.
If you are a fan of the original Half Life, this will serve as a fantastic return to the titular doomed research facility. If you're new to Half Life, while it may not be as good as the original in my personnal opinion, it's an excellent way to get into the universe and discover where it all kicked off.
A lot of people complain that the developers aren't releasing Xen for the free mod version (Still available to download by the way) and that they said it would always be free. Those people need to consider how much of their lives the developers spent on this while working or being in full time education. Modding isn't easy and the scale of this project is undeniable. If nothing else, they have the right to go back on what they said in the earlier years of development.
On top of that, Xen is on the way and I cannot wait to see Crowbar Collective's take on the border world!

Gameplay: 5/5. This is the best part of Dark Souls 2. Enemies have good tells, level design is fun to explore and gear provided lots of options.
Multiplayer: The improvements from Dark Souls 1 are very welcome, but it would be really nice if they would make co-oping with a specific friend easier. It is quite a hassle and a lot of online research is needed if you feel like playing through a boss fight with someone you know. It would also be good to be able to opt out of invasions at times as that is a huge stumbling block for some players.
Story: 3/5. This game has a very well build world, that within itself is believeable. All gameplay systems are wrapped into the story and the world has a feel of history to it.
Graphics: 3/5. The game looks pretty, with the textures and lighting, but it is a bit rough around the edges.
Sound: 3/5. Somehow a lot of sounds seem to be played without any positional information. The grass sound for example is really loud and suprises me each time. The hinting of enemies and sounds themselves are fine, it is only the technical playback that bugged me.

This game is great, I really loved the parts when Sebastian said "What the..."

CONS: Thoughtless storyline, kringy dialogue, lack of attention to detail and repetitive scenarios (IE. YELLS "MYRA WAIT!" or "LILLY ITS ME!" in just about every scenario you encounter, and with each time enemies will rise up from the ground or enter your current area, where the guided response is to wip out your guns and clear the room or crouch it out and move around them). Boss battles are simple and unsatisfying to defeat. Ammo and other ordanance is much too easy to stock up on, taking away from unsettling feeling of scarcity and leaving it to feel more like an action shooter. Pace of the game itself is much faster than the first EVIL WITHIN, and it feels rushed, since side quests are quick and usually just present you with more ammo or crafting supplies; even with the open world concept you feel constrained to a single path since the doors to practically all other buildings stay locked until you reach a further part of the story. OVERALL, if you're looking for that same feeling you got with the first EVIL WITHIN, you wont find it here.
PROS: Artstyle is beautiful, Game mechanics are fluent, and the character upgrading and development is very satisfying. The full game length is well worth the price, where as I was just shy of 14 hours after completion. The flashback scenarios to the original EVIL WITHIN were alot of fun to get phsycologically plunged back into, and the phsycological instability of Sebastian throughout the whole campaign makes it quite the adventure, just dont rely on the story to satisfy you. Just as a summary, I wholeheartedly recommend this game to pretty much anybody old enough/mature enough to handle it, even my girlfriend is a little scaredy cat and she ended up loving sitting by my side and helping me finish this masterpiece.
So let's go through the checklist
Gameplay: This game has improved pretty much all mechanics and controls from the first game, first of all expanding to a much more sandbox approach, which actually makes things a lot more enjoyable. They've redesigned everything to make it far more accessible for the average user playing with a gamepad, and the keyboard gives you hugely expanded accessibility in terms of additional options ( more weapon slots, excellent mouse accuracy and good button placement on keyboard)
The stealth mechanics are also massively improved, enemies react a little more "Game-like" in terms of predictability and pattern recognition, this time around you definitely have a stealth option for the vast majority of the game.
Shooting mechanics are pretty nicely improved, with a huge array of weapons to select from, with a variety of the pistol weapon type.
Enemies broadcast their attacks which gives you the opportunity to play skillfully, but at the same time, your restricted field of view can mean you are unaware of enemies on the other side of you, this forces the player to constantly be checking their surroundings, and to place themselves strategically in all firefight situations.
8/10
Graphics: The environmental scenes can be bland, but at the same time beautiful, with a small variety in the colour pallette, but excellent attention to detail, and a wide variety in assets. Textures are at a pretty high bit-rate overall, but this game shines specifically with animations; enemies move in a horrifying way, which adds to the terror and makes things a little more frantic.
8/10
Sound: Just phenomenal, just as the first game. This game presents insanely thematic music, that really just couldn't set the tone any better if it tried, enemies make unique and terrifying noises, voice acting is the only thing that didn't quite hit in this game, for some reason the protagonist just didn't really hit the right tone in about half the scenes, which is a real shame, some of the secondary voices (Myra in particular) are excellent.
Replayability: This game takes a leaf out of the classic survival horror games like Resident Evil and Silent Hill, with tons of replayability options, New Game +, additional weapons, new costumes, additional difficulty settings and lots of achievements to hunt the second time around.
This is my game of the year so far for 2017, thoroughly recommended

A simple bare bones indie rpgmaker game, with inspirations from OFF. Got the game for a song and I thought it was worth the price.
You play an all purpose businessman in an exaggerated black and white capitalist universe, where everything is a satire of everything that goes along with the nature of economics, politics, entertainment, etc. Enemies are hand drawn in a rough style, with some of them being parodies of real world people. There's a great deal of 420 humor, references, and some♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes. I found a lot of it just blurred together.
You can control up to 3 unspeaking characters, although I was able to finish the non-joke ending with just 2, as the third arrives very late in the game. Outside of one or two moments, the game is not hard whatsoever. Combat is extremely simple and requires little to no resource hoarding, nor tactics. I wasn't a fan of that- it's a little too basic. I got through the entire game with just my main character auto attacking and my one side character doing an ability with a single crowd control effect, with the rare occasion of using an area effect attack. You don't really get interesting abilities and a LOT of what you have is too expensive to use more than one or twice without reloading resources out of battle, but you don't really need those abilities either.
At about 4 hours long, taking my time, but not grinding anything for xp, the game is of fair length for the price. It's not an amazing title in the sense of other really 'out there' indie games like OFF, Yume Nikki, or Space Funeral, but it's fair for what it is and I don't think it's trying to be anything more than that. And that's really just how Suits is. It's not terribly interesting to read the text in the game and the imagery is fairly dull, but it's not bad either. It's just average. I am, however, figuring the price of the game into this. You get what you pay for, and for that, it's quite fair. I didn't mind playing it, it just didn't 'wow'.

When I first heard of Ron Gilbert's new adventure I was very sceptical. The failure that was Broken Age made me weary of yet-another-old-dev-bringing-back-the-magic. I did not donate to the kickstarter at that time but closely observed the making of the game through various media. The closer the premiere the more I felt like it was a good investment.
The game is weird, but in a good way. I expected a bit less surreal humour, but instead of something akin to Maniac Mansion, I got something closer to Zak McKraken. It has that nice touch of horror/tension to it. Even with the 4th wall breaking humour it has that aura of creepiness that X-Files/Twin Peaks had of small Americana towns where the outsider is usually not sure what to see as weird and what to see as normal.
The gameplay is a throwback to classic SCUMM adventure games with the same array of verbs at our disposal, but don't be fooled - this game was not written in AGS, but has been coded from grounds up, which is an achievement cause it looks damn gorgeous at times. The only thing I can find negative is that when you're doing pixel art, don't make it move so smoothly, ruining that whole chunky pixel feeling.
As far as the sound design goes - props to voice actors. Very good voice acting - Reyes newbie enthusiasm, Ray's sarcastic and tired veteran commentary, Ransome's Krusty-like voice... the characters are very much alive thanks to all of that. Music is quite good and gives the nice atmosphere, but sometimes, just sometimes it's way too faint to hear it properly. Sound bug?
As for the story... can't say much - it's a murder mystery but I'm loving it so far. The biggest problem so far is that sometimes the 4th wall breaking jokes get a bit too tiresome in one conversation. There's a lot of nice Lucasfilms tribues that anyone that follow Lucasfilms/Lucasarts should recognize but the subtle references are better than the in-your-face ones. There's a ton of side-stuff to do and the dialogue options are great to explore so definitely a good game in that regard. Oh and no character deaths... yet.

So the bottom line is: Was it worth it? Is it worth it? For adventure game fan? Yes. For a newbie... no. The game requires a certain logic. Mind you I have not checked the causal mode because I always went for the Mega-Monkey in Monkey Island games, but it might be a bit easier there. Overall the game just requires you to think in that surreal fashion like back in a day. Analyze the clues and work out solutions. It's not that hard but a newbie is gonna quickly get lost.
The pricing of a game could be $5 dollar lower IMO, or at least the Euro price could be adjusted so it's lower than $20. But I'm not complaining. These days a $20 game can have so little content it hurts. This is not the case.

Not having been alive/being a young child when the original King's Quests were released, I was unsure about purchasing this game. A lot of resurrections/long awaited sequals are hardly understandable, or at the very least humorless, if you are unfamiliar with the original content. Such is not the case with King's Quest. I found this game to be a delighful romp, a heart warming tale, and at times it left me with tears welling. Having now seen LPs of early KQ games I can say there is not much missing if you have not experienced the original games.
Now, let us adress what might chap some peoples khakis. This game is in episodic format; a format that is, in the grand scheme of time, relatively new. Some games do this well, some do not, and it is all very subjective anyway. In Kings Quest, each episode is unique in form and function. I can see how this might be jarring or make the game seem inconsistant for some people. I've seen people go so far as to say it felt like the developers were experimenting wildly. I, however, feel that this makes each episode a unique experience, as each episode is a different story that takes place at a different time; filling in a larger narrative as the game unfolds.
Another thing that rubs some people the wrong way is how the game handles choice, as it is want to do in any storytelling adventure game with any semblance of choice. There are a fair amount of choices in KQ. Not all of them necessarily feel important, nor are there many paths or endings, but the choices change the flavor of the story being told. "What does it matter if it all leads to the same conclusion?" You may ask. Well, this game is one of those "it's about the journey, not the destination" kind of experiences. There are subtle to obvious tone shifts in the story, both in the episode and over the whole game, dependent upon player choices. Another mechanic I found quite poetic, if a bit morbid, is that as the story goes on, and the protagonist grows older in his stories, you get less and less choice in your options on how to handle or "flavor" things. You become locked on the path you have chosen. The game calls this out in a rather melancholic dialogue. The way this is implemented in the game is a real deep commentary on life and aging, as well as regret, opportunity, and burning bridges.
Now, on to less serious stuff. The grapics are pretty, and Graham's billowing cloak never gets old. The writing is top notch for, and this is important here, its genre. If you don't like fun, simple, pun filled, and fantastical adventure you won't like this game. The voice acting is amazing, and includes the talents of Wallace Shawn, Tom Kenny, Zelda Williams, and Cherami Leigh. The musical score is wonderful and greatly adds to the story. The puzzles are challenging, yet fair, and you you won't run into crazy, moon logic, timer triggering, if-you-don't-pick-this-up-you-die-way-later kind of nonsense. Now, nothing is randomly generated so the solutions will always be the same, but the different flavors you can make the story warrent replaying. The added ability to skip cutscenes from episode 2 and on makes things better as well.
So, if you are still in after all you've read I guarantee you will have a good time. If you're hesitant, you may want to wait for a sale. Either way, if you are a fan of King's Quest, if you are a fan of the genre, or if you want a nice storytelling experience I recommend picking this up at some point. Fingers crossed for a season 2!

After how much I loved Dark Souls in spite of its flaws, this was always going to be a tough game to summarise, especially with the personnel changes at Fromsoft and creative differences.
Compared to Dark Souls 1, there are a lot of differences. It's technically in many respects a superior game to the original. It doesn't need a ton of changes to get it working like Dark Souls did and it flows a lot better. It's world and PVE is fantastic.
However, there are plenty of faults with Dark Souls 2. The bosses for a start are lacklustre in comparison to the original, the first had some woefully bad fights like the Gaping Dragon but the environment they were in and the sound worked to make it feel like they fitted in. The experience of that aspect didn't feel at all great or worthwhile, and too many of the boss arena fights are on small circular areas.
There's a couple of cool bosses in the game, but there's nothing as grabbing as any of the Ornstein and Smough/Manus/Kalameet/Artorias/Four Kings fights.
Co-op works a lot better than the GFWL fest, invading seems to work better too but the combat feels off and cartoony at points,  Hopefully it will change with patches. The Geography with the world is broken too; for example one zone you take a lift up to you don't see it's subsequent environment anywhere in the previous area. The world is disjointed and Dangleic, while being pretty cool, seems completely out of joint and nowhere near as well constructed as Lordran.
It's still a good game and if you love Dark Souls like I did, you won't be too disappointed. However, if you've not played the original I recommend playing that first and taking it from there. I'm hoping the game improves drastically with the new DLC like the Prepare To Die Edition worked for the first.

This new bad guy felt really fresh and to follow in the wake of his distruction was pheonominal. Saddly it soon moves on to less interesting enemies and finally to the least challenging last boss in a game that I have ever played.
On that note, the enemy AI is not good. I like that once being seen it does not draw the whole area's worth of enemies upon you, however maybe they should try at least a little to find you after you crouch behind the nearest corner. They just wander back to their very obvious patrol, worse so in my opinion then the first game.
The atmosphere was somewhat mixed in this one as well, the first game was throwing you head first into a seemingly endless abyss of constant danger. Evil Within 2 however, you could easily stealth kill anything you came across (mini bosses being the only exception) and if you failed you could run 10 feet and they would walk back allowing you to stealth kill them anyways. Call me crazy but any dark and cramped moment in either game sent me on high alert where being out in the open allows me to see every little ambush coming from a mile away. All in all, I did not find this title scary. Well, except for the ghost lady (that never really gets explained) she was pretty terrifying.
They traded horror for drama and in a "scary game" it leaves me with a lot to be desired. The decision to change the models was unnecessary; and the change in voice actors (for whatever reason that may be) was done well enough that it didnt bother me too much. The "haunted heroic father righting his wrongs" was enough to engage me with the story, but it is still a trope. On the technical end I had a few crashes and some visual glitches, but it was minimal. In the end, it was a good game that had great moments, but should have stayed a little closer to the roots of the first game in my opinion. 8/10

Hello folks!
For someone who really disliked Evil WIthin 1, (Because of the game design structure and boring set pieces.) I was horrifyingly surprised by Evil Within 2 and how awesome the overall game design is!
Positives:
- No performance issues whatsoever! (Nvidia GPU and i7 CPU)
- Super Creepy without overloading on jump scares
- Gunplay is satisfying and it is tricky to aim while you're panicking
- Semi-Open World mechanic is actually good (Personally, I dislike open world games)
- Redesigned and fun crafting system
- Side quests are interesting to finish and the game motivates you to do them (I usually skip side quests on most games)
- Progression system is much better than Evil Within 1
- The story has an interesting premise (I am yet to finish the game, will update once I complete the game)
- No cheap cash grab tactics from the dev team. I will definitely buy future DLCs for this game!
Negatives:
- Texture Filtering gets annoying (Far away objects are low resolution but, turn into high resolution when you reach them)
- Dialogs are uninspiring throughout the game (Not a major issue but, would love some philosophical depth)
I would personally recommend The Evil Within 2 to all horror game fans, who loved classics like Silent Hill and Resident Evil. This is a must play at full price! The dev team deserves their efforts' worth!
However, I will not compare this game to Alan Wake. As Alan Wake had a lot of layers of philosopy and narrational depth which is clearly absent in Evil Within 2.

Disclaimer: I received a press copy to do my review, but I am also a backer (and Ransome Swear Jar contributor), so I spent my own money on it. I am a big fan of the game (and LucasArts adventures), so I was eager to fall in love with it. This review was originally published in Retronator Magazine (and it's way longer there).
Thimbleweed Park delivers on the promise of being a true old-school point-and-click adventure. It’s as if Maniac Mansion 2 wasn’t developed by Tim Schafer, Dave Grossman and others, but stayed in the hands of Ron Gilbert, Gary Winnick, David Fox and Mark Ferrari. Lucky for us, since both games ♥♥♥♥ing rule, I’m glad the two alternative histories both live in our lifetimes.
This comparison hits closer to home than expected. Just like in Day of the Tentacle, in Thimbleweed Park you don’t choose which characters will be part of the story — they all slowly unlock as the plot develops. Except instead of three, we get 5 of them.
You start with the two federal agents: experienced (and bitter) Ray and younger (and eager) Reyes. They are mostly interchangeable and give a nice choice of a cynical or cheerful commentary of the game’s world. Even though their lines are the same for the most part, the voice actors did a great job at breathing different life into each character.
You soon meet the supporting cast, which is an unexpectedly pleasant mix of bizarre, weird and humorous-a-reno.
As you investigate the murder, you cross paths with the other three playable characters and soon take control of their fate. Whereas the agents can both do the same things (with rare puzzles that involve both of them), the others are more specific as their backgrounds tie deeply into the history of Thimbleweed Park (the name of the degenerating town where the game takes place).
First we have Delores, a lovable game developer who’s in town for the will reading of her late uncle.
Franklin is Delores’ dad. Like the uncle, he is also dead. But still plenty kicking, even though he lacks a bit in the self-confidence department.
Finally, we have Ransome the ♥♥♥♥ing Insult Clown. Ah, Ransome. I need to give a special shout out to Ian Corlett who voiced the offensive clown. The hilarious writing together with his delivery make Ransome one of the best characters in the game — and I hate clowns, so this means a lot. In the game, all Ransome’s lines are beeped out, but Ian actually went all-out swearing in the recording sessions, so there’s a chance we’ll get an uncensored version at some point. I’d replay the game for that.
The five character arcs develop in parallel, but are mostly independent. Time-travel interactions in Day of the Tentacle were much more involved in that regard.
Each of the five characters is equipped with a list of goals that progress their story further. Some goals are shared (especially between the agents), and you’ll occasionally have to hand over an item from a character to another to help them out. Thimbleweed Park is very clear like that—you always know what you’re trying to do. In 1989, Ron Gilbert wrote an article titled Why Adventure Games Suck where he laid out rules of thumb he used while designing Monkey Island. Thanks to his rules, Monkey Island did away with stuff like dead ends, dying and arbitrary puzzles.
If Thimbleweed Park follows Maniac Mansion in its setting, the puzzle design clearly follows the later predecessor. While Monkey Island still had a sour monkey wrench in there or two, Thimbleweed Park perfects Ron’s philosophy.
I don’t remember when I last finished an adventure game without looking at a walkthrough at least once. Maybe even never. I finished Thimbleweed Park without any help though. That is not to say the game is easy. I was playing on ♥♥♥♥ing Hard mode, alright?
It’s true that I was forced to not look at walkthroughs, since there weren’t any by the time I finished it (what with the game not being released and all). I was handed a real simulation of the eighties. Back then, if you got stuck in a game, you wrote a letter to your favorite magazine, they would print the letter in the readers section and if you were lucky, another reader who solved the puzzle would respond in the next month’s issue. It was kind of like having Internet with the latency of two months. Not something you can use when you have two weeks to write a review. The press were given a walkthrough a few days before the release though (when I’ve already licked all my fingers), so be suspicious of cheating ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s at other journalistic establishments.
But my success did not come (just) because I was forced to think with my own head (as you know, once you look up a single walkthrough clue, it’s an instant drug addiction and every time you get stuck, you go for the easy way out). No, puzzles in Thimbleweed Park simply make sense.
When I say puzzles, don’t forget that this is an old-school adventure game. Gameplay is a never-ending (well, after-15-hours ending) sequence of well-designed hurdles the game throws at you, mainly the townsfolk refusing to do what you want, or missing an item to do it. Coming up with solutions is most alike riddles: you have a setup with a bunch of clues, and when you figure the item or action that fits the problem, you feel really clever.
You always have a few open problems at hand, but it’s never so overwhelming that you’d have to resort to old-school frustrations such as trying to combine every possible item in your inventory. That will get you nowhere since there are no arbitrary solutions.
When I depleted my ideas on all loose ends, I simply turned off the game for the day and next time, with a fresh motivation to retrace my steps, the solution would always show up in a clue I missed. I can’t stress how much pride you get from being able to solve everything on your own.
Without getting into spoiler territory, I’ll say that the game’s ending holds up to a 10/10 rating for me. It’s not exactly the love/hate plot twist of Monkey Island 2, but close enough and it left me completely satisfied. Catharsis was strong.
It’s hard not to have a warm fuzzy feeling thinking about the game. I fell in love with the weird-a-reno town, and as funky as it is, I was always delighted to return. I don’t think I need to praise the art and voice actors any more (the art is fantastic, and I go into it in great detail in my Retronator Magazine article), but the music also contributes majorly to the Twin Peaks vibe the authors set to recreate. It’s a perfect match.

The second one is set in his stories when you play through Graham's experience and sometimes broken memories. You can see how the main character develops and throughout the stories identify with him. Every chapter takes place in different time so you can see how Graham became a king in the first part, then how he dealt with the power he seized. You relive Graham's meeeting with his future wife and consequently 18 years later you help Graham bring his family together. At last you experience Graham's last adventure in his advanced age of 77.

✪ Funny and entertaining most of the time
✪ Unpredictability in story
✪ Pleasant graphics + Good voiceacting
✪ Puzzles - there are a lot of them, some intriguing and some only about guessing

✪ Descending quality of the game
✪ Poor controllability
✪ Simplicity - some characters seem underdeveloped, their behaviour is very simple.

I have to say that Technomancy Studios offers this game at a really modest price, and I can see why.
The things I really enjoyed about this game is the overall presentation.  It's nice, unique, and I can appreciate the crudely drawn graphics and weird sound track.  Some may say that it draws parallels with OFF (a free game), and LISA (another steam game), and that wouldn't be too far from the truth, but not entirely correct either.  It ends up being its own unique experience from beginning to the end that is worth sitting through, along with its many comedic moments to break up the otherwise dark and demented atmosphere.
With that said, there are problems I have with this game that is hard to complain about because of its value.  However, as I do appreciate the end product, I feel the need to address this in hopes to see improvement in the future.
For one thing, the battle system may look like it has a decent amount of options, but there is hardly any strategy and variety involved.  Most of the special moves the protagonist can perform have a high miss chance (so I've noticed).  Even the move that lets him recharge his TP has a chance to not work at all, which I find ridiculous.  It gets to the point that his special abilities that he earns are just underminded entirely.  Once you recruit Jerome, the game just gets easy from there to where I just employed one strategy: attack with the Protagonist, use the staple move with Jerome to stun the enemy (or staple storm if there are multiple).  Once the enemy is stunned, keep spamming attack (or briefcase toss if possible), and repeat until I win.  Early on, you do have to manage your inventory, but any novice can catch on and abuse this strategy quickly.  Just remember to upgrade your equipment every now and then, have some healing items and water bottles for Jerome, and you never need to change up your strategy.  Once you recruit the third party member, the game just gets stupidly easy from there.  I'm not asking for anything complex, but I feel that the combat system really bogged down the overall experience for me.  It hurts that there is hardly any replay value.  I am aware that there is a hidden ending, but that involves getting the one item that you lose forever once you've completed half the game.  Some of the jokes presented at the end game felt forced too in retrospect.
Should that steer your decision from buying the game?  Honestly, I cannot say.  The price does make the experience worth while over all despite the lack of replay value, and I still encourage you to at least give this game a try.  It won't take up too much of your time, and it costs about the same as a soda, and you don't have to worry about the excessive amounts of sugar and having to buy the soda again and again.
Yeah, that was forced, but my point is, I would give this game a chance.

Suits: A Business RPG is one of those games you pick up for under a dollar not expecting much. Upon playing it for about fifteen minutes however, you realize you've come across a gem. Suits: A Business RPG is a hilarious take on white collar culture in the form of a Final Fantasy 4-esque RPG. You'll do battle with demented coffee cups, evil corporate bosses (putting a whole new meaning on “boss fight”), and other business-related denizens using staplers and other office supplies in a turn-based battle system. The game is divided into five main areas, and can be completed in about 2 to 2.5 hours if you stick to completing the main quest. Finding all the secret areas and cleverly hidden jokes within the game however, may take you upwards of 3 to 4 hours, due to the sheer number of Easter eggs included. The developers could have charged more for the game, and I would still feel like I got my money's worth, on merit of the game's humor, story, and Easter eggs.

There's a lot of things that Suits gets wrong. And I mean a
. But there's an interesting sort of creative mind at work behind all of the black and white, and it's at least an interesting experience to see which ways the game'll turn. Less than the price of a double cheese at Mickey Dee's too, there's uh, not much sacrifice in snagging this. I'd stay away if you're not interested by the initial look and feel of the game, but otherwise, it's not going to be a waste.

Fun and surreal experiential game. The sound design and graphics are nicely done, and the real joy of the game comes from seeing unexpected things happen in the environments. It's fun to see the scenes transform, and watching weird stuff unfold in otherwise normal-looking spaces reminded me of Myst. The sounds are really evocative as well, especially in the parking lot scene. A VR mode would be fun...it would be cool to be able to explore in more than the fixed rotational perspective.
That all being said, it's short, minimalist, and more like a showpiece for environmental design than a full-fledged game.  This reminded me of the Diorama series for the Vive in that you get to experience a well-designed environment but there really isn't much of a game mechanic. The interaction feels perfunctory and there's no branching - you hunt for the next trigger to click and once you find it the next thing happens. I think some people will be turned off by the lack of variation, but for me, it was satisfying and kind of sublime. I recommend it, especially if you're interested in game design.

When I was younger - that is, a much younger version of myself - there was this toy that siphoned all of my attention every time I caught a glimpse of it in the catalogue. Every image was brief, but illustrious, overflowing with colours, like a ROYGBIV eclair that I couldn't bite into.
It was the Tomy Racing Turbo.
The invitation to my eyes was received and I was fortunate enough to get one, thanks to the generosity of my parents. I put aside an entire night for it; it was going to be glorious. The lighting was soporific in my room and I prepared myself, mentally and physically, for a marathon joy-festival.
And then I played it. In under an hour, all of my visions of grandeur and joy; pomp and circumstance; elation and hypersensitivty were disrupted by inexcusable hyperbole and unforgivable brevity. For a short moment, yes, it was everything I had hoped; and I applauded and lauded the creator for bringing it to me.
After? I realized that feeling, that sensation and expectation I had would never come to fruition.
It's a really pretty interactive screensaver with some great bits of ASMR. If that's what you want, enjoy. Beyond that, it's nothing different from the trailer you see above - really.

It's an art game, and that will not appeal to some people. I really enjoyed Burton's mixtures of mundane urban objects, mundane urban sounds and artistic reimagings of them outside their otherwise mundane urban environments, and as a longtime urban dweller myself, I found this concept quite delightful. It's really far too simple in concept and in execution to be remotely pretentious, but some will still insist on calling it that, because perhaps its whimsy is a little too understated for some people. But don't think that by simple I mean it is lacking--I mean that more in the classical sense of elegance. There is no excess here at all--every detail is purposeful and thoughtful, and so it seems effortless. That sense of effortlessness works in favor of its intent: to make you smile and step outside of the ordinary for a little while, and then send you on your way with the encouragemet to reimage your world on your own. And it does a really good job at that.

Alien: Isolation is about you Amanda, who has boarded a ship which has a distress signal. When you enter you soon realise that there is an Alien aboard which is killing everyone. You have to try to escape or trap the Alien while figering out what happend.
+ The grathics are great. They look amazing and give a great atmosphere thoughout the game. Not one point did the game look rushed, you can really tell the the developers really enjoyed working on the game. One small problem would be the anti aliasing which could be better. You probaby wont notice.
+ The storys a very creative and diffrent, the first half feels and works great but towards the end it can get tiresome. The main reason why would be becasue you have to backtrack more than once which leaves you feeling like you want to see more of the ship.
+ The controls are spot on and I have no problem with them, if you did then you can change the keys to your liking or you can play with a controller as they have supported them.
+ Music in Alien: Isolation is perfect since they remastered the original soundtrack from the movie Alien. Because of this the game feels alot like the film with fans will love.
+ The difficulty is how most games should be. Not many save points which means you really dont want to die and the game is always challanging.
+ The AI is the best I have ever seen in any game, well for the Alien. The Alien learns your tactics and roams freely which means you can never predict what/were the Alien is. This is great since the game will always feel diffrent every time you play. The humans are good but not as good as the Alien.
+ length of the game is around 15 hours, but is can be alot more depending on how you play. If you run around and dont look around your surroundings you will finish alot quicker than if you looked around and walked slowly. Really depends on how you play games.
+ Threre are some replayability to be had such as achievements and timed missions which are fun. There is some DLC you could buy if you want to play more missions.
+ The voice acting is fits well and they even voiced actors from the movie which is great. It makes you feel like your playing a Alien game.
- The only downside if a few tiny things... These are Story backtracking, anti aliasing and the game models/lip syncing is bad. They are very tiny to added up together they could have been fixed in development. They hardly do anything to the game which is good.
Overall I think that Alien: Isolation is an amazing horror game which is taken back to it's roots. I would definitely recommend it to anyone who likes horror, Aliens. I rate Alien: Isolation 9 out of 10!

First off, I'm a huge Alien(s) fan.  Love the movies, games, toys, everything.  However, this game I have a love hate thing going with it.
First, what I love:  The look, the feel, the graphics.  This is all amazing.  I felt like I was right back in 79.  I wanted to adjust the tracking on the loading screens!  The crafting wasn't too bad.  Killing (when you actually GET to kill) was a blast.  Let you be very creative.  I also liked the story though it gets to the point in some places where you go, what next will you throw at me?  And another big draw.  They got the original crew back together!  That's huge.
Now to what I hate: The Alien.  First off and this is the biggest problem I have with the game is... it doesn't work.  The alien DOESN'T!  HAVE!  EYES!!!  Hiding under a friggin' desk or behind a chair is NOT going to work.  It knows where you are.  At all times.  The other problem is that not only does the Alien now see, but it also seems to be nearsighted.  There were many instances where it would just walk right past me as I was standing in a corner.  Standing.  Out in the open.  For all to see.  Now I understand, this is how the game is played, but come on.  A poor sighted Alien is not as faithful as the rest of the game was.  The other thing I hated was that the game does not let you kill the alien but simply drive it off and erase it's short term memory.  Fire will drive it off but not kill it.  No matter how much fire or firepower to bring down on it, it will not die.  Which... makes the Alien dumb in addition to being poor sighted.  So, ok.  Fire hurts it but won't kill it, it needs to come and kill Ripley and the pain will stop.  Things aren't going to change just because it runs away to let it's carapace cool off.  I'm still going to burn it next time it finds me.  If it's so damn smart it would figure this out and just leave me the hell alone or set a trap or something.
Overall though, I will recommend the game.  There are parts I never want to ever have to play through again but in the end I had a good time.  As I said, I both love and hate this game.

It's safe to say a dedicated following (including myself) have been eagerly anticipating Thimbleweed Park for the sole reason that it comes from the folks who helped to establish LucasArts as a particularly important milestone in the history of tthe point and click adventure genre. Ron Gilbert in particular has a reputation that precedes him for his Monkey Island series and in spite of their age, those games easily hold up even now as some of the most pivotal adventure games ever made. Gary Winnick, while involved primarily in Maniac Mansion rather than its extremely successful sequel Day of the Tentacle, played a large part in the success of the genre in the mainstream as well.
I am happy to report that the homecoming of two of adventure's heroes is a resounding success, through and through. The characters, almost immediately, strike a chord, and the humor is easily reminiscent of Monkey Island's punny, quirky style. The attention to detail is uniquely important in a genre that too little receives the attention or the care that it deserves. Dialogue is entertaining, and one of the biggest appeals for me is the exploration of choice, which can certainly lead to some hilarious and memorable methods of breaking the fourth wall. The game deftly reminds you that yes, you are playing a game, and yes, it has tropes, and yes, those tropes have come a little ways from the games you remember in the 90's.
I would say more but I want to play the game, so I'll leave it at this: pick up the game for yourself and don't miss out on possibly the most important adventure release since The Curse of Monkey Island. It's that good.

This is not a detailed review by any means, as I cannot yet speak for 100% of the content; However, it is rare that such detailed completion can be claimed by reviewers of MMOs. At any rate, The Elder Scrolls Online appeals to me strongly, as it does with many gamers, due to its direct ties with Bethesda's Elder Scrolls series. After spending roughly 50 hours in game, I can attest to several negatives and positives of this title though I endeavor to be brief. My primary critique so far (In being a veteran of MMO titles) is in the control system itself. To be clear.. I do not have a problem with their intended method, only that I am fairly locked down to that method barring the use of some unknown addon. I have always mapped abilities to either key-mouse combinations or to clickable macros in other MMO experiences, so I was upset (at first) that I could not click abilities or control their assignment past 6 predetermined keys. This was further agitated by my own preferences as, though I may be alone in this, I have never fancied using the number keys as shortcuts. I felt that this game forced this playstyle. HOWEVER, this leads me to my primary positive note: The control system itself. 'Wait.. but you said..' I know what I said, but I also pointed out that this was my initial feeling. I found, after around 20 hours, that Zenimax knew better than me how to provide a combat experience, and after avoiding my keyboard related griefs by using numbered mouse keys, I found myself thoroughly enjoying an experience that I had once dreamed about: The Elder Scrolls in a massive online setting, with no extended action bars to take away from the experience. Furthermore, the limited action bar spaces served in the end as their own brilliant mechanic, keeping (most) fights varied and fresh due to a requirement of resourcefulness in opposition to the lackluster buttonmashing of the many proc based abilities on other games' always visible action bars.
I said I would keep it short, so I have. As I mentioned, I do have several pros and cons, but for the purpose of this being quick ( I am strapped for time at the moment) I will keep it simple with one + and one - sentiment.
However I will leave you with this: I am a HUGE fan of lore, and I am in most games for their story, and the Elder Scrolls series is far from an exception. This game thus far has both elated and disappointed on this front. My disappointment has come in the form of inconsistancies pointed out by a respected youtuber, but KNOW THIS: Even though dialogue may sometimes be quick and the stories bring other lore into question, any good nerd can look past these bothers and see ESO for what it is: A  wonderful representation of the future of MMOs with thousands upon thousands of brilliantly voice acted lines that tell a fantastic story from a time in Elder Scrolls lore that we honestly dont know enough about to complain. Any piece of Tamriel that I can get in this format is fine with me. Overall I recommend, but know that due to a fairly limited number of complaints, I must hold it to a modest 8.5 out of 10.
** continuation **
A further complaint is with an almost pay-to-play environment. In lieu of most similar games allowing for a rested experience gain after logging out in taverns, cities, etc. ESO has provided smaller in-game gains such as the Ring of Mara (I would make a list but can literally think of no other example) with the largest gains only being available to those spending real world coin. I understand the necessity of money making in the business model, and it has to happen somewhere; however, there are no real alternitives for the players that cannot afford a subscription or random crown purchases. The primary experience boost is in the form of a consumable item available ONLY in the crown store. While there is the scroll's redeeming quality of persisting (and pausing) during logouts, this is an item that carries a real world price tag and lasts a measly 2 hours with a 50% boosted gain. WHAT?! A free system of doubled experience with a bar percentage limitation would be much more welcome. Take some notes from Blizzard, Zenimax, they have been in this 'game' a LONG time for a reason.
Discouragingly high in-game prices seem to further penalize players who keep responsible pocketbooks. I understand that this is an inflated economy where 1000g is easy to come by with a couple quests and a vendor selling spree, but almost 50k for a very basic mount? I do have other things to spend my coin on... Who wouldn't rather subscribe and buy a horse with their 'complimentary' crowns?
On a more positive note, this is NOT the worst system I have seen for microtransactions. Given the price of a subscription vs the real world price of crowns, it's actually quite fair as your subscription grants you access to otherwise paid content and an allowance of crowns that are roughly the value of your sub itself. For the gamer that is responsible with his or her wallet, this makes the previous complaint somewhat moot.
Now let's address the things that keep me playing. Despite its questionable continuity and how easy it would be to miss when rushing to keep up with friends, the story is still, in my humble opinion, worthy of the series, and far superior in the MMO genre itself. If one takes the time to listen and follows the quests from area to area, he or she will discover a brilliant slew of voice actors backing up an intriguing story of enemies and alliances in a world that I personally can't get enough of.
Meanwhile, the aforementioned combat system has grown on me and mixes extremely well with a concept that can't be praised enough: classless classes. In ESO you choose a class during character creation that, instead of locking you down to specific skills like most MMOs, provides you with a guideline for the type of hero that you wish the Vestige to be. Skill lines are divided between weapons, guilds, classes, and more. You really want to be an assassin that heals and is particularly brilliant with maces? Go for it.
Another bit of praise falls on just how good this game looks. Remember, you have to be fair; this is not a fully loadable file that you alone exist in like its single player brothers, this is a system that relies heavily on cached data and internet speeds to deliver a highly playable experience. With that in mind, to the people who say this game looks bad, and continues to compare it to a fully-modded Skyrim:  Have you ever played an MMO before? Do you understand what sacrifices must be made to make them playable by more than 1% of gamers? Finally, when exactly was the last time you actually played Skyrim?
Ok, ok, I get it. Some things could look better, but come on! The game looks beautiful with some truly breathtaking vistas! Don't be a troll!

I bought this game during the Sqaure Enix sale for $40. I played for about 3 hours, mainly flying and blowing stuff up. That's what the majority of the game is. The story is basically nonexistent, and the characters are flat and boring. I didn't really mind this, I had expected as much based on other reviews. The gameplay was very fun, though the movement is a bit diffucult at times with the parachute and wingsuit and grapple all combined. It takes some getting used to.
The campaign is really awful. Four hours in, I'd had 4 or 5 escort missions. Really? Escort missions? After I had completed about 10 missions, I was told that I had to liberate 2 provinces to continue in the story. Why isn't liberating provinces just part of the story in the missions? Great question. It quickly devolved into a repetitive, grinding style game, in which you fly from town to town pulling down billboards and loud speakers. One province typically has 5 or 6 settlements to liberate, and each settlement takes about 10 minutes. That's about an hour per province. After two hours of the same gameplay, I really didn't care about the story anymore.
Then, the game crashed. It had done this once before, at which point I had just restarted and gotten back to it. But this time, my effort to restart was met with a 15 minute loading screen. I didn't take it as a huge deal at the time; the game is very big and has a lot to proccess. Once it loaded, I realized that there was a bigger problem. I was getting about 5 fps, and the entire thing was choppy. I tried to lower my grahpical settings, which took about 5 minutes becuase even the menu was slow and unresponsive. I decided to restart the game, then steam, then my computer. This was to no avail. I tried timing the loading screen to see how long it actually took. I gave up 35 minutes in. The game froze in the loading screen. I've now decided that it simply doesn't work.
Tl;dr: No story, repetitive, grinding gameplay, frame rate drops, crashes, ungodly long load times, and freezing in the loading screen. This steaming pile of garbage in unlpayable.

I find myself torn with King's Quest here. Why? Before I say anything I'd like to preface this entire ramble by saying it's not a BAD game on its own. My frustrations come from how misguided its priorities are and just how intense the entire game is with references and homages to games of old. Much to its own detriment in my opinion when it could've easily done without them.
So let's hop to it. At its core this new title is a so-called “re-imagining” of a venerable point & click adventure series, but it also happens to be stuck in this weird place where it still feels entirely justified to make callbacks to previous events and exists in some mismatched continuity where certain events, as evident from items and people that get name dropped or seen outright, have obviously unfolded but are relegated to sidelines. Time-skipping nature of the game also works against it in this regard as characters and locations come and go without, for the most part, getting enough screen time to really shine on their own. We'll get to it later on in the piece but this structure King's Quest went with, while helping to give the illusion of passage of time needed for a grand epic tale, doesn't hold up in terms of some semblance of consistency. You could blame that on the fact not all episodes are created equal and there was obviously some front-loading going on here to make a good first impression, even though I'd be far more inclined to point the finger at inconsistent storytelling in general.
Let's get some good news here to clear the air of all the negativity first, though – we assume the role of knight-to-be Graham who, and this isn't much of a spoiler, over the course of some chapters goes from a wannabe to being the king of Daventry. Over the course of this journey which takes many many years, and is narrated by elderly Graham to his granddaughter Gwendolyn as the action cuts from his intricate stories to present day when old king is bedridden, we get to assume control in an adventure game crossed with a platformer. Is this good or bad? Depends on your taste, but considering the latter parts are really in no way challenging and are just a way to make the game more appealing to an audience that might fall asleep if they had a close encounter with a proper P&C adventure I think it works against the game in this particular instance. Fortunately, it is the game's wit and characters that largely work in its favor, backed by a decent soundtrack when it has something to tell and isn't just background ambient noise. Characters will come and go as the years run by and depending on your choices, although this is not a Telltale game and King's Quest even takes a few jabs at those, but puzzles themselves never really ascend beyond very basic “everything you need to solve this is never further than couple of rooms away” and later on... well, let's get to it.
Further on game abandons puzzles traditional to the genre aka using X on Y, combine X and Y, etc. in favor of more logical puzzles where you have to work out a tune, riddle or saying and then apply what you learned to figure out the problem. Is this bad? No, and I welcome puzzle variety, but when your ENTIRE FINALE essentially boils down to glorified minesweeper you've ticked me off. In fact, entire last two chapters are puzzle-heavy which suited my taste just fine, but said puzzles are re-used to a point of exhaustion and clearly showed developers ran out of ideas. How many permutations of “follow the line to unlock the door or you die” do you really need?
But really, my biggest problem with the game and why it's getting what it's getting from me is a singular one – I was not invested in the plot. Don't get me wrong, story itself is decent, but without going into spoiler territory that entire deal with the main bad guy, his motivation and entire train of thought felt like an unwarranted escalation that kinda came out of nowhere. Are there chapters missing? Just how much was left on the cutting room floor? I don't know and probably never will. What they really should've focused was more on Graham's personal story and his family because those were honestly the parts that worked much better for me and actually got me emotional towards the end of the game. There is payoff and you grow attached to characters. Even disregarding a lot of re-told of existing events from the series, I mean. Problem is game is split between chapters one through three which end up being Charming Shenanigans: the Game, and chapters four and five where all the DRAMA kicks in just for the sake of drama. Developers have shown they can hold an emotional thread with the Graham and Gwendolyn's interactions, but this thread is so thin and barely there most of the time. Why? I think they took the “last adventure” concept to an extreme and it backfired, with bulk of chapter five really coming off as a sad half-remembered last hoorah.
So... would I recommend it? My answer depends entirely on whether you A) are familiar with King's Quest at large, B) want to see it brought back and C) expect a Telltale game out of this. I won't dope out the multiple choices answer here, but for my taste I'd go with NO and this opinion was sadly heavily influenced by the decline in the last two chapters. I was on-board with all of it early on even with all the heavy-handed callbacks and questionable creative blocks developers found themselves facing.
Game did not hold out for me, but it might for you if all you're looking for is some humor and genuinely touching moments that can trump everything else.

Disclaimer: I've not played any of the other King's Quest games and will be judging this installment entirely on its own.
King's Quest biggest mistake is that you can get the first chapter for free and experience a much better game that ay than if you were to play the full package. It's kind of sad because the story beats are great. Every chapter explains certain parts of King Grahams life like how he became a knight, his search for his true life and his relationship with his family. The story beats make a lot sense with chapter 2 as the only exception which comes off as filler. Unfortunately while the game is capable of tugging on your heartstrings mostly thanks to the great performances such as Christopher Lloyd and the Josh Keaton, the writing itself can be atrocious. The cast is great with very likeable characters and fantastic voicework, but they feel underutilized and/or mishandled. This especially applies to the main villain which is a damn shame because the actor is doing his best, but everything else leaves a lot to be desired. Most of the time his plans make no sense (even for a villain of a point & click game) and you feel like the developers left in some holes they were going to answer later in a next chapter but then forgot to add it in. The game doesn't take the time to fully flesh out the characters and makes a lot of strange decisions when it comes to the storytelling such as awkward timeskips, important developments we don't see happen for ourselves and just weird glaring holes that could have been explained very easily but just weren't.
The gameplay is decent. It has the standard moon logic based puzzles. Though chapter five feels very lazy until the very end, but 1-4 are actually pretty good when it comes to that. I won't really comment on the choices, because that's not the main focus, but I do feel like something is off there. I was trying to go for a compassionate playthrough but ended up with a brute strengh one instead somehow. Eventually I learned there were different triggers to how it works, but I do feel cheated out of the "kindness" playthrough I was going for because of poorly explained setpieces and how the game occasionally railroads you to a certain path if you want to get a better ending. Though all in all, the puzzles are fine. Gameplay gets a pass.
The presentation is also pretty good. The graphics are great minus some awkward facial animations during cutscenes and the music is fantastic. Unfortunately it's the story that brings it down. It has a great start, but the game loses steam very quickly. Chapter 1 is the best one with many memorable characters and moments. It's probably the most varied one too but it loses that edge by the fact that a lot of things are reused in later chapters. 2 is probably my least favourite. It feels the most fillery. The story is brought to a complete halt and there's too much backtracking in boring cave areas and just moronic moral choices. 3 is actually pretty decent because you get to choose your own waifu and love her in your own special way. 4 has a lot of neat ideas but are poorly executed. The introduction to the son character is poorly done and he has the worst dialog in the entire game. The twist is pretty forced too and doesn't make a lick of sense. 5 has the best emotion but as a climax it suffers from having the worst puzzles and challenged. As a showdown between the hero and the main villain, it really fails. There's also an epilogue that you can only acces if you bought the complete edition and not the season pass. Whoever made that decision or enforced the developers to do that needs to be shot into the sun. The epilogue itself however is nothing to write home about and I don't think your choices really affect on how it plays out. oh, did I mention it took forever for these episodes to come out?
So if you want to scratch that moon logic itch, just play chapter 1. It's free and the best thing to come out of this whole thing. Only pick this up if you're very curious as how the rest plays out and if it has a very large discount.
