So I've just acquired 100% of the achievements to the game, and although it was totally unnecessary, I feel I'm qualified to write a review now.
First of all; I started the game and I finished the game with keyboard and mouse. The default keybindings I found pretty terrible to be honest, and the game using Xbox controller key prompts made it all the more frustrating. After having played with a controller and changing the keys to my liking though, I have to say that I couldn't bring myself to go back to the controller.
Dark Souls II has fairly decent graphics, but falls short of triple A releases. It makes up for that with a smooth 60 frames per second which is absolutely vital in a game like this which requires you to patiently learn enemies moves while dodging death by the breadth of a hair. Fortunately you don't need a beast of a PC to run it either, with my average (or below) set up of an AMD Radeon HD 6780 + four gigs of RAM I experienced maybe three or four frame drops through my ten characters.
The game itself is really quite challenging. Casual gamers I'd imagine would have a hell of a time trying to adapt and I'd highly reccommend searching for the hidden attributes in some stats and what they fully affect, while Hardcore gamers will have plenty of room to trip up as well. Don't fret if the game feels too intimidating, failing is a large part of every Souls players first experience, it's the ecstacy in beating the jerk after your tenth try for some sweet revenge and coming back later in the game when you're more experienced to take the time to torture them.
As far as Online Play goes... You'll find a lot of fantastic people willing to engage in jolly cooperation, but keep in mind that there are no rules in the Dark Souls universe, in a broken and decaying Kingdom it's every man for themselves and some people just want to watch the world burn.

So this is some sort of art exhibition. But what is it about?
For visitors searching for an actual game it is rotating the view and clicking things, something happens, rotating the view and clicking things again, something different happens, moving on to the next level, finishing the last level in under one hour.
For visitors searching for an inspiring new experience it is exploring ten minimalistic installations in a wonderful relaxing atmosphere, watching them evolving into surreal dreams of aesthetic perfection, being enchanted by rich colored tints and experimental sounds, by living terminals and dancing suitcases, knowing that something special and magical is going on.
I expected the last level to be a bit more of a climax, the ending was not bad at all but felt slightly underwhelming for me, overall the settings could have gone even more crazy for my tastes. Apart from that I can say that I thoroughly enjoyed ISLANDS: Non-Places and had a very good time with it.

Nothing can eat my time up like a 4x game. The total war series, like Civilation, has been around a long time and what they do well is real time battles with pause, and histoical settings. Total War Rome, was in my opinion one of the top three 4x games of all times. So obviously I was excited for the new Rome. The battles are very similar however after about 4 hours I realized that all my strategies of the past were not going to work. This is a very different game, and it's obvious they took some chances. Many of the early reviews will point out that the changes they went with didnt really work and dissappointed players looking for Total War Rome with better graphics.
The largest disparity is in the city development. No longer can you just max out every building type in every city you own. Cities need to be carefully managed and you need to think globally about wether you want a city that builds infantry, or ships. Doing both with strain your citizens happiness and lead to huge consequences. Better realism? You bet. Frustrating to get the hang of? Absolutely.
Once you do get the hang of these changes there is still a great game here. Just look at it like a brand new entry into the 4x genre and its fine, a solid game that I can recommend to fans of 4x games. The original's just better.

Black Mesa is remastered Half Life 1 - the game which might be the best pc game of the last millenia. After 12 years hard work we can finally play this classic from the beggining to the near end with modern graphics and physics powered by Source Engine.
The game which was started as a mod back in 2004, is a remake in all its glory: it does not only upgreade visuals, but it also remakes the audio of both speak and weapon sounds. Enviroment has also met several changes and areas are larger, wider and much more detailed than in Half Life vanilla. All these enchantments have been done carefully without interfering too much into level design. Especially chapter "Surface Tension" has met various changes and the immersion of catastrophy is well delivered.  This is why I lift Black Mesa above Half Life vanilla - thanks to all succesfull enchantments it has made the storytelling is much more alluring and entertaining. It is not appropriate to forget of giving Valve credit though, because they created hell of a game and Black Mesa respects that legacy.

First off, I'm a huge Alien(s) fan.  Love the movies, games, toys, everything.  However, this game I have a love hate thing going with it.
First, what I love:  The look, the feel, the graphics.  This is all amazing.  I felt like I was right back in 79.  I wanted to adjust the tracking on the loading screens!  The crafting wasn't too bad.  Killing (when you actually GET to kill) was a blast.  Let you be very creative.  I also liked the story though it gets to the point in some places where you go, what next will you throw at me?  And another big draw.  They got the original crew back together!  That's huge.
Now to what I hate: The Alien.  First off and this is the biggest problem I have with the game is... it doesn't work.  The alien DOESN'T!  HAVE!  EYES!!!  Hiding under a friggin' desk or behind a chair is NOT going to work.  It knows where you are.  At all times.  The other problem is that not only does the Alien now see, but it also seems to be nearsighted.  There were many instances where it would just walk right past me as I was standing in a corner.  Standing.  Out in the open.  For all to see.  Now I understand, this is how the game is played, but come on.  A poor sighted Alien is not as faithful as the rest of the game was.  The other thing I hated was that the game does not let you kill the alien but simply drive it off and erase it's short term memory.  Fire will drive it off but not kill it.  No matter how much fire or firepower to bring down on it, it will not die.  Which... makes the Alien dumb in addition to being poor sighted.  So, ok.  Fire hurts it but won't kill it, it needs to come and kill Ripley and the pain will stop.  Things aren't going to change just because it runs away to let it's carapace cool off. The town of Thimbleweed Park is the perfect setting for a gripping story: we have a small population of 80, a murder, two federal agents coming in to investigate said murder, as well as a seemingly ever-present local sheriff who appears quite eager to stick his nose into everyone’s business. The premise appears by-the-book, yet as the plot is untangled, you soon realize that in Thimbleweed Park, not everything is as it seems at first glance...
Thimbleweed Park is a modern representative of a genre that once dominated the game industry. As such, it logically follows that the game itself takes us back to this world – to the world of Ron Gilbert and Gary Winick, all the way back to 1987. In fact, Delores – one of the playable characters – serves as a window into Gilbert’s early career, though not without a healthy dose of self-critical humor.

Thimbleweed Park is an instant classic. It returns to the days of classics like Maniac Mansion and Day of the Tentacle but modernizes the experience with less obtuse puzzles and better visuals.

Provided you can look past ye olde timey papier mache graphics, System Shock 2 still holds up and can still rattle nerves. Whether your taste steers towards patient, psychologically infused torment or ADD addled jump scare-addict mayhem, you'll find plenty to gnaw away at your courage amidst the cyberpunk inspired, body-horror infested hallways of the starship Von Braun. I could laud the wonderfully written, if blandly acted characters whose final moments you pick up from audio files (done properly before this became such a staple horror game cliche); or the flailing grotesqueries that line up with differing, challenging tactics to test your trigger hungry nerves as you calculate how much carefully scavanged ammo a moment's piece is worth. Yet the true value of System Shock 2 comes from it's unrivaled sound design (courtesy of Eric Brosius): Giant spiders hiss like an unravelling nest of cockroaches while cyber-midwives clunk and plod with every agonized step. Shodan, specifically, will find permanent residence in your nightmares as a godhood-seeking mad computer that dreams humanity trapped in unending, surrealist torture to service sadism incarnate. (this will be your one and only ALLY)
The game does have short-commings. I wouldn't bother experimenting with RPG elements and upgrades as many builds will leave you crippled and frustrated. (Find a GameFAQ and just let it plan your build for you) The complex menu screens will be clunky to those not initiated in old-PC game interfaces. Weapon degradation is an uncreative and unnecessary bother you'll have to add to your survivalist anxieties. Oh, and of course, you'll have to properly map the navigation keys if you don't want to rotate clockwise every time you press the right arrow key. Look past this and you'll find even the blocky graphics add to the surrealist aesthetic to one of Ken Levine's most enduring masterpieces.

This review is from the perspective of someone who has played the first Evil Within and its DLC's multiple times.
The first Evil Within, to me, was a game with tremendous potential, but significant issues. The art direction, visual variation and general premise were top notch, but almost every other aspect was half-baked and/or flawed in some way. The story was obtuse and uninteresting; the controls were finicky and at times unresponsive; the graphics and performance were sub par; and the gameplay was marred with random difficulty spikes and annoying sequences. Despite all of this, as a fan of the dying genre of survival horror, I still really enjoyed the first game, and I was excited for the sequel. Now that it is out, the best thing I can say about it is that it improves upon the original in almost every aspect.
The Evil Within 2's story is, like the original, its weakest component. Voice acting is better, but still passable at best and only a few hours after beating the game I'm already having trouble remembering any characters outside of the protagonist, Sebastian, and the two main villains. That said, unlike the first game, the story is much less convoluted this time and actually hits some really strong chords in its final hours that actually made me care about what happened to the characters involved.
Graphics and performance are, also like the original, the game's second weakest aspect. The game undoubtedly looks better than the first, but still struggles to match the visual fidelity of most other modern games. Many textures look very low resolution and pop-in semi-frequently during cutscenes, and while I maintained a steady 60 fps for most of the game on a GTX 1070, the game would occasionally dip below, even when nothing much was happening on screen.
With story and technical performance gripes out of the way, The Evil Within 2 makes significant improvements in the gameplay department. Put simply, the game is a lot more fun to play than the first. The controls, while still off-putting at first, are much tighter and more responsive than before. A large variety of guns are available throughout the game, and they all feel really satisfying to use. The new crafting and upgrade system is more complex than before, but simple enough to understand almost immediately and implemented very well. Stealth is still flawed, but leagues better than the first, and even better when upgraded with some skills from the proper upgrade tree. Enemies are more varied and actually require different tactics to approach certain enemy types or enemy groupings.
The gameplay is most significantly changed by the move to an "open world" design. I put this in quotes because it is far removed from true open world games like Fallout or The Elder Scrolls. Instead, at certain times, the game will drop you in an open area and allow you to explore at your own pace. During these sections you can search for supplies, hunt for new weapons and items, complete side missions, or just continue straight on with the main story line. I was initially skeptical about these sections, but I ended up finding them really cool. They give you more freedom of progression and force you to constantly make fight-or-flight choices when confronted with strong enemies or large groups. In between these sections are linear style levels more in-line with traditional survival horror games. Overall, switching between these two level design styles keeps the game feeling fresh throughout its 15-20 hour run.
When I told people I enjoyed The Evil Within, I always felt like I needed to explain myself. It almost felt like I had to apologize for liking it. With The Evil Within 2, I have no qualms telling people I unapologetically enjoyed the game. It is a marked improvement over the original and a great game in its own right. I would definitely recommend it to all fans of the survival horror genre.

As a huge fan of Its predecessor, this was the first game I was eagerly awaiting all year. I am glad to announce that the sequel has done the game justice and improved on almost every element the first game was criticised for.
You find yourself once again playing bitter old Sebastion Castellanos, set some time after the events of Beakin mental hospital, events quickly transpire throwing him directly back into STEM, the “inception” machine. Your main goal for the entirety of the games duration is to find your lost daughter Lily, However despite the very noticeable story quality improvement personally I still couldn’t get into it.
The Voice acting is very sub-par, Laughable lines of dialogue whilst a dramatic scene in in the works is common place. It’s also hard to be invested in the Daughter when we know not a single thing about her; she was only mentioned very briefly in the original game.
Classic survival horror traits apply here; you will spend a lot of time scavenging, conserving and shooting enemies in the head! Shortly after starting you will be thrown into a semi sandbox town, which has left some players feeling weird. It definitely is a change but a good one at that. It doesn’t wear out its welcome as 60% of the game is still linier chapters. Enemies are much more aggressive this time round and much easier to outnumber you. Gunplay has a strange clunkiness to it; you will find yourself aiming directly at an enemy to only miss an entire clip. However that makes it so much more satisfying when you land that headshot to blow off that zombie’s head!
The Evil Within 2 is a great instalment to the franchise and I personally hope you try it out, In this current video game industry we need all the survival horror single games we can muster!
PS: Big thumbs up for not having any microtransactions!

Evil Within 2 has kept every positive gameplay element from the original while massively improving most everything else. The gameplay, story, graphics, and many other aspects are hugely upgraded from the original. There has even been some open world gameplay added (not to its detriment, surprisingly) that allows for exploration and the ability to familiarize yourself with the world instead of jumping from scenario to scenario as with the previous game. Unfortunately, the quality of life improvements undid some of the gritty charm of the original – if the first one was a low budget horror movie, the sequel is what happened after Hollywood got it and pumped a bunch of cash into it. This isn’t a complaint so much as an observation.
My biggest complaint is that Evil Within 2 happens to not be that scary very often. I know that is totally subjective – but losing some of the clunky controls and difficulty, Evil Within 2 feels a little less nerve wracking than the first. There are higher difficulty settings that emulate the first game’s experience, but it isn’t quite the same.
This is good survival horror. I recommend picking this up.

The Evil Within 2 is a sequel that I can best describe as "good." Not "great" or "amazing" or "jaw dropping" or "omg best game ever." Just "good." The Evil Within 2 is a good game on it's own merits and even a good sequel. However it is marginally worse the the original due to the sheer fact that much of the mystery around the plot is gone. Knowing where you are and what's going on makes everything feel a bit more familiar even if it's still in the depths of somewhere very screwed up.
Much of the gameplay is similar to the point that you're going to find yourself right at home if you remember playing the original. And that's a good thing. The original didn't need too much of an update and the changes here are almost all welcome.
If you enjoyed the original, you're going to enjoy this one as well.

I bought this game during the Sqaure Enix sale for $40. I played for about 3 hours, mainly flying and blowing stuff up. That's what the majority of the game is. The story is basically nonexistent, and the characters are flat and boring. I didn't really mind this, I had expected as much based on other reviews. The gameplay was very fun, though the movement is a bit diffucult at times with the parachute and wingsuit and grapple all combined. It takes some getting used to.
The campaign is really awful. Four hours in, I'd had 4 or 5 escort missions. Really? Escort missions? After I had completed about 10 missions, I was told that I had to liberate 2 provinces to continue in the story. Why isn't liberating provinces just part of the story in the missions? Great question. It quickly devolved into a repetitive, grinding style game, in which you fly from town to town pulling down billboards and loud speakers. One province typically has 5 or 6 settlements to liberate, and each settlement takes about 10 minutes. That's about an hour per province. After two hours of the same gameplay, I really didn't care about the story anymore.
Then, the game crashed. It had done this once before, at which point I had just restarted and gotten back to it. But this time, my effort to restart was met with a 15 minute loading screen. I didn't take it as a huge deal at the time; the game is very big and has a lot to proccess. Once it loaded, I realized that there was a bigger problem. I was getting about 5 fps, and the entire thing was choppy. I tried to lower my grahpical settings, which took about 5 minutes becuase even the menu was slow and unresponsive. I decided to restart the game, then steam, then my computer. This was to no avail. I tried timing the loading screen to see how long it actually took. I gave up 35 minutes in. The game froze in the loading screen. I've now decided that it simply doesn't work.
Tl;dr: No story, repetitive, grinding gameplay, frame rate drops, crashes, ungodly long load times, and freezing in the loading screen. This steaming pile of garbage in unlpayable.

At one point, big game companies cared about their product, because vidya wasn't mainstream at the time, so they had to be quallity to turn any profit.
Unfortunately, that isn't the case anymore, as video games have become a huge part of society, and big game companies are well aware of this fact, and care about money above all else.
Why go through so much effort to produce something great, when you can literally just take a dump on a plate and sell it for just as much?
Fortunately though, every once in a blue moon, you get gems like the Souls series, that shine like a glistening diamond above the rancid pile of arid feces that is most modern games.
Dark Souls 2 brings back a welcome feeling of challenging game-play that is as every bit as rewarding as it is unforgiving. This is not an easy game by any means, and every aspect of your skill as a gamer will be tested to its limits.
The world is beautiful, and brings back a sort of exploration feeling that you would get from games like Ocarina of Time. The level design, while not as good as Dark Souls 1, is still brilliant, with many traps, secrets, and the like. I find something new every time I play through.
The game's story and lore are told in the sense that the game doesn't tell them, but rather, lets the player discover it for himself if he so pleases. The story and theme of the game blends in with the game play on such a deep and creative level, that I can think of no word short of masterpiece to describe it.
Despite its few short-comings, Dark Souls 2 is the closest thing to perfection the gaming community has seen in a very long time, and it serves not only as a giant, much needed middle finger to the craptacular games that dominate the casual scene, but also as a beacon of light to remind real gamers that there is still hope for a creative, challenging, and fun tommorow for gaming.

I was a little dubious about this remake at first but it turns out the The Odd Gentleman handled it really quite well.
Things get off to a rather rocky start in episode 1, as the game at first appears to have stripped itself down to an action platformer. To my relief, this brief section is just a fashback and once the game proper starts, it begins to feel like a proper adventure game. Even then I was still wary, a particular salesman character that is doing a cheap knock off version of Billy Crystal was so grating I ground my teeth every time he appeared on screen. Fortunately the devs seemed to have realised this and after episode 1 he makes much more fleeting appearances, to me relief. After you get to the castle and begin to take part in the tournament, I started to feel much more at home.
I'm not going to go too much into the story, but I will mention that it has a neat framing device, with an elderly king Graham telling the stories of his adventures to his grand daughter, while you actually play the adventures as the young Graham. It works quite well, really helped by a solid performance by Christopher Lloyd as the elderly Graham.
The episodes vary a bit in gameplay style, with the first and second episodes being defintely the most like traditional adventures with lots of inventory based puzzles. Later episodes move more in the direction of recent Telltale games, very cinematic and with great narratives, but the puzzles get a bit on the light side. While this tonal shift is odd, the overall story helps carry things along, and I never at any point felt like not continuing.
Each episode deals with a slightly older Graham and covers a new stage of his life. Episode 1 is starting out, episode 2 is finding his feet as king, episode 3 is finding love.....and so on. It works well, and its nice to see Graham grow both physically and in character. There are a lot of call outs to fans of the original series, from references to characters and scenes from the original game, to some familair music.
This is definitely a reimagining of the old series though and is it's own canon, which might rub purists the wrong way, but I always felt it's heart was in the right place. If you are willing to get on board, the game will both make you laugh and also pull at your heart strings. If you are a long time fan you might even shed a tear or two at the end.
The graphics are quite good and it feels very much like playing an animated film. On the sound front the voice cast does a great job (Barring back alley rent boy Billy Crystal wannabe) and the music is thrilling and melancholy in equal measure, depending on the scene.
Overall I really reccommend this title. It is not without it's rough patches here and there, but given this is the first project of this scale that The Odd Gentlemen have attempted, I'm willing to forgive a few teething problems, and I heartily await the next season.

I spent a sick day playing Suits and I have to say that that sick day was one of the best I've had recently. I was able to complete Suits in about 4 hours, however those 4 hours were quite dense with content. The art style of Suits is akin to OFF, Space Funeral(2 tablets to paradise), and Thank God for the Rain(never completed). The gameplay is like a typical RPGMaker game, so it's not overly complicated in any way. You don't have to grind very much, and if you buy the equipment upgrades every now and again, you'll be fine. There's a handful of silly political missions to be done if you take up the jobs offered by the left and right wings in some areas, but what I found to be the most interesting political aspect of Suits is that the game seems to take a more bipartisan stance (well, okay, there WERE some marxist themes to be fair...) to politics and focuses more on The Guy's process of detangling the grip of an unregulated, dominating corporation(stick it to the man, man.) on Suits City. It seems to paint politics as a side issue to a larger one at hand, rather than weaving a less than subtle political agenda into it.
I found the save feature to be amusing, but would've liked a health/FU/MP restore upon save like other RPGMaker games, but that's not entirely necessary as you can restore your health easily with some disposable income. You can also skip one of the tasks if you take the secret passage in one of the bushes to the left of the W. bank if you want to get into the bank in the Financial district faster.
My favorite songs (in the BGM folder) would have to be WallPuncher, AdvancedSharkness, and PainStation; each were catchy but unique while supplying the game's environment with an almost ambient sense of dread.
Or maybe it's just Marxist overthrow simulator....
Lastly, check out the bushes on top of the office building for a fun little reference, go into the painting, and of course THANK YOU BASED MJ

Short and sweet. Free and worth a price.
Though short in scale and scope, Eternal Senia is a complete joyful experience. It is perfect for when you want to break away from all the high-action, high-adrenaline games of today, and despite the
still get a rewarding experience.
The plot is sweet and simple. There's no complicated politics, nor salvation from mayhem, nor ultimate confrontations with God or Evil. It's just the main protagonist looking to reunite with her missing sister. Easy to grasp, easy to understand,
And it has 3 endings.
The gameplay is full of surprises. At first I expected this game to be turn-based, but no, it is actually real-time. Just as the plot, it is simple to understand and delve into it. If you want to get all of the items in this game, then you must keep in mind all the options you have. Even sometimes backtrack a little.
The soundtrack is where the game falls short, but not by much. The variety may leave something to be desired depending on how harsh you are with a free game, but the few tunes it has are catchy and emotional, full of color where it needs to be.
The graphics are actually really cute and rich for a free game. Here, you won't find sprites that change according to your equipment, but you also won't find recolors of a previously encountered enemy to denote a stronger enemy, other than the mini-bosses.
Speaking of mini-bosses, if you want to call them that, those are the only actual bad point of the game. Simply put, they have no AI, so they don't do much to harm you by themselves. That said, you shouldn't get too cocky with them either, all enemies reflect damage when you deal normal attacks, and these guys hit hard.
The bosses, though, oh man are they fun to fight. This is where the game asks something more of you, and they can actually be a challenge. Still, the game tells you when you're about to fight a boss, so you can choose not to fight it yet if you just don't want to do it.
Overall, the package is very good.

I saw ISLANDS: Non-Places on Steam yesterday, and seeing as how I'm always in the market for a new gaming experience, I thought I would go ahead and grab it, see what it had to offer. I'm glad I did. Initially, my thoughts were that the game looked really cool and was quite bizarre. After playing through it, my first reaction was, "what did I just witness?" Upon further reflection however, I realized that ISLANDS: Non-Places carried an almost intricate and yet surprisingly delicate sense of depth. So, without further ado, let's get to the meat of this game review.
The story in ISLANDS: Non-Places isn't really a story told, but rather a sensibility conveyed. It goes into great detail, both visually and audibly, allowing the player a glimpse at what could lie underneath seemingly mundane places and circumstances. For example, one of the puzzles begins with an idyllic fountain. As you explore underneath the fountain, you start to see all the moving pieces and natural interactions that make the fountain what it is. Not only the mechanics of it, but also the natural interactions of dirt, tree roots, and so on. So, while there isn't an actual story per se, the depth of experience bears witness to a more transcendental, subjective tale. Essentially, it is meant to convey an evocative if brief moment of reflection and introspection
9 out of 10
The gameplay in ISLANDS: Non-Places is simply a means to an end. At its core, ISLANDS: Non-Places is a casual puzzle game. What you realize early on however, is that this is a game about experience rather than challenge. You are simply guiding the game along its chosen path.
This is accomplished by simply clicking on anomalies in the little islands of mundanity provided. These take the form of either flickering lights or moving objects. After clicking on the requisite item or items, it unlocks the next link in the chain of events you are to witness.
Despite its very casual and simplistic nature, the gameplay in ISLANDS: Non-Places is the very definition of perfection for what it has set out to accomplish.Rather than get in the way, it seamlessly guides you through your 45 minute or so journey.
10 out of 10
Graphics in ISLANDS: Non-Places are a featured device for conveying the atmospheric little ecosystems that breathe life into each mundane scenario. This is truly a beautiful game. While functional and minimalist to an extent, the moments that highlight the inner life of simple things like a drink cooler or a cafe patio are both compelling and evocative. You can feel the intricacy of a delicate and sublime, typically unseen other world that helps to create a synchronicity between the visual and audio experience in this game.
8.5 out of 10
It is recommended that you wear a headset when you play ISLANDS: Non-Places so as to get the maximum benefit of the subtleties in sound offered in this game. However, they arent required, and I played through half the game without just be sure of this. Like the graphics, the audio serves to take the player to a world within the world, where, upon witnessing the grandeur of a simple bus stop, you have no choice but to ponder the relevance and meaning of existence beyond what our overt senses tell us. To that effect, the audio in this game is really the star. While always present, it doesn't burden you in any way and really instead helps to create a fully immersive experience.
8.5 out of 10
While ISLANDS: Non-Places wont be a game that everybody appreciates, for those of you who enjoy a more subtle and fulfilling, if short experience, I can easily recommend this game. There are ten little islands of mundanity in this game, but their transcendent nature will keep you thinking about this game long after you finish it. That said, once you finish you can also replay any level you want at any time, and this is something I would actually also recommend as you will find yourself noticing things you may have missed on your first play through.

I consider myself to be a person of few words, so I'll try to keep this short and in small points.
System Shock 2 is the sequel I didn't ask for and I sure as hell didn't want either. The blend of FPS-RPG elements seems haphazard at best and very clunky in implementation. The gameplay doesn't help either. The Dark Engine clearly wasn't meant for head-on combat (as exhibited by the Thief games where combat is mostly avoided) but unfortunately the player is forced to combat enemies all throughout the game. The pacing isn't very good either; I spent four hours just trying to get off the first floor I started on. The story is okay in most areas and I did like the concept of The Many, but the ending literally♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off to no end because it ruined an otherwise satisfying sequence and basically turned the entire game into one big joke. However, the voice acting for characters, the textures, and the sound design was top notch, just like the first game. Now comes the points on why this isn't a very good game and some points on it being good:
- Gameplay is clunky and very bad in some areas (guns constantly breaking in the beginning and the middle section of the game, movement is awful and feels very awkward compared to other games at the time, melee combat is also literally the worst thing I have ever experienced in a game like this; I fail to understand how you could be standing in front of someone and miss with a melee weapon, etc.)
- Skills are often split into seperate skills for absolutely no reason other than to overly-complicate things (Why is maintenance and repair seperate skills? Doesn't it take some maintenance knowledge to be able to repair something and vice versa?)
- Story is alright mostly, but the ending is quite possibly the worst videogame ending I have experienced in quite a long time. (The comedic relief was completely out of place and ruined the whole ending sequence turning the game almost into one big joke.)
- Pacing isn't very good. I spent four to five hours just trying to get off the medical / science (and engineering) deck to be able to explore the rest of the damn ship. After finally getting off those floors, the game started to pick up again but falls flat once again once I reached the Command deck and boarded the Rickenbacker. The Many's flesh home also suffers from being terribly boring and monotonous (kinda like Half-Life's Xen section) and also slightly ridiculous at the same time!
There are some good things about this game however:
- The voice acting is excellent for the time and is top notch just like the voice acting from the first game was.
- The textures are great and the level design is alright, but somewhat monotonous as I managed to get lost a few times.
- The sound design is excellent, nothing more to say.
All in all, this isn't really that great of a game, and I don't understand how this overshadows the first game so much. The first game is superior in literally every way. I might have missed a few things so I might come back and edit this review later.

As a huge fan of Its predecessor, this was the first game I was eagerly awaiting all year. I am glad to announce that the sequel has done the game justice and improved on almost every element the first game was criticised for.
You find yourself once again playing bitter old Sebastion Castellanos, set some time after the events of Beakin mental hospital, events quickly transpire throwing him directly back into STEM, the “inception” machine. Your main goal for the entirety of the games duration is to find your lost daughter Lily, However despite the very noticeable story quality improvement personally I still couldn’t get into it.
The Voice acting is very sub-par, Laughable lines of dialogue whilst a dramatic scene in in the works is common place. It’s also hard to be invested in the Daughter when we know not a single thing about her; she was only mentioned very briefly in the original game.
Classic survival horror traits apply here; you will spend a lot of time scavenging, conserving and shooting enemies in the head! Shortly after starting you will be thrown into a semi sandbox town, which has left some players feeling weird. It definitely is a change but a good one at that. It doesn’t wear out its welcome as 60% of the game is still linier chapters. Enemies are much more aggressive this time round and much easier to outnumber you. Gunplay has a strange clunkiness to it; you will find yourself aiming directly at an enemy to only miss an entire clip. However that makes it so much more satisfying when you land that headshot to blow off that zombie’s head!
The Evil Within 2 is a great instalment to the franchise and I personally hope you try it out, In this current video game industry we need all the survival horror single games we can muster!
PS: Big thumbs up for not having any microtransactions!

Evil Within 2 has kept every positive gameplay element from the original while massively improving most everything else. The gameplay, story, graphics, and many other aspects are hugely upgraded from the original. There has even been some open world gameplay added (not to its detriment, surprisingly) that allows for exploration and the ability to familiarize yourself with the world instead of jumping from scenario to scenario as with the previous game. Unfortunately, the quality of life improvements undid some of the gritty charm of the original – if the first one was a low budget horror movie, the sequel is what happened after Hollywood got it and pumped a bunch of cash into it. This isn’t a complaint so much as an observation.
My biggest complaint is that Evil Within 2 happens to not be that scary very often. I know that is totally subjective – but losing some of the clunky controls and difficulty, Evil Within 2 feels a little less nerve wracking than the first. There are higher difficulty settings that emulate the first game’s experience, but it isn’t quite the same.
This is good survival horror. I recommend picking this up.

I bought this game during the Sqaure Enix sale for $40. I played for about 3 hours, mainly flying and blowing stuff up. That's what the majority of the game is. The story is basically nonexistent, and the characters are flat and boring. I didn't really mind this, I had expected as much based on other reviews. The gameplay was very fun, though the movement is a bit diffucult at times with the parachute and wingsuit and grapple all combined. It takes some getting used to.
The campaign is really awful. Four hours in, I'd had 4 or 5 escort missions. Really? Escort missions? After I had completed about 10 missions, I was told that I had to liberate 2 provinces to continue in the story. Why isn't liberating provinces just part of the story in the missions? Great question. It quickly devolved into a repetitive, grinding style game, in which you fly from town to town pulling down billboards and loud speakers. One province typically has 5 or 6 settlements to liberate, and each settlement takes about 10 minutes. That's about an hour per province. After two hours of the same gameplay, I really didn't care about the story anymore.
Then, the game crashed. It had done this once before, at which point I had just restarted and gotten back to it. But this time, my effort to restart was met with a 15 minute loading screen. I didn't take it as a huge deal at the time; the game is very big and has a lot to proccess. Once it loaded, I realized that there was a bigger problem. I was getting about 5 fps, and the entire thing was choppy. I tried to lower my grahpical settings, which took about 5 minutes becuase even the menu was slow and unresponsive. I decided to restart the game, then steam, then my computer. This was to no avail. I tried timing the loading screen to see how long it actually took. I gave up 35 minutes in. The game froze in the loading screen. I've now decided that it simply doesn't work.
Tl;dr: No story, repetitive, grinding gameplay, frame rate drops, crashes, ungodly long load times, and freezing in the loading screen. This steaming pile of garbage in unlpayable.

9/10. *NOTE: If you're into games where you are ALL POWERFUL and rain bullets on your foes with ease, this game is NOT for you. However, if you like the challenge of being hunted and vulnerable, in a very well put together survival space sim that pays homage to Alien fans like myself, get this. If you wanted to ever know what it felt like to be the lone survivor on a derelict space station, then this game is for you.
+Solid AI: Hiding in the vent doesn't make the Alien forget you. If you accidentally open the vent door and the Alien sees you thru the glass window of another room, it WILL come try to find you. If you manage to close the vent door, and wait 30 seconds for the Alien to go away, it WILL remember you're still in there and crawl in the vent to chop your brains out.
+Excellent Graphics and Performance: PC was running on Ultra for all settings. The animations are smooth and not choppy. The alien and NPC's look pretty good, but also I wish their models looked a bit less generic.
+Atmosphere: Superb sound mechanics. You creep thru the halls hearing the alien move around in the vents. You can hear other NPC's walking up on you around corners, giving you the chance to hide. This game is meant to be played with headphones in the dark (provided your little gamer heart can handle that). All the textures are rich and true to the first Alien and Aliens movie. The devs did this game a justice, because five minutes after I quit the game I'm still on edge...YOU are RIPLEY's daughter in this game and the fear of being vulnerable is what this game is all about.
+Story: It's not the best story for a game I've ever seen. You get tasked with finding this, or going there, etc etc.
+Replayability: I've yet to finish the game, so it wouldn't be fair for me to say anything here. However, I will say that there's a satisfaction in going different routes to get to the same goal.

Let me tell you a story of my biggest fear in the world.
It all started when I was in school, probably 8 or 9. I was a quiet, shy kid who thankfully had a kickass dad. He loved watching grownup things like the X-Files and horror movies, and he let me watch them with him. One fateful day, he let me watch Alien with him. It was a lifechanging experience: I haven't seen such a scary movie before! It was amazing. I had a nightmare about the xenomorph later in the night, I was really terrified of this otherworldly beast.
Anyway, the next day, I went to school, and in those days I was a timid nerd. And like any such nerd, I had a gang of bullies who picked on me. They noticed me in the school hallway, and rightly stuck my sorry, weak♥♥♥♥♥inside a locker they padlocked from the outside before class. It was very dark; I was locked in there for the whole hour! Finally, a janitor heard me crying inside, curled into the fetal position.
Ever since then, I had feared the inside of a locker. As I grew older, I have learned the value of strength. I turned from a timid nerd to a buff jock - yet, my most primal fear loomed over me still, reminding me of my past failures every time I changed my clothes in the gym dressing room. The inside of a locker, so foreboding, so dangerous, so claustrophobic. I had thought this fear would cripple me my whole life.
Then, I played Alien: Isolation. And it made me realize something that eluded me my whole adulthood. The locker is not my enemy. The locker has always cared. It is always there, waiting openly to embrace me when I need it the most. It is everlasting and dependable in ways that make me hold my breath. The locker... is the safest place there is. It is the only friend that won't betray me. It keeps me safe from... well, the things I *should* actually fear.
Thank you, Alien: Isolation. Your ability to give me heart palpitations gave me the clear mind needed to discover the error of my ways. And oh, locker? If you're reading this... I'm sorry I have kept you waiting so long. I know you're there for me; I'm here for you, too.
Hell, these days, I spend more time inside you than inside my girlfriend, anyway.

UPDATE: Other frustrated Steam users have figured out how to solve this problem. To purchase the Complete Collection, we first need to remove the complimentary license for Chapter 1. To do this, follow these steps:
(1) In the Steam client, open the settings window (View->Settings)
(2) Click on Account
(3) Click on View Account Details
(4) Click on View licenses and product key activations
(a) You should see a list of items. One of the lines should be "King's Quest - Chapter 1: A Knight to Remember.....Remove....Complimentary"
(b) Click on "Remove"
(c) It will ask if you are sure. Click "OK".
Now the store page should no longer say that you already own this game. You will then be able to add the Complete Collection to your cart and purchase it for yourself.
As for the game itself, Chapter 1 was fun and I expect the Complete Collection will be worth the 50% off price. Still, I'm going to leave my recommendation at "No" just because of these stupid problems. You can blame Steam if you want, but it's only an issue because Sierra didn't include the epilogue in the Season Pass.

Chapter 1 - 4/5 ; I've played this chapter so many times that it's physically painful, but in the best way possible. It's only a 4 because of the lack of skips for cut scenes and talking. The music is beautiful, as is the art, and the characters are so amazing. I love them all, my dude.

Chapter 3 - 5/5 ; GIRL IN THE TOWEEEEEEEEEERRRR -- okay, sorry. This chapter is pretty amazing. I adore it. The new characters introduced are both so charming and lovable. The music, by far, is my favorite part of the chapter, though. I want the soundtrack for it real bad.

Some parts were fairly nonsensical, mirroring something that happens at the beginning of Chapter 3 that didn't make sense either. However, this chapter was the chapter to make me cry during my first playthrough of it. So, that's a plus.
Epilogue - 4/5 ; I WISH IT HAD BEEN LONGER. I was an idiot and spent too much time on this, ngl. But ultimately, it was pretty good.

Where to start with this game? I wanted to like this game, the artstyle and surreal atmosphere/setting drew me in, having thoroughly enjoyed titles such as undertale and LISA, I imaged I was in for a similar ride. Unfortunately this was not so, this game was generally not very enjoyable, simply due to how it was executed. I'll start off with what I liked first though.
If you don't want to read a wall of text, skip to the conclusion at the bottom
The artstyle is, very very interesting, it is something that has drawn alot of people in, it gives the game a unique feel, and enemy sprites were generally interesting to look at, surreal, pen drawn abominations in suits and political cartoons. Secondly, the music is another striking feature of this game. Like the art style, it is very atmospheric, and just fits very well with the setting of the game. There isn't loads of music, but there isn't a lack of it either. Another "strong" point of the game is the humour. I have mixed feelings about the humour, I did chuckle at the various references to modern politics and some puns did make me laugh, but at times the humour felt very forced, or just, didn't make any sense. Lastly, there is Jerome. Jerome is good.
Now, onto the negative aspects, the first main issue is combat. Combat is extremely simplistic, you only ever have two party members (apparently there is a third somewhere?) with an incredibly simplistic and limited range of abilities. Fights mainly consist of stocking up on sandwichs, and just attacking enemies in a war of endurance. Sandwichs get you through this game, not any strategy. Random encounters are also extremely common and frequent. Secondly, there is plot, the game's plot is apparently a business man's descent into corruption.
. Everything about the plot is dull, forced and just badly executed. Another strong negative point is the writing in general, again, everything is just forced. Some jokes, as stated did make me laugh, but there's alot of dialogue that, seemed to be a joke, but just wasn't funny. The last thing, is that, it just doesn't feel like there's any point to the game, it's wasted potential. This game is very quirky in some ways, with it's artstyle, curious setting and the fact that all plants have female names. There is potential here to make a really damn good and unique RPG. But this game fails to say anything about politics other than "Corporations are bad!" or really make you feel anything. The plot is just a series of events that happen.
Oh, one very last point, Jerome should say more, you don't hear a peep from him after he becomes a party member, he could've been a great comic relief character.
In conclusion
Great artstyle
Unique music
Interesting setting
Jerome
Humour covers a diverse range of topics, seems to be based more on personal tastes
Extremely cheap
Extremely Monotonous gameplay
Humour and writing seems forced at times
Plot doesn't make any sense, just a sequence of events
Poor execution in general, wasted potential
Not enough Jerome
As a final point, other people seemed to have liked this game alot more, so it is quite possible you'll enjoy it more than me, plus the price is extremely low.

, but TL;DR: Buy this! You will not regret it.

-Fantastic Dialog/Voice Acting
-Smooth Interface/Controls (plus excellerated movement options!)
-Plenty of mature humor, and tongue-in-cheek references to Pop Culture
-References to previous Gilbert/Winnick games!
-Satisfying puzzles that are challenging without being infuriating or obtuse
-A clever cast of intriguing characters
-Snarky banter, ghost shenanigans, and a murder mystery
-It's like being back in 1990, playing Maniac Mansion, but better, modern, and polished
Cons:
-I want more, please give us more, make another game! (Not that this one is "Short" by any means!)
-I cannot come up with more cons.

A beautiful looking world of death and ancient creatures. To those not familiar with the first Dark Souls or Demon Souls; Dark Souls is a game that doesn't coddle you. It doesn't prevent you from falling off edges, it doesn't save you from dieing, it doesn't reward your mistakes and in fact punishes you for it by lowering your health (unless you consume an item). There is no explicit difficulty option but you can make it easier by summoning other players to help or make it much harder by increasing the difficulty of the area, joining a certain covenant, and striking out alone. I would say most gamers either love the dark souls series or hate it.
There is a lot of story and lore to the game but it's not presented at it's surface, you have to find it by looking at item descriptions and talking to npc's. The multiplayer can make a lot of things easier by summoning others to help you get through areas and boss battles. It can also make it harder when you get invaded but that is pretty infrequent and it is pretty satisfying to kill an invader. If you want to play with friends I don't recommend trying. The system is set up to rely on the random help of others in this lost and lonely place.
If you want a game that can challenge you to the limit and/or like dungeon crawling then yes it completly worth it. If you're easily frusterated, want to play with friends, more into casual gaming, I would probably pass on this.
But what does it matter? You're going to die in Dark Souls anyway, Keh, heh, heh, heh, heh, heh...

This is the Alien game you have been waiting for!
For once the Xenomorph is given proper respects as the unstoppable killing machine it is designed to be. You really feel powerless and hopeless in this game, and when that Alien pops out at you and there isn’t a damned thing you can do about it, it will make you panic and feel defeated. I really enjoyed going after mission objectives while playing cat and mouse with the Xeno, and trying to out think it. There are more dangers you will face during your time on Sevastopol Station like malfunctioning androids, and stranded colonists that have lost their minds to fear. The station itself is almost a villain in this game as it dark corridors and dim lighted areas will play tricks on your mind. I can’t tell you how many times I thought the Xeno was after me just to be relieved it was some pipes and boxes. Another thing I like in this game is the crafting system and making use of what small of tools you can use to get yourself out of situations, and of course we cannot forget our dumbed down motion tracker that does not work as well as the ones the Marines have in Aliens but next to using your ears, it’s about the only way to know if you are being hunted.
I don’t normally like survival horror games, and I might be biased as I am an Alien fanboy, but this game is a must play, and I would recommend it to anybody. That does not mean it is a perfect game by any stretch. The one fatal flaw of this game is that it is absolutely frustrating at times. I actually have yet to finish it as I am stuck about 60% through the game, and my desire to go on any longer has faded. For one this is 2015… Why the hell do we have such an ancient save system? I understand the save system was to ramp up the difficulty but that should be a choice of players not a developers. They could have implemented a “hardcore” mode that disabled auto saving and what not. It is absolutely just painful to lose so much progress because of a death, for myself that is almost a deal breaker as it just sucks the fun out of the game. Auto saves please! Hopefully somebody will mod it, until then I am not sure if I will go back, it is just too frustrating.
Flaws aside though, this game was a massive leap forward for Alien franchise games. The atmosphere of the game is the real winner here, the lighting is perfect, fire effects are perfect. It really just looks amazing. Also don’t forget to look out the windows of the space station, the view is amazing! I applaud the Creative Assembly team for a job well done. Hopefully this leads to something greater!

Alien:Isolation has masterful art direction, superb visuals and atmospherics, and well executed music. It also has some of the best voice and character animation I've ever seen in a game set in the Alien universe. In short, as far as immersing itself in an established franchise, it is by far one of the absolute best games ever made. It in many ways perfectly captures the feel and look of the original movie. It leans heavily, and successfully, on cues from the movie. It comes very close to breaching the barrier between video games and art

LATER EDIT: After the developer response concerning the "full bright mode" I simply reinstalled the game. Launched directly into “surface tension” and there is a HUGE difference on the visuals. I might even start it all over again and see what I missed. It’s still not the eye candy you’d expect in 2016 but this feels miles apart from what I found on my first run. I still have issues with this game, it’s not loyal enough to the original to be considered “redux” and yet too close to the original for me to take it as a sort of fan-made-extended-version of the great Halflife. But as the visual part (or lack thereof) weighted a lot in my initial dissatisfaction I think it’s fair to switch my recommendation.
ORIGINAL REVIEW: This is a free mod turned commercial and after playing it I unfortunately must say it shows a lot of shortcomings.
The visuals are not that great. What am I talking about, they are not good at all! I was expecting something closer to Halflife 2, but I got nothing better than Halflife Source with some mods. A shocker, right? It looks tired and old. When you get to the exterior scenes things improves a bit but not enough. I can only hope Xen, being exterior and also alien looking, would turn up good enough to save the best for last. After all Xen was the letdown of the original, so there is nowhere to go but up. Right?
Choices have been made, too many of them bad. Rooms (and maps) tend to be bigger and more complex, that’s the whole thing with Black Mesa. Complexity is achieved usually by interlocking what were different areas before in single areas with multiple layers, usually. Bigger is achieved by making things… big. Bigger is bad when it feels empty though. The Initial train ride on the credit roll felt amazing back in the day when I first ran Halflife. It was meant to be a showcase for skeletal animation and the graphical capabilities of the day, a promise for what awaits you further in. It was. Now it’s just a tired delayed start for the game, clearly subpar even for the average Black Mesa delivers. Bigger is not better if you can’t fill it with purpose and logical industrial design.
After the look warm start the first thing I did is try to open the first door on the right. What a shock I had when I discovered that not only it was locked (waaaaay too many locked doors all over the place are a blight in this mod) but it became apparent that I was looking directly at the keyhole of the lock. So Freeman is in fact a midget in this game, looking up at everything.
Halflife games are essentially linear cinematic experiences. Black Mesa has a lot of doors (at first locked) that you can open from the other side… for no purpose whatsoever. Sometimes it felt like a maze. Unrewarding experience.
There were good choices too. For example I never cared for the train ride mini maze in the original. In this the train is exactly what is supposed to be: a vehicle to advance you forwards, no need to worry about getting left or right. Also the dismissal of the second coming of the tentacle monster that you kill first in the blast pit I think is a correct decision. Recycling bosses is always a bad thing.
So, I hope we’ll see Xen soon enough and it will be good, allowing this mod to go out with a bang. So far paying 20 bucks for this feels like exploiting the kindness (or wekness) of the original’s fans.

I've been waiting for over four years to get Xen, since the release of the original free mod, and then they announce that I'm going to have to wait almost a whole 'nother year to get it. Seriously guys, what have you been doing these past few years, I know these people have lives, but this is their only game, the least they could do is finish the damn thing. If Xen is worth the wait then I will give a positive review.
Edit: Now is as good of a time as any to come back and edit my review, Xen was just pushed back to December of this year, and with that makes me even more worried for the end result of a project I have been following for years. Normally when a game is delayed I don't mind, since it usually means that the developers are making some much needed improvments to their game, but when an indie company delays a game/game feature, AND fails to update their audience for half a year, AND tells them about the delay WHEN THE INNITIAL RELEASE WAS ADVERTISED, it leads me to believe that all Xen will ever be is the No Man's Sky of Black Mesa. It pains me to see a game with so much potential failing to deliver on the one feature that I bought the game for, the one feature that seperated it from the FREE mod, and even try telling me that the multiplayer was also something they added, multiplayer has basically been dead since day one. At this point I don't even know if releasing Xen could ever change my opinion on this game, after two years of waiting it's impossible to make it worth the wait, unless this area adds something like an extra 30 hours of content, or are the greatest game levels ever developed, so much so that they make even the greatest games ever made look like f-ing Shaq Fu. All in all, if I could get a refund I would, then I would buy the game again when it went on sale for somewhere around 5$, and enjoy it in it's entirety, but because I can't I just look back and think about that one time I was robbed of my money by and indie dev, then I stop thinking about Hello Games and remember Black Mesa, I think about how good it was when I first played it, and I remember how good it was when I played the Steam release, but then I remember all the anger of waiting two years for the finished product and then being told I have to wait about another 6 months, and that is how I will always remember Black Mesa, whether its two years from now or ten, all the possible good memories of playing this game have been forgotten by time due to all of my waiting and anguish. I wish the best of everyone at the Crowbar Collective, and how the next six months are productive, and I wish you a lot of luck for your new December release date, since if you don't reach it, I won't be the only one with a negative outlook on Black Mesa.
Edit #2: It got delayed AGAIN, my level of dissapointment is through the roof right now, and here I thought I might finally be able to delete this review.

Devs replied very fast with a fix to the game breaking bug I encountered and I was able to play again
In chapter 3, upon death a bug causes all AI to be disabled, stopping any progress since they cant open doors for you. Its noticable by having text appear on screen that says "A.I. Disab"
The devs gave me a temporary fix and it seems to be working, though I had to slightly alter their instructions
*First enable the developer console. This is found on the main menu, under options>keyboard>advanced>enable developer console.
*Load save file, the ai should still be disabled.
*Press the ` (tilde) key to enable the console, and type
map bm_c1a1a
(this will reload the current map, and for me removed "A.I. Disab")
*Now type
sv_cheats 1
ai_norebuildgraph 1
ai_disable 1 (NOT 0, as the devs said, as this turns "A.I. Disab" back on!)
*If that doesnt work (even though it did for me) just try retyping ai_disable with either 1 or 0 till the words "A.I. Disab" are cleared from the screen
Now upon death the bug no longer triggers!

TL;DR: A decent RPGMaker game with a fairly unique art style and aesthetic. Nothing outstanding about it, but the low price point and short play time means it doesn't overstay its welcome.
The first point of comparison to this game comes easily to OFF, an RPGMaker game made with a similar aesthetic style. The comparisons are really only skin deep though, as the game itself is much shallower than its inspiration. While the inspiration for this game is freely available and this costs about a dollar, it doesn't mean you should pass this up entirely.
It is clear that this is not a work of laziness at all. The art style is consistent and the enemies encountered tend to be fairly unique, with the exceptions of random encounter areas and a few repeated enemies. The sprites and hand drawn works fit well together, and nothing looks jarringly out of place. The only offense art wise is that practically all encounters start by talking to a generic looking suited dude, who turns out to be something far more interesting in the combat screen. Some of them could have used unique sprites, but that is a small complaint.
Game-play is bog standard. You start with one character, and can acquire two more through a bit of exploration. Notably, the first party member is easily missed if you don't take the time to get him, and he can be lost forever, just like the second one. If the game suffers anywhere, it is that the game is exceedingly easy if you have a remote skill at RPGs. Every encounter, boss or not, can be solved by a combination of the second characters staple ability to paralyze them, and then wailing on them till it needs repeating. Some healing might be required, but the game doles out cash and healing/recovery items quite often. Any more complex strategies are not needed, and there are no elements or weaknesses to worry about, and very few buffs get used outside boss self-buffs or debuffs. No grinding is really necessary, but the game could have used some variety in the challenge, as there is really nothing to differentiate bosses from each other, other than attack animations and some spikes in damage.
The story is clearly trying to style itself after OFF, with that weird world-vibe, dystopian appeal, and twisted characters in battle. The main way it falters is that the game really doesn't build on the world at all. OFF has characters telling tales to you as you go through the areas, and its clear the place has a mythology. This game attempts that, but so much of its writing is spent telling one-off pop culture jokes and references that any potential world building is lost. Half of your encounters are jokes or references to something, when the game time could have been spent building the world. Where OFF tells a story of a world where everything is, well, off, this game tells a story about a world where everything is a reference that will become dated in time, with a vague plot about huge faceless corporations and drones beneath.
In summary, the game is short, cheap, and doesn't overstay its welcome. It hints at a sequel, and it would be nice if they built on what they have to be more than pop-culture references, but that is not in this game. Buy it, play it for four hours or so to fully complete it, and decide for yourself if you want to give the developers a chance to further develop it.

I love this game so far, and it is totally worth the $60. I haven't played too many mmorpgs before this game, and that was because of one thing. The class system. Most mmos have a class system that restricts your skills, weapons, and armor, and I find it to be ridiculous because you can't choose how you play. In Elder Scrolls Online, there is a class system, yes, but unlike all other mmos I've seen, you have full control over your path. There are specific skills only a certain class may have, which makes sense, but there are plenty of other skills you get, regardless of your class. You decide the armor style you use, light, medium, or heavy, and you choose your own weapons. You can even craft your own! Also, the combat system works smoothly, there are plenty of quests to complete (I haven't scratched the surface), and a huge map to explore! I say don't even hesitate in buying this game.

Thimbleweed Park is about as on the nose as video games get.  It has a retro style akin more to Maniac Mansion than Monkey Island, great music in parts with middling music in others but the voice acting for some characters seems out of place or reused, not counting the character for which this is obviously intentional.  Overall it is an excellent throwback to the point and click games from the LucasArts era that any current or nostalgic fan will really enjoy, though folks who have never played those older games might miss some of the references and jokes.  But even up to the very end, Ron Gilbert keeps his sense of humour all the way down to the price.  To quote Guybrush Threepwood from Monkey Island, never pay more than 20 bucks for a computer game.

Do you enjoy old-school zombies? Old-school gameplay? Not paying for games? Then No More Room in Hell (NMRiH) is the game for you! NMRiH is not designed for solo-play, so keep this in mind when starting-out.
NMRiH is not going to hold your hand, as it punishes you for the mistakes you make. There are no tutorials available, so you're required to figure-out most of its intricacies on your own. This, of course, will discourage those that are looking for a relaxed experience. If you can't accept the fact that you can't adjust the game's difficulty, or your health does not regenerate over time, or there's no checkpoints, or that even a common foe can inflict an immense amount of damage to you (along with nasty status effects like bleeding or infection), then you will not like this game. However, the game's difficulty is balanced-out by how stupid the zombies are (they're zombies).
Unless you're aiming for the head, you're not going to take-out the "shamblers" very easily, especially if they're wearing armour. However, the "runners", "crawlers", and "children" have relatively low health, but this does not rule them out as threats! Yes, you can kill children, but remember that they're not real! Okay, that's rather insensitive of me, but remember that they're... not human? Just try it out for yourself and see if you can stomach it.
NMRiH has two game modes: "objective" and "survival", with maps designed for both. In objective maps, the player's goal is to navigate from the start (point A) to some sort of rescue area (point B) while dealing with zombie and environmental threats along the way. Weapons, recovery items, and ammunition are spread throughout the map, with some maps being a little more stingy with supplies than others. In survival maps, the player must defend a position and its "zones" while waiting for rescue to arrive, protecting said zones from 9-10 waves of zombies. The zones will become damaged when zombies enter them if no players are present, but can be repaired by dropping FEMA bags in them. I feel that both game modes are handled relatively well and are different enough from one another to keep the NMRiH experience fresh enough.
The first thing you'll notice when you start playing is your lack of HUD (heads-up display). NMRiH will only alert you of your changing condition through auditory and/or visual cues, such as your screen's colours becoming less saturated (closer to black-and-white) when you're lower on health; a brief splash of blood around your screen's edges every couple of seconds when you're bleeding; damage arrows appearing when you're being hit/burning; some grisley veins along with darkness appearing over time when you're infected; and the sound of your heart racing/the lowering of your melee weapon when you're low/out of stamina. I believe this minimalistic approach provides substantial "atmosphere", but it sometimes causes more problems than it's worth, especially regarding current health levels.
By-far the most important thing to keep an eye on is your character's "stamina". Stamina, unlike health, DOES regenerate over time, but only if you're not doing anything that requires it. Stamina is required for jumping, sprinting, and swinging (but not throwing) melee weaponry. Jumping is necessary for navigating certain obstacles or eluding pesky zombies, but it normally costs much more stamina than it's worth. Sprinting allows you to zip through a mob of zombies with relative ease, but drains stamina quickly. Unlike other games that have a form of stamina, I feel that NMRiH's interpretation is the most realistic, and, if not managed properly, the most punishing.
There are two status effects in NMRiH: Bleeding and infection. Bleeding makes the player take 1% health damage every couple of seconds and disables sprinting, and infection will kill the player after a few minutes and turn them into a runner. Both status effects offer varying degrees of deadliess, with infection being by-far the worst, but the player can find recovery items to keep them at bay. Bleeding is normally a non-issue unless an objective is very time-sensitive, and I honestly wish it dealt more damage than it currently does. The player can also burn, but it only applies if the player is standing in fire. Burning deals varying damage depending on the source.
The most-important survival tool in the game is "shoving". Shoving interrupts a zombie and makes them stumble backwards no matter what they're doing. This means that you can get a shove in and interrupt a rather deadly attack. Shoving is also instantaneous, which means you can execute a shove no matter what you're doing. There isn't enough health to go around a lot of the time, especially during the objective maps, so shoving is a necessity. I feel that shoving should cost at least a small amount of stamina because, if you shove when you need to, you can easily take no damage through entire sections of maps (or sometimes a whole map). However, you can't shove when drained of stamina!
Melee weapons each cost different amounts of stamina per swing, and the amount increases exponentially if you strike multiple targets at the same time. If you hold left-click down with a melee weapon, the weapon will begin to "charge", increasing damage until it reaches a set maximum. Charging will cost a bit more stamina, but the damage increase is noticable for most weapons, and the time required is longer the weaker a weapon is.
Guns are plentiful, just like melee weapons. There are pistols, shotguns, SMGs, assault rifles, sniper rifles... the only problem with there being so many types is the large assortment of ammunition. Sure, a lot of guns share ammo types, but you usually won't find as much ammunition as you're comfortable with (especially if you're a newbie), so it's a good idea to carry a melee weapon as a back-up.
One problem with NMRiH is its lack of weapon balance: there are plenty of weapons that are almost pointless to use in comparison to others. For example, the Colt 1911 (a pistol) kills in one headshot at the cost of slightly-lower accuracy and a small magazine, while the Beretta M92FS (another pistol) has double the clipsize, but requires two headshots (unless pot-shotting). In almost all cases, the Colt 1911 is the best choice, as being able to immediately one-shot a zombie is invaluable. There are similiar issues with melee, such as the crowbar/hatchet out-classing every other melee weapon.
Another problem with the game itself is enemy pathing. A lot of zombies, especially runners and children, have difficulties navigating around or over certain obstactles, and will often run back and forth between two spots with awkward timing, making them very unpredictable in nature. This is mostly an annoyance, but can be a rather large problem when there are more than a couple suffering from this very issue, especially when there are a group of children (as they are smaller and require more precise aiming than other zombie types). You'll most-likely survive such encounters, but usually not unscathed.
Recently, a new difficulty setting called "Nightmare" was added to the game. Unfortunately, it's limited to increasing zombie health and chance to get infected, with some additional minute modifications. This hurts melee weapons as charging is required for reaching maximum damage, something that gun users don't need to do.
Playing online can be fun, but, like any other online game, you WILL encounter disrespectful and immature players. Also, there are plenty of modded servers, such as those with "unlimited spawns" or "unlimited ammo/items", which takes away a lot of the game's intended challenge and immersion.  :'(
Overall, I fully recommend NMRiH if you enjoy an in-depth zombie experience. While the combat is engaging and satisfying, some balance is needed. I also want more maps and game modes to play! I'd even pay!
