Let me start off with a small history lesson: I have seen the first Alien movie in 2002 or so, and I really liked it. Coincidentally, this was one year after I got my first gaming computer and was actually getting into videogames in a big way. The first thing I thought was "This would make for an amazing videogame!"
But a shining beacon of hope appeared in the distance as I have discovered that there indeed is a game which is considered good from Alien universe (sort of), Aliens vs Predator by Rebellion. So I got that. And while it was scary enough as a Marine, Alien wasn't this constant, ever present threat which was to be feared - Aliens were just common monsters, which would give you a scare, but weren't really all that difficult to defeat. I liked the game, sure, but something just wasn't quite there. It reminded me of the second movie far more than it did of the first, and the fact that I seemed to move at warp speed didn't help either. Since then, two more Aliens vs Predator games got released, and shortly after those, Aliens: Colonial Marines came out. And finally, 12 years in which I have revisited the original movie a few times and every time hoped for a proper Alien game to exist, one came out. And it is nearly all I hoped it would be.
Alien: Isolation throws everything you would traditionally do when returning to a movie that old out of the window and executes everything with a beautiful attention to detail, replicating everything from visual design, sounds of the original, music, hell, the game even got the original cast of the fist movie on board to do voice acting. The game doesn't try to modernize, it doesn't try to make the game 'more believable' for a 21st century consumer - nah, it just says ♥♥♥♥ that, converts everything we could see in the original movie into in-game assets and ends up being that much more thrilling, nostalgic and believable for it. It's a game made by fans of the movie, for fans of the movie, a huge love letter to everything the original is.
I could probably start talking about the game tho, right? Yeah, I should do that. So, you're playing as Amanda Ripley, daughter of Ellen Ripley. Ellen Ripley has been considered lost for 15 years, and Amanda has been informed about black box of Nostromo finding its way to Sevastopol space station. Soon after arriving on station, she finds that everything has gone to hell, surviving people are fighting for remaining resources, androids kill on sight for trespassing, and on top of that, there is talk of some creature murdering people.
The game is mostly a stealth-based survival horror, with very few tools to defend yourself with (and while you get more of those as you progress trough the game, you very rarely get to have enough ammo), so you're left to a motion tracker and your wit to stay alive. The game gives you many tools for distracting your enemies, be it humans, androids or the Alien. You can craft items, some of which can cause direct damage, others which can serve to distract. Some levels have conveniently placed 'rewire boxes', which allow you to turn off cameras, open doors or cause distractions in various parts of a level. You can hide in lockers, vents or just low spaces like under desks or beds. These elements, and parts of the game where you need to get around humanoid opponents, mostly reminded me of games similar to Outlast or Amnesia. Individual areas tend to be open enough to allow for a decent amount of ways to get around various obstacles, and the level design itself is quite beautiful, varied and clever to keep you interested. All in all, when you're up against more traditional threats, Alien: Isolation is a good stealth game, and a decent shooter in the rare occassions you choose to approach it that way. When you explore the station, it also very rarely happens that you'd get locked out of a section of it, and so you can go back to most places you've already been - and there's even a reason to do so as more equipment you gain will open up more secret areas for you.
However, all of this changes after the Alien makes its first appearance. Suddenly, you're not just worrying about the traditional opponents. There's always the threat of the Alien, lurking above you, making its way trough ventilation ducts of the entire station. If you run too fast - you may attract the Alien. If you hit a wall with your maintenance jack, it might distract your opponents, but it might also attract the Alien. If you fire your gun, you don't just fire your gun - you may attract the Alien. (that also applies to human opposition tho - while the Alien ignores androids, when someone shoots at you and the Alien is nearby, it will jump out of airduct and start working its way trough any human it sees. Including you of course.)
The creature's AI is good enough to differenciate it from all other opponents, to make it a constant threat and to make you nervous about it, as you see a green dot on your movement tracker, circling around you somewhere above. Those are the calm bits of the game tho - when it emerges and you can see it, everything gets a lot worse as, most of the time, it only takes the Alien to notice you once for you to pretty much instantly die. Oh, and it can kill you from the vents if you miss the dribbling ooze or are foolish enough to take a look what exactly is it dribbling from. All of these aspects are frustrating, yes, along with the fact that the Alien is a lot more perceptive than the other opponents, you are going to die a lot and the only way to save your game is at fixed save stations (which are placed fairly close to each other so it's not that bad), but all of this successfully leads to one end - not cheapening the creature. Alien is terrifying, it's constantly there, stalking you, trying to pinpoint your exact location and to kill you. You'll feel that most of encounters with it are close, and that you are always one wrong step from dying. While it is, in reality, a lot more forgiving than that, the feeling of paranoia is always there, scratching at the back of your head.
All of this is backed up by a decent storyline and solid writing, with fantastic music, graphic and sound design. While some bits of the game feel a bit padded, it generally manages to make you feel like its always quite fresh (I don't want to spoil anything so I'm not going to reveal how exactly), and while the game is quite long, it feels captivating enough to make me finish it. The game takes good care to pace itself properly - the first time you even get to see the alien is about 1,5 hours into it
All in all, Alien: Isolation is the best survival horror game I have played in a very long time, possibly since Dead Space, and this time, it places emphasis on the 'survival' bit. It's beautifully put together, very well crafted and it's such an innovative gaming experience that I'm pondering on making it my GOTY of 2014. Well worth your money, well worth playing.

In a world of mostly bad Alien games, Alien: Isolation is easily the best one of them ever made.  This is not a FPS or RPG, but rather a stealth/survival horror game.  Whether or not those gameplay mechanics are fun is entirely up to you.
The game has stunning level design, archetecture, and overall look and feel.  It replicates the first Alien movie's environment in sound, music, and visual style perfectly.  Never before did I ever feel like I was literally walking through a living version of one of the movies. All the technology in the game is the same 1970s "vision of the future" from the films as well, and is appropriately clicky, glitchy, bulky, boxy, and otherwise primitive. The Alien creature itself feels, acts, and moves as if it were a real living thing, its AI being one of the most realistic ever in a game.
That all being said, several things about the gameplay annoy me to no end:
1.  The controls are very clunky.  Your character almost moves as if in slow motion, and the camera sway is sort of nauseating.  You scroll through the weapons with the mouse wheel (as typically done these days) but the other items (medkit, pipe bomb, etc) are done with an ingame "wheel" that is very odd to operate.  I often found myself going into the "crafting mode" when I was actually trying to select one the few weapons available, usually when a Working Joe was sneaking up to throttle the living crap out of me.
2.  It's not an FPS game and cannot be approached as if it were one.  The weapons provided in the game pretty much do jack sh!t and are useless overall.  While I never expected Colonial Marines type of play, there should have been better ways to deal with enemies.  For example - Working Joes:  How about being able to trip them and then smash their head in with a wrench or something?  And why can't I hear their foot steps?  Are they programmed for stealth walking by default?  Why isn't there a control on one of the terminals to shut down all the WJs on that level?
3.  There are times when you get stuck in an animation of doing something (i.e., typing on a terminal, opening up a welding tool, etc) and it puts you at complete risk of being discovered or killed.  Naysayers will argue this is part of the experience, but if we are truly going for realism here, then a person attempting to do these things in real life would simply stop what they are doing (if they value their life) and go back to hiding, etc.
4.  There are times when I swear the Working Joes or the Alien are looking right at me and they do nothing, then other times when I sneak past them and somehow they either spot me and/or come out of nowhere and maul me.  Does that make for "realistic" or sh!t gameplay?  You decide.
5.  It's not a fast moving game by any stretch.  While the length is completely subjective based on your skill, etc it just goes on way too long for my liking regardless. For all of the work spent of the game environments, it all boils down to fetch quests/switch flipping/locate a key type of play, which gets horribly repetitive after a while.  If you are not a patient player, this game will probably test your patience.  It certainly tested mine, especially toward the end.
6.  If you've seen the movies, you will be able to guess much (though possibly not all) of what happens in the game.
Bottom Line:
Though it's the most well done Alien game to date, I really don't enjoy all the sneaking around and not having more gameplay options to deal with enemies.  After getting mauled by the Alien so many times, the horror is completely lost to what becomes horribly repetitive and boring gameplay.
Considering the first Alien movie is one of my favorites of all time, I think that's a shame really. I've played it thru completely just once, having retried several times since only to uninstal it and move onto something else.
At the end of the day, it's just not fun...Not for me, at least.

Devs replied very fast with a fix to the game breaking bug I encountered and I was able to play again
In chapter 3, upon death a bug causes all AI to be disabled, stopping any progress since they cant open doors for you. Its noticable by having text appear on screen that says "A.I. Disab"
The devs gave me a temporary fix and it seems to be working, though I had to slightly alter their instructions
*First enable the developer console. This is found on the main menu, under options>keyboard>advanced>enable developer console.
*Load save file, the ai should still be disabled.
*Press the ` (tilde) key to enable the console, and type
map bm_c1a1a
(this will reload the current map, and for me removed "A.I. Disab")
*Now type
sv_cheats 1
ai_norebuildgraph 1
ai_disable 1 (NOT 0, as the devs said, as this turns "A.I. Disab" back on!)
*If that doesnt work (even though it did for me) just try retyping ai_disable with either 1 or 0 till the words "A.I. Disab" are cleared from the screen
Now upon death the bug no longer triggers!

I've only played a short while on two days, and this game has captivated me like no other online game has, but maybe that's 'cause I only played online FPS games.
As a TES game, it's okay. Not quite the lore of Skyrim, or Oblivion, and certainly not Morrowind. There will be arguments whether or not it's canon. There will be arguments whether it actually counts as an Elder Scrolls games. Take them with a grain of salt.
As an MMO, I cannot say whether it's good or bad, as this is the only MMO I've played. I have found it highly enjoyable in the few hours (less than 10 at the time of writing this) I have played. The quests seemed a little grind-y, but I figured that's typical of an MMO. The community is incredibly friendly to new players, answering questions patiently from people such as myself who were daunted by the vast amount of content. Within an hour of playing I was questing with another player all over Betnikh (I think that's how you spell it) and Daggerfall for the next 8 hours. it was incredible.
I've found the game highly enjoyable, and well worth the wait for the download. (Install isn't quite 85 gigs, and the download was compressed to about 30, massively reducing the download time). I cannot thank my sister enough for buying me this over the Christmas sale. If I knew it was this good, I would have bought it months ago.
The game, even on my Intel integrated GPU, runs quite smoothly. System requirements are quite low so even if you have a toaster, you should get at least 24 FPS as you adjust the settings according to your hardware.
My only disappointment in this game is that I cannot play it much due to having only a limited amount of internet data per month at home, thusly my need to go to public wifi sources to play.
All in all, I find this game incredibly fun. Maybe it's the "new game" hype I have every time I play a game for the first 50 or so hours, so maybe if my view changes over time, I'll adjust this review. But for now, I cannot stress enough how much I love this game. I highly recommend it to any MMO or ES fan for it's solid gameplay.

I have about 1200 hours played out of steam, and another 145 on steam. I can say this game is really great, and a lot of fun especially with friends. I've read some of the negative reviews, and for the most part it seems that they are not lvl 30 yet. Keep talking about matchmaking, and afk people in every match. Once you hit account lvl 30 is where the matchmaking starts to become somewhat competent, and afk players won't be as big of an occurence like they are in the lower level brackets. Now I will say that sometimes it is pretty crap especially when it's not prime time for whichever region you're from.

Smite really does have some cool gods to choose from, and at the time of writing the count is up to 72. With many more to come. The character design is overall pretty good. Some gods definitely have bloated kits, and need to be trimmed down, but I would say the balance is in the best state it's ever been. Minus a few exceptions. The variety of game modes is also a big difference from other mobas who focus only on conquest like modes. Helps keep the game from getting overly stale.

Performance wise it runs pretty good as well, but it does seem to be getting worse for some people. Some can run the game max settings without a hitch, and others with the same hardware have bad drops during a match. Something they did after the season 2 patch changed the performance, and it can be hit or miss. Honestly judging from quite a few posts I've read on the smite reddit it seems people with older hardware actually have better performance than people with newer components. I'm guessing it has to do with smite using dx9, and being only 32 bit, but until Hi-Rez says something about it, it's only my speculation.

Finals thoughts are this game can be a ton of fun, and with friends you can have some great moments. I would suggest at least trying it. It's free so you don't have anything to lose.
P.S. If you really start to play smite a lot then do yourself a favor and buy the godpack. All current and future gods for $30 is a hell of a deal compared to league.

First and foremost, I love this game but with this statement I will say this game is no where near the level of its predecessors. The gameplay itself tries too hard to emulate Dark Souls and Demon's Souls at the same time and ending up pleasing none. It tried to make death this thing you want to avoid at all costs but around the 60% mark of the game, you've been loaded up with tons of human effigies and death isn't even that big of a deal. The game also tries too hard to be hard. Instead of presenting a challenge it relies on cheap tactics to tack on a few unavoidable deaths. Enemies placed near ledges that will stunlock you off the ledge and kiling you. Since the game doesn't have a working Poise system, you will get stunlocked by absolutly everything.
This also affects PvP. The addition of dedicated servers is welcomed, this does not mean they are fully functional and optimal. I have met my fair share of random lag spikes that will result in more than a few deaths. The game also has a bad balance issue, with Miracles being the most destructive thing in the planet and everything else being inferior in comparison. When you can just cast one miracle and take 70% less damage, PvP tends to take a large hit and it all becomes the same build with no insperation for unique builds.
The Lore in this game seems to be hampered by taking place in the Dark Souls universe. It keeps hinting at Drangleic being Lordran. This point is done almost to death, characters repeating that "This kingdom went by a different name which is now lost" and item descriptions doing the same thing. The call-backs to the old bosses seems forced in and not really that necessary. The lore could do more but it seems to not want to deviate from the old formula.
The bosses in the game are of three variations, One big humanoid boss, a boss with multiple minions or just a large demonic boss with each boss being easily beaten. Aside from the optional bosses and a few necessary bosses, everything else can be beat in one try. The Royal Rat Vanguard is one boss that did something new. A room with infinitly respawning rats and one rat that you need to kill. This rat is not special aside from the fact it doesn't display a health bar while locked in. The Royal Rat Authority is just a rehash of Sif and the same goes for the Lost Sinner with Artorias. The game didn't want to deviate just in case the fanbase disliked it.
While I recommend this game I still cannot say it is without it's fauls and it has many. The Directors just tried to stick with what they knew worked and that ended up working against them. Some of these issues can be patched out to be fixed but some, like the bosses, cannot and they are a perminent blemish on the game's rather fine "body."
If I were to score I'd give it a 7/10. If you want more Dark Souls then you will enjoy this game, but hardcore fans of the series will be slightly disappointed.
Edit: One thing I forgot is that unlike the first game, the world isn't connected in the same way. In Dark Souls 1 you could see where you were going. One example is that you can see Undead Burg and Parish from Darkroot Basin. Dark Souls 2 has the "We have an elevator to take you everywhere else." Asides from Majula to Drangleic Castle and maybe somewhere else, the whole game feels disconnected. Even Demon's Souls Felt more connected, You could visably see where you were headed next in an area. In Valley of Defilement before you headed to the swamp, you had a large view from a cliff. You see how the area looks and a few items. It really feels like each area is just a cube that doesn't connect to the rest. The map viewer for Dark Souls 2 shows how everything is basically overlapped. Dark Souls 1's map viewer shows they're all connected. This is something that was lost that I found very cool.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

I'm going to right ahead and state that this game stands as a testimate to the fact that a game need not be long to be breathtaking.  Eternal Senia is concise; it does not bog itself down with meaningless excess, focusing instead on a simplistic but powerful and clearly defined narrative.  It knows what it wants to do, and does so unerringly.
To give an example of the time necessary for completion, I personally have seen every ending, visited the "bonus stage", and found/unlocked every item, all while sometimes tabbing out to find out what I might be missing, in roughly 7 hours.  Naturally, the exact amount of time will vary from person to person, but the simple truth is that you can reasonably expect to open the game for the first time and reach an ending within a single afternoon.
As for the gameplay, namely combat, I'd say the easiest way to describe it would be, "unassuming, yet engaging."  It is simplistic without being dull, and though there are instances where combat boils down to "stat checking," for the most part, it focuses more on movement and spacial awareness.  It is nothing spectacular, but is certainly enough to discourage complacency and keep things from getting monotonous while you continue on your journey through the various zones.
Moving on, when it comes to the music, I'm admittedly bias.  The style used is one that I am personally already rather infatuated with, so it was innevitable that I was going to adore it.  With that said, the tracks are instrumental, atmospheric, and will often times be attached to a single emotion or desire, like hope, dread, curiosity,, and sorrow.  If you like music from N64/Playstation era RPGs and Adventure games, Eternal Senia's choice in style will likely strike your fancy.
Oh, and don't worry about the Ragnarok Online references in the leads, knowledge of their characters are not at all necessary to enjoy this game, and in fact, the characters from Eternal Senia probably have more lore on them than the characters they were based on.
But I've gone on entirely too long about this already.  The real message I'd like to get across is this: Eternal Senia is an exceptionally well-crafted experience that is free, has a great story to tell, and all it asks of you in turn is that you free up a few hours so it may do so.  And, to be perfectly forthright, if you're reading this part of my review right now, as in literally these words near the bottom of the fifth paragraph I've typed up on this subject, just download the game if you haven't already.  The only real reasons why you'd be here are either you've played it already and are reading this to see what other people thought, or you're curious about what it has in store and if it's worth the download, and to the latter I can only say that yes, yes it is, and you've already demonstrated that you have an adequate enough amount of free time, so you really might as well just give it a go; the only thing you stand to lose is a bit of that aforementioned free time, and considering you actually read all of this, those terms should be more than agreeable.

Eternal Senia is an RPG Maker game but do not hold that against it, a lot of people have become annoyed by all the RPG Maker games appearing on steam lately and that is unfortunate as many of them are very outstanding games and Eternal Senia is one of these games.
I have spent so much time playing this game and I have become so immersed in its story that I can almost tell you about it off the top of my head, nevertheless I will try my best to give you a good idea of what its all about without spoiling anything.
Eternal Senia, a romantic drama story of the struggles one human will go to save the person they care most for. This story may very well draw you in from the start, as it did me I couldnt help but keep going to find out what will happen.
The combat for this game is a fairly standard for those who have played a lot of RPG Maker games and is much easier than most games not saying that thats a bad thing though. The battles can all be  won using strategy rather than sheer force, some grinding may be needed.
For the most part if you keep your wits about you, you will get through with no real trouble. However grinding can be very worth it, there is huge amounts of loot which can be crafted to make the game more enjoyable.
Length wise Eternal Senia is not the longest RPG Maker games I have come across, but it doesn't need to be it tells its story well in the period of time needed, any longer and the feel would be completely off, as if to make it worse by drawing it out so though some will be disappointed at its short length it is for the best.
As for replayability, the game has 3 endings These do not require the game to be replayed from the start, as you can just save before the final boss and change your accessories before the fight each time.
These accessory combinations will provide the various endings of the game. Having said that I replayed the game from the start each time as I found that more rewarding.
Overall Eternal Senia is beautifully written piece of work it has an Interesting Storyline; It is visually appealing, the characters are interesting, a simplistic and fluid combat system, and  3 diferent endings which make those replays worth it.
I'll leave you with this, I have replayed this game so many times, it is perhaps one of the best  RPG Maker games Ive played in a little while and given how much time Ive sunken into it I guess thats sort of evident huh?
Eternal Senia is just that good of a game and will no doubt keep you interested throughout its duration, and its absolutely free, if thats not a good reason to check it out I dont know what is....so why not give it a try.
(Like all my reviews I do not put a score as it is my belief that games like all forms of art are subjective and therefore it is impossible to afix a number to them)

I like it.  The developer has released it FOR FREE, which is pretty cool.  The story has a little sweetness to it, a plot where an emotionally broken big sister tries to obtain "the power of eternity" to save her little sister, only to have the little sister try to rescue her from that very same power.  The gameplay is pretty simple:  wander through three pretty big levels that are loaded with enemies as you try to reach the final confrontation.  In terms of graphics and sound, it's about what you would expect from "RPG Maker" and similar to the original "Legend of Zelda."  It's got that 16-bit feel to it, slightly better than NES but not on par with the Gamecube or Playstation generation.  It has three different endings, all depending on how you complete that final battle.  It has a few side quests and hidden treasures.  And instead of "shopping" it has a system where you use items dropped by enemies to improve your weapon and armor.  The crafting system is simple and easy to use; not too much grinding needed.  The XP system is just about perfect in terms of when you should be leveling up vs. the strength of monsters you face at that time.  It even has a system in place to use SP (earned from killing enemies) to boost the effective power of your four special skill attacks.
In terms of time, you're probably looking at a solid 8 hours of gameplay to finish it.  Then another half hour or so to see the other two endings.  Then if you want to replay, it does have "hard mode" for an added challenge.  But there are no achievements available for this game (at least not yet?).
The only real problem I had with it is:  NO CONTROLLER SUPPORT AT ALL.  Sure you can use the L-stick to run around, but the skill attacks are not able to be mapped to the controller unless you want to use some crazy 3rd party software like a real programmer... and I'm not like that.  So, expect to be using the keyboard controls instead.  You only need the arrow keys, Z (or spacebar), X, Q, W, E, and R.  Pretty simple controls, if a bit awkward to get used to.

This was a risky game for Sierra to publish but I think, after the epilogue's release, I can finally say with certainty that I recommend it. Oh, and sorry for the wall of text you may or may not be about to read.
Ch1: 4/5 - Obviously, being free is a plus and it did succeed in bringing the King's Quest franchise to a modern platform without feeling aged, even adding branching pathways without making them feel too important, however it doesn't quite capture the feel of the originals.
Ch2: 2/5 - Probably my least favourite chapter in the game, due in part to its addition of needless survival mechanics. While it did follow up from Chapter 1 as promised, this was one mechanic change I was not a fan of.
Ch3: 3/5 - Definitely a step up from the last one, starting with time travel elements and later featuring a twist on the end of King's Quest II, seeing you attempt to woo two candidates for your queen, urging you to answer a quiz honestly and solve problems with either brain or brawn in a series of tests not disimilar to the questions you would see in dating sims to find your wife. Despite the dating sim exterior and a slightly more linear playstyle in comparison with the first two chapters, it still manages to return to the charm of the first one.
Ch4: 3/5 - A lot of puzzles. Needless to say, do not play this chapter if you don't like puzzles. Although there are a lot, most of them are only slightly challenging, so feel satisfying to complete without having to mean 10 minutes to solve a puzzle. Follows up from the previous chapter a lot more smoothly than most other chapters do.
Ch5: 4/5 - King Graham, on his deathbed, tries to remember his final adventure with his misremembering playing a key role this time around. A very creative game mechanic, giving an excuse to show cut content and makes it arguably the best chapter. Switches to retro graphics at one point and... (I can't really add much more without giving major spoilers)
Epilogue: 4/5 - Some of the most creative uses of items in a much more animal based adventure starring King Graham's granddaughter. Would be 5/5 if it were longer, had any achievements and wasn't exclusive to Complete Collection. While I might not be in the majority here, I feel that the Complete Collection is worth buying purely for this.
Tip for people who have played Chapter 1 but not bought any others (and a reward for reading): Go to Help, then Steam Support and remove King's Quest from your games, as you cannot buy the Complete Collection with it in your library. As long as you do not uninstall the game, you will not lose your progress and achievements will be kept.

Let me start off with a small history lesson: I have seen the first Alien movie in 2002 or so, and I really liked it. Coincidentally, this was one year after I got my first gaming computer and was actually getting into videogames in a big way. The first thing I thought was "This would make for an amazing videogame!"
But a shining beacon of hope appeared in the distance as I have discovered that there indeed is a game which is considered good from Alien universe (sort of), Aliens vs Predator by Rebellion. So I got that. And while it was scary enough as a Marine, Alien wasn't this constant, ever present threat which was to be feared - Aliens were just common monsters, which would give you a scare, but weren't really all that difficult to defeat. I liked the game, sure, but something just wasn't quite there. It reminded me of the second movie far more than it did of the first, and the fact that I seemed to move at warp speed didn't help either. Since then, two more Aliens vs Predator games got released, and shortly after those, Aliens: Colonial Marines came out. And finally, 12 years in which I have revisited the original movie a few times and every time hoped for a proper Alien game to exist, one came out. And it is nearly all I hoped it would be.
Alien: Isolation throws everything you would traditionally do when returning to a movie that old out of the window and executes everything with a beautiful attention to detail, replicating everything from visual design, sounds of the original, music, hell, the game even got the original cast of the fist movie on board to do voice acting. The game doesn't try to modernize, it doesn't try to make the game 'more believable' for a 21st century consumer - nah, it just says ♥♥♥♥ that, converts everything we could see in the original movie into in-game assets and ends up being that much more thrilling, nostalgic and believable for it. It's a game made by fans of the movie, for fans of the movie, a huge love letter to everything the original is.
I could probably start talking about the game tho, right? Yeah, I should do that. So, you're playing as Amanda Ripley, daughter of Ellen Ripley. Ellen Ripley has been considered lost for 15 years, and Amanda has been informed about black box of Nostromo finding its way to Sevastopol space station. Soon after arriving on station, she finds that everything has gone to hell, surviving people are fighting for remaining resources, androids kill on sight for trespassing, and on top of that, there is talk of some creature murdering people.
The game is mostly a stealth-based survival horror, with very few tools to defend yourself with (and while you get more of those as you progress trough the game, you very rarely get to have enough ammo), so you're left to a motion tracker and your wit to stay alive. The game gives you many tools for distracting your enemies, be it humans, androids or the Alien. You can craft items, some of which can cause direct damage, others which can serve to distract. Some levels have conveniently placed 'rewire boxes', which allow you to turn off cameras, open doors or cause distractions in various parts of a level. You can hide in lockers, vents or just low spaces like under desks or beds. These elements, and parts of the game where you need to get around humanoid opponents, mostly reminded me of games similar to Outlast or Amnesia. Individual areas tend to be open enough to allow for a decent amount of ways to get around various obstacles, and the level design itself is quite beautiful, varied and clever to keep you interested. All in all, when you're up against more traditional threats, Alien: Isolation is a good stealth game, and a decent shooter in the rare occassions you choose to approach it that way. When you explore the station, it also very rarely happens that you'd get locked out of a section of it, and so you can go back to most places you've already been - and there's even a reason to do so as more equipment you gain will open up more secret areas for you.
However, all of this changes after the Alien makes its first appearance. Suddenly, you're not just worrying about the traditional opponents. There's always the threat of the Alien, lurking above you, making its way trough ventilation ducts of the entire station. If you run too fast - you may attract the Alien. If you hit a wall with your maintenance jack, it might distract your opponents, but it might also attract the Alien. If you fire your gun, you don't just fire your gun - you may attract the Alien. (that also applies to human opposition tho - while the Alien ignores androids, when someone shoots at you and the Alien is nearby, it will jump out of airduct and start working its way trough any human it sees. Including you of course.)
The creature's AI is good enough to differenciate it from all other opponents, to make it a constant threat and to make you nervous about it, as you see a green dot on your movement tracker, circling around you somewhere above. Those are the calm bits of the game tho - when it emerges and you can see it, everything gets a lot worse as, most of the time, it only takes the Alien to notice you once for you to pretty much instantly die. Oh, and it can kill you from the vents if you miss the dribbling ooze or are foolish enough to take a look what exactly is it dribbling from. All of these aspects are frustrating, yes, along with the fact that the Alien is a lot more perceptive than the other opponents, you are going to die a lot and the only way to save your game is at fixed save stations (which are placed fairly close to each other so it's not that bad), but all of this successfully leads to one end - not cheapening the creature. Alien is terrifying, it's constantly there, stalking you, trying to pinpoint your exact location and to kill you. You'll feel that most of encounters with it are close, and that you are always one wrong step from dying. While it is, in reality, a lot more forgiving than that, the feeling of paranoia is always there, scratching at the back of your head.
All of this is backed up by a decent storyline and solid writing, with fantastic music, graphic and sound design. While some bits of the game feel a bit padded, it generally manages to make you feel like its always quite fresh (I don't want to spoil anything so I'm not going to reveal how exactly), and while the game is quite long, it feels captivating enough to make me finish it. The game takes good care to pace itself properly - the first time you even get to see the alien is about 1,5 hours into it
All in all, Alien: Isolation is the best survival horror game I have played in a very long time, possibly since Dead Space, and this time, it places emphasis on the 'survival' bit. It's beautifully put together, very well crafted and it's such an innovative gaming experience that I'm pondering on making it my GOTY of 2014. Well worth your money, well worth playing.

In a world of mostly bad Alien games, Alien: Isolation is easily the best one of them ever made.  This is not a FPS or RPG, but rather a stealth/survival horror game.  Whether or not those gameplay mechanics are fun is entirely up to you.
The game has stunning level design, archetecture, and overall look and feel.  It replicates the first Alien movie's environment in sound, music, and visual style perfectly.  Never before did I ever feel like I was literally walking through a living version of one of the movies. All the technology in the game is the same 1970s "vision of the future" from the films as well, and is appropriately clicky, glitchy, bulky, boxy, and otherwise primitive. The Alien creature itself feels, acts, and moves as if it were a real living thing, its AI being one of the most realistic ever in a game.
That all being said, several things about the gameplay annoy me to no end:
1.  The controls are very clunky.  Your character almost moves as if in slow motion, and the camera sway is sort of nauseating.  You scroll through the weapons with the mouse wheel (as typically done these days) but the other items (medkit, pipe bomb, etc) are done with an ingame "wheel" that is very odd to operate.  I often found myself going into the "crafting mode" when I was actually trying to select one the few weapons available, usually when a Working Joe was sneaking up to throttle the living crap out of me.
2.  It's not an FPS game and cannot be approached as if it were one.  The weapons provided in the game pretty much do jack sh!t and are useless overall.  While I never expected Colonial Marines type of play, there should have been better ways to deal with enemies.  For example - Working Joes:  How about being able to trip them and then smash their head in with a wrench or something?  And why can't I hear their foot steps?  Are they programmed for stealth walking by default?  Why isn't there a control on one of the terminals to shut down all the WJs on that level?
3.  There are times when you get stuck in an animation of doing something (i.e., typing on a terminal, opening up a welding tool, etc) and it puts you at complete risk of being discovered or killed.  Naysayers will argue this is part of the experience, but if we are truly going for realism here, then a person attempting to do these things in real life would simply stop what they are doing (if they value their life) and go back to hiding, etc.
4.  There are times when I swear the Working Joes or the Alien are looking right at me and they do nothing, then other times when I sneak past them and somehow they either spot me and/or come out of nowhere and maul me.  Does that make for "realistic" or sh!t gameplay?  You decide.
5.  It's not a fast moving game by any stretch.  While the length is completely subjective based on your skill, etc it just goes on way too long for my liking regardless. For all of the work spent of the game environments, it all boils down to fetch quests/switch flipping/locate a key type of play, which gets horribly repetitive after a while.  If you are not a patient player, this game will probably test your patience.  It certainly tested mine, especially toward the end.
6.  If you've seen the movies, you will be able to guess much (though possibly not all) of what happens in the game.
Bottom Line:
Though it's the most well done Alien game to date, I really don't enjoy all the sneaking around and not having more gameplay options to deal with enemies.  After getting mauled by the Alien so many times, the horror is completely lost to what becomes horribly repetitive and boring gameplay.
Considering the first Alien movie is one of my favorites of all time, I think that's a shame really. I've played it thru completely just once, having retried several times since only to uninstal it and move onto something else.
At the end of the day, it's just not fun...Not for me, at least.

The short version is: This game has a great concept but gets ruined by it's bland as hell Combat, Story and by it's downright terrible sense of humor which only consists of references to internet memes and jokes or puns which is so heavily forced the entire game that this was just painful in the end. I don't recommend it, even for this price.
The long version is: Suits is a RPG that sparked my interest, not only because of the visuals, but also because it seemed like  funny, kinda new idea in doing so. That the game would be a bizzare trip with dark humour mixed in it, i knew from the start, the screenshots kinda gave it away.
What i didn't expect was, that the game accomplishes nothing throughout the entire 5 hours of my playtime. The entire game is heavenly inspired by Earthbound or in general the mother series, one boss battle even being a straight homage to one of the bosses in Mother 3. Even one of the companions you find on your way (which there are only 2 to find in total anyway) has a move similiar to the character Duster from Mother 3, even almost looking the exact same. The problem is, that every single battle feels exactly the same. There is no real strategy or no real difficulty, go with the same strategy as before and you are sure to win the entire game without a problem.
Like mentioned before, the artstyle is what got me interested in the game, i really adored the mix of pixel characters and the handdrawn, clumsy, dark and gritty pen drawings. No enemy in this world looks normal, all of them take the form as some deranged and weird creatures and monsters.
The music score is nice and one of the stronger points, but one thing, ONE big thing that ruined the entire game for me:
The writing and the humour.
The humour is such pure and utter cancer it ruined every single serious, dark or good tone the game had for me, even the story. This game is worse with it's jokes than games like Borderlands and Undertale combined, that just don't manage to shut up with their jokes for even a second. But i think Suits takes the cake for me in this category. There wasn't one joke that wasn't a reference to an internet joke, memes, puns, selfirony (man this game sure sucks right guys??), current pop culture or video game jokes.
Sometimes the characters were talking downright jibberish or random nonsense, presented to you as a joke, that was unsuprisingly, not funny at all. On occasions, the game tries jokes on politics or, well, business, but they fall down flat on their nose aswell. They usually end up that both parties are dumb and thats it, there isn't much to it. There is nothing clever, nothing makes a statement about anything and so forth. And this goes on throughout the entire game, making you not caring at all for anything in this game. Because, well, everything is just a joke right?
And if the point really just is "yeah it's supposed to be dumb because business is dumb and it's self irony" or similar, then sorry, i can't take your game serious in anyway, this has been overdone without end by other games and it will always just strike me as a bad excuse for your lazy effort.
But when i look at what Youtubers they put in for a gag, i'm not suprised the developers would find constant 420 jokes hilarious and what the final product looks like. It's just a shame, that such a good concept and idea gets ruined by such trivial needs of portraying yourself funny or witty.
I don't recommend this, not for 1 dollar or for less. With that cash you can buy a drink, and that one is probably more refreshing than this game.

Maybe it's the "new game" hype I have every time I play a game for the first 50 or so hours, so maybe if my view changes over time, I'll adjust this review. First and foremost, the mods made in the community were able to recover most of this games lost potential. There are still many frustrating aspects to the gameplay, the most fustrating being the fact that "realism was sacrificed for balance." I understand that there is a desired balance of gameplay ( lets face it, if it was realistic playing as Rome would be remarkably OP) but its a bad excuse for how the AI interacts and how faction development falls apart late game (No circo maximvs with the colloseum in Rome, as in you cant build both in the same city.... thats just dumb, no excuse). However, user mods do repair the AI TO A CERTAIN EXTENT and manage to even increase the agressiveness of certain factions that were known for this (Suebi, more precisely german tribal coalitions).
Also, although the scale of war may be difficult to achieve, it is annoying to see that CA has kept the size of battles relatively small (maximum 10k vs 10k units). The average size of a battle in Roman times was around 40k vs 40k (estimate, there were many smaller battles and many larger battles) but the tiny scale of the military in TW:R2 really hurts the game.
Overall, with mods i would give this game an 8.5/10 (wihout mods its a 7/10) but due to my frustration with the lame excuse CA has given in regards to maintaining faction balance (lets face it, you CAN be realistic and have balance..... look at Europa Univ.) I have to give this game a final score of:
8/10

Having played the original King's Quest series, I can vouch for the accuracy of the description "reimagined". The stories, setting, and puzzles are different, and the graphics updated, but the general idea and feel are quite similiar to the original. Each of the 5 episodes is a self-contained story, within the over-arching story of the life of the principal character.
The good:
- nice graphics (cartoon style)
- excellent voice acting!
- good range of characters (main character and protagonist, plus several secondary characters)
- heart-warming overall story
- humor well done - not overdone
- good range of puzzle types
- almost no combat (not everyone will agree that this is a good thing, but I appreciated it)
- it's almost always clear when a puzzle component has been found/solved (although not necessarily for which puzzle)
- major choices matter
The bad:
- not much clue-following; many puzzles require only straightforward (if sometimes complex) reasoning, while many other puzzles have arbitrary solution components (solveable only by exhaustive search)
- puzzle solution components are oftern widely separated, requiring a lot of repetitive travel that does nothing to advance the story
- sometimes solution component "hot spots" are very small, and not necessarily in the most expected precise location, making them easy to miss; no cross-hair assist
- some puzzles require a change in state that is triggered solely by leaving and re-entering the area
-
- it's often unclear which choices matter, until after they have been made (sometimes long after); with limited save/load ability, re-do is usually not practical
FYI: I bought the first chapter on PSN for my PS3. Switched to Steam when the full suite went on sale for $15.
The bottom line: 9/10 for on-sale value (7/10 at original price).

Hell, yes, do I recommend this game!
But please keep in mind, that it was released in 1999. Graphics at this time relied stronger on your sense of imagination than today!
But if you want to play the grand father of Dead Space and Bioshock and have a look, what ancient knowledge these games remember (and which they did forget!), then this is the adress to go to!
Story writing of System Shock is on eye level with stuff like Dead Space 1. Not great, but definetely servicable. Voice acting is great (and everything is voice acted!).
The graphics are... well... ancient. But work well enough as to not being confusing. You will be able to tell apart enemies from kitchen wear.
The game mechanics are... awesome! Really, not by 1999 standards, but by today's standards. You got different weapon types, you can specialize on, different psy abilities, you might learn, but you also have to learn, how to maintain and repair your equipment. You need to manage your resources... honestly: Quite a few of today's survival games should REALLY have a close look on System Shock 2 and reconsider their mechanics!
So, good game with lots of nostalgia value (remember the waxd as your default move keys?). Play it, if haven't already. That is, if you are into shooters and you can stand the rather old graphics. Check them out, before you buy the game.
For those, who want to try it out, here are's a word of advice, so you don't mess up your character and have to start over again:
-The most powerful weapons in the game are the pistol, the grenade launcher (and to a smaller degree the shotgun). Learn to use these and don't mind about the other weapons, unless you got some leftover points late in the game.
-Psy is funny, but not that powerful. Don't spend too much on it. Cyber affinity is a must have, though.
-Hacking is very useful! Lvl 4 is recommended. Repair 1 is the only thing you need for the important weapons. Maintenance needs a few points.
-I didn't find the stats, besides strength all that useful.
-Save ammo and nanites, whenever you can! There are a few rather tough sections during which you'll go through your resources as if you there'd be no tomorrow! Make sure, you got some!
Otherwise... there are plenty of ways to play the game (even pure psy run-throughs oO), though some are more difficult than other. But, hey! Try to find your own way through the Von Braun ;)

Playing this vanilla.
+ Has a wide range of customizable play styles which you also can play with a "Jack-Of-All-Trades" kind of style.
+ Although clunky at first the UI gets familiar with a sense of nostalgia and makes other UI's feel inferior because of how much you can do with it.
+ If you care about stories with or without the gameplay the story will take a strong grip on you. It is fascinating and inspired.
+ Has a wide range of weaponry with both "space-magic", laser guns and standard bullet type and otherworldy alien arms.
+ Enemies are downright scary and will make you feel uncomfortable right away. They'll give you an enclosed feeling of loneliness.
+ Game is very difficult at first since you don't know what you're doing. But is rewarding once you get used to it in both fun and skill.
+ The ambience and music are well thought out, it will throw you right into the frey with fast-paced techno music giving you an alarmed feeling whilst still keeping its creepy atmosphere. And by God if Med Sci 1 isn't the best techno tune ever I don't know what is.
+ Ammunition and other resources can be quite scarce if you're not careful, making you want to avoid combat. You must be cautious of how you use/manage your items. Learn melee combat!
+ Very easy to mod.
+ The map design is why I love both System Shock and System Shock 2. While still being a game level it still feels like a workplace and actually looks livable.
- The game has very out-dated graphics, especially character models.
- Might want to change the default controller settings, they're not good at all.

I snagged this for $24.99 and that's a good price for it in my opinion. This is the second best game with xenomorphs in it that I've ever played, the best being Aliens Vs Predator 2 if aged graphics don't upset you. In this game, you play as Ellen Ripley's (Sigourney Weaver) daughter, Amanda Ripley, going to a space station where her mom's blown up ship's flight recorder is being held, because she wants closure on what happened to her mom since she'd been missing 15 years (a la the end of ALIEN). It's a great setup and the characters' motivations in this game are totally believable; all of the characters, really. Any xenomorph enthusiast who likes stealth games needs to play this game, as I definitely recommend it, but it's not without disappointing elements. So before I complain about those, let me just say that the alien will have your pulse raised while you watch it from hiding, moving yourself around a low object like a crate while the xeno walks around , peeking at it and just wishing the damn thing would go away. The stealth is great, and the alien can pop down out of vents and your motion tracker just makes this stealth experience wonderful. Lastly on the game's pros, it looks pretty darn good and it is an absolute -love letter- to the visuals of the first movie, ALIEN. Quite a few little homages and stuff to the film as well.
On to the downsides...this game is just too long. You think "I want to get my money's worth!" Well, a horror game with only 4 real enemy types should not be 20+ hours long, 15 hours for a first-timer not rushing things wouldn't have gotten as boring, because that's how I felt before the game's climactic last leg: bored. Sure, I'd get nervous when the xeno was around, but no longer was I enchanted by the locations or the computer logs. I just wanted it to end on a high note. The game hardly fizzles out at its conclusion, but that feeling of wishing it would just end out of the whole thing finally getting dull isn't one I want when I'm playing a game that I had such fun with earlier.
Another gripe for me is the ammo...I'm fairly certain that on Normal difficulty, I could have killed every single non-xeno enemy (you can't shoot the xeno to death) in the game with the ammo I found just looting containers and finding it on the floor, but the game, being "survival horror," made me think that I would need to be sparing with the stuff. So by the end of the game, I had enough pistol bullets, shotgun shells, and bolt gun rounds to kill 40 more androids, which is like 3-4 times as many as I snuck past and left alone, so now I feel like an idiot for not blowing everything away like a standard first person shooter when the xeno wasn't after me. =/
Final complaint would be the false Metroidvania vibe it gives you. If you've played any of the Batman Arkham games, or even Metroid games, you'll know that you will see stuff you want to get, such as bonus XP (Riddler Trophies) or Missle Capacity upgrades for Samus, but you can't get to them yet...there will be something visually marking that you need a certain upgrade to get in later. It makes you want to backtrack and I find it fun. However, in this game, the xenomorph is stalking you like 75% of the game, and is definitely stalking you during the small window of time that you have every upgrade. This makes backtracking through all the levels to get ID tags and Nostromo audio logs (only relevant for achievements and listening to the logs, no upgrades) a total chore to do. I couldn't bring myself to bother with going back to do that because I just wanted the game to end.
I know I'm throwing up a few things that I really didn't like about the game, but this really was a good game, despite these flaws. If you like horror stealth kinda games, then you should get this for $24.99 or less. If you're really into xenomorphs and like stealth, then you should definitely pick this up, but I really would get it on sale. If you've waited this long since it launched, you can wait for another sale. I hope this has helped you out!

Albeit with a few quirks, a fantastic game with a interweaving fantastic story.  The voice acting was good, although there were some points where the script went a little cliche.  Very good use of suspense, and the cinematics and soundtrack nailed it.  I also appreciated some of the interesting things the developers did with the enemies (especially the bosses).  I even found the lore items interesting and not overwhelming.  The environments were interesting and very diverse.  Played it on "normal" and it was a decent challenge.  It really had the orignial Resident Evil zest for requiring smart use of items.  You don't find ammo all over the place, and you have to be choosy about when to go for that headshot.    Although, I regret that I wasn't able to spend much time with some of the arsenal to due the high price of making bullets.  The inability to max everything out in one run also meant you had to be choosy about what attributes mattered most.  Taking everything I just wrote, I can say that most of the game I was in a state of pucker, if you catch my drift.  Game mechanics were decent, but there were more than a few times that the intended action was not the one I got (e.g., quick turnaround, corner stealth kill, etc.).  To me, that is the only big gripe I have for an otherwise extraordinary sequel.

With the release of Emperor Edition, Total War: ROME II has finally launched the game they meant to make back in 2013, a full year ago.  What this means is ROME II no longer has fatal bugs, crashes, humorously rendered faces, poorly designed building trees, poorly designed tech trees, or painful wait times between turns.  The bugs are gone, the polish is there, it is safe to say this is a completed game.
This might be too long for people, so I'll put my final thoughts here and then if you wish you can read the justification for them below:
Rome 2 is more of a management game than a strategy game.  There are very few strategic descisions to be made in this game after 30 turns into a campaign.  You simply build buildings, train troops, give movement orders, and upgrade generals because if you don't the game gives you a pop up telling you what you forgot to do.  There's a shameful lack of interesting battles to be fought, and it hardly matters what buildings you choose to upgrade or build, and it certainly doesn't matter what general traits you choose.  So you click the buttons to get the pop ups to go away, and eventually you start wondering why you started the game up in the first place, because there's no game to be had here.
I'll start with the Campaign.
The map is pretty, but a pain to navigate when your empire is large, as the camera does not zoom out enough on the main screen, forcing you to go into 'strategic mode' and double click and have the game zip the camera over there.  Despite there being several views of the map: the normal camera, the strategic map, and the diplomatic map (the latter of the two having options to change different overlays) there is still no good way to get a picture of what is going on in your empire.  The Strategic map will show you the position of your armies and enemy armies, but it doesn't tell you how big the armies are, or how much movement they have left.  So when you see an enemy flag in your territory, you still have to zoom your camera over there to see if its a full army or one of the small, threatless stacks the AI likes to create.
On the campaign you will develope your cities and move your armies.  The UI for these functions is minimalistic with lots of tool tips that pop up.  This allows you to get a good look at the graphics, and a poor look at what the buildings do and what affects are on your armies and generals.  To compare two different buildings you have to hover over one, wait for the tool tip, memorize the stats then hover over another, wait for the tool tip and mentaly compare the stats of the first option.  There is no side by side view, or a list of effects or anything.  This leaves you mousing back and forth frequently trying to pick which building you want.  The buildings themselves often offer small percentage bonuses to one type of income (cultural for example) and cost food.  Thus one must balance their food and food-demanding buildings appropriately.  This is an ok mechanic.  It's not great, but it's something to break up the monotony or the linear upgrades of other Total War titles.  However once you have a large empire, it is very easy to lose interest in min-maxing your buildings, because you end up conquering so many cities so quickly that you always have food and you always have money, so balancing the economy and food tends to go away at a certain size.  The technology tree feels rather pointless and linear.  It provides either a flat bonus to troops (like upkeep, movement speed, or combat effectiveness) and access to buildings which allow higher teir troops to be trained.  This mechanic is hollow.  It primarily serves to gateway what troops are available at what times of the game, because the flat bonuses are small and inconsequential.  Some of the religious buildings will increase your research rate by a small amount, but the technology tree still fees shallow and arbitrary.  In Rome 1 units were gated by buildings, and occasionally (in the case of Roman legionaries) the date.  This functioned better, and was more transparent, which allowed for better planning.
I like the feature of generals and armies leveling up, but they get too many bonuses and they seem so small and unnoticeable.  This leaves me clicking one at random and not really caring, similar to buildings.
Other aspects of the campaign map are simmilar enough to the other Total Wars that I can't expect anything more or less from them.
On to the battles.
Battles are pretty.  There's plenty of nice effects that let you see your army of antiquity on the battlefield in high fidelity.  However, due to the nature of Total War AI (which is SLIGHTLY improved in Rome 2) the battles are boring.  As long as you line your men up to face the enemy properly and prevent any sad attempts the AI makes at flanking you, you'll probably win.  This is a problem because the battles are supposed to be the best part.  That's where they spent all the money, right?  Right?
The unit variety is nice, and I could complain about the way pikemen don't really feel like pikemen, and that the difference between heavy cav and light cav is very minimal, but there's no point, because it takes a special kind of idiot to lose to a Total War AI.  I haven't played much multiplayer, I presume the battles are decently interesting when they're both controlled by a human.
Over-all.
There's a mysterious and unfortunate paradox to the Total War series.  If you are playing correctly on the strategy map, you would make sure you have the highest chance to win a battle as you possibly could.  This means that most of the battles you fight you will have overwhelming odds and you can auto resolve them with 95% of your army remaining.  Fighting it out would be boring, and you probably wouldn't save that many casualties commanding yourself so what's the point?  This means that there's a small 20-30 turn window at the start of a game where you actually fight the battles because you only have one or two armies and you need to put them in 'risky' situations.  And since in a fair fight you will always defeat the AI you win those risky situations.  But once you're large enough you tend not to fight battles, and just auto resolve as you blob over the entire map.  Which leads me to the short sampler from the top of the page.

Maybe it gets better if you get deeper into it, but my experience with the game can be summarized as a bunch of people with spears and bows running around killing everyone they see.
The land was so littered with fruit and game that survival was never even remotely a challenge.
In order to actually do anything in the game you need to collect amber, a rare resource that is randomly dropped sometimes when you harvest something. You need amber in order to claim land so that you can then start building things. You also need amber in order to make the tool you need to start building things. You also need amber in order to make a little prefab shack. If you do end up building something, the game makes sure you know that it is temporary and will dissapear within a day if you don't throw more amber at it.
Basically you can't touch the world until you get a rare item that is randomly dropped. I only know this because I looked it up online because the entire time I played I never saw any amber. It felt like running around in a minecraft server on observer mode, you're not allowed to touch anything, but you can look at the buildings other people put up.

This game evokes all the magic and fun of the original King's Quest and Monkey Island games.  Its puzzles aren't difficult, but nevertheless left me with a feeling of cleverness when I solved them.  Throughout, the game's puns and tongue-in-cheek humor kept me delighted.  Throw in excellent graphics and a heartfelt story and the game is a perfect one to share with the next generation of point-and-click gamers in your life.

The original King's Quest and most of the sequels were incredible. You have to imagine that it was sometime in the 80's, and my single uncle had a PC Jr. and played King's Quest with friends. Always trying to figure out the puzzles. There was no Google or even an Internet to speak of. At Christmas, I managed to sneak away from the grandparents, parents, and dog to play a bit. I never got to fully experience the game at that time, but I have very fond memories of those days. Asking my Uncle about how to get past a hard puzzle, with him replying, "Yeah, Stan and I haven't figured that out yet." No access to information. Nintendo Power didn't have the answers and the Sierra Hint Line was expensive.
This is a beautifully drawn recreation of those times. Most of the episodes incorporate excellent voice acting, puzzles ranging from pretty easy to mildly difficult to mind-bogglingly insane, excellent artwork and coloring, and a sense of humor which hearkens to the 80's. For those of you far removed from the 80's: puns, innuendoes, irony are the norm. The series gives a sweeping picture of young Graham (the hero) the squire, the King, and the adventurer, and so forth. Even if you haven't played the originals, though, and don't notice some of the inside jokes, there is a lot to like.
It reminds me of the Telltale Games series, but set in a different world, and with more adventure puzzles. It's not Myst, mind you. I'm not a huge fan of adventure games unless we're talking King's Quest or the Blackwell Conspiracy (great indie adventure) or even Grim Fandango. But this game shines. That's not to say there aren't problems.
Episode 4 is somewhat mind numbing, with exposition and annoying puzzles. I didn't find any of them difficult, exactly, and they were fun in a way, but it was basically a bunch of pushing blocks and making paths that would light up. While they were clever, they just weren't fun.
Wallace Shawn does a spectacular job of acting, and his character plays a part in each Episode. Without question, for fans new or old, King's Quest is a very solid entry into the realm of Adventure games, replete with excellent acting, beautifully drawn locales and characters, and enjoyable humor. It's not for everyone, but Adventure gamers and those who like a bit of a brain tease will find something to enjoy and make their own.

I'm always a fan of point & click adventure since the old Sierrra & LucasFilm days (changed to LucasArts, but I think now it's no more). I'm more toward the LucasArts style of adventure (you can't go wrong nor die in the game) instead of the old Sierra style, although I liked them too.
This is the way the new modern point & click adventure should be. It's retains its old beloved style, yet the gameplay and graphics have been adjusted to modern times, Full 3D with moving cameras, yet still maintain that look & feel of the traditional games.
Some devs still stick with pixel arts style (mostly indies because of the lack of funding), but AAA point & click adventure should be like this. Middle tiers developers usually go with 3D characters on 2D rendered backgrounds (Gray Matter, etc), which is also nice, OR with high quality & high resolution 2D hand drawn sprites (Secret of Monkey Island Remake, Days of Tentacle remake, Broken Sword 5, Runaway 3, etc) which is also nice.
Just like old Sierra style, you can still die in the game (sometimes you need to for achievements), but the whole mechanism feel so polished and you're put right back before you die, thus giving no penalty for exploration, which is a good thing. In fact, this game encourages you for exploring as multiple solutions are sometimes provided for a puzzle.
The humors and the whole atmosphere of the game feel good so it doesn't feel boring.
Chapter 1 is more like the old traditional style, with multiple paths for solutions and mostly inventory based puzzles. Most of the puzzles are logical, although a few here and there not so much, but still feel very entertaining and you don't feel like you're cheated.
Chapter 2 is smaller and have a slightly different mechanism. More paths for solutions are in this chapter 2. You're probably want to re-play ch. 2 more than one time if you're curious on "what if I chose that path" in the game.
Highly recommended, and I still have 3 more chapters to go :)

Suits: A Business RPG is a new RPGMaker RPG designed by Technomancy Studios. That's the standard stuff out of the way, so let's get into the weird.  Suits starts you off as The Guy, another businessman in line to join the ranks in a world run entirely by corporations, built as corporations. The satire of consumerism and greed is done well, and helps to add to the game's very offbeat sense of humor. The jokes range from the clocks always set to 4:20 as it's simplest, to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on a dinosaur's floor at its strangest. This, along wth the setting and atmosphere is what I think makes Suits such a fun game; it's absurd while still being relevant to modern times. The Payday 2 microtransactions joke is a good example, and is done well. The story itself is rather straightforward; notes are placed around to provide back story and clues and the ending sums up the purpose of the world itself and your actions nicely. Oh, and the art and music. Some people were put off by the crude sketch design and music; personally I found them both surrelastic, funny and disturbing enough that they made a perfect fit for the plot.
To sum it up, Suits is a straightforward PRG mechanically; there are some special abilities like a instant kill that only works 1% of the time, and being able to pay your enemies to lose. There's not much that changes the gameplay itself from other RPG's; instead the focus is on the creative art of the game. Whether you'll like this or not will depend on what you're looking for in an RPG game, but for it's price it's got a decent story length to it and potential for follow up. Also: dinosaur dinosaur diunosaur dinosaur dinosaur

Let me start out by noting Suits is a game inspired by OFF, a game by Mortis Ghost. In all honesty, I liked OFF a little more, but I did enjoy this game. For a dollar, it's totally worth it, even if it's only a couple hours long.
The gameplay itself wasn't very inspired. I found myself using the same three strategies the entire game: Use Staple Down to disable strong, single enemies, use Staple Storm to beat groups, and attack the rest of the time. Ultimately, you should sail through it, as long as you be sure to get the best equips at all times. One interesting note is that most of your funds come from doing optional things, rather than only battling. That's pretty cool, because it gives you a reason to explore a little, even thought it's not exactly a vast world.
The visuals are very unique and interesting, but if you don't love the general uniqueness, you'll likely hate it, because it's all drawn in black and white. The music is pretty good actually, though not good enough to go searching Youtube for it. Overall, I'd say these are both nice for what they are.
The most important thing is the adventure, despite everything previously mentioned. The story is an interesting social commentary, with witty bits of comedy scattered through the entire game. The generallly cynical atmosphere is a great change of pace, and the whole game experience is one huge satirical parody of the greed and corruption of those in power and the mundane lives people are programmed to live, working as small cogs their whole lives for these powers. It's really frightening to have to accept this reality, but it's unfortunately accurate. People are expected to live as workers. As for the corporate and political corruption, that's all true as well, just not to a degree where society is openly a place where justice is bought, the poor are used as spare parts and people are punished for not buying things. You cannot deny that there are scandals, however. I believe the CEO of McDonald's once stated that if any of his competitors were to drown, he'd put a hose in their mouth.
To wrap things up, this game is not expensive at all and a very unique experience, and I would reccommend it for those reasons.
Amazing game. For a dollar, this game provides humor, a good story, and well crafted fighting. I highly recommend playing this game, and am excited for any further developments to the series.

A simple, yet surreal little RPG heavily inspired by OFF.  You play as The Guy (no really), just another Suit in Suit City, where Corporations run everything and your worth begins and ends with your work output.  What begins as a simple job to sue an uncooperative potential buyer quickly spirals into a conspiracy and civil war, with you stuck in the middle.
Gameplay is the standard RPG Maker combat.  Its turnbased, and the enemies are surprisingly colorful, varied and unique.  Most of the enemies are handplaced and unique.  In fact, random encounters don't actually become commonplace until halfway through the game after a certain plot development.
The game really shines in its writing.  It is an unapologetic pastiche of capitalism, materialism, and other kinds of -isms.  Its wacky, surreal, and surprisingly dark at times.
Its short, but given the low low price its acceptable.  If you want a quick, quirky and fun RPG, give it a go.  Its literally pocket change.

TL:DR; Great game aside from some issues that I note below. Not worth full price as one low chaos playthrough takes about 10 hours on your first go. Try to pickup this game on sale if you can.
I enjoyed this game, I got it discounted and I'm not sure if I would reccomend it for the full $60. But anyway heres some things I really enjoyed and some warnings.
These are some things Arkane could of improved on:
- This game doesn't deliever the same experience as Dishonored, that game was special and provided a totally new and insane experience all on its own with a deep story filled with twists and betrayal. Not to forget it created the legendary combat system that this game very well expands on in every way possible. But overall the very themes of this game aren't anything like Dishonored, this game is quite hopeful and the cities you explore are filled with life and people; which is nice but produces different themes and you might not be as interested in it due to this. Whereas Dishonored's themes were dark and diseased, and everything from the city and dialouge showed this, it was sureal being in a city filled with death and suffering like Dunwall.
- The characters aren't as good as in Dishonored. In Dishonored 2 we see meet many characters and some of them have the potential to be some of the best in the series, esspecially the inventor, but none of them live up to it and heres why: no characters in this game get any chances to draw out their personalities and show who they really are, and because of this every character you meet is very 2 dimensional. The only character in this game that had their personality drawn out to show they're more than a blank slate was Corvo, mainly due to his new found voice as he actually speaks in this game, and quite allot at that. Personally I hated this decision to make Corvo talk as much as he did, in Dishonored he was a slient protanist and this was the basis for his identity, you see a silhouette of his face on the cover and thats as much as you get to see. And I loved it, I loved the powerful, silent character Arkane made Corvo and wish that they had toned it down a bit in this game as its kind of ruined that perfect character they had made in Dishonored.
- The story is actually a little sub-par, esspecially compared to the orginal Dishonored. Delilah just shows up, kicks you off the throne and freezes the other character. Thats it, thats the motivation. You wont ever see Delilah again until the climax of the story. Arkane seemily tries very hard to build her character in forced void sequences, but because you cant tell the different between the truth and her lies its mostly usless as its just left to your interpretation anyway: "she might be lying, she might not be? Who knows, you cant tell".
- They compromised less missions for bigger levels, which means you can be spending 1 hour on a single level if its your first low chaos playthrough; as you're spending most of that time trying to figure out where things are in these huge levels, which is a little annoying. But a nice thing about Dishonored was all the different targets and types of missions you got to do over all these levels, even if the mission levels weren't anywhere as big as Dishonored 2's. And the places you vist in Dishonored accross these missions built the world in far more ways than one big level ever could of.
- Game isn't incredibly optimized either.
- Everything else. Notably building on the combat systems from Dishonored and adding even cooler, newer abilties. Also NG+ is the♥♥♥♥♥♥
