TL;DR - The Evil Within 2 is a vast improvement over its predecessor, placing more focus on building up the atmosphere and environment rather than overemphasis of blood and gore.
---
Gameplay for TEW2 is vastly improved. Gunplay is pretty much the same as the original but the stealth aspect of the game is better now with the cover mechanic. There are different types of weapons for each categories that each serve their different purposes which caters to the different needs of players. i.e. stealthy players may focus more on the silenced pistol to draw enemies one by one, whereas players who prefer straight up combat may go for the more powerful revolver or the more accurate laser-sighted pistol.
Upgrades for weapons and stats for Sebastian are now separated, with weapon parts for upgrading weapons and green gels for upgrading Sebastian and granting him new abilities. In that way, not only can the player build their character according to the playstyle they like, it's is also more difficult to get into the situation whereby the player feels like he/she wasted the materials they used. In addition, green gels actually grants certain useful abilities to Sebastian, such as the ability to strike at unaware enemies from cover, automatically freeing themselves from a grab with a bottle or increased weapon damage with consecutive hits. This is a great departure from the small, minute improvements you get from green gels in the original game.
Crafting is also introduced and seems to draw heavily from Resident Evil 7. This feature gives the player some leeway in using their supplies when venturing through the world, easing them from some on the situations possibly face in the original game whereby they just have not enough bullets to take any boss down. Yet at the same time to prevent this from being abused, the great idea of increased cost when not crafting at a crafting table is greatly increased to deter the wasting of materials unless absolutely desperate for them. I thought this is a really good idea.
Instead of the mostly linear path like the original, TEW2 is now set in an open-world-ish town with a few sidequests that gives more insight on what the background of this game is about.
Story is still whack depending on how invested you were in the lore of the previous title. Newly-inducted players are more likely to find everything more acceptable while the veterans might find the sudden introduction of the new characters (i.e. the daughter) to be more...abrupt.
The best part of this game is the atmosphere and some of the disturbing monsters that haunt you throughout your exploration of the world. With minute usage of jumpscares, the focus and details on the background, eerie music and sometimes cramped environment keeps the players constantly on guard.
I have only one complain - the length of the game feels a bit too short. For a game of this price, i'd expect the story to run on a bit over 25 hours. Playing through the game trying to find all the extra events nets me a total of 15 hours, although to be fair i did not manage to find anything. I also did not try the new game plus mode or higher difficulties.
Whether you liked the original game or not, TEW2 is sure to be a welcomed addition to your library of games.

It has a few issues but Alien: Isolation stands as one of the best survival horror games in recent years.
The reason Alien: Isolation works so well as a horror game is because it largely uses unscripted horror elements. Sure there are a few scripted jump scarry things but they are few and far between. The jumpscares in this case help elevate the tension rather than being the main horror conceit of the piece. The horror in this title is created near perfectly by the tension in the gameplay, the result of attempting to get from point A to point B while a giant human blender stomps around actively searching for a tasty human nuggets. There are also human and android enemies which aren't too scary in their own right but come with their own sense of dread because dealing with them may mean you will attract the attention of something far worse, plus those android guys are tough as nails to kill. The AI for all the enemies is really ingenous, just when I think I had figured out the the alien or the androids AI enough to trick the game sytems to getting past it they do something the completely surprises me. The humans were always pretty stupid but they more or less act as canon fodder. Dealing with the alien though is always so nerve wracking because you never quite know what you can get away with. I know this may be a sticking point for some but I like the approach that sometimes you can fire a gun and the alien will not be alerted and then sometimes he will be on top of you in like 2 seconds. It creates a great sense of risk and reward to gameplay that immersed me even further into the situations.
The game reminded me a bit of System Shock 2, except with more cowering in the corner, oh wait that's exactly like system shock 2. Also like in SS2, you spend a lot of the game just trying to figure out how to repair the broken down space station so you can get to your objective point, which means you often have to organically search about the environment for things like key codes or key cards to open doors, or use distractions on enemies so you have enough time to cut through a door with a blow torch. This means a lot of sections will probably feel very tedious to some because it will have you get a keycard to open a door, to get in a vent, to get to a room where you can turn on a generator, so that you can power up another door, and so on. But, the tedium never bothered me most of the time because I was completely immersed in nearly every situation.
While the active storytelling, like what you see in cutscenes and diologue, is pretty mediocre, what really shines is the storytelling through environment design. Sevasterpol has got to be one of my favorite sci-fi worlds explored in a video game because of how beautifully crafted it is. I am such a sucker for retrofuturism especially retrofuturism where all the computer systems run on a DOS-like operating system on old green and black crt monitors. The story of Sevasterpol is a more interesting story than Amanda Ripley's and I loved reading about its history through various audio logs and computer database entries like some kind of digital archeologist. The rich environment design is also paired with probably one of the best audio-designs ever put in a game. A great soundtrack paired with incredibly detailed sound effects really contribute to an extremely immersible environment.
Overall, I highly recomend this game. While I will say that it may be a tad over-long for some and the ending goes a little chaotic at the end at least it builds up to that rather than starting the game at chaos and at least it is a game that understands the fragile subtly of genuine horror. I'm just honestly glad this game exists. It may not have perfected everything but it stands as an exception to the samey AAA video game market and really stands out because of it. Lastly, I would definitely recomend that most players play the game on Hard.

As the sequel to my absolute favourite game ever, I expected A LOT from this game, and for the most part it delivered. Dark Souls II has improved very much on the first game specifically fixing the frame rate and online issues, but seems to fall short a little gameplay wise. The mechanics are almost the exact same as Dark Souls, which is good because the original Dark Souls mechanics were near perfect, the main difference being the implimentation of dual wielding. The first game seemed to attempt dual wielding, but it turned out very wrong, making the player's left-hand weapon act closer to a sheild than a sword, axe, mace, etc. But Dark Souls II has implimented a dual wielding system which very effectivly allows the use of each individual weapon as well as both together; however this added mechanic doesn't make up for this game's decently worse gameplay. One of the main problems I have with Dark Souls II is the difficulty. While this game is, without a doubt, hard, it is most often in a much different way than the previous title. Rather than making bosses and enemies have hard to work around movesets, more often than not this game just throws tons of the same enemies at you, which makes building AoE heavy incredibly easy, and building single target damage incredibly hard: I often times had to unequip my ceastus and pull out my claymore just due to the shear amount of "minions", to use a D&D term.
In conclusion, the mechanics of the game are fleshed out and flow better, but the story, enemies, and world are very much less engaging. While this is the worse of the two Dark Souls games, it absolutly does live up to its predecessor's name, and thus I would still recomend it to any and everyone.

Right. So what do I say about Black Mesa? I have to be perfectly honest, I really loved this game. Black Mesa is a fantastic remaster of the first Half Life game that came out in 1998. Black Mesa is the remaster of that game.
The game runs on the standard source engine but the graphics and textures in this game are sooo damm good, im running this game on a I5 4460 and a Gigabyte GTX 960 IX OC 2GB edition graphics card and the game runs at more than 80 frames per second, some of the times it might drop the frame rate, I had the frame rate drop to 44 and even 24 sometimes for me but then again, a lot of things were going on in that specific area. I would have to say that the PC optimization is really great, it gets an A+ from me.
The new weapon models and textures in this game are also really good, you have some of your classic weapons like the MP5 with the grenade launcher or the Spas 12 shotgun remade in the new remastered version. The sound effects are really very designed, definitely a big improvement from the original game.
Now while I like this game a lot and I think it’s a perfect remaster of the original Half Life game, it’s not finished. It’s in early access for a reason and that is because it’s missing a huge part of the game which is known as Xen. At first I thought that Xen was some kind of DLC story for the original Half Life game, well it turns out that it’s not. To put it in a way for people to understand. Xen is the ending of the game and the final level and it’s missing from the game, yea so the final area that you were supposed to be where you would finish the game is missing, it is kind of disappointing and I was a bit sad about it. But the developers did say that they are working on it, when can we expect an ETA? We don’t know unfortunately.
The other little problem that I had with this game is the broken AI, luckily there is a fix for it that I made, check out my guide right here to fix this issue -
Right as for the issue, basically what it does is basically makes the enemies stupidly overpowered, you can’t hide anywhere because they will rush your position, you can’t peak out on them because they will start shooting you before you can, they deal huge amount of damage and it just ruins the game experience, you can use my guide to fix this issue until the developers decide to fix this issue.
Another small little issue is that sometimes when im playing the game becomes rather confusing, sometimes im stuck in a game area for around 20 minutes and I have no idea on what to do because the game doesn’t hint it to you or anything of that kind, it becomes rather frustrating trying to figure out what to do when you in fact have no idea what to do. The Developers could definitely work on this.
And so we come forward to my final words, do I recommend this game? It’s a tough question, at one hand Black Mesa is a fantastic remaster of the original 1998 Half Life but at the same time it’s missing Xen which is in fact an entire game ending, but even without Xen the game will give you hours upon hours of content before you even get to the suppose ending of the game.
In my opinion, buy Black Mesa on a sale or buy it now, while it does miss Xen it does feature a big amount of content that will keep you playing for a few days or maybe even weeks, the other option is that you can wait and buy Black Mesa when the Xen update comes out making it the full game. But this game deserves an 8/10 from me, really fantastic remaster of the original Half Life but it has some issues and is missing some content.
I will update my review if Xen ever comes out or if we get some new exciting content to give it a look at.

There's most likely going to be a lot of criticism towards anyones opinions that are 'against' this mod, and for those who do so, you're simply going to be ignored.
Firstly, NMRIH does well on atmosphere and environment. The level design could do with some work, I've noticed some areas on maps that are just ridiculous and not well suited for the mods style of gameplay. However the settings it portrays are realistic and very immersive. The atmosphere is created very well not only from the map design but also from the sounds, the lighting as well as the gloomy soundtrack in the background. It all creates for a eery and perfectly matched apocalyptic setting.
The core gameplay mixes dependant on the gamemode and maps and other aspects. Most of the time you'll be doing pretty much the same thing, but it can get pretty intense and NMRIH does well to remind you just how realisitcly challenging a zombie apocalypse could really be. You'll have to spare ammo to other surivors or saviour your firearms for when you really need them. You'll have to quickly decide what tools and weapons to take as you only have a set limit of items you can carry. You'll have to learn to identify ammo types and weather or not you need them for your weapons or not. You'd be wise to avoid combat with zombies unless you really need to...
That last bit of advice goes without saying, the melee system in this mod is flawed. If you can manage it, you'll be lucky to club a zombie around the head as hard as you humanly can (forceful blunt weapon trauma to the head clearly isn't the way to KO a zombie) and get away with it.  Most of the time, you'll get grabbed and be forced to shove the zombie off of you, before realising that you've almost instantantiously been infected from barely seconds of being throttled...
Personally I'm all for realism but NMRIH really fails to deliver a satisying approach to the melee and survival approach when you've been, pardon my French, "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥tted" by a mere shambler despite how full your health is or despite your best efforts to redecorate a zombies face. The melee system isn't rewarding in the slightest, it's damn right awkward and just ridiculous. The way around I found is to charge up your attack, then carefully execute an attack from behind or at a distance. A lot of livid fans have spoken up and mentioned that this adds to the realism. It doesn't. It makes the gameplay an annoying struggle. The concept of little ammo and salvaging precious items is fun, but badly made melee combat in a zombie apocalypse game that offers that concept of combat more, over firing precious rounds is scandalous.
I guess in a sense, it adds to the realism of how difficult a zombie outbreak really is. There are servers that offer infinite ammo if you do get sick of every other player stealing the goods or just being selfish, these servers are usually pretty fun to play on and still offer a challenge as you can't sprint around and you still have the realistically slow reload times. Other than that, the gamemodes offer, or rather push the players to test their survival skills as well as teamwork capability. However when so many players are used to being the lone wolf, it's often hard to succeed in this area. The gamemodes are rather fun and do offer a challenge and be you lucky to make it to the end - you might be met with a satisfying achievement!
The mod feels fantastic, I personally love immersion and atmosphere. I've often been terrified when turning round to see a zombie spawn out of no-where right behind me - even after double checking the area was clear. I kid of course, I won't punish this mod any further, but the child zombies - yes if you've not played NMRIH yet, there are child zombies (Which I personally found quite interesting considering it would possibly bring controversy, however it didn't... so good job guys :D). NMRIH definitely brings a fresh experience to the zombie apocalypse theme, however nothing ground breaking. If you're looking for a fairly substantial and "realistic" experience, NMRIH might just be for you.
Oh and it's free, so it really won't hurt you at all to pick it up and have a shot ;) (Unless the mods flaws♥♥♥♥♥♥you off xD)
A good mod that really still needs a bit of tweaking to make things more enjoyable, however it is a solid and well created mod. I recommend this game to zombie lovers and fps fans, also realism lovers too.
I rate NMRIH a 7.1/10

I grew up playing King's Quest 5 and 6. King's Quest 6 is possibly my favorite game ever, not because it is the 'best game' or the 'best story'.... but because it was the perfect game at the perfect time for me in my child hood. Fast forward to King's Quest by Odd Gentlemen. It hit the tone, humor, and wonder that I remember from the early King's Quests.
At times the emphasis on puzzles was tedious, but the story and tone of the adventure was perfect. The 'story within a story' method was wonderful and I truly cared about the characters by the end. For old school adventurers, note: I found itmore enjoyable to play with game controller, because the mechanisms worked better.
The references back to older games in artwork and characters truly made me enjoy playing all the chapters. When I heard "Girl in the Tower" in Episode 3 playing my wife rushed up to me in concern because I was crying with joy.
Episode 1 is the longest and best.
Episode 3 and 5 are my next favorites with great story and emotion.
Episode 2 had a good hurry up mechanic, but was a bit frustrating at times with "what do I do next"
Episode 4 was my least favorite because of its emphasis on "puzzles" instead of typical point and click mechanics.
Definitely worth playing through for the story, especially because decisions int he first Episode effect the later episodes. For those of you who played the originals, you will enjoy!

I really enjoyed this game, not just as a tribute to the original games but as an adventure on it's own. Each chapter can be finished with multiple solutions and the story is affected by various choices. The chapters are much longer than the Telltale games and expand upon the original stories without changing anything too much.

This series was such a surprise, and one of my favorite of the year. While none of the individual chapters, except Ch1, could be called great, the overall package is excellent. I actually appreciated how different some of the chapters were, and how they often focused of different sub-genres that the Adventure game genre has branched out to.  For anyone with any memories of the previous King's Quest games, or like adventure games with characters that you WILL get emotionally attached to, I fully recommend.
I completed all chapters with several different paths (Xbone and Steam).

Loving this game so far, having played 4 of 5 chapters. King's Quest has a wonderful sense of humour, great aesthetics and fun puzzles. What stands out most to me though is how touching it can be. Is it worth a buy? Yes, if you have friends. No, if you don't.

We don't see the same things happening on our screens. Characters, both players and NPC, teleport all the time. I am dead but do not appear so on his screen. He walks through walls that appear intact to me but are destroyed for him... And also, everytime there is a cutscene, a super annoying bug happens where the game restarts after the cutscene for one player, but not the other who has no choice but have his character remain static and most likely die.
What a shame. This game is full of good ideas.
Until now we gave it some slack, saying "it is early access, they will fix it, we believe". We have tried coming back to this game several times and the problem was always here, but we decided to cope with it because we had hope for the future. In part because the game was easier and with less enemies, making lag more forgiving.
The issue is even more problematic now that there are new harder levels with more ennemies : those levels are just an unplayable lagfest.
You even have lag against the final boss, which should not happen as it is a single enemy. But my guess is that the guys who programmed this game have no idea what "dead reckoning" is, or can't implement it. (FYI it's a basic netcode technique).
Developers, you now have removed the early access tag from your game, so there is no excuse anymore. This is supposed to be a complete working product. And it's not.
Multiplayer, which is supposed to be the best thing about the game, does not work. maybe it does for soime other people, but for us both it didn't.
I bought that game hoping to have fun with that friend which I can't often see in real life. Technically we did have a little fun, but I can't in all honesty recommend a game that caused this much frustrations because it does not work properly.
Maybe get this game if you can play multiplayer local. But do
get it for online mode, disappointment is likely.

The Elder Scrolls: Online looks and feels (relatively) like an Elder scrolls game. Many of Elder Scroll's signature features         (pick-pocketing, sneaking, lock-picking, etc.) exist in this MMO.
However, one of the few things I'm not a huge fan of is being limited to 5 spells/abilities on your castbar. This technially exceeds to 10 upon reaching level 15, where you can switch out an alternate set of weapon(s) and spells. However, despite being limited to 5 spells, the game pulls it off.
TESO provides technially no limitations to players who don't subscribe to a monthly fee. While subscribers get all DLC with their game, non-subscribers can easily just purchase each individual DLC, and even purchase bundles of said DLC with some little extra goodies.
The microtransactions (Crown Store) are mostly cosmetic, with of course the optional purchase of DLC/Expansions included in the Crown Store, and very few items that actually help with gameplay (Such as purchasing extra bag space for real money, or purchasing experience boosts, and "Crafting Motifs" which allow for the skill to craft specific racial armor styles) Some may argue the Crown Store is ridiculous; it's really not. Everything in the Crown Store that is not cosmetic can be earned in-game without real purchase. (Experience boosts being the exception)
The game so far has provided plenty of content to satisfy my $60 purchase, and that's just in the first 15 levels of the game in one area of the entire map. There are still plenty more zones and levels and quests to accomplish beyond that, and then there are the expansion packs.
This game is not just a generic MMO with Elder Scrolls slapped onto it, and if you're looking for an MMO to get into, I strongly recommend this one.

Review: Dishonored 2 in my opinion is the closest thing we'll ever get to a Thief 4. While most people will shout negatives at this game on steam for performance. The only negative I have with the game is that it's not "Thief" enough. The sound design is not as good as the Thief series and that is integral to a First Person Stealth Sim like Dishonored wants to be. The fact that sound does not matter until 'Very Hard' and even then it's not really a true mechanic is quite puzzeling to me. The only other negative I have is that I cannot retract Corvo's blade and use it as an equivalent to the Black Jack from Thief. I am fine with choking people out but the fact that it's almost my only option to knock people out is kinda lame IMO.
Before I move forward with my review I would like to say that if they make a Dishonored 3 PLEASE give us that choice. I think it would be cool to be in situations where some guards have metal helmets, so that, I have no other choice BUT to choke them out. Then a lot of guards would be wearing hats or nothing at all and I could just run up to them and bop them on the head. It would be so much more interesting to me from a gameplay perspective.Then If they also made sound matter imagine having to worry about being on Marble, Stone, Metal, and anything that makes a lot of noise. Those are the gameplay elements of Thief that I loved to death. Jumping down from above onto my Moss Arrow patch and then smacking a guard on the head. It was seamless gameplay, no context sensitive BS.
Anyways, sorry for that loooong tangent but it had to be said. Overall I DO LOVE this game a lot. It and DOOM are my favorite games of the entire year. The performance issues on my end have been completely ironed out. Plus, I bought it on sale so not having to pay that full sixty was definitely a plus. The game definitely captures MOST of Thief's style. It's like 80% there. Stephen Russell voicing Corvo alone is literally enough to bump that up to 85% if I'm being totally honest. Just like Thief and Garrett of the past Corvo will comment on things around him and make witty quips. The dialogue is pretty damn good so far and I would say it's pretty on par with Thief. This game was my dream come true in a nutshell. I totally say give it a shot if you loved Thief.

It has a few issues but Alien: Isolation stands as one of the best survival horror games in recent years.
The reason Alien: Isolation works so well as a horror game is because it largely uses unscripted horror elements. Sure there are a few scripted jump scarry things but they are few and far between. The jumpscares in this case help elevate the tension rather than being the main horror conceit of the piece. The horror in this title is created near perfectly by the tension in the gameplay, the result of attempting to get from point A to point B while a giant human blender stomps around actively searching for a tasty human nuggets. There are also human and android enemies which aren't too scary in their own right but come with their own sense of dread because dealing with them may mean you will attract the attention of something far worse, plus those android guys are tough as nails to kill. The AI for all the enemies is really ingenous, just when I think I had figured out the the alien or the androids AI enough to trick the game sytems to getting past it they do something the completely surprises me. The humans were always pretty stupid but they more or less act as canon fodder. Dealing with the alien though is always so nerve wracking because you never quite know what you can get away with. I know this may be a sticking point for some but I like the approach that sometimes you can fire a gun and the alien will not be alerted and then sometimes he will be on top of you in like 2 seconds. It creates a great sense of risk and reward to gameplay that immersed me even further into the situations.
The game reminded me a bit of System Shock 2, except with more cowering in the corner, oh wait that's exactly like system shock 2. Also like in SS2, you spend a lot of the game just trying to figure out how to repair the broken down space station so you can get to your objective point, which means you often have to organically search about the environment for things like key codes or key cards to open doors, or use distractions on enemies so you have enough time to cut through a door with a blow torch. This means a lot of sections will probably feel very tedious to some because it will have you get a keycard to open a door, to get in a vent, to get to a room where you can turn on a generator, so that you can power up another door, and so on. But, the tedium never bothered me most of the time because I was completely immersed in nearly every situation.
While the active storytelling, like what you see in cutscenes and diologue, is pretty mediocre, what really shines is the storytelling through environment design. Sevasterpol has got to be one of my favorite sci-fi worlds explored in a video game because of how beautifully crafted it is. I am such a sucker for retrofuturism especially retrofuturism where all the computer systems run on a DOS-like operating system on old green and black crt monitors. The story of Sevasterpol is a more interesting story than Amanda Ripley's and I loved reading about its history through various audio logs and computer database entries like some kind of digital archeologist. The rich environment design is also paired with probably one of the best audio-designs ever put in a game. A great soundtrack paired with incredibly detailed sound effects really contribute to an extremely immersible environment.
Overall, I highly recomend this game. While I will say that it may be a tad over-long for some and the ending goes a little chaotic at the end at least it builds up to that rather than starting the game at chaos and at least it is a game that understands the fragile subtly of genuine horror. I'm just honestly glad this game exists. It may not have perfected everything but it stands as an exception to the samey AAA video game market and really stands out because of it. Lastly, I would definitely recomend that most players play the game on Hard.

As the sequel to my absolute favourite game ever, I expected A LOT from this game, and for the most part it delivered. Dark Souls II has improved very much on the first game specifically fixing the frame rate and online issues, but seems to fall short a little gameplay wise. The mechanics are almost the exact same as Dark Souls, which is good because the original Dark Souls mechanics were near perfect, the main difference being the implimentation of dual wielding. The first game seemed to attempt dual wielding, but it turned out very wrong, making the player's left-hand weapon act closer to a sheild than a sword, axe, mace, etc. But Dark Souls II has implimented a dual wielding system which very effectivly allows the use of each individual weapon as well as both together; however this added mechanic doesn't make up for this game's decently worse gameplay. One of the main problems I have with Dark Souls II is the difficulty. While this game is, without a doubt, hard, it is most often in a much different way than the previous title. Rather than making bosses and enemies have hard to work around movesets, more often than not this game just throws tons of the same enemies at you, which makes building AoE heavy incredibly easy, and building single target damage incredibly hard: I often times had to unequip my ceastus and pull out my claymore just due to the shear amount of "minions", to use a D&D term.
In conclusion, the mechanics of the game are fleshed out and flow better, but the story, enemies, and world are very much less engaging. While this is the worse of the two Dark Souls games, it absolutly does live up to its predecessor's name, and thus I would still recomend it to any and everyone.

This game is a love letter to Roberta Williams and our childhoods.  It is full of heart and pays great respect to the original games, while forging ahead to make a new story.
The graphics and sound are wonderful, and the voice acting is superb.  The choice of Christopher Lloyd for the aged King Graham is perfect and he brings the character to life in a way only he could.
If there was anything not to like about it, it would be the excessive use of puzzle-gimmicks...one of the chapters is dedicated to (I thought) annoying puzzles that didn't do too much to advance the story...but even these were wrapped around a father's love for his children.
There are plenty of references to the original games, both obvious and subtle, and plenty of new interpretations on them that don't make you say: "but that's not what happened."
The user interface is incredibly, perhaps overly, simple.  King's Quest I-IV had parser interfaces, in which you could type whatever sentences you want.  KQV-VI had point and click interfaces with five options...this new KQ reduces it down to one button, which is context sensitive, and does feel a bit oversimple.  The game isn't hard, but it is fun.
I nominated this game for the 'something in my eye' category.  The Sierra Games were a big part of my youth and seeing Graham so well handled made me very happy.  I hope you'll give this game a chance, it really deserves it.
But is it King's Quest?
Yes. Yes, it is.  I really believe that Roberta would be proud of this.

I highly recommend this game if:
-You enjoyed the first Evil Within (albeit the 2nd one I found was far less "horrific" but had just as many tense moments and twisted environments)
-You are a fan of the survival horror genre in general, most notably games such as RE4, Dead Space series-the gameplay is very similar, 3rd person, some RPG elements/and stealth.
-You want to experience taking LSD without actually taking LSD.
-Psychological torture manifesting itself in the form of ghastly killers is something you'd like to learn a bit more about
I don't recommend this game if:
-You are very averse to horror-it's not as scary as the first, but as far as games go it's still pretty scary/demented at times
-A top notch story is a must-the story isn't bad but definitely not what carries the game, I'd rate it a B.
-You have any heart conditions-some moments will make your heart pound!!
If I had to name the biggest development from the first game to the second, it would definitely have to be the addition of the more "open world" feel. While the game isn't completely open world, as once you go past certain chapters, you can only go forward (or on rails), there is still the addition of side quests in this game if you want to get special unlocks or additional story that is not required to actually complete the game.
The gameplay is definitely an improvement over the first, the first game was definitely frustrating at times on PC but issues were few and far between in the 2nd game on PC.
With deaths included, the game on nightmare mode took me about 20 hours to complete with all the side missions I could find, I doubt I missed more than one or two. I still missed plenty of unlockables though so I'd say if you want a "100%" completion (no real way to track), it'd probably take around 25-30 hours.
All in all, I loved this game and look forward to New Game+, a definite must play if you are a fan of the Resident Evil/Silent Hill/Dead Space survival horror series.
Gameplay rating:9/10-Aside from toggling wall hugs, there were very little issues with the controls, stealth feels great, shooting felt great even on nightmare without auto assist aiming.
Graphics rating: 9/10- Cinematic scenes looked great, and gameplay graphics were not far behind
Story rating: 8.5/10-Better than the first game, lots of answered questions that went unanswered
in first game, but overall typical Dad trying to save daughter story.
Survival rating:10/10-You have to pull all the stops on Nightmare, and Survival difficulty is probably no cake walk either.
Horror Rating: 9.5/10: Not as in your face ♥♥♥♥ing demented like the first, but still has plenty of shock value/heart-pounding moments that will have you on the edge of your seat.
Sound rating: 10/10- The music (or lack thereof in some areas) controls the ambience so well, makes you cringe at times, and drives the suspense as it should in any game in the genre.
Overall rating: 9.3/10

My oh my there is so much wrong with this game.
I know this review will frustrate and offend some people, so let's start with a disclaimer: you may like this game.
It's perfectly fine. Sometimes people love bad games. I can even say that the fist Evil Within might be arguably bad game that I really liked.
I would not mind people highlighting the flaws in EW1, because, boy, did this game have a lot of them.
I don't see much of the same critique of the EW2.
So before you would start downvoting this review without even reading it, let me note that the goal of this review is not to criticize whether you should like EW2 or not, but to highlight all of the stuff that is wrong with it.
Disclaimer 2: there was always a certain trend of common opinion about games, a certain consensus of what is good or what is bad driven by a game journalism and media.
For example EW2 is considered as a good game, while, say, Dead Space 3 was considered as a bad game. Why do I think there is a trend and it is relevant?
Because, honestly, EW2 and DS3 have almost identical set of gameplay problems and narrative issues.
It is very difficult to go against this kind of trends. It's very difficult to say, that, let's say RE6 was good or RE7 was bad because pretty much everyone arround you saying exactly the opposite and fueling this self-sustaing loop of self-conviction and conformity.
I don't mind going against common consensus, because, frankly, I don't really care what other people think and Bethesda is not paying me.
===============
This review assume that you played the first game and liked it, or at least tolerated it.
Q: I did not play the first game.
A: It is a mix of GTA and dead space 3. If you like this kind of stuff, you will like EW2.
Q: I did not play the first game and I don't care, second one is good.
A: It is incredibly tricky situation. The big problem about EW2 is that it is not a standalone game. It's not even a reboot like RE7 was. A lot of stuff in EW2 or gameplay elements will make you scratch your head if you did not play the first one. The whole cast of characters and their motivations would make no sense to you if you did not play original.
1. Introduction
Let me repeat that EW1 was not a perfect game. It was incredibly difficult and frustrating and suffered from a huge pacing issues. However if it could not be the only thing, than it was not DULL.
Secondary, the game was made by a Shinji Mikami, a guy who designed almost all clasic Resident Evils (RE1, RE2, RE4). While he is listed as a producer and supervisor of EW2, I think he was about as much of a supervisor as Hideo Kojima was a supervisor for Castlevania. I.e. not related to game at all.
This fact is important because EW1 was a game made in a genre that the creator of the game established in a first place. EW1 is not just a Survivor Horror, it's Mikami Survival Horror.
Imagine watching George Romero movie and discovering it's a documentary war drama. Or magine playing Silent Hill 3 and discovering it is a flight simulator. This is a kind of thinks you usually don't do and for a reason, continuity of the genre is really important.
So we have a flaved game with a lot of good ideas. All what Studio Tango should've done is to take it and to fix the problems and iterate on them. So basically do what RE2 did to RE1. Fix what is broken, keep what is working.
What a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥it turned into.
2. Story and setting.
How did it happened? EW2 is directed by John Johanas, the guy who directed EW1 Kidman DLC. It was not perfect, not quite EW1, but an interesting and refreshing derivation from the original. I was not happy of him being director of the sequel, but I hoped that at least he can immitate the style of Mikami. I can imagine him sitting at night full of hatred to the original work. "I will make the thing that will mock and humilate your work, Shinji, that will destroy the very spirit of it, and, worst, people will *love* it".
What is a first word that comes to your mind when you think of EW1? *Nightmare*
The world of EW1 is essentially the collective uncontiosness of different people merged in a single reality that is slowly transforming into a horror world.
We don't know what is happening in the game. For the 75% of the story we don't even suspect that the world around us is not even /real/.
This is a nightmare that does not have rules and structure, that is formed and shaped in a dreamscape panorama by deep fears and desires of game characters. Why do we stuck in the land of abandoned villages and decaying mansions? Because this was a kind of chilhood Kidman had. Why there are pieces of almost mundane clarity where everything looks normal and stable? Becasue this is the kind of reality Sebastian and Leslie would expect. Why everything is getting corrupted and destroyed? Because the main antoganist is an incredibly psychotic and unstable person.
The is nothing like this in EW2.
What is a first word you would use to discribe EW2? "A videogame". Or "a virtual reality".
I think the only biggest crime EW1 did is to introdeuce the concept of STEM. Maybe they though the story would be too confusing for people, so they did give some explanation that there is a machine that link minds together. EW2 is all about trying to explain how STEM works and establish it rules.
The nightmare turned into a huge hollow predictable open world, where monsters respawn in animated cuscenes and game points exactly where and when it happens.
Every  item is glowing, no GLOWING so you wont miss it. Every active zone is highlighted or marked with icon. The game constantly breaks the immersion with cutscenes or intermissions, the first enemy in this game is not even _introduced_, it's just "Hey, look, there are zombies, go hit them with knife or something".
(I found it peculiar that the story, in a nutshell, is a tale of soulles burecrats lackign any imagination who turned the world of endless possibilities and incredible depths into a hollow formalistic husk that falls apart around the seams, which, is, if you think about it a bit, ironically what happened to the game itself.
I don't know if it is a clever shoutout of the game aware of this meta nature, or just a random act of divine serendipity.)
-
3. Design and writing
The problem with setting is hugely reinforced by a design.
EW1 was released in 2014. EW2 three years later. You would never guess by the game graphics, EW2 looks at least five years older than the original.
Every single location in EW1 was very detailed, unique and beautifully crafted. EW2, now facing the challenges of the open world, replaced it with a bunch of empty tunnels and boxes connected together.
Evil Within 1 monsters were unusual and interesting. The first zombie you met are glitchy and corrupted humans with missing limbs and barberd wire coils growing from their faces.
Ewil Within 2 mosters are zombies with glowing eyes. Just zombies.
The boss designs of EW2 are either lazy or just a copy from the other games. Laura in EW1 was a Grade A nightmare fuel. EW2 replaced here with a ghost lady that just sings and floats, because, ghosts are apparently shpooky. Camera lady is a weak copy of Warden.
Characters have no story or motivation or any depth around it.
Existing characters were turned into completely opposite versions of themself. Sebastian is now a whiny ♥♥♥♥♥. Kidman is not a naive Jill Valentine-style newcomer, but an edgy teen listenign to the nightcore. (Also she seems never washing her head or sleeping in the last 3 month).
New characters are so generic that I don't even remember their names and roles. They are either shown for 2 seconds in some cutscene as a plot device to completely disappear for the rest of the game, or just keep annoying you as an NPC in a safe zone. (But they don't have anything interesting to say or give you).

Great game.
I'll be brief.
For new players:
Game is a limited, semi-open world segmented by chapters and linear set pieces. To give an example, the first two chapters are small and linear, while the third chapter is larger and open world. This is the template the entire game follows from the first to the last chapter.
It is a third person shooter not unlike Dead Space, however, there is greater emphasis in stealth and cautious gameplay than the run-and-gun style of the Dead Space series and RE:5 - 6.
All in all, a rather atmospheric and excellent horror game to play.
For returning (Played Evil Within 1):
My feelings upon finishing this game were mixed; I can tell that Shinji Mikami was not the director behind the game's development. It lacks the typical asian flair of horror games with absurd plots, eccentric, garrish, or flamboyant characters, and the extreme dark and gritty violent, tense atmosphere from the first game. I honestly did miss the first game's atmosphere; the first game was a descent into hell. Beacon was a far more foreboding place than Union could have ever hoped to have been. This may be a dissenting opinion, but I feel that the story/atmosphere in the sequel was weaker than that of its predecessor. That is not to say it isn't decent; it holds itself well enough and has a distinctly American feel to it. (American made plotlines tend to be far more cohesive and grounded than that of the Japanese) Of course, it is all still campy and insane as hell but magnitudes less.
However, the combat systems, stealth, weapon upgrade and character upgrades are far better than that of the first game. It is a far more streamlined system that was clearly designed with quality of life in mind. The open world was a welcome diversion and the movement and gunplay was much improved.
That being said, I did feel that enemy variety and design was not quite as frightening/engaging as the original. One enemy in particular in the game (the typical grunt or haunted) was essentially carbon copied with a different model in three different flavors (regular, fiery, white clay). I felt it somewhat jarring as I had really hoped to have more variety and behaviors in enemies. The first game was better in that regard as well.
I could continue to go on and discuss the differences at length, but I will simply say this; from a design perspective, The Evil Within 2 improved upon many of the original's flaws. However, I do miss some of the magic from the insanity of the first game.
I would still heartily recommend anyone who liked the first game to pick up the second. You won't be disapointed.

While the first game in the series was a half-baked horror/action hybrid with a character that can't run for more than 2 seconds without getting winded and a cast of characters that are forgettable at best, The Evil Within 2 released under my radar and turned out to be an astounding improvement to the original.
General spoiler warning.
I'm a hardened horror veteran who's played many popular and niche horror games and I've been pretty unfulfilled with newer horror games that end up resembling a "spooky action game" more than what typical players are hoping for. With that in mind, I can promise you this game is very different from the original.
Tango Gameworks and their parent company ZeniMax media decided to give the director's chair to John Johanas, the man who directed TEW1's DLC segments, and he really made some good changes overall. The matches/burning bodies system have been removed, as have grenades (for some reason), but more than anything the new "Open World" style of level design is a decided improvement, with not only dedicated stealth and cover mechanics the first game lacked, but enemies that can't see you through some all-seeing eye that ruined stealth-attempts, which the first game had.
The biggest gameplay enhancement is the ability to actually sneak your way behind enemies, with the highest upgrade tier giving you the ability to quietly run behind the enemy for a quick stealth kill. On top of that, the issue of the first game blending inventory expansion and character upgrades together has been fixed, with character augmentation using Green Gel and weapon upgrades & ammo crafting using "parts." Some people call the game more "combat-heavy," but I'd gladly take that over TEW1's constant teleportations and confusing scene transitions that added nothing to the final game.
While there ARE some boring enemies like the ghost-lady Anima who simply wanders aimlessly, dashing towards you when spotted and finishing you with a one-hit kill cutscene, the vast majority of the enemies in this game are very intimidating - there's a reoccuring miniboss named Sentinel that takes the fire-vulnerable Laura (spider demon thing) from the first game and cranks the fear factor up to 11. She has a buzzsaw and she's much faster than you, requiring a lot of ammo necessary to put her down. Multiples of these bosses can be found roaming around fixed areas in the overworld, making stealth a feasible battle strategy; landing a few blows and then losing the enemy. There's also a few intimidating enemies like the double-headed dog characters that rush you and tear you apart (and are also unable to be stealth-killed), but later after fighting a bullet-sponge flamethrower psychopath, you leave the level and re-enter the city only to find THREE MORE flamethrower minibosses wandering around the city, which drop flamethrower parts needed to unlock your very own, as well as patrol according to where you move. If you hang out near the safehouse, the first one will chill near the small park adjacent, but if you move to the nearby gas station, you can see the moment his animation changes to make a BEELINE for your location.
Some people might be put-off knowing an enemy's AI is scripted, but I find it really panic-inducing to find a safe-looking bush to hide in, only for an enemy to walk right up to me, sniff around angrily, and then turn away - or even worse, for me to hide behind cover before a boss wanders over and does a huge conal-AOE guess attack. There's a particularly unsettling boss you have to avoid in one area - it just patrols the area you're hiding in, wandering away briefly to give the player a chance to escape. Once you make a break for the exit, it suddenly knows and starts walking towards your location. This kind of telepathic enemy AI is what made Outlast so terrifying to me - where I'd pull a switch and an enemy would bust down the door to investigate.
Exploring is MUCH more rewarding in 2, as 1 would have you breaking boxes to find very little supplies, or walking around a corner to find a few bullets, but in TEW2 there are little doodads; collectibles from other Bethesda games, as well as documents and supplies. The environment plays a much greater role, possessing optional side-quests that can net you ammo capacity upgrades and weapon unlocks.
Probably my favorite fix is, as previously mentioned, how Sebastian can now sprint for MORE THAN TWO SECONDS and doesn't need to upgrade his ability to aim his gun without getting a mad case of the tremors. That was terrible. He now controls like a competent police officer.
Very solid game. Even better sequel. I'm not bold enough to call this game a classic, but it's very very fun and feels MUCH more balanced and well-designed than the first game. I don't regret buying it for full price somehow.

Right. So what do I say about Black Mesa? I have to be perfectly honest, I really loved this game. Black Mesa is a fantastic remaster of the first Half Life game that came out in 1998. Black Mesa is the remaster of that game.
The game runs on the standard source engine but the graphics and textures in this game are sooo damm good, im running this game on a I5 4460 and a Gigabyte GTX 960 IX OC 2GB edition graphics card and the game runs at more than 80 frames per second, some of the times it might drop the frame rate, I had the frame rate drop to 44 and even 24 sometimes for me but then again, a lot of things were going on in that specific area. I would have to say that the PC optimization is really great, it gets an A+ from me.
The new weapon models and textures in this game are also really good, you have some of your classic weapons like the MP5 with the grenade launcher or the Spas 12 shotgun remade in the new remastered version. The sound effects are really very designed, definitely a big improvement from the original game.
Now while I like this game a lot and I think it’s a perfect remaster of the original Half Life game, it’s not finished. It’s in early access for a reason and that is because it’s missing a huge part of the game which is known as Xen. At first I thought that Xen was some kind of DLC story for the original Half Life game, well it turns out that it’s not. To put it in a way for people to understand. Xen is the ending of the game and the final level and it’s missing from the game, yea so the final area that you were supposed to be where you would finish the game is missing, it is kind of disappointing and I was a bit sad about it. But the developers did say that they are working on it, when can we expect an ETA? We don’t know unfortunately.
The other little problem that I had with this game is the broken AI, luckily there is a fix for it that I made, check out my guide right here to fix this issue -
Right as for the issue, basically what it does is basically makes the enemies stupidly overpowered, you can’t hide anywhere because they will rush your position, you can’t peak out on them because they will start shooting you before you can, they deal huge amount of damage and it just ruins the game experience, you can use my guide to fix this issue until the developers decide to fix this issue.
Another small little issue is that sometimes when im playing the game becomes rather confusing, sometimes im stuck in a game area for around 20 minutes and I have no idea on what to do because the game doesn’t hint it to you or anything of that kind, it becomes rather frustrating trying to figure out what to do when you in fact have no idea what to do. The Developers could definitely work on this.
And so we come forward to my final words, do I recommend this game? It’s a tough question, at one hand Black Mesa is a fantastic remaster of the original 1998 Half Life but at the same time it’s missing Xen which is in fact an entire game ending, but even without Xen the game will give you hours upon hours of content before you even get to the suppose ending of the game.
In my opinion, buy Black Mesa on a sale or buy it now, while it does miss Xen it does feature a big amount of content that will keep you playing for a few days or maybe even weeks, the other option is that you can wait and buy Black Mesa when the Xen update comes out making it the full game. But this game deserves an 8/10 from me, really fantastic remaster of the original Half Life but it has some issues and is missing some content.
I will update my review if Xen ever comes out or if we get some new exciting content to give it a look at.

Having only played this game for the first time now long after finishing the Bioshock series... i can definitely say that System Shock 2 is a much better game.
There is a lot of cunkiness with going back and playing such an old game. Combat is stiff and can be confusing. Objectives require an absurd amount of backtracking. The key is that the storyline is absolutely amazing. If you download a bundle of graphic overhaul mods, things can get very playable (this is what I did). They can't bring it up to date, but at least make it feel like a slightly newer game. Once you get past that barrier to find a really interesting and unusual story.
Shodan is this game seems to be the spiritual grandmother of GlaDos from Portal. Your experience with Shodan is similar as you start by trusting her and then she slowly becomes the enemy. Unlike Portal, there is no comedy in this and the game as a very serious tone from start to finish. What is really interesting is that Shodan is not your enemy until really the final boss battle. You're instead trying to destroy her creation: a massive organic muscle monster. It is hard to put into words, but every enemy you face is part of this giant organic mass that is grwoing through the ship. All of it is Shodan's creation and you have to help this AI take control of the ship again and wipe out this infestation. You do it all the while as she insults you and reminds you of her superiority over you.
Just do yourself one favor. Don't watch the final cutscene. The player character only says 1 word throughout the entire game and it is in this little video. it pretty much ruins most of what you've come to experience. The cutscene also leaves room for a sequel with a cliffhanger. There will never be a sequel so do yourself a favor and when you finish that final battle, just turn off the game.
The game is really worth a play... even if it really is an antique by now.
If you want to know what inspired and sparked the Bioshock series, this is it.

Review: Dishonored 2 in my opinion is the closest thing we'll ever get to a Thief 4. While most people will shout negatives at this game on steam for performance. The only negative I have with the game is that it's not "Thief" enough. The sound design is not as good as the Thief series and that is integral to a First Person Stealth Sim like Dishonored wants to be. The fact that sound does not matter until 'Very Hard' and even then it's not really a true mechanic is quite puzzeling to me. The only other negative I have is that I cannot retract Corvo's blade and use it as an equivalent to the Black Jack from Thief. I am fine with choking people out but the fact that it's almost my only option to knock people out is kinda lame IMO.
Before I move forward with my review I would like to say that if they make a Dishonored 3 PLEASE give us that choice. I think it would be cool to be in situations where some guards have metal helmets, so that, I have no other choice BUT to choke them out. Then a lot of guards would be wearing hats or nothing at all and I could just run up to them and bop them on the head. It would be so much more interesting to me from a gameplay perspective.Then If they also made sound matter imagine having to worry about being on Marble, Stone, Metal, and anything that makes a lot of noise. Those are the gameplay elements of Thief that I loved to death. Jumping down from above onto my Moss Arrow patch and then smacking a guard on the head. It was seamless gameplay, no context sensitive BS.
Anyways, sorry for that loooong tangent but it had to be said. Overall I DO LOVE this game a lot. It and DOOM are my favorite games of the entire year. The performance issues on my end have been completely ironed out. Plus, I bought it on sale so not having to pay that full sixty was definitely a plus. The game definitely captures MOST of Thief's style. It's like 80% there. Stephen Russell voicing Corvo alone is literally enough to bump that up to 85% if I'm being totally honest. Just like Thief and Garrett of the past Corvo will comment on things around him and make witty quips. The dialogue is pretty damn good so far and I would say it's pretty on par with Thief. This game was my dream come true in a nutshell. I totally say give it a shot if you loved Thief.

Having played the first Dishonored (inclusive of all its DLCs) and absolutely loving it, I was super pumped to play Dishonored 2, so much that I preordered it. Although some would call this a mistake as you can never be sure of the quality of a game on its release, I didn’t mind one bit. I’m going to be honest here, I wouldn’t exactly call my computer flash or top of the range. It’s an old Toshiba laptop with an outdated Nvidia graphics card, and a small amount of RAM, so I knew that I was going to experience some graphical issues. That is exactly what I got, however it didn’t affect my game play all too much. I guess once you get used to poor playing conditions, you end up living with it. So although a framerate of 15fps wasn’t ideal, I made do.
Despite this, the rest of the game was phenomenal. One of the things that I loved in the first Dishonored was its level design. The ability to play each level so differently, where Bethesda catered for various playing styles, was one of the things that made it so memorable. Dishonored 2 did not fail to meet this mark, but rather exceeded it. Whether you were an assassin, a ghost, a killing machine or a sprinter, it was easy to make your way through the level in whatever fashion you desired. While going back through different levels, I’m still finding areas that I didn’t know existed and paths that would have made certain bits a hell of a lot easier. I truly believe that Bethesda have outdone themselves with the level design, including my favourite level of the Clockwork Mansion. This is where this aspect shines. Even trying to comprehend the planning that went into this level, making sure that everything worked as it should, blows me away. I can’t even begin to work how they would even build this level, let alone complete it. To me, Bethesda have skilfully incorporated this aspect into the game, forming a unique world and gaming experience.
Beautifully paired with the level design is the game’s mechanics. Building on the mechanics from the first game, Bethesda have added, changed and improved certain aspects across the board. When Bethesda first announced that you could play as either Emily Kaldwin or Corvo Attano, I was torn as to which to play. However, in order to get a new gaming experience, I played as Emily. Although I did miss certain abilities that came with Corvo, I was excited to try out something different, and boy is that what I got. Having the addition of these new mechanics meant that I had to think differently, and take a new approach when solving certain challenges. They were fun to play with when both sneaking and doing full on attacks. I am eager however to do the new game plus mode (which you unlock after a full run through), which means that I’ll be able to select my powers from both characters. With that said, I’ll probably pick Corvo for that run, just to see the difference.
The other addition of mechanics was to that of the game world. Unlike in the first Dishonored where you had could buy equipment from the hub, this game added the black markets. These were little shops that could be found in levels, enabling you to buy supplies, favours, and surprisingly runes. This addition became a life saver to me too many times to count. Whenever I was running low on sleep darts or stun mines, these shops would be my saviour, so I’m thankful they were added. Other than the black market, I was greatly pleased with the ability to craft bone charms meaning I could have more perks in less space. Although there is probably an endless list of all the mechanics which I felt improved the game from its predecessor I must say that there was one thing that I felt let down the game.
Although Bethesda clearly captured the world of Karnaca through the journals, newprints and audiographs that you find throughout the place, the main story was a little bit less encaptivating. To me it was too linear and didn’t have a lot of depth, and when they tried to add depth
, they didn’t fully carry through with it, giving us unanswered question.
To me this was the only area that flopped and I felt it was more of a way to facilitate the amazing level design and mechanics that had been implemented, rather than being the game’s focus.
However, with that said, I would strongly recommend for anyone to play this game. It covers a whole range of play types, and the level design is beautiful. I have heard currently that there are a lot of problems with its graphics and with that I would say hold off for a bit. Wait until those are sorted out if you think they will be the make or break of your experience, because this game is one should and can be thoroughly enjoyed.
With that, I think it’s time to delve into a second run.

It's getting increasingly harder and harder to wade through the amount of games that gets released onto Steam these days and find a game that manages to impress in its own interesting, albeit flawed, way. Suits: A Business RPG was sleepily released amongst the end of the 2015 Winter Sale, and one could be easily forgiven for missing this game's late arrival to the scene. After all, buying another game after the massive winter sale was through? Most people were likely bloated on games and their wallets drained of the almighty dollar. But you're in luck! Because one United States dollar is exactly how much this little package costs (perhaps it's being too meta with how tongue in cheek the price is), and at this time of review, the game is discounted to a mere 59 cents.
This asking price alone for this title is enough to warrant a purchase, but there's more that can and will be said about this title. About a year ago, back in late December 2014, a game called LISA: The Painful RPG was released to little fanfare (not unlike Suits) and quickly became a hit with a small, but dedicated number of people. It became a cult favorite, and has a lot of similarities to Suits - both were made in RPG Maker, both have nearly identical combat mechanics, both share a similar name, and they both share a similar world design and aesthetic. But that's about where the similarities end for the two titles. While LISA took place in a post-apocalyptic world with no women, Suits places you in a, literal, grey world where commerce, industry, media, government, and society itself are ran with cold efficiency by the omnipresent hands of capitalism and corporations. Big business rules the world, and, hey, congrats, you've just been accepted as an employee for one of the CEO's. Put your suit and tie on, drink some water from the water cooler, and let's get to work.
Right away you'll notice the graphics for this game are pretty unique; everything has been hand drawn...badly, if I may have an opinion on it. But this doesn't detract from the game, instead I think it gives the game it's own unique look. I can only imagine the artist for this game scribbling away at his desk late at night. A cold, yellow light beams from his lamp as he puts on the finishing touches to some bizarre monstrosity. And that's the exact kind of attitude that permeates this game. Everywhere you're inundated with outrageous, often unnerving imagery of amoral officials, corrupt businessmen, and deformed and dejected lowlifes. But with that chaos comes uniformity and normalcy, and even casual humor. Characters think nothing of the situations they find themselves in, and this is compounded by the ever present fact that no matter what happens, no matter what disturbing or unusual or strange circumstance you might come across it is all according to plan. Everything happens according to the machine, the macabre punches in and it punches out like any other day job.
And if there's one thing that completely ties everything together, it's the music. It's without a doubt the best aspect of Suits. Whomever composed the music did a wonderful job, it really brings everything to life (if life is calculated, controlled, and quantified that is). The music gives the game a real sense of hopelessness and oppression - it feels crippling at times, but playful on several small occasions. The music is muted with a lot of low, droning brass that echoes in each track. I think sometimes it even tries to replicate the offbeat and extremely dry humor the game conjures up from time to time. It wants you to be happy, it wants you to think everythink is okay. After all, a happy and content worker is an efficient one. The world may have gone to hell, but hey, Friday is wacky tie day. Lastly, there's one track in particular that stands out from the rest and the story behind it is quite humorous. I won't give it away, it's best if you find it for yourself.
I'll touch briefly on the combat as it's not terribly important to this game, it's more of a means of reaching the end of the game's narrative. It behaves like LISA did. You fight (through random or scripted encounters), you gain experience and money, you level up, learn new moves and techniques, and use the money to buy new and better equipment and items. So far I've only encountered one other party member, and skill usage works the same as it did in LISA. The main character uses TP (or Technique Points) and the other party member uses SP (or FUEL in this game, which means water. Gotta stay hydrated in this economy, after all). You gain TP by being attacked or attacking, and FUEL works like mana. You buy water bottles to replenish your reserves. It's a pretty simple, pretty easy engine and anybody can pick up and do well at this game with a little grinding every now and again to get the proper upgrades when you come across them.
Suits: A Business RPG is a dark game, and that may be redundant to say by this point, but the atmosphere, visuals, music, and aesthetics make for a very unique playing experience. It feels like it came straight out of the 1970's, when dystopian science fiction films were commonplace.  The soundtrack for this game sounds more like a film score than tracks recorded separately. The music blends and accommodates in the same way Morricone's score did for John Carpenter's The Thing. And the material for this game, while occasionally hamfisted and silly, does a good enough job to convince me it wouldn't be too out of place in a Kubrick film or other work about suppression of emotions and oppression. The game actually reminds me in a way of Upton Sinclair's "The Jungle."
I wouldn't dare put this game necessarily in the same league as such legendary works, not at all. However, I do think you probably won't find another game on Steam that hits the same sort of tonal pitches those films and stories did. Suits: A Business RPG is fairly short, fairly hamfisted, and somewhat chokes on its own material at times but the overall package definitely tries and I think it succeeds in most avenues.

Probably the most realistic Zombie FPS on Steam, No More Room In Hell brings alot to the table, and leaves none to be desired. There are so many aspects that make this game great. I haven't played that long, but I've enjoyed it thoroughly.
Gameplay Elements: Probably the best part of the game is it's reliance on teamwork and strategy (in a way). If you run off on your own, 9/10 chance you are gonna die. If you run, guns blazing through a crowded street, you will most likely die. If you decide to waste that one shot you have saved, you will probably die (but not in the way you have planned.) If you stick together, and work smart, you will most likely live to see the light of the next day.
Another great element is how if you get bit, it might have a long-lasting effect. In most other games you get bit, and meh, shrug it off. In NMRiH, you get bit, you might get infected. You get infected, you turn in a short time to one of them.  You can do two things to save you at this point, either take some pills (which are fairly hard to find) to delay the effects, or you can use a gun and one bullet to off yourself and save your allies the problem of you coming back and fighting them. Either way, once you are infected, you WILL die. Remember though, you can still fight up until the point you turn.
Atmosphere: This atmosphere has clearly been inspired by many zombie movies (one level is pretty much just Night of The Living Dead) and it makes it so much better. Most levels have that creepy, abandoned feel, and in my opinion, really ties the feel of this game together.
Multiplayer: This is the one aspect that I kind of dislike. The community can be real♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Pick up a rifle someone else wants? They might just smack you over the head with a fire axe. Get infected and call out to your team? Oh, look! A bullet to your brain when you could have done something in the time you have. Sometimes, the players you are put with are ruthless, and will literally screw you over twice and a half just to get that extra bullet, just to get that better weapon, just to get those pills to extend their life. Some people can be really terrible to play with. So if you do play, bring friends.
TOTAL RATING: 8.5/10

What every game aspires to.

• Spectacular atmosphere, where horrible sights are abundant.
• Great objective-based maps, that usually switch from different sets of objectives to complete, in order to finish a level.
• Very good soundtrack, mixing tension and desolation with its electronic vibe.
• Gruesome combat (some zombie maiming is missing, but it's not a big deal).
• Simple and functional co-op: the more players there are, the easier it gets to complete the objectives, and zombies don't focus on only one player. Also, helping other people to get past a hoard, healing them, preventing them from becoming a walking corpse, feels great, as well as when they help you in return.
• Zombies are disgusting, very dangerous and hard to kill, making you hate the moment they grab you, or when they decide to swing their arms at you. The sheer number of them helps build the desperation in the player's mind.
• The inclusion of zombie children is nice, because it helps with immersion and realism, as well as freaking the player out.
• Scarcity of weapons and ammo keep the tensions high, especially when there are 8 players in the server.
• Both firearms and melee weapons are very satisfying to use and pack a punch.
• The minimalistic HUD is excellent and surprisingly comfortable to use (at least in my experience).
• Bleeding and infection are some good game mechanics that up the difficulty and realism
• Realism + Hardcore mode is hard but very, very thrilling to play, once you have the skill for it.
• Nightmare difficulty is brutal and unforgiving. A paradise for adrenaline junkies.
• Some of the achievements are really good and can prove a real challenge, like "We Got This!" or "New York Minute".
• Even after completing all objective maps several times and learning all the tricks, it's still a thrill to complete each of them. As an extra challenge, you can try finishing every objective map on your own, which feels like a fantastic accomplishment (for example, "nmo_brooklyn").
• An abundance of free, fan-made maps can keep you entertained for a long time, because many of them are really hard (namely, underground_v1, subside_v5, sweden1_v1, urbanhazard_v4, in_the_dark, anxiety, ghostbuster, ravenholm_v2, ocwd_a1, emergency_1101, torn_b2, camilla_v2, and many more).
• It's free to play, as if everything before that wasn't enough for you to try it out.
• It's still a mod, so some clunkyness, bugs and glitches will be present at all times, breaking some of the immersion.
• Although gruesome, the combat is finicky and requires some serious practice and experience to fully dominate.
• Hitboxes are really bugged. Pushing, melee hits and shots don't register consistently.
• If you are being followed by two or more runners, it's really inconsistent to kill them all in a straight line, because they clip into each other, and they can instantly kill you if one of them grabs you (you can push them, but it's random if you push the zombie that's actually grabing you).
• The random chance of infection can be incredibly frustrating, especially when you get infected on your first bite, and you are in the begining of a really long map, like nmo_anxiety. Yes, the chance increases the lower your health is, but I've had many instances where I got infected on full health, first bite, and others where I could finish hard maps like nmo_underground_a9 having been bitten many times on low health, and showing no signs of infection.
• Objective maps can be broken with ease. Just throw a vital item over a fence and you're done, no more progress. This is a problem that server admins, have to face many times, and I, personally, punish players severely for breaking nmo maps.
• Survival maps tend to be somewhat boring and stale, not to mention how easy it is to beat them with 5-ish players, unless Realism is enabled, but very hard to solo them. Also, they are very laggy when playing online, where more than 100 zombies can spawn at a time.
• The tutorial is limited to an image of the main keyboard controls during the loading screens, which isn't the best way to teach players. It all ends up in a good old trial and error type of learning curve. No info on game mechanics, like charging your melee weapon, whatsoever.
• Co-op is quite bad when your team is filled with new players that are still figuring out the controls (or even trolls), and if you haven't mastered the game, it can prove difficult to complete most of the maps. However, if you have mastered the game, then you can usually ignore other players and win.
• Zombie models lack variety which breaks the realistic gameplay to some degree. It's kind of dumb when you encounter the same old man zombie for the tenth time on a single map. Also, there are only two skins available for zombie children.
• Third person character animations are a little bit funky. Walk, run and melee attack cycles are stiff.

The things Black Mesa perfectly nails as an update of Half Life are the Shotgun, Gluon Gun (way improved) and Long Jump (also way improved). The voice acting is largely on par with the original, and the fleshing out of characters who later appear in Half Life 2 was a welcome addition.
But, there are many areas where the game is significantly weaker than the classic masterpiece. The gunplay (especially with the pistols) is quite different, and I didn't like it. I also hated the nuetered ammo carrying capacity. Only 12 spare magnum rounds? Please!
The hive hand is as OP as ever (am I the only one who basically uses it all the time after getting it?) and can clear entire rooms from behind cover.
I enjoyed the basic physics puzzles and felt like this is the level of physics puzzles Half Life 2 should have had if it weren't so enthralled with showing its physics engine and gravity gun off.
Overall, it's a good game, and I reccomend it, but I encourage anyone interested to see it as it is: a love letter that fans of the game wrote, and not a replacement for the original.
