Finally i finished this game in 2015 but its well worth it, im writing this review from personal enjoyment and satisfaction.
First of all this game is developed by Looking Glass Studios who has also developed game franchises like Ultima Underworld and Thief.Also this game was designed by the almighty Ken Levine and co-developed by Irrational Games.
System Shock 2 is a first-person shooting game which incorporates role-playing system elements, also survival horror at its best.The setting of the game is in a starship when an infection begin and devastated the ship,so as a lone survivor you start with the weapon we might say its memorable to Ken Levine games "the wrench", so the player has to progress through the ship levels along side of that is the awesome dark atmosphere that keeps you on your toes because enemies are always near you and you cant feel safe.The rpg elements in this game are strong because you have a large inventory and exploring is probably the main thing you have to do to survive in this infected ship, from the class you choose you can have certain benifts in weapons,hacking or psi power.The player can hack turrets,devices,crates,vending machines also skills called "cyber-modules" which can upgrade stats,weapon skill,psi powers,abilities and for every item picked there is a description what is used for cause if you are like me you will get confused a lot.
The weapons have their own strengths and weaknesses and you will have to repair,maintain and modify them.The plot gets interesting more and more as you pick audio logs through the levels which explains the events that occurred on the ship.Not the mention as you progress through the plot appears one of the best villains of all time SHODAN with the amazing sound it makes the plot interesting to the end.I dont want to go too much on the storyline there's no way to do so without totally spoiling the game.The graphics are outdated but they are acceptable for those who want a good story although there are some mods that would make the models and other things better,the sound overall is amazing and the overall presentation is amazing.
System Shock 2 is a masterpiece,unrivaled in many ways it shows quality that will fulfill enjoyment even today.

8.5/10 Very nicely detailed, great updates, MODs and add-ons; but if you're not in for a marathon style, unforgiving RPG, this might not be the game for you. The graphics options and gameplay are delightful, and with the most recent patch, one is allowed more 'flavour' with town and province set-up - opposed to pre-patch where there were very few building combinations which would give one an advantage. This game, speaking as a huge RTS fan, has only two flaws I've yet to uncover: 1) There is the occasional glitch, whether it is my PC or a game-side error, I do not know, but every now and again an option will become unavailable (like character promotion) or an action or mini-video (Triumph, as Rome) will cause the game to crash, and 2) The load and turn times. I am a patient man, and love my RTSs, but when I am able to fire up the 3DS and goof around on Pokémon after I end my turn due to long AI times, that might be indiciative of too much attention to detail. That being said, the battles are fantastic, the units are diverse and strategy actually comes in to play; especially when compared with Medieval II total war, where you could just train enough elite troops, throw them at the enemy, and know you'll eventually win, and the multiple factions, sub-factions and politicking actually make for a nerve-wracking, encompassing and downright fun time.

If you enjoyed The Evil Within, you'll certainly want to pick this up, too. Tango addressed most of the issues critics pointed out from the first game, and made numerous improvements. Sebastian is now a more-human character, the story is easier to follow, and the inclusion of sanbox/quest elements were all pleasant surprises. It is also optimized very well, as I was able to play it on ultra settings with minimal performance issues. The game took me a little over 15 hours to complete, but it could easily take longer if you explore all of the corners of Union.
My only complaint would be inventory management during some of the later boss battles in the game. Sometimes, ammo is so scarce that you have to keep running in cricles while being chased just so you can get lucky to pick up three randomly-generating bullets. It broke the immersion for me, but I suppose that's part of what makes it survival horror.
Anyways, all-in-all it's a great game for anyone who loves survival horror.

Ok i don´t usually write reviews about any game but still i think this one desserves alittle time from me to explain you guys why this MMO its so unique and fun.
Ok a certain clarification about this game, this isn't skyrim and its not gonna be 100% like it that or any elder scrolls game, although it doesn´t mean its a bad thing, it take some elements from previous elder scrolls game and adapt them to the MMO style it should have since its a Massive Multiplayer Online game!
Lets start by inmersion, they really do a good job on this aspect of the game, you find public world bosses and certain events called dolmen scattered around all the map, it has collectibles and resources for your crafting jobs as well so it encourages that you explore around their beatiful made maps, for every faction i must say it takes roughly 150+ hours to complete theese maps and they are beginning to add more content to the game so it doesnt end that quickly.
Ok this is no ordinary mark target then spell cast MMO you are used to, it´s combat system its kinda unique it reminds me a bit of Tera online but way better, you have 2 bars where you can allocate certain spells that you intent to make part of your specialised build, certain spells are actually skill shots or require you to be targetting the mob with your camera so its not the usual jump and spam buttons from other MMOs, in dungeons and in pvp positioning is actually key for your success, and not only that you can actually block and dodge (dodge roll) spells to minimize their effect on you, its more action based without skipping the RPG because depending the way you built theese bars affects hugely the play style of your characters, you have a really big skill tree where you can allocate like 300 skill points in crafting passives,combat passives, weapon passives and actives, and 4 direrent classes each with 3 skill sets actives and passives as well. It´s really flexible to do a really original build ive seen crazy builds like sorcerer healers or tanks etc it really lets you do really personalized stuff. AND NO not only that! when you reach end game you unlock a thing called Championship System where you unlock points every certain exp amount that you can allocate within a really wide skill tree that looks alike skyrim tree (theese are passive skills) to tweak your character to your own needs.
Dungeon wise it has a really big spam of dungeons around 15 or more dungeons each with unique boss fights and mechanics and around 10 more End game dungeons, 3 trials (raids), so its kinda hard to get bored specially on the endgame dungeons since they require skilled players to beat, also you have with the DLCs are big solo player Arena and a huge PVPVE map where you have a hybrid of story and pvp.
Talking about PvE it has a really really big map where you fight for the dominance between the 3 factions available, with diferent mechanics, you can even use siege weapons to break down walls on Forts and so (i don´t wanna talk much about it because i dont wanna spoil the fun of seeing it for yourself).
In conclusion this game it´s a gem specially for thoose who are TES games fans, no its not a pure TES game but it uses a lot of it´s elements, and also players who just want to play a MMO can be delighted with it, specially if you are bored of the same usual MMO.

Unfortunately this game has turned out to be a huge frustration and I cannot recommend it in it's current state.  I was a huge fan of the first Dishonored, I purchased this over the holidays only to find it unplayable. The engine is so not optimized for PC it's tragic. I had a 32GB RAM/FX-8350/GTX 760 config and the game would only run using the absolute lowest settings. I say had because the card config changed.
I get that the old card was a few years old but the jump in system requirements for this game is ridiculous. The game aggravatingly insists on displaying on a smaller secondary monitor and using it's crappy built in speakers instead of the primary sound card and Logitec speakers hooked to it. I disabled the sound feed from the computer to the built in speakers but it still displays on the secondary monitor, albeit now with no sound. And there is no way I can find (short of using third party apps) to change this behavior.
Luckily I received a new 1060 for Xmas that I went ahead and installed, hoping it would fix the monitor issue. No dice. So at this point I've said screw it, hopefully I will stumble across a fix at some point in the future. I do know I will not be purchasing any more Arkane titles going forward until they hit the cheapie bin, and then only after doing some thorough player commentary research.
TLDR: You are taking your chances if you purchase this game, in my opinion Arkane did a terrible job with the PC version and frankly no AAA title should have this many issues this far after initial release. I haven't had this many issues even with indie titles.

I can safely count Just Cause 3 as one of my all time favourite games. Why? Read below to know!
Graphics:
I'm running an Nvidia GTX 980 OC version from MSI 4GB with an i7 processor at 3.4Gh and 16GB of RAM. This allows me to take advantage of the game's stunning beauty. I am originally from the South of Europe and many games tend to have a cold sun, i.e. the light in-game looks artificial. Just Cause 3's Sun is vibrant and warm. That fact alone makes the game more realistic to me than any other try hard graphism betting game (Crysis amongst others). But coupled to that amazing Sun and lightning, the water effects from Nvidia Gameworks are simply the most immersive water I have seen in a game. It's beatiful especially since they fixed the foam glitch. Everything has been fine tuned to be apealing to the eye. Just Cause 3 even uses a custom ambiant oclusion that works amazingly well. The environment is beautiful and diverse, although I regret the later part of the game having huge areas of forrest. Wingsuit and tree don't really like each other...Anyway, I know that AMD people havent' been really blessed in this regard due to many launch issues, but imo if you chose AMD over Nvidia your asking for trouble anyway. There are only a handful of games developped with an AMD partnership, while all the others have Nvidia as a partner...
Gameplay:
It's pollished and fun fun fun! Did I say it was fun? Seriously though: it's fun! If you love realistic games, just move along, because here realysm has been thrown out the window in order to remove any sort of frustration (unless you're going for 5 gears in the wing suit challenges). You can fall from incredibly high and collide with things at incredible speed without dying. The wingsuit is basically a small turbojet as it doesn't just reduce your fall, but it actually speeds up your velocity! You also get unlimited grappling hook with an unlimited self folding parachute! Acrobatics are the central point of anything you do while in the air! I admit, you might have to gain some skill, but once you've mastered the grapling hook, wingsuit, parachute combo you will be unstoppable and faster than any maritime or land vehicle! If you get tired of flying you can always call in an airdrop with a new set of weapons and a vehicle of your choice. And why not enjoy a fully upgraded sports car with nitrous boost and jump? That's right, you read jump and that's what I meant!
Explosions!:
The game has tons of stuff to explode and more. You get the feel that each car you drive gets micro charges of C4 in each of its bumpers so you can screw physics and ram other things into oblivion! If ramming is not enough for you, no worries! You get tanks, helicopters with rocket launchers, gatlings and jet fighters dropping their bombs! Don't want to use vehicles? The game got you covered, everything from mortars, to assaults, pistols, smg's, rpg's, grenade launchers and prototype weapons fill your arsenal! Why not use that weapon who calls in an aerial carpet bombing? No? Could I interest you into a nuke launcher then? Got your pick? Then have a go at refineries, water towers, vehicles, fuel and hydrogen tanks, transformers and other huge antennas! But wait, there's some nasty propaganda there, get rid of it with sticky explosives or homing grenades, your pick!
Quests/Story:
The story? Well, I remember freeing towns and bases while getting rid of some opressing general, but WHO CARES! I'M FLYING SUPERMAN-STYLE WHILE BLOWING STUFF UP IN A ZEUS LIKE FASHION! That's all you really need to relax after a long day of work. And if that is not enough enough there are many different challenges involving races, destruction goals, wing suit courses (attention frustration disclaimer unless you got som Skillz) and even some more esoteric magnetic ball ore catcher thing. IF you buy this only for the main story, don't bother. You should get it for the blowing stuff up deal. Definitely the blowing stuff up thing. Nothing else. And all that blowing stuff up will take you about 30h or more. Add on top of that some secret searching, like parts for secret vehicles, recordings and candle lighting that gives you free fast travel and you've got a consequent life time.
Negative aspects:
Well the only negative things I encountered were the long intro video, which you can easily skip using an easy to instal mod. And the other issue was the lack of steam cloud synchronisation. This actual made me lose my save game when I formatted my PC while being unaware of the lack of said feature. Now I'm replaying the game from start.
I wanted to only rush it this time, but I got caught up with blowing stuff up again... I might need a support group here... Nah! I love blowing stuff up in Just Cause 3!
And this is what JC3 is all about: fun while doing random blowing up of random stuff. The funniest moments I had were trying to take a boat up a mountain tied up to my helicopter, or the time I dragged a bus on it's side through the country side with my huge dump truck stolen from the quarry, or the time I got a cow stuck to my hood that would just refuse to leave, stayed unaffected all the way and sank with the car in the middle of a lake after a glorious jump off a cliff. Why did I do those things in the first place? Why the hell not. Life is too much spent losing time thinking about what makes sense and what should be done or not. Just Cause doesn't ask you to think, it doesn't even ask you to do things, it just gives you tools, alot of awesome tools and you just do with it what the hell you want, without even thinking of it. And there lies the magic.

Now, after finishing
on the hardest difficulty setting, I feel the urge to express my enthusiasm about this terrifying horror experience. I got so traumatized by playing it, even my wife had to hold my hand and wipe my tears while encouraging me to play along after the first few hours. Yes, the game takes a lot of time, twenty-nine hours in my case. Some journalists even complained about its rather exceptional length. Maybe the press got used to expect short games fitting their editorial deadlines so much that a bit more of content nowadays seems to be a problem, but how could I know about objective reporting? :-)
I recommend choosing the hardest difficulty setting when starting a new game. The Alien behaves just like a complete idiot on easy difficulty and on normal it still can be seen as the nice extraterrestrial next door. You don't want to be stalked by a friendly ret♥rd whereas being given the creeps is the point of a survival horror game. Just remember: The Alien from the movie of the same name represents such a danger because it possesses heightened sensens and instincts superior to ours.
unfortunately reveals another complicated thing to handle than the Artificial Intelligence: save points. Though I like how The Creative Assembly made them part of the virtual world: Your progress on Sevastopol station can be saved by putting your personal ID card, which looks like a twenty year old graphics board with a handle, into an emergency telephone. But how did I suffer in the Medical Facility trying to find and reach the next phone after the sudden activation of the quarantine lock-down! Goddammit!
The game's horrifying atmosphere not only benefits from the well-designed AI, but also from the feeling of overwhelming loneliness you get while sneaking through the recently abandoned space station. There are apparently some horror cliches that just can't be avoided, but I suppose some mechanics have just proven themselves, like the scarce lighting on Sevastopol Station. You often encounter nothing but silent and dim-lit areas, sometimes accompanied and confused by different sounds from afar, for example the station's own drumming noises, not knowing what situation your next insecure step might get you into. I'll never forget the Torrens (the ship that brought you to Sevastopol) surprisingly enlightening the room with its search lights and floating past the station just to leave me alone again in the station's chaos, where everything went wrong with the evacuation procedures...

Being a fan of the Alien series, the last game which came right before this one - Aliens: Colonial Marines - was a bit disappointing to me. You probably expected me to not have high hopes for a new game in the series, but that wasn't the case. My hopes were very high, and the game didn't disappoint in any way I can think of.
First of all, it's a survival horror game, and it's based mostly on the first movie in the franchise, seen as a sort of continuation of it, and the action takes place between Alien and Aliens.
That being said, don't ever expect to be able to kill the alien. It's one of those games where you are forced to constantly use stealth and immediately hide when the monster is in the area (which you will probably do about 90% of the time), except that you can defend yourself, but from anything but the alien. After all, they couldn't kill it in the Alien movie either, could they?
The graphics and atmosphere are quite beautiful, and the game really does make you feel like you're in the movie - and if you get the DLC, on the actual Nostromo.
So... if you're a true fan of the Alien series and you enjoy survival horror games with a bit of a twist, this is definitely the game for you! 10/10

The scariest game out now.
This is the best game made for the IP, certainly, but that's almost damning the title with faint praise. What it really is, is the most accomplished and sophisticated of the first person horror games released so far.
I'm a big fan of Penumbra: Overture and Black Plague, I very much enjoyed Amnesia too. They came along when first person and adventure games were becoming quite stale, so I'll always be very fond of them. I played them with relish and love them for incepting a whole genre, essentially. But they were far from flawless. Likewise the Bioshock franchise, which has many positive qualities, also lacks somewhat. It fails to recreate the sense of tension System Shock 2 had, and it also fails to create a realistic sense of place in its game levels. Atmospheric as Rapture is, it only vaguely felt like a city, and much more specifically like a dungeon for you to kill people in.
The reason these games are relevant to this review is because Alien: Isolation recreates them mechanically almost blow for blow. A crafting system not unlike that found in Bioshock exists here, but it's far stripped back, Being lean and always useful but never overpowering you or giving you a too great sense of confidence, in contrast to Bioshocks items and abilities systems which always were, quite frankly, bloated. I initially ignored the system, as I do most crafting systems, be cause they usually ARE ignorable distractions from playing the main game. But here, medpacks, molotovs, noisemakers and all kinds of other junk you can make save you a world of trouble, and you quickly learn to pay attention to the little side areas that contain treasure troves of crafting materials and ammo.
Further, Alien: Isolation is imbued with an aesthetic sense far finer than its inspirations. Dialogue and story, especially at the crucial opening act of the game, are subtle, well measured, realistic and feel quite human. Most commendable is Amanda Ripley herself, who functions perfectly as the voice of the player. She never just accepts the bizarrely violent  world on board the station as the half-mute protagonists of Bioshock usually do, and demands explanations from word go. Such a feature is crucial because it allows the player to accept the in-universe situation as an emotional one, not just one with mechanical obstacles and story as pretense for it.
This subtle, detail oriented mentality extends to the visuals of the game. Art direction is not just slavishly devoted to the design patterns used for the environments in the original Alien, but also to creating a sense of humanity. Environments are scaled to human use, stuffed with normal human rubbish (candy bars, cokes, pens, papers, the fodder of workstations) and their layouts are logical in the sense of their utility first (a medical centre is planned out just like a medical centre should be), not in the service of gameplay, a mistake both Bioshock and the Frictional games make.
And that's the secret to Alien: Isolation. I enjoyed this game immensely. Not because it showed me something new, but because it showed how taking something that's already popular and done well, then adding the extra 10% of love and thought, creates much more than just 10% more fun, it can give a game a reason to be remembered for being more than just "the best of the three good games amongst dozens of mediocrity that were produced for X movie franchise".

Arguably the best game of 2014, which is unfortunately saying very little since 2014 was a pretty crap year for good games.
Before I say what I liked about the game, I'll go over the parts I didn't like so much. The story and characters are largely forgettable, characters I'm supposed to care about die and I don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥ In one instance someone is doing something in the story which, to me at least, seems like a good idea, but apparently I'm not supposed to like what they're doing because heroes have to be paragons and can't have any blood on their hands whatsoever. The whole thing was just silly. It just came off like Amanda was a big baby and didn't want to sacrifice herself for the greater good. Maybe this is just a matter of philosophy and I'm the dumb one, but it seemed to me like the whole thing could have been handled better. Anyway. The only character I found interesting at all was Samuels. Died too young.
Whenever they do finally get around to making a sequel to this, they have to work on the AI, above all else. Hiding from the alien, taking a few steps, then having the alien jump down behind you from a vent; forcing you to hide in a closet again for another few minutes, isn't fun. Something else that bothers me is that you don't seem to be able to hide from anything by running away and ducking behind some furniture or crates. You always have to hide inside a closet or some vents. That's something I hope they really fix in the future. Hiding out in the open is way more intense and keeps the player active. Compared to just sitting on your hands in some closet and maybe having to hold your breath every once in a while when you're around some droids.
The last bad thing I have to say about the game is the beyond awful cutscenes. The lip synching is probably some of the worst I've ever seen in anything. Going from 60fps to 20fps or whatever terrible framerate the cutscenes are running at is incredibly jarring. It made me wish the entire game just had a cutscene at the beginning and end, with everything inbetween just being that first-person in-game stuff. Apparently the game employs motion-capture. I really hope that doesn't apply to the cutscenes. That is laughably bad if it does.
Now. Alien: Isolation is a very beautiful game. The art department deserves a big raise after the work they did on this. The way they did the lighting and smoke/steam in the game is pretty incredible, some sections in the game look nearly photorealistic. People love to throw around the term "atmospheric" for every game nowadays, but it really does apply to this. It's still a little hard to believe how much the game got right in that area. Their use of the classic Alien musical themes and their nailing of the art style from the movies. It's just so good.
Another thing they really nailed was the Alien itself. The thing is pretty terrifying. Hearing it crawling around in the vents and eventually dropping down somewhere nearby is something to experience. Also, having it in a dead sprint coming after you is also bad news.
Isolation is the best AAA game we've gotten in a long time, and that it has pretty successfully revived the survival horror genre. It's a really good game, not a perfect one. They were close, but some of the stuff (mainly the AI) brought it down. I really hope that the people that made Isolation get a chance to refine everything they've got here and create a fantastic sequel. I'd also like them to take a crack at making an Aliens game, to wash away the taste of Colonial Marines.
Short answer: nice game
Lastly, I'd like to thank Ganymede for gifting me the game. I probably wouldn't have played it for many, many years otherwise. Thanks.

So this review has long been over due.  I had pre-ordered this game with high expectations as it just seemed like finaly we would have an alien game.  And was I right on the money.  I played this game over the course of a few days at night with the lights off with amazing sound and using steam streaming to my 55" tv using my wireless 360 controller cause I can, and what a treat.
The official reviews out there for the most part I thought were harsh for all the wrong reasons. That it was just to unforgiving. The reason being that we have raised a generation of gamers who have it to easy and quit when it gets to hard.  In the prime of PC gaming which is always, but i'm talking pre 2000's where games made you think, were unforgiving and amazing on it's own right were the reward and satifcation of completing the task lead to greater satisfaction and you felt smarter for it. We can see the tone of it changed from it's initial inception from the critics after they had time to calm down from their rage quitting.  I think even PC Gamer chose it as their game of the year and it was definitely mine.  The scores were artifially lowered due to the difficulty.
Here is the best part in all of this the game is amazing.  The atmosphere, sounds, xenomorph details & brutality bring you a world of constant dread knawing at the back of your mind as you travel and unravel the lore of your surroundings to a satifying conclusion.  The impossible notion of knowing this lethal entity is programmed to hunt you down and kill you at all cost as well as other elements in this game.  I found myself often times holding my breath as the creature approached, hiding in the shadows a arms reach away from being destroyed by this lethal killing machine.  I think at one time I sat there for 20 min just waiting for the right moment to move or make a run for the exit.  I've given it the middle finger, I've cust at it as I knew I would die and the adrenaline of making it to the exit in one piece.  Hah the one time my wife came down and sat for a few minutes to watch me play and we were talking not expecting to turn and realizing the damn thing joined us in the vents o.O and the yelp that ensued.  And the many other deaths i've experienced unique in each it's own :)
They did a good job of capturing the feel of the original movies I found myself in nostalgic moments of my youth when I first experienced those movies that's how well they did on that.  The sounds are amazing.  The visuals on ultra are amazing.  If there is one truth to pc gaming, never skimp out on the video card.
With all that out of the way dont forget games are about having fun and the fun is only limited by your own imagination and willingness to escape to these worlds that are created for us to enjoy.

Bought this game on a whim because I liked the art style and I've spent €0,59 on dumber things before. And I didn't regret - especially at its price it's a fairly enjoyable (although very easy) RPG.
The humor is quite surreal and the artwork is a pretty great black and white pencil style. I enjoyed the weird soundtrack as well (reminded me in part by the soundtrack for LISA: The Painful RPG... except perhaps for the dinosaur song).
It's not a perfect game by any means. The controls are a little buggy sometimes and the enemies are oddly unbalanced depending on where you are (although you're usually given enough healing items so it's not a big deal - I went through the entire playthrough without having a single game over). The story definitely has some great moments, although is somewhat incoherent in places. In my playthrough the F12 hadn't been fixed so trying to take a screenshot with F12 would result in the game going back to the main menu and me having to start again from my latest save - this should definitely be fixed.
In summary I found the game enjoyable for its price and found that the humor and art in itself was worth it. I spent roughly 5 hours to complete it (and it appears I missed a few things), but I took my time so it can probably be beaten faster than that,
If you like odd RPGs and aren't offended by the artstyle then I'll definitely recommend this for the low price.

Broforce is a game that is rooted deep in the arcade shooters of the past. Contra, Commando, The Revenge of Shinobi, all of these games and more were made in a time when John Rambo and John Matrix were the superheroes of the silver screen, and game developers shamelessly translated these characters again and again. Entire genres were created in pursuit of capturing the essence of Rambo in an interactive sense. The developers at Free Lives have perfected this ideal in a way that neither the official Rambo video game or Stallone’s own nostalgia trips can. Simply put, Broforce is the ur-action movie game, combining the ridiculous tone of Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon with an attention to detail that can only come with a true love for that strange and ridiculous time when Arnold and friends shooting and screaming into the forrest was the pinnacle of cinema.

The series tells a wonderful story of Graham as he becomes King, rescues his people, finds a wife, bonds with his family and ultimately saves his kingdom. The story is told episodically starting with the becoming King tale which sets up the series very well. It has the user solve puzzles and problems through the use of items they find about the levels and also allows the player to choose different approaches on how to solve them. The game is above and beyond a very concerted and commendable game that effectively conveys the emotional toil that occurs through grahams life that shape the person he becomes. The graphics are a whimsically well chosen style that really reflects the tone of te series but doesn't stop it from conveying dark tones when necessary.
The series does falter somewhat in episodes 2 + 4 (especially 4) mainly due to either very little story development or in the case of episode 4 just repeated use  of the same puzzle and forced/badly explained character development that leaves you feeling confused/annoyed at the mishandled story telling. But the series overall is above par one of the best series i've ever played and i look forward to a sequel.

There's very few games in this world that have literally brought me to tears, and this is one of them. Having been a player since Chapter 1 way back last year, the pacing of the chapters over the course of time was a welcome change from the mountain of content you usually get from a game studio game, so the time investment felt very worth it (I had several playthroughs chapter-by-chapter)
The thing that really got me, was the character development and story telling. I know this is what these kinds of games are all about, but the way the story was told, and how it all ties together at the end, draws the player in and really engages them with their decisions has real impact on the story. I felt sad along the way for some of the choices I made, but never to the point where I felt I was missing out on part of the game. I'd like to play through again at some point and make very different decisions to see what's different.
The puzzles, while they can become challenging, are certainly not overwhelming. The most difficult ones I felt were in Chapter 2, not because of the actual difficulty, but because you literally were making life and death decisions. While there felt like a way to optimally solve it, it was not clear and really had an impact on how you felt about the characters in the game. The rest of the puzzles were challenging to the point where they were solvable with enough patience, and I did not feel like I had to look up many of them online (I did for a few... I will admit)
Anyway, this game is amazing. Well worth the time investment and I would highly recommend for any player, either having played King's Quest in the past, or not.

An adorable, puntastic adventure that rekindles the soul of the
series for another generation... and when I say PUNtastic I certainly mean it!
The dialog is rich with pun after whitty pun, sometimes firing at you in rapid succession. It is a bit of a dry sense of humor at times, but more often than not had me laughing out loud. I have never heard so many bakery puns in my life! They really got a rise out of me when I yeast expected it. The developers didn't loaf around on the physical comedy either. They did a really knead job of it & add lot of bun to the experience!
Ok enough, this isn't a half-baked review, and this is getting mold fast...
All puns aside, the story itself is well written, split into mostly individual episodic adventures taking place at different timelines in King Graham's past, with some crossover via the storytelling by 'Grandfather Graham' to his granddaughter/son in the present. The narrative taken puts you firmly into the story, giving the sense you are experiencing it through the innocent & wonder-filled eyes of one of Graham's grandchildren. Taking this approach really worked well to bring that magic of fairytales, those heroic quests of adventure, & the larger-than-life stories of legend to life. There is a mash up of references to classic fables, albeit a bit more traditional approach than taken in say
, for example.
There are also some unique storytelling techniques are interwoven within the game mechanics, such as timelapse section where Graham has a "senior moment", forgets & has to back track the same section retelling the story, or where your granddaughter interrupts you and says adorably "do we really need to see this again?" when running back over a location, skipping you forward.
At times the story does feel like it takes a bit more of a back seat to the action or puzzles, and although you can make different decision paths throughout, the differences made on the story are relatively minor. Ultimately, most of your custom choices fall into a bravery, wisdom or compassion decision tree depending on how you want to play it out.
There are a lot of puzzles to sink your teeth into across all of the chapters, but particulary later in the game. Some larger sequences of puzzles do make the game more linear in its design, rather than offering more discovery/adventure/experimentation. Difficulty of the puzzles would range in the easy-to-medium category, although the music related ones specifically seemed to personally give me a bit of grief, you should find that your progress doesn't stall for long. The design of the puzzles were very well done, offering a good variety of challenges to keep you engaged between story progression.
Graham meets a number of intriguing & querky characters in his travels. Even the minor characters are well thought out, full of personality & brought to life with some great animations & energetic voice acting. You really do not know what to expect with the wackiness of it all sometimes. Although there wasn't a weak link in the voice casting, my favorite would have to be Christoper Lloyd's performance as the warm & endearing 'Old Graham'. Could listen to that husky voice for hours, athough I was still half expecting/hoping for a
reference to be snuck in there somewhere!
The villian Manny, superbly voiced by veteran
& the enthusiasticly nerdy performance of 'Young Graham' by Josh Keaton captured the persona of Graham perfectly. His geek-out moments where
are hilarious!
The beauty & attention to detail in the world & enviroments is impressive
. You can see a lot of love went into it. Dynamic camera movement is smooth, mixing up the angles as you navigate around the hand-painted maps. Although fully 3D, there is a good mix of 2D elements that give a retro touch
.
There is not much that I found detracting from this adventure, although I would like to have seen it
to be possible to skip the story until you have completed the first playthrough. I knocked it accidentally in one section and had to replay to hear it, but it also resulted in many of my screenshots showing the
UI overlay when pressing F12 for a Steam screenshot even when playing with a controller. Strangely chapter 1 was not like that but the remaining were.
The lack of in-chapter save points will also mean for the achievement hunters out there, you will need to replay the entire chapter again if miss something. With a larger number of hidden & creative achievements already requiring multiple playthroughs to get, this can induce some frustration for those chasing the 100%.
I was also very surprised after such an exciting introduction that <
> did not bear any influence or part of later chapters. It was one of the most memorable scenes of the game & that encounter
should have been a bigger part of Graham's legacy.
It felt like quite a long time coming for the full chronicle of
to be released, but playing through all the chapters together over the past few weeks, I haven't not been disappointed by what
have accomplished. Nostalgic, yet fresh, it has kept the spirit of the originals alive.

You're in for a world of pain.
No More Room in Hell (NMRiH for short) is a zombie-survival game with intense themes. You can see blood, death, and despair everywhere. Body bags on the street, with crashed cars and stores that are boarded up. There's a few weapons left, and you plus up to 5 other survivors have to make it to an extraction point by doing many different objectives. One objective could be quick as hell. Another might take tons of minutes.
There are tons of zombies that are all really slow. It'll take a while before they'll get you, Barbara, but when they do, unless you're prepared you're pretty much dead. There are normal zombies, fast zombies, and child zombies. Normal are easy to kill, just hold down Mouse 1, release and then quickly press the V button (THIS IS VERY IMPORTANT! It pushes zombies back, and has saved my life A♥♥♥♥♥♥TON of times) and then do it again until they're dead. Fast zombies are the same as normal zombies, but they go faster and attack faster. Child zombies are quick too, but they can't bite you, only make you bleed. Melee weapons usually take two or three hits to the head, charged before they'll kill one zombie. If you just sway your weapon back and forth you'll find yourself either empty on stamina, or dead.
A gun is good, but they're not common and ammo for the right gun, YOUR gun, is even more rare. A Beretta 92 or a Glock 17 will take 2 hits to the head (Or 1 if you stand still for a while, this is called "Deadeye") but their ammo is common and they have a large capacity. A 1911 will only need 1 bullet to the head, but ammo for that is rare and so is the gun itself, and it's only got a capacity of 7+1, but it will bring a world of pain to the zombies. A revolver is handy but it's got a lot of recoil, 6 shots and rare as hell ammo. Then there's big guns, MAC-10, MP5, M16A4, CZ858, Shotguns and Sniper Rifles, all of which take a lot of inventory space and have rare ammo (Except for MAC-10 and MP5, who uses .45ACP and 9mm), and they're all rare too. What I'm trying to say here is that all you need is a pistol and a good melee weapon to survive.
Then there are survival maps, which are about you and your team bunkering down and trying to protect one, two or three areas at the same time. These maps are very intense, and your team has to survive some waves with limited supplies and a horde of zombies. Hammer and planks are going to be your best friend, since they can slow down the zombies, but not forever. And sometimes The National Guard will drop in supplies for you and your team. This can include melee weapons, guns & ammo, medical supplies and other useful and handy supplies.
However, do not download this game if you are easily scared, this is a pretty scary games with dark enviroments and scary enemies.
Although the graphics of the game were not top-notch, the list of weapons and the character selection far surpased my expectations.

The game strays away from the survival horror elements compared to the first one and the focus this time around is action. If you are a Mikami fan you will notice the lack of his signature style, with the game taking a more hollywood-esque safer approach to enemy encounters as well as cinematics. The difficulty is drastically toned down with plentiful ammo and easily accessible save points. If you are a survival horror fan, the normal/survivor difficulty is quite easy and i recommend to start with nightmare difficulty, which puts up a challenge until one gets used to the controls. The classic mode is a neat addition but rather forgiving compared to the Akumu difficulty in the first.
The transition to semi-open world dilutes the entire experience and atmosphere is rather lacking, which is suprising considering the freedom given to players. Similar to the first game there are plenty of scripted events that take control away from the players, but the core shooting RE4 mechanics kept me on the hook.
There are definitely some survival horror moments within the sidequests but they are short lived and lacking much content. The art direction took a step down from the first one and the bosses are rather not intuitive except for a select few. Still a good game with a more coherent and emotional plot. The soundtrack elevates the title quite a bit and sets it apart from the first one.
Hopefully it gets a third one and would make a great trilogy.

Its the cynical by-the-numbers sequel we were all secretly expecting. Dark Souls 1 is the better game in most aspects, but DKS2 triumphs in a couple places.
1, the new game+ has seen a lot of hard work and theres chunks of content you cant even see until youve beat the game several times.
2, secrets are way more prominent, be they the new super-hidden false walls or inaccessable parts of old areas you can revisit.
3, there was a revamped lighting system planned in development, where you could forego your off-hand to carry a torch and illuminate dark areas. The lighting plan was more or less ruined by release, but theres still a good 2 or 3 levels where a torch is viable, and those levels tend to be pretty awesome (except for shrine of amana, for unrelated reasons).
4, dks2 is a better PC port than dark souls, with steamworks instead of GFWL, passable keyboard controls and a less insulting options menu.
Otherwise, you get more for less by just getting the first game. Lore, combat, exploration, enemy variety, level design, bosses and multiplayer; whatever 2 actually improves upon, it simultaneously breaks so much that it may as well have not bothered.
If you loved dks1 and just want more dark souls, this product more or less performs as advertised.

Ok i don´t usually write reviews about any game but still i think this one desserves alittle time from me to explain you guys why this MMO its so unique and fun.
Ok a certain clarification about this game, this isn't skyrim and its not gonna be 100% like it that or any elder scrolls game, although it doesn´t mean its a bad thing, it take some elements from previous elder scrolls game and adapt them to the MMO style it should have since its a Massive Multiplayer Online game!
Lets start by inmersion, they really do a good job on this aspect of the game, you find public world bosses and certain events called dolmen scattered around all the map, it has collectibles and resources for your crafting jobs as well so it encourages that you explore around their beatiful made maps, for every faction i must say it takes roughly 150+ hours to complete theese maps and they are beginning to add more content to the game so it doesnt end that quickly.
Ok this is no ordinary mark target then spell cast MMO you are used to, it´s combat system its kinda unique it reminds me a bit of Tera online but way better, you have 2 bars where you can allocate certain spells that you intent to make part of your specialised build, certain spells are actually skill shots or require you to be targetting the mob with your camera so its not the usual jump and spam buttons from other MMOs, in dungeons and in pvp positioning is actually key for your success, and not only that you can actually block and dodge (dodge roll) spells to minimize their effect on you, its more action based without skipping the RPG because depending the way you built theese bars affects hugely the play style of your characters, you have a really big skill tree where you can allocate like 300 skill points in crafting passives,combat passives, weapon passives and actives, and 4 direrent classes each with 3 skill sets actives and passives as well. It´s really flexible to do a really original build ive seen crazy builds like sorcerer healers or tanks etc it really lets you do really personalized stuff. AND NO not only that! when you reach end game you unlock a thing called Championship System where you unlock points every certain exp amount that you can allocate within a really wide skill tree that looks alike skyrim tree (theese are passive skills) to tweak your character to your own needs.
Dungeon wise it has a really big spam of dungeons around 15 or more dungeons each with unique boss fights and mechanics and around 10 more End game dungeons, 3 trials (raids), so its kinda hard to get bored specially on the endgame dungeons since they require skilled players to beat, also you have with the DLCs are big solo player Arena and a huge PVPVE map where you have a hybrid of story and pvp.
Talking about PvE it has a really really big map where you fight for the dominance between the 3 factions available, with diferent mechanics, you can even use siege weapons to break down walls on Forts and so (i don´t wanna talk much about it because i dont wanna spoil the fun of seeing it for yourself).
In conclusion this game it´s a gem specially for thoose who are TES games fans, no its not a pure TES game but it uses a lot of it´s elements, and also players who just want to play a MMO can be delighted with it, specially if you are bored of the same usual MMO.

I'm not often compelled to write reviews for games I play, even ones I greatly enjoy... but this game was truly something. I completed it in two sittings.
It took me a few attempts to figure out how things worked in the game, especially line of sight and sound. Once you understand how the different enemy types react to specific stimuli, it becomes rather easy, at least on Medium difficulty. However, this is one of those Metroidvania FPS games where you revisit certain locations of the game multiple times with new tools--and I LOVE that.
This game nails the atmosphere. Sound effects, music, voice acting--all stellar. I highly recommend using surround sound, even if it's virtual.
There are some trial and error moments in the game, but they are few and far between. Those usually set you back a few minutes and can cause some frustration, but it's as simple as learning basic traversal patterns.
As a horror game, this is one of the best. Nothing comes quite close to holding your breath in a locker while the Alien stares into it, or hiding under a table as its tail slithers by. And nothing is quite as heart-pounding as hearing it scream as it spots you, and you make a mad dash around corners looking for a hiding spot. WHEW!
There are set pieces which made me pause and take numerous screenshots. This is a work of art! I will one day (maybe soon) go back into it and play on Nightmare difficulty, but because this game is so long (around 20 hours if you take your time and explore and find collectibles), it may have to wait a bit.
PLAY THIS GAME!

Quick Review:
Overall score 9/10. Much like the original Alien film, AI’s biggest strength is its incredibly immersive atmosphere. Even when the alien isn’t around, the constant sense of paranoia that the game creates is outstanding. I wouldn’t call this game “scary” in the typical horror sense, but no game has ever made me feel so on edge or filled with pulse-pounding tension. As other reviews elaborate on, the action-oriented sequences leave a lot to be desired and are completely underwhelming in comparison to being stalked by the perfect organism. In the end though, be prepared for the most tense and stressful gaming experience in recent memory, if not ever.
Full Review:
Gameplay 9/10 – Intense. That is, perhaps, the best one-word summary of the gameplay in AI. Much like seemingly all of its recent horror-gaming cousins, AI sticks you in a violent world that you are simply not prepared to face head on. You must hide, stay in the shadows, and keep your composure if you want to survive. The few weapons you do find in your travels on Sevastopol are only effective against the scattered human and android enemies you’ll come across. Go ahead, try them on the alien. Just make sure you tape it so I can laugh at your feeble attempt to live. Where this game differs from other related games is, to me, in the masterful sense of tension that it creates. Even playing games like the much-lauded and deservedly so Amnesia, I never felt the same level of drawn out, heart thumping goodness on display here. Every bump behind you or above you, every creak of the ships’ hull will have you anxiously scanning your surroundings. When you find yourself caught in a cat and mouse game with the alien, especially for the first time, your every waking second will feel like an eternity as you struggle to push on and predict what your hunter will do next. Some of the most memorable moments in my gaming history were when I breathed a sigh of relief as I found a clever way around the alien’s path only to hear it scurry into the vents and appear just beyond the next door, mere feet from my face. As I crouch on the other side of a table with the alien across from me, sniffing the air, it begins to move around toward me and all I can do is a delicate dance of almost certain death as I try to keep just that one inch ahead of its gaze. Unfortunately, these amazing moments of terror are sometimes interrupted by haphazard bargain bin FPS action sequences where you must ward off the far less menacing threat of humans and androids. While I certainly agree that the player needs a break from the unbearable tension of being hunted, I’m disappointed that this was the best way the developers could think of. Still though, what this game gets right, it really gets right and if a pulse-raising thrill ride is what you’re after, then I guarantee you will find it here.
Graphics 9/10 – The graphics in AI aren’t jaw-dropping in their majestic beauty or surreal color palette, but for what they are trying to do, they are close to perfect. Every detail is faithfully recreated from the original Ridley Scott vision of the environment and the optional film grain adds a nice touch of nostalgic ambience. The mood lighting in the game is also excellent with brilliant contrast between dark corridors and hopeful glimmers of light, though it never feels too dark. My biggest gripe with the graphics is in the animations. The alien sometimes appears to move about a bit awkwardly and when it does, it takes some of the menacing quality away. The way that the game forces you into completing every single animation also has a tendency to annoy, especially when it’s simply logging off a computer.
Sound 10/10 – A huge part of why the gameplay is so effective is because of the phenomenal sound design. With headphones (you better use headphones foo!) the sound is so immersive and detailed that you will truly feel like you are trapped on the deadliest space station in the universe. Echoes in the halls, the slow creaks of the walls, and certainly not least, the adrenaline boosting thumps and shrieks of the alien itself. I prefer to play with music off as I find it much more immersive, though for the purposes of this review I tested it and found it genuinely effective at fleshing out the atmosphere.

As someone who grew up loving the King's Quest series, and who is still an avid point-and-click fan, I wanted to love this game.  And while certain elements of it were really wonderful, bringing back fond memories (the creaters clearly also loved the original series, throwing many classic references into the mix), I do have to admit to some fairly significant disappointment.
First the pros:
Music -- The music is wonderful, fitting, and, with the occasional remixes of original songs from the franchise, perfect for the experience.
Graphics -- While I wouldn't describe them as "stunning" they are lush, filling Daventry (and other areas) with the correct mood and ambiance than one would expect, allowing the story to be told with its own unique style.
Gameplay -- While the controls were a little awkward at first (I had expected mouse controls, as with most point-and-click adventures), as someone also used to RPG controls, I quickly adapted.
Script -- Dialogue was pithy, clever, and very entertaining.
Unfortunately, the game also came along with some major cons:
Story -- This is where the game really falls on its♥♥♥♥♥  As a brief summary, King Graham, now an old man, retells some of the highlights of his adventuring life to his grand-daughter, beginning before he became a knight all the way to his present as an old man.  A few recurring characters appear along the way, some who weave themselves into the larger narrative that was the original King's Quest series.  THIS...is a great idea.  However, the execution needed some SERIOUS editing.  Character motivations and feelings (especially in the "modern day" with Graham's grandchildren) seemed to vary at whim and certain sections were FAR too long and tedious as cut-scenes.  The past was better in terms of its storytelling, but, at times there was a lot of shoe-horning things in or forcing connections that don't really make sense or feel genuine.  Generally, the story with Graham's grandchildren wasn't interesting enough for the time given to it, and the storyline in the past wasn't consistant enough with trying to weave it with the original series to make it anything other than unsatisfying.  Which is such a shame because all the parts for a great game were here...they just needed a little more work than it felt was put into them.
Puzzles -- The game couldn't seem to decide if it was a puzzle game or an inventory puzzle game, and I think this is one of the major reasons for the mixed reviews.  I get that this game couldn't be as challenging or incorporate the unforgiving Sierra-logic of my youth, nor would I have the patience for that anymore, but at least one chapter was reduced to almost entirely logic puzzles, which many won't expect from King's Quest.  It made the game feel a little like those areas were added to bulk up a somewhat lacking storyline, and, while no game should have padding, a game that is standing on the backs of a legendary series like King's Quest should have returned to the drawing board instead of resorting to it.
Verdict:
I'm still giving this "recommended" (although I hate Steam's binary system just for games like this), because I can't bring myself to not.  However, that recommendation comes with a warning: don't expect old-school King's Quest, and be prepared for a flawed, but entertaining, game.  This will never really feel like part of the King's Quest series to me...for that maybe go download The Silver Lining.  Overall, perhaps wait for a sale.

This game needs no introduction. It's regarded as one of the best games for PC ever made, as well as one of the best for its genre... and it is wholly deserving of all its praise. System Shock 2 is a game that defies any real review, to do so would to really spoil the experience. It needs to be played to understand why it is so good, and that is what playing it is: an experience.
The game is a rare example of design, gameplay, aesthetic, atmosphere, and presentation all working in near perfect harmony to deliver an engrossing experience that pulls you in and keeps you going until the final hours are passed. The RPG elements are almost completely free form, allowing you to build your character in almost any way you like focusing on what you want as you want it (though in the early game you'll do well to focus on your initial strengths as to not spread yourself too thin), and while initial enemy placement is pre-determined you'll find out that they respawn with alarming frequency in random numbers and placements to constantly keep you on your toes.
The game is not perfect, mind, and has some flaws. Most notable are the level designs for the final areas of the game don't seem quite as well designed as the rest of the game and some other small nitpicks, but these are minor gaffes in System Shock 2's excellent imageand are easily forgiven. If you like science fiction, survival horror, cyberpunk, body or eldritch horror, free form RPGs, first person shooters, adventure games, or any combination thereof of them, then System Shock 2 is well deserving of your attention. And hell, even if you don't like any of that stuff, it may be worth looking into just to try new things! You might just find yourself surprised.

This game is too good for a normal review so he is a recipe for a bacon explosion:
INGREDIENTS:
2 lbs thick cut bacon
2 lbs Italian sausage
3⁄4 cup barbecue sauce (your favorite)
3 tablespoons barbecue seasoning (your favorite rub, recommended Bad Byron's Butt Rub, Rendezvous Famous Seasoning, or Steven Raichlen)
DIRECTIONS:
To kick off the construction of this pork medley you’ll need to create a 5x5 bacon weave. If the strips you’re using aren’t wide enough to span 5x5 inches, then you may need to use a few extra slices to fill out the pattern. Just make sure your weave is tight and that you end up with a nice square shape to work with.
The next step is to add some barbecue seasoning on top of your bacon weave. (BBQ Addict recommends Bad Byron's Butt Rub, Rendezvous Famous Seasoning, or Steven Raichlen's All-Purpose Rub).
Now that your pork is well seasoned, it’s time to add more pork. Take two pounds of Italian sausage and layer it directly on top of your bacon weave. Be sure to press the sausage to the outer edges of the bacon creating a patty that is the same thickness all the way across. Most grocery stores carry loose sausage, so just pick out one you like.
Next up is bacon layer number two. Take the remaining bacon slices and fry them up the same way you would for breakfast. If you like soft bacon, make it soft. If you like crunchy bacon, make it crunchy.
Since this is a barbecue recipe, we need to add another layer of barbecue flavor. Take your favorite sauce and drizzle it all over the top of the bacon pieces. (BBQ Addict recommends Burnt Finger BBQ’s homemade competition sauce). Once you’ve sauced the bacon, sprinkle on some more of the barbecue seasoning you used on the bacon weave.
Very carefully separate the front edge of the sausage layer from the bacon weave and begin rolling backwards. You want to include all layers EXCEPT the bacon weave in your roll. Try and keep the sausage as tight as possible and be sure to release any air pockets that may have formed. Once the sausage is fully rolled up, pinch together the seams and ends to seal all of the bacon goodness inside.
At this point we can start to see the final shape of our Bacon Explosion, but we’re missing one key item. To complete the construction process, roll the sausage forward completely wrapping it in the bacon weave. Make sure it sits with the seam facing downward to help keep it all sealed up.
Sprinkle some barbecue seasoning on the outside of the bacon weave, and now it is ready for the smoker. Cook your Bacon Explosion at 225°F in a constant cloud of hickory smoke until your meat thermometer gives an internal temperature reading of 165°F Normally this will take about 1 hour for each inch of thickness, but that could vary depending on how well you maintain your fire and also how many times you open the smoker to take a peek. BBQ Addict recommends 2.5 hours, for a roll 2.5 inches in diameter.
Now that the Bacon Explosion is fully cooked, you need to add some finishing flavors. Remember that barbecue sauce you used for inner flavor? You'll be using that same sauce to glaze the cooked bacon weave. Using a basting brush, coat the entire surface with a thin layer of sauce. Sweet sauces are loaded with sugars, so they’ll give your fatty a nice glossy finish. Spicy and vinegar based sauces don’t contain as much, so they won’t set up as well. If you’re dead set on using those sauces, just cut them with a bit of honey and you’ll get the same effect.
Slice the Bacon Explosion into quarter to half inch rounds to serve. If your roll was good and tight, you should now see a nice bacon pinwheel pattern throughout the sausage.
Obviously pork is best served by itself, but if you feel the need to make this meat monster into a sandwich, BBQ Addict recommends placing a couple Bacon Explosion slices on a warm Pillsbury’s Grands Biscuit.

It's been about 3 years since the first Evil Within was released and boy, there is a pretty good jump when it comes to comparing gameplay as well as story between the two. Note, you don't have to play the first prior to playing this but there are a good amount of references in this game from the former that will give you good chills, especially when you obtain the final projector slide imo. Anyway, gameplay has evolved with the transition of levels as in the first game to semi-open world in the second. Upgrade trees are streamlined and an eclectic amount of new weapons as well as old appear. Overall, the sequel allows increased freedom and options in how you want to take down enemies. The pacing of the story has also improved compared to the first game. Sebastian (the main protagonist) is better fleshed out as a dynamic character with legitimate motivations rather than "the guy that was there at the wrong time and wants to get out alive" role that he played in the first game.
TL;DR Best survival horror game I've played in awhile, even better than RE7 imo. Interesting cast of characters and simple, yet poignant story. Last 2-3 acts made the game a memorable one for me. First steam review I've ever written because I hope to draw more attention to this game for others.
PS References "you're the best" and hercules meme. 10/10.

You are
Sebastian, trying to find a girl in a town where everything went wrong and must use everything at your disposal to get to her...if you are playing on classic mode difficulty, that is. The game is not that hard to be honest, even in nightmare difficulty after you upgraded some abilities and guns. If you are familiar to action-adventure genre, this game won't challenge you much.
The design of the monsters that appear in the town are good enough for me, but it's the boss designs that I'm underwhelmed with. In the first game, every boss was unique and some of them even had their own little backstory. They were memorable. In this one, the antagonists are unique and do have their backstory which is great but they lost their creepiness. Only the chainsaw lady freak and the ''obscura'' is what I liked in terms of looks. Also, the final boss is better than the final boss of the first game but is still bad.

The semi-open world style areas are not a bad addition in my opinion but I can understand if some players don't like it. It's a good thing the developers didn't just make the whole game resolve around in the same big area. There is variety, as you progress you start to visit different linear and semi-open areas. The environment design is nice and detailed, it is not boring to look at.
Now, onto the good parts :)
+ Controls are much better! You don't automatically stand up when you aim anymore, don't have to stand still while using syringes, can reload while sprinting and stealth is much more polished with the addition of stealth upgrades for Sebastian.
+ Upgrades are separated into two parts and the addition of crafting! No more using green gels for upgrading guns. Instead, you have to collect weapon parts to upgrade your guns. Another new addition is high-grade weapon parts and red gel, you use these two items to unlock the next tier in upgrades, these are found or given to you as you progress in the story. This system prevents you from upgrading to the top tier from the very start so you don't get overpowered in one category. Also, you can craft ammunition in workbenches using less crafting items or on the run using more items.
+ Better voice acting! I admit the lines can be cheesy at times but still Sebastian is not dull and actually has a personality.
+ The story! A father who feels guilty and trying to find his own daughter story is as generic as it sounds but what makes the story interesting is the involvement of mobius and STEM. I also would like to thank the developers for answering most of the questions that were asked in the first game and not forgetting the events of it AND building up on it. But I still have two questions:
1.

2.
+ You don't find the story interesting? It is still fun to play!
+ A polished game overall!

+ Tatiana!
+ That part after you reach Theodore!
+ That feeling I got when I opened last projector slide ;_; and after I talked to kidman about it!
In the end, I think this is a solid sequel. Thank you Tango Gameworks!

I recommend Slime Rancher with a large caveat in that the game lastability and longevity comes from a tumultuous grind in Slime Science and the devaluation of plorts.
Positives:
+ Disgustingly adroable and cute - the titular slimes will squeak and mew with delight as they bounce around with happy smiles plastered across their faces. There are even ones with cat ears and you can eventually shoot sunglasses (or other accessories) onto their faces
+ Incredibly relaxing - A calming experience that rarely presents much of a challenge as you farm food and feed slimes
+ Genuinely pleasant
Negatives:
- Thighs of steel required - You'll spend most of your time running around. Whether it be sprinting across your ranch or sprinting through the wilderness or back.
- Oh my, the grind - the late game effects are slow and laborious requiring numerous items to create a a single pump and a single pump then taking 10 minutes of your life for not much to come out of it.
- The Great Plort Market Crash - The plort market, how you'll make money, will inevitably plummet to measely funds and never recover, no matter how much you stockpile plorts. Rare slimes and tricky slimes become equally as valuable as those you gained in the first couple of hours.
Slime Rancher is wonderful enough just for the premise and the physical running of the ranch. Getting lost in the wilderness looking for slimes or mangos is greatly fun, but there's an awful lot of busy work that can get in the way. Whether it's running back and forth across your farm to sell everything due to a very limited inventory or even having to run all the way back to the latest zone because you'd picked up the four different things you could hold and needed some more. The fast travel is very limiting so travel rapidly no longer becomes fast. There are items that can fix these issues, such as your own personal teleports, but to acquire these items will take hours of slime science, trying to gain that single Royal Jelly you need, only to be shown the face of failure time and time again at 10 minute intervals, but also with your inventory constantly filling up and needing to be emptied. So many gosh darn laps and not a single jelly.
It's still fun and cute and good for several hours as you get every slime and combine them, but don't expect anything too grand, the world is a little empty and it feels a tad lonely.

I'm not often compelled to write reviews for games I play, even ones I greatly enjoy... but this game was truly something. I completed it in two sittings.
It took me a few attempts to figure out how things worked in the game, especially line of sight and sound. Once you understand how the different enemy types react to specific stimuli, it becomes rather easy, at least on Medium difficulty. However, this is one of those Metroidvania FPS games where you revisit certain locations of the game multiple times with new tools--and I LOVE that.
This game nails the atmosphere. Sound effects, music, voice acting--all stellar. I highly recommend using surround sound, even if it's virtual.
There are some trial and error moments in the game, but they are few and far between. Those usually set you back a few minutes and can cause some frustration, but it's as simple as learning basic traversal patterns.
As a horror game, this is one of the best. Nothing comes quite close to holding your breath in a locker while the Alien stares into it, or hiding under a table as its tail slithers by. And nothing is quite as heart-pounding as hearing it scream as it spots you, and you make a mad dash around corners looking for a hiding spot. WHEW!
There are set pieces which made me pause and take numerous screenshots. This is a work of art! I will one day (maybe soon) go back into it and play on Nightmare difficulty, but because this game is so long (around 20 hours if you take your time and explore and find collectibles), it may have to wait a bit.
PLAY THIS GAME!

Quick Review:
Overall score 9/10. Much like the original Alien film, AI’s biggest strength is its incredibly immersive atmosphere. Even when the alien isn’t around, the constant sense of paranoia that the game creates is outstanding. I wouldn’t call this game “scary” in the typical horror sense, but no game has ever made me feel so on edge or filled with pulse-pounding tension. As other reviews elaborate on, the action-oriented sequences leave a lot to be desired and are completely underwhelming in comparison to being stalked by the perfect organism. In the end though, be prepared for the most tense and stressful gaming experience in recent memory, if not ever.
Full Review:
Gameplay 9/10 – Intense. That is, perhaps, the best one-word summary of the gameplay in AI. Much like seemingly all of its recent horror-gaming cousins, AI sticks you in a violent world that you are simply not prepared to face head on. You must hide, stay in the shadows, and keep your composure if you want to survive. The few weapons you do find in your travels on Sevastopol are only effective against the scattered human and android enemies you’ll come across. Go ahead, try them on the alien. Just make sure you tape it so I can laugh at your feeble attempt to live. Where this game differs from other related games is, to me, in the masterful sense of tension that it creates. Even playing games like the much-lauded and deservedly so Amnesia, I never felt the same level of drawn out, heart thumping goodness on display here. Every bump behind you or above you, every creak of the ships’ hull will have you anxiously scanning your surroundings. When you find yourself caught in a cat and mouse game with the alien, especially for the first time, your every waking second will feel like an eternity as you struggle to push on and predict what your hunter will do next. Some of the most memorable moments in my gaming history were when I breathed a sigh of relief as I found a clever way around the alien’s path only to hear it scurry into the vents and appear just beyond the next door, mere feet from my face. As I crouch on the other side of a table with the alien across from me, sniffing the air, it begins to move around toward me and all I can do is a delicate dance of almost certain death as I try to keep just that one inch ahead of its gaze. Unfortunately, these amazing moments of terror are sometimes interrupted by haphazard bargain bin FPS action sequences where you must ward off the far less menacing threat of humans and androids. While I certainly agree that the player needs a break from the unbearable tension of being hunted, I’m disappointed that this was the best way the developers could think of. Still though, what this game gets right, it really gets right and if a pulse-raising thrill ride is what you’re after, then I guarantee you will find it here.
Graphics 9/10 – The graphics in AI aren’t jaw-dropping in their majestic beauty or surreal color palette, but for what they are trying to do, they are close to perfect. Every detail is faithfully recreated from the original Ridley Scott vision of the environment and the optional film grain adds a nice touch of nostalgic ambience. The mood lighting in the game is also excellent with brilliant contrast between dark corridors and hopeful glimmers of light, though it never feels too dark. My biggest gripe with the graphics is in the animations. The alien sometimes appears to move about a bit awkwardly and when it does, it takes some of the menacing quality away. The way that the game forces you into completing every single animation also has a tendency to annoy, especially when it’s simply logging off a computer.
Sound 10/10 – A huge part of why the gameplay is so effective is because of the phenomenal sound design. With headphones (you better use headphones foo!) the sound is so immersive and detailed that you will truly feel like you are trapped on the deadliest space station in the universe. Echoes in the halls, the slow creaks of the walls, and certainly not least, the adrenaline boosting thumps and shrieks of the alien itself. I prefer to play with music off as I find it much more immersive, though for the purposes of this review I tested it and found it genuinely effective at fleshing out the atmosphere.

This was one of the most intense games I have ever played. I am not even sure I would say it was fun, rather it COMPELLED me to continue playing either out of morbid curiosity or fascination with terror. Either way, it held my rapt attention throughout the entire campaign. This is not an 'easy' game, nor is it a casual way to spend a few hours. Expect to be drawn into the ultimate horror survival experience, where every mis-step can mean instant death. Impatient players will no doubt be rewarded with numerous up close and personal encounters with Alien fangs, and any time you engage in gunplay carries the virtual certainty of attracting death incarnate.
This is an enemy you cannot kill, only hope to avoid or eventually scare off for a few minutes. Add rogue synthetics (they hate being called androids) and fear-crazed humans into the mix, as well as a random Alien AI (you never know when the damn thing is going to show) you have the recipe for the stuff of nightmares. An immersive space-based 'world', with gorgeous graphics and true to the original movie in terms of art direction and 70's-ish future technology, this is the seminal Alien experience. Expect to have your heart pounding in your throat while you try and summon the courage to leave your hiding place to move forward. You'll really need to grow a pair to finish this game.

The gameplay is pretty grindy and linear--the player walks through a non-branching series of hallways and repeats rooms until gathering enough of whatever resource to get the desired upgrade. There is a live action combat mechanic and the rooms contain puzzles, but the controls are awkward: picking up unintended inputs and not clearly communicating to the player when input is being locked out.
The majority of the upgrades only provide differences in scale, and many become locked behind Points of No Return later. The story is a bit contrived, relying most on exposition and character monologue, rather than expressing any of that to the player through gameplay or character interaction.
To be fair, many of these weaknesses are actually weaknesses inherent to the RPG Maker engine, but knowing that doesn't make the game fun in its own right.

The game's main problems are that it's excessively long, and poorly paced.
There is a lot of waiting, laborious time consuming actions, and a lot of pointless filler, sometimes including quicktime events. Also a lot of arbitrary objectives, and collectathon situations. And in terms of narrative it contains a lot of boring technical dialogue that no one cares about, and a lot mainstream cheesiness.
But encounters with the alien make it all worth while.
The alien itself is a dramatically terrific creature, and the complex AI puts you into situations requiring carefulness and strategy to maneuver past. It mantains dominance and a level of uncertainty that keeps you on the edge of your seat, and it always manages to try to keep the battle close, but not unfair.
The game's also stunningly beautiful, with great polish, incredible lighting, and visceral sound effects which really help immerse you into the atmosphere of the space station, Sevastapol, based on the Nostromo from Alien (1979). Those elements + the AI still hold up even now.
If it were boiled down to just stealth and challenge, and they cut out all the pointless crap, I would give it a 10/10. Unfortunately that didn't happen so it's 8/10.
