What can I say about this series after marathoning through it? As a King's Quest fan, I enjoyed it. As an adventure game fan, I mostly enjoyed it. Let's explain.
Episode 1: Very strong with fun characters, a good mix of conversations and puzzles, and intuitive design. The only issue were non-skippable dialogues on repeats.
Episode 2: By far the weakest of the chapters. While it does try to establish a darker story and I will admit that it was unique having meters to juggle and deal with, I feel like the game didn't do enough to establish the villains as a legitimate threat. Kinda hard to feel captive when you're facing some weak bad guys with a weaker motivation. I'd say the early conversation with Olfie and the voice acting of the villagers is the strongest part here.
Episode 3: Amazing. While it's mostly a dialogue heavy fare with light simple puzzles and rather linear, the characters  were amazing, the nods to previous king's quest including amazing remixes of "Girl in the tower" and a great sense of timing and character building made this one worth it.
Episode 4: While I enjoyed angst-e-xander, and the voice acting was again top notch, I feel like aside from a scene towards the end this was also weak. It relied overly much on the same puzzle type which made the puzzle solving boring and there were no chances to make meaningful choices. I found the dinner conversations with Gwendolyn and her family FAR more interesting.
Episode 5: The use of white space to signify memory loss and the doddering early parts were uncomfortable. Especially after marathoning the series over two days, there weren't any real clues of it happening so it felt like a cerberus switch. That said, the themes it presents were intended to be uncomfortable so it did it's job well. The ending and explanation at the end was also quite amazing. This does wrap up the series quite well, making way to a new adventure with new characters potentially down the line.
So, I like this, but Episodes 2 and 4 drag down the experience somewhat.

I've been a KIng's Quest fan for the past a couple decades.  I've always enjoyed the series (except for the horrible King's Quest Mask of Eternity).  This series was, for the most part, a delightful return to those long ago games.  The storytelling was rich, the graphics beautiful, and the gameplay fun and smooth.  Players have the option of three different story routes Bravery, Wisdom or Compassion, which gives the game some slight replay value.   The early chapters are light-hearted and are most aligned with the old game series.  The later chapters place more emphasis on solving puzzles and less on collecting objects.  The puzzles themselves pose some challenge, but no overbearingly so, which I enjoyed.  Also, the storyline in the later chapters beoomes rather dark, and I can't say I was too thrilled with it, though I will concede it was good storytelling.  It's just not what I'm looking for in a King's Quest game.  If you're a fan of the old series definitely check this one out.
That being said, I'm really disappointed that the game developers are releasing an Epilogue chapter that will be unavailable to those players who purchased the Season Pass.  I think that's utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. If you're planning on purchasing, then I suggest getting the complete series or you will be unable to get the extra chapter like me.

This game is Half Life as it was always meant to be seen and played, but our computers couldn't handle it in the 90s. Black Mesa incorperates all the best that the Source engine has to offer; it's drop-dead gorgeous in the graphics department and the developers deserve a huge round of applause for all the work they must have put into this.
At the same time, I should point out that it's not exactly the same game as the original Half Life. In the original I always thought it was intended to be comical how the dumb looking scientists kept getting killed left and right or blindly blundering into danger only to be splattered into half a dozen pieces. Black Mesa on the other hand borrows a lot of the darker and sometimes tragic atmosphere of the HL2 games. The scientists feel more like real people trying to survive a disaster now, and you feel bad when they die, rather than thinking it's part of a joke. I think that level of immersion though makes the game that much more of a triumph.
The gameplay is much more sophisticated now as well. I remember in the original one of my favorite tricks was to hide behind a box and wait for Vortigaunts to turn the corner before blasting them with the shotgun; I can't do that now because Black Mesa made them too smart for that. Nevertheless, that makes the gameplay more chalanging, more realistic, and therefore more fun.
I only have one real complaint about the game and it's that the bullsquids' eyes are on the tops of their heads instead of on the sides like in the original HL, but that's just a little detail only a nerd like me would take notice of.
At the time I'm writing this, they still haven't finished the Xen levels of the game but it's absolutely worth buying as it stands right now. Whether you're a hard-core HL fan like me, or you've never heard of it before, if you like FPS games, this one's an absolute treat.

Clandestine is one of the most underrated stealth games I've ever played.
I'll start with what I don't like: out of all the things to randomly place they chose collectables you'll need to upgrade your armory.
The game is coded in Unity, so the facial animations are questionable, and the animations overall are very stiff and the  collision detection on the environment isn't great.
The AI is competent, but not particularly complex since guards won't notice doors opened or trace left by the player.
So why do I love Clandestine?
Despite marketing itself as a cooperative experience, Clandestine is a very solid single player campaign as well, and one that reacted to my playstyle and performance more than any other stealth game I've ever played along with more attention to detail than most games released with far, far bigger budgets.
Despite just having pistols for a firearm, several different ammo types are available all of which are balanced to ensure people who treat the game as a murder simulator have some systems to mess around with. You can have different rounds in the chamber than you have in the clip, something so few games do I can't count them on more than one hand.
The game tracks your pacifism, the amount of footprint you've left behind and whether you've been spotted separately, and reacts to all of it individually in gameplay, dialogue (written notes and e-mails as well as conversations) and score.
The soundtrack is smooth guitar and electric synth that dynamically ramps up and down based on your performance and the levels events.
To top it all off, the game does something I haven't seen since Splinter Cell Chaos Theory! It goes the extra mile to make sure everyone who should be speaking a specific language is actively speaking that language, so your Russian character when speaking to other Russians will be speaking in subtitled Russian. Mexican cops in Mexico City will speak accurate Spanish. The attention to the international settings astounded me.
Lastly, the game is one of the very few to include depleted uranium shells (armor piercing and hollow points in one bullet, but leaving so much footprint you would never want to use one while concealing your presence), salvo squeezebore (splitting bullets) shots and nerve gas, incredibly going out of it's way to describe in detail the laws of the time that would nullify the legality of the grenades and the horror that inspired the treaties that banned them.
All of these amazing things, wrapped around a genuine, solid post-Cold War spy plot that actively calls to attention and accurately draws on the alphabet agencies, international diplomacy and darker aspects of the time.
All of this while essentially doing Watch_Dogs concept (hacking + stealth) far better than Ubisoft managed as well as tapping into a rarely touched upon period in videogames (the post Cold War confusion of the mid 90's) means I can absolutely give Clandestine a recommendation, and a rare commendation as the best game on Unity I've ever played by a country mile.
If you've played your fair share of stealth games and want something a little more experimental this is absolutely worth picking up.
Oh, and to those into hardcore stealth the game actively encourages minimalist gameplay in it's scoring system, pushing the player to finish levels with the least gadget use and the least knockouts and kills. The entire game can be played nonlethally, with only one knockout and no item or weapon use.

Clandestine is a game that I should have found earlier. The concept of this game is very unique, as it requires 2 players to get the best experience. One is hacker, the other the spy. You have to rely on each other to get the job done, because both players have completely different tasks and abilities.
This game stays true to its stealth core. The spy isn't overpowered as hell, and the game rewards you for avoiding any conflict with guards and such. Playing as the spy is fun, because you are given just the right amount of tools you need to finish the mission: A gun, some gadgets and the shadows.
Sadly, it doesn't come without its flaws. Getting used to the controls was a bit tricky and the voice acting isn't the best. The story was ok, but nothing really new. Clandestine relies on its gameplay a lot, maybe a bit too much. Another point is that there isn't really much to do as the hacker. You monitor enemy patrols, hack email accounts and find passwords. Usually, the hacker is ahead of the spy, because as the hacker you have much more power on the internet than the spy has in the field.
But that's fine by me. My friend and I are both having a great time playing this game, and it's the coop part that makes this game so good. Thankfully, singleplayer is also available, allowing you to switch between the spy and the hacker. But like I said, playing with friends is way better.

This game got some bad press, but I disagree with those that said it was too hard. I played through on the recommended "hard" difficulty. Don't get me wrong, this game is very challenging, sometimes frustrating, but I think that's exaclty what drives the chest-pounding tension. perfectly spaced save points and an atmosphere that replicates the creepiness of Alien (1979) with uncanny detail. I can't say the game will have much replay value, so do what I didn't in my pl;aythrough: use good directional headphones or surroundsound for the best experience. A caveat: you really need to like survival horror/stealh games to enjoy this. If you want to get through every section in only a few attempts you will probably not like the punishment this game can deal out. Still, when I did manage to get everything right on the first try, it felt amazingly satisfying. If you like survial horror AND the Alien movies ( the first two) don't misss this one.

This game is everything an Alien game should be but for one, at times agonising, flaw... Why can't I climb over stuff?! I know it can be difficult to add that kind of functionality and I'm not imagining it should be Mirror's Edge style parkour, sliding over desks and under damage, but there are times when game progression or simply survival would be easily, and far more logically solved if I could climb over an obstruction instead of having to work my way around obstacles that wouldn't really hold you back. The effect is massively damaging as I get yanked out of the immersion, something the game painstakingly creates and one of its biggest draws.
The very occasional glitch also made for some frustrating moments and I had to restart a section at one point because I blew up a lot of androids instead of fleeing at one point.
Let me be clear though; these issues, whilst painful sometimes, do not stop this being one of the greatest stealth games I've ever played. I've heard people criticise the story but I have to say that the written word of it is fairly irrelevant as the real fabric of the story is created by the player and how they tackle one of the most terrifying creatures in film (and now game) history.
The devs have managed to perfectly recreate the dread you'd feel in a situation like this to the extent that at points I just had to switch the game off because it was so tense. Yeah, it's just a game, but when you can't save at every corner, and one mistep could cost you a good chunk of progress you find yourself cursing when you spot some vital flamethrower fuel across a room that you just crossed without alerting the giant murder beast that's stalking you.
This is especially harder on players like myself who like to explore every corner of the environment to try and find everything. In most games, if I realise I've forgotten something and have to go back, it really isn't that big of a deal as repetetive mechanics and knowing that most threats are scripted means I can waltz back the way, even if I'm being told everything's blowing up around me (if there ain't a timer on the screen, then nothings going to happen.) In Alien, I feel genuine regret and curse myself for failing to see something important and really have to force myself to go back for it.
And I LOVE it.
If you're a fan of stealth games or survival horror (not the action shooty kind) then you've probably already got and played this game. If you haven't, and you're still unsure after previous treatments of the Alien universe leaving a bitter taste in your mouth, then this game is what you want. Not only is it increadible to play, but the level of detail they've put into recreating Ridley Scott's version of the Alien world is flawless, with fan-pleasingly perfect attention to detail.
I look forwards to going back and finding the logs and tags I missed on the first play through, but frankly my heart rate needs a chance to calm down for a while. Maybe skydiving without a chute, or running headlong into speeding traffic will do the trick.

I really really hate to do this, but I feel backed into a corner.
WHAT a disappointment!  We so loved Sierra Games when they ruled the RPG roost.  And in many ways this revisitation of the King's Quest series is a beautiful tribute to those games.
But here's the problem.  As beautiful, humourous and interesting as this game is, they have done some really weird things that are totally out of character for the series that just blew it for me.
The main issue is the extraneous and totally unwarranted intrusion into this game of the same kind of mouse-athletics required by the old side scrollers like Donkey Kong and all their ilk.  Sierra Games was NEVER about making you (literally) jump through hoops.  All the crap they've injected where you have to time your jumps or you die; time and aim your arrows or you die; etc etc is just totally off-putting.
In the first place I am disabled and the fact that I can pass ANY of these "tests" of mouse dexterity at all tells me that these intrusions into the game are not sufficient to keep anybody who likes that stuff happy, but for those of us who are not dextrous for whatever reason they are a giagantic annoying hateful pain in the butt.  I don't play those types of games for a reason.  To find this stuff in a King's Quest game is terribly annoying.  So that is both too much and not enough.
I understand that gaming has changed since Sierra ruled supreme. But I had expectations of Sierra Games, and the expectation was NOT to find I have to satisfactorily perform mouse calisthenics or be stuck at a bottleneck.
The solution to that is to make these harder (to make button mashers happy), but SKIPPABLE.  Why is there only one difficulty level?  This was financed by a major gaming company, there's no reason for a feature like that to be missing.
If I even had the option of changing the key bindings it would have helped.  But NOOOOOOOOOoooooOOOOOooOOo.
The other main issue I have is the choice to release this in chapters.  I hate chapters.  They enforce a level of linearity that I find totally off-putting and annoying.
I love the characters.  I love the voicing.  I love the story line. I love the humor.  I love the look of the animation.  I get the Princess Bride references etc.
But because of the injection of mouse-olympics, I will most likely just find a playthrough on youtube and watch it like its a movie.  It is just too frustrating to have to spend an hour trying to get through the rapids or across the chasm or whatever.
It is unlikely, much to my sorrow, that I will buy the remaining "chapters" of this game.  I am simply not physically capable of performing the mouse athletics that have been spuriously injected into this game in any reasonable amount of time - and desperately disappointed to find this is the case.

GIRL IN THE TOOOWWEEERRRR, I'M REACHING OUT, PLEASE TELL ME WHAT TO DOOOO.
HERE IN THE TOWER, I'M CALLING OUT, MY HEART GOES OUT TO YOUUUUUUU.
In all seriousness, this ♥♥♥♥ing game is a 10/10, If looked at episode by episode each and every episode has it's own style and story telling methods. Overall this game has everything you ever wanted from a rebooted King's Quest and it does Telltale better than Telltale ever did, or ever will. Your choices, believe it or not, actually ♥♥♥♥ing matter, and they follow you every single step of the way, right up to the ending. But let's break down each and every episode.
Episode 1 feels more like a classic King's Quest game where you pick up everything in sight and use them all together in strange but somewhow logical ways to solve puzzles, which usually centers around three core ideas, and none of which are wrong choices, and will impact the rest of the game appropiately, unlike every single Telltale game ever made. You'll notice these choices following you almost every step of the way, and not just some throwback right at the final episode, "hey remember that thing you did in episode 1? Yeah, we remember too!"
Episode 2 is the same idea, but in a prison setting. This time you are given game mechanics that are really quite interesting. This episode takes place over several days, or weeks if you let it. Every day you sleep you get once piece of meat, and you can use that meat to either, feed yourself, or feed one of your friends (Amaya the Blacksmith, who is healther than the rest at the start, your partners in deception The Cobblepots, and the loveable Wenty and his wife Bramble. You also have the option to feed Mr. Fuzzycakes and a giant rat that gives you access to a chest where you can stash contraband and cigarettes). This mechanics really makes you think and plan out your strategy because only some things can be accomplished when certain pairs are at full health, and knowing if one of them reaches 0 they will die, adding a very real emotional attachment to wanting to save everybody you can.
Episode 3 strikes a personal chord for me, considering it's basically a retelling of an older King's Quest game, featuring a sountrack very reminescent of "Girl in the Tower" a song played at the ending of King's Quest VI (one of my personal favorites). In this episode, without spoiling much, you set out to find a princess worthy of your affection, and newly acquired cuddling biceps, but once you reach the tower where your true love is located you run into a dillemma, and the choice of which will alter the rest of the game. This episode in particular is a bit lacking in dialogue choices and exploring while trying every item together, but it definitely makes up for it by sacrificing the exploring for greater storytelling.
Episode 4 is pretty cool. If you haven't had your fill of puzzles yet, here is where you'll be getting it! This episode in particular is very linear (as even pointed out by one of the characters) however it's forgiven due to how damn fun these puzzles are. If you're not the puzzling type then you may despise this episode, but you probably shouldn't be playing a King's Quest game in the first place.
And finally Episode 5: Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ where to start. This episode takes the absolute best parts of every episode and combines them all for one epic finale. Complete with throwbacks to the previous episodes, and even the previous games. There are a few puzzles near the end of the game, and these may be the most fun riddle/puzzles I've ever played in a video game, even moreso than Portal 1 and 2. They really make you think, and the sense of satisfaction when completing these puzzles is just incredible. There are so many good feels in this episode I can't even begin to describe how awesome this game turned out to be.
In conclusion / tl;dr: Whether you're a fan of King's Quest, or not, this is a must buy for pretty much everybody. The only people I can say to stay away from this game are those that despise using their mind. If you want to brainlessly mow through hordes of enemies with a shakily written plot, then Call of Duty is the game for you. However if you have even a little bit of intellect and want a really well written story that makes you feel emotions every step of the way, then King's Quest is the game for you. Thanks for reading.

Well, could you believe it? A first RPG Maker game that I have played (because other games looked identical to each other) and I've quite enjoyed it. To be fair, it is only a short game (at least 2 hours) but there was something in this game to admire.
First of all, probably in everybody's minds, the graphics put me off at first, indicating poor production value but later throughout the game, I sooner realized that it was the style it was going for. Mirroring the reality of business and the economy of the everyday world/man and how they see the world from a business perspective (not surprising, in the least).
Also, this game did surprisingly make me laugh. It is full of meta references, political satire it it enjoys making fun of EVERYTHING, even making fun of itself from time to time. So, obviously, this game does not take itself seriously as it's one of those games that it taken with a grain of salt and does make you laugh at yourself, no matter if it's a joke or not.
If you're one of those people who is only in the game for its story, don't expect much with this one. This game has the meta references, the style, the weirdness it portrays and its simplistic RPG combat, equipment system, etc. And for 79p, compared to the price of Breath of Fire VII, it's not too bad to check out. Don't be put off by the lack of quality the game has. Looks of the game can deceive you. Give it a shot and judge it for yourself.

Quite good. Solid controls and beautiful visuals. The story isnt amazing, but its presented in a way that doesn't get in the way of gameplay with tons of cutscenes or dialogue. Dark Souls 2 is an improvement on Dark Souls 1 in the sense it runs smoother and handles better.
There is an issue with health regenerating items in that in Dark Souls 1, Estus (your healing item) was limited between bonfires(checkpoints) and would replenish at a bonfire, but enemies would respawn aswell. In Dark Souls 2 you have Estus (and it works as it did before) but there is also Life Gems which regenerate health slowly. The issue here is that estus made health a precious resource where if you ran out of estus you'd likely have to go back to the bonfire to refill your estus charges which inturn would reset enemy spawns. Now you can farm life gems, and health is no longer a precious resource.
The addition of the Emerald herald, who acts as a means to upgrade your character is good because it forces you to return to a specific area, making said area feel special to you. Though nothing noteworthy happens in said area.
Another issue is that of enemy respawns. If you kill an enemy, reset the spawn with a bonfire, and repeat that, eventually the enemy will stop respawning. This can to easily manipulated to kill a single enemy over and over again untill it stops respawning. It allows for the removal of the dangerous walks between bonfires. Dark Souls 1 never felt slow or as though i was just walking for a long time, though revisting old areas in dark souls 2 makes this a reality. Many times i would walk through an old area with nothing to do.
The upside of no respawns means it limits the ability for people to grind souls in easy areas. There is a trade off. Obviously.
There is also an issue with being able to teleport between bonfires at the beginning of the game. It makes walking anywhere not needed unless it is for the sake of progression. This might seem like a good thing but in reality it makes the areas of the world unimportant and it fragments the world making it seem smaller than it actually is because there is no time spent traveling between areas, getting to know the environments.
There is an issue of fairness in the game. The difficulty of the Souls games was a means to get players invested and engaged into the world of the game. Focusing so heavily the game, because it is so difficult, causes players to see things they wouldn't normally notice. Dark souls 2 is hard for the sake of being hard though, where the game is not punishing players for being stupid or careless, but rather is trying to be unfair. An example of this is the insane amount of enemies with an overhead swing that heavil tracks player movement.
The final issue i have is that the game is just not as creative as Dark Souls 1. The story rehashes alot of concepts and only serves to say "everything is a cycle" and "your choices do not matter because it is a cycle". Its interesting at first but all in all amounts to nothing. The lack of creativity is seen within the bosses aswell, where a majority of them are large humanoids with a large weapon. They all have a horizontal sweep, an overhead strike, and a lunging attack. Alot of these bosses felt the same but at different sizes.
Those issues aside the game is really fun and the controls are so smooth they are almost invisible. Fighting enemies is satisfying and customizing your character always works, and i've yet to see a faulty character build. The game is beautiful and still really fun with those issues i mentioned. If you liked Dark Souls 1, this might be worth getting just to have better online pvp on PC. If you are new to the series it will be good, but if not you might be dissapointed. It doesn't further the series like Dark Souls did with Demon's Souls.

System Shock 2 is a top notch survival horror game!  I completed this game when it first came out, and it was one of the most gripping and exciting experiences I've ever had in a video game. The models looked a little dorky then and still do, and sometimes the balance of your choices can make the game harder than you might like, but aside from that the game was spot on!
The Dead Space and Bioshock series offer a similar eperience that this game offers (System Shock 2 probably inspired them both).  While the aforementioned games have better graphics, in my opinion their experiences are a bit watered down in comparision to System Shock 2.  So, if you're a fan of those games, and want to see where they got their stuff from, this is the game to try!
With the mods to update the graphics and sound as well as the ability to play in linux (all covered in the community hub), this is a must-have game - it's a classic!!!  If you still haven't bought it yet, or are still on the fence about it, wait for it to go on sale and get it - this is one you won't regret!!

Eternal Senia is a basic Anime RPG that is meant to give a relaxing take on RPG games.
Magaleta, Senia's older sister, goes missing and Senia is determined to find her. Throughout the game, Senia will regain flashbacks and discover her past and what really happened to Magaleta.
This is a very basic RPG. I like to think of it as Pokemon, but you instantly attack enemies by simply walking into them (Note that you can also take damage from them). You have a normal attack with your sword and multiple special attacks that consume SP.
Crafting and upgrading your gear is very important, as you may have trouble getting past areas if you don't have the best armor or an upgraded sword. Open the craft menu every once in a while to see if you can craft something better.
You will also encounter stationary bosses. These can be annoying since you attack and wait for your health to come back and you keep repeating this process. Though, its worth it since you will get a huge amount of XP and maybe a cool item.
Soundtrack is quite pleasant. You have music ranging from violin, piano, and some electronic bass. Game sounds are a throwback to the nostalgia days of top down RPG games.
If you have never played an RPG before, this is a simple game to start. It takes around 3-5 hours to complete. Three if you just want to get to the ending(s) as fast as possible.
P.S. You might want some tissues if you get feels.

I am a HUGE Alien fan, and so I was really hesitant to pick up this game in fear that it would disappoint me…. I am VERY GLAD that I chose to give it a chance!
Alien Isolation stays true to the source by capturing and adapting every detail (big and small) from the movie. From the eerie soundtrack and sound effects, down to the 1980s computer terminals. To say that I was impressed by the game’s environment would be an understatement. While the art and sound helps set the right atmosphere, the game also has a wonderful story that made me want to keep playing just to find out what’s going to happen next…. No matter how scared I was, I kept pushing forward.  And on that note, the true icing on the cake is the masterfully terrifying AI that was bestowed on the Alien creature that is hunting you down on the station. It is very unpredictable, to such a degree that I would spend 5-10 minutes hiding in a locker still wondering whether or not it’s safe to come out. I played the game on medium difficulty, I am sure on Hard the AI is even more intense. Definitely adds a whole new level of terror to the horror FPS genre.
In conclusion, if you love nearly flat-lining while playing a video game, Alien Isolation won’t disappoint you. And if you love Alien and you ever wanted to know what it would feel like to try and outsmart a Xenomorph, this game captures that experience wonderfully! I was scared all throughout, and I enjoyed every second of it.

This wasn't the finest of years for AAA games.
First, everything got delayed to the point where it might as well exist on the surface of Pluto. That happened in the first quarter, leading to a sense that we'd see very little in terms of actual releases.
This is the first reason why Alien: Isolation is so good. More on that in a second.
Second, from May onward, a good chunk of the high-profile releases came out and disappointed.
From Watch Dogs to Destiny to even Far Cry 4 (which I admit I liked!), games that were supposed to be, well, game-changing almost routinely.. weren't.
So, what do we, as a gaming public, do in this scenario, where only a handful of AAA releases come out that are really notably good? We could simply go outside, but ha, as if. We could play classics, and indeed, I did.
Or, we can take a second look at games no one expected to be earth-shattering at all.
Shovel Knight says hello. This War of Mine waves in our direction.
And, despite having literally every effort working against it, from a developer who's not famous for survival horror, to a franchise that's been doomed to mediocrity for some time, Alien: Isolation stomps in the room and angrily demands we give it a look.
And it's completely right to do that.
Let's get one thing straight. This game is not fun, not in any traditional sense of the word. It's unlike any title I've played before. It lacks the morbid dream-like nature of Penumbra or Amnesia, the predictability of Outlast, or the methodical atmosphere of traditional survival horror. The most apt comparison I can think of is a much more desperate Call of Cthulhu: Dark Corners of the Earth, but even that's a stretch.
Alien: Isolation is a unique game, one that never empowers the player, one where the literal only defense is quick spatial reasoning and close attention to sound design. I suggest trying it on hard difficulty at first. The AI, damage, sound system, and a few other quirks all contribute to a more terrifying game, where survival becomes near impossible. Alien: Isolation is better for that tension.
The game itself, minus its adversaries, is kind of mundane. It's really a series of open maps with must-be-completed QTEs at various points.
Note that I said "minus its adversaries", though. The real reason we're here is to avoid and soil ourselves over the titular alien and his merry mates. They're worth addressing categorically, I think.
One of the things that makes the setting of Alien: Isolation so unique is that humans still live on the station. The game argues, however, that human does not inherently mean ally. Most are driven tense and mad with fear, and they're all too quick to attack the player. They may be killed, but killing means noise. Noise isn't our friend here.
Androids are one reason why. They're comparatively dim-witted and slow, but they require serious power to put down. Generally, attacking them is a waste of resources until a certain late-game weapon is acquired.
The Alien is really why we're here. It's powerful. It's fast. The most you'll ever do to it is scare it off for a few seconds. Most notably, it is easily the most intelligent foe I have ever encountered in a video game. It's almost frightening, game aside, that a piece of software could read human action so proficiently. It flanked me. It used sound to fool me. It learned from my actions, and adjusted its behavior so that the same tricks failed me if used too often. The sections of Alien: Isolation where the player is being stalked by this thing are legitimately the scariest moments to be found in any game, period. There has never been an AI so convincing in a horror game, and it is singularly Alien: Isolation's greatest achievement.
This is not a perfect title in spite of that. It does drag on long after it runs out of new ideas. The plot never really goes anywhere, and the most interesting characters always seem to exist somewhere far outside the world of the protagonist. The androids also simply aren't scary. They can be outrun, easily fooled, and generally feel more like padding than a real threat. I did run into a few odd mid-game crashes as well.
I disagree that the save system is a bad thing about this game, to address a concern I've seen. Being forced to save at specific points is merely another piece of control the game takes away from the player, and I think it amplifies the horror immensely.
As a final note, the aesthetic presented here is fantastic. Screenshots don't do it justice. It's a near-perfect replica of the original Alien film, and goes a long way to establishing the sense that everything is dangerous.
So what we have here is a game that isn't fun. It's depressing. It's tense. It's hopeless. It does its best to suffocate the player under a weight that is never lifted.
It also just about represents the best of what can be done when a studio has the confidence to make something that is all of those things, and so much more.

Alien: Isolation is in a class of its own when it comes to the horror genre. Many games boast horror elements, or are outright horror games as their very premise (see Outlast and Amnesia: The Dark Descent for excellent examples of other horror games), but Alien: Isolation's success occurs on so many levels, culminating in one of the finest examples of horror I have come across in the video game medium (and possibly beyond).
The storyline is very well told, and has a natural flow to it. There is extremely well paced game progression (it plays out pretty much in real time) and well developed, sympathetic characters. The dialogue in the game is excellent, which provides an excellent platform for characters to develop. You take on the role of Amanda Ripley, an engineer, and daughter to Ellen Ripley (the protagonist from the original
movie. Amanda is invited on an expedition to retrieve the Flight recorder from the Nostromo (of which Ellen Ripley was crew, when she met the Alien) from Sevastopol Space Station. Amanda is separate from her crew as they attempt to board Sevastopol, only to find the station is essentially in lock down and is falling apart.
The horror atmosphere of Alien: Isolation is a key aspect, pivotal to the success of the game. This is created through a mixture of the environmental design, the sounds and the actual gameplay itself. There is this constant, looming feeling of dread which accompanied me throughout the game. You are in danger pretty much throughout the game. There is little opportunity to rest or breathe. Even when you're hiding, you're still not entirely safe. The actions of the alien are often unpredictable, giving it the element of surprise at many turns. Your means of tracking the alien can also alert the alien to your presence, further enhancing the difficulties in your flight from the xenomorph. The alien is hunting you, and detects the sounds you make (or chases you if it sees you), so even when in hiding you have to keep your character(Amanda Ripley) quiet and out of sight by leaning into the shadows, or holding your breath.
The feeling of dread is further enhanced by the level design - claustrophobic, dark corridors (much akin to what made the original
movie so scary), dark corners, shadows, and a feeling of being lost. Everything isn't sign posted to you in game, you actually have to find your goals, while being hunted. This can be very challenging, as you have to deduce your way through levels (by reading computer terminals or signs) and avoid the alien. In addition to this, your exploration takes you to various parts of the space station complex, varying the scenery and layouts of the levels – avoiding repetition and keeping the experience fresh.
The actual gameplay of the game is a real asset to aiding the horror atmosphere. The scarcity of resources meaning you can't just  go on a bullet fuelled killing spree. Most of your weapons are very believable in the context, as in you don't suddenly become a super soldier with a rocket launcher and a machine gun. You can craft a couple of basic bombs (which is believable in the context of Amanda Ripley being an engineer), in addition to other offensive weapons you pick up from security personnel. You can craft various other non offensive devices to provide further tactics for survival.
In my opinion, the aural delivery of the game was an outstanding feature, and perhaps one of the best utilisations of the sense of sound to generate atmosphere I have come across. The sounds of the station can be disconcerting, and may often signify something completely harmless, but when you're tiptoeing through the dark corridors of Sevastopol station, listening out for the alien tracking you through the vents (and able to jump out at you at virtually any time), the sudden sound of a vent or door automatically opening as you creep by can startle you. The echoing sounds of the other inhabitants of the station can be ambiguous - friend or foe? You must eavesdrop so determine if it is safe to waltz past, or to stealthily dodge, or even attack. The ambient sounds of Sevastopol space station,; the hum of generators, engines, the droning voice of the working joe androids, the dripping of water all add up to provide a convincing ambience. Add these to the visuals; the shadows, lighting effects, high resolution textures and we have an immersive universe to lose ourselves in.
And once you're immersed, the horror becomes real.

Alien Isolation is an excellent game!
It's a tense, white knuckled (If you're using a controller), heart pounding game! Alien Isolation has it's moments of being truly terrifying. If you want PTSD this is your game! I spent my time crawling through hallways and jumping my gaze from motion tracker to environment. The AI was truly unpredictable, for the alien at least. The others well….
Isolation is at it's best when you're exploring and dodging the alien. There are times when you encounter humans, but their AI is god awful and ALL OF THEM are hostile, not a few like we were told. You also encounter Working Joe's, which are creepy, but no where near as fun as encountering the alien.
In terms of presentation Isolation is one of the biggest mixed bags out there. The environments are drop dead gorgeous. The lighting, fog, sound effects (OH MY GOD THE SOUND DESIGN IS AMAZING), and movie accurate models are excellent. But the characters and their animations are horrible; they all look like sausage links. At one point when Amanda is held at gunpoint her face wasn't animated and she looked bored. Speaking of Amanda she seems like a ghost, she doesn't cast any shadows or reflect from water, visors, or mirrors. This is baffling to me since it's clear that CA spent a lot of time with detailing the environments. Textures are also mixed; on some objects they're jaw dropping; the alien is beautifully detailed and so is the motion tracker. But a good majority of other objects lack detail. The cutscenes were the most jarring, suffering from random black screens (I guess the editor never checked his edits), along with stuttering and lifeless animations.
The story is easily what made me so mad about the game; it sucks! Lacking competent storytelling,  Amanda's story screams wasted potential. The voice actors are horrible, except the alien (wink wink). The dialogue is horrible and I didn't give two craps about anyone. None of the characters go through any arcs! I was at least expecting that out of Amanda. Literally no one has a personality to them other than this one guy you meet for about ten minutes at the games start. The story of finding Ellen is overshadowed by such gripping sub plots such as: get a med kit for that one girl, doing other survivor's work, and stopping a person from doing explosions. There was one moment where a character flew into a window and I burst out laughing at how poorly animated it was and at Amanda's "No!" scream.
Over all though Isolation is an excellent game, it may lack in story and graphics but it gets the most important thing right: the gameplay.
It was a great idea for a new Alien game with great gameplay and the fact that it follows along the Alien timeline. All in all it was a very fun game to play!

Some chapters are easily better than others with Ch. 1, 5, and 3. Leagues better than chapters 2 and 4.
That said when taken as a whole package King's Quest is surprisingly funny and full of heart with an exceptionally emotionally charged ending.
I would recommend it if you'd like to try something with a little bit more story oomph than what Telltale has been providing.
That said prepare yourself for variation in quality between chapters.

This game is good. It is. Let's take a look at why.
Gameplay:
The game simply plays well. Well designed fully destructable environments. There seems to always be a way to navigate a level even after you blow a lot of it up.
Tight controls and enemies that are satisfying to kill. Each "Bro" plays differently, with their own abilities and subtle nuances that makes them even more special. They all have a different super move,  from throwing a grenade, slowing down time, using a companion of some sort, or shooting a bigger gun.
Some of them have different melee attacks, while some of them are shared, you'll find more than a few with a unique attack.
Humour:
The game is, obviously, a parody and satire of United States patriotism. American foreign policy jokes abound! You "liberate" areas by absolutely destroying everything in sight. Lots of shouting and muscles. The physical/slapstick humor is on point.
Replayability:
You get different bros in different orders for every level. That alone makes one level infinitely replayable. It hasn't gotten old yet, and I'm not sure if it ever will.
Graphics:
The game looks pleasing. Characters muscles are exaggerated greatly. It's simplistic but very easy to look at art style makes explosions and terrain damage more obvious. There are a variety of death animations that enemies can go through, but most of the time you'll end up shooting them to pieces.
Difficulty:
The game has a strange difficulty curve. Some levels are harder than others, and they don't really come in any particular order. You'll often die in a cluster-gaggle of explosions. Once you die, the game pretty much throws you right back into the action. Instant respawn at checkpoints. But if you run out of lives, you have to start the entire level over. Makes sense.
Notes:
The game has a nice little system where if you're struggling on a hard level, the over-top-narrator will encourage you to "make them pay" or "You can do it, BRO!" And after you beat he congratulates you. I liked that touch. It's good to know that the developers don't hate you and want to upset you.
I wholly recommend Broforce.

DISCLAIMER:
Before you judge his review based on my "2 Hours" of playtime. Please let me inform you, I played this before it came to steam and was free. I only recently purhased it because I want to support the DEVs, see how it has grown, and I wanted to play it again :)
Now to the review
Black Mesa is a recreation of the classic Half Life on the Source Engine. The difference between this one and the Valve released "Half Life: Source" is that Black Mesa is taken a step further, with an overhaul on damn near everything. Textures, Sound Effects, Maps, Voice Acting, Particle Effects, NPC Interaction, and a lot more in between.
Black Mesa mantains the feel of what Half Life was and still is, just more finely tuned and more detailed (Not to say the original HL and HL: Source were not, this just gives them a more modern touch).
The graphics look absolutely stunning and very well optimised (I played with EVERYTHING Maximum Settings).
The Voice acting is wonderul, the voice actors did a great job at not only staying true to the original script, but also adding many new lines to the mix as well. They paid real close attention to the small details from the orignal HL voice acting and kept them in game (ex: "They are waiting for you Gordon, in the test Chamberrrr").
On top of the voice acting, the NPC's feel much more alive and have more depth and sentience compared to their HL counterparts.
The story remains as it was, some minor differences here and there (new puzzles, different routes, new threats, change of scenery, ect) but in the grand sceme of things it is still Gordon Freeman's adventure we all know very well.
And this is all while the game is in early access, which means it should only keep improving. Which it has vastly from the version back in 2012. That goes without saying, it is a bummer that Xen is not out, but the DEVs are hard at work on it.
Overall I would say this is definitely worth buying, hardcore Half Life fan or not. It is a wonderful experience and brought a tear to my eye getting to play one of my favortie games once again in such a glorious new form.

In life you tend to not pay attention to certain things because you feel like maybe its not for me and you just ignore it. I play games but not every game and I tend to stay in my lane with certain types of games. I had never heard of Demon Souls or Dark Souls until earlier this year. I decided to play Dark Souls for the first time in February and I fell in love with what the game had to offer. I love games that challenge you in every way possible. Games that try to kill you at all times with no remorse. Dark Souls gives me that and then the thrill to complete that challenge is awesome!
That leads me to Dark Souls II and how it keeps that style of gaming going stronger into the future. When I first started playing Dark Souls II, I noticed the complete overhaul in the graphic department. This game looks incredible when you first start playing it. The lighting and colors are really good. There are nice wind physics while you run around in the game as well. WInd physics also come into play when you do simple things like light your sword on fire or cast a spell. This effects everybody on screen. The amount of weapons available to master is almost too much to comprehend. I have played almost 230 hours and still have mulitiple weapons that I deem my favorite. The game is deep and on going that it may take a few play throughs to figure out which weapon you think is your number one. Level design also has been done with lore in mind. When you are playing the game, make sure to pay attention to your surroundings and what you see because it plays a HUGE part in finding out what happened in the game and the story as you move along. Improvements from Dark Souls includes the ability to duel wield great swords and do double attacks with weapons. You can now equpied 4 rings instead of 2 and 6 weapon slots(3 in each hand) The developers also made it easier to change into your human form which effigies and the estus flask upgrade has bee altered too. The ability to teleport is avaialbe from the start and the item box as well. PVP is not the greatest thing about the game though. It can be a bit of a bore sometimes and then alot of times it becomes a bit of a bother especially when your trying to complete a task in the game. Certain areas are almost automaic PVP areas with no choice being yours. Other than that, Dark Souls II is a great game with limitless depth and options. The replayability of this game in my opinion is infinate because of the aspect to build your character and challenge others who play the game during or after you have beaten the game mulitple times. I'm not going to spoil the details on bosses but I will say that the bosses of Dark Souls II are incredible and they each challenge your intelect and patience.
Have fun with this game and I encourage all of you to play it but make sure you play or know the story of Dark Souls I before or while you play, it will help you understand a few things that are mentioned.
Rating: 9.5/10

Probably one of the better coop games i've played in a while. The graphics aren't anything crazy tbh, it's a little dated for something that was released in 2015 and the voice acting leaves much to be desired. The true gem in the game is that you really do need to play with a friend. The asymetric coop really makes the game as the field operative can't see everything or get all the information. Whereas the hacker can't move between systems without the operative plugging him in. As well as the operative is the only one able to pick up physical stuff as they're the only ones in the field.
The other bit that i love is that it's ACTUALLY CO-OP. I can't tell you how many games I've looked thru that claim the tag "coop" only to be brutally reminded that apparently MOBAs and arena shooters are coop games as well. . . . yea, no. Back to this game tho, even with the outdated graphics and poor voice acting the story isn't too bad and you can go about finishing the game in multiple different ways. Stealthy, considering you're a covert operative this is prolly the easiest way because you do die pretty quick in the game if spotted. Light force, meaning shooting some guards and cameras but using non-lethal rounds or subduing them physically. Or the hardest method (yes i like that in a stealth game this is the hardest way to complete the obj) Gung ho kill everyone and everything on the map.
Now even considering how short the game is, i put it roughly around 10-13 hours of solid gameplay. Switching it up, playing the hacker side while your partner plays the operative, still makes the game feel fresh. Especially if you don't give each other clues and whatnot about where everything you or they found while playing is. That being the case the game is definitely 20-28 hours worth of gameplay.
Please note tho, this isn't metal gear solid stealth or tom clancey stealth where killing someone doesn't matter. It does count bodies and evidence you left at the end and I believe it has an outcome to how difficult the last few missions are. Being stealthy actually gets you an easier time where leaving evidence everywhere probably makes it much tougher.

Alien: Isolation is in a class of its own when it comes to the horror genre. Many games boast horror elements, or are outright horror games as their very premise (see Outlast and Amnesia: The Dark Descent for excellent examples of other horror games), but Alien: Isolation's success occurs on so many levels, culminating in one of the finest examples of horror I have come across in the video game medium (and possibly beyond).
The storyline is very well told, and has a natural flow to it. There is extremely well paced game progression (it plays out pretty much in real time) and well developed, sympathetic characters. The dialogue in the game is excellent, which provides an excellent platform for characters to develop. You take on the role of Amanda Ripley, an engineer, and daughter to Ellen Ripley (the protagonist from the original
movie. Amanda is invited on an expedition to retrieve the Flight recorder from the Nostromo (of which Ellen Ripley was crew, when she met the Alien) from Sevastopol Space Station. Amanda is separate from her crew as they attempt to board Sevastopol, only to find the station is essentially in lock down and is falling apart.
The horror atmosphere of Alien: Isolation is a key aspect, pivotal to the success of the game. This is created through a mixture of the environmental design, the sounds and the actual gameplay itself. There is this constant, looming feeling of dread which accompanied me throughout the game. You are in danger pretty much throughout the game. There is little opportunity to rest or breathe. Even when you're hiding, you're still not entirely safe. The actions of the alien are often unpredictable, giving it the element of surprise at many turns. Your means of tracking the alien can also alert the alien to your presence, further enhancing the difficulties in your flight from the xenomorph. The alien is hunting you, and detects the sounds you make (or chases you if it sees you), so even when in hiding you have to keep your character(Amanda Ripley) quiet and out of sight by leaning into the shadows, or holding your breath.
The feeling of dread is further enhanced by the level design - claustrophobic, dark corridors (much akin to what made the original
movie so scary), dark corners, shadows, and a feeling of being lost. Everything isn't sign posted to you in game, you actually have to find your goals, while being hunted. This can be very challenging, as you have to deduce your way through levels (by reading computer terminals or signs) and avoid the alien. In addition to this, your exploration takes you to various parts of the space station complex, varying the scenery and layouts of the levels – avoiding repetition and keeping the experience fresh.
The actual gameplay of the game is a real asset to aiding the horror atmosphere. The scarcity of resources meaning you can't just  go on a bullet fuelled killing spree. Most of your weapons are very believable in the context, as in you don't suddenly become a super soldier with a rocket launcher and a machine gun. You can craft a couple of basic bombs (which is believable in the context of Amanda Ripley being an engineer), in addition to other offensive weapons you pick up from security personnel. You can craft various other non offensive devices to provide further tactics for survival.
In my opinion, the aural delivery of the game was an outstanding feature, and perhaps one of the best utilisations of the sense of sound to generate atmosphere I have come across. The sounds of the station can be disconcerting, and may often signify something completely harmless, but when you're tiptoeing through the dark corridors of Sevastopol station, listening out for the alien tracking you through the vents (and able to jump out at you at virtually any time), the sudden sound of a vent or door automatically opening as you creep by can startle you. The echoing sounds of the other inhabitants of the station can be ambiguous - friend or foe? You must eavesdrop so determine if it is safe to waltz past, or to stealthily dodge, or even attack. The ambient sounds of Sevastopol space station,; the hum of generators, engines, the droning voice of the working joe androids, the dripping of water all add up to provide a convincing ambience. Add these to the visuals; the shadows, lighting effects, high resolution textures and we have an immersive universe to lose ourselves in.
And once you're immersed, the horror becomes real.

Alien Isolation is an excellent game!
It's a tense, white knuckled (If you're using a controller), heart pounding game! Alien Isolation has it's moments of being truly terrifying. If you want PTSD this is your game! I spent my time crawling through hallways and jumping my gaze from motion tracker to environment. The AI was truly unpredictable, for the alien at least. The others well….
Isolation is at it's best when you're exploring and dodging the alien. There are times when you encounter humans, but their AI is god awful and ALL OF THEM are hostile, not a few like we were told. You also encounter Working Joe's, which are creepy, but no where near as fun as encountering the alien.
In terms of presentation Isolation is one of the biggest mixed bags out there. The environments are drop dead gorgeous. The lighting, fog, sound effects (OH MY GOD THE SOUND DESIGN IS AMAZING), and movie accurate models are excellent. But the characters and their animations are horrible; they all look like sausage links. At one point when Amanda is held at gunpoint her face wasn't animated and she looked bored. Speaking of Amanda she seems like a ghost, she doesn't cast any shadows or reflect from water, visors, or mirrors. This is baffling to me since it's clear that CA spent a lot of time with detailing the environments. Textures are also mixed; on some objects they're jaw dropping; the alien is beautifully detailed and so is the motion tracker. But a good majority of other objects lack detail. The cutscenes were the most jarring, suffering from random black screens (I guess the editor never checked his edits), along with stuttering and lifeless animations.
The story is easily what made me so mad about the game; it sucks! Lacking competent storytelling,  Amanda's story screams wasted potential. The voice actors are horrible, except the alien (wink wink). The dialogue is horrible and I didn't give two craps about anyone. None of the characters go through any arcs! I was at least expecting that out of Amanda. Literally no one has a personality to them other than this one guy you meet for about ten minutes at the games start. The story of finding Ellen is overshadowed by such gripping sub plots such as: get a med kit for that one girl, doing other survivor's work, and stopping a person from doing explosions. There was one moment where a character flew into a window and I burst out laughing at how poorly animated it was and at Amanda's "No!" scream.
Over all though Isolation is an excellent game, it may lack in story and graphics but it gets the most important thing right: the gameplay.

This game excels in terms of aesthetic design and faithfulness to the source material, and is competent in most fundamental mechanical regards. But it drops the ball a bit on its horror ambitions by desensitizing the player to the alien's presence. And without the alien being frightening (or present, as the case may be), the rest of the game is just a boring walk through a decrepit space station.
I've definitely played better horror games, and Alien: Isolation doesn't quite live up to the film on which it is based. But this is still a very solid horror title and easily the single, best game based on the Alien (or Aliens) franchise that I've ever played. If you're a fan of the franchise, then it should be very easy to overlook this game's shortcomings and frustrations, and it will likely make you forget all about last year's abysmal Aliens: Colonial Marines.

I rarely play ARPG's, but since this one was free and got great reviews i figured "Hey, why not? These kinds of games usually have appealing storys, just like The Crooked Man, Ib, Mad Father and Corpse Party".
And so began my 3 hour journey towards the unknown, i was feeling rather optimistic and ready for adventure. So i started playing as a cute sword fighting girl named Senia, who also happens to have more balls then i'll ever have... She's looking for her sister Magaleta who's gone out to find a mysterious power called Eternal, which is said to grant any wish when controlled. This can't be done without risk however, there is a chance that anyone who approaches the Eternal will eventually get consumed by it and turned into a mindless slave. (I may have said too much so i'll stop).
The first thing that suprised me was the fast paced combat, i expected turn based combat like pokemon. You just walk up to an enemy to swing your sword then SWISH!!! Done.
Well that got sworded out rather quickly. Get it! SWORD-ed out ha ha "gasp" ehh, i'm gonna jump off a cliff later...
This exludes bosses, of course, as they need to learn a bigger lesson than the rest of the bunch to not ♥♥♥♥ with little girls wielding swords twice their size (i notably exaggerated). But as you continue on you learn different skills that comes in handy for certain foes/ situations. You get up to 4 skills that can also be upgraded with points earned by slaying enemies, the costs for upgrades gets gradually higher after each purchase.
It doesn't take long before the game introduces you to the crafting system, were you gather materials from fallen enemies/ chests and use them to craft new and improved weapons and armor. This is a necessity as you face stronger foes you will need better gear. Thankfully did the creator add optional areas for these special "farming" occasions. Let me point out that you don't necessarily need to max out all your equipment before facing each main boss, it would definitely make things easier and quicker.
Together there are 4-5 different biomes to explore. Each biome includes a new set of enemies, some with different abilities that slightly mixes up the gameplay. Areas are crafted with your classic ARPG textures, although the environments gradually get more detailed the further you go. A new soundtrack is also used to set up the atmosphere for each area, while fitting in, the songs can get annoying if you play in one section for too long.
As the story unfolds by jumping between flashbacks and the present, you learn more about the sisters backstory and why their strong bond is what makes them stay determined till the very end. There are 3 different endings that brings a
conclusion for the game that basically screams for a sequel. Together with the amazing artwork that expresses the final moments with beautiful music in the background, creates the perfect moment that brings up emotions (possibly tears) which encourages you to see the other endings as well.
Conclusion:
Pros:
+ A short yet sweet and captivating story
+ Fast-paced, satisfying and slightly addicting combat
+ Good looking environments
+ Artwork is amazing
+ All soundtracks, except the main meny theme (according to me), are all well placed and above all astonishing
+ 3 different endings
+ It's free
Cons:
- GIMME MOAR!!!!
Overall, i enjoyed every bit of this game and encourage anyone who has an interest in ARPG's to check out this hidden gem.

It's cutesie, so be sure that's what you want.  I have a nine-year-old niece who loves this game, and it's what we do together most of the time she's here.  Even if it weren't for her, though, there's still a lot to appreciate.
You play as Beatrix LeBeau, greenhorn rancher just landed on the Far, Far, Range--an entire planet infested with living balls of slime.  Fortunately for you, these slimes are prime profit material.  See, whenever a slime eats food, it deposits a crystaline "plort".  In the wild, plorts usually get eaten by another slime, who becomes a mixed-state slime called a Largo.  However, it's possible to coral slimes so they only eat what you want them to eat, meaning you're free to sell the plorts on the market.  Most slimes only eat a certain type of food, and almost all of them have exactly one favorite type of food for which they'll thank you twice.
With the right kind of strategy and diversification, all that's left is to explore new parts of the Far, Far, Range and discover new types of slimes.
Well, that's not exactly true.  You only have a limited amount of space on your ranch, and some of it will have to be used to generate food for your slimes.  Plus, the market for plorts actually updates according to your sales.  Prices fall drastically on oversold items, so there's no set system for maximum plort profits.
And besides all that, you may wish to get into slime science at some point.  What's slime science you ask?  Just the real meat of the game, that's all.  We're talking crafting, fast-travel, advanced resource-management.  Everything it takes to run a state-of-the-art slime ranch for pleasure and profit in today's tough economy.
So I don't know if you yourself like cutesie titles, or if you've got a little someone special in your life to make it worth it, but listen, if you are not directly put off by the cuteness?  Go ahead and try Slime Rancher.  It's a well-developed game with lots of freedom for your playstyle to shine.  Maybe you're more into exploration, and ranching is just a means to that end.  Maybe you'd rather run a slimestead full of happy, exploding, irradiating, sneaking, oozing, singing, flying doggies--and going out on the Range is just a means to that end.  Maybe you're a typical power-gamer tool who wants to mastermind the best way to maximize productivity and profits the fastest because why else try to do anything in life other than to deconcstruct the experience and impose cold, hard equations instead of human reactions.  Maybe you got tired of your previous playstyle and want to do something completely different for a second or two.
That's the beauty of the Far, Far, Range, kiddo.  It's just you and the slimes out here, and they ain't judgin'.  ;)
9.5/10

I bought this gem when it came out in Eerie Access (no typo).
Didn't expect much but was suprised much.
It is:
Dumb, has a shallow boring story, isn't technically the fanciest stuff and its gameplay can be very repetitive.
But who cares? It's supercute, partly funny, relaxing, pretty unique, and overall a very cool relaxing and chilly game.
I even played it two times in EA and will again now after its release.
The whole game is actually: You gathering slimes for "herding purposes". You build pens where you will then throw tons of slimeys in there and wait for them to...errr....poop. Which you will then collect and sell. That currency you spend on new pen-upgrades (like auto-feeding or preventing them from escaping) or gadgets to improve yourself.
The market-prices for "poop" vary, so you can try to bunker some until the price is right and then sell.
You also have to feed them. For that you have to grow different types of food. Each slime has a special diet and a favourite food. For optimal results you want to give every one their favourite food.
Blahblah, and there is lots to explore and discover on a rather big map.
One big remark: It's really more a relaxing game than a challenging. No time-limits, no perma-death, you can't really screw up. Just start the game, enjoy your time, leave whenever you want.
It's one of the VERY RARE examples of how Early Access actually can provide GOOD things. The devs were always active, showing and improving. You could literally log in every other day to see something new. And they finally delivered.
Totally worth the money if you somehow find the gameplay interesting enough.
Oh and it has cat-slimes. Cutest things ever :-)

This game is truly spectactular, don't be turned off from it thinking it's just another rpg maker game, because it is much more than that.
One of the absolute highlights of this game is it's quirky humor.  From going on an acid trip to beating up old ladies with super wheelchairs, this game never fails to amuse.  Many games attempt to be humorous and end up sacrificing the integrity of the story for a few laughs, however the humor in this game only compliments the story, emphasizing just how messed up the corporate world of the game is.
Being an rpg maker game, obviously this game doesn't have the best graphics in the world.  However, the aesthetic that the designers went for fits in perfectly with the game and the story.  If you hate games with pixelated graphics then this isn't for you, but it certainly isn't visually unappealing.
The music in this game is pretty good, but it's nothing special.  It helps to emphasize the mood of the game pretty well, but it's nothing I would ever listen to outside of the game.
As far as gameplay goes, it's just a basic rpg.  You encounter enemies and fight them, but with a business twist to the combat.  Overall I felt the leveling system and the enemies were very well balanced, I didn't really feel the need to grind at all.  One unique element I really enjoyed was the ability to "buy out" enemies, where you can pay the enemies to lose the fight.  The more powerful the enemy, the higher the cost to buy them out.
One downside I've found is there are a few bugs and spelling errors, however the developer has been very active in the discussion boards, and has been responding to any bug reports or spelling corrections very actively, and the game has updated several times already since its release a few days ago.  None of the bugs I've encountered are game breaking, and the developer is in the process of fixing them.  By the time you've read this review, there might not even be any left to worry about, so I really wouldn't let this deter you from buying this game.

I was unsure what I was expecting. The original game, while good, had its fair share of flaws, so I was a bit wary before the release of The Evil Within 2. I actively avoided reading any news or watching any trailers before release, afraid that it would be a disappointment. Oh, how wrong I was!
This game had me hooked from the very beginning. It improves on every aspect that the original had and adds so much more to the table, it's honestly one of the better games I've played in quite a while. It's like a hodgepodge of some of the survival-horror genres best aspects, combining ideas from Resident Evil (both old AND new), Silent Hill, Dead Space, Alan Wake and even some Condemned.
The combat is thrilling, both when you're fighting head-on as well as when you use a more stealthy approach. The world is much more open this time, allowing you to explore it at your leisure at most times, finding hidden collectables and crafting materials. The enemy designs are fantastic, they are both varied as well as often times grotesque and horrifying.
Visually, the game is also superb, oozing with a fantastic atmosphere from beginning to end, but some environments in particular stand out as flawless staples of horror set pieces. The levels are very varied, and you never truly grow bored of the world as it always hides some pretty neat surprises around almost every corner.
The icing on the cake are some pretty fun boss-battles, and while they’re never extremely challenging, they remind me a lot of the bosses from Resident Evil, which any fan of the franchise knows is a good thing.
If you are a fan of horror games, give this one a try, I absolutely loved every moment of it!

Recommended without reservation!
If you've played stealth or hybrid games such as Hitman, Alpha Protocol, or Deus Ex, you'll have a basic idea what being the Agent is like.  That type of game is pretty fun.  Here, the extra dimension of the Hacker support player makes things far more interesting.  Definitely make time to play this with a friend.  As a single-player game, it's fine, I guess; but the co-op experience is outstanding.
It's probably not the best shooter you've ever played, nor the best stealth game you've ever played, nor the best hacking game you've ever played; the enemy AI isn't cutting edge; it doesn't have the best graphics you've ever seen; the writing isn't the most provocative ever ... I could perhaps go on.  These individual elements are important, and sure, it'd be nice if they were all As instead of B+s, but it's not so important in light of how well everything comes together.  What's important is the overall design, and
delivers.  Levels are well designed to keep both players highly engaged, and the asymmetrical nature of your abilities really magnifies the need for good communication.
Get a friend and try it, dammit.  It's good.

Just about 3 and a half hours in, and this game is so cool.  While not flawless by any regard, it's unlike much of anything else out there, and the ambition shows far stronger than the shaky parts.  Interesting writing, a tense atmosphere, and the two styles of play meld so well together.
I would definitely -not- recommend this as a solo experience, especially when you're new to the game.  The two styles of play are so drastically different, and learning just one side of it took a lot of effort in its own right.  I've been playing as the hacker with a good friend of mine, and keeping things running smoothly is for sure a challenge on both of our parts, but it feels so fun and rewarding especially when you concoct your own alternate paths and objectives.
I've seen some comments about bugs and glitches, but we've only experienced one major one and that was the game locking when we first failed just after our tutorial.  The graphics leave a bit to be desired, but they're serviceable.  I think the odd-sounding voice acting is actually intentional and that is so cool to me, as many of the characters (and actors, I think) aren't native English speakers, and that's reflected in their intonation and dialogue, purposely showcased when they do speak their native language.  No complaints from either of us with the controls.
The price point is almost steep as it's effectively a $40 game, but so far I think it is fair in the end.  I was lucky enough to acquire it on a sale, no regrets.

It's cutesie, so be sure that's what you want.  I have a nine-year-old niece who loves this game, and it's what we do together most of the time she's here.  Even if it weren't for her, though, there's still a lot to appreciate.
You play as Beatrix LeBeau, greenhorn rancher just landed on the Far, Far, Range--an entire planet infested with living balls of slime.  Fortunately for you, these slimes are prime profit material.  See, whenever a slime eats food, it deposits a crystaline "plort".  In the wild, plorts usually get eaten by another slime, who becomes a mixed-state slime called a Largo.  However, it's possible to coral slimes so they only eat what you want them to eat, meaning you're free to sell the plorts on the market.  Most slimes only eat a certain type of food, and almost all of them have exactly one favorite type of food for which they'll thank you twice.
With the right kind of strategy and diversification, all that's left is to explore new parts of the Far, Far, Range and discover new types of slimes.
Well, that's not exactly true.  You only have a limited amount of space on your ranch, and some of it will have to be used to generate food for your slimes.  Plus, the market for plorts actually updates according to your sales.  Prices fall drastically on oversold items, so there's no set system for maximum plort profits.
And besides all that, you may wish to get into slime science at some point.  What's slime science you ask?  Just the real meat of the game, that's all.  We're talking crafting, fast-travel, advanced resource-management.  Everything it takes to run a state-of-the-art slime ranch for pleasure and profit in today's tough economy.
So I don't know if you yourself like cutesie titles, or if you've got a little someone special in your life to make it worth it, but listen, if you are not directly put off by the cuteness?  Go ahead and try Slime Rancher.  It's a well-developed game with lots of freedom for your playstyle to shine.  Maybe you're more into exploration, and ranching is just a means to that end.  Maybe you'd rather run a slimestead full of happy, exploding, irradiating, sneaking, oozing, singing, flying doggies--and going out on the Range is just a means to that end.  Maybe you're a typical power-gamer tool who wants to mastermind the best way to maximize productivity and profits the fastest because why else try to do anything in life other than to deconcstruct the experience and impose cold, hard equations instead of human reactions.  Maybe you got tired of your previous playstyle and want to do something completely different for a second or two.
That's the beauty of the Far, Far, Range, kiddo.  It's just you and the slimes out here, and they ain't judgin'.  ;)
9.5/10
