TLDR: Buy it. Very likely to grab game of the year awards from many reviewers this year. Also my game of the year by far. High quality game which does justice to its pedigree. Is not without its problems, though.
Positives:
- For everyone who liked Dishonored, this one provides the same experience, with a new continuation story. The "Dishonored experience" is an excellent one, I can't recommend it enough.
- Much more direct sequel than most games with the number 2 in their name. While 10+ years did pass between the games, many of the characters are the same and the story is directly linked to the first one (+ its DLC).
- The ability to choose the protagonist is very refreshing for a game like this.
- Serkonos and the various locales are very pretty. Visual map design is excellent. Even run down mansions are really cool in their own way, while the inhabited, lavish ones make me want to live there.
- Audio design is pretty good and quite immersive.
- Voice acting is pretty good also. Not amazing. High point for me are probably the Clockwork Soldiers. The human characters are just quite normal. Even the protagonists are just passable, I guess. There wasn't ever a point where I thought any of the voice acting was terrible, though.
- Stealth mechanics are just amazing and now a step above Deus Ex (it used to be the reverse). In stealth mechanics I count what the NPCs do when they start searching. They are very thorough and act logically. The AI is just excellent overall.
- Level design is on par with Deus Ex and leaves little to be desired. I saw someone saying: "If you find yourself thinking, 'I wonder if I can...' then the answer is probably yes." It's a true statement. The level design allows for very many approaches to the mission objectives. Just navigating the maps themselves is very fluid and open-ended. I guess the maps could be bigger still, but on the other hand they already took 4-6 hours to complete (each).
- I can't stress enough how many nooks and crannies there are to explore and to find stuff. Including lore of course. It's really the salt and pepper of Dishonored and they didn't skimp on that. Running straight for the objectives really is a waste in this game.
- Aramis Stilton's mansion, with the mechanics present there, is probably this decade's coolest map of any game.
- Very Hard (the hardest difficulty) is really brutally hard. Almost too hard in places but I guess there's no such thing as "too hard" for some people. Personally I thought in some spots that they could give me a break, while they were pushing unfair situation after unfair situation, but most importantly, each one was solvable with patience and some ingenuity.
Negatives:
- Really awful PC launch. I guess I don't need to go into details as the problems are now widely printed across gaming media. But I'll say that a few patches later with the new NVIDIA drivers (375.95), I'm getting like 3x the performance compared to launch day, and running 45-60fps @ 4K Ultra already (as opposed to 15-25fps on launch). Like I said, it took some serious patching, and also some settings tweaking on my side. It's getting better and I've no problems recommending it by now.
- Some situations you run into are very gamey and need to be cheesed in order to progress. I prefer a more organic system of difficulty/challenge. Thankfully most of the game is like that. The cheesy places are the exception.
- Some things don't make mechanical sense. For example, you can and must kill some things (magic hounds and Clockwork Soldiers), even when doing the Clean Hands run. Mostly you can avoid it but sometimes you can't. I wonder what the design challenge was that prevented them from making a truly ghostable path everywhere.
- Some things don't make sense even in the in-universe context. One example is the Jindosh riddle. IMHO better to not have that bit in the game, and leverage the strengths of the franchise, which is a truly map-design-centric approach to ghost through the level.
- Speaking of achievements, Dishonored still doesn't award achievements for difficulty. Not exactly a gamebreaking issue but it bugs me that I've nothing to show for beating it on Very Hard.
- Not really a full-on negative, but I'm not sure what to think about the Powers. Obviously first I need to say I beat the game without powers. But all the time I was thinking: "oh look at that ledge/jump/window, this would be so easy with Blink". Or "this would be so easy if I could see through walls where those guys are looking/walking". I understand the concept of "play how you want", I did, and even got the achievement to show for it. But, while others surely had fun playing with superpowers, and the powers are "quintessentially Dishonored", I still think they make the game just laughably easy and unchallenging. I think the truest way to play a stealth game like this, with incredible stealth mechanics, is to play it "in the raw" - no overpowered game-breaking superpowers like Jesse Cox put it (paraphrasing).
- Something is really off with the crossbow. Most importantly, sleep darts get caught on pretty much everything (including bushes). Also the darts don't quite land where you point, so when shooting from cover or lean, the darts usually just miss or get caught on something vaguely in the way. For these reasons the crossbow was mostly useless. I couldn't trust it except for the most dire emergencies where all the other options were already explored.
- Loot is completely useless for a no powers ghost run. The first couple of runes (200g each) every map are enough to float your economy for the whole game. There's an arbitrary scarcity of sleep darts (can't trust to find them anywhere except Black Markets) but all other loot is plentiful. IMO the best way to approach loot would've been to make it respond to your game mode. For no powers ghost, it should emphasize sleep darts, because you can't just run around shooting sleep darts into people anyway. You need to be intelligent about where to use the weapon, but the artificial resource scarcity made it so sometimes it was impossible even when it was the right or only thing to do.
Fantastic game. Not as impressive as the first, but a wonderful game nonetheless.

in clandestine you either take on the role of the spy who has to get to specific destinations without being seen

This is a third person stealth game in which you play two characters: the operator, who plays as you'd expect, and the hacker, who has to retrieve data from computers, spot enemies, take care of cameras, obtain the access codes for doors, manipulate the envionrment to distract enemies, and so on. You can also play co-operatively, in which case the host plays as the operator and the guest plays as the hacker. Voice comms recommended!
This is not a slickly produced AAA game like Splinter Cell, and in order to enjoy it you have to be willing to look past the jankiness and imperfect voice acting. This is balanced by the surprisingly substantial worldbuilding and low-key, actaully-somewhat-plausible storyline (think more le Carré instead of Ian Fleming) that was presumably inspired by the revelations surrounding Room 641A and later PRISM. The main characters also have a lot more depth to them than you would expect (and it's always a pleasant surprise to find an honest to goodness actaul Strong Female Character, especially in a game in this genre!)
I get the impression that the developers of this game really care about their craft, even though they don't have access to a huge budget. For instance, the tactics you use and choices you make in missions effect conversations that take place later on, and can even alter the tactics that your enemies will use later in the game.
This is not a perfect game, but it is perfectly worth playing and I hope that the developers earn enough that they can produce a second iteration in the future.

Personally for someone who meets only the minimum system specs and can't afford to go any higher, this review is biased, decently.
I've played through only the whole campaign and honestly... the multiplayer maps aren't too much to rave about.
First the campaign. Looking back on it, it indeed did use alot of tropes that I wish writers of the campaign levels would take a step back and look at other games in general. Just as always, you're a hardened marine or something, who is always in the thick of it, unlike the other comrades who are usually less in danger.
You're also a marine once more who has Turtle symdrome most of the time, once knocked down, something story-related or relevant to survival has to happen before your character decides to act, even if this trope is old and stale and instead detracts from the game now.
The only thing I really totally enjoyed, were the totally new things. I loved the grappling hook, scaling up buildings, up to overpasses in a city, made me feel awesome like some modern military ninja, or spiderman if he was a special forces operative.
Luckily this time, the story is actually not really based off of anything that's happened so far, because even if that is plentiful enough to do in military shooters, it's nice that the story writers actually had to think past characters for once.
Basically, ARES is a military for hire. you hire them and get an entire army and can even get your country restored in a shorter time frame than you can yourself. They soon become the largest army on the planet and near the end, low and behold, they literally declare war on the states. Because... you're american as always usually, so why not.
The campaign has some chasing segments, but the most intense moment was when in the story, there's a sniper, and instead of the usual fare for snipers, this guy has a very pathetic railgun. I say pathetic because REAL railguns cannot be stopped by even titanium walls unless they're like... 5 feet thick atleast and a solid chunk of metal.
But this sniper is coming after only you (ofcourse) and if you get hit even once, you're literally dead. And so you're trying to get to the objective as fast as possible, while trying to bait the sniper and avoid being shot by him/her, and they're up in a tall-freaking clock tower, so pretty much any form of window is a shooting zone.
The only real intense moment in the game is right there. You even have to fight other guys with the sniper sniffing up your butt, it's honestly the only really unique part about the story.
As usual military-shooters, you're shooting people using guns you spawn with instead of some nice realism flavrs, like keeping the same weapon throughout the campaign, only needing to eventually swap it out in combat for another, having to manage your ammo maybe with a similar thing.
The game however finally hasa real reason to have melee attacks be a for-sure instant kill as now you punch people with your exoskeleton-powered fists.
The cutscenes in the game are all done with pretty good motion capture and honestly the people in them are almost as real as real people can get. Ofcourse the cutscenes aren't as realistic and nice-looking as the game and as such it makes a slightly wierd visual disconnect like with any Diablo cutscene ever.
I like how in the campaign, the bad guys aren't stereotypical. Sure, it's a corporation, but it's also Kevin Spacey, and I'm sure in the game he too is American.
Is it as awesome as it was advertised? Ofcourse not. You get the drops for random loot in the campaign, but honestly even if you can upgrade your abilities in the campaign too, it doesn't affect anything else at all.
Altogether, the Campaign isn't really as different as any other CoD game, the game's focus seems to be more with the multiplayer, as the campaign more or less just functions as a tutorial for how everything in multiplayer works, save for gamemodes. Some multiplayer map bits are even used in the Campaign here and there, which is kind of nice, but also kind of lazy.
Now for Multiplayer.
Multiplayer works like this... as you play, you get supply drops which basically award you your stuff. You get these for things like leveling up, doing challenges probably, and probably other things too. They award you random items, camo patterns and accessories, which is actually really cool because it's sort of an RNG, but it's nothing you wouldn't otherwise get in Battlefield 4.
You can customize how killstreaks work, doing so will limit what you can pik in other areas of a loadout. Loadouts use the pick 14 system, which is just a bigger version of the pick 9 system from call of duty black ops 2/1 (forgot which has it).
Ofcorse there's zombies, but I think they're DLC, and honestly... I could hardly play multiplayer.
Just like in Ghosts, if you try to load a multiplayer game, but have it take enough time to load, it'll kick you from the server, even though a bunch of other games with AFK kick time, atleast acknowledges load times in that kicking process. This game doesn't.
Indeed, this is made by new hands for once, no Treyarch or Infinity Ward, but SledgeHammer Games, and honestly... for a call of Duty game, the multiplayer and campaign are actually nice and pretty stable once you can play. There's the actual ability to dodge melee attacks which are executed in the right range, and honestly... altogether the game was rather fun to play.
So what's so bad about game? This review indeed has been saving them for last, but here's for the negatives.
When I play anything in this game, it takes me 5 minutes of literal load time to get bakc into the action form a death, entering a level or a match, and... due to that alone and the fact that it has such requirements, I don't recommend the game to anyone.
Let's jsut look at Unreal Tournament 4. I can paly that fine though it's in the Pre-alpha stage, but it looks amazingly detailed on low settings. No combination of setting adjusments on this game will make it load quickly if you don't have the recommended settings available.
I'd recommend this game in a few years when it's inevitably replaced by 3 or 4 clones... but it's be replaced and you wouldn't remember my review anymore.
The game altogether gets a 5/10. Score is based upon bias ofcourse due to not being able to play the multiplayer, and honestly not alot of people were even playing multiplayer.
The game has plenty of modes and options, but as usual, the most played game modes are Deathmatch, Kill Confirmed, Search and Destroy... and that's actually about it.
Alot of the campaign has cool and nice moments, I recommend it for the story alone, and it keeps it from falling to a 4/10. The weapons aren't actually high-tech as you'd expect in a FUTURISTIC MILITARY SHOOTER, with only one actual high-tech weapon, the railgun sniper rifle (don't remember the actual name) and some pretending to be it, when it's just a gun whose projectiles have been reskinned to look high-tech.
Indeed, bullet weapons will still be used in our future, but these will eventually be replaced by obviously superior beam and mass driver-type weapons like laser rifles, and rail guns, and honestly, for someone expecting a game with like... a laser gatling gun, or even a chargeable plasma launcher or something... it disappointed me.
Sledgehammer and everyone else, take note, to me, this is only a 5/10 and not a 7/10 because of the weapons. Enough of the "Every weapon in a category are usually only slight variations of eachother" weapon formula that's been repeated since the series' beginning. It's nice, but it's time to change honestly.
The Exos are a good step in the right direction and alot of the killstreaks are actually futuristic, like a mech walker you can pilot, though.

ALIEN ISOLATION
Most of the game isn't too hard, as it plays on my honed skills of social avoidance. Imagine that you are Ripley, a 20 yo college student who shares a house with some people. You are an introvert and like to avoid conversations every time you want food. So you start listening to the old house you share, learning the patterns of your roommates and where to hide to avoid contact. That is this game. Honestly, the alien is quite pleasant to live with in comparison. There's only one, and it'll stomp around and make itself known like an angry upstairs neighbor. This thought also makes the games more humorous than scary, as you play hide and seek, or use noisemakers to direct the alien to the human hunting parties. Fetch boy.
Weird spikes in difficulty annoyed me early on, as you lack most devices for distraction, offense, or even knowing where to go next. Even when you get the motion tracker that points you in the correct direction, the game drags on longer than it should. You keep having to do nested sidequests to move on. You want to leave the station, but your friend is hurt so you need a med pack, so you need to go to the hospital, but you need to find a keycard and password  to open the door, so you must restore the power, but the facility catches fire and you need to escape. The game is about the journey more than the destination, and I enjoyed the details to the sound (7.1 headphones helped track), and the retrofuture design of the technology. It captures the thrill of the original Alien, the stalking and evasion.
Now some hate. Worthless ♥♥♥♥ing character development and npcs. Half attack on site, the other half fail the game if you do the same to them. Why would I want to read another person's emails while an alien is stalking me? Reading my own is tedious enough.
Most of the game time is searching for the one thing in the environment that advances the plot. Can't find the plasma torch on the dead guy in the corner after 5 rounds on the area? ♥♥♥♥ you. Trouble finding the 3 small green lights that lock the area down for an alien trap. Do it anyways, Marco or whoever mucks it up anyway. All this backtracking and walking mocks my precious free time.
I started sprinting around and then giving the Alien a flame bath whenever he wanted a hug. Then I'd go to use a terminal and helplessly mash B to abort the uninterruptible 10 second log on time, while Alien had the chances to drop from the vent, scan the area, kill me, have tea, file his taxes, and kill me again.
The enjoyable bits of terror you get from hiding in the cupboards is quickly diluted by repetition, since the game dynamics remain the same for the nearly 25 hour journey. The save system magnifies these issues when they can literally be 20 min apart in an area where death is common.
Kevin Vanord's review on Gamespot mirrors my sentiments.

As it currently stands I highly do not recommend this game with the current $20 price tag for numerous reasons which I will go into detail about below.
IN GENERAL:
The game has a multitude of flaws and problems that you notice right from the beginning when you first start playing it and it gets worse as the game goes on. There have been times where I've gotten so frustrated at the game that I've quit entirely and pushed it aside because of the flaws it brings to the table.
IN-DEPTH (May cover things not mentioned above):
Horrible HECU AI:
One of the biggest things you will notice is how stupid the soldier AI is yet they manage to shoot you with almost perfect accuracy from across the map with no recoil and even while out of view their magic bullets still seem to find there way into your body. Even with their Godlike accuracy they still manage to act like total idiots, I've had many times where they run into cover after I've started shooting and run back out standing in the exact spot they were when I shot them. All I have to do is keep my crosshair on that same spot and wait for them to run right back into it for an easy kill. Not only that but there are several times where they simply just stand in one place and do nothing, even when I approach them they still stand there in a dazed stupor not shooting or moving or anything until I kill them. Even when they run up to the player to shoot them there's times when they just stand there starring at the player waiting for them to be killed.
Damage Boost:
Another gigantic problem in this mod is the damage boost done by enemies, it seems like it takes only a few shots to reduce the player's full health and suit charge to zero in seconds, same with the Agrunt's Hivehand projectiles.
Animations:
For the most part the animations in this game are bad, from the metropolice run animations for Barney to the goofy stumbling animations of the zombies, even the HECU are simply combine soldiers with different skins and sounds. Because BM is using stock HL2 animations you can see how they don't fit well with the new NPC's such as the scientists with their weird finger animations or Barney who likes to have his arms go through his chest when he has the pistol in his hand.
Bugs:
This game has plenty of bugs from bad collisions on props, constant game crashes, buggy AI, and unfair player deaths that shouldn't have happened in the first place. The workshop, not to mention, is a horribly implemented mess. Not only is the workshop system in-game a poorly designed tacked on mess but it serves no functionality other then to tell players what they are subscribed to. You can't turn things on or off, you can't unsub from the menu, and to make things worse the devs broke most workshop support and haven't fixed it yet and because we can't disable workshop items in-game we have to unsub and completely re-install BM to play it without more crashes and errors.
Textures/Models:
You'd think that an HD remake of Half-Life 1 would be just that, an HD remake but over the course of the game you start to see how bad the textures are. There are places where the textures are so bad and blurry that the original Gldsrc engine would do a better job rendering the textures than the BM team did on the new engine. The various car models in the maps are under-detailed on the inside looking like something out of an N64 game and the textures for the damaged Truck and APC are so low res that it looks like they took them straight from a SNES console. These are just a couple examples but if you take the time to look you will start to see how bad things look. Not only that but the BM team is still using stock HL2 and L4D assets without even giving them an upgrade so you see extremely low res HL2 props next to HD BM props, it doesn't look nice. Even some of the NPC's are still from the stock HL2 such as the Barnacle and Headcrab, they didn't even try to make them look faithful to Half-Life 1.
Overall Black Mesa is nowhere close to justifying their $20 price tag, I get it's an early access title but asking for $20 when the game has all these issues is greedy and unnecessary. I highly suggest you get this game when it goes on sale for 75% off or you get it dirt cheap from a third-party website but I caution you not to buy it for full price. Don't buy this until they put more effort into it, as it stands it's a nice $20 pack of maps but it is NOT a complete Half-Life remake. If you want to play BM play the mod, you aren't missing anything and at least some of these problems can be justified.
If you would like to see examples from some of the things I've mentioned check my BM screenshots on my profile, I point out a lot of bugs and problems there.

It started off as a simple gang, four of us, on a seemingly fresh server. We made a vow to rise up to power and control the lands of this hidden land! Or so we thought.
It was only the first day, and food was scarce. We were stuck, bare to all elements of the outside world, living between two rocks and a campfire. One of our friends decided he was gonna go hunting, and so he ran, attacking any living thing.
It was only a matter of time before we reached the news, that he was attacked by a hostile boar, killed by surprise. He had rage quited. It was apparent to us that we were too close to a junkyard and had fled atleast four miles before settling on a mountain rock. We had not known of the cold that would soon engulf us.
It was only day 2, the campfire was expected to run out of fuel. Eventually we had decided that two of us would go and gather supplies, before expanding our newly formed "Empire".
We had gathered some owong so we could satisfy our growing hunger, but that wasn't the only problem.
A band of looters had joined the server, apparently had more hours on it than us, and screams of rage in the chatroom was beginning to be more and more apparent. They were hunting down treasureless poor folk, not for survival, but for a 'game', which is what they'd call it.
When Day 3 rolled around, we were engulfed by the fact of getting hunted down. So we gathered our last resources and moved to a seemingly nice neighbourhood, where they had happily let us settle down, and gave us clothes and all a wood bow, each five arrows.
Day 7, we had a small shack we had built, were barely the three of us could manage to fit in it. It helped atleast, keeping us safe from the unknowledgable dangers outside. When morning rolled around, we had heard three russian kids screaming in their voice chat, most likely a sign of dominance in ones opponent. We ran outside, were we came to the conclusion that we were being raided.
Three kids pointed their pistols at the crouched settlers, dropping loot so they won't be killed. A body would lay next to the other, maybe he had protested. We ran for as far as we could, two of them shot and screamed at us. They were so bad at aiming we barely managed to run to a mountain top and snipe them with our bows. Killing one, the other two ran after his body, in a weak effort to take his loot to his rightful owner. We ran after them, killing another one, before the other one had escaped out of our grasp. We were praised, took our earned loot, and continued the days work.
Day 30 rolled around.
It was an army, atleast eight people with spears and axes running in the settlement.
We were safe inside, but we had to do something.
My friend yelled at them, attempting to scare them off. "I got a gun!"
We ran outside guns blazing, killing three of them before the rest scattered off.
Three people came behind us and attacked and killed two of my friends.
Barely managing to survive, bleeding profusely, I slowly walked to my death.
Apparently, the people we killed were apart of some parade, and we got punished.

After Bethesda announced the sequel to Evil Within, I have been really anticipating this game. The main reason being is that they couldn't do the same thing again. The first game was a little clunky, had the mandatory widescreen (I know DLC was different), and didn't hold your hand much in the story. So many changes have been made this time around as they all feel like improvements instead of changing the formula. The main character hasn't changed but the motive has; find your daughter and figure out who/what Mobius is and what they are doing. I like this because no I'm willingly going into this and I feel like I'm going back into the Matrix to figure out what in the heck it really is. The other big standout in the game is how much bigger it feels. The first game was an endless stream of rooms and hallways, and without spoiling anything, you have a lot more elbow room this time around. This gives you a chance to breathe but now wonder how in the heck they are going to freak you out in new ways. The gameplay itself feels similar but more fluid. Like I said, they greased the gears on this new game and it makes it feel so much better. Finally, presentation-wise the game looks a lot better but still doesn't have the drop dead gorgeous textures that some games do, and it's ok! 9 times out of 10, you are playing this game for the ambiance, the unique world, and the lack of understanding what is going on. Overall:
+The gameplay feels SO much better
+The world has been more thought out, and with that, the environments are larger
+Scares and music are back and keeping you on your toes
+Visuals are great and are a step up from the previous game
+The story has a stronger emphasis with a more distinct motive

I have no way to describe how bad of a game this is.
TL;DR: No immersion, bad storytelling, too many genres packed into one game, bad difficulty scaling, no fun.
It feels like the Tango Gameworks put visuals over plot and gameplay. Massive letdown after the 1st game
(It visually looks good, which is a plus, I guess)
There is almost no storybuilding or world building in this game. You get the "Your daughter died in a fire" motive but that's really it. Even after playing the first one *again* to get into the mood for this game's release, it was hard for me to connect with the characters. Sebastion and Kidman have no depth to them outside of what was built in TEW1. There is NO immersion at all. I found myself fighting just to keep playing the game. It felt like the same♥♥♥♥♥♥over and over again. The "open world" is just 3-5 maps broken up by the Marrow, which is like a hub for world travel. I shouldn't be locked into a single city block  in an open world game. I can not think of a single reason for why the whole map couldn't be together. The difficulty scaling is horrid. When I was first introduced to the zombies after the prologue, I hit them with 5-6 shots and they didn't go down. You have to stealth kill them...? What? Until half way into the game, the run-of-the-mill zombie was one of the hardest things to take down, but after I hit chapter 6-7 I could dispatch them with ease. There was no challenge to moving around the map(s) after that point, the zombies just becuase annoying and it felt like a grind just to get the next part of the story done. As a horror game, I would hope there would be actual horror...this game just throws in one or two cheap jumpscares and then relies on the gore factor for the rest of the game. It was intimidating at first, of course, but it's everywhere all the time and you get desensatized to it after like an hour. It just becomes background noise that nobody pays attention to.  Another issue is the genres. It feels like Tango Gameworks looked at every successful game in the past 5 years and tried to smush all of that into one game. It's a shooter/stealth/progression/horror/ survival/upgradeable character/minigames/mystery/open world/linear/exploring/puzzle game. Too many genres make it hard to play becuase of so many conflicting ideas. Literally the ONLY time I wanted to play the game was right before the final boss. Right at that area in the game, it was really good. The plot started to thicken and the characters seemed to actually be people, instead of a shallow character. The ending was really good, bummer you had to play through 11 hours of♥♥♥♥♥♥to get to ~20 minutes of good game. Oh well...I'll remember to let the game come out and read reviews before buying anything next time. I wasted good money on this game.

One of my favorite survival horror games in quite a while, The Evil Within 2 is a wonderful sequel to a wonderful game. I had my doubts at the beginning, as the game initially feels a lot different in both playstyle and mechanics than The Evil Within, however the more I played the more I realized these were welcome changes that served to evolve this series.
Gathering materials to craft ammunition and medicine is a huge focus of this game, as ammo and materials are scare throughout the game world, especially late game. This scarcity really brings out the survival horror elements as you find yourself with one bullet in your pistol having to stealth around or die. For survival horror fans, I imagine this is extremely refreshing. I know it was for me.
The Evil Within 2 also separates quite a bit from the first game in that is is a lot more 'wide linear' in level design, at least in early game. I had a lot of fun exploring one of the earlier maps without a ton of hand holding, gathering supplies, and seeing what I could find. This was a step up IMO from the much more linear design of the first game.
There is a decent variety of monsters to encounter in this game, although I would have loved to see more, the game more than enough delivers on a fair amount of sick and twisted creatures for you to battle or walk away from.
No game is perfect but I believe The Evil Within 2 to be a great addition to the series and would recommend it to survival horror fans.
ALSO to mention: The amount of nostalgia I had playing this game was unreal, they really paid homage to some older survival horror titles and they did it extremely well ( Target Practice anyone? ) to the point of being one of my favorite parts of my initial playthrough.

What an excellent title. I was a fan of the first one, but I'll admit it wasn't amazing it mostly just had a lot of potential. The second evil within takes advantage of a lot of that potential. It fixes a lot of gripes I had about the first game - More concise and interesting story, more fluid movement, characters feel like real human beings. Not to mention Tango Gameworks added some new elements I wasn't expecting. The semi open world yet linear progression was a huge welcoming addition. There are mini side quests and world events that trigger and actually add substance to what's happenning in the crazy world around you. I know graphics aren't everything but wow - the game looks fantastic. Especially when you compare it to the first which looked awkward and janky at times. I didn't run into performance problems or bugs once.
I'm honestly a little upset with critics not rating this game higher. It was a huge step forward from the last game yet it recieved a somewhat similar metacritic. We need to encourage more high quality, single player focus games in an era where big companies are mostly focused on microtransactions/loot boxes/multiplayer (which this game has ZERO of!). Absolutely listen to the Very Positive steam reviews it is exactly that - the fans know what's good. I was also pretty confused to not see this game anywhere on the steam front page the week it came out. I really hope Tango keeps up the excellent work and delivers us another awesome game, whether it's another The Evil Within or a new IP.

I just completed the game with 100% province and story completion, so my opinion in light of that:
The Good: This is a spectacle shooter. If you like explosions, Rambo-like action, think 80s shooter movie, then you'll enjoy that aspect. The graphics are much better than Just Cause 2, and there are a few (not many) tweaks and changes made to your arsenal to open up some possiblities.
The Bad: This isn't much of an evolution from Just Cause 2. It isn't worth $60, although it held my attention for 25+ hours, I do think it is a solid pick in the $30-$40 range, but I'd wait for a Steam Sale.
The story is by-the-numbers, and there isn't much in the way of depth. Not much changed from the first province taken to the last. By the end I was just tired and wanting to complete it. The best part of the game is the voice acting of the Medici radio announcer, which is no surprise since I'm a Doctor Who fan. I was more concerned about his fate than the rest of the story.
In any event, pick it up on a sale and if you go in with low expectations you'll have a great time. If there were a star rating, I'd give it a 3/5.

Ever since I first played the first dishonoured, I have been patiently waiting for the second one to come out. The second that I heard about Dishonoured 2 coming out, I wanted to cry tears of joy. As soon as I got the game (Christmas Day), I began the download. My internet isnt the greatest so it took roughly a day and a few hours, but i was willing to put this time in for a game that I knew I was going to love. After the game downloads, I practically cried tears of joy and pressed play. The game opens, and I doubt I was running 5 FPS. I could barely navigate my way through the main screen to get to the settings to turn down the quality on some settings, just to find out they are already as low as possible. I then do the best I can to get them even lower, and proceed to simply click on the tutorial. It took a solid 3-4 minutes for that to even get to the first view of the tutorial, and even then I didnt even take 3 steps because the frame rate was horrible. I understand that I have a semi-potato computer, but it runs every other game I have with ease. Its honestly very saddening that I can't play the game that ive been dying to play for years now because the technical errors are far to great. I have done nothing but brag on this game ever since it first came out, the first dishonoured was a masterpiece and I can easilly say that it was my favorite game of the time, and I thought that the second one would take its spot. I doubt I will be able to find that out until the game is fixed to the point of being mutally playable. Its a shame that anybody would release a game with this much hype, but not have betta testers play it first, or have it in a completely unstable state. I very sadly would not reccomend this game until these errors are fixed, simply because the game is literally unplayable in the state that it is in. I will be that happiest man on earth when my computer can run this game, but until then, I'll continue to cry over the fact that this beautiful piece of art has been ruined for lots of people because the game was released when it still needed lots of work.

On my end, all performance issues have been resolved and I can finally enjoy the game as it should be played and what a game it is!
Pros:
-Huge expansive levels that make the first one pale in comparison
-Two characters to chose from, each with their own skill set and perspective/commentary on the narrative
-Smarter AI and more varied enemy types (soldiers, witches, clockwork soldiers etc.)
-A lot easier to play non-lethally than the first game
-Excellent art style and gorgeous graphics
-A whole wack of new powers to chose from and new abilities added to pre-existing ones
Cons:
-Chaos meter is still weird. I find it was actually a lot harder to tell what you were doing to cause chaos in this one than the first one. Its also strange because it seems as if Shadow kill, a key ability in the first one  which almost guarenteed a low chaos/lethal playthrough, now adds chaos. Either was, the chaos meter still really needs to be fixed
-Stuff that should've been in the game at launch isn't in the game. While New Game Plus has been added, there is still no mission replay function, which is really frustrating
-Story is meh, not terrible, not great, just in the middle
TLDR- A solid sequel which improves upon most of what was wrong with the first one. While performance issues for most are fixed, I'd still recommend waiting for the inevitable DLC and future patches. If you're a die hard Dishonored fan like myself, than you'll enjoy it. Recommend it on a sale.

My partner and I bought this in the winter sale to play together. The concept excited us and 50% off seemed like a good deal. The graphics aren't anything to write home about but we figured if the gameplay was as good as reviews suggested we could look past it. We couldn't. This game is broken. Challenge and gameplay are replaced with confusion, tedium and unnecessary stress. A scarcity of ammo would be understandable if every enemy you took down didn't *have a gun*. Confusing hacking mechanics could be overlooked if the hacking was *actually fun*. Don't misunderstand me here: I like hard hacking games. The hacking mechanics in Clandestine are simplistic, but there were too many things to watch at once, not enough information about how to do this or why you can't do that and it just /wasn't fun/. Finally, the ability to take down enemies through walls is unforgivable, as is the sponge-like ability of enemy torsos to soak up bullets. Other unforgivable sins include godawful writing and the fact that no one is more obviously aware how crappy the writing is than the game's voice actors.

Few bugs here and there, but still a masterpiece, both the original game and Black Mesa.

The good:
1. Incredible work, visually, in re-imagining the original Half-life locations, which started off (and completed a significant part of the project) as a fan project.
2. Great soundtrack.
3. I liked the voice-overs a lot. I remember reading complaints about them, but I found all of them very professional and near perfect.
The bad:
1. Level design was updated and changed (in comparison with the original Half-Life maps) to make more sense. Which would be great but, unfortunately, this in conjunction I guess with insufficient QA testing has resulted to:
a) Too many objects obstructing your movement. Quite a few of those are even fixed in place, even though it doesn't make sense for them to be (eg some chairs are fixed, others aren't).
b) On some occasions the map design is bad to the point that you can't even walk normally around the level and for example you have to jump over a stair railing to reach the stairs (because objects, pillars, walls in the map make the available path, which yes there is one - you can see it, too narrow to cross/ fit into. Residue Processing map is particularly guilty of this.
c) Objects in the map are in too big scale with respect to  the player's proportions (eg many doors have handles that are near or above Freeman's head).
d) A few times I got stuck behind a door which I opened, because its "opening" animation, pushed me and got me stuck between the door and the wall. The door then had no option to be closed again for me to get freed. Only loading a previous save game can take you out of that.
2. Quite often it's difficult to navigate in the maps. There are pointless pathways (again, they went for maps making sense, but gameplay-wise... they got confusing in the process), and there are eg levers to be triggered that are obscured or not very obvious. You can get stuck in a room searching for exits, unbeknownst to you that there is a lever somewhere (eg under-water) or a missing wheel that you need to find, and restore in place before you can turn it to open a door or access a vent or something).
3. Enemy placement and choreography is too troll-oriented many times. The game expects you to die again and again (and maybe resort to quick-save quick-load) to overcome certain battles and environmental hazards.
4. They have kept all the annoyning stuff from the original Half-Life that I remember. I don't blame them, but I would expect them to tone them down. But nope. The awful first person platforming is as awful here, if not more. You are expected to jump on pipes, shimmy across thin pipes, jump on (moving) platforms, jump through holes in gates, jump and climb onto ledges while you keep sliding for some reason (bad controls maybe?).
5. Xen levels/ chapters are still missing. No updates yet about that, no WIP screenshots. Nothing. The developers have written recently that there is going to be an update (announcement) about that soon. But no Xen and no allowsed questions about Xen (the topics are locked) is not a very promising attitude anymore (yes, when it was a free fan made/ community project, you bear with them, you have to be patien. This is no longer that).

Eternal Senia is a free ARPG (action rpg, meaning the combat is not turn based) made in RPG maker. The game was simple but quite fun while it lasted. For a game that's 100% free, there's really no reason not to try it.
Pros:
+Great soundtrack. Admittedly it's small and loops a lot, but the game is free, so I can't complain.
+Gameplay is simple but sucks you in. Nothing too complicated here, this is a relaxation game. (Except for the final boss, which is unexpectedly difficult.) Just touch enemies to auto-attack. There's also a set of special skills that consume a magic meter.
+Touching story
+Character art is scant but what's there is excellent. It looks much better than most doujinsoft on Steam. Almost professional level.
+I got eight hours of gameplay out of it
Cons:
-Final boss is MUCH harder than the rest of the bosses; it feels slightly unbalanced with the rest of the game.
This game was better than a lot of games you have to pay for. I think the creator could have easily gotten away with charging $2.99 for it; people would still have loved it.

This is an MMO of individuality. It isn't like most MMOs that ask you to kill this X amount of times then turn it in. It asks you to do actual tasks, from being an errand boy to helping recover books for the Mages guild. Which is also a nice feature, the Mages guild and the Fighters guild both have their own main story quests, along with side quests (Just like the regular and main story quests). These not-so-mindless tasks also involve some puzzles and wordplay that makes it a bit more necessary to get into the lore instead of just speed running to max level (Even though you can do that, and most people try to).
The game immerses you in a world that is not just pretty to the eye, but beyond adventurable. You can go into the darkest most off the wall location on the map and find treasure chests and materials. There's always something new to see.
There is an in-game store that allows you to buy certain things with real money, but none of these things give you an edge in PvP, making it not a p2w game. Most of the items are costumes, exclusive mounts, pets, and DLC's.
Definitely my best game purchase of 2015, next to Killing Floor 2, which I will recommend playing both. At least giving it a try won't kill you and the game isn't all that expensive when it comes down to it.

What a visceral, immersive experience! The buyer gets his money’s worth within the first few hours of this atmospheric Sci-Fi Horror game if racing heartbeat and sweaty palms are a measure. Mostly I play action or soldier games and usually I’m running into the action even if I have to replay an area several times to get to the next. But frustration is the dominant feeling in those games, not the dread and terror of creeping down a dimly lit corridor, all the while hearing bumping and thumping all around and above me (and the unsettling soundtrack) as the alien hunts for me. The squawky detector is a help to tell you when the alien is near but sometimes the random pips and scratches send a false alarm that need to be checked out.
Fans of the Alien series of movies will love wandering around the nearly-abandoned, deep-space manufacturing complex which truly captures the look and feel of the style in the movies. But it’s obvious that something went very wrong here, and it’s your job to explore where needed to fulfill the missions (rather than Chapters) as the game progresses.
The difficulty can be changed under Options but only within the game.  Game Save is only allowed at specific stations which means in some levels you have to redo many minutes of nerve-shattering creeping around only to get skewered again by “that thing”. So I recommend taking the time to slink back to the save station when mini-tasks are completed even when it’s out of your way and you’d rather not backtrack more than you have to.  Another minor complaint is the sometimes contrived reason you have to put yourself in harm’s way but that is just another convention of the genre.
There are many visual and auditory references to iconic games such as Half-Life and Portal (and probably others I miss). An earlier Alien game got terrible reviews due to hang-up and crashing problems but this one is a winner on par with these other benchmark games. If you don’t want to buy it at the reasonable market pricing at least put it on your Steam wishlist and buy it when you get the email that it’s on sale. That will limit your financial exposure, but nothing but heightened awareness and a fuelled-up flamethrower will protect you when you creep out of your hiding place to see what’s beyond the next sliding door…

Early Access Watcher Reviews Hurtworld
Update Version: 0.3.5.3
Disclosure: The game copy was bought by the review.
Simulation style games can always be a hit or miss depending on the trends set by any active game's predecessor. For the survival branch of this genre, most of the early access players decided to throw their hat into the ring around the end of 2013. The next two years would see the addition of many ambitious, if not underwhelming, survival games with very few managing to see release. Hurtworld is one of the newer attempts at revitalizing the genre and has been separating itself from the competition with the addition of craft-able vehicles. Is this one difference enough to carve a mark into the interests of the consumer or just another worn out gimmick?
As usual, the visual appeal of the game manages to maintain a distinct look. It has a robust, cel shaded modeling choice that makes everything from buildings to animal models stand out in a decent manner. Campfires, fruits, ore, vehicles and even weapons are detailed, even if most of these items look like crates if dropped from the player. The one complaint I would have derives from the lack of environment change for some areas which mostly make up cubicles of rock formations. It makes travel confusing as hell before arriving to the later biomes that change things up with grasslands, snowy ground and abandoned structures. Granted it is not the best looking game out there, but what is here doesn't hurt the eyes. Sound effects and music on the other hand is rather forgettable with the majority of your time listening to pick axe cracks and the character complaining of hunger.
Survival is the name of the game if you can manage to escape the instant death of player kill. Materials are strewn around in the form of single rocks or mining nodes with animals and oranges to gather to stave of hunger. Clothing can be made to counter freezing and heat stroke while structures provide access to a respawn and storage hub. Vehicles are the only real difference available in this game, but they work and provide an excellent mode of transportation. Outside of building and exploring the single map, there is nothing else to do. Player interaction in the community is the only reason this game could survive. The majority of players resort to killing on sight principles and make it nearly impossible for new players to join servers without being annihilated on initial spawn. If you can find a private server with some friends then maybe you can avoid this issue.
As with any other early access game, the lack of optimization seems to carry the burden of technical issues along with it. Crashes were prevalent when attempting to connect to servers; the loading screen would freeze and then force me to the desktop. Frame rates took a hit as well during select weather events, driving and even running. I could be in a empty area and start to feel the slowdown as I launched a arrow or two into a boar. Speaking of boars, a strange and mostly annoying bug caused animals to stand perfectly still and absorb hit after hit before deciding to disappear. Optimization can fix a lot of these issues and hopefully they will take the time to see it happen.
Hurtworld has experienced the same development hiccups as most other survival simulators. The process generally provides a slow start with content updates while the online community forms and makes a foothold in primary servers. Time will go on and the content updates begin to stop all together and leave behind optimization problems made worse with unsuccessful bug fixes. At the same time, the communities begin to implement basic "kill on sight" and a ripple effect occurs that leaves a nasty scar on the game's reputation. While I cannot fault the response of the community on the developer, I can say the lack of content and optimization make this game a lot harder to deal with. While the community's aggressive nature will decide the fate of the game, the technical side prevents me from recommending Hurtworld. By the time I revisit this game in six months, I hope the developers will return to a regular update schedule.
Pros
- Cel shaded look is easy on the eyes

Cons

- Single map with very little biome diversity
- Content is slim at best

- Amount of deaths reported in just first thirty minutes is staggering (how did I never die to anyone?)

God, where to start?
I am sure there are tons of other people out there who have glorified this game better than I can, so rather than go crazy about how much I like this game I will just focus on a few highlights.
1 - It isn't that often that you can find a game on Steam that is 100% family friendly.  Sure, there are some games like Subnautica that don't necessarily have swear words or graphic material, but I've had my siblings give it a go and most of them freak out whenever they go outside of the starting zone because of the vast, alien ocean the game takes place in.  This is a game that I could give to my baby niece when she grows old enough to play games and feel confident that I won't be everyone's least favorite uncle.  Would love to see more games like that.
2 - It's music is amazing.  There's nothing to hate about this game's soundtrack.  Every track fits its zone perfectly, be it the rustic farmer track on the Ranch to the upbeat tunes of the Moss Blanket to the mysterious awe of the Glass Desert.  It functions really well with the game's aesthetic which I will get to in a moment.
3 - The game's visuals are like eye candy.  You can never go wrong with making your game focus on toon graphics.  It's pleasing to the eye and brings about less strain on your computer, so you can focus more on adding cool content instead of balancing between something that looks realistic and something that can function on a computer without dropping performance.
4 - It sucks you in.  Literally the first night I played it I spent around 10 hours playing, which would make me feel guilty if not for the fact that I was having a lot of fun.  There are some aspects that do feel grindy, granted - once you establish a working system that sets up the maximum amount of plorts per largo gathering your plorts to get loot can become a chore.  Implementing other means to use said plorts rather than just use it to get currency to spend on cosmetics on your ranch, such as the Slime Scientist Lab, helps break the monotony and gives you an excuse to visit old areas to get new resources.  Even though I finished the base game already I am definitely coming back for more.
5 - It is nice and short.  I beat this game up to 63% achievements in 20 hours, and over half of that was kerfuffing around dealing with stuff in my slime ranch.  Realistically you can beat this game's story in about half that time if you wanted, though I don't recommend you do.  Where this game works well is how everything is balanced together.  There's just the right amount of everything in the experience that you can't just speedrun it.  Take your time and enjoy it, and when you have you'll be able to enjoy one of the sweetest heartfelt endings a simple indie game like this can give.  (Although if you REALLY feel like giving a speedrun a go, there is an optional mode that essentially acts as a 5 hour challenge to get as many newbucks as possible in the allotted timeframe, definitely trying that next).
This is a game I'm definitely going to be replaying for a while until I've completed everything, and then I'll definitely give it a replay in the future.  9/10.
Before I close this off, if the devs are paying attention, there are a few things I would like to include at the end of this review.
- Keep adding content to this game.  It is great, but now I want even more.  I'd love to encounter a volcanic-themed island or perhaps a snow-themed island in the Far Range with equivalent slimes and other resources.  Don't add too much - too much of a good thing won't help anybody - but I would love to see more challenge and more fun like what we got with the Glass Desert.

9.8/10 I actually really really liked The Evil Within 2. And I haven't had a really good and engaging single-player campaign game in a long time and this game REALLY quenched my thirst for that! Before I started this game I looked online to estimate how long this game would take and a couple of sources said around 20 hours of gameplay. For me, I think, I got ~14.5hrs on Survival and I looked around and really took my time with the game. And to be quite frank, I probably could've beaten this game around 11-12hrs, if I didn't take my time. A friend also told me that in the Evil Within 1 (I never played Evil Within 1, f*** me right, looking back on it, maybe I should play it) there were a lot of puzzles that were pretty hard (don't take my word on it, thats just what he told me). So I thought yeah this game will be really fun cause I love puzzles. Only came to know that there were like no puzzles at all (for me at least). I'll be honest I only died once throughout my run, on survival difficulty, and it was because I was doing an interactable and something came up to me and one shot me (won't spoil by what or how it killed me). Also the game was very easy for me on survival, I don't know if anyone else feels that way but I didn't really struggle at all, the only thing I struggeled with was maintaining ammo. I ran out of resources for medical and ammunition like two times throughout the run, other than that I was pretty stacked because I conserved my supplies. But I 100% garrentee that this game will be way harder on Classic mode and I'm excited to start the new playthrough with this new challenge (for those of you who don't know, Classic mode is the hardest difficulty and you can only obtain the option for it after you've beaten the game once). And to be fairly honest, I felt the boss fights were extremely easy to beat and 2 of them you can kind of exploit where the boss can't really do anything to you because your positioning just some how is in the sweet spot. My friend also said that this game was nothing how he thought it was going to be like. He said the abilities, the interactions, the somewhat open-world feel to it too (that's how you know you're playing a Bethesda game xd) were all just so different and way better than the first game. The graphics were, for the most part, really stunning (nothing new) and the audio was really good. I'm mean like the voiceacting for some mobs were just outstanding.
The story wasn't boring and the gameplay wasn't repetitve, everything was dynamic. So why did I rate this game a 9.8/10, why not a perfect score? I don't know, I just feel like if some elements were touched up then this game would be perfect, I don't know I could just be really picky about it. But to me, this game kind of feels like Resident Evil and The Last of Us had a baby, but the baby had better characteristics than their predecessors. For the multiplayer platform freak that I am, I really loved this game and I would recommend it for anyone and everyone. Also this game isn't one of those single player games were you can beat once and then not feel like beating it again. The Evil Within 2 really encourages the player to keep playing after they've beaten it, chears to Tango Gameworks for that and for making a masterpiece of a game!

Its also strange because it seems as if Shadow kill, a key ability in the first one  which almost guarenteed a low chaos/lethal playthrough, now adds chaos. ♥♥♥♥♥is pretty much a given, but how do I stop this suffering? Maybe if I shift my brain for the first time in fourteen years, the answer will come. Oh, lord. Such unpolished development. The ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ization of co-op gameplay has altered the mass in my head. My brain is being reconstructed. I've become a god! Power Lances through my body. The planes of this and all worlds are opened to me as pages from the book of Johndavid consume my being.

A perfect example of a game that's more than the sum of its parts. The game features you either playing the agent or the hacker, each having a very different perspective on each mission. The agent is your typical 3rd person view that interacts with the world, while the hacker is stuck somewhere far away with access to the level's networking structure. Each mission requires you to honor both these diciplines, either in single player or in online co-op - which is the way the game SHOULD be played anyway.
Clandestine also manages to establish an environment and somewhat of a story outside each mission, allowing you to run around in HQ doing various tasks, talking to people and further advancing the story. Most of these are optional though. The game also changes some of its dialogue trees based upon how you've done it in previous missions, and even changes future missions!
While being anywhere near state of the art graphically-wise it serves the game well enough to not pay it much mind once you have a couple of missions in your pocket. The soundtrack is atmospheric, but voice talents are subpar with often hilariously bad dialogue and pronounciations. There's also an (un)healthy dose of broken in-game cinematics that are more the standard of the norm than random occurences. Expect to see people and items glitch through floors, walls and not even honor you being stealthy/hidden! Thankfully you can also be just as shady, allowing you to take out guards through walls and doors!
For a game that so heavily relies on stealth you're forced to play around the game in way that damages the experience and immersion - a thing that should've been patched a long time ago. Net code also seemed way off at times, requiring a really good internet connection unless you wanted your co-op partner to drop out. Swapping roles are also inadvertedly awkward, as the game host will always play the agent and the joining player will play the hacker. If you want to switch roles in between missions you have to send your save game to the other person! Seriously!?
There are many thing that Clandestine should have fixed or done better, but as I said initally it is an experience that is better than the sum of its parts. Because when it works it's an experience like no other. You have to pay attention, keep a close dialogue (a VOIP is a MUST) with your team mate and work together to make it through the levels. There are plenty of exilirating moments to be had when the game allows it and this is where Clandestine shines. It makes one wonder why there aren't any more games of this type.
If stealth is your forté and can compromize with the game's apparent faults and some its wonky mechanics are wonky and lackluster dialogue there is a unique experience to be had here. It is a shame that it requires a bit of work to see this diamond in the rough.

Borderlands 2 works some weird magic. Something about the game is so mysteriously charming - its storyline that doesn't take itself very seriously can immediately turn heads and leave you speechless.  Its thoroughly-designed central antagonist will evoke strong feelings of hatred, but will also draw out an incredible and unexplainable curiosity toward his personality and actions. Its gameplay feels tight, discrete, and responsive, especially when accompanied with the unique but also 'solid' graphics, providing you with hours of satisfying gibs, explosions, and laughs.
I find it hard to pinpoint what's so good about this game. It really has to be a culmination of multiple factors, which makes sense since Borderlands 2 draws inspiration from multiple genres. It has an RPG element to it, arising from the loot-based/farming gameplay and character skills/skill trees, which by the way, creates a plethora of playstyles and strong replayability. Its chaotic but crisp combat mixed with hilarious commentary incorporates elements from first-person shooters and story-based singleplayers. Maybe the most interesting part is its relatively simple but ridiculously fun multiplayer system - because experiencing the ups and downs of a well-written storyline alone can only be beat by doing the same thing but with your friends.
Yes, it has its flaws. The game can try a little bit too hard to be funny at times, and it can get on your nerves if you're not into its kind of crude humor. The plot also isn't the most engaging until later on, since it takes a while to build its characters and your feelings for them. Side quests are abundant, and one might get sidetracked (no pun intended) which causes the plot to be even less engaging, not to mention an awkward inbalance of levels might occur - enemies in the default difficulty have set levels, and don't scale with your character. If a person focuses only on doing the plot, they will also miss out on some loot and world exploration which may or may not be a problem.
Nonetheless, it's been years since the release of Borderlands 2, and I definitely don't play it as much as I used to, but it's the only game that still sits in my library, unchanged by the sands of time. I guess it is quite literally timeless, but perhaps you'd take that as a metaphor and just buy the damn game already.

9.8/10 I actually really really liked The Evil Within 2. And I haven't had a really good and engaging single-player campaign game in a long time and this game REALLY quenched my thirst for that! Before I started this game I looked online to estimate how long this game would take and a couple of sources said around 20 hours of gameplay. For me, I think, I got ~14.5hrs on Survival and I looked around and really took my time with the game. And to be quite frank, I probably could've beaten this game around 11-12hrs, if I didn't take my time. A friend also told me that in the Evil Within 1 (I never played Evil Within 1, f*** me right, looking back on it, maybe I should play it) there were a lot of puzzles that were pretty hard (don't take my word on it, thats just what he told me). So I thought yeah this game will be really fun cause I love puzzles. Only came to know that there were like no puzzles at all (for me at least). I'll be honest I only died once throughout my run, on survival difficulty, and it was because I was doing an interactable and something came up to me and one shot me (won't spoil by what or how it killed me). Also the game was very easy for me on survival, I don't know if anyone else feels that way but I didn't really struggle at all, the only thing I struggeled with was maintaining ammo. I ran out of resources for medical and ammunition like two times throughout the run, other than that I was pretty stacked because I conserved my supplies. But I 100% garrentee that this game will be way harder on Classic mode and I'm excited to start the new playthrough with this new challenge (for those of you who don't know, Classic mode is the hardest difficulty and you can only obtain the option for it after you've beaten the game once). And to be fairly honest, I felt the boss fights were extremely easy to beat and 2 of them you can kind of exploit where the boss can't really do anything to you because your positioning just some how is in the sweet spot. My friend also said that this game was nothing how he thought it was going to be like. He said the abilities, the interactions, the somewhat open-world feel to it too (that's how you know you're playing a Bethesda game xd) were all just so different and way better than the first game. The graphics were, for the most part, really stunning (nothing new) and the audio was really good. I'm mean like the voiceacting for some mobs were just outstanding.
The story wasn't boring and the gameplay wasn't repetitve, everything was dynamic. So why did I rate this game a 9.8/10, why not a perfect score? I don't know, I just feel like if some elements were touched up then this game would be perfect, I don't know I could just be really picky about it. But to me, this game kind of feels like Resident Evil and The Last of Us had a baby, but the baby had better characteristics than their predecessors. For the multiplayer platform freak that I am, I really loved this game and I would recommend it for anyone and everyone. Also this game isn't one of those single player games were you can beat once and then not feel like beating it again. The Evil Within 2 really encourages the player to keep playing after they've beaten it, chears to Tango Gameworks for that and for making a masterpiece of a game!
At this point I see know why I rated it 9.8/10. It is a cult classic which failed to sell as well as it deserved when it was first released, but those that did buy into it at the time almost unanimously agreed that it was a great experience.
While the gameplay is admittedly more clunky than most modern games, it still functions well and doesn't have too steep of a learning curve, allowing for relative ease of use. The only real drawback in this regard being it's rather odd default control bindings which will doubtlessly be very uncomfortable for anyone used to modern controls. For all I know, they may even be unusual by the standards of the time in which it was released. This issue is easiy solved by going through the controls and rebinding them to your liking. I most definitely did this.
It's atmosphere is incredibly well-maintained, never breaking and remaining consistent throguhout the game. The events occuring within the game are somewhat plausible too, and don't feel entirely impossible, further adding to the dread that it will instill into those who play it. The game's "fear-factor" doesn't lie in producing outright terror in those that play it, but rather in gradually exposing the player to increasingly disturbing events and revealing the backstory regarding how these events took place over time through the use of audio logs. Needless to say, it was this game that popularized the use of audio logs and many other elements in the BioShock games.
All in all, it's an amazing game that you should most definitely check out if you have the moeny for it. And be sure to look up mods for it. They can really polish the game up and make it all that much more enjoyable.

[TL;DR at the bottom]
Eternal Senia surprised me quite a bit. As a free ARPG made through the RPG Maker, I really did not have high expectations and downloaded it mainly due to the “Overwhelmingly Positive” response by the community.
As such the game sat months in my Steam Library before today I finally thought “Man, would I love to play through a quick Adventure.” – and man did I get that.
To start off, you’re playing as Senia. A slightly 2-Dimensional character, who at first glance doesn’t care about anything other than saving her “sister” Magaleta” who went into the “Tower of Eternity” for reasons unknown at the start of the game. The first ten minutes you’re fighting through a couple of trashmobs and get introduced to the games mechanics. Most notably the combat mechanics, which I’ll talk about in a bit.
Essentially the game is divided in three separate parts outside of the tutorial. Each of them is basically one big dungeon with 2-3 Cutscene’s, which is also the only time in which you’ll find any dialogue, exposition or character development, as there are barely any characters besides Senia and Magaleta, but every one follows the same structure.
What I mean by that is, that you have your dungeon, with your fair share of enemies, which after the first dungeon do not pose any threat whatsoever, if you’re somewhat decently equipped, but each dungeon has an “Arcane” version as well, in which you simply go through around 10 rooms, grinding again for crafting material. Which you’ll do, since the Upgrades are quite important, especially if you’re attempting the Hard-Modes of each of the three bosses.
Each of the 3 dungeons introduces a minor gimmick, which however isn’t really enough to set them apart and thus the gameplay can become quite stale if you’re not used to “grindy” games like other games from the ARPG-Genre.
Also at the end of each dungeon you’ll find 3 NPC’s who award you with special and sometimes important items for essentially 100% completing each segment. It’s a neat little bonus which you’ll most likely be going for anyway if you’re even interested in maxing out your Equipment before shooting for the next dungeon.
The game does have a really simplistic crafting system, which you’ll have to use, since there aren’t any drops from the enemies you defeat. Additionally you only have 1 Set of Armor and Weapons for each dungeon. As such you’ll be playing as a Swordsman and only as a Swordsman, which can get quite boring, adding to the stale combat system and the grind for equipment.
The combat system being quite simple: Through the game you unlock 4 special attacks which use Mana-Points and any other attack is done by simple bumping into enemies – quite like the first YS game. Having completed the game 100% (every challenge) and every Boss on Hard Mode, I did only actively use the first 2 Special Attacks and the 3. as an activator for some of the puzzles and even the second one only for Groups of enemies. As such only a single skill was somewhat important for any of the boss fights.
Speaking of which, the boss-fights are quite challenging, though basically share many attack patterns with one another, which can more or less be blamed on the game being made with RPG-Maker. Nonetheless all were fun to play through and each one had just enough innovation over the last one to keep the fight somewhat new and exciting.
The last thing I do want to talk about, since it somewhat surprised me – is the conclusion of the game. Like I mentioned earlier: the characters are quite 2-Dimensional, not only do we exclusively hear about Senia only caring about Magaleta, but also only learn about a tiny part of her backstory. On the other hand, Magaleta’s only exposition is during the finale of the game. The story very much falls apart by not explaining the concept of the “Eternity” Senia is plagued with throughout the game and we also do not learn about any of the few other characters we do encounter.
So that begs the question, if the story, lacking so much detail is good enough to justify a playthrough, especially if any given person isn’t that much used to ARPG’s?
I’d argue yes. For a number of reasons: The most important being, that the story heavily relies on the conclusion, which is filled to the brim with emotional and somewhat manipulative dialogue and great exposition about the true feelings of both Magaleta and Senia. Each of the endings is smartly designed, the first one basically asking the player the question: “Did you pay attention to the dialogue, we DID present to you?” – which for me was a great feeling to then see this detail playing a role in the finale.
I’ll obviously not spoil any of the endings, but just say that it reminded me a bit of the Key-Visual Novels, especially planetarian in terms of writing style.
In conclusion, I’m not sure if I’d recommend Eternal Senia solely for the ending and I do have to say “for the ending”, since I can’t recommend the story in its entirety. What I can do whoever is recommend Eternal Senia for the great conclusion, the ability to make the player bond with characters he/she barely gets to know over the course of just a couple of hours, I can recommend it for the surprisingly good Soundtrack, throughout the entire game and lastly for making the albeit negative grind a very rewarding experience, once you finally finish any of the dungeons and finally get to face one of the bosses.
TL;DR
+ Fluent difficulty (Easy Mode / Hard Mode)
+ Rewards Completionism
+ Great ending (The entire last dungeon)
+ Good Soundtrack
+ Solid length
+ Great art
+ It’s free
+/- Very grind-heavy
- Not enough character development
- Senia’s exposition can get a bit repetitive
- Lackluster in detail (Eternity / Sidecharacters)
- Overworld “Boss” Monster completely lacking AI - why not make the Gems they drop a reward from the Arcane Dungeons?
Keep in mind that my critique of the story is quite subjective, as one could argue, that the story doesn’t need to flesh out those details to get its point across – and I’d agree with that, although presenting me with those elements and then just “forgetting” about them (e.g. the game completely forgets about Senia’ sidekick during post-finale) did seem a bit silly to me. However none of it is a reason not to give Eternal Senia try.

Yes, the AI will follow the patterns it sees most offten and it allows the alien to track you. So honestly if you think your safe, you're ♥♥♥♥ed. (Based on Chapter 1) Wonderful story, atmosphere and voice acting. Puzzles are fun and logical (for the most part). The game looks and runs great on my old PC. I highly recommend to give the first (free) chapter a go, especially if you loved the classic adventure games back in the day.

Played only the first 3 episodes, but I love how it still respects the original King's Quest games by making references to them. They're also filling in the blanks of what happened between each original KQ game, and how they tie it all together is quite gripping! It's also a fine adventure game for new players. Though the game is quite railroaded and choice-based, it has a different feel than TellTale games with more action sequences and driving home the METHOD of solving problems rather than two different TellTale-like choices (either using Compassion, Wits, or Strength, to solve a problem in KQ).

For those who complain that you can't get the Complete Edition (with Epilogue) after having installed the free Chapter 1 - this is possible. Go to the to Steam Store with a web browser, log in, click "Support", "King's Quest", then "I want to permanently remove this game from my account". Confirm and et voila, the free Chapter 1 will be gone, and you can now buy the Complete Edition. Do this at your own risk - but it worked fine for me (I'm downloading the other chapters right now).
Otherwise, it's very much a declaration of love for the original games. The puzzles feel similar (hey, it's been 25-30 years since I played them), the UI has its quirks but works fine - and, best of all, it's not over-the-top comic-y like the Monkey Island remake. I can even stomach the soundtrack (something I mostly can't in other games).
There's some quicktime events (like in other Telltale games), but they're slow enough so they don't get in the way of good old adventure-style gameplay.
Speaking of "good old adventure-style gameplay": don't expect a fast-paced environment. It's a modern take on a classic adventure, so you
be going back&forth lots, and trying lots of different combinations of environment&inventory. YHBW ;-)
