I'm only a few hours into it, but I'm thoroughly impressed by this late 90s classic. There's a surprising amount of realism available. Firearms degrade with use (A bit quickly, granted, but it's still interesting to see a mechanic like that in such a relatively old game), and those stim pack things slowly improve your health as apposed to automatically switch you from severely wounded to mildly wounded, or mildly wounded to suddenly completely healthy. There's some mild parkour abilities, like holding space to grab onto a ledge at about chest height after a jump, and pull yourself up the rest of the way. There's the ability to level up VARIOUS different abilities/stats. Lots of food/drink/booze/cigarettes available, and there's also no regenerative ability (so far), which is cool. After all, how does one heal in seconds or minutes from blunt force trauma, funky psi attacks, or gunshot wounds? You have limited inventory space, which is larger or smaller depending on your strength.
Oh, this game also doesn't hold your hand. Even on Normal difficulty, it's not an easy game. There's no arrows pointing you in the direction to go, and so far there isn't even a minimap. You have to wander around, start to become familiar with your surroundings, and try to manage your way to where you figure you have to go. Ammo is also QUITE scarce, so try to conserve what you can. Luckily there's surgical table things that are automated, and they're scattered around the area. Not very common, however they only cost you 5 nano-whatsits, which is essentially money, so it's worth it to use one if you find yourself under half health.
The atmosphere is very well done, the graphics are dated of course, but not exactly an eyesore. The story thus far is quite engaging, I find myself enjoying the game immensely in spite of the difficulty and lack of in-game assistance, and I look forward to finding out more. Searching new areas is always enjoyable because you never know what stuff you might find, and you can also backtrack to previous areas if you like. I have kind of an OCD where I have to do things in sequence; I've owned this game for months, but didn't play it because I wanted to find the first one. Finally I decided to give it a try, and I'm glad I did. I was missing out. I don't know what else to say about the game other than that I am really enjoying it. If you enjoy survival horror games, then I advise you to check this out.
Even if you're not into using firearms, there's different ways of defending yourself. Different modes of attack, as it were. There's even select fire capabilities, kinda lol Anyways, I look forward to playing it more and seeing how the story turns out. If you don't minds somewhat dated late-90s graphics, enjoy FPS games, survival horror, and the ability to upgrade your character to your own play style, then I truly believe you'll come to enjoy this experience as much, or possibly even more, than I am.

The Evil Within was my favorite Survival Horror game. Running on id Tech 5, Shinji Mikami's first release with new studio Tango Gameworks was a breath of fresh air in the survival horror space that had been cluttered with spin-offs of 2010's brilliant Amnesia: The Dark Descent (Designed by Thomas Grip and Jens Nilsson of Frictional Games). Running on the HPL Engine 2 the game was rather attractive although not state of the art at the time; it made up for its lack of visual fidelity with creating some intense bone chilling moments. Then... Endless hiding which worked for the game but did not always work in games that came after.
Luckily The Evil Within followed where Shinji Mikami the creator of the genre and master behind RE and RE4 left off: revisiting his original vision for Resident Evil 4 and going bananas with it. id Tech 5 to this day is an under-rated graphics engine that introduced megatextures to the industry with the release of RAGE. The game was paced in a heart pounding set of chapters that on stream while in some hellish Carnival in a factory esque environment with blades I had to duck under had me state "I am having a panic attack".
The Evil Within 2 takes everything that was loved from the original and expands upon the mechanics while adopting an altered version of early id Tech 6 build which they state as being powered by id Tech. (Doom (2016) / Wolfenstein 2 so far are the two titles running on the id Tech 6 engine while Dishonored 2/DOTO/TEW2 are running on modified versions of early code). The visauls are indeed quite pleasing! some may miss the grainy rusted textures seen in the original game although we must remember these textures had been bashed by many gamers and critics as part of the mega-texture / id tech 5 slamming which was going on at the time. Some have said that enemies are too easy to see now along with items; but I cannot state that being able to see something horrifying that looks far sexier makes it any less horifying.
The gunplay and gameplay mechanics are top-notch. The open world hubs leave plenty to be explored and I was giddy finding the Quake 1 Rocket Launcher collectible to add to my desk collection in game. Shooting is VERY satisfying with the Double Barreled shotgun having one of the most satifying BOOMSTICK! blasts in the genre. A good sort of distraction is using these weapons while ensuring I complete every side objective to find more ammo pouches and crafting utilities.
Once you have completed the game EX abilities become usable on the second play-thru including the returning burning Harpoon bolts from the original, the awesome slo-mo Max Payne (if he was ASH from Evil Dead) ability along with the chain kill (kills continue to grant stronger offensive damage when chained together).
The story is bonkers even for the bar the first game set. I need not ruin anything and suggest you just dive in and prepare for one hell of a ride!

While I can only praise Amnesia's take on survival-horror, a game where you can only flee and not fight, it suffered from a critical flaw : surviving an encounter was as simple as hiding in a dark corner and wait for the scary music to stop. You could tear through the entire game without seeing a single monster save for the few mandatory moments just by sitting motionless behind the nearest piece of furniture, in the reassuring knowledge that he's never going to find you where you are. That just sucked all the tension from the game.
While there's a lot of positive things going for Isolation, one thing particularly stood out : it succeeded where Amnesia failed for me. The Alien truly is unpredictable, and he is definitely not going to disappear in a puff of smoke after 20 seconds of wandering around. When hiding under furniture and seeing him leave the room, he might very well suddenly decide to turn around and double-check. Walking in a corridor when he's out is taking the risk to stumble upon him. It's not a cheap game of chance either, though, you just have to be extra cautious and pay attention to your surroundings, especially to what your ears tell you.
Playing through the game a few times will definitely help you understand the rules, but you'll never be truly safe. That was one of the objectives the developpers gave themselves when designing the game, and they nailed it.
So far... it is very good, my kinda game really. I need to finish this beautiful thing.

Save points are strategically positioned at key locations but are sometimes hard to get to adding to the anxiety that if you die it will set you back. A true remake of Half-Life 1 on the Source Engine created by modders who worked on it for around 8 years, to which they then released the mod for free, and then put it on Steam for people to buy. That's some serious dedication. It all began in 2004 when Half-Life: Source was a major disappointment. Because of this, Black Mesa was concieved.
The game itself though, very solid, very fun. It's pretty much Half-Life 1 but everything has been modernised (or 'remastered') and to be somewhat more realistic (in a good way!). No old sounds, no old textures, all of it is new and original. Definitely worth buying if you want to re-live Half-Life 1 again in high quality. I definitely miss the old GoldSrc (HL1 Engine) feel though.
There's also multiplayer as well which is alright. It's very much like Half-Life 2: Deathmatch. Minus the sprint key (because by default you always run).

This reimagining of the FPS classic Half-Life brings the world of Gordon Freeman and Black Mesa to life and into the modern era.  Completely revamped but still familiar, Black Mesa achieves all of its lofty goals with ease.

"Let's develop our own engine for a AAA-game with hi-end visuals using a small team of unexperienced programmers! What could possibly go wrong?"
- Historical moment when the Void Engine was born
I would like to write something about the game mechanics, quality of level design etc, but what's the point if the majority of potential players won't be able to enjoy any of this stuff because someone make a monumentally dumb decision to replace Unreal Engine (that worked fine in Dishonored 1) with some sort of eldritch abomination that manages (for some people, including myself) to run the game at 20fps on lowest settings when there is literally ONE FLAT WALL on a screen.
As a programmer I wonder, what is even happening inside this thing? Is it trying to render the whole level regardless of what is actually visible? Is it implementing some sort of revolutionary stupid technique for post-processing that works terribly slow regardless of the complexity of the scene? We know for the fact that this engine was based on the latest idTech (and go read some reviews for the new Doom, the game that uses the same version of idTech and runs silky smooth for pretty much everyone), so Arkane probably put an immense amount of effort to ruin something that was actially quite good.
According to one of the interviews, they had to rewrite ~80% of the engine code. Why? We'll never know. The result is quite sad: a game that would probably be quite good is borderline unplayable for so many players.

I bought this game on a whim since it piqued my interest and I'm always on the lookout for co-op games to play with my best friend. I was not disappointed! Yes, this game has it flaws and could definitly use some polishing, but overall I really enjoyed it. It has such an innovative co-op mode that is severely lacking in the gaming industry today. It actually requires good teamwork. I played as the hacker and guided my friend, who played the field agent, as safely as possible to the target in question. Even though the hacker role might feel a bit "passive" to some, since basically all you do is watch different computer screens, blueprints and live feed from various cameras, I, personally, never got bored. I had a full time job disabling security messures, keeping an eye on the surroundings, setting up traps and so on.
So, if you're looking for a good co-op game that adds something new the the genre, I highly recommend this one. It also has great replay value since you can switch the roles and play the game from a competely different angle.

This game. This is one of those hidden gems we crave for. The one amongst dozens of others who show promise but fall through, except this one prevails. First of all, the story is certain to claw you in. The game definetly rewards you for being meticulous, search everywhere and you are bound to find something helpful or just interesting. The mechanics are certainly some to talk about, the way that the game is made around Co-Op but works just the same in Single is extremely well though through. Although you kinda have to play both roles when in Single, the co-op doesn't make it "Easier", it just changes the play style to require a lot more communication between the players, which I think it's amazing and they didn't cut off the single player people from any of the experience. Also, the game gives you alot of precise feedback on how you did on your past missions, which I find to be lacking in even AAA games nowadays, where the feedback (even when there is any) is pretty much black or white.
But Ok, it's not perfect, some things will probably bother people. First off, the clunky controls. Takes time to get used to them and even then they are still kind of hard to deal with. While playing I did indeed meet my fair share of bugs, but nothing game breaking really. Just annoying for the most part. And also the music could have been better. But that is pretty much it. I certainly believe that most of these things will be getting fixed in the near future anyways.
In summary, if you like spy movies and stealth, get this, you won't regret it.

A very refreshing take on the MOBA genre! There's the traditional MOBA games modes of 5v5 with jungle creeps and buffs to take, but being down in third person view as opposed to the traditional 2.5D isometric ish view of normal MOBAs, you can really appreciate the gorgeous background scenery. My preferred game mode is called Arena, where you're pitted 5v5 in a literal arena much like World Of Warcraft's PVP, with no tower or lane objectives, pure all-out battling.
Almost every single ability and attack in this game is a skill shot - which is great for those who like a challenge, but auto attacking as a ranged god can be frustratingly difficult to land hits with as people can strafe and jump about to try and avoid damage. Similarly, 'Assassin' gods can get right into your face and run around you, making it even harder to hit them..but that doesn't stop the fun :)
Definitely a worthy addition to the somewhat stale same-old-game-with-new-look genre, and definitely worth checking out!

Other thoughts: Yes, TEWII runs a bit better than TEWI but there's some technical problem, in regards to PC Port Optimization. Indeed, the game uses derived id Tech 5 Stem Engine and vast majority of PC players are not happy with GPU performance. For instance, most PC players have their GPU usage around 60-80% on average, and it seems like CPU, RAM, and VRAM allocation are not doing as much work as PC players expect. Also, SLI is not scaling properly since some SLI users reported that running two-way, three-way, or four-way SLIs perform worse than single GPU. To fix performance, running single GPU seems to run consistent and framerate was stable too. But in the meantime, let's hope that Tango Gameworks/Bethesda are working around the clock to release the patch soon to address performance optimization issues!

I have roughly around 9 hours of actual gameplay in. Currently I am on chapter 6 of 17 if I'm not mistaken. My review will be spoiler free and as detailed as I can be.
THE GRAPHICS: Im working on building a new PC so I'm currently playing on a gaming laptop. The laptop holds a 980m graphics card which gets the job done but isn't too powerful. However, even with that card the visuals are amazing! The level of detail is exquisite! Even though I am currently running the game at around 40 frames (which is pretty low for most games) (also I'm having it set lower as to not have frame rate drops because of my weaker card) and the game still runs smoothly.
THE STORY: Horror movies tend to have a pretty basic storyline. Theres the protagonist who has to go through whatever horrors that the story has ahead of them whether its zombies, ghosts, or killer clowns. This game doesn't stray too far from that. Its definitely what you would expect from a horror game. The story is simple and easy to follow. As previously stated I will not include any spoilers so I will not be giving a synopsis of any part of the story.
THE GAMEPLAY: Here is the important part! The first game was filled with tight corridors will monsters that would scare the actual crap out of you. In the sequel, those tight corridors are replaced with small sections of a town called Union which you can explore freely. Within Union are multiple sidquests that MAY reward you with ammo, weapon parts, green gel, or even weapons. I repeat, MAY reward you. Thats the fun part of the game. You never know what you are going to get! Within Union there are also many buildings that you can go through to find all kinds of loot. Thanks to the ever changing scenery, I have not gotten bored in the slightest. I have completed every sidequest or side job so far. Every mission adds a little bit more to the story but aren't needed to beat the game. However, many of the missions are very rewarding so I suggest checking them out. Did I mention that you can craft many different items like health packs and ammo based on the parts that you find around the town? You can create them at workbenches or while you're out exploring but it will cost you more if you're not at a workbench.
THE UPGRADES: The upgrade system is very similar to the first game but also very different but its for the better. Like the first game, green gel will be used to upgrade Sebastian's stats. Nothing different there. Weapon upgrades on the other hand are upgraded by collecting weapon parts. This makes the game run much smoother than the first game but also makes the game a bit easier in my opinion. I remember sitting and staring at the screen trying to decide whether to upgreade my health or the damage on my pistol while playing the first game. That is no longer an issue. Personally, I think that this game is much better when it comes down to upgrades. Of course upgrades cost alot so you will have to grind to find the parts or green gel for your upgrades. Back to the green gel! In the first game, it felt like a godsend when you found some green gel. In this one, it is dropped many more enemies that you run into. Any of the higher difficulty enemies are guarenteed to drop the green gel. This made gettin my upgrades much easier but of course it cost me alot of time and ammo.
RANDOM MINIGAMES: So....there are minigames. One of which is a shooting range at varying difficulties that will reward you with different types of loot. I completed all of the difficulties and I can say that the loot is amazing. Make sure to complete it as it is much easier than the other minigame. The second minigame that I have ran into is much like Bejeweled or CandyCrush. The only difference is that instead of moving tiles, you shoot them trying to make the largest combo possible to get a high score. The higher the score, the better the loot. Both of these minigames make for a good break during the horror filled adventure that is The Evil Within 2.
Overall I have really enjoyed this game so far. It passes up the last game by a longshot because of the way that it built off of it. The game keeps you on your toes as you never know what enemies lie ahead. Just because you cleared an area out doesn't mean that they won't come back. The game doesn't rely too much on jumpscares but more on the psychological side. The situations that the game puts you in can resemble some of the classic horror games like Resident Evil or Silent Hill but then other parts of the game where you are rendered helpless since you can't use your weapons make it feel more like Outlast. The changing pace makes the game amazing and keeps you wondering as to what you will have to face next.

Considered by many to be the spiritual precurser to Bioshock, System Shock 2 is a FPS-RPG with stealth and horror elements.
The gameplay still holds up to this date. While not overly complex, you'll find that the gameplay is more advanced than your average shooter. There are some puzzles here and there that will require you to use your brain or require you to obtain a certain object in order to proceed. The gunplay is fairly standard as well, you point and shoot. Guns have a efficiency rating, so the more you use your gun, the more it will deteriorate. This can be fixed by repairing it.
The RPG elements come in the form of player stats and classes. There's four categories: Stat, Tech, Combat and O/S. The Stat skill comes in the form of your average stats: strength, endurance, psionics, agility and cyber affinity. Tech comes in hacking, repair, modify, maintain and research. Combat deals with standard guns, energy guns, heavy guns and exotic weapons. O/S helps with your body's operating system, and can enhance it with modifications such as being able to run faster, jump higher, increased stats or being able to do other things.
The classes include Marine, Navy and O.S.A. Agent. Marines are for the people who love to use guns and overall combat. You first learn to use standard weapons, then later learn to use other weapons. The Navy class is for players who want to play with the Tech side of the game. They are better at hacking, repairing items, modifying weapons and things like that. O.S.A. Agents are the most interesting and fun classes to play, but can also be the most challenging. This class uses Psionic Abilities, which gives you this ball that you hold in your hand that can allow you to do many different things, such as shoot energy balls, telekenisis, heal your self automatically or give you stat advantages.
The graphics in this game still hold up today. The game looks a lot better than any other game that came out around that time, so better than HL1 or Deus Ex. The textures are smooth and nice, and with a few Steam updates, it runs really well. The athmosphere is at first a somewhat familiar one if you're a fan of Deus Ex or Mass Effect. Set in a futuristic space station, it's been overrun by an AI O/S called Xerxes. Pretty much, him and SHODAN (another AI) control the whole ship and there's zombies on it and other monsters on it. They've also programmed the robots to be hostile towards you. The whole ship is very unsettling. The whole ship has a cramped feeling to it, and combined with it being dark a lot of the times does not help it at all. It really provides a very scary athomosphere when playing.
The sounds in this game are phenominal. If you're a audiophile, you will not be dissapointed by this. The ambient noises are eerie, the voice acting is surprisingly well for it's time and the music is awesome. I'd recommend using a pair of headphones for this game. Hearing the Hybrid zombies in the other room or the hostile mechs marching across the hallway is always frightening.
Now, for some cons about the game.
First off, I feel the interface is dated. It's really small, and doesn't upscale good enough on large monitors. It takes a while to get used to and it's hard to use if you don't have great eyesight.
This game can be pretty challenging even on easy modes, and while this isn't really a con, it does put a lot of new players off, especially people who don't play older games too often.
Along with being challenging, the controls are a little wonky. They make sense after you get used to them, but that's the thing, you have to get used to them.
The lack of a journal system can leave you flustered. You have to make sure you pay attention to the lady speaking to you telling you what to do. PDA's help a little bit though.
Overall, this game is very great, with very few bugs and cons. Challenging, fun and exciting everytime I play it. I recommend this game for people who are just getting into retro gaming. This is a good introduction into what games were like 15+ years ago. Other than that, I also recommend this to players who like horror games, FPS with more depth than your SHOOT DA BAD GUYZ muscleman games and RPG fans.

"Let's develop our own engine for a AAA-game with hi-end visuals using a small team of unexperienced programmers! What could possibly go wrong?"
- Historical moment when the Void Engine was born
I would like to write something about the game mechanics, quality of level design etc, but what's the point if the majority of potential players won't be able to enjoy any of this stuff because someone make a monumentally dumb decision to replace Unreal Engine (that worked fine in Dishonored 1) with some sort of eldritch abomination that manages (for some people, including myself) to run the game at 20fps on lowest settings when there is literally ONE FLAT WALL on a screen.
As a programmer I wonder, what is even happening inside this thing? Is it trying to render the whole level regardless of what is actually visible? Is it implementing some sort of revolutionary stupid technique for post-processing that works terribly slow regardless of the complexity of the scene? We know for the fact that this engine was based on the latest idTech (and go read some reviews for the new Doom, the game that uses the same version of idTech and runs silky smooth for pretty much everyone), so Arkane probably put an immense amount of effort to ruin something that was actially quite good.
According to one of the interviews, they had to rewrite ~80% of the engine code. Why? We'll never know. The result is quite sad: a game that would probably be quite good is borderline unplayable for so many players.

The Pitch: You are Senia. Your older sister has entered the Tower of Eternity. It's a bad place. Go save her with your action RPG swordplay skills.
The good: The music is catchy (though sometimes not fitting,) the boss fights are fun and challenging on hard mode, and collecting the stuff to make you strong enough to fight them is strangely addicting without being a long grindfest. I was also invested in the characters throughout the story. Short playtime (8 hours on hard for me,) so it doesn't get stale.
The bad: Non-boss gameplay is so easy you could do it blindfolded. The translation is rough. It regularly drew me out of the story and made things less clear. The ending(s) is a sudden, sharp turn in the storytelling, and not in a good way. No spoilies, but I feel it soured the whole experience. Props to the author for doing something different, but it wasn't justified in the course of the story. Sometimes the sheer simplicity of the gameplay can make for frustrating moments, since you attack AND move with the arrow keys.
The verdict: If you can handle the translation and don't mind most of the game being easy, this is a lot of fun. If you need a consistent challenge and quality story all the way through, look elsewhere.

An old hand of the Half Life series or a wet behind the ears gamer eager to understand the game that revolutionised modern gaming? Then look no further.
Black Mesa originally started out as a free mod for HL2 that eventually made the jump to a Valve sanctioned game in its own right. Black Mesa combines the game play and story that captured the hearts of gamers with the venerable source engine bringing physics, improved performance and some pretty slick visuals even by today's standards.
Black Mesa is a near faithful recreation of Half Life and Gordon Freeman's leap into video game history. The major changes compared to the original range from slight level redesign to completely new and reworked areas that just work. Some weapons are relocated compared to the original and I did feel a bit sad having to soldier on further to finally get that sweet, sweet MP5.
The cons? I played the game on Normal, I wasn't exactly chasing a challenge, I was more interested in having a nostalgia overload (by the way CHECK). And throughout the course of my playthrough, I died to gunfire / combat ONCE.
Enemies are smarter than the original but feel very fragile. At times the Marine AI is questionable as one member will stand fully upright unawares despite the other six members of his squad tactically moving on your position.
Overall Black Mesa is a great game, it's not yet finished with the final XEN chapter yet to be released but in its current stage it is definitely worth your time, regardless of your previous Half Life experience. And the same mob who made Black Mesa are also working on remakes of the old Half Life expansions, Opposing Force and Blue Shift respectively, so watch out for those someday too.

Other thoughts: Yes, TEWII runs a bit better than TEWI but there's some technical problem, in regards to PC Port Optimization. Indeed, the game uses derived id Tech 5 Stem Engine and vast majority of PC players are not happy with GPU performance. For instance, most PC players have their GPU usage around 60-80% on average, and it seems like CPU, RAM, and VRAM allocation are not doing as much work as PC players expect. Also, SLI is not scaling properly since some SLI users reported that running two-way, three-way, or four-way SLIs perform worse than single GPU. To fix performance, running single GPU seems to run consistent and framerate was stable too. But in the meantime, let's hope that Tango Gameworks/Bethesda are working around the clock to release the patch soon to address performance optimization issues!

I have roughly around 9 hours of actual gameplay in. Currently I am on chapter 6 of 17 if I'm not mistaken. My review will be spoiler free and as detailed as I can be.
THE GRAPHICS: Im working on building a new PC so I'm currently playing on a gaming laptop. The laptop holds a 980m graphics card which gets the job done but isn't too powerful. However, even with that card the visuals are amazing! The level of detail is exquisite! Even though I am currently running the game at around 40 frames (which is pretty low for most games) (also I'm having it set lower as to not have frame rate drops because of my weaker card) and the game still runs smoothly.
THE STORY: Horror movies tend to have a pretty basic storyline. Theres the protagonist who has to go through whatever horrors that the story has ahead of them whether its zombies, ghosts, or killer clowns. This game doesn't stray too far from that. Its definitely what you would expect from a horror game. The story is simple and easy to follow. As previously stated I will not include any spoilers so I will not be giving a synopsis of any part of the story.
THE GAMEPLAY: Here is the important part! The first game was filled with tight corridors will monsters that would scare the actual crap out of you. In the sequel, those tight corridors are replaced with small sections of a town called Union which you can explore freely. Within Union are multiple sidquests that MAY reward you with ammo, weapon parts, green gel, or even weapons. I repeat, MAY reward you. Thats the fun part of the game. You never know what you are going to get! Within Union there are also many buildings that you can go through to find all kinds of loot. Thanks to the ever changing scenery, I have not gotten bored in the slightest. I have completed every sidequest or side job so far. Every mission adds a little bit more to the story but aren't needed to beat the game. However, many of the missions are very rewarding so I suggest checking them out. Did I mention that you can craft many different items like health packs and ammo based on the parts that you find around the town? You can create them at workbenches or while you're out exploring but it will cost you more if you're not at a workbench.
THE UPGRADES: The upgrade system is very similar to the first game but also very different but its for the better. Like the first game, green gel will be used to upgrade Sebastian's stats. Nothing different there. Weapon upgrades on the other hand are upgraded by collecting weapon parts. This makes the game run much smoother than the first game but also makes the game a bit easier in my opinion. I remember sitting and staring at the screen trying to decide whether to upgreade my health or the damage on my pistol while playing the first game. That is no longer an issue. Personally, I think that this game is much better when it comes down to upgrades. Of course upgrades cost alot so you will have to grind to find the parts or green gel for your upgrades. Back to the green gel! In the first game, it felt like a godsend when you found some green gel. In this one, it is dropped many more enemies that you run into. Any of the higher difficulty enemies are guarenteed to drop the green gel. This made gettin my upgrades much easier but of course it cost me alot of time and ammo.
RANDOM MINIGAMES: So....there are minigames. One of which is a shooting range at varying difficulties that will reward you with different types of loot. I completed all of the difficulties and I can say that the loot is amazing. Make sure to complete it as it is much easier than the other minigame. The second minigame that I have ran into is much like Bejeweled or CandyCrush. The only difference is that instead of moving tiles, you shoot them trying to make the largest combo possible to get a high score. The higher the score, the better the loot. Both of these minigames make for a good break during the horror filled adventure that is The Evil Within 2.
Overall I have really enjoyed this game so far. It passes up the last game by a longshot because of the way that it built off of it. The game keeps you on your toes as you never know what enemies lie ahead. Just because you cleared an area out doesn't mean that they won't come back. The game doesn't rely too much on jumpscares but more on the psychological side. The situations that the game puts you in can resemble some of the classic horror games like Resident Evil or Silent Hill but then other parts of the game where you are rendered helpless since you can't use your weapons make it feel more like Outlast. The changing pace makes the game amazing and keeps you wondering as to what you will have to face next.

While I can only praise Amnesia's take on survival-horror, a game where you can only flee and not fight, it suffered from a critical flaw : surviving an encounter was as simple as hiding in a dark corner and wait for the scary music to stop. You could tear through the entire game without seeing a single monster save for the few mandatory moments just by sitting motionless behind the nearest piece of furniture, in the reassuring knowledge that he's never going to find you where you are. That just sucked all the tension from the game.
While there's a lot of positive things going for Isolation, one thing particularly stood out : it succeeded where Amnesia failed for me. The Alien truly is unpredictable, and he is definitely not going to disappear in a puff of smoke after 20 seconds of wandering around. When hiding under furniture and seeing him leave the room, he might very well suddenly decide to turn around and double-check. Walking in a corridor when he's out is taking the risk to stumble upon him. It's not a cheap game of chance either, though, you just have to be extra cautious and pay attention to your surroundings, especially to what your ears tell you.
Playing through the game a few times will definitely help you understand the rules, but you'll never be truly safe. That was one of the objectives the developpers gave themselves when designing the game, and they nailed it.

I was incredibly suprised at this game and I feel that I currently have enough hours to do an honest review. I have never ever owned a Call of Duty game in my life and once I saw this game I thought it could be my first. The exo suit is a great addition to the game allowing more diverse maps including heights that are not accessible without the exo. It is a dramatic change from "first to spot" slogan in Ghosts, which was terrible. Even now if you were to be spotted first you can still outplay and I feel that if you are good with the exo you will outplay most players.
The campaign is nice but I never really got into it since I'm a much more competitive person. The supply drops and huge customization is a great feature to get players to keep playing as it is almost addictive to open supply drops looking for those elites. The gun play is great and although there are some underpowered weapons and some slightly over powered weapons the gameplay is balanced and enjoyable.
I don't understand all these complaints about the servers. I live in the UK and I have only once, in 56 hours, been placed into a laggy server. You might want to research your region and the server lag before purchasing but for me it is perfect and I don't have any issues with the servers.
Overall I reccommend this game for many reasons. The gun play is great, complimented with the new mobility from the exo. The customization and addiction to acquiring supply drops is amazing feature that allows you to be unique and stand out from the crowd. Micro transactions are nothing special and it definitely isn't a pay to win, although the DLCs are pretty overpriced considering this is a £40 title and they charge around £12 per DLC, of which the full set cost more than the actual game. The servers are no issue for me but I advise you research your region before purchasing. I have enjoyed this game thouroughly and if the following are just as good, if not better then I will definitely pick them up.
TL;DR Great gunplay with new exo // Customization and supply drops are amazing // Servers are never laggy // DLC is annoying // First COD game I have ever played, thouroughly enjoyed.

Considered by many to be the spiritual precurser to Bioshock, System Shock 2 is a FPS-RPG with stealth and horror elements.
The gameplay still holds up to this date. While not overly complex, you'll find that the gameplay is more advanced than your average shooter. There are some puzzles here and there that will require you to use your brain or require you to obtain a certain object in order to proceed. The gunplay is fairly standard as well, you point and shoot. Guns have a efficiency rating, so the more you use your gun, the more it will deteriorate. This can be fixed by repairing it.
The RPG elements come in the form of player stats and classes. There's four categories: Stat, Tech, Combat and O/S. The Stat skill comes in the form of your average stats: strength, endurance, psionics, agility and cyber affinity. Tech comes in hacking, repair, modify, maintain and research. Combat deals with standard guns, energy guns, heavy guns and exotic weapons. O/S helps with your body's operating system, and can enhance it with modifications such as being able to run faster, jump higher, increased stats or being able to do other things.
The classes include Marine, Navy and O.S.A. Agent. Marines are for the people who love to use guns and overall combat. You first learn to use standard weapons, then later learn to use other weapons. The Navy class is for players who want to play with the Tech side of the game. They are better at hacking, repairing items, modifying weapons and things like that. O.S.A. Agents are the most interesting and fun classes to play, but can also be the most challenging. This class uses Psionic Abilities, which gives you this ball that you hold in your hand that can allow you to do many different things, such as shoot energy balls, telekenisis, heal your self automatically or give you stat advantages.
The graphics in this game still hold up today. The game looks a lot better than any other game that came out around that time, so better than HL1 or Deus Ex. The textures are smooth and nice, and with a few Steam updates, it runs really well. The athmosphere is at first a somewhat familiar one if you're a fan of Deus Ex or Mass Effect. Set in a futuristic space station, it's been overrun by an AI O/S called Xerxes. Pretty much, him and SHODAN (another AI) control the whole ship and there's zombies on it and other monsters on it. They've also programmed the robots to be hostile towards you. The whole ship is very unsettling. The whole ship has a cramped feeling to it, and combined with it being dark a lot of the times does not help it at all. It really provides a very scary athomosphere when playing.
The sounds in this game are phenominal. If you're a audiophile, you will not be dissapointed by this. The ambient noises are eerie, the voice acting is surprisingly well for it's time and the music is awesome. I'd recommend using a pair of headphones for this game. Hearing the Hybrid zombies in the other room or the hostile mechs marching across the hallway is always frightening.
Now, for some cons about the game.
First off, I feel the interface is dated. It's really small, and doesn't upscale good enough on large monitors. It takes a while to get used to and it's hard to use if you don't have great eyesight.
This game can be pretty challenging even on easy modes, and while this isn't really a con, it does put a lot of new players off, especially people who don't play older games too often.
Along with being challenging, the controls are a little wonky. They make sense after you get used to them, but that's the thing, you have to get used to them.
The lack of a journal system can leave you flustered. You have to make sure you pay attention to the lady speaking to you telling you what to do. PDA's help a little bit though.
Overall, this game is very great, with very few bugs and cons. Challenging, fun and exciting everytime I play it. I recommend this game for people who are just getting into retro gaming. This is a good introduction into what games were like 15+ years ago. Other than that, I also recommend this to players who like horror games, FPS with more depth than your SHOOT DA BAD GUYZ muscleman games and RPG fans.
My personal score: 9/10 [MUST PLAY]

This game has an amusing cyber-retro sheen mainly accomplished through the environment and UI. Sound effects, windows, and text prompts all contribute to an atmosphere that makes it seem like the player is managing the level rather playing an FPS.
Too many audio logs, or at least too many focusing on the couple. Voice acting is once again very well done, Terri Brosius once again giving a solid performance as the central character. Compared to the very in-your-face punk techno of the first game, the music is much more subdued in this game, and you'll be playing through most of the game with no backing music. The story is a reasonable progression from the first game, although the ending sequence leaves a lot to be desired. Additions to the game like nanites, upgrade units, and cyber-modules are never really explained in the context of the world.
The first game had only one enemy that was unredeemable garbage, so the sequel ups the ante by adding several enemies whose only purpose is to annoy, inconvenience, and waste ammunition. Worms, exploding eggs, invisible spiders, enjoy trying to kill these with the woefully inadequate melee weapon range.
The RPG aspects of the game are designed in mind around multiple playthroughs, on your first game you'll have a hard time as you flounder around not knowing what to do. Once you start repeat playthroughs you can make specialized builds that take advantage of stuff like hacking and Psi. Unfortunately running counter to this idea of a "pure" run is the dedicated weakness triangle the game has, making some weapons vastly superior to others in terms of damage output.
Map design has faltered from the first game, giving the impression that the spaceships are smaller than they appear, and often have layouts that don't match geographically. Maps cannot be used to view an entire deck, only the current portion of the deck. Combine this with the more sprawling map design and backtracking is far more of a chore than in the first game.
It's a good game, but unlike the first game a lot more of the enjoyment is centered on its visuals and audio rather than the gameplay as well.

I did not play System Shock 2 until 2014, and have never played its namesake.
System Shock 2 is not a good FPS. It was never designed to be a great FPS. It is an old game that shows many signs of age. The textures are dated. The models are dated.
It is an old game.
What then, makes me recommend System Shock 2? What is its relevance along technically advanced games of more modern times? It is the marriage of forgettable FPS and engaging RPG mechanics that surprise me. It is the interesting characters and fleshed out backstory that make me want to see it through. It is the complex level designs that show me attention to detail. All of these elements are reason why I review the title positively. SS2 was made before its time and yet its creation still influences games today. It is an important part of gaming as a whole and deserves to be looked at.
If you can see past the age and the odd hitch, pick System Shock 2 up, tweak the controls, slap on a texture mod, and experience SHODAN.
Please Consider: There are no mission arrows. The map can be unhelpful. Codes from audio logs must be typed manually.

This game is incredibly immersive, challenging, fun, and is the original idea behind many modern games.
Pros: Gameplay, soundtrack, immersion, creativity, story, voice-acting, terrifying.
Cons: Dated graphics...*sigh* rats. Oh, and that's about it. This game still stands on its own.

I really wanted to like this series, after enjoying so many of the classic King's Quest games.
I had high hopes for the series after the first episode, which was pretty good.  My two minor complaints for that one were that you cannot skip cutscenes (this is fixed for most of them in ep 2 and 3), and there was way too much running around.  Otherwise, it was a decent adventure game with a couple interesting puzzles.  However, it's downhill from there.
The second episode is interesting, because it forces you to make some tough choices and there is no way to complete it "perfectly" (though you can get close).  It's not easy to figure out how your choices will affect things, which I think is part of the challenge of it.  But I ended up regretting most of what I did.
The third episode was extremely disappointing, and basically not worth playing at all.  It is extremely linear, and has way more cutscenes than puzzles.  The puzzles that there are are not that challenging.  So it's like a slightly interactive movie.  Episode 3 had very little content at all in the way of puzzles.
All three episodes suffered from limited inventory items, and more or less one use per item.  So, in a lot of cases you can revert to trying all 5 items in your inventory to see what you were supposed to do.
The series seems to give you some choices that (might) change the course of the game, and seem to persist across episodes.  It seems like it would be interesting to see how things could turn out differently, but I couldn't stand to play through again to find out.  Since the game uses save slots, there's no way to go back to a certain point and change you choice.
I also dislike the reliance on timed sequences.  They aren't intellectually challenging or fun, just boring and/or frustrating.  Some of them didn't seem to serve any real purpose, other than to give you the illusion of interaction between cutscenes.  One in particular in episode 1 I found really unintuitive to complete.
The main improvements from the classic series/classic adventure games are:
1. You can't put yourself in a state where you can't finish the game from.  If you die, you die immediately.
2. The game auto-saves, which is both a pro and a con, but the main benefit is that when you die, you immediately continue from the last choice you made and can try something else.  No needing to save the game before every choice.  I do like that there are still ways to die, for me that's part of the adventure experience.  But they've taken the frustration out of it, so you can try stupid stuff for fun.
3. It was generally clear when you completed a puzzle and no longer needed to interact with a game area, and inventory items were consumed when no longer needed.
I really hope that the remaining chapters will return to the classic brilliance of this series.  For the moment, I wouldn't recommend this series for people who like serious adventure games that require actual thinking.

I've never played the original King's Quest games, but if they are anything like this I need to get on that! I love this game, great writing, great story (so far), and great gameplay. Don't miss out on this game if you are any sort of fan of adventure games and puzzle/thinking games.

I'm hooked. To say the first episode exceeded expectations would be an understatement -- I put it off for quite some time under the assumption that it'd be a massive disappointment. After all, I cut my teeth on KQ 1, 2 and 3 on my mom's 286 and then 386 IBM pc, back when VGA graphics were a luxury we just couldn't afford. I played those games for years -- there was no internet available to most of us back then, and I have memories of having a hint book for one game as a bday gift, and calling a 900 number from my grandmother's house for another -- and to finally finish them felt like a tremendous achievement.
by contrast, this game (part one of it, anyway) I finished in five hours. And it was one five-hour sitting -- I generally only play pc games in fifteen-minute sprees these days. The fact that time flew by as I kept wanting to go deeper into the story speaks so well to the game as faar as I'm concerned, because that hasn't happened to me since.. well, since the early days of Sierra adventure gaming. Even though it was brief in comparison, I felt that I had gone on a journey by the time I finished the episode.
Here's what I think made the game great:
1) Excellent writing, filled with the goofy puns and double entendres that the games were known for. The characters were engaging and believable even when they were silly and at times monstrously so. (Does that count as a pun?) the writing was well represented by very good voice acting.
2) Beautiful graphics. I didn't expect that. And I'm on a laptop. I met the minimum requirements by a bit more than a little, but not much more. The colors were striking, the character models looked fantastic. Wait till you see the bridge trolls.
3) The puzzles aren't insanely difficult like they were in the originals -- when they needed the length of play to justify a $50ish purchase -- but not overly simple, either, as some of the more disappointing neo-adventure games have contained. I feel like it was just enough to make me feel engaged on an active level with the story, but not enough to force any rage-quits. (If I'd been strong enough to lift my mom's IBM when I was six years old, I might have thrown it out the window at times during the first 3 games).
4) It has all the in-jokes and nostalgia-based representation of things and places in Daventry that will help old-school sierra folks get back into the KQ spirit, but it struck me that none of these elements is overdone, it's all very subtle yet still effective, so newcomers to these games will definitely not feel left out.
Finally, I'll say at first i thought they were making a departure from the norm by having you use the keyboard, but then I remembered that's how we used to control Graham (and his progeny) in the old days. Thankfully, you no longer have to type just the right words to make things happen, but the mechanic feels nicely updated and seems like a natural way for other developers to do adventure games moving forward.
In sum, just as the original King's Quest set a standard for a renassiance of adventure games that followed back in the 80s and 90s, my hope is that this one is successful enough to do the same. i have played a lot of the newer adventure games, and with the exception of wadjet eye games and one or two other notables, they've been massive letdowns. Hope that developers can follow the example of this one. It really was the most pleasurable adventure game experience I've had in my adult life, and making episode 1 free was smart, because now i'm hooked for the rest. I guess I'll have to give in to that humble bundle after all.

First game was heavily inspired by Resident Evil 4, but was more focused on the horror and gimmicky mechanics that worked well in their favor of selling it as it's own game. I enjoyed it a lot.
Second game threw all that♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the window and decided to fully become it's own game. Now it's an open world, and even though it's not the biggest one out there it fits surprisingly well with the game. I certainly didn't expect that many successfully scripted events in an open world game, but it all goes so well together. You can truly feel their need of making it *just* right.
Story is infinitely better than the first one and Sebastian's character got a whole lot more development than the first's game notes you'd find littered around. He's honestly one of my favorite characters in recent years, the voice actor did a swell job.
All in all, it's just a good game. Everything is pretty effective, even with the adding crafting system that every game nowadays seems to have; it didn't feel that terrible to use actually.
One thing i missed though, was more enemy types or perhaps more mini-bosses. The few bosses there are gets re-used taking some of the originality away from the otherwise great monster designs in both the first and recent game.
It's still worth a buy though, even with the small mistakes they made.

HOLY ♥♥♥♥ THIS GAME IS SO SCARY AND AWESOME AND GREAT THE ATMOSPHERE IS SO PERFECT AND IT LOOKS SO GOOD AND JESUS ♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥ING CHRIST. But fo' real, this is a fantastic game that really does what it does well, stealth and horror are well executed. There is nothing more heart-pounding than hiding in a locker. Then, watching the Alien look at you, and walk away You start to think your safe, you step out of your hiding spot, and see that the Alien hadn't left yet and watched you step out of your hiding spot because you though you heard the door close behind the beast.

After the assterpiece that was Colonial Marines, this is a breath of fresh air that treats the license with dignity and respect. Kinda like a good marriage I suppose. The game features a pretty bad♥♥♥♥♥A.I. for the alien that allows the creature to learn patterns the player may use frequently, check popular hiding spots, and perform some pretty horrifying counter stealth. The stealth system is done pretty well, though it does have the occasional hiccup where you can be seen through a crate or some other similarly solid object. The game does a good job of keeping a familiar atmosphere to the original Ridley Scott movie, and the setting invokes a certain kind of nostalgia for some, sporting a distinctly late 70s to early 80s visual style to really deliver the sci-fi vision of the time.
The Good
- A truly awe inspiring visual style, complete with (toggleable) film grain and vivid, cinematic lighting. The environment looks like it was ripped straight from the movie, but that is not to say that it isnt original. Everything is clearly inspired and clearly unique, which I like a lot.
- Focus on survival through escape, stealth, and hiding. Combat is NOT a reliable option for the engineer you play as, so if you want an Alien themed FPS, this game is not really for you.
- Great voice acting. Andrea Deck (Amanda Ripley) did a pretty impressive job with the role. Also it's nice to hear somebody other than Nolan North or Steve Blum for once.
- Well optimized all around, which is a relief considering it was made with the new line of consoles in mind in terms of graphics. Very good performance throughout the entire game.
The Not-So-Good
- Tips and hints. The tips and tutorials that are provided to introduce and familiarize yourself with some of the mechanics are a bit lacking, many of them slightly confusing. Honestly, I stopped even trying to understand them eventually and just figured it out as I went. Not a huge problem but it is something to consider.
- The difficulty curve. I am all for a challenging game, but when I run through a game specifically for review purposes, it is a bit discouraging to die over and over because the stealth is a bit basic. Satisfying yes, but only because once you actually succeed you've most likely died a dozen times trying to get out of a room with some other survivers in it. This is my biggest issue with the game.
Overall, if you like the Alien universe and you are okay with a pretty tough experience with sneaking around on a station full of crazy people, this game is or you. At 49.99 though, you may want to wait until it goes on sale for 35 or so.

This game is riddled with glitches and oversights. Maybe Sega's a bad publisher or maybe Creative Assembly is losing it's edge. Despite its flaws, Total War: Rome II is well worth buying if you enjoyed the original Rome: Total War. Updated graphics and altered combat mechanics are definitely a step forward in the right direction. Unfortunately, the combat A.I. is a large step back, so don't expect to be challenged tactically. The technology tree is more or less the same as Shogun II, with two main parts: military and infrastructure. The character system is a not one, not two, but three full steps backward. Due to time passing so quickly, characters will usually die before you can start remembering their names. The skill tree system for characters is completely simplified and your characters will only ever grant very minor bonuses to your armies; such as, +5% weapon damage (5% of 35?... Great). The Army Traditions system is the best thing to come out of this game. Your armies will gain experience on their own, gain traits specific to them, and you will likely become more attached to your military units than the swinging door of generals who parade in and out of life. All in all, not nearly as good as the masterpiece that's Shogun II, but worth buying if you're a fan of the series and the original Rome.

I enjoy the title so much I've played it twice, once on either side. The beauty of the game is the asymmetric co-op. One of you is an agent in the field, the Ethan Hunt (Mission Impossible) if you will. The other is the Benji Dunn (or the Simon Pegg) character, directing your movements. The agent is given a choice from multiple guns, ammo, and gadgets. The man on overwatch can direct the agent to the best route to the objective, tag enemies, hack computers, locate passcodes, and even kill enemies with malfunctioning electrical boxes and steam pipes. The only drawbacks are 1) the gameplay as the agent isn't particularly smooth, 2) there isn't much of a consequence for failure as the overwatch guy, and 3) there is a lot of juicy intel, but it's difficult to really devise a plan to consume it. For instance, the agent needs the overwatch player to aid him relatively consistently; however, the overwatch player also has access to a large number of e-mails. Also, whenever the players visit the headquarters, there are many objectives for the agent but none for the overwatch guy. However, none of those drawbacks kept me from loving the game. I just wanted the throw that out there in case the devs take another stab at a game like this.

- Excellent, classic, stealth game. The game-play is true to the original Splintercell or Deus-Ex stealth style.
- The voice-acting is authentic and heartfelt, even if it's slightly amateurish at times. The developers don't coddle the player. The all dialogue is in the speaker's language: if two Russian's talk in a cut-scene they use Russian, not accented English with flavor words. However the guards (even danish police) do use English while searching/patrolling/shooting.
- The Humor is 100% on the money with slightly corny jokes, some lightly-hidden gems, and many 1990's references (i.e. cat facts, ultra sheriff, SR-71/Aspen-20, and the "Don't print the door-codes in this email" trope).
- There is plenty of emotional depth if you look for it: Read the right emails at a certain point in the game, and you will cry when you realize what has happened.
- The story is refreshing, new, believable, and carefully revealed. Your first play-through you will be actively trying to discover the plot, how it works, and who the baddie(s) is/are. Once you reach the end or play it again, it will all fall into place.
I bought two copies. The game is highly playable in SP but MP truly shines as you and your friend learn to work as an asymmetric team. (MP voice is all but a must!) As of three months after the release, all problems aren't still ironed out. Crossfire support is still missing, and basically eyefinity/4K would need multigpu support, even a TitanX / FuryX would not be enough. Frame rates still vary, however you can expect somewhere around 50fps on 1080p ultra with a 390X, with around 35 fps in cities and 30fps on worst case. Oh, and the frametime variance is still way too high.
In case you got AMD, get the 16.2 driver, it improves performance compared to 15.11 with 10-40% in practice. At least 12/16GB is a must, the game also utilizes a huge page file (as long as it is present), even with 32GB of memory. The game is also partially CPU bound, an i7-3820 was doing fine, however was thread limited in some cases. It seems like the game has one or two threads which are using quite high CPU time. Oh, and load times are still very high, but at least it can be played for 5-6 hours without the game crashing. But then again, we are speaking about a rig with 32GB DDR3-21333 memory, and two separate SSDs for the game and for the operating system.
So, the performance is still bad, but we are coming there.
For the good news: This is Just Cause 2++, most of the mechanics are intact, so if you liked the previous installment, this is a game for you. You will have fun. On the negative side, the game is much shorter than JC2. 32 hours was enough for to get to the end of the game and liberate everything, but I did only the weapon related challenges.
The missions are less memorable, the landscape varies less than in JC2 and overall, the second installment feels better. But, this can have to do with the less-than-optimal performance (I had better framerates on the second one).
Oh yeah: The collectors edition is HUGE, but I'm unsure about the replica grappling hook. Less would be more actually in this case.

HOLY ♥♥♥♥ THIS GAME IS SO SCARY AND AWESOME AND GREAT THE ATMOSPHERE IS SO PERFECT AND IT LOOKS SO GOOD AND JESUS ♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥ING CHRIST. But fo' real, this is a fantastic game that really does what it does well, stealth and horror are well executed. There is nothing more heart-pounding than hiding in a locker. Then, watching the Alien look at you, and walk away You start to think your safe, you step out of your hiding spot, and see that the Alien hadn't left yet and watched you step out of your hiding spot because you though you heard the door close behind the beast.

After the assterpiece that was Colonial Marines, this is a breath of fresh air that treats the license with dignity and respect. Kinda like a good marriage I suppose. The game features a pretty bad♥♥♥♥♥A.I. for the alien that allows the creature to learn patterns the player may use frequently, check popular hiding spots, and perform some pretty horrifying counter stealth. The stealth system is done pretty well, though it does have the occasional hiccup where you can be seen through a crate or some other similarly solid object. The game does a good job of keeping a familiar atmosphere to the original Ridley Scott movie, and the setting invokes a certain kind of nostalgia for some, sporting a distinctly late 70s to early 80s visual style to really deliver the sci-fi vision of the time.
The Good
- A truly awe inspiring visual style, complete with (toggleable) film grain and vivid, cinematic lighting. The environment looks like it was ripped straight from the movie, but that is not to say that it isnt original. Everything is clearly inspired and clearly unique, which I like a lot.
- Focus on survival through escape, stealth, and hiding. Combat is NOT a reliable option for the engineer you play as, so if you want an Alien themed FPS, this game is not really for you.
- Great voice acting. Andrea Deck (Amanda Ripley) did a pretty impressive job with the role. Also it's nice to hear somebody other than Nolan North or Steve Blum for once.
- Well optimized all around, which is a relief considering it was made with the new line of consoles in mind in terms of graphics. Very good performance throughout the entire game.
The Not-So-Good
- Tips and hints. The tips and tutorials that are provided to introduce and familiarize yourself with some of the mechanics are a bit lacking, many of them slightly confusing. Honestly, I stopped even trying to understand them eventually and just figured it out as I went. Not a huge problem but it is something to consider.
- The difficulty curve. I am all for a challenging game, but when I run through a game specifically for review purposes, it is a bit discouraging to die over and over because the stealth is a bit basic. Satisfying yes, but only because once you actually succeed you've most likely died a dozen times trying to get out of a room with some other survivers in it. This is my biggest issue with the game.
Overall, if you like the Alien universe and you are okay with a pretty tough experience with sneaking around on a station full of crazy people, this game is or you. At 49.99 though, you may want to wait until it goes on sale for 35 or so.

I really do have to give COD Advanced Warfare credit; it truly got me back into playing Call of Duty. To my delight, there were still a good amount of people playing COD 4 online , and with that said,  I feel as though I never need to play the multiplayer of AW again, which makes me very happy.
Alright, so I'm just going to review the multiplayer here, as I am sure the single player is good, but just more of the same COD style, but one of the main components of playing COD is multiplayer, so that's what I am going to focus on.  I really found it insufferable.  The game play seemed just about the same as it did in COD 4 and the other MW's with some obvious changes such as the guns and exo suits which really just made the game worse.
I found all of the exo suits dumb and just not fun.  Multiplayer was easy, I had never played before and was close to if not top fragging, but it just got boring very quickly.  The maps weren't very fun, and the exo suits were more annoying than anything.  When trying to strafe left or right, if you double click you are propelled in that direction, people are flying all around the map because of how much you can jump with the exo suit, it just got to be too much.  Now if you like that stuff, then you might like this game, but with all of that, I'd rather just go play Halo.  They also added laser guns which made the game play terrible.
It seemed as though someone could just hold the laser down and it was pretty much a one shot kill in hardcore if they touched you with it.  So with players just holding it down, it just got to be annoying.  Truly, advanced warfare just seemed like more of the same COD with worse changes.  It's an expensive game that I felt wasn't worth the money.  I'd much rather get any of the other COD's or even get 3 copies of COD 4 and give the others as gifts.  It's not a bad game, just not nearly as fun as any of the other COD's and definitely not worth the money. The changes in the gameplay are not significant enough or fun enough to make this game worth getting.  The franchise has become a cash cow and it is becoming evident in the games which are being put out.  At least they attempted to try something different with AW but it just falls flat on its face.
Simply put, this game is not worth the money.
Also, its 55 Gigs of space I will be very happy to get back.  Hell, I’d rather use every kb of that space storing Randy Newman songs where he describe sthe sounds of Honey Boo Boo’s stomach growling.  That would be a better use of the space than keeping AW installed…

Well this is actually my first Steam review, after picking this game up after reading about a lot of the fixes - and my setup being pretty decent: 3.4ghz i5, GTX 1070, 24gb DDR4 ram, I figured I'd at least be able to brute force the games performance to a decent level. Whilst the first 1hrs of gaming ran relatively decently, after landing in a bigger open city I had some serious slowdown - and experienced 2 crashes in the space of 2 hrs. All the latest graphics drivers from Nvidia were installed.
I have a few positives to say:
+ First, the story seemed fantastic - it drew me in pretty much straight away, and the charatcers and voice acting seemed great. The atmosphere is well and truly nailed, despite the game being really choppy in the bigger cities it was great seeing NPCs go about their business in a delapidated city that shows flashes of interesting objects and architecture. While throughout getting a great sense of lore and narrative.
And some negatives:
- Slowdown and choppiness aside, I noticed when the graphics options were cranked right up that the visuals felt seriouslly off key. High levels of blur in the enviroment felt like I was staring through a vasaline covered window, just for the record I turn motion blur off, and tried switching off depth of field but the issue persisted. Also despite anti aliasing being cranked right up it felt like the environments off in the distance had some serious jaggies. Again these points are a shame, because sometimes the visuals show huge promise in some areas.
And a conclusion:
= All in all it's an absolute shame I'm having to write this review, I'm dying to play the game since it seems like the story and gameplay are ace, but with it's current state in performance I'm going to wait until everything is a little more stable. It absolutely shouldn't have been released with these issues, and I'm sure other people, like myself would prefer they'd of held off on the PC version until it was better optimised.
And a side note:
For all the people claming they're not having any problems - while that may be true, also consider that there are just as many people that are having issues. It would be better for everyone if these issues were not swept under the rug.

For all the problems the first game had, I was still able to look past them and enjoy it for what it was, a fun, action-horror romp similar to Resident Evil 4 and Dead Space with a decent, but pretty all over the place story.
This one fixes pretty much every problem the first game had. The gameplay is much closer to something like The Last Of Us than Resident Evil 4, and the game all in all is the closest I've seen to the classic Silent Hill games since the PS2. It's like if Konami actually gave the developers of Silent Hill Downpour the budget and time they deserved to finish that game. The story is much better this time, and they've given Sebastian some very welcome character development.
Another downfall of the original was, while a fun game with great atmosphere, it wasn't really scary. This game has had me on edge several times, the monsters are creepy and threatening, and the stealth set pieces really keep you on your toes, but just enough for you to stay on edge the entire time and actually finish the section. Far, far less unfair and 1 hit kills. I'm on chapter 13 and I've died only a handful of times, always my fault, where in the first game I finished with 58 deaths. Combat is always tense, and challenging, but I feel I've done a significantly better job than I did the first game.
The open-ended approach really helps out. Exploring was key in the first game, and here it takes a 2 steps forward, 1 step back approach where you'll use some ammo and health supplies getting to your side destination, yet be rewarded with more than you used on your way to get it. When the game wants you on a linear path, you'll know it, and you'll know it when it's open for you to run around.
The PC port is great as well, I'm running on an i5 7600k/GTX 1070 and solid 60 FPS/1080p throughout, no stutter or pop-in.
All in all, even before the ending, it really is one of the best horror games I've played in quite some time.

CG:AD is a member of the "True Stinkers of the Steam", a game that is so appallingly unfinished and un-optimized, so poor in all its aspects, that its sole redeeming factor is that it works, barely.
The game tries to be a Hard Sci-Fi shooter/platformer/hacking simulation where you control a robot on a mission to hunt other robots, long after the humanity has been wiped away. Story makes little sense, especially with barely understandable sentences and grammar errors aplenty.
Controls are overly-complex and counter-intuitive, visual and audio aspect are assault on all senses: graphics are not staggeringly bad, but there's an interlaced shtick and quick flashes of colors CG:AD likes to employ to evoke cyberpunk feeling, but they only employ massive headaches and eye-bleeds. Bugs in this game are the main things that you are going to encounter and will follow you all the way until you try to exit the game, along with an exception error caused by the game. In closure, CG:AD is really bad, and among my top 10 worst games in library. Avoid it like you are trying to avoid catching a cold: You'll never have fun with it, and it will leave you in a foul mood every single time.

This game is riddled with glitches and oversights. Maybe Sega's a bad publisher or maybe Creative Assembly is losing it's edge. Despite its flaws, Total War: Rome II is well worth buying if you enjoyed the original Rome: Total War. Updated graphics and altered combat mechanics are definitely a step forward in the right direction. Unfortunately, the combat A.I. is a large step back, so don't expect to be challenged tactically. The technology tree is more or less the same as Shogun II, with two main parts: military and infrastructure. The character system is a not one, not two, but three full steps backward. Due to time passing so quickly, characters will usually die before you can start remembering their names. The skill tree system for characters is completely simplified and your characters will only ever grant very minor bonuses to your armies; such as, +5% weapon damage (5% of 35?... Great). The Army Traditions system is the best thing to come out of this game. Your armies will gain experience on their own, gain traits specific to them, and you will likely become more attached to your military units than the swinging door of generals who parade in and out of life. All in all, not nearly as good as the masterpiece that's Shogun II, but worth buying if you're a fan of the series and the original Rome.

When it was first anounced I was one of the many rabid fans drooling over returning to the command of Legionaries, Phalanxes, Sacred Band, Berserkers, and the Pink Pajama Brigade (Parthia). When the interactive map was revealed, I spent countless hours planning which factions I will play first, who will I conquer first, where are the resources, etc... I didn't preorder though as I had no money to spare at the time. Sadly, this turned out to be a good thing.
We all know what happened next... Terrible launch, possibly rivaling Empire's... Controversial On Disk DLC (Greek States anyone?)... An expansion that came out not too long after release... etc...
Many patches later, a good deal of the bugs and optimization issues have been fixed. Also, some bad features were removed/fixed (capture the flag in field battles) and removed staples of the series made a partial comeback (loose formation, fire-at-will for melee troops, guardmode/formation figthing... but only to certian units). However, due to it still being way overpriced to get everything, I still refused to get it.
Then the free weekend comes along... "why not?" I said to myself... I began by dropping into custom battles and played around with rome, parthia, and egypt. The experiance was... ok at best. nothing groundbreaking or anything. Next I wanted to try a historical battle... then quickly decided against it remembering youtube videos of them and remembering they weren't all that great (seige of carthage)... so I went into the campaign. Took a moment to decide. The release of Rome II was such a buzzkill that I had actually forgotten who I was most excited to play as. Eventually I remembered it was Parthia (btw I was doing the new augustus campaing so parthia was a pretty good size). Loading screen was a little slow but not too bad. It loaded about the speed of Shogun 2. Anyways I was waiting for an inspiring faction intro cinematic or something (which has been a part of the series since the first rome except for Empire+Napoleon.) Sadly this did not happen. All I got was a lousy dialog with forgetable music in the background. I almost exited the game right there, but I convinced myself to go a little further.
The UI is... kinda awful. I tried to find my capitol, but either it is just poorly marked or not marked at all. I could find my provencial capitols though. I messed around in the politics screen... nothing in there seemed to do much of anything... diplomacy was pretty bad too. Couldn't get anything accepted by the AI (even my satraps). City Development is the worst I've seen in the entire series. Army limit still pisses me off. Add that to the fact that you can't detach a few units and send them elsewhere and you've essentially taken away most of my cav operations on the campaign map. I always have multiple small, highly mobile cav forces to conduct recon, raids, misdirection, and other kinds of havok in enemy territory. but can I do that in Rome 2? NOPE!
I tried to keep going, But the more times I clicked end turn the more I wanted to go back to prior games. I do not recommend especially at its current total price (including all content).

If you've played BioShock and don't at least want to try Shock 2, well, slap yourself.
System Shock 2 is one of the most influential games of all times, yadda yadda, masterpiece, yadda  yadda. Long story short this is where BioShock came from. You can trace it back to System Shock, but System shock even in comparison to 2 is a primitive, vastly inferior game.
Essentially SS2 plays out very similarly to BioShock games. You're a dude, thrust into a situation - although System Shock 2 being far heavier on the RPG elements actually gives you a training course and an entire section during which you create your character and choose their path - and things spiral out of control as you, the player, move the story forward and realize you're nothing but a pawn. Setting those nuances aside, SS2 is still very much an FPS first and an RPG second. You will be killing a lot of things, with a lot of different weapons, and a lot of them will probably break too, not to mention be beyond your ability to mod or repair for a significant portion of the game. Fortunately for you, if you're terrible at aiming, the hit boxes for enemies are very large, considering the game is from 1999.
And yes, you'll probably get killed by a monkey, and turrets, and radiation.
Many sources will tell you SS2 was a landmark for storytelling and player driven narrative (though HL1 is probably more so) but SS2 basically took the concept of finding plot bits in written form - like in Resident Evil - and converting them to audio. It gives life to the characters, and adds a new layer of immersion when you unravel a story as if you are actually listening to the audio logs or reports or whatever left by these people. Just like BioShock 1, 2, 3, and Dead Space 1, 2, and 3. Other than that, SS2 is definitely one of the first games that screwed with you - a lot.
You can easily get this game for 1 dollar on Steam and pretty much anywhere else, when the sales are right, and after you do that, there are a wealth of well preserved mods on the internet to try and update the 16 year old graphics to something slightly more pleasant on the eyes. Unfortunately there is no complete remake, and likely never will be, but if you're going to take the leap, you may as well play the original anyway.
