Played through it four times, and had a great time doing so. The newly released Nightmare difficulty rebalances the game such that it managed to recapture the first half of the first playthrough for me in terms of tension and terror, whereas the vanilla experience's mechanics and alien became somewhat exploitable after some time with the game. The new difficulty also tweaks the AI of the enemies, most notably the alien, which in my opinion delivered on the promise of a truly reactive and menacing antagonist. Of course, the game looks great, great recreation of the film's atmosphere and environment with just the right amount of nostalgia. Sound design, especially the audio cues of the alien and the environment, and the dynamic music mixer that is driven by what's going on in-game really help to nail that sense of anxiety that the game needs to be engaging. Overall, it's a good experience, so long as you don't mind playing a game with some older game design philosophy, and if the long winded pacing of the story doesn't put you off. You may find yourself actually having to work hard to get past a section or set piece, but I found this refreshing. It's uncommon lately  when a game actually challenges you to complete it, especially in the context of a game that lives or dies on how much discomfort it can cause in its player. There are still several technical issues in the current build of the game three months after release, some of them game breaking, but none of the ones that I encountered detracted from my enjoyment with the game as a whole.

Alien: Isolation is the single most terrifying game experience I have ever had the pleasure to enjoy.
As an Alien fan that was dying for a genuinely good horror game from the franchise, I was both incredibly excited and nail-bitingly nervous when I first preordered Isolation. I was so afraid that it was going to bomb, and that I was going to be severely disappointed.
My fears were for naught.
Isolation is
, without the crutch that is constant jump scares that so many horror games like to rely on. The horror in Isolation is purely in its brilliant atmosphere and the ambiance. (Believe me, there is nothing more unsettling than walking along a dark and quiet corridor and hearing the distant banging of the Xenomorph making its way through the ventilation shafts.)
The Alien itself is also
. Not only does it look amazing and is animated well, it’s
. I swear its AI is some of the best I’ve seen in any game I’ve played. It felt as though a Xenomorph was plucked straight from the universe of Alien and dropped right into the game. If you encounter it, and you get its attention, there’s no running or hiding from it. You can scare it away with the flamethrower later on, but it only stays away for a short period before coming back. It is fast, and it is deadly. It
catch you. It doesn’t help the motion tracker (the most reliable method of tracking the Alien’s position) is purposefully not 100% accurate, making relying on it solely to figure out where the Xeno is a poor life choice.
Isolation is also a
survival horror. You can fight back, yes; but ammo is painfully scarce and enemies (such as the endlessly unsettling Working Joes) absorb a lot of bullets before they go down. It is always better to creep past or craft a diversion item to distract the enemies than go in guns blazing, believe me. Plus the noise will attract the Alien, and you don’t want that.
The only complaint that I have is that the save stations felt a little sporadically placed at times, but really, it was only in a few areas, so it isn’t very relevant.
EDIT: I can't believe I published this without talking about the Working Joes in more detail.
The Working Joes are Androids, but nothing like the ones we know from the Alien movies (
and Bishop). They are primitive and more like basic drones than intelligent robots, programmed with basic orders and functions. Automatonophobics beware: they are more visually akin to walking mannequins than the fully humanoid androids you're used to from the franchise.
And holy crap are they ever
, even when they're peaceful. Their unnervingly monotonous voices and scripted dialogue (things such as "You are becoming hysterical", "You always know a Working Joe" and "I am going to catch you") make them all that more unsettling. To make it worse they're tough, too; as I said, it takes a lot of shots to take them down, and most of the time it's better if you just ran or hid instead of fighting back.

This game has lots of setbacks. So how can I recommend it, considering that? Two words: asymmetric co-op — this single factor is so important that it changes the perception of this game and its overall experience. There are pretty much no other games on PC with asymmetric co-op of this kind. This feature makes Clandestine a unique experience which has to be appreciated despite its flaws.
Let's get clear with the setbacks first:
1. Poor optimization (average 40 FPS on a decent rig).
2. Visuals and overall production values will remind you of mid 2000s (except for music, which is spot on).
3. Story and characters are nothing to blow your wad over.
So how can a single feature outweigh all of the above?
Just get a friend for co-op and now all of a sudden you're no longer playing a generic indie stealth-action game with dated visuals, but engaging in deep & realistic spy missions all over the world. Go in as a spy and do whatever it takes to get the job done, or put yourself in the shoes of the all-seeing internet wizard and help your spy friend in any way you can. There are plenty of approaches to the missions at hand, both from the perspective of the spy and hacker: you can be totally stealth, without leaving any traces in either physical or digital form, or go in guns blazing / server DDOS'ing, wiping out any resistance in your way. But playstyle isn't the only thing that's left at your discretion, with it also expanding to side objectives, in-mission decisions, choosing routes, equipment and the like.
What's usually just a generic gaming convention, e.g. hacking electronic door locks and disabling security cameras, now becomes a real game mechanic, with those jobs being reserved for your co-op hacker partner. Need to know the location of those security guards? Ask your partner to tag them for you. Want to make an extreme, highly dangerous stealth run between the routes of security guards? Have your hacker partner carefully guide you, tracking both your and their movement. Seriously, open a voice chat via Steam, Teamspeak, Skype, Hangouts or any similar app and the game becomes an experience like no other.
It also isn't a walk in the park if you're playing as a hacker — you'll need to be really good at multi-tasking, providing spot-on help for your spy partner, digesting and extracting useful information from data you obtained, spotting enemies through cameras and disabling them with the right timing and playing hide-and-seek with the network administrator. Sometimes, all at the same time. You won't be bored.
Usually in spy games mission control is reserved only for supplying player some info. And in hacker games, usually you can do everything remotely, leaping from host to host. In Clandestine, you're nothing without your partner, there are some thing that only your partner can do, and this goes for both hacker and spy characters. Hacker won't be able to reach non-connected machines or designated networks without a help from a spy. Spy is a blind puppy without a hacker.
This game develops great sense of trust between players, resulting in jolly co-operation.
Clandestine is a great example of a flawed masterpiece or a diamond in the rough, that almost nobody gave a chance to, with SteamSpy estimating sales at just 9K copies sold. Sure, it's hard to see what's so good about this game just by its description and some screenshots, but that's just more reason for you to try it yourself — just remember to get a friend along for the ride.

I'm going to come out and say it: I like this game not as a Sierra game, but as a fresh, original take on the series. Here's why.
I know there are a lot of people who complain that this doesn't feel like a King's Quest game. It doesn't have all the puzzle, the plot, the mystery behind it, etc. And although this game contains so much energy and entertainment, it simply isn't a Sierra game. If you are looking for an "epilogue" to the original King's Quest games, you won't find it here. But that doesn't mean you'll be wasting your time.
I love the original King's Quest games, but I had long forgotten about them when I picked up this gem several months ago. I only remembered that it was connected to an older series when I googled the name and several older, pixellated images came up.
This game is graphically gorgeous, funny, heart-wrenching, and will leave you with a mixing pot of emotions, from frustration to pride to disappointment, in such a way that makes you feel like you went on an adventure yourself. I loved it from beginning to end, and I replayed it again and again to fully experience all of the potential it holds.
HOWEVER, there are several reasons why it doesn't have a big following now. Firstly, it's not by Sierra. I think this is a silly reason to avoid it because it still holds the essence of the original games, just casting a fresh, modern light on it (i.e. goofier puns and more cartoonish actions). Secondly, there's a lot of rumors going around about the issues between the Odd Gentlemen and Andrew Hussie, creator of Homestuck. Since, at the moment, we don't have much information aside from speculation, I feel it is important to wait for full disclosure of information and, in the meantime, step into the game objectively. Besides, you can play the first chapter for free! And that, in my opinion, is the best one.
On a side note, I feel I should mention that this game has several different gameplay routes. If you're clever, gentle, or adventurous, you'll enjoy the emotion and energy in this game as long as you don't hinge on the background of the game.
If you're the type of person who cares about where a game comes from and who makes it, you may be biased and want to avoid this game. I went into it unawares, so I fell in love with it before I learned of all the muck behind it. I'm not going to say that you should ignore the rumors, or accept this as a "continuation" of the King's Quest series, but you really can't go into this game expecting one thing or another. Go into it blind, and you'll totally lose yourself in it.
All in all, 8.5/10.

Rome II was terrible when it launched. Now it's pretty damn good.

Just to start off with, I'd like to point out that I'm a big TW fan. I've played nearly all of the games, and loved both Medieval games and the original Rome. However, in my opinion, this game suffers from a few issues which stop it from being at quite the same level. Whilst the way in which there are dozens of tiny tribes, each controlling a small amount of land is probably accurate to the times, it also makes it incredibly easy to defeat them, as they simply don't have the strength to fight off a genuine attack from even a semi-decent player. This, in turn, makes the rest of the game too simple, as you can simply snap up relatively undefended territories and then use them to constantly spam troops in the direction of nations which otherwise would stand a chance against you. I'm also not a fan of the new trait system, but I'll get to that in a minute. In the original Rome, the only real limit to your army size was the unit cap for each army, (about 20) and what you could afford to maintain. In this, that is still the same, however you can only field a set number of armies at a time, and this makes it incredibly difficult to be able to bring reinforcing armies into play, as the AI is ridiculously, hilariously aggressive for the moment, and is not above launching a war it cannot win, just because it feels like it, meaning that you constantly have to keep most of your forces on standby to defend you. This makes it difficult to fight against a similar strength foe, as they will then launch all their forces against your armies one at a time, ensuring either quick defeat or massive frustration. However, this is also a good thing, as it means that you have to learn and adapt to what can be a sometimes difficult and constantly changing situation, meaning that every country you conquer comes with a sense of achievement, even if it's still very annoying when an army that should easily win a fight is destroyed by a handful of low level units. Anyway, the trait system. Previous games had a long list of traits that characters could gain, ranging from incredibly helpful stuff that dramatically boosted your characters stats or absolutely slaying them. Whilst sometimes these traits seemed to appear with no real rhyme or reason, (with combinations such as being a raving lunatic but a masterful diplomatic influence) they added a real sense of connection to characters who, in some cases, were only going to last a relatively short period of time. There were also no particular limits to how many traits a character could gain, although this was decided by the AI, you could affect it by pushing this character as a main army general, an ambusher, etc. In Rome II, a character can only have 3 active traits, and once this limit is achieved, that's your lot. The same goes with a character's retinue. It was the same idea as the traits, although in this case it was an ancillary character or item usually added to a general's bodyguard or affecting their stats in some way. In this, a character has a limited number of slots. One for a spouse, and a one or two others for an item, which can be swapped out with any excess items which you have collected from amongst all the generals you have, and these can be pinged around between all your generals, meaning that a particularly useful item can be shifted amongst all your generals as the situation dictates.
Having made these complaints, I do have a few things to say in favour of this game. It's still a very deep game, with a lot of empire building options, and the battle map is still as good as always, with tactics, perhaps, having become more and more important in this, especially amongst the more powerful empires such as carthage or the romans. The historical accuracy is also impressive. The number of individual factions within what may have been seen as a singular nation in the original is brilliant, and the fact that they all have their own mindsets (war-like, expansionist, peaceful etc) is a sign that Creative Assembly have created a game that you can tell they cared about and put a lot of effort in. There are a lot of flaws in this game, but it has a lot of really good features too, and if you can cope with those issues and have the patience to put up with a lot of early game a*** kickings, then you can find out just how good this game can be, and how much fun you can have setting up your own empire and ruling in the way that you choose to. Overall, I'd have to say that this game is just about worth getting, but be aware that it's not the same game you may know from earlier titles.

Well I do not understand why it was possible to read so many bad reviews about this game while actually IT IS AMAZING !
Yes there are some differences with Rome Total War I but I didn't find Rome II neither simplicistic,dumbed down or bugged at all (maybe because I just played the Emperor version already heavily fixed).
The army limit for me is better than the old system, it's a new rule that I like, I find the combat much better than older games : troops stay a lot more fighting and you can watch them, try to plan your strategy and try to win enjoying every second of the battle. From my point of view combat had huge improvement in this game.
About other complaints like the "simplicistic" province management well I thought the people saying this may be playing another game ! You just have icons now and towns are grouped in provinces, the building management is quite deep and you have to decide if to develop a city more economic oriented or a military city troop producing oriented. This will affect the buildings you can build there (each building has different effects on your province) and also in this aspect Rome II is a huge improvement compared to past.
If you need a challange play on legendary level and prepare to get your *** kicked so bad and be prepared to fight with all your strenght to keep your territories against foes that wants your head !
To keep this short I found Rome II a huge improvement over the past in all aspects : more details (not only graphic) in everything, lots of units, amazing combat, some changes that for me are all step forward compared to past and also more difficulty if you ask for it.
There is also a possibility to make a Multiplayer campaign with a friend Online or on local LAN where you choose two different nations and play Co-Op or Head to Head (each one on its own and all the other factions of the world are still there of course) and it works great, you can save and continue...no lags at all, each player has its turn and you spectate his battle. This also is a great add-on.
Give it a try, and don't listen to such criticism. This game is really GREAT !

System Shock 2may have flew under the radar for many gamers like myself, However and i am glad to have stumbled upon this gem.
The game is set in the distant future, where the first FTL spacecraft was created through earth's technological advancement. The creation of Intelligent AI was also one of them.
You, the hacker must unravel the mystery of the ship, the Von Braun which had been taken over by a strange presence in the ship which had caused the slaughter of 1000s of crewmembers on-board.
At first glance, I knew this game was something a little more complicated then your average shooter, by no means is this a 'Doom' or 'Quake' or even halflife game. Its something deeper. The addition of RPG elements much like Deus Ex adds a bit more depth upon choosing 3 distict paths in the game. The marines, The Navi and The OSA.
Each class will determine the way you will pass each challenge throughout the game. By choosing the navi, you have more technical abilities then the others. You are able to disable cameras and turrets from a security terminal to remain undetected as you advance through each stage.
If you were to take the OSA approach, which focuses on your 'Psi' powers (doing things with your mind), you are able to possibly go invisible, disable a camera or turret, or just use a blast of cryo energy.
if you were the marines perhaps, you could get your hands on an arsenal of different weaponary ranging from laser pistols to fully fledged alien assault rifles and even grenade launchers! using your leaning ability you can shoot around corners with out getting hit (but the game cheats sometimes and you can get hit through a wall).
With all these in mind, you are not resticted to your class qualities alone. you can spend your cyber modules on skills from the other classes and not feel guilty either. Although the impulse is to go for a Jack of all trades approach, its best to stay loyal to the chosen path.
The games difficulty is an interesting aspect of the game. You will be underpowered, and you will be killed faster then your pc rig can play pong. the vunerablility of the player gives a sense of danger, what could possibly be around the corner, or what could possibliy bring me to an end? thats the intention. The game wants you to pay attention to its surrounding, where one wrong move could mean your life, or slow you down from progressing.
The atmosphere of the game is astounding! It has that Half life and dead space feel to it, but darker and scarier. the corridors have mutant crewmembers, rouge cyborgs and even (monkeys?) ready to snap you in half. And even as you progress further through the game you are constantly Taunted by SHODAN (the antagonist) as if you were just a mere bug. nothing encourages you as you progress, but you feel the reward of going against that.
The audio logs of crewmembers found throughout the ship helps the player to understand what has happened to them or the events in a personal manner. You are sunken into the mystery of what happened to the crew member as you find audio log after the other, just like chapters in a book. I absolutley love when developers give characters more depth through audio logs or written passages.
The music and all dont always give the atmospheric vibe you should expect from a game of this caliber, but sometimes, silence is the best kind of music.
In all, I was satisfied with the ending of the game and the twists and turns inbetween, and for any of those wondering whether to buy this or not, i reckon its a worthy investment of your time and money.

This game is almost as good if not better than the original. I was blasted through the game for the third time on average difficulty and I loved it. The game is certainly harder than the original Half-Life, but I don't think thats a problem. I owned the original mod and this is certainly a big improvment.
The atmosphere is much better than the original Half-Life, which is mostly down to the music. This game has the best soundtrack I have heard in any game. The improved lighting also helps to give the game that survival horror element at the beginning and the hard core shooter element at the end. I have to admit that I dread when ever you have to enter the water with the fish thing in it, that if one of my biggest fears; being attacked while in water. Its frantic and scary, my skin crawls whenever I see it swimming toward me, its mouth gaping open like your mum at the cake shop.
The guns are all useful with few being OP, except maybe the Hive Hand but even then it isn't that over-powered. I died alot. I've seen alot of reviews complaining about how the game isn't ready yet, but I assume that the Crowbar collective is operating on VALVe time.
The last thing I want to touch on is the art design. This game is the best looking Half-Life game, maybe even Source 1 game. It has such vibrant colours and everything is clean and sharp. I always felt in Half-Life 2 that Gordon was in his mid-thirties, mostly due to the somewhat lack of colour in the world and his movement, but in this game I for some reason feel that Gordon is young and is ready to fight, whereas in HL2 he seemed weary, even in the climactic moment, although maybe that was just me.
To conclude, I would definately reccomend Black Mesa as a fantastic contribution to the Half-Life cannon.

As this is a Retelling of the King's Quest Games, King Graham, who's now old as King Edward, shares his previous adventures with his curious granddaughter, Gwendolyn. It is through these tales that Gwendolyn learns about the life led by her grandfather. The game uses vocal performances by actors such as Christopher Lloyd, Wallace Shawn, Tom Kenny, Josh Keaton, Maggie Elizabeth Jones, and Zelda Williams.
In Episode 1: Graham's journey to knighthood begins in this chapter. It takes place before the original King's Quest as memories of the present day Graham (who is now aged), narrated to his granddaughter Gwendolyn. Later, Episode 1 was released for Free which I consider as Modern Day Free Shareware.
In Chapter 2: Graham recounts his first adventure as the newly crowned king of Daventry saving the kingdom from invading goblins which is set around after King's Quest 1 but before King's Quest 2.
In Chapter 3: Graham recounts the tale of how he met his beloved Valanice which is set around King's Quest 2.
In Chapter 4: After Graham's son, Alexander, escapes his life of enslavement to Manannan they celebrate by taking the family on vacation. However, they find the resort has been transformed into a snowy palace of lethal traps by an icy queen and a sphinx which is set around Kings Quest 3-4.
In Chapter 5: As the elderly King Graham reaches the end of his life he has enough time to tell Gwendolyn about his final confrontation with Manannan as he promised the Magic Mirror one last adventure to recount & recall which is set around Kings Quest 5-6. Afterwards, the fate of Daventry's Throne in both the Past & Present are all based on the choices you made in the previous Episodes.
The Epilogue is Coming Soon.

This game has its flaws, and it's not going to appeal to everyone - or even most people, probably. It has a certain PS1-era charm to it that may resonate more with "older" folks that don't necessarily care if every single texture isn't 4K and animations are bemusingly clunky. When it comes to content, the actual experience, there's a lot here to love. The asymmetrical approach to coop works very well, as long as the hacker player doesn't need to be engaged in high-adrenaline activity every second - there are periods of time where the hacker will be doing little other than observing their partner, and that's ok. So far, I've been playing the field agent while my friend plays the hacker, and I tend to be slow and patient, preferring maximum stealth and to avoid contact whenever possible. This very much feels like the way the game is intended to be played; getting spotted is almost always a quick death.
My biggest and really only complaint is the seemingly inconsistent checkpoint system. There have been a handful of occasions where I've spent 30+ real-world minutes completing several objectives, only to be spotted by a guard, restart, and find myself having to redo all of it. But then, on my second or third attempt, a checkpoint will trigger where one never did before. It's little more than a mild frustration if you're patient, in which case it doesn't happen very often, but it is something that needs to be addressed.
The tutorial is also a little bit lacking, as there are certain features that aren't explained very well and need to be figured out by accident or through trial and error, but once you know what you're doing, everything actually works and works well.
Overall, highly recommended. Certainly worth a purchase if it's on sale, and even at full price - $25 is more than fair for what you get.

Just one of the many grammatical/spelling errors within the game.
Sound: As mentioned before there were weird voices/sounds popping up in the background with no discernible purpose.
Overall, a dreadful, dreadful game. Never buy this.

If you manage to think to look behind you, you will find the main menu, where you can start the game. Maybe. If you can figure out how. The 'start' button seems to allow you to choose which save file you are using. It does not, in fact, start the freaking game.

The second time I got it working, I did use the 'alpha simulation' button, which brought me to a long, very gray area with lots of boxes. A weapon, another droid thing... Some ammo... Some... Well, not much, actually. Basically nothing of use. After attacking the green thingy some and jumping around a lot, I closed the game so I could look at the controls again. The controls did not help. I fruitlessly started the alpha simulation once more before I just gave up because THIS GAME IS USELESS. I HATE IT. I HATE IT MORE THAN ANYTHING.
I SPENT ELEVEN MINUTES OF MY LIFE ON THIS USELESS PIECE OF TRASH AND I WANT THEM BACK.
Edit: I forgot to mention one of the other 'features' in this useless thing. If you happen to press the wrong button (it's either x or c, I'm not sure), your character gives up on life and self destructs, which will always cause the game to freeze. Enjoy.

Well I do not understand why it was possible to read so many bad reviews about this game while actually IT IS AMAZING !
Yes there are some differences with Rome Total War I but I didn't find Rome II neither simplicistic,dumbed down or bugged at all (maybe because I just played the Emperor version already heavily fixed).
The army limit for me is better than the old system, it's a new rule that I like, I find the combat much better than older games : troops stay a lot more fighting and you can watch them, try to plan your strategy and try to win enjoying every second of the battle. If you need a challange play on legendary level and prepare to get your *** kicked so bad and be prepared to fight with all your strenght to keep your territories against foes that wants your head !
To keep this short I found Rome II a huge improvement over the past in all aspects : more details (not only graphic) in everything, lots of units, amazing combat, some changes that for me are all step forward compared to past and also more difficulty if you ask for it.
There is also a possibility to make a Multiplayer campaign with a friend Online or on local LAN where you choose two different nations and play Co-Op or Head to Head (each one on its own and all the other factions of the world are still there of course) and it works great, you can save and continue...no lags at all, each player has its turn and you spectate his battle. Give it a try, and don't listen to such criticism. This game is really GREAT !

Ridley Scott's 1979 "Alien" was one of the first horror movies I ever saw as a kid. I grew up loving the Alien movies and this game was an awesome homage and add on to the story of the original.
Although this game scored higher postive review scores than negative ones, I was confused about some of the gamer complaints....."It's too hard. I have to hide all the time. " I'm not sure what mode they played it on, but I played it on normal and had a f****** blast! This is by far the best "Alien" game out of the many disasters and the only one people should play.
PROS:
*GORGEOUS graphics and attention to detail (I wondered around for hours just reading posted notes attached to desks)
*Amanda Riply is a fantastic lead character, who for once said MANY of the things I was thinking when I have played similar "fix-and-fetch" quests. For example: "Why is this ship a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥" "WHy don't you go fix the power reactor?" "Why are you all so worthless at fixing ANYTHING?!" I chuckled several times.
*The gadgets you can make are pretty cool and not just "balls-to-the-walls" machine guns and grenande launchers. You have to rely on stealth.
*The Working Joe androids were scarier than the Alien itself. The little things they mutter to themselves and to others are f****** creepy.
*The DLC "Crew Expendable" and "Lone Survivor" are great because they allow you to play actual characters from the original Alien story. These are short, but sweet.
CONS:
Although I probably loved everything about this game there was one CON that I agreed with when reading the other gamer/critic reviews.
The game play is consistent and the story line awesome, but it reaches a  point around hour 16 when you REALLY think the game is going to wrap up and finish and then........it continues for another four hours. This is not necessarily a bad thing because you are having fun, but it needs to be trimmed down. Not only that, I found the final four hours of the entire game to be the only times I became frustrated.

Scary as hell, ranks up there with Resident Evil 2 and Slender as one of the scariest games of all time.  The game is well paced, for the most part, and it doesn't overuse placing the player in scare mode.  The timing of the music has to be commended as well, along with the jump scares.
That being said, there are times when you might get killed for cheap reasons, especially on the harder levels of difficulty.  Using the motion tracker to determine when you should move beneath an open vent, or move at all, does help.  But there will come times when you have to take a chance and move when the enemy is nearby, because there are some rooms/levels where the enemy will always search near where you hide.  You will spend a decent portion of the game moving, hiding when you detect a threat (either with motion scanner, by sight, or by sound), rinse and repeat, save for a few moments when you craft a weapon to use on some robot Joes.  The cheap kills done on you are not that big of a deal on easy mode, maybe even on normal mode.  But on Hard mode and Nightmare, it can get unfair and ridiculous at times.
Hiding doesn't always work, especially on higher difficulties.  On those levels, when you are in a locker or other hiding spot, the alien won't just slowly walk past you.  If it senses you hiding in their (and it almost always does on Nightmare mode), it will lean in close to see if you are there.  You will then have to press a couple buttons to lean back and hold your breath.  The longer you hold your breath, the more health you lose.  Hold it too long, and you will gasp for air, and then the alien will hear you, open the door, and kill you.  So you will be forced to quickly but stealthily maneuver around the hallways and rooms as best as you can, and only use hiding spots when absolutely necessary.
That being said, I played through the game twice, once on easy (14 hours), once on Nightmare (13 hours).  Yes, I beat the game on Nightmare mode, and thought the game was worth playing twice.
One last note about Nightmare mode.  You are going to need health kits and pipe bombs, and maybe one EMP.  And try to save your ammunition for the Joes, except the flamethrower because that weapon is the only thing you'll have to save you against the alien, and flames don't do squat against Joes.  I never had to use any other crafting item on that level of difficulty.  Be bery careful with what you craft, because crafting materials are very hard to come by on Nightmare mode.  And try not to use the flamethrower.  While handy, it burns through ammunition very fast on Nightmare mode.  But there is a neat trick with the flamethrower.  As I ran for an elevator, with the alien charging after me, I pointed the weapon at the alien ready to blast it.  But the alien stopped.  It flinched, knowing that the flames burn and it doesn't want to get hit by them.  It's a very useful bluff tactic to use if you are low on ammo to keep the alien away for just another couple seconds, just the amount of time needed to get that elevator going.
Brilliant emmersion.  A true survival horror gem in an era where most AAA survival horror games get that aspect so wrong (ala Dead Space).

I never really liked these types of games, but Just Cause 3 has left me wasting away hours upon hours of messing around and wreaking havoc. System Shock 2may have flew under the radar for many gamers like myself, However and i am glad to have stumbled upon this gem.
The game is set in the distant future, where the first FTL spacecraft was created through earth's technological advancement. The creation of Intelligent AI was also one of them.
You, the hacker must unravel the mystery of the ship, the Von Braun which had been taken over by a strange presence in the ship which had caused the slaughter of 1000s of crewmembers on-board.
At first glance, I knew this game was something a little more complicated then your average shooter, by no means is this a 'Doom' or 'Quake' or even halflife game. Its something deeper. The addition of RPG elements much like Deus Ex adds a bit more depth upon choosing 3 distict paths in the game. The marines, The Navi and The OSA.
Each class will determine the way you will pass each challenge throughout the game. By choosing the navi, you have more technical abilities then the others. You are able to disable cameras and turrets from a security terminal to remain undetected as you advance through each stage.
If you were to take the OSA approach, which focuses on your 'Psi' powers (doing things with your mind), you are able to possibly go invisible, disable a camera or turret, or just use a blast of cryo energy.
if you were the marines perhaps, you could get your hands on an arsenal of different weaponary ranging from laser pistols to fully fledged alien assault rifles and even grenade launchers! using your leaning ability you can shoot around corners with out getting hit (but the game cheats sometimes and you can get hit through a wall).
With all these in mind, you are not resticted to your class qualities alone. you can spend your cyber modules on skills from the other classes and not feel guilty either. Although the impulse is to go for a Jack of all trades approach, its best to stay loyal to the chosen path.
The games difficulty is an interesting aspect of the game. You will be underpowered, and you will be killed faster then your pc rig can play pong. the vunerablility of the player gives a sense of danger, what could possibly be around the corner, or what could possibliy bring me to an end? thats the intention. The game wants you to pay attention to its surrounding, where one wrong move could mean your life, or slow you down from progressing.
The atmosphere of the game is astounding! It has that Half life and dead space feel to it, but darker and scarier. the corridors have mutant crewmembers, rouge cyborgs and even (monkeys?) ready to snap you in half. And even as you progress further through the game you are constantly Taunted by SHODAN (the antagonist) as if you were just a mere bug. nothing encourages you as you progress, but you feel the reward of going against that.
The audio logs of crewmembers found throughout the ship helps the player to understand what has happened to them or the events in a personal manner. You are sunken into the mystery of what happened to the crew member as you find audio log after the other, just like chapters in a book. I absolutley love when developers give characters more depth through audio logs or written passages.
The music and all dont always give the atmospheric vibe you should expect from a game of this caliber, but sometimes, silence is the best kind of music.
In all, I was satisfied with the ending of the game and the twists and turns inbetween, and for any of those wondering whether to buy this or not, i reckon its a worthy investment of your time and money.

System Shock 2 is a wonderful atmospheric game. It's different than many FPS' in that there's more focus on the story, experience, and exploration. The story unfolds as you discover audible recordings and make progress through the game.
There's also different stats, skills, and abilities which allow you to create your own unique character and focus on the skills you'd like to improve. Main skills focus around: weapon types, hacking, fixing, and cybernetics (magic). Typically you specialize rather than try to have all of them low level.
There a bit of inventory management--you can only carry so much. You must make room for quest/progress items--other than key-cards.
A few warnings. The game is buggy. However, there's some on-line tutorials about patching the game to a more stable version (PC Version). There's also some great mods--for the PC version--that improve the textures, models, etc. Also, be wary of multi-player--which is also buggy. I wanted to play this with a friend, however, the game would freeze, and it became a bit challenging to play the game. You also will only see each others characters after selecting you character path (abilities)--post fourth year.
In all, if you've yet to ever play this game, you might enjoy it the most playing it single player first anyway. It's easier to get into the atmosphere/environment.

Old but gold. That is the best way to describe System Shock 2.
The game itself plays like it's predecessor System Shock and it's spiritual successors, the Bioshock series. What makes it different is that players are given the choice on what class to pick based on the military: Navy, Marines, and OSI. The atmosphere is suspensful and oppresive. You'll never know if the next corner has a pipe-wielding crewman with worms sticking out from his head to the torso, a kamikaze service droid, or even spider that was once human.
Despite the graphics being outdated (It was made in 1999 so cut it some slack. There are mods that make it look better), the gameplay itself shines like a diamond, giving replayability for those that want to literally adjust the skills of their character, whether it's spending some cyber-modules on an OSI upgrade to run past enemies undetected or improving your hacking skill so the crate doesn't explode when you hit a bad node.
Another high point to mention aside from the atmosphere and gameplay is are the audio logs. Each log found gives off a bit of backstory as to what is going within the game, whether it's a conversation between to leaders of the ship you are on or of a scientist who is voicing her concerns regarding what enemey is worse. Another high point to mention is a key character of the game, SHODAN. So as not to spoil too much, SHODAN is someone who will help you out though not without voicing her or its displeasure towards you, especially since you are a fleshy insect.
System Shock 2 a game to recommend to anyone that would want to play a good game. If you want an FPS game that has good atmosphere, gameplay, and replayability, look no further than at System Shock 2.

Clandestine is a unique, innovative, and engaging co-op stealth game. While it was clearly made on a small budget, and potentially limited game design experience ( I don't know these things, I'm just guessing ) it shines as a very unique, memorable experience when played with a buddy.
Story feels rather forgettable, and the NPCs all look really strange - I kept making fun of this one guy who looked like a Sim from the Sims 2 - but there are some fun parts in what I've seen. The dialouge seems rather dynamic, and the NPCs will react to how your missions go down and some other small things - My friend wandered into the men's restroom in the hub area, for instance, and when he went to talk to the big boss guy he asked that they please refrained from doing so.
...The spy is female, for those unaware.
The characters will either compliment or berate you based on your performance in the missions - How lethal you were, or how much of a trace you left. Some of them have different overall desires in how you handle things, but I don't think it affects anything aside from dialog.
One thing I noticed is that later missions may get harder if you leave more evidence. It was brought up during a mission briefing that the security on the level would be low, because the previous mission was so flawless they just assumed it was an inside job, and that there was no reason to step up security.
The gameplay, while unrefined in some ways, is very unique and engaging. Controlling the Spy feels clunky and awkward at times, but you can get the job done easily. The Hacker works like a charm, though, which is impressive considering how they manage and keep track of four different windows.
If you want more specifics, read other reviews - But I have to say that this is a big recommend - If you get a friend. The solo seems just a little too scatterbrained with switching between hacker and spy. And if you get a friend, you should probably keep in mind if they would like the Hacker or the Spy, and what you would rather play yourself. A scatterbrained hacker is not something you want or need.
I recommend Clandestine to anyone who enjoys co-operative stealth games that require some planning, and a bit of experimentation.

This is a flawed game.
But that does not make it a bad game. In fact, Clandestine is a good game. A friend of mine and I purchased Clandestine and played through, co-op and streaming online the blind run. I played the Spy, my friend the Hacker. Some things were goofy, especially the controls. For one thing, you don't smoothly leave cover when you try to walk away, you have to press the cover button again. Doorways can catch you for seemingly no reason. Giving directions (Left! No, right!) can be silly when the camera the Hacker is using faces the direction the Spy facing while you have the camera facing another direction. Some game mechanics are unintuitive (Reloading, for example: hold R, scroll mouse to another magazine, then release R). Animations are wonky, and the faces on a few characters are... well... I may see Sarah in my nightmares tonight.
But when we ended for the night, we both agreed that we had had fun. The netcode didn't hiccup, which is a great plus in a heavy co-op game. The stealth is a great blend of tense and forgiving, and getting caught doesn't signify the end of the world. This is one of the few stealth games where getting caught doesn't necessitate an immediate reload. Finding the right path is not a chore, but rather an interesting puzzle. There are consequences to your actions in the after-mission debriefings, and the story, while not seat-of-your-pants-exciting, is still better than quite a few games out there.
Overall, the game has its flaws. The controls and animations could use polish. But the game does well at being an enjoyable game, blending together things in a way AAA game makers should note. If you have a friend, get this game and play through it with them. Especially if they like telling you where to go. Left, no, right, those double doors you silly goose.

The same dark and twisted world full of hellish abominations that you'd expect to find in the Evil Within series, only now it's less linear and more open world in design, harking back to the earlier days of the Silent Hill series and its portrayal of psychological horror in a middle-America town. Stealth is still just as importanat as it was in the 1st Evil Within, but now with an emphasis on exploration and the ability to craft ammo, weapon upgrades and even health items, regular ammo is in very limited suppply and so stealth is perhaps even more crucial than before. You can directly engage an enemy or you can often work your way around them and even use bushes as cover to conceal your presence. The hot, though vaguely creepy, 50s-era nurse puts in an appearance, offering up her services to allow you to level up skills using green/red jell and unlock those beloved little lockers with keys gotten from breaking statuettes. For Alien fans this game is a must have, it make great use of the license to make a truly atmospheric experience. The game is challenging on hard mode but still enjoyable. A few parts in the game can be annoying when it is just you taking on Working Joes rather than the Xenomorph, but the Alien is where the fun is at.

Scary as hell, ranks up there with Resident Evil 2 and Slender as one of the scariest games of all time.  The game is well paced, for the most part, and it doesn't overuse placing the player in scare mode.  The timing of the music has to be commended as well, along with the jump scares.
That being said, there are times when you might get killed for cheap reasons, especially on the harder levels of difficulty.  Using the motion tracker to determine when you should move beneath an open vent, or move at all, does help.  But there will come times when you have to take a chance and move when the enemy is nearby, because there are some rooms/levels where the enemy will always search near where you hide.  You will spend a decent portion of the game moving, hiding when you detect a threat (either with motion scanner, by sight, or by sound), rinse and repeat, save for a few moments when you craft a weapon to use on some robot Joes.  The cheap kills done on you are not that big of a deal on easy mode, maybe even on normal mode.  But on Hard mode and Nightmare, it can get unfair and ridiculous at times.
Hiding doesn't always work, especially on higher difficulties.  On those levels, when you are in a locker or other hiding spot, the alien won't just slowly walk past you.  If it senses you hiding in their (and it almost always does on Nightmare mode), it will lean in close to see if you are there.  You will then have to press a couple buttons to lean back and hold your breath.  The longer you hold your breath, the more health you lose.  Hold it too long, and you will gasp for air, and then the alien will hear you, open the door, and kill you.  So you will be forced to quickly but stealthily maneuver around the hallways and rooms as best as you can, and only use hiding spots when absolutely necessary.
That being said, I played through the game twice, once on easy (14 hours), once on Nightmare (13 hours).  Yes, I beat the game on Nightmare mode, and thought the game was worth playing twice.
One last note about Nightmare mode.  You are going to need health kits and pipe bombs, and maybe one EMP.  And try to save your ammunition for the Joes, except the flamethrower because that weapon is the only thing you'll have to save you against the alien, and flames don't do squat against Joes.  I never had to use any other crafting item on that level of difficulty.  Be bery careful with what you craft, because crafting materials are very hard to come by on Nightmare mode.  And try not to use the flamethrower.  While handy, it burns through ammunition very fast on Nightmare mode.  But there is a neat trick with the flamethrower.  As I ran for an elevator, with the alien charging after me, I pointed the weapon at the alien ready to blast it.  But the alien stopped.  It flinched, knowing that the flames burn and it doesn't want to get hit by them.  It's a very useful bluff tactic to use if you are low on ammo to keep the alien away for just another couple seconds, just the amount of time needed to get that elevator going.
Brilliant emmersion.  A true survival horror gem in an era where most AAA survival horror games get that aspect so wrong (ala Dead Space).

Where to begin?  Very few games give me a headache when playing them.  This is one of those games.
This game really needs someone with incredible patience to create a video walkthru just to explain how to play this crazy game.   So far no one has done this.  Not sure anyone will.  I'm sure as hell not going to try.  I didn't even get through what I think was the tutorial before giving up in frustration.
I got to a wall where it said hold W to climb wall.  Uh no.  That doesn't work.  Not at all.  You have to use a combination of hitting W and the space bar in the right way to get up that wall.  And that is provided you didn't waste energy sprinting around and stuff.
The game doesn't bother to tell you that sprinting or using your "jet pack" consumes energy.  And if you consume too much energy, then you cannot get past the next obstacle.  Too bad.  What to do?  Hit X and autodestruct and start over.  My first attempt I did just that in trying to get over that stupid wall, where I didn't have enough jet pack whatever to get me high enough.  Except I didn't know to hit X, until I accidentally hit in randomly hitting keys on the keyboard.  There is a way to get a list of the controls, including the magic use of X, but it's not obvious why you would want to autodestruct, so it's easy to overlook.
After the wall, I got to a switch of some kind.  I tried everything, but I could not figure out for the life of me how to flip that freaking switch.  It's probably some use of the E button with the cursor positioned just so, maybe with CTRL mode on, maybe not.  After futzing with it for a few minutes, I decided I no longer cared to play this game.  It was giving me a headache.  And not the fun kind of a headache either.  If such a thing exists.  No.  This is get an aspirin and not ever play the game again kind of headache.
This game might be playable, or possibly in some alternate universe, enjoyable even, if you had any idea of what you were doing half the time.
The game boasts that it is the hardest sci-fi side scroller.  Ever.  Yeah right.  Having a game where not enough time was taken on basic stuff, like spelling or creating a descent tutorial, doesn't make a game "hard", it just makes it "unplayable", or more precisely, "frustrating to the point where you don't want to play it anymore".
As a side note,  it's kind of amazing really how bad the spelling is at times.  Instead of the word "destroy", you have "destrov".  Instead of the world "following" you have "follawing" and so on.   But I digrees and I'm getting yet another headache even thinking about all this.

As I mentioned earlier, it's possible for your character to become infected; this sometimes happens when a zombie grabs you. When your character becomes infected, the infection will gradually worsen until it kills you. The infection can be held off by consuming pills; but doing so only buys you some extra time, and the infection will eventually come back. And don't forget what I said earlier about medical items being scarce.
The worst part about dying from infection (or just getting killed by a zombie while you're infected), is that your character will then turn into a zombie that is stronger, faster, and more aggressive than the standard zombies. This isn't really your problem (other than the part where you die), but your teammates will have to deal with zombified you (and like I said, zombie you is more dangerous than a normal zombie). If you don't want to turn (or don't want a friend to turn) and nobody has any pills, zombification can be prevented if an infected player is killed by another player. Speaking of which, friendly fire only applies to infected players by default; so if somebody says they're not infected but you think they're lying, you can just swing at them with your melee weapon and see if they take damage (I don't really recommend this, since some servers have friendly fire on at all times).
There are two main gamemodes: survival and objective. Survival maps require you to maintain control of certain areas of the map, with supplies being airdropped to you occasionaly so that you have a fighting chance. Objective maps are kind of like left 4 dead; get from the start of the map to the end with the occasional objective showing up that you have to complete to progress.

On the outside this game looks like an unoptimised mediocre game with glitches, enemies who look like each other, unpolished piece of software one could easily pass on the market. And in solo game it absolutely is just that a 6/10 mediocre game about spy stuff (which i might add are rare and few, almost no one really makes games about spyies these days).
However, the game really shows what it was made for in a 2 man co op this is when the game from a blank canvas with a few brushstrokes over becomes a masterpiece to remember and to set example for generations to come. Its sort of like that old spy trick with invisible inc or concealing something in the plain view - game is so much more then it is when there are 2 people playing it at the same time. The camera monitoring, escaping people on the ground and admins in cyberspace you are both are gonna be always under pressure with just brief moments of respite in between them.
AI is not very good, and difficulty mostly just amps how fast they spot you, with no reaction to opening doors, blood on walls or dropped shell casings.
Maps are few but done with a lot of effort (except tutorial which is absolute garbage). Speaking of tutorial, in game there is a 'footprint' mechanic which tracks down how much evidence you leave behind. Not only does it not explain in detail what counts towards it, whats the error margin, OR you cant check how much you accumulated during mission, i wasted 2.6 hours crawling around for my 'perfect' completion of a single level only to find out that somehow i tripped the security network via hacker interface which i didnt even touch for 99.9% time of that mission. Proposterous.
Futhermore the footprint is supposed to give away how much your activity leaves things visible for all those who want to see on the macro level (the CIA , FSB, MI6 etc) even if we take in my total ♥♥♥♥ up count in an entire playthrough, which were: 1 broken lock, 1 tripped cyber alarm without me tripping it  (THATS IT) the game goes out and says: "Oh you know, you did great and all but we still found you : ) enjoy the base getting wrecked!" Which leads me to think that even if i did it with 0 footprint they would have still found me. Picture this: no visual of me ever caught, not a single gunshot, no one saw me, no camera footage, no KO'ed or killed people.... they still somehow by some miracle know you are there and coming.
Yes it matters for gameplay a bit, since if you are quiet there will be less security the less aware enemies are of your existance, but those few extra guards wont ammount to anything really, it is the macro scale that is supposed to matter.
Next up: inventory ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Before you start mission you need to pick your inventory AFTER that is a briefing. During one of those i hear 'you'll need a gun' i didnt take firearms with me, and im not allowed to drop by the armory to pick one up. Which ultimately worked out great ( NPC just believed that i have a weapon which i didnt scene was hilarious). However for the last mission where i specifically didnt pick a weapon main character WHIPS IT OUT no problem out of thin air like a magician for the cutscene. I wish i could get pagers that way.
All in all game is good, there are very few people who own or even heard about the game making the co op part hard, but its really worth it. For the bold effort and innovative gameplay i give this game a total score of 8/10. It lacks polish, its not very good but it did things AAA projects wont in half a decade. And i know some things could have really made it easier like say pinging on the map to mark things, but this is 1996 there was no such technology back then, hell the bloody entire hacking thing is under a big questionmark as to could you really do all that crazy stuff back then from such distance?
Final Score: 8/10                   (Co-op: 10/10  Solo: 6/10)

If you enjoy eerie games of the 90s, System Shock 2 is the perfect game for you. You are an unnamed soldier given cybernetic upgrades after being recruited as a crew member of U.S.S Iforgotthenameoftheship (sorry). Your recruitment is essential, as it gives tutorials of the different play-styles (guns, technology, and psionics) and, more importantly, your customization options. You're given 3 classes, or rather careers: Marines, Navy, and OSA members. Marines are your standard class if you want to have a run 'n gun experience. Navy Seals specialize in hacking and strength, and OSA members specialize in Psionic abilities. Customization options continue depending on "missions" you take during a "tour" preparing for your career while aboard the ship. I quote these terms because they are not actual missions filled with action, merely filler explanations as to why you start with certain skills.
After performing a your "tours" for three years you are upgraded in your cybernetic form and placed in a cryo pod, only to wake up to ship-wreck crawling with parasite-human hybrids and monkeys. This is where the gameplay begins. It resembles a survival horror game at first, with your only weapon being a bloody wrench. Soon you will discover nanites, or currency, data logs, and cybernetic modules. Data Logs actually contain quintessential information for learning more about the game's story. I actually enjoy listening to them, as they add a new layer of depth to the game. Listening to the logs of now deceased crew members is awfully eerie, meaning that this game is fulfilling its purpose in trying to make the player immersed in an uncomfortable fashion. Cybernetic Modules are the experience points of the game, allowing you to upgrade skills or psionic abilities. These, however, come far and few between, and you have to be prepared to make certain decisions regarding upgrading your skills at upgrade stations because said upgrades are permanent. Do not, I repeat, do not spread your skill points thin. You won't have enough to make it beyond mediocre.
The general atmosphere of the game is very creepy and unsettling. What makes it even more unsettling is the fact that game is set in space, the setting one would least suspect as a subject for horror. Thoughts of a starship exploring the vastness of space usually leaves one with a sense of pride and overall positive thoughts. But this is no U.S.S Enterprise voyage accompanied by Captain Jean Luc Picard himself, or anyone for that matter. You're essentially alone, left to fend off against twisted creatures that were once human, and, more importantly, the highly intimidating, highly intelligent, highly creepy computer AI known as SHODAN. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥is she creepy. Once in a while, when you least expect it, she'll begin a short monologue describing how much inferior you are. Her voice is mangled, fluctuating between an almost human, female tone and a demonic, twisted, deep voice. I almost jumped when she first spoke.
I can safely say that the gunplay is alright, but it is clunky. If you're skill set does not have strong Maintenance, you will discover that guns break quickly, which really gets annoying at times. Furthermore, ammo either runs out quickly, or they cost too many nanites at dispensers (the equivalent to shops). This could either be a good or bad thing. The advantage of limited, expensive ammo is that it adds to the survival-horror element of the game, as it forces the player to conserve ammo and strategize how to plan their next move. The disadvantage is that it can be near impossible to progress without it, especially later in the game when there are more long-ranged threats. Luckily your psionic abilities counter this problem, if you're skilled. Psionic abilities essentially feed off of an energy meter, granting you super powers of sorts. They can come handy, such as the defense and cryokinesis (basic attack) abilities. It definitely adds to the otherwise sketchy combat.
My biggest problem with the game, however, is your inventory interface. The game does not pause while it's up, which leads to many problems. For instance, the only way to switch weapons is to manually do so through the inventory interface. Now imagine that you run out of ammo for a particular weapon while a few hybrids are chasing you down. You don't have enough time to manually switch weapons before being clubbed to death by the hybrids. But you have to switch weapons if you don't want to lose progress being forced to run back. Furthermore, enemies respawn, meaning that if you visit an old area you might run into even more hybrids and monkeys. There is absolutely nothing you can do except die. I tried switching weapons in a similar scenario and managed to survive, only with 11 hit points and no health packs or healing station in sight. It was even against one basic hybrid while I had armor on. To top it all off, when I made it back, there was another hybrid, waiting for me. The enemy-respawn and user hostile inventory interface add questionable difficulty.
If you're a newcomer to this game, like I am, I warn you that this is a very difficult game, even on the normal difficulty. However, System Shock remains as one of the more positively sophisticated and creepy games I have ever played, a game that still deserves to be critically acclaimed by many. Just turn off the music while playing; it ruins the creepy atmosphere.

Played the new Emperor Edition during the free weekend. It seems simplistic next to some of the other Total War titles, but it's strangely addicting and you have to be much more careful in the choices you make, both in building structures and moving armies around. Building an empire feels much longer and more satisfying, as you can't do as much per turn as in some of the other ones.
Land battles are fun but tend to turn into a grindfest. Units take FOREVER to break even if you have them completely surrounded. But you are rewarded for good tactics by taking fewer losses. Unlike other games, losses in battle automatically regenerate, which I really like because in the other games I was always pretty anal about retraining my units. So taking fewer losses doesn't save you money, but it does save you a lot of time regenerating units to their full capacity. Also unlike other games, cities have automatic garrisons in them. In exchange, you cannot station extra troops anywhere you don't have a general, and the number of generals is capped by the size of your empire. Some people complain about this but I actually like it because it forces you to be very careful about positioning. It makes the game more strategic IMO.
I really enjoyed the naval combat, but ships are SLOW on the campaign map. It takes three turns just to get from Italy to Corsica, although I think the fleet slows down as it gets bigger and/or carries more troops. As other reviewers have noted, it's pointless to build a dedicated navy. Just build regular units and instantly transform them into a navy whenever you want. I don't actually mind this because I did really enjoy naval battles.
The political element is okay but seems pointless except to force you to spend money on promoting your leader, only to have him die. The random political problems are annoying because there's no way to tell whether your choice will have a positive or negative effect. Seems random to me. *shrug*
My biggest peeve is the technology research is way too slow to keep up with your economic development, but it does mean you have extra money for armies pretty quickly.
Overall Rome II is worlds better than Rome I, and looks like a great addition to the franchise. It's simple enough to appeal to new players and has enough new game mechanics and twists to appeal to old Total War players. I will definitely buy this game when the price goes down.
(I have played Medieval: Total War, Medieval II: Total War, Rome and Empire)

Product:
"Total War: Rome II" is a major dissapointment for diehard RTW fans, maybe even for fans of Total War in general. The first day of launch was plagued by bugs, glitches, bad optimization and graphic promises that were not kept by developers and advertising. Don't get me wrong I really, really, enjoyed this game for over 50 hours mostly spent on the multiplayer battles. But that didn't stop me from noticing that this game had major flaws. The sale strategy also known as a "Money Grab" is growing daily in the gaming market and will probably become even bigger as the years progress. This game is the perfect example of this. Selling you factions and DLC content that should have been given to players at the start of the game. If not that then as an apology for releasing a close to unplayable product that fell short of promises made durring the eager wait for the release date. I will give them credit though, they did patch 80-90% of the problems... Until the recent update.
Total War: Rome II - Emperor Edition Update
The recent update that hands out "Emperor Edition" makes players re-learn the entire strategy of each faction! Rome has been nerfed to a near useless margin and other factions such as Suebi or Arverni have become more powerful. Armies containing missile cavalry, missile units, and elephants have become the dominant forces seen on the battlefield. What happened to having a long bloody battle with sword units slashing it out untill the bitter end with the game changing cavalry flank? This has mostly been replaced by having a large body of missile units showering your opponent from behind on horses or from almost every meele unit! Thats right! Many, many, many units now have the ability to be more or less javalin throwing troops. This creates an overwhelming habbit of just bringing more and more missile units to finish off the enemy as quickly as possible without actually fighting them.
Conclusion:
Although I am a HUGE fan of the Total War series, things aren't looking good for their community morale. I do have fun on this game, but those moments of fun are quickly followed by the farmiliar realization that this game does have major flaws. This game was a disapointment for me, but it will not stop me from getting excited about the next Total War game. This company has treated me well with HUNDREDS of hours of enjoyment and fresh situations and challenges throughout all of their games. I rate this game 6/10

Alien isolation is a game I've been wanting. Its a deadly game of cat and mouse that tells the story of amanda ripley as she faces what her mother ran into in deep space. Fans who appretiate a stealth game of trial and error all the while dealing with a deteriorating space station and its psychotic AI robots will like this game. If you were expecting a game involving nothing but a complete shooting gallery of alien creatures this game is not for you. If you were expecting a game you can play with friends, this is not for you. If however you like tension and the feeling of being helpless facing things alone I recommend playing it on its hardest difficulty. Its not perfect but it plays on what has been lacking in an Alien game in the past decade.

It was always going to be difficult to make a game worthy of the original Alien movie but Creative Assemby rose to the task and created an absolute classic. Not only was the game filled with tension and terror, it was filled with so much nostalgia that you almost felt like you were back watching the original movie at times.
The graphics are great, although the aliasing is an issue due to the AA options not being great. The sound fits perfectly from the creepy ambient noises to the epic music. And the design of everything in the game was a true nod to the original movie. Everything looked like it had been dreamt up by someone in the 70s trying to predict what the future would look like and for old fans like me, it worked perfectly, even down to the addition of a slight film grain (which could be turned off).
The game itself was terrifying, with the alien AI being brutally good at stalking you, and although there are a few places it feels too scripted, the general feeling you get is one of facing a supremely good predator who is learning your movements just as much as you are trying to learn his.
The game could probably have been a little shorter and still been great, but in general I recommend this game without hesitation to any horror game fans, or any old timers who remember the original Alien movie with fondness (or terror).

Even though i'm not the kind of guy who usually writes reviews (as a matter of fact, this is my first), i thought this masterpiece deserved at least a few (maybe more) worlds of appreciation.
First, let me say that this is, by far, the best game i've probably ever played. Before playing it, my all-time favourite was Half Life 2. Even though this isn't, strictly speaking, an fps, it successfully manages to blend several kinds of gameplay, including the fps, the stealth and the action ones.
What actually blew me away was the attention to details and the general care put in the game. The space station, in which most of the game is played, resembles closely the one of the original, Scott's, "Alien". The technology "feels" the same (lots of analog controls, buttons and textual interfaces) which is exactly, how at the time, the authors of the franchise perceived a possible future. Textures and general aestethics of the game are just great. I usually like to stop from time to time to see things up close out of curiosity and i was astonished by the fact that they apparently never. slacked. off. Every room in every level is rendered meticously. Even though you could argue that artificial environments are easier to get right than vegetation and nature in general, still, they've done a great job.
Apparently, they built their own game engine instead of relying on the usual bloated ones. This is, on its own, a great feat and in my opinion, it further enchance the gamer experience by providing him with unfamiliar but clean and neat-looking visual effects.
The strong point of the game is of course, the struggle to survive the relentless Alien hunt. The creature mostly preys on his sense of hearing and during most of the game, you will be kept on edge to make as little as noise as possible (or as much as possibile, if you want to make a decoy). The alien is basically immortal and is only scared off by fire. Also, this may seem like nothing important, but i found this game does a great job in portraying fire in general (which i always felt was rendered very poorly in games). Synthetics (or androids, if you want) on the other hand, are not as unbeatable as the alien, but offer greater resistance then ostile humans. They're vulnerable to physical attacks, but are highly resistent to fire and will keep advancing even when ignited. They'll usually try to strangle you and you will lose focus while gasping for air (the peculiar use of focus and motion blur is another great thing about this game). For the moment, i've only tried the normal level of difficulty, and i found the a.i. of the enemies very good (especially the alien), however in a few occasions when i was standing right next to them i felt like they should have catched me easily and yet they didn't.
Last but not least, audio-wise this game is just top-notch.
Cons:
1) Approaching the end of the single player campaign, the gameplay will begin to feel a tad bit repetitive (get from point a to b, push this button, restore power, get back to point a, etc..).
2) The characters felt unrealistic and stereotypical. Fortunately, they don't interveen enough to ruin the general experience.
3) <Spoiler alert> I only mention it because i noticed but i don't believe it to be really an issue. In the second Alien movie, it is stated Xenomorph eggs are layed by a queen (which is huge). In the game, the queen can't be seen anywhere in the campaign and yet we can see eggs and facehuggers coming from them. These eggs are also found in strange places like small conduits, where a queen couldn't possibly get. Even so, i'm no alien fanboy (although i enjoyed the movies) so no biggie here.
Verdict:
I have no game-dev experience whatsoever, but, as a programmer myself, this is the game i would certainly love to have made.

This game has a feel for the new when it comes to the Alien franchise. For me, Alien: Isolation was a 15 hour struggle of cat and mouse, the alien hunting me down and sniffing me out; the impact of the first few encounters with the monster felt huge.
The game's been a critical success, getting a lot of great press and making many game of the year lists. Steam at the moment of writing has 5000+ reviews logged which are flagged as 'very positive'. I too would agree, this a great game – outstanding really – but certainly not without its problems which I found close to immersion breaking.
I enjoyed the way the game forces you to sneak. It suits the narrative of the game and makes your controlled protagonist's actions seem believable. I believe Amanda Ripley would sneak around this space station, the survivors and androids being relatively unpredictable along with the alien being lethal. You sneak to avoid the risk of alarm and I thought this was very fitting.
On the other hand, I found constantly sneaking around very tiresome. The alien controls the pacing of the game far too much and as a player you're forced to go along with how the AI has been developed. Stay still and the games pacing is wrecked - move too fast and you get punished. I found it frustrating that the AI seemingly does not adapt to the individual player but rather, you find yourself adapting to the AI's systems.
The uncertainty of the games rules is interesting; throw a flare and distract the alien for a while knowing that it's now close in your vicinity and can potentially hunt you down. Yet after a while the game does show fault here. With enough subtlety and patience you can sneak past any threat.
The narrative is paperthin, and I think it's the games rules which cause a very undercooked story. I focused on saving my game far too much than what was going on in the world. Ripley's own story became tedious for me, as my biggest objective was saving the game. Really, the game became a save-area-loot style game, with the story not mattering much.
Tension is a huge part of Alien: Isolation, and the game creates an amazingly tense atmosphere through the aliens empowerment and your lack of power over the creature.
However, this focus on challenge to create tension was another problem for me. It made the game feel extremely linear and I didn't explore the world much because of the constant threat. My influence in the game world didn't matter so long as I could save the game. The actual narrative itself is not so great either. Frankly, I did not care much for Amanda Ripley or her crew – which is surprising because the world of Alien: Isolation is teeming with nuggets of info and audio dialogs.
If the narrative does not drive this game – and it really doesn't – then it's about putting the player into situations against the alien and having that play out. Indeed, that is enthralling and quite incredible at times. But the games length also turns this into tedium.
It must be said, none of the above is game breaking either. This the first 'survival-horror' game I've played and truly enjoyed in many years (since maybe the first Resident Evil). The atmosphere of the game is wonderful and visually its jaw-droppingly faithful to the 1979 classic. Incidentally, I'm not a huge fan of the film, yet the visual similarities to Ridley Scott's universe in Alien: Isolation are breathtaking.
Despite the problems above, this is a fine game for reasons already explained in the dozens of reviews found elsewhere.
