Clandestine is a unique experience with good writing and a somewhat poor graphics and performance attached to it.
Let's just get right to business with the bad. Yes, it looks like it came straight from the Playstation 2 era and this is not at all encouraging to modern gamers. It even has some occasional issues with the performance, bugs that are somewhat obvious, clunky movement and controls, and it definitely does not look like it brings much new to the stealth genre.
But then why the positive recommendation?
Because where the graphics and performance are questionable, the gameplay itself is solid, the writing is great with excellent attention to detail, and the co-op is a good way to spend time with a friend working things out together. and getting through the story. Which, by the way, changes based on what you do. If you kill everyone because dead men don't tell tales, then you will have a different experience after a few missions than if you went through as a ghost, unseen and unheard.
While some things are easy to see coming from far away, the story as far as I've experienced it makes sense and is intriguing enough to keep you coming back for more. As for the co-op gameplay, it does exactly what many people wanted to do for their stealth games. As the spy, you will rely on your co-op partner to hack into the computer net, get you the information you need to play your undercover role out, block cameras from seeing you, and mess with anything electronic that needs messing with. As the hacker, you will be multitasking to hack into their system in one screen, check the cameras for guards approaching your partner from behind, and work with a map to make sure your partner doesn't get lost in the facilities you're infiltrating. Both roles are rewarding, and working together as a team makes for a unique experience that so far I've not been able to find anywhere else in a game.
(I have not played single player, so I can not mention much on that)
Clandestine can be a real hit, something you will remember for years to come and will hope to see more of if you can see past the obvious flaws and outdated graphics. If you can, I can certainly recommend it.
But if you are big into graphics and are easily frustrated it may not be your kind of thing. Clandestine is a flawed gem. If you can look past the flaws you will have a great time.

Let me preface this with a disclaimer: If you hold appreciation or amusement for the culture of the 90's then you'll love this game, if you're too young to know or remember much of them this game probably isn't for you.
Being the former this was one big nostalgia trip which involved a lot of "WOWWWWW" and laughter; dev's really nailed the immersion and level design. I probably spent 40 minutes or so just running around the agency building marvelling at it all.
Had this game been set in a more modern era I would deride the absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it for being a terrible waste of money. In my honest opinion the AI and stealth is mediocre, the guns and gunplay are♥♥♥♥♥♥ your gadgets are♥♥♥♥♥♥ controls are♥♥♥♥♥♥ the "social engineering" is shallow if you give it so much as a second glance and the graphics are atrocious. Unreal 3, anyone? Now 4? What about Unity 4 and now 5? These kind of graphics really aren't excusable for this kind of genre.
All that said though, whether by design or luck, it all ties into and feeds off each other to create something entirely 90's. Those clunky controls, bad guns and gadgets, the dumb AI, that fairly bad voice acting and occassionally buggy cutscenes. This♥♥♥♥♥♥is glorious, when I play I feel like I'm playing a game in the 90's (Realtalk: It plays how games back then worked when thinking back with nostalgia, not how terrible they are when you actually try). So, I am very unsatisfied with the combat system: as I've played many games that are tagged with survival horror (SH), here's my comparison on why I don't like playing this.
Stealth might not be in every SH game (RE4, Dead Space vs. The Last Of Us), when it is part of it, it should be rewarding. When using stealth, you trade "not using sparse resources" for "waiting for the moment". So, when you sneak upon your enemies to take them down silently, they should be dead. That will not hold with this game, as some (and not the large hunky sort) enemies just don't care and have at you at point blank range, as demonstrated here:
So let's try Melee.
Melee combat: you trade "not getting hit by enemy melee" for "possibly getting hit, while not using resources". In most games I played so far, melee is either your last resort or you decide to do it instead of wasting bullets (stagger zombie, slash face).
Well, first of all, Mr. Detective is using a knife like an Axe or a Hammer. You know, something with weight on it. Not sure who was in charge of that animation.
That might explain why hitting (not slashing, mind you) enemies does next to no damage.
So you'd have to resort to either outlive frantic enemies in your face or start shooting.
Ranged combat: In most games, you kill zombies by aiming for the head, trading "I might miss it and waste ammo" for "if I hit, it's gone". In this game, headshots are nothing zombies have to worry about, as you'll have to upgrade your weapon to even get to a 60% chance of a critical hit counting as such. That's great(?) in RPGs like Mass Effect, but not in a SH genre game.
Enemies behave as frantic as Fallout 4 ghouls or the Dying Light zombies at night. That's fine when I have ample supplies of ammo or high-damage melee attacks, but you get neither.
The weapon "upgrade" system is a joke, very unimaginative nothing interesting to see here.
Larger magazine, more damage, faster reload or upgraded range. That's all I've seen so far.
"Traps": Most traps are easy to spot, as the blinking trigger rope is screaming right at you. Not sure what the point of that is.
1st encounter: in a train, you get into a dead end. Magically, a trapped rope appears out of view and blocks the way. Disable? No. Slash it? No. Shoot it? No. Nothing works, so you walk through it to receive a scripted enemy. Nice reward.
2nd encounter: you spot the rope in after exiting a car shop through the secret cellar. Between the rope and yourself, you see zombies. So you lie in wait for one to spot you, and to die by the trap you spotted. Nice try, u ded. Next try, you trigger the rope, another trapped rope appears and now you'll be able to explode zombies. Nice logic.
So after getting screwed over several times by this games logic I lowered the difficulty setting once and again shortly after. Now I'm stuck with the same mechanics that won't work on the lowest difficulty setting. Nice. Upping the difficulty is disabled, because achievements?
I'm sure that there is great content to be found, as is tradition in Zenimax games. If I could get to it without getting screwed several times by the game's weird logic, it would be fun I guess.

The Evil Within 2 exceeded all my expectations. It is worth every penny.
The game starts out subtle... eventually the tension bleeds its way into your mind until your on the edge of your seat. I'll be playing this game over and over again just like Resident Evil 4, but this game is much more than Resident Evil 4
The Evil Within 2 has open gameplay for you to choose how you want to approach the horror, with a mix of linear connections in between, it has many different weapons, and a great line of characters.
But most importantly the story was beautiful, heart melting, and nerve racking. Like I said... I'll be playing this game over and over and over again.

TL;DR
A vast improvement over the first game in almost every aspect.
If you haven't played the first game, then my review probably wouldn't make much sense because in this review, I am comparing The Evil Within 2 to The Evil Within. Though, I could still argue that this game is objectively good, even when not being compared to The Evil Within.
PROS:
- Graphics are now prettier (Obviously, lmao)
- Gameplay is now open-world while still retaining that survival horror atmosphere. Feel free to explore the area (carefully), find secrets / loot, and pursue secondary objectives!
- New resources are introduced (Weapon parts, red gel) , separate upgrade system for Weapons and Abilities, compared to the first game which uses the green gel to upgrade everything.
- More options for stealthy approaches (e.g: Silenced pistol, using foliage to hide, ambush from cover, and more!) other than just sneak-kills and bottle-tossing in the first game.
- Crafting is introduced. Instead of just crafting crossbow bolts, you can now gather materials to craft some ammunition, or medicine.
- The writers did a lot of good filling the gaps of the story that the first game left behind. We get a lot more about Sebastian's background and his psyche (The main character). The story in this second game is also more captivating and has a direction, unlike in the first game.
- Enemies are still agile. They sprint and dodge more than the first game (At least in the "nightmare"  difficulty that I'm playing in).
- Enemies are still stupid.
- The atmosphere and environmental design is surreal and terrifyingly beautiful, in my opinion.
CONS:
- The Evil Within 2 still has the same framerate issues like its predecessor when it was released. I'm hoping there will  be a patch to fix this soon. That's all the flaws I could think of at the moment.
Overall, I enjoy this game very much.

Black Mesa is a proper up-to-date (for like 2013) remake of
with some artistic license here and there (which I believe was an improvement every time), but mostly sticks 1:1 to the original game. 20€ is not too high a price for this well done creation.
I had played through the much earlier Black Mesa version that was (Or still is.) available for free, and while I enjoyed most of it, I found the sound of trooper radio messages extremely off-putting.
It has convincing soldiers-in-the-field speech that feels like humans, not any longer like someone with sound effects at their disposal tried to make something sound bigger-than-thou.
Gameplay is super hard at times, but you'll manage if you wisely use the toys you have at your disposal (one of which certainly is quickload :P). If all fails (like in the lobby roughly half way through the game), there's still the console that allows you to use god mode. I don't remember if there was a proper FOV slider, but the console certainly has that covered.
If you think "I'll recommend this to people to show them what was so great about Half Life back then.", think again: Scripted events, industrial hazards, and the campaign story to ride on almost every place you get, that was something that broke new ground back then, it showed us the potential of what could be by giving us the first instance of it (as far as I know). But while it's sure a good game, and the right thing to recommend in case you want to talk about Half Life 1, you can hardly convey the discovery of the new world to people who weren't there when it happened.

Dont know what to write, so I will write a recipie for pancakes.
ingredients
100g plain flour
2 eggs
300ml semi-skimmed milk
1 tbsp sunflower oil or vegetable, plus extra for frying
pinch salt
Method
Blending in the flour: Put the flour and a pinch of salt into a large mixing bowl and make a well in the centre. Crack the eggs into the middle, then pour in about 50ml milk and 1 tbsp oil. Start whisking from the centre, gradually drawing the flour into the eggs, milk and oil. Once all the flour is incorporated, beat until you have a smooth, thick paste. Add a little more milk if it is too stiff to beat.
Finishing the batter: Add a good splash of milk and whisk to loosen the thick batter. While still whisking, pour in a steady stream of the remaining milk. Continue pouring and whisking until you have a batter that is the consistency of slightly thick single cream. Traditionally, people would say to now leave the batter for 30 mins, to allow the starch in the flour to swell, but there’s no need.
Getting the right thickness: Heat the pan over a moderate heat, then wipe it with oiled kitchen paper. Ladle some batter into the pan, tilting the pan to move the mixture around for a thin and even layer. Quickly pour any excess batter into a jug, return the pan to the heat, then leave to cook, undisturbed, for about 30 secs. Pour the excess batter from the jug back into the mixing bowl. If the pan is the right temperature, the pancake should turn golden underneath after about 30 secs and will be ready to turn.
Flipping pancakes: Hold the pan handle, ease a fish slice under the pancake, then quickly lift and flip it over. Make sure the pancake is lying flat against base of the pan with no folds, then cook for another 30 secs before turning out onto a warm plate. Continue with the rest of the batter, serving them as you cook or stack onto a plate. You can freeze the pancakes for 1 month, wrapped in cling film or make them up to a day ahead.

Slime Rancher is a cute, fuzzy and warm farming simulator esque game where you explore the wild to find Slimes of various breeds to collect and nurture at your farm.
You start off with in the eyes of Beatrix *who now has a very neat looking 3D model* with little to nothing on a farm containing empty plots, armed with a vac-pack you venture through the currently explorable land to find small slime's who want to hug you and drop "plorts" which are essentially their poop so you sell them for money, or you can use them to fabricate gear in the Slime Science lab once unlocked.
Eventually you will have sold enough wild plorts to start building up your farm, making corral's, farm's, coop's and silo's. You can being to house your own slimes rather than find them in the wild, grow your own assortment of fruit and veg that you discover, look after and breed chicken's as well as store plenty of resources that your pockets can't quite hold yet, but not to worry, you can upgrade your inventory slot capacity as well as your health, maximum energy capacity, lower energy consumption and more. Various upgrades become avaiable as you progress through the game, allowing you to access more, along with the progression comes discovering new lands.
You'll find some large, light-hearted looking slimes called Gordos, these lovable lumps of joy require feeding, a lot of it too. Feed them and something might happen, who knows?
It's important to know what your slimes love, cross-breeding slimes helps with this, you can feed 1 type of slime, say a pink slime, a phosphor plort, doing so will create a Largo, which are slimes that have cross-bred, it will now produce 1 pink slime plort and 1 phosphor slime plort, meaning you can be more efficiant with your food while making more plorts. The reason I mentioned learning about what your slimes love is because not all type of slimes will eat the same thing, some will only eat veg, some fruit, others meat, but if you know what their favourite food is, largos will love both types of food from either of their original breed, producing double the plorts upon feeding.
This game is all about exploring, enjoying the company of your slimes, expanding your farm and snazzing out your equipment.
Considering this game is about £15/$19/16EURO, I'd say it's worth it, even if it was breaching the £20 mark, I would still get it, the models and visuals for this game are very pleasent, the gameplay is very relaxing and almost therapeutic, simple down to the core but engaging at the same time. The soundtrack is made by none other than Harry Mack, so it's got the feint Spiral Knights hint to it which is pleasent. Updates are regular too which is a bonus that cannot be ignored, the team have a Roadmap showing what ideas they have for future updates, the work and love behind this game is great and of course the community too.

Half of the fun of the original King's (and especially Space) Quest was finding ways to die, since the animations were often funny or gruesome, and typically had mocking quips from the narration. An awesome idea hampered by very poor execution. Bugs, glitches, terrible stealth stickyness hamper a really clever idea for asymmetrical stealth.

It would be better to have a bunch of entirely unlinked missions with no background.
Hacking is fun, but could stand improvement. For one, there is absolutely no indication ANYWHERE that you need to press the magic button "v" to jack into remote systems. In addition, most nodes are useless and don't do anything. It'd be fantastic if I could actually disable cameras for a few minutes instead of just babysitting them and not being able to see anything of the agent.
Stealth suffers severely from bad sticky mechanics, and forcing doors is painful - there's no ui hint and it's easy to alert a lot of guards. It'd also be nice if stealth had some semblance of a map that the hacker could point things out on or draw on instead of "Go East... now go South.. Now go east again"
Great basic idea, bad execution. Would love to see this remade on a remotely modern engine. Might be a viable buy if it's < $5.

EDIT: I have tried to go through and make changes to my review where the game has changed (e.g. bug fixes, tutorial improvements, etc), but I may have missed some.  The game has gotten several patches since this was initially posted, so I might be shining a slightly harsher light on it than it now deserves.
Warning: Unmarked Potential Spoilers Ahead
The game is definitely rough around the edges, there's no denying that.  I discovered in Copenhagen that I can grab guards through walls (they'll just teleport to me), and I've had some other assorted bugs, but on the whole my friend and I had a good time playing the game.  Overall I think I'd give it a 7/10; the cutscene graphics definitely drag it down a bit, and the voice acting could be better, but the core concept and gameplay are well done.
Some negative observations/thoughts:
There's kind of a disconnect in between what the spy is doing and what the hacker is doing.  It took me a while to figure out that little blue cross cursor is what the hacker is currently accessing, which helps.  Maybe the asymmetry of it took us some getting used to because my hacker friend seemed to be doing things more fluidly after a while.  The disconnect comment comes right from him.  Also, marking more than three enemies would be useful; three seems to be a tad too small.  EDIT: The hacker bug mentioned previously (hacker can't move in the HQ between missions) was acknowledged as a bug and quickly fixed.
The game could use some better explanations of how the various mechanics work.  The starting tutorial is good, but could use some more explanations of things like Footprint.  EDIT: The confusion with breaking locks has been cleared up in the forums and an improved tutorial bubble has been implemented /EDIT.  Copenhagen was an utter disaster in terms of getting spotted; at the end I had seven bodies.  My friend went to use Cleaner, but we didn't know exactly how it worked.  So on our way out, having failed to use it properly, the bodies were discovered, leaving witnesses and a giant footprint.  What's the difference between crouching and walking, if neither makes noise?  Maybe I missed it, but why would you use one over the other?  How does the hacker gets more/refill their abilities?  I know they unlock via Intel scores, but do they refresh every mission?  I think so because I haven't found a way to buy any.
As I said above, I encountered a bunch of bugs.  I didn't get any gamebreaking bugs, but I would say they definitely qualify as something bigger than minor.  For example, while in the crime scene in Copenhagen, I was able to grab one of the guards through the wall.  He just teleported into the room and I went through the knockout animation.  In Warsaw, after the conversation with Baxter, I chose to knock him out and my hacker partner didn't see the knockout; just him falling over.  Also in Warsaw, I had an ammo drop fail to give me any ammo for my PPK; it said that I had refilled my ammo, but when I went to use the PPK it said I had no ammo left!  I think there was an issue loading, though; I had just blown my cover a minute earlier (the ammo pickup worked fine then) and had to reload the checkpoint, after which I got the buggy ammo pickup.  Fortunately, I didn't need the PPK again that mission.  The game could also use a pass over the collision detection, as well.  I had a handful of clips through various objects/NPCs during the levels.  A Bug Reports subforum would probably be of use.
Crashes: a few for both of us.  One of his crashes was related to mine, I believe, because I crashed and he followed suit a moment later.  I think my crashes were related to using NVidia's Dynamic Super Resolution, where it renders at at 3840x2160 and then downsamples to 1920x1080; I set the resolution just to 1920x1080 and I haven't had a problem since.  Of course, I verified the game cache, and it validated all the files.
The graphics could use a pick me up.  They're not terrible, and I'm perfectly fine with the mission graphics, but the cutscene graphics are pretty rough for a 2015 game.  Sarah especially looks like she's perpetually sucking lemons.  EDIT: Unfortunately, Josiah's fumanchu no longer does that hysterical clipping with his chin (aka it was fixed).
Positive observations/thoughts:
The core idea is brilliant.  I compare it to a coop Alpha Protocol, a game which was panned by critics (and similarly buggy lol), but a game I personally still love and play through every now and again.  Where this game really started to shine was the London and Warsaw missions.  Not every mission is like Mexico or Copenhagen, where you have to always sneak around in the shadows.  It was really thrilling to be wandering around the London office and the Warsaw party blending in with the enemies and then branching off to quickly do a task.  I think it was wonderfully executed, and I hope the same pattern continues for the last few missions.  This is, I think, where the game really shines and excels.
I think the spy's controls were well done.  There's nothing too crazy to do as the spy, but the movement and mantling especially felt much improved even just from version 0.9, which is when I picked it up.  It seems like you've got a good range on your cover takedowns, although I wish the enemies didn't teleport a foot or two over if they're too far.
Gunplay is decent.  You're not quite as in trouble if it comes to shooting as you would be in older Splinter Cell games (can't speak to Conviction+), and if you're quick on the draw you can shoot before your enemies draw, but the gunplay isn't anything out of the ordinary, either.  I feel like a tightening of the cursor over time would be of benefit instead of the quick shrink to the size that it is.  There's no zoom either, which is ok I guess since it's close range, but it would be "nice".
Once you get into a groove, it's possible to really synergize well with your coop partner.  The game would have benefitted from in game voice chat, however, having played both with the text chat and on TeamSpeak with a friend, there's just no substitute for the voice chat.
Overall, like I said, I think I'd give it a 7.5/10.  It's rough and it needs a good coat of polish (EDIT: Which they seem to be sticking around to give), but there's a solid game under there.  I bought multiple copies during an Early Access sale (sorry to see the two pack go!) and I don't regret any of my purchases.  We both had fun tonight, and will definitely continue even after we beat it; it'll be my turn to be the hacker and we'll see if we can beat our previous performance.  I believe there's some element of randomization in the levels so hopefully it won't be just us memorizing patterns/locations.
I don't want to make it seem like I used reams of paper for the negatives and just have a few tiny paragraphs for the positives, but I wanted to a) be specific about the negatives in the hopes that it can help improve the game, b) I'm a little tired, but more importantly c) I'm having trouble putting my thoughts into words for the positives.  It's easy to point out the bugs and the things you believe need improvement, but aside from saying I think they have a wonderful idea here and really nailed some of these missions (Warsaw!) with how you weave in and out of clandestine actions (pardon the pun), it's hard to describe it.  I don't make YouTube videos but I hope someone can make some and show off more gameplay post-release to give people an idea of what I'm talking about.
Anyway, I hope this will give prospective buyers a decent look into the state of the game immediately post release, maybe help assuage some fears, or pique some curiousities.  I mark it as Recommended, but caveat it with "if you're planning on playing coop".  Singleplayer, I think the roles are two complex to try to multitask them.

Clandestine is a third person (two player co-op) (action-)stealth game that personally reminded me a bit of Alpha Protocol. Both are heavily focused on stealth and hacking, but both also control kind of similar.
Let it be known, however, that Clandestine is a game of its own and while there’s definitely room for technical improvements the game in this state is already fun to play. That’s right, even in single-player. It’s still best played with a friend or partner, though, since the game is focused on a co-op experience. In any case; let us talk about the single-player aspect of the game a bit more, which is was I played for myself.
You’re pretty much dropped right into the first level without too much of an explanation. You’re then taught the basic movements and how to hack electronic devices. If you play by yourself then this information might be a little overwhelming at first, especially if you’re being taught the hacker side of the game. Still, it’s nothing too complex and with a little practice you should do just fine.
The first level is, for a prologue, rather large, and after an introduction of about 10 minutes, you’re tasked with planting several bugs (optional) and getting to the basement, preferably without being seen/spotted. As a single-player experience you will have to do everything yourself and this in turn lowers the tension a bit, which is to be expected and I’m not going to blame the game for it. In co-op, however, each player will just see his or her part of the game: the hacker will see the four panels (camera, map, network and console) while the other person will have to physically get through the level by (quietly) moving around, collecting data and killing/knocking out/distracting enemies.
There are a total of 7 levels, excluding the prologue/tutorial level and each one can be played with a completely different playstyle. You don’t have to use stealth per se. The choice is yours: if you want go to through a level trying to remain undetected that’s fine. And if you want to go in guns blazing you can do this, too. And if that still doesn’t suit you then you can mix things up and use a combination of both, for example. You are completely free to choose how you want to approach each level.
Controls wise – and this is for the third person part - the game plays a bit similar to games like Alpha Protocol or the Gothic or Risen series. It doesn’t feel really fluent or even connected, but it doesn’t feel weird or slow either. I think people call it ‘janky’ these days. If you’ve played the game I just mentioned then you should understand what I mean.
The third person part of the game is really good and feels grounded: enemies don’t have superhuman sight or hearing and they react mostly realistically. It has an authentic, realistic feel, while also still feeling like an actual game. I appreciated that a lot personally.
Should an enemy notice your attention then a meter fills up until you get either out of sight or kill him/knock him out. If the meter fills up entirely then all guards in the nearby area will be alerted. Same goes for being detected on security cameras, by the way.
Enemies don’t have the ability to ‘one-shot’ you but they do inflict a lot of damage if you’re reckless. If you’re caught between several guards then it’s likely you will not even survive the fight so it’s important that you’re careful and just take your time. Overall, the game seems to have a good balance in difficulty.
Playing the hacker is a little more passive, but I think it can still be very rewarding if you can pull of
perfect mission. Although it may be more passive it’s in no way boring.
Anyway, as a hacker you will have to keep an eye on things with the office and building cameras and tag potential enemies for your buddy to see. Tagged enemies can be seen through the walls so it’s a good way to prevent your team member from getting spotted. You will also have access to the map so you can give directions and whenever your buddy logs in to an electronic device you can then try to hack it. Sometimes you will also have to get access codes and these then have to be sent by chat (or remembered in case of single-player) which adds to the authenticity of it all. It’s a really cool and neat idea.
Both characters play completely different and that’s why it’s so great to have a game like this.
While the game is pretty linear - as in: there’s really only one way to complete a level - there still are plenty of big areas and rooms where you can take a different route. But these routes nearly always end up at the same location so it’s more an illusion of freedom, really. But it’s still way better than making/keeping everything linear; I appreciate the effort that was put into making it feel like you have freedom, although ‘true’ freedom would obviously be better (but I understand there are constraints to game developing).
The audio is pretty good. Characters use their native language (Russians speak Russian, et cetera) and the voice acting is mostly solid. Sounds effects are also generally well done.
Graphically it isn’t the most advanced game. Characters have just enough detail but the faces could definitely use some work. The textures range from okay to good. The environments on the other hand sometimes feel a bit empty. It’s a bit of a mixed bag, but this is yet another game that’s all about the gameplay and not the graphics. Still, there’s some work to be done.
If you each take your time each mission could take anywhere between 30-60 minutes to complete. And then you can switch characters. Or try go get a better score. Or try a different playstyle. I think that with a solid friend/partner you could put at least 15 hours or more into it.
For single-player it might not be completely worth the full asking price, but if you can find someone to play it with then it’s well worth your time, and money.
Pros:
+ A great mix of stealth (active) and hacking (more passive)
+ Large, semi-linear, levels
+ Feels realistic/authentic
+ Cool, asymmetrical experience
Mixed:
+/- Enemies aren’t terribly clever/observant
+/- To get the best experience you really need to have a friend or partner.
Cons:
- It still has a bit of a janky feel at the moment
(Ratings aren’t calculated based on a formula, but on my personal feelings)

Lets start off with what this game is comparable to.
The first Rome total war spans over a much longer period of time with many more factions. It was much more complex with city management but there was an auto-manage button. The AI wasn't to great but it didnt ruin the game.
Now Rome II is garbage.
Pros
Graphics(as if that would be a reason to buy the game)
Prologue was actually fun
Total war Encyclopedia in game
Generals are also politician
Cons
Tutorial teaches you NOTHING
City management
Poor AI
Difficulty Jump
Autoresolve
Naval System
Confusing Tech tree
Confusing building system
UI is a mess
Diplomatic AI
Limited units unless you buy the dlc
Can't Merge Units
Multiplayer bugs
Lets tackle these individually
Pros
The total war encyclopedia is very helpful when you want to look up a units stats and maybe a little history. It was not helpful however when looking up tech trees and building trees
A Cool Aspect of the game is your generals can rise through the ranks of your family as you use them
Cons
-Doing all of the tutorials and they don't teach you about: Tactics, Diplomacy, Politics, Regional management, Unrest.
-City management is a confusing mess. Each city has smaller cities part of their region. They all share bonuses(including population). So if you can recruit in one city you can recruit in the whole region. My problem is they don't tell you that. They also don't tell you anything about edicts and the requirements for those. You also can't build things like walls in sub-cities(I am looking at your Jerusalem)
-The AI is consistently dumb. Sometimes they get stuck on boats when doing a landing, and sometimes the enemies general will walk to the edge of the map and stay there. Your long term "Friends" will betray you instantly if you don't have your cities well guarded(even if you share a common enemy).
-There is a massive difficulty jump when switching from any faction besides Rome. Rome can just walk across the map, but you can easily spend 50 turns doing nothing as the germans or british. This is because each city has a large garrison and they can reinforce armies.
-In Rome 2 they added a little more control over autoresolve. However autoresolve has no idea how to judge your odds. 1 extra group for the enemy will drop your chances down to 1/5. Also expert units don't seem to make a difference, and you can destroy anyone with just a ton of slingers.
-The naval system is completely over powered. Each ship carries a full set of troops that can get off their boats and attack cities. Even if you kill an entire unit the boat doesn't disappear. They also require less researches to get epic boats(including onagers).
-The tech tree and buildings are mostly unique to the faction(which is a plus) but it offers no advice on what to get or what future things offer. Sometimes you can unlock powerful unique troops by getting a religous building but you wont know unless you make those choices. The tech tree is split up into obscure categories that don't offer you any real reason to go for a specific tech when you start. Unless you know what everything unlocks you will find yourself starting a research when you can't build something, and you have to waste time to advance.
-The user interface is so confusing and is very pointless. You will find yourself search through all the tabs just to figure out why you are having a civil war. You can easily ignore most of the buttons until you have a problem because the tutorial doesn't go over the interface at all, and you won't bother figuring them all out because some of them do nothing.
-Diplomacy is probably the most frustrating thing in the entire game. Your allies will betray you. You sometimes have to pay thousands of gold for a non-agression pact. Sometimes people from across the world will give you money and ask for ridiculous things(like an alliance). Some people will completely refuse to trade even if you offer 4k gold. Their diplomats will want something but via audio will insult you.
-You are seriously limited in gameplay unless you buy dlc. More then half the nations you cannot play.
-You can't merge injured units(like in the previous games). I even went out of my way to look this up. You have to either disband them all and re-recruit or what like 8 turns in a city.
-In Multiplayer, desyncs were frequent and sometimes you will find out 10 turns in the future that you desynced ruining the save. You have to start over or manually send them the save file.
Overall, This game was a huge disappointment. I have played all the total wars and beaten them all except this one. The most I'd pay for this broken unfocused game is 10 bucks with all the dlc. It is seriously disappointing that their is so much dlc and they still want 60 bucks for this game. They seem to have invested in things that the total war fans don't care much about. If you have any interest in playing a total war game save your time and money and just play shogun 2 which is a much more polished and focused game. Rome 2 was a catastophic failure and couldn't deliver on any level of satisfaction. With buggy AI and completely lame intricacies this game has destroyed my hopes for this series, and alienated me with Creative Assembly's future projects.

Let's start of by talking about the game.

-Eternal Senia is a free, storytelling focused ARPG. It largely references Ragnarok Online (both Senia and Magalena are based on enemies of Ragnarok Online) since it's the creator's favourite game.

You don't need to click anything to attack, you just walk towards the enemy and you deal damage, while suffering some damage at the same time. That's it, simple as that.
>Skills
You also have acess to skills, that you unlock during gameplay. As you kill enemies you get SP points, that you use to upgrade your skills.
>Crafting
Yea, this game has crafting. Every time an enemie dies, it has a chance to drop a crafting material, that you can use to make better weapons and armor. Materials are dungeon specific, so don't expect to find some
in the
. You can also upgrade the weapons/armor you craft, by using the weapon/armor you crafted and the extra materials you need. You can upgrade an item 3 times, and at the 3rd time the item will be of Legendary Class (important if you want to complete all the quests).
>Quests
Of couse, you have the main quest, that is to
, but you also have the secondary quests. Every time you get to the end of a dungeon, in the room immediatly before the boss room, there will be 3 NPC's: Jack in the Chest, Slime and the LEGENDARY SHEEP! These 3 will give you a quest (the same for all the dungeons). Jack's quest is to
, Slime's quest is to
and LEGENDARY SHEEP's LEGENDARY QUEST is to
. These quests aren't mandatory (you can complete the game without doing any of these quests), but I strongly recommend you to do these quests, expecially Jack's quest, because

>Dungeons
As you play the game, you are going to go through 3 Dungeons,
, each with their own enemies, drops and items. (Not going to say more because there isn't anything more to say xD)
>Bosses
In each dungeon you will find huge versions of the normal enemies of said dungeon, those are bosses and you need to kill them if you want to get the stuff to craft LEGENDARY ITEMS. They are very, very easy to beat, because they don't have ANY AI. They won't attack you, they won't even move. TIP:

As I said in the beggining, you can change the difficulty of the bosses. That only applies to the floor bosses. Before you enter the boss room, when you interact with the door to the boss room, you will get the options to put the boss in easy, normal or hard difficulty. This doesn't affect the ending.
>Endings
Eternal Senia has 3 endings. One "bad", one "feels" and one "normal?". Your performance before the ending doesn't affect what ending you get. Go read a guide about that. I recommend
>Final Thoughts
This game is marvelous. The story is good, the gameplay is good and simple, the music is awesome and, best of all, it's FREE! You seriously don't have any reason NOT to try out this game.

Ok first off, this isn't so much a bad game. This game could very well have the best graphics of any Total War game Ive ever played. Ive also been very impressed with Creative assembly and their Total War sries for providing great strategy games, historical notes, and a realness to the campaigns that just isn't on other RTS games. Sadly, this game has alot of problems that other TW games dont have, thus the thumbs down.
The cons of this game:
Soldier cards while in battle. They're black shapes of men, like ancient artwork. Which is really annoying in battle. Cause, while Im trying to move my troops around to engage, and hopefully, get the best results from the engagement, I got to keep hovering over the troop cards to ensure Im not sending my slingers to the front and my spearmen to a slingers position. The fact that, 2-4 versions of the spearmen are available, and only difference is how they are holding the spear, only adds to the confusion.
The Grand Capmaign. Where to begin with that? Ill start off with, the map. Feels like the Ice Age is over and the cavemen are now starting to form tribes, despite the fact the starting year is listed as 272 BC. Next, the map is only so big. Yet, there is SO many Ai tribes, with strange, unheard of names and every shield emblem imaginable.  Its hard to believe the map is even big enough for all of them. The campaign also needs help explaining the different researchs, how to increase food production, etc. Felt like the more I researched, the less production! And, didn't seem to be any farming building to build. Yet, my soldiers were dieing of food shortage.
Battlefield camera controls. They stink. As you go left and right, it swings you in a wide arc, making it hard to be sure your even moving towards the units you wished to move/command. Which then makes it tough to do your battle plan and ensure you dont take heavy loss's.
The units seem to not be numbered. On medieval TW or Empires TW, you might recruit a unit of 45 calvary. On Rome, you dont seem to have a set number of soldiers in any unit.
The few pros I did find:
The battles are a bit realistic. I saw a horse riding away from the battle, riderless. Empires and Medieval dont have that.
Each general character you recruit, his army is given a name and can choose an emblem, which does not happen on Medieval or Empires.
Overall, not worth the $60 price it has. $20 is the highest I would ever pay for this, if I ever chose to buy this game. Its not a bad game and at least worth a try. But its not the best Total War game and I wouldn't recommend it to new Total War fans. I'd recommend Medieval Total War 2 for swords, spears, and archer warfare or Empires Total War for much better experiences.
Note: I bought Medieval Total War through Amazon, not Steam, thus why Medieval TW aint on my Steam library.

Black Mesa is a proper up-to-date (for like 2013) remake of
with some artistic license here and there (which I believe was an improvement every time), but mostly sticks 1:1 to the original game. 20€ is not too high a price for this well done creation.
I had played through the much earlier Black Mesa version that was (Or still is.) available for free, and while I enjoyed most of it, I found the sound of trooper radio messages extremely off-putting.
It has convincing soldiers-in-the-field speech that feels like humans, not any longer like someone with sound effects at their disposal tried to make something sound bigger-than-thou.
Gameplay is super hard at times, but you'll manage if you wisely use the toys you have at your disposal (one of which certainly is quickload :P). If all fails (like in the lobby roughly half way through the game), there's still the console that allows you to use god mode. I don't remember if there was a proper FOV slider, but the console certainly has that covered.
If you think "I'll recommend this to people to show them what was so great about Half Life back then.", think again: Scripted events, industrial hazards, and the campaign story to ride on almost every place you get, that was something that broke new ground back then, it showed us the potential of what could be by giving us the first instance of it (as far as I know). But while it's sure a good game, and the right thing to recommend in case you want to talk about Half Life 1, you can hardly convey the discovery of the new world to people who weren't there when it happened.

TL;DR
Pros:
- Good Story
- Thrill of being hunted from beginning to end
- Unexpected shock moments
- Good Graphics and lightning
- Crafting system (!)
- Scarce resources
- "Rare" Safe Points (not rare, but you'll be happy to reach some)
Cons:
- some minor bugs (not game blocking at all, should probably not even put it into Cons)
- not correct lip sync (at least for me)
- backtracking (running through the same areas again seemed to be a bit boring and mindnumbing)
- crashed 2-3x on me
Details:
I LOVE this game.
This is THE Alien game I've been waiting for and what the Alien series deserves.
Okay, it's not perfect (had some very minor bugs, the game crashed on me 2-3 times and the backtracking in the game can be a bit annoying and mind numbing), but appart from those small issues it's just awesome!
I've played through the game on Hard (well, discription said this is the best experience, so I went from it from the start :P) and never changed the difficulty, though I was cursing sometimes.
Humans and Working Joes (they are annoying...) are pretty predictable and easy to avoid.
But the Alien, ohhh, the Alien. It's soo unpredictable in it's movement. The AI for it is BRILLIANT.
It checks out stuff and seems to be constantly on your trail.
It seems to change direction randomly and also the speed it moves when searching for you.
The creepiest moment I had was when it was completely silent.
Usually when you hide you can hear it (tab, tab, tab - from it walking), but at one point I was hiding under a table and it walked just past it, shock moment for me, seeing the feet and tail from it suddenly walk past it, without any sound, then it turned around and moved faster again and I could hear the walking sound again - OMG - scary. If I went out a bit earlier cause I assumed it was safe, I'd be dead.
You also can not outrun it (maybe if you're lucky to break line of sight quick enough and hide, but in the rarest of cases you'll manage to). If it spots you, usually you are dead.
Later on you can scare it off with your Flamethrower and Molotovs - but fuel and resources are scarce and it takes ~50 Flamethrower fuel to scare it off (except it was already charging at you and very close to you, but then you lose HP, not something you really want either - since holding breath in lockers when the Alien checks it out costs you HP).
I was sneaking through almost the whole game, not even walking normally and never sprinting (except at the beginning and the end of the game, when it was safe and when you kinda had to), always afraid I'd attract the Alien, which I wanted to avoid, since when it comes to check out the area, it stays for a while - much easier to get around if it's just crawling in the vents above you (even though hearing it clattering through it is creepy too....).
And a Working Joe + Alien combination? Me curseing!
The Saving System is great too!
I was never so happy to see Safe Points.
No real autosafe (just sometimes after some major points), no quick safe - only specific points you can safe.
And those even require you to stand still for ~3 secs before you can use it.
My friend was laughing at me, when we were talking while I played the game and I was like "OMG, A SAFE POINT - quick, I gotta get to it!"
The game also has its intense shock moments.
Like: I was checking out a room, no enemies close by, quest pointer guiding me different direction (I just wanted to explore), no music indicator something might happen, and then BOOM, huge explosion with intense sound out of no where, knocking me back. Shocked in first moment - once I recovered I was so excited and happy. THIS is what I want from a game, a thrill.
And that's what I got.
Voice Acting is good too (lip sync seemed to be a bit off, might just have been me though)
I didn't buy the DLCs, and I most likly wont's (I'm not a fan of DLCs, silly money baiting for minor content), so I can't say anything about that and I still gotta try out Survivor Mode - but the Story Mode is just great.
So I can fully recommand this game (I bought it with a Christmas Deal - but to be honest, it's worth the full price of 50€)

The Evil Within 2 exceeded all my expectations. It is worth every penny.
The game starts out subtle... eventually the tension bleeds its way into your mind until your on the edge of your seat. I'll be playing this game over and over again just like Resident Evil 4, but this game is much more than Resident Evil 4
The Evil Within 2 has open gameplay for you to choose how you want to approach the horror, with a mix of linear connections in between, it has many different weapons, and a great line of characters.
But most importantly the story was beautiful, heart melting, and nerve racking. Like I said... I'll be playing this game over and over and over again.

TL;DR
A vast improvement over the first game in almost every aspect.
If you haven't played the first game, then my review probably wouldn't make much sense because in this review, I am comparing The Evil Within 2 to The Evil Within. Though, I could still argue that this game is objectively good, even when not being compared to The Evil Within.
PROS:
- Graphics are now prettier (Obviously, lmao)
- Gameplay is now open-world while still retaining that survival horror atmosphere. Feel free to explore the area (carefully), find secrets / loot, and pursue secondary objectives!
- New resources are introduced (Weapon parts, red gel) , separate upgrade system for Weapons and Abilities, compared to the first game which uses the green gel to upgrade everything.
- More options for stealthy approaches (e.g: Silenced pistol, using foliage to hide, ambush from cover, and more!) other than just sneak-kills and bottle-tossing in the first game.
- Crafting is introduced. Instead of just crafting crossbow bolts, you can now gather materials to craft some ammunition, or medicine.
- The writers did a lot of good filling the gaps of the story that the first game left behind. We get a lot more about Sebastian's background and his psyche (The main character). The story in this second game is also more captivating and has a direction, unlike in the first game.
- Enemies are still agile. They sprint and dodge more than the first game (At least in the "nightmare"  difficulty that I'm playing in).
- Enemies are still stupid.
- The atmosphere and environmental design is surreal and terrifyingly beautiful, in my opinion.
CONS:
- The Evil Within 2 still has the same framerate issues like its predecessor when it was released. I'm hoping there will  be a patch to fix this soon. That's all the flaws I could think of at the moment.
Overall, I enjoy this game very much.

This game isn't what I was hoping for. I loved the first EW, but this one just lost whatever it was the first game had. The mobs almost are always in 3's, walking the same pattern, and are often complete bullet sponges. Stealth just doesn't feel right and you can tell all the enemies have the same detection radius. The controls are fairly unresponsive. You need to crank up the default sensitivity. Dodging and spending your green goop on the kick reflex appears to be broken. You'll find yourself running away from mobs at times, only to be stopped by invisible barriers. Some boxes you can climb, others you can't. There will be boxes with a gap just big enough to fit though, at least that's what you'll think. There are a lot of boxes. I've died serveral times being cornered running into what I thought was an escape path, only to find an invisble wall. Oh, and you'll be placed before the cut scene after you die more often than not, making you watch the same garbage again.
It feels like it's trying to be open world, but it grabs the controls out of your hand so often to say, "Hey! You need to look at this! LOOK AT IT!!! Go THIS WAY!!!" It gives you strange dialog choices, but they don't matter at all. You get three dialog options, and none of them matter. You can completely ignore them, listen to all three, but it makes no difference. After you exhausted the dialog options, it will prompt you to speak again, but there is nothing new. I like the corny dialog, but I see no reason to give you any options in these dialog trees other than to give you a false sence of choice. They could have just had them in a cut scene, which are plenty.
The game has it's moments, the beggining is very well done. Once you get to the main section of the game, it just loses itself. I would not call it a horror game. It's an action game with mild gore. It has it's edgy moments, but they're pretty tame. You can feel the games desire to be psychological horror, like Twin Peaks or Silent Hill. However, it relies on telling the player how to feel and completely misses the point.
Performance was fine for me. I see a lot of folks complain, but I'm running a 960 on high settings and it runs just fine. However, the laziness of the environment creation is nothing a graphics card will make up for. I've seen trees clipping through fences, floating boxes, horrible lighting that feels like some playstaion 2 era stuff. It feels rushed. Some areas got the polish, but most didn't. Unfortunatley, the area that you are mostly in, did not get said polish.
Story has no mystery. You're a detective, but there is no detecting. The game just tells you flat out, hey, this is where you are. In the first game, I was asking myself "What's going on?" This one, you know the answer from the start.
Overall, I'm going to keep playing it. Only becuase I dropped $60 on it.

Hmm I see still no neutral way to comment on game, so guess Ill have to use the thumbs down.
Ok first off, this isn't so much a bad game. This game could very well have the best graphics of any Total War game Ive ever played. Ive also been very impressed with Creative assembly and their Total War sries for providing great strategy games, historical notes, and a realness to the campaigns that just isn't on other RTS games. Sadly, this game has alot of problems that other TW games dont have, thus the thumbs down.
The cons of this game:
Soldier cards while in battle. They're black shapes of men, like ancient artwork. Which is really annoying in battle. Cause, while Im trying to move my troops around to engage, and hopefully, get the best results from the engagement, I got to keep hovering over the troop cards to ensure Im not sending my slingers to the front and my spearmen to a slingers position. The fact that, 2-4 versions of the spearmen are available, and only difference is how they are holding the spear, only adds to the confusion.
The Grand Capmaign. Where to begin with that? Ill start off with, the map. Feels like the Ice Age is over and the cavemen are now starting to form tribes, despite the fact the starting year is listed as 272 BC. Next, the map is only so big. Yet, there is SO many Ai tribes, with strange, unheard of names and every shield emblem imaginable.  Its hard to believe the map is even big enough for all of them. The campaign also needs help explaining the different researchs, how to increase food production, etc. Felt like the more I researched, the less production! And, didn't seem to be any farming building to build. Yet, my soldiers were dieing of food shortage.
Battlefield camera controls. They stink. As you go left and right, it swings you in a wide arc, making it hard to be sure your even moving towards the units you wished to move/command. Which then makes it tough to do your battle plan and ensure you dont take heavy loss's.
The units seem to not be numbered. On medieval TW or Empires TW, you might recruit a unit of 45 calvary. On Rome, you dont seem to have a set number of soldiers in any unit.
The few pros I did find:
The battles are a bit realistic. I saw a horse riding away from the battle, riderless. Empires and Medieval dont have that.
Each general character you recruit, his army is given a name and can choose an emblem, which does not happen on Medieval or Empires.
Overall, not worth the $60 price it has. $20 is the highest I would ever pay for this, if I ever chose to buy this game. Its not a bad game and at least worth a try. But its not the best Total War game and I wouldn't recommend it to new Total War fans. I'd recommend Medieval Total War 2 for swords, spears, and archer warfare or Empires Total War for much better experiences.
Note: I bought Medieval Total War through Amazon, not Steam, thus why Medieval TW aint on my Steam library.

Minimal expectations in mind, I took my time to look at all the playable factions; theres a "decent" amount regardless of DLC, however the number of actual nations is just so vast compared to other games.
Anyway, picked the Kingdom of Pontus in what is modern day turkey or so, and soon as i started playing I was hooked.
Diplomacy has improved slightly since Shogun 2, AI nations actively try to earn favour and security from their neighbours with a will to survive rather than conquer others, unless survival means to conquer (unless their barbarians, to which they will only listen if you're giving them a swirly).
On a strategic view battles now feel more important to me, due to the lack of armies; it makes victory more valuable and losing will have a relatively severe affect on the security of your nation, leaving gaps in your frontlines; and in that respect wars should be planned accordingly.
Knowing the crushing details about this games release, I feel that most of the ideas and details have been decently ironed out over the past year or so, thought it is missing a few things that would have been nice to include, such as trading territory. Still I genuinely think the 30 hours I've put into it was time well spent.

As a preface, I feel a need to mention that this game is a fine purchase for about ten dollars, not sixty.
The UI is incredibly convoluted. You cannot just click on  a province and get all the information. You have to choose from a submenu of villages, which makes sense somewhat, and adjacent provinces, which makes absolutely no sense. Everything has its own button, so things get a little cumbersome. You also cannot zoom out far enough to see more than one province, probably because the game hasn't been optimized since that would leave no time for making DLC, and allowing the player to do so with any level of graphics settings would result in a melty plastic and metal pizza where the video card once was.
This same paradigm has been employed in the battle mode, where things get really frantic really fast. The most commonly used formation, spread formation, has been hidden under two submenus. I cannot concieve of a reason of why this has been done. Units still clump on top of each other like they always have.
The game sometimes freaks out and renders the units in 2D, making the game resemble Medieval Total War. Yes, the first one. I know why this happens, I'm sure the programmers could figure it out if they really wanted to. They clearly do not have the time or the willpower, or are simply too busy making more DLC.
Actually, that isn't fair. They are not distracted by making more DLC. They are distracted by selling cut content and selling it for a few dollars on top of the sixty dollar entry fee.
Here is what you do to fix this. Buy Rome: Total War. Install Rome: Total War. Install one of about 20 well known mods ranging from historical to Middle Earth flavor. Play Rome: Total War. Be glad that you didn't pay 60USD for Rome II: Total War - Rebranded Edition.

It's terrible.
The cutscenes, including simple "look at an item" ones, are all unskippable, even if you've seen them before or are reloading after death. If a three-line dialogue pops up on screen when you look at a road sign, then you get to spend 10 seconds listening to the (awful) narrator read it to you, even if you can read it yourself in a fraction of that. God help you if you accidentally click that thing again.
Half of the fun of the original King's (and especially Space) Quest was finding ways to die, since the animations were often funny or gruesome, and typically had mocking quips from the narration. The deaths in this game are dull and sanitary. They use Prince of Persia: Sand's of Time's "wait, that's not what happened" reload gimmick, but the KQ narrator is unpleasant to listen to. Adding insult to injury, dying means reloading and being forced to watch unskippable cutscenes again, so I quickly lost my desire to find ways to die.
The puzzles are cake. There's no satisfaction in clicking on the only usable thing on the screen and watching a cutscene. The one time I felt some tension to solve a puzzle, the game dissolved it immediately. After recovering the magic mirror from the dragon, the dragon notices you. I started thinking of how I would get away, but it didn't matter; Cutscene Graham handled it himself with what could've been a fun little puzzle sequence. After that, the game turned into a rail shooter with quick-time events, and then more boring cutscenes with unskippable dialogue.
Don't bother.

If you couldn't guess by the trailers and other reviews, Clandestine is a co-op, stealth based game. Grab a buddy and play as the spy, who sneaks around, shanks guards, rescues targets and retrieves intel. OR play as a hacker and hack into the environment, manipulating cameras, water mains, and transformers, all while avoiding the security systems, which kick you out of the system, give you the blue screen  of death and reset all your hard earned anarchy.
As the first game of its kind, Logic Artists could've done better, but they certainly couldn't do any worse. They could've easily made this game such that the hacker just sits there, occasionally opening a door while the spy sneaks around and knifes everyone in the room, or the spy hiding in a corner while the hacker bursts water mains and explodes transformers left and right. Luckily, the game is fairly balanced, and both parties involved have to have good communication skills to reach their objective. This is definitely the game to play with a close friend or significant other. Although they have public matchmaking and single player options, it's clear that this game was made for friends. While I wouldn't suggest getting it in early access (as there's a pretty good amount of polish that needs to go into this game before it's done), be sure to keep it on your radar, as it sets a precedent for both co-op and stealth fans alike.

That's your tl;dr. It sums up the game, to be honest. The Evil Within 2 is indeed fun in certain parts, don't get me wrong, but the game isn't scary. It has one or two good moments for someone not used to horror games and...that's about it.
Here are the pros: combat is sort of fun, level design is pretty good, game has good visuals and even some creatively designed monsters. Shooting enemies is fun, and being able to give your character skills is good. And that's about it.
The Evil Within 2 markets itself as an open world rpg horror game with shooter elements. Don't be fooled, though; the open world areas are fairly small and there are very linear sections. It might be more accurate to call the game a 'game that calls itself open world which really means you can explore a bit if you want'. There's not really that much exploration and the side quests don't really matter to the overall plot. A truly open world horror game would have been great, but I guess the developers couldn't make that work.
The monsters in the game are slightly challenging before you learn the mechanics, and then almost laughably easy. I played on the Normal difficulty and I could have done Nightmare pretty easily. None of the boss fights were even close to intense; I died in only one of the fights and generally only died while playing if I forgot to heal up.
Are all these flaws unforgivable? No, they wouldn't drag down a game with great storytelling or amazing scares. Too bad The Evil Within 2 has neither. I got scared at the start because I thought the game would be scarier than it was. But it never suprised me or made me feel uncomfortable. Clearly one of the villains is meant to be a horrific monster who pushes the boundaries of what we consider normal...he's almost laughably silly. For a horror game, the greatest sin it can commit is being boring and predictable, and that's the biggest flaw this game has right now: the story sucks.
The villains are not scary or captivating, and the side characters are as interesting as a plastic bag. Not that the first game had an amazing villain either; he was cliched as well. But at least you had two side characters, Kidman and Joseph who had a tiny bit of personality you could care about. In this game, all the side characters are like sticks you occasionally interact with.
And then there's our main character, good old Sebastian Castellanos. He's...the most cliche of stereotypes. He's the suffering detective, the bitter alcoholic seeking redemption, the desperate father who lost his daughter and has to get her back. Nothing about him will suprise you, and it's depressing how unoriginal Tango Gameworks made this character.
Honestly, it annoyed me how much I stopped liking this game. I'm not a horror fan, but I liked watching people play the first game on Youtube enough to play it myself. And it had some fun moments. But this game...no. There's a ton of positive reviews for it, but I don't see how people can call this game intriguing or provocative unless they truly are newcomers to horror games. The Evil Within 2 has the most reused plot lines, the lamest villains, and the most cardboard protagonist I've seen in a while. Some of the monsters look cool, but that's it.
The game developers should be ashamed of themselves for creating something so forgettable. This game is definitely not worth your $60, and maybe not $30 either. If you want to be entertained and you don't mind wading through some boring scenes, I'd still recommend you try this out. For $10, maybe. But if you're looking for a scary game, a fun game that will keep you invested in the characters, or a classic game you won't forget, look somewhere else.

TL;DR
Pros:
- Good Story
- Thrill of being hunted from beginning to end
- Unexpected shock moments
- Good Graphics and lightning
- Crafting system (!)
- Scarce resources
- "Rare" Safe Points (not rare, but you'll be happy to reach some)
Cons:
- some minor bugs (not game blocking at all, should probably not even put it into Cons)
- not correct lip sync (at least for me)
- backtracking (running through the same areas again seemed to be a bit boring and mindnumbing)
- crashed 2-3x on me
Details:
I LOVE this game.
This is THE Alien game I've been waiting for and what the Alien series deserves.
Okay, it's not perfect (had some very minor bugs, the game crashed on me 2-3 times and the backtracking in the game can be a bit annoying and mind numbing), but appart from those small issues it's just awesome!
I've played through the game on Hard (well, discription said this is the best experience, so I went from it from the start :P) and never changed the difficulty, though I was cursing sometimes.
Humans and Working Joes (they are annoying...) are pretty predictable and easy to avoid.
But the Alien, ohhh, the Alien. It's soo unpredictable in it's movement. The AI for it is BRILLIANT.
It checks out stuff and seems to be constantly on your trail.
It seems to change direction randomly and also the speed it moves when searching for you.
The creepiest moment I had was when it was completely silent.
Usually when you hide you can hear it (tab, tab, tab - from it walking), but at one point I was hiding under a table and it walked just past it, shock moment for me, seeing the feet and tail from it suddenly walk past it, without any sound, then it turned around and moved faster again and I could hear the walking sound again - OMG - scary. If I went out a bit earlier cause I assumed it was safe, I'd be dead.
You also can not outrun it (maybe if you're lucky to break line of sight quick enough and hide, but in the rarest of cases you'll manage to). If it spots you, usually you are dead.
Later on you can scare it off with your Flamethrower and Molotovs - but fuel and resources are scarce and it takes ~50 Flamethrower fuel to scare it off (except it was already charging at you and very close to you, but then you lose HP, not something you really want either - since holding breath in lockers when the Alien checks it out costs you HP).
I was sneaking through almost the whole game, not even walking normally and never sprinting (except at the beginning and the end of the game, when it was safe and when you kinda had to), always afraid I'd attract the Alien, which I wanted to avoid, since when it comes to check out the area, it stays for a while - much easier to get around if it's just crawling in the vents above you (even though hearing it clattering through it is creepy too....).
And a Working Joe + Alien combination? Me curseing!
The Saving System is great too!

My friend and I play a lot of games together, and we're big on maximizing our communication to really make a difference in multiplayer games. In Clandestine co-op, communication is key. A good hacker is streamlining, guiding, and scouting the route for the infiltrator.
The infiltrator is taking care of objectives and relaying their needs back to the hacker for support. The gameplay on the infiltrator side (my prefered side) handles like an older third-person stealth game would (see Hitman or Splinter Cell) while the hacker is much more of problem solving and gathering as much information about the playing field as possible. With a good team, and an appreciation for a co-op game where cooperation is integral (neither party can get anything done without the others help), I found it very easy to overlook some of the basic flaws that this beta has and enjoyed playing it thoroghly.

TL;DR:
Pros: Awesome co-op gameplay, okay solo, okay graphics (It's Early Access, so...)
Cons: Awkward Spy movement and cover, not too optimized.
Clandestine is an asymmetrical hardcore stealth game. I say hardcore because it takes 3 shots to kill the Spy. Sometimes guards get headshots that insta-kill you. Anyway, this game is asymmetrical in the fact that there are two modes: the Spy (Agent, Spy, they're called different things) and the Hacker. The Spy plays a lot like stealth games you see in other places. There's cover (clunky at the moment), takedowns, all that stuff. However, the Spy herself doesn't know where any guards or cameras are, or even where her goal is.
This is where the Hacker comes in. This is the most interesting concept of this game in my opinion. The Hacker has access to all of the cameras and alarms and stuff, as well as a tactical map (minimap, but no color or depth, just wall outlines). The Hacker's job is to tell where the Spy to go, disable any cameras that might be an issue, and tag guards (when the Hacker tags guards, the Spy sees a number over that guard that can be seen through walls). However, the Hacker has opposition of his own: he has to avoid the "system admin" so that he doesn't get disconnected from the network. When he gets disconnected, everything the Hacker has done resets, so cameras turn back on, door passcodes change, etc.
This game is absolutely amazing on co-op mode. One person plays as the Spy, the other as the Hacker. I can see how some people would think that being the Hacker could be boring, since you just manage things and keep an eye on a map for the entire level. But it's actually a lot of fun, and I prefer being the Hacker than the Spy. It's fun warning the Spy of a guard, or telling him where to go next, and it's also fun being fed that information. Of course, failing gloriously is always a possibility, and it's a ton of fun anyway. One mistake on one person's end could kill you.
The game is okay on solo mode as of now. You have to fill in for both roles, which can be tedious. You'll move forward into cover or some other place as the Spy, then go into Hacker mode and scout things out. Note that when you switch into Hacker mode, the Spy can still be seen and shot at, which can be really frustrating.
Version 0.7 is on it's way, which contains the first story mission and a better tutorial level, as well as some other additions and optimizations. So it might be good to wait a bit until that comes out. It'll have a nice polish om it by then.

TL;DR: This game's asymmetric co-op system offers a unique and fun two-player experience that makes this game very enjoyable, even through the notable bugs in the game's current alpha state.
Longer Review:
With one player playing from a 3rd person shooter point of view, and the other from a unique "hacker" point of view, co-op is made -very- important in this game. The field agent, on their own, simply sees what's right in front of them. No objective markers, no map, and limited ammo. The hacker has all the info, but isn't in the field to act on that info. They have the map, they see the objectives, they can look through the camera, they can call out guards, they can bribe, they can drop ammo/health-kits, they can hack passwords for locked doors, and so forth.
This system lends itself to an extremely co-op oriented, yet still responsibility-flexible experience. A skilled field-agent player can probably go all out as an mostly independent Sam Fisher sort of role, only needing help with a couple doors. On the other hand, a skilled hacker can quickly seek out most guard positions, disable all cameras, drop ammo near the field agent when they see fire-fights going down, drop health kits when the heart monitor shows injury, pre-hack all door passwords, bribe guards in stickier situation, and general make things a LOT easier on the field agent player.
This is part of what makes the system so fun, is that the system causes the two players to rely on each other to succeed, yet gives room for inexperience on either role to further reinforce that co-op "helping each other out" feel. Currently there are several notable bugs in the game that can be hindering, but the fun that comes out of this game very much outweighs any annoyances. I look forward to this game being a hit, and seeing more players online.

I should be thankful that someone told me this was on a free weekend; this games been out for a while now and I'd still not seen what sort of crap I was missing out on for myself...
Minimal expectations in mind, I took my time to look at all the playable factions; theres a "decent" amount regardless of DLC, however the number of actual nations is just so vast compared to other games.
Anyway, picked the Kingdom of Pontus in what is modern day turkey or so, and soon as i started playing I was hooked.
Diplomacy has improved slightly since Shogun 2, AI nations actively try to earn favour and security from their neighbours with a will to survive rather than conquer others, unless survival means to conquer (unless their barbarians, to which they will only listen if you're giving them a swirly).
On a strategic view battles now feel more important to me, due to the lack of armies; it makes victory more valuable and losing will have a relatively severe affect on the security of your nation, leaving gaps in your frontlines; and in that respect wars should be planned accordingly.
Knowing the crushing details about this games release, I feel that most of the ideas and details have been decently ironed out over the past year or so, thought it is missing a few things that would have been nice to include, such as trading territory. Still I genuinely think the 30 hours I've put into it was time well spent.

As a preface, I feel a need to mention that this game is a fine purchase for about ten dollars, not sixty.
The UI is incredibly convoluted. You cannot just click on  a province and get all the information. You have to choose from a submenu of villages, which makes sense somewhat, and adjacent provinces, which makes absolutely no sense. Everything has its own button, so things get a little cumbersome. You also cannot zoom out far enough to see more than one province, probably because the game hasn't been optimized since that would leave no time for making DLC, and allowing the player to do so with any level of graphics settings would result in a melty plastic and metal pizza where the video card once was.
This same paradigm has been employed in the battle mode, where things get really frantic really fast. The most commonly used formation, spread formation, has been hidden under two submenus. I cannot concieve of a reason of why this has been done. Units still clump on top of each other like they always have.
The game sometimes freaks out and renders the units in 2D, making the game resemble Medieval Total War. Yes, the first one. I know why this happens, I'm sure the programmers could figure it out if they really wanted to. They clearly do not have the time or the willpower, or are simply too busy making more DLC.
Actually, that isn't fair. They are not distracted by making more DLC. They are distracted by selling cut content and selling it for a few dollars on top of the sixty dollar entry fee.
Here is what you do to fix this. Buy Rome: Total War. Install Rome: Total War. Install one of about 20 well known mods ranging from historical to Middle Earth flavor. Play Rome: Total War. Be glad that you didn't pay 60USD for Rome II: Total War - Rebranded Edition.
