I walk up to the first boss battle in the game - "The Last Giant", after traversing through many enemies I find myself here, now the real fight begins. Before I walk through the mist, I summon a phantom to aid me in my battle and see a message written next to it. I examined it and it read 'destroy but hole'. I stood there in confusion, not knowing what the message was trying to say. I walk through the mist and there it is - The Last Giant.
It wakes up and breaks free of its constraints and stares right at me, there are no eyes, no mouth, no nose, no nothing but a huge gaping hole that looked like the result of both too much Chilli "Ringburner" sausages and a freaky one night stand with someone that has a fetish for the 'uncharted'.
It stumbles towards me, I look to my left and see the phantom rush towards the boss recklessly and within 2 swoops from the  Last Giant; die. Now it is just me alone, I run for it, dodging his attacks and doing little damage to his gigantic health bar. I think to myself 'He must have some sort of weakness' and then I hear an ominous voice call to me, the voice started whispering and the sound got louder, repeating itself until I finally understood what it was saying. It said 'destroy but hole'.
With no other option, I try and attack the Last Giants rear, with a trickle of his health left, it only took one more hit to kill more first boss in Dark Souls 2. Then the Last Giant raised its foot and stamped down on me, I run away, about to heal up until the Last Giant tore off its own arm and killed me.
I sat there in shock to what has happened until I see a message pop up on the lower right of my screen, it was an acheivement and it read 'This is Dark Souls'.
Great game, a must buy.

I'm really glad there are indie developers out there providing free content, and this game has clearly been a labour of love for the developer, which makes me feel bad giving a negative review, but unfortunately that's the impression this game left on me.  I'd hoped for more, and I can't fathom how this game has so many positive reviews. I guess being free helps a LOT.
The gameplay itself is meaningless, just filler to pad out a visual novel. A mix of simple combat and tedious, unwanted, grinding to get ingredients to craft better gear. Although, I did like the boss fights.
Really the reason to play is the story right? But that is the least satisfying part of the game. The main characters are both very damaged, and have an unhealthy obsessive relationship with each other. It came across to me as plain creepy, not "love" as I think it was intended. I think this game lost a lot in translation, culturally and linguistically.
There are moments of fine storytelling, and the storytelling techniques the developer has employed like flashbacks and multiple points of view do enrich the game, but it's the story constructs themselves - the characters, the plot, the dialogue - that is poor, even cringeworthy in places. The worst part being the endings. Endings #2 and #3 were so ludicrous and clumsily executed that I'm sorry to say, I laughed and shook my head.
It's free though right so why so negative? If you don't mind throwing away a couple of hours on a low quality free game, then go for it. If you like to play games that are worthy of your limited time, look elsewhere. Go and replay To The Moon or Actual Sunlight if you can afford their modest price. If you really are destitute, and free is all you can afford, go to your local library and borrow a book for free instead.

I want this game to be longer or have a sequel but i doubt that will ever happen given the fact that it's heavily influenced by Ragnarok Online (which i never played).
The game can be beaten in 4-6 hours depending on how badly you want to collect and upgrade your gear, which in the end works out really well for how big this game is, it's small but high quality. That high quality shows in just about every part of the game, the skill and crafting system works pretty damn well as they are easy to understand given how cumbersome the menues are in the average rpg are. The gameplay and level design work incredibly well together as you are given more skills as the game and story progresses, every skill has its use (there are four) and they are tied story directly.
Eternal Senia is about a girl who is trying to rescue her older sister from the forces of evil that reside in a tower called the Tower of Eternity. Our protagonist, Senia, is a walking anime trope of the sensitive but determined type, but thats okay, as you progress through the game you learn each characters back story and whats at stake and you can easily see that this story has weight to it. However i felt that there could have been something more than just one objective to the story and that the characters could have been fleshed out a little more but you can pretty much chalk it up to the games length (4-6 hours!)...

and that is the hallmark of a successfull game.

I've included a short version for those who don't want to do all this reading.
Short Version:
Pros:
-Excellent variety in weapons, the skill tree, and enemies
-Good hacking mechanic
-Good research mechanic
-Open-world
-Enemies dialog=chilling
-Excellent soundtrack
-Outdated graphics
Cons:
-Outdated graphics
-Animations in this game leave something to be desired
-Overly dramatic death animations from most enemies
-Researching could get annoying at times
Long Version:
While outdated, this game still has a lot to it.
The gameplay is extremely varied, from the number of different weapons you can get, to the psionic abilities, to skills. You can get different skills over time, and choose which of those skills to upgrade, allowing you to customize your character according to your playstyle. Your weapons get damaged over time, which means that you must perform maintenance on them periodically, which could get annoying at times. The hacking mechanic isn't as good as Bioshocks, but it's still very well done. The research function was a nice feature, which sometimes requires you to find the appropriate elements for your research. This could also get annoying, since you may be carrying around this or that slab of meat for a long time to find the correct chemical you need.
You can go almost anywhere in this game. You can return to earlier sections of the ship to look for stuff you might have missed or left, and all the different decks have their own unique style. There's a large variety of enemies, each with their own weaknesses and strengths, which you can learn about by researching their organs after you kill them. Most of the enemies you face are downright chilling, enhanced by the bad graphics. If you think you won't like this because of bad graphics, think again. The animations in this game are kind of bad, but that's to be expected in a game this old. One thing about the enemies I disliked though, is that once they were killed they had to have this long, dramatic death animation.
The game also has a terrific soundtrack and story, which really helps you get immersed in the game.
This game, is a true classic.

My favorite PC classic. If you are willing and able to look past the dated graphics, you will find a very immersive FPSRPG with a memorable villain. Although the game is labeled a "horror FPS", its not really scary. It's one of those games that is just creepy, but it's that kind of creepyness that grows on you as you immerse yourself further. The gameplay may seem overwhelmingly complex at first, but once you get used to it, it's quite good. Backtracking exists in this game, and that might ruin it for some, but I felt the level design was good enough that doing so was relatively quick. If you dislike techno, turn off the music. Some might say this makes the game more haunting. Personally I enjoyed the music. The difficulty can really spike at times, but this is part of what I like about this game. It does not forgive you. You will manage your resources and upgrades carefully and you will like it. Otherwise you will die.

The Evil Within 2 is a fantastic game, and I would recomend it to anyone that has played the first. Not only did the game rekindle my interest in the series that Tango Gameworks is creating here, but it also made me want to play through the original game all over again!
The game has some substantial differences from the original but that is what can make a follow-up or sequel really shine, and I find in this game is does rather well. They did away with being completely linear to allow a semi-open world feel and environment--while being a "plain old suburb". The creepy atmosphere and interesting world building is still there, however in lower amounts, as the developers have already shown you the world of STEM and how truly messed up it can and will be. Though that doesn't mean that development is gone. They have shown that the world of STEM is fragile and can be manipulated on multiple levels, which is more than the first game showed. There are some ties back to the original which help the game shine too, and there are some revisits to some of the more memorable scenes in the first game to help Sebastian come to grips with his inner demons and conquer them once and for all. It's a story deeper than just "rescuing your dauther", it's a game about fighting your inner demons in a attempt to right wrongs and repair a life now broken.
All-in-all, The Evil Within 2 is a very good game that you should try out if you like a steathy horror experience with some atmospheric chills thrown in. And I'm not scared easily at all, but I thought the creepiness and the setting was awesome. Psychological horror is one of my favourite genres and this fit the bill nicely! The weirder the atmosphere and the harder it is to piece environments together, the better!
On a side note, it should be mentioned that the game has a little bit of framerate/performance issues, but I didn't experience all that many. With a patch or two, the game will more than likely be running completely fine. Should have been something that was corrected before launch, but it didn't detract from my overall enjoyment of the game.

A fun horror survival game was pretty good balancing and wonderful visual designs. It can be really brought down at times by its extremely poor writting. The biggest issue being that often there are whimsical moments that are so painfully over the top and badly written. I presume they were going for a contrast to the dark horror world but in the end, it just sucks you out of the horror experience. At times it's all "I LOVE YOU SO MUCH WIFE!" with painfully over the top happy music, i was half expecting a pony to start ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ rainbows in the background. It really sucks you out of this dark and cruel horror world and hurts the game as a whole.
With that said, as i said before when you're left to roam the open areas or on a mission, the special effects and monster designs are wonderful. The combat is simple but rewarding and satisfying. Just the dialogue is just so terrible at times, so don't expect a fully engaging story.
The game seems to struggle in the last third, suffering from Far Cry 3 syndrome in which you kill the most interesting character first. You end up losing a lot of extremely creative monster designs to "generic muscle monster" towards the end as well as a significantly less interesting antagonist.
With all its flaws however, it's certainly worth picking up if you're looking for an engaging horror survival game, especially when it comes to the open world areas. Though they're small, it's plenty enough to keep you satisfied for 10+ hours. I just hope in the future they improve on the writting and instead of making a happy/evil contrast just focus on making a never endingly cruel and horror world if they make a sequel.

For those who love challenging games with big bosses and tough mobs, there are few games which I would recommend more than Dark Souls II. A worthy successor to Dark Souls and to the Souls franchise, Dark Souls II manages to keep every gamer stuck hours upon hours on the chair until they finally defeat all the bosses. But the fun doesn't stop once you have finished the game. Exploring the world, trying to solve a rather intricate story, which the developers of the game have hidden in the items and scenery you find throughout your jurney and fighting with other players makes Dark Souls II appeal to many gamers even after finishing the game. Dark Souls II also gives you the possibility of challenging yourself even more by trying new builds or by starting a new, more difficult journey.
All in all Dark Souls II is a great game with great controls (if you die, it is our own fault), great gameplay, great bosses, beautiful sceneries, fun co-op and pvp experience and a game which will make you challenge yourself through an almost limitless variety of ways.

Dark Souls II is the third in a semi-linked series of games, including Demon's Souls, a PS3 exclusive, and the absolutely fantastic multi-platform game, Dark Souls, and it's subsequent DLC package, Dark Souls : Prepare to Die Edition.  Dark Souls II does quite a lot to embrace its heritage, but, at the same time, manages to bring some new things to the table, while leaving some, unfortunately, behind.  I would argue that Dark Souls II is easily the most accessible game within the franchise to date.  I do not mean the easiest, by this.  Dark Souls II goes out of its way to provide helpful context menus to explain to what effect each statistic works, such as the new seperation between endurance and vigor, and the all-new adaptibility mechanic.  Also, there are many new weapons brought to the table, and a distinct new way that many spells, including pyromancies, and the way dark magics are handled.  However, despite these wonderful additions, there is a pretty major flaw that has prevented me from placing this game above the original, in terms of quality.  Dark Souls 1 was less accessible, buggier, and had tons of inherent problems at launch, but it did a few things better than Dark Souls II.  The most major was the ability it had to completely engross the player within its world, a feature that Dark Souls II seems to be lacking.  Dark Souls I felt like an adventure, whereas Dark Souls II almost feels like a roller-coaster ride, rather than a self-contained narrative.  This does not mean, however it is a bad game, or even a mediocre one.  Dark Souls II is fantastic if only for the gameplay itself.  Quite simply, it feels good to play.  With this in mind, I completely suggest this game, even at its launch price.  Hopefully we will get to experience more of the world when the DLC drops next month.

Ah Just Cause 3, a good game? A bad game? A fun game? A boring game?...  If these were statements instead of questions they'd all be true of JC3. This is a game of systems and mechanics and what is there works great, however I think sadly there isn't enough mechanics to keep the game interesting all of the time.
A typical play session of JC3 would be travel some where and blow everything up, then rinse and repeat. It doesn't matter why you're there and the context of your destruction, that is what it boils down to, explosions. Now nearly every game ever made could be described in such over simplified terms and I know that, but what JC3 fails to do is disguise this fact in a way that you don't realise that is all your doing.
Now don't get me wrong, how you go about exploding everything around you is immense fun. Grenades, rockets, grenade launchers, high jacking Tanks, combat Helicopters, fighter jets, using grappling hooks to pull down structures, topple fuel tanks etc etc...  it goes on and on and it also looks really good too, the explosions in particular are something to behold. They have made this a spectacle and it is awesome to see, at least for a while.
Like with any spectacle, it has a shelf life, you can't watch fireworks for 30 hours straight and not get bored, but in small bursts here and there... fireworks are great! That pretty much sums up the game for me, good in small bursts but it does get tired quickly over an extended play period.
Does this make it a bad game? Not in my book, but it does make it a shallow game and sadly an imperfect experience. Difficulty isn't high (which I am fine with by the way) so the challenge will come from destroying things in the most spectacular way or efficient way you can think of.
The story missions are ok and the final boss is an expected anti climax, but there is a narrative if you're interested. There is loads to do, upgrades to unlock, challenge missions that test your skills and collectables, you aren't short of content but like me you might find yourself asking if you *want* to do it all...  as I said,  you'll be more or less doing the game thing over and over again in a very noticeable way which at times felt like a chore.
It is what it is, it never advertised itself as anything other than a fun explosive romp, so no complaints that it delivered on it's promise, but whether that will be enough for you or not, will boil down to own personal tastes.

First of all: IT'S FREE!
A couple of years ago, I played a little free game called King Story. It was an unfinished game, the first in a series, but it's combat system was pretty neat. Like in Eternal Senia, you attack by charging into the enemy. Even if it is more limited due to RPG Maker mechanics, it was really cool to see this concept again - one that I really missed from the first game, that let me longing for a sequel that will never come out.
The character design was incredible. I am not familiar with RPG Maker so I do not know if all the sprites are original from the creator (they too are superb btw), but the drawings for the protagonists and bosses were wonderful for a free game, better than a lot of paid games with anime visuals. The story was great, it is simple but manage to immerse you into the plot, and actually like the characters.
What really got into me was the secret chamber - don't read if you want to discover for yourself. Until then, it was a really good game that I pretty much enjoyed and became attached to the characters; but to see the love invested in this game, and the care the developer devoted to it really moved me. The reference to old games, specially Legend of Mana, made it something special. It was like it could be any of us there, determined to create a game moved by childhood memories, and sharing with people that could possibly get the same feeling. Maybe I am reading too much between the lines, but this line of thought amuses me, and make the fact that it's free even more interesting. I don't know, I give it some thought and this game may as well figure between my favorite games.

The Evil Within 2 is a fantastic game, and I would recomend it to anyone that has played the first. Not only did the game rekindle my interest in the series that Tango Gameworks is creating here, but it also made me want to play through the original game all over again!
The game has some substantial differences from the original but that is what can make a follow-up or sequel really shine, and I find in this game is does rather well. They did away with being completely linear to allow a semi-open world feel and environment--while being a "plain old suburb". The creepy atmosphere and interesting world building is still there, however in lower amounts, as the developers have already shown you the world of STEM and how truly messed up it can and will be. Though that doesn't mean that development is gone. They have shown that the world of STEM is fragile and can be manipulated on multiple levels, which is more than the first game showed. There are some ties back to the original which help the game shine too, and there are some revisits to some of the more memorable scenes in the first game to help Sebastian come to grips with his inner demons and conquer them once and for all. It's a story deeper than just "rescuing your dauther", it's a game about fighting your inner demons in a attempt to right wrongs and repair a life now broken.
All-in-all, The Evil Within 2 is a very good game that you should try out if you like a steathy horror experience with some atmospheric chills thrown in. And I'm not scared easily at all, but I thought the creepiness and the setting was awesome. Psychological horror is one of my favourite genres and this fit the bill nicely! The weirder the atmosphere and the harder it is to piece environments together, the better!
On a side note, it should be mentioned that the game has a little bit of framerate/performance issues, but I didn't experience all that many. With a patch or two, the game will more than likely be running completely fine. Should have been something that was corrected before launch, but it didn't detract from my overall enjoyment of the game.

System Shock 2 takes place a few decades after its predecessor. The stories aren't directly related so don't worry about jumping straight into this one. The first took place on Citadel Station, where an AI named SHODAN, stripped of her ethical restrictions, went batshit crazy with dreams of Godhood. She failed. Fast-forward 40-some years and you play a soldier on the maiden voyage of a FTL spaceship, built by the same company who was responsible for Citadel Station - TriOptimum. You wake up after cryo-sleep and, conveniently, suffer from amnesia - the favorite theme of infinite game developers world-wide. Needless to say, something bad is happening on board, but I'll leave the rest for you to find out in game.
It reminded me a bit of Dead Space (or, rather, the other way around - if I had played the games by their chronological release), but it isn't a jump-scare "horror" game as I was led to believe. Creepy, yes. Disturbing, indeed. But it's not frightening in that traditional sense of changing your underwear. There aren't shocking twists and turns in the plot - no wheel is reinvented in this sci-fi space crisis. If you're approaching this at 2014 after being around the gaming and movie block for a while, you'll probably be familiar with most of the developments. You probably know SHODAN as the iconic villain from the game that is well-loved (out of character). I'm sorry for the upcoming blasphemy, but I didn't find her too different from the generic granduer-obsessed villain. Maybe it's because I'm playing this game 15-years late and I've been exposed to all sorts of antagonists. Maybe I'm just a dim-witted gamer who can't see the sophistication. She did have some shining moments, however, that made me realize that this is one messed-up cyber girl. And while my remarks here might make it seem as if I consider the game bland, that isn't the case. I enjoyed the ride, just more due to the gameplay rather than the story (which is the other way around with BioShock: Infinite).
I played System Shock 2 after the BioShock trilogy and was immediately surprised. The amount of gameplay functions was a bit overwhelming at first, especially when you're used to modern gaming standards. I won't list these said functions down because I don't think it'll make any sense to a reader who hasn't played the game. You need to experience it to understand. After the tutorial and an hour or so into the campaign, however, I got the hang of it. More or less. Once I grasped the basics, the further I got into the game the more I felt a growing regret about how criminally streamlined the last installment in the BioShock series - Infinite - is, compared to its ancient ancestor. Now, I ike BioShock: Infinite, I really do. But it pains me to think how magnificent it could have been if it maintained some of SS2's complexity in RPG mechanics.
If you've played the BioShock trilogy you'll quickly notice the shared DNA. Shock 2 has the audio recordings you probably like (I certainly do) that help tell the story. It has its "magic" abilities (like Plasmids and Vigors), it has hacking of security cameras and turrets, it has vending machines, it has research of enemies, it has big maze-like levels that make you open your map time and time again - and as I wrote earlier, it has a lot more than that; things I enjoyed a helluva lot that I wish were in later games, too. The RPG is strong in this one. From ability scores to expertise in different sorts of weapons, this game offers you much more than your average shooting (which is good, considering shooting in 99's standard isn't as exciting and challenging as it is today).
Actually, I should confess about the challenge - I started out on Nightmare (the last out of four difficulty levels), and early on lowered it to Easy. I know, I know. "A filthy casual." Maybe it's becuase I didn't have a lot of time per day to play and didn't want to waste what little of it I had respawning and refighting the same fights. Maybe I didn't enjoy the combat mechancis of a 15-year-old game. Maybe it was just honestly too tough for me. Maybe a bit of all, or something else entirely. I can speculate that on Nightmare this game truly /is/ a challenge. Your HP is extremely lessened, I suspect enemies do more damage, and every upgrade requires many more "Cybernetic Modules" (think of them as XP points you find throughout the game). Maybe one day I'll replay it as a different class (I went for a Tech\Hacker sort) on the highest difficulty, because SS2 certainly has replay value between a Tech focused character or a "Magic" (Psi) one. But it is not this day.
Speaking of 90s game - the graphics are, obviously, dated. However, I played it with mods which made the game look surprisingly pleasant and I strongly suggest Googling quickly for some prime graphical enhancements.
System Shock 2 is a brilliant game whose age isn't half as felt as you might expect it to be, and shockingly offers more complexity than many modern products. A creepy sci-fi setting with an iconic villain, complex RPG mechanics while still capable of being played as a shooter, and a challenge to be found if you have the patience for it. I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoyed the BioShock trilogy in particular, and FPS-RPG games that amount to more than taking cover and shooting in general.

This is a great Alien game and a strong stealth game by itself. The aesthetics are excellent: ambiance sounds, lighting, music, textures, rooms design, graphics, etc... It uses the movie's lore very well, and gives a lot of fanservice.
The gameplay is generally slow-paced and sometimes frustrating (specially if you are trying to save resources or avoiding unnecessary encounters). The crafting system and the item menu aren't very intuitive and can be hard to realize what are you doing in the most urgent moments. The use of save points instead of auto-saves increases the stress and difficulty (sometimes it can become annoying when you die and you have to repeat a lot of actions). There are a lot of interactions with mechanism that involve interesting button combos or minigames. There is backtracking and exploration almost at Metroid level (some places are visited only once, others can or are visited twice or more times).
I recommend Alien: Frustration for its difficulty, its ambiance and sense of freedom in the gameplay and exploration.

I did not play this game at release, but whatever bugs which plagued this game on it's release, that people complained of, seem to have been addressed. The game runs incredibly smooth, it feels very well optimized so I get very good dps, the grand strategy campaign is indepth and detailed, everything runs seemingly perfectly.
The art direction taken by this game puts you right into ancient times, the music, the textures, the drawings etc, all add an immersive element to the game. The graphics are very good as well.
Also the game capture the brutality of ancient times, everything from the combat, to even the quotes chosen for loading screens, seem to communicate this. I wouldn't recommend this game to a young person or child, just because of the brutal element in this title.
The game plays like a movie at times, battles seem to run so smoothly, that it may seem like you are recreating a battle from Troy or Alexander. For example, you can have large unit formations battling in phalanx formation, or be attacking a town, with reinforcements sailing in on boats and disembarking on the beach to join the fight.
I also love that they brought back the speeches made by Generals at the start of battles. I don't believe they were in Empire or Napoleon Total War, as I dont think I heard them since Medieval 2 Total War - but I may be wrong. The speeches are always witty, clever, very funny while still seeming relatively genuine, even the commanders of specific units will speak to thier men at times.
The game also imploys likewise clever events you will come across in the grand campaign, as well as historically accurate and interesting events. The grand campaign I find is where lots of replay value is hidden, like other Total War titles, but if you are interested in antiquity, then this title is for you definetely.
I really recommend this game for anyone who is interested in ancient history, and who wants a game with top cinematic quality and historical, even emotional, depth.

TL;DR:
SBMM - Not a great idea, Ranked Play is ther for a reason. Just cuases added lag and kind of takes away the fun for better players.
DLC - Separation of the regular and DLC maps is really stupid, should be some form of tickboxes to select which maps you want to search for. e.g. Regular maps + Havoc + 3rd pack, or rather just all the DLC map packs.
Gun balancing - Fire rate is determined by FPS, some wepaons with high fire rate to begin with just get so much powerful and the TTK goes down dramatically.
Supply Drops - Needs to be system with some sort of Elite/Prestige, current system can just give duplicates only every few prestiges or so.
DEDICATED SERVERS - Give them to us, NOW. Or at least in Treyarchs upcoming game.
So after 36+ hours in just Multiplayer, I think I have a good perspective of AW.
First off, SBMM, objectively, it's amazing, matching good players with good payers, and not so good players also with not so good players. However, it just doesn't work well enough tbh. Because there is such a small amount of people in AW on PC, there's bound to be connection issues. I've been dealing with several bad connections as of late because I am getting quite good at the game, and versing players who are at or above my skill with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ ping is horrible.
Though, these are rare, and only sometimes noticable. And additionally, if you want to play against people of the same skill as you, go into Ranked Play, though, good luck finding a match.
Sledgehammer's addition of DLC weapons is nice, gives the Season Pass some more value, but the separation of the DLC maps and the regular maps is just stupid.
As I said before, there is already a limited amount of people who play AW on PC, and by factoring in SBMM and the fact that only a selective amount have the DLC pack, it's literally impossible to get a match.
On the same line, almost of the game modes have no people in them as well. The only time when I play a different game type other than TDM is if I get into a lobby in Mosh Pit, and that doesn't even include all of the game types.
I do think there are some balancing issues as well, the EM1 is a prime example of OP. Because the game runs on the same ol' engine used in Quake, the fire rate of weapons is determined by framerate. So obviously if someone is getting 91fps (cap) than they will absolutely destroy because the EM1 has a super high fire rate with low damage, so not like and actual laser.
This is a personal one of mine, but seriously, Supply Drops. I bloody hate them. I have a Silver Bullet and Chicanery (not sure on the spelling), and there are the only decent Elites I have, after 3 Prestiges and 36 hours...
I think there needs to be some garuntee of an Elite at least every Prestige that you don't have already.
Also, the Nigerian crap needs to be taken out, they look♥♥♥♥♥♥and they just take up space and reduce the chance of getting something good.
Dedicated servers is also a hot topic, and I think they really, really need to be implemented in Treyarchs upcoming installment into the franchise.
You may be thinking why the hell I've played the game for so much and why I've recommended it. It's simply because it's fun sliding around, boosting above others and time-to-time reking some noobs.
It hasn't drifted away from the traditional CoD formula, which I still think it fine, but the additions are what makes this game so much more fun than Ghosts for example.
So all in all, I'm not bashing on Advacned Warfare or SL (except for them ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Supply Drops), but rather I'm just making suggestions as to what should be improved upon and fixed.
So that took ages, good job if you read that all.

A fun horror survival game was pretty good balancing and wonderful visual designs. It can be really brought down at times by its extremely poor writting. The biggest issue being that often there are whimsical moments that are so painfully over the top and badly written. I presume they were going for a contrast to the dark horror world but in the end, it just sucks you out of the horror experience. At times it's all "I LOVE YOU SO MUCH WIFE!" with painfully over the top happy music, i was half expecting a pony to start ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ rainbows in the background. It really sucks you out of this dark and cruel horror world and hurts the game as a whole.
With that said, as i said before when you're left to roam the open areas or on a mission, the special effects and monster designs are wonderful. The combat is simple but rewarding and satisfying. Just the dialogue is just so terrible at times, so don't expect a fully engaging story.
The game seems to struggle in the last third, suffering from Far Cry 3 syndrome in which you kill the most interesting character first. You end up losing a lot of extremely creative monster designs to "generic muscle monster" towards the end as well as a significantly less interesting antagonist.
With all its flaws however, it's certainly worth picking up if you're looking for an engaging horror survival game, especially when it comes to the open world areas. Though they're small, it's plenty enough to keep you satisfied for 10+ hours. I just hope in the future they improve on the writting and instead of making a happy/evil contrast just focus on making a never endingly cruel and horror world if they make a sequel.

If you're a bit skeptical or on the fence like I was before I bought this game then wait till it's on sale and try it out - you can always refund it if you don't like it. A lot of people on here complain saying this game is disappointing, that it isn't a "true Elder Scrolls game". Well I disagree completely!
This game IS a proper Elder Scrolls game. At its core it is everything you would expect from a proper TES game - freedom to explore, freedom to forge your own character and playstyle, freedom of choice and freedom of approach to situations - do you go into a dungeon shouting battlecries and swinging your battleaxe, or do you take the stealthier approach? Both can be done, and are not mutually exclusive at all - you have total freedom in skill choice. It plays very similarly to the older titles in general, and you start off as a prisoner, escape and then go on to explore the world as you see fit. There is no linear progression path like in other MMOs. You could start in Morrowind for example but run around the entire zone in an unrestrained manner, killing monsters and exploring dungeons and ignoring quests if you so choose.
You can do almost everything in this game that you could in the older titles: Sneak around, steal things, murder people, join factions, make choices that affect the world, make your own unique character build, play in FIRST PERSON with the same / similar combat system to the older games with great new features, find hidden dungeons, secret lore, uncover mysteries etc. Even better is that more features will be added as time goes on.
But what this game does also is enhance the experience by adding new features from other MMOs. This makes it feel fresh and new, because it combines the best aspects of the singleplayer TES games and MMOs like WoW - you have an action bar associated with your weapon, with abilities hotkeyed to the number keys, which you use alongside your standard attacks, power attacks, blocking and bashing.
It breathes new life into the MMO genre I think by having a unique combat system that is addictive, intuitive, much more tactical, and above all FUN. It doesn't feel grindy at all either because the quests are all genuinely interesting and fun, the stories are meaningful and touching, as you would expect from an Elder Scrolls game, and the world is one I am deeply fond of and immersed in already from playing the older games for thousands of hours. Plus you can explore areas that haven't been available in a TES game since Arena or Daggerfall, like Summerset Isle and Valenwood - games which you can't exactly call high-tech.
The music is another strongpoint of this game, because even though it's clearly been designed to be as ambient and non-intrusive as possible for the MMO format, you can still hear familiar themes rise up from the pleasant ambience from time to time, like Watchman's Ease from Oblivion and Blessing of Vivec from Morrowind. The theme is also excellent and was composed by none other than Jeremy Soule, adding to the authentic feeling of the game.
Then of course you have the multiplayer. I have yet to experience this, but from what almost everyone else has said it is supposed to be excellent. Time will tell for me, I've only scratched the surface of this beautiful game.
Speaking of beautiful, the GRAPHICS in this game are excellent and miles better than Skyrim's. The colours are vivid and rich, the shadows are excellent and free of striping that plagued the older games, all the animations are wonderful and smooth, the scenery is amazing and the flora / fauna of the world is highly consistent with older games - giant mushrooms, Alits, Netches and more in Morrowind for example.
On top of all this, we get to meet characters that have always been mentioned in books in previous games but whom we never met -  Mannimarco, Molag Bal, Sotha Sil in the upcoming Clockwork City DLC, to name a few. Speaking of DLC, this game is constantly being updated. They frequently add new areas, such as the recently added Orsinium, and factions such as the upcoming Dark Brotherhood. Eventually I hope they will add every last area of Tamriel, especially Vvardenfell!
I think ultimately that the reason someone would dislike this game is not because it's objectively "bad" but simply because it isn't their cup of tea. I however love it - I would go so far as to say that it ranks alongside the older, legendary titles.

I had heard great things about this game, which BioShock is said to be a spiritual sequel of, so when I saw it on sale, I decided to buy it to give it a try. And I don't regret it. The comparisons between this and BioShock are pretty much spot on, but I must say that this game seems like a more complex version of BioShock; a great thing, in my opinion.
The gameplay is pretty varied, from the number of different weapons you can get, to the psionic abilities. The RPG aspects are pretty good as well, allowing you to customize your character according to your playstyle. The weapons get damaged over time, which means that you must perform maintenance on them periodically, otherwise they'll end up breaking (you can still repair them, though). The hacking mechanic is good, and the research function, which sometimes requires you to find the appropriate elements for your research is excellent.
As far as environments go, you can go almost anywhere. You can return to earlier sections of the ship to look for stuff you left there, and all the different decks have their unique style. There's a good variety of enemies, each with their own weaknesses and strength, which you can learn about by researching their organs after you kill them. It also has a good soundtrack, and the story, without spoilers, is excellent.
I really recommend this game, especially if you enjoyed the original BioShock.

First off, I feel the need to express that I'm a passionate fan of the Alien series: I've seen/played/read every movie, game and piece of literature there is. Some I loved, some I struggled through. Unfortunately, Isolation straddles the line between those points with a fair lean to the bad side of things. The story is great, the voice acting and atmosphere is great - the gameplay, however, falls flat on its face and then painfully drags itself, still lying face-down, for 25+ hours. I'm not sure what the dev team were thinking when they were fleshing out the game but they evidently latched onto the notion that turning power on is the most interesting activity that anyone could partake in. The Alien itself is just about the only thing in the damn game you don't have to restore power to. At one point I was required to restore power to a generator. I don't f**king even. There are sections of the game that are amazing and incredibly tense, but these moments are few and quite literally far between.These moments are marred by the frustrating and boring tedium of the filler material between them. Expect to do a lot of walking to and from powerless doors and generators through some pretty, though repetitive corridors. Make a mistake and woe be you, because the save points are spaced quite far apart with seemingly no consideration to the relative difficulty of the gameplay between them. The game does capture the essence of the first film and really tries to (and mostly suceeds to) deliver the best interactive Alien experience to date. It just feels like it was stretched out to a point where the action couldn't support the narrative. As much as I want to recommend the game, as it truly does have shining moments, wait till Gaben flogs it off for $5, because that's about all it is worth. It's more Agoraphobic-Blackout simulator than survival horror. Disappointed fan, signing off.

Don't bother with this one. Get Total War: Shogun 2 for much less (start with the base game -- Fall of the samurai or Rise of the samurai are not *as* good) and avoid the urge to bang your head against the wall yelling "why, why, WHY?!?!?!?!?!?!?!?"

As Total War games go, I feel fairly justified in referring to this one as the worst so far. Probably the most disappointing aspect is that it fails to live up to its older brother, the original Rome: Total War since the Creative Assembly decided to take the original Rome game, improve the graphics and then make it worse in every other possible way. That cool feature allowing you to see a city on the battle map outside of combat? Gone. Family trees? Gone.
About the only decent thing added is naval combat and the ability to perform amphibious landings, but the glitches therein where the AI are concerned do tarnish that somewhat (the AI likes to land troops on the beach and then just leave them standing there).
Even the helpful information pieces on each unit and building to tell you what each of them do and to provide historical context has been moved to an online service, so if you don't have an internet connection you have no idea what anything does until you can build it. Honestly, what was wrong with just having that as part of the game?
Then there's the fact that the game has glaring mechanical issues too - perhaps most pronounced in the closed system of the Britannic tribes, where often times if you start as the Iceni you can find yourself in a ridiculous stalemate where everyone has a 20 stack of identical units and can't take anybody else's city because of the garrisons and can't build more/better units due to a lack of cash. The root cause of this ofc is the fact that even across cultures all the units are fundamentally the same - they're all either swordsmen, spearmen, cavalry or missile units, and since all the units are equally terrible it comes down to a simple matter of whoever has the most men wins - which may be fairly accurate historically but it doesn't make for an enjoyable experience in-game, particularly since you can't have any more than 20 units per army.
The blandness of the uni choices is further compounded by the fact that a lot of the abilities and formations don't do what they're supposed to; the testudo is underpowered if not totally useless and when last I checked the shield wall had literally no effect whatsoever.
I'd recommend the original Rome: Total War game over this (or any other Total War game really if you're not set on the time period) any day of the week.

First off, I played the original non-Steam version of Half-Life so I knew what the game was going to be like from the get-go. However, I never thought the experience would be completely fresh despite being a remake of the game. I thoroughly enjoyed the combat, it's fast-paced and I feel each gun you use has a specific purpose for a specific time so there's no redundancy in the vast arsenal that Gordon Freeman will carry over the course of the game. The game paces itself well however, I personally felt they streamlined the "On a Rail" chapter a bit too much, so it felt underwhelming compared to the original. Overall, the plot remains completely intact aside from the Xen chapters, which are still in development for who knows how long. Despite that, Black Mesa retains the spirit of the original Half-Life and the quality you would expect from a Valve game. It amazes me that a modding team with enough dedication would aspire to create such a great game. If you're looking for a fast-paced shooter atypical of the FPS genre, Black Mesa is definitely the game to consider.

By far the most fun I've had in a game in a while! 9.5/10.
While my review can not be called "thorough" my enthusiasm to report how amazing this game is should say something at the least. What I feel is the best feature of Just Cause 3 is the fact it plays like a game, not like a pseudo movie. The idea of fun was obviously on the creator's mind during the whole development process where as I feel a lot of developers these days are prioritizing graphics or practicing wallet vamprisim over making a fun and memorable experience for their players.
+ The controls are tight and clean. They make me feel when I die it is my fault, not the game's. The gunplay is not only responsive but tie that in with the Spiderman-esque movement and you've got yourself one hell of a good time. The traveling via hook/parachute/wingsuit felt almost perfect if it were not for the delay with being able to quickly deploy then hide the parachute when trying to zip around the battle. All in all this flaw only took the game down about a 0.1 in my books.
+ The new grapnel hook makes for a world of fun. I recall playing Just Cause 2 way back when on my 360 (sorry) and two things really made me feel the game fell short. One, The idea of only having one hook to tether two things together. And  two; The fact the hook immediately broke under pressure. With these small hook adjustments it made the game so much more enjoyable than it's predecessor.
+ It's big. Ok now I know that bigger aint always better (See: Banjo Kazooie: Nuts and Bolts.) but that's only when the huge area to explore is filled with nothing! Thus far I've been able to be a quick 1 minute float away from yet another fun thing to do!
+ Fixed Rico's voice. One of the things I HATED about just Cause 2 was Rico's voice, it was so fake and cringey I couldn't stand any scene where that cardboard box of a man would try to sputter out a thick stream of camel spit coated words.
~ Day one bugs. I've heard a lot of complaints about some people not being able to play the game since launch. While I feel for those people, I REALLY do, there are also a lot of people able to jump straight into the action.
- Lack of direction. There is quite a fine line between "freedom to choose" and "freedom to wander until something comes up" I found myself at the top of a mountain staring, hungrily at the base ahead of me, when I see a message pop up and my screen go white. Turns out, I had to take care of some base defenses. "No problem!" I thought, unknowingly. I searched around the place for a way to shut off the defenses that would bombard where I was standing every 2 seconds but to no avail. (Remember, I have not played this game for long so I could have missed something.) But as I had not been given any form or direction to help me disable the defenses I felt a little thrown int othe deep end.

The general consensus so far seems to be that The Evil Within 2 is, at the very least, a significant improvement over the original. Personally, I really don't see it. It has ideas that look good on paper, like making the levels more explorable in a semi-open-world design, but it takes all of an hour or two of playing to realize that their idea of "open world gameplay" is setting the entire game in a generic suburb town where every house looks exactly the same and almost everything there is to "explore" amounts to big empty garages with nothing interesting in them but random tidbits for you to tape together in the crafting menu. Sebastian Castellanos has fallen victim to "edgy sequel character development syndrome", and with the addition of a beard he's completed his transition into that one alcoholic washed-up detective that's only capable of speaking in breathy mumbles that plagues games that are too lazy to actually write an interesting continuation of their main character's development. The enemy design has gone from bad to worse, and aside from the bigger enemies (which are mostly just the same generic J-horror long-haired girls you saw enough of in TEW1 mixed with "we gorilla glued a bunch of corpses together, you won't believe what happens next", guest starring "that spotlight monster from TEW1 except now it has a camera instead of a spotlight, how spooky") most of the things you'll fight are just zombies, or various forms of zombies I'd be willing to bet money you've already seen somewhere else before, like "scraggly female zombie that screams a lot and takes more damage", "fat zombie that explodes", or "slightly less fat zombie that leaks poison", as if the only research the developers did when making the game was playing Left 4 Dead 2 every night.
The big issue with the game isn't that it's bad, it's just that it's boring. The game's idea of "scary" is just funneling in as much blood as they can afford, and it very rarely bothers to actually even attempt any form of atmospheric build-up or tension and when it does try it usually just fails miserably. When you add in the various bugs I hit during playing, it only takes away from the vibe even more; a lot of times I would think that the lights were flickering to indicate that something was about to happen, only to realize that it was actually just the game's janky physics engine causing a hanging lantern to spaz out. The controls are clunky and sometimes buggy to the point that if you just hold the sprint button while holding back to try to run away from a monster, occasionally all you'll succeed in doing is doing a rapid series of spins and faceplanting into the monster. There's a reoccuring ghost-ish thing that pops up in the "open" world sometimes, and whenever it does it shifts the world into a frozen version where all the enemies and items turn invisible, but her AI is so bad that she just sort of wanders around, and most of the time I just ended up stuck not being able to interact with anything until I ran as far away from what I was trying to do as I can, wait for her to disappear, and then run back, which is just frustrating instead of even remotely scary (this is a reocurring trend throughout the game, but not just from her; the entire game is plagued with horrendous AI that was clearly not made with the new, more-open design in mind). Any time you have to climb on top of something the game seems to roll a dice to determine whether it works normally or you end up floating in the air, and in general the controls are clunky to the point that it becomes difficult to determine which parts are intentional for the survival horror factor and which parts are just bugs (for example, while the game occasionally forcing you to use Page Up and Page Down to scroll through documents is horrifying, it's horrifying in a way that I would consider not conducive to good survival horror).
In the end, they trade in all of their more interesting ideas for "cohesiveness". People complained about the original game being a compliation of ideas that lacked any sort of direction, and it was, but at least that kept things interesting, instead of abandoning all of their more creative ideas in favor of slapping long hair onto a pile of body parts and setting nearly the entire game in a boring-looking suburb. The story is predictable and uninteresting, and certain very obvious ties from the end of the first game are just outright forgotten and never brought up. It's a passable game, but it has even less original bones in it than the first game did, and it's not at all worth paying full price for in my opinion considering you've almost certainly seen every part of it somewhere else before.

I had heard great things about this game, which BioShock is said to be a spiritual sequel of, so when I saw it on sale, I decided to buy it to give it a try. And I don't regret it. The comparisons between this and BioShock are pretty much spot on, but I must say that this game seems like a more complex version of BioShock; a great thing, in my opinion.
The gameplay is pretty varied, from the number of different weapons you can get, to the psionic abilities. The RPG aspects are pretty good as well, allowing you to customize your character according to your playstyle. The weapons get damaged over time, which means that you must perform maintenance on them periodically, otherwise they'll end up breaking (you can still repair them, though). The hacking mechanic is good, and the research function, which sometimes requires you to find the appropriate elements for your research is excellent.
As far as environments go, you can go almost anywhere. You can return to earlier sections of the ship to look for stuff you left there, and all the different decks have their unique style. There's a good variety of enemies, each with their own weaknesses and strength, which you can learn about by researching their organs after you kill them. It also has a good soundtrack, and the story, without spoilers, is excellent.
I really recommend this game, especially if you enjoyed the original BioShock.

Incredibly deep and IMO overall superior experience to the wonderful Bioshock.
I didn't play System Shock 2 back in the day but love it all the same.  SS2 has all of the tactical depth and strong RPG elements lacking in the more recent Irrational releases; nonetheless you can clearly see the blueprint developing for the more simplified 'spiritual' sequels to come.  These similarities include hacking turrets and vending machines, non-linear exploration, stats-based real-time combat, powers, weapon modding, regeneration upon death, alarms adn security, researching enemies to improve your damage and many more.
SS2 is a technical, detailed, atmospheric, lengthy, challenging shooter/RPG hybrid and a triumph in originality and level design, even by today's standards.  Also, the Sci-fi/horror storyline is incredibly rich and interesting if you're in to that kind of thing like myself, and is fleshed out through countless audio recordings as well as communication from the ruthless AI SHODAN, one of the greatest game villains ever realized.
I urge you to overlook the aged 3D engine (which I find charming btw) and persist through the initial few hours until you can develop a play style that suits you because let me tell you when it clicks, the payoff is staggering revealing a rewarding and satisfying level of depth seen in few games today.
Once you're hooked on SS2, you won't want to stop until you've seen the ending. 10

This is one of those games that trancends the medium, this is high art. Being a huge fan of the franchise I was astonished to see how every detail from the first film has been carefully implemented into this game. The lighting, fog effects the sense of dread looming over you while creeping in and out of vents. There are multiple enemies such as androids and scavangers that try to kill you along the way. Creative Assembly unlike Gearbox are true fans of the franchise and by no means have they deviated from Ridley Scott's original vision of this horrific monster. There are couple of problems I encoutered with this game and to me, they are egregious enough to me that I feel the need to warn other potential consumers.
Harvesting:
You start with literally nothing. Your avatar may have some boxer shorts on, but they are part of the character model and you truly have nothing. So you start your journey picking up whatever tidbits are on the floor in order to build some basic tools, which would be fine if the harvesting wasn't partially RNG based. Often times, completely identical looking stones on the ground will give you different resources, so you can never be sure that you are ever getting closer towards your goal.
Once you have some Tools, perhaps the Axe, a persons first thought would be to hack at trees right? Trees must give wood, that's logical.
Wrong.
You can only harvest fallen logs in the world and dried up dead trees that exist in certain places in the world. Healthy trees cause your Axe to bounce off harmlessly.
The other resource node you can harvest look like sculptures of colored rocks, which require that you have a pick on you. Different colored nodes yield different quantities of resources, but you will never be certain of exactly what you will harvest due to the inane RNG harvesting thing I mentioned before.
This is further made frustrating in the way harvesting takes place. You left click on the resource node with the appropriate tool until the node breaks apart and only at the end of the break do you gain resources. If someone comes running by and has a higher level harvesting tool, they end up dealing more damage to the node and will manage to harvest your node before you could ever do.
Combine this with absurd costs of various items and the rarity of certain resources, this creates a scenario where a player is likely never to know exactly what they need in order to get the goals they desire.
Which leads me to the second bit I despise.
Player Killing:
This game handles player vs player interactions with a sort of karma system. When a player with no bad karma kills another player with no bad karma, they get a visible timer on them that shows how long they are marked. I forget the in game name of this mechanic, but suffice to say, this is something that is often abused.
Let me explain.
A player with no karma timer on them, when killed, retains all their gear and clothes upon death and spawns with it in their inventory. A player who dies while their karma timer is still active loses all their items.
This sounds like a nice way for non-violent players to play the game, but any player who dies still loses all their resources. Often times, groups of players will harass other players into killing them just so that their buddies can come and kill the now karma marked player and loot all his items.
This system manages to not solve the horrid KOS problem prevalent with these survival games at all and even makes the experience worse for those players who successfullly defend themselves only to then be killed and lose EVERYTHING as opposed to just their resources.
It's dispicable.
The last problem I had with this had to the frequent server restarts.
Every 20 minutes, it seemed, servers have to restart, which requires that every player on the server get disconnected, wait a few moments and then manually reconnect.
Players only get a 5 minute warning of when this will happen, which is never enough time for players to find a safe area to be in before the restart.
When a player finally logs back in, they may find that other players are there already and have killed the player while they were spawning into the world.
It's awfully annoying for a server to have to restart so frequently to start with, but then logging back into the game just to find yourself dead is just unacceptable to me.
I do not recommend this game. 24 dollars is just not a sensible price when there are games in the survival genre that are much MUCH more developed and thought out than this game and also cost less.
YOU GUYS COULD BE PLAYING SOMETHING THAT IS SLIGHTLY MORE FUN THAN THIS FOR SLIGHTLY LESS THAN THIS GAME COSTS!!
Anyway, I didn't realy have fun with this game at all, I didn't find it's crafting intuitive in the least nor did I enjoy the combat or survival systems. The community was meh, but that's to be expected in these games.
All in all, I'd say look elsewhere for your survival gaming. This game is just not fun.

If you're a bit skeptical or on the fence like I was before I bought this game then wait till it's on sale and try it out - you can always refund it if you don't like it. A lot of people on here complain saying this game is disappointing, that it isn't a "true Elder Scrolls game". Well I disagree completely!
This game IS a proper Elder Scrolls game. At its core it is everything you would expect from a proper TES game - freedom to explore, freedom to forge your own character and playstyle, freedom of choice and freedom of approach to situations - do you go into a dungeon shouting battlecries and swinging your battleaxe, or do you take the stealthier approach? Both can be done, and are not mutually exclusive at all - you have total freedom in skill choice. It plays very similarly to the older titles in general, and you start off as a prisoner, escape and then go on to explore the world as you see fit. There is no linear progression path like in other MMOs. You could start in Morrowind for example but run around the entire zone in an unrestrained manner, killing monsters and exploring dungeons and ignoring quests if you so choose.
You can do almost everything in this game that you could in the older titles: Sneak around, steal things, murder people, join factions, make choices that affect the world, make your own unique character build, play in FIRST PERSON with the same / similar combat system to the older games with great new features, find hidden dungeons, secret lore, uncover mysteries etc. Even better is that more features will be added as time goes on.
But what this game does also is enhance the experience by adding new features from other MMOs. This makes it feel fresh and new, because it combines the best aspects of the singleplayer TES games and MMOs like WoW - you have an action bar associated with your weapon, with abilities hotkeyed to the number keys, which you use alongside your standard attacks, power attacks, blocking and bashing.
It breathes new life into the MMO genre I think by having a unique combat system that is addictive, intuitive, much more tactical, and above all FUN. It doesn't feel grindy at all either because the quests are all genuinely interesting and fun, the stories are meaningful and touching, as you would expect from an Elder Scrolls game, and the world is one I am deeply fond of and immersed in already from playing the older games for thousands of hours. Plus you can explore areas that haven't been available in a TES game since Arena or Daggerfall, like Summerset Isle and Valenwood - games which you can't exactly call high-tech.
The music is another strongpoint of this game, because even though it's clearly been designed to be as ambient and non-intrusive as possible for the MMO format, you can still hear familiar themes rise up from the pleasant ambience from time to time, like Watchman's Ease from Oblivion and Blessing of Vivec from Morrowind. The theme is also excellent and was composed by none other than Jeremy Soule, adding to the authentic feeling of the game.
Then of course you have the multiplayer. I have yet to experience this, but from what almost everyone else has said it is supposed to be excellent. Time will tell for me, I've only scratched the surface of this beautiful game.
Speaking of beautiful, the GRAPHICS in this game are excellent and miles better than Skyrim's. The colours are vivid and rich, the shadows are excellent and free of striping that plagued the older games, all the animations are wonderful and smooth, the scenery is amazing and the flora / fauna of the world is highly consistent with older games - giant mushrooms, Alits, Netches and more in Morrowind for example.
On top of all this, we get to meet characters that have always been mentioned in books in previous games but whom we never met -  Mannimarco, Molag Bal, Sotha Sil in the upcoming Clockwork City DLC, to name a few. Speaking of DLC, this game is constantly being updated. They frequently add new areas, such as the recently added Orsinium, and factions such as the upcoming Dark Brotherhood. Eventually I hope they will add every last area of Tamriel, especially Vvardenfell!
I think ultimately that the reason someone would dislike this game is not because it's objectively "bad" but simply because it isn't their cup of tea. I however love it - I would go so far as to say that it ranks alongside the older, legendary titles.

Brilliant game.  The core product has beautiful artwork and quests that are engaging.  In fact the storylines are so expertly constructed that it feels as though I'm a character in an online epic.  They've moved me, made me laugh, and made me go "awww" at times.  The quests force you to make decisions that will have consequences later in the game, such as which friends and enemies you will make that might help or block you later on (individual NPCs, not entire factions).  I like the way crafting progression is based around destruction rather than construction.  They've thrown out the rulebook on how different classes must structure their gear and skills and this is really refreshing - it leaves a sense of a limitless and rich structure for defining the characters you want to play.
There are a couple of issues that I've noticed on the periphery of the game.  First is that prices advertised in the in-game Crown Store are not always applied as advertised, resulting in my paying around 30% more than expected in two occasions.  The customer service experience in trying to have this rectified via Steam was not helpful at all.  A friend who had the same problem was sorted with a refund but I was not - so it is "hit and miss" with the service level you can expect.  Second is the erotic Role Players who insist on putting their liaisons out there in public channels, the content of which can be brutal and distasteful.  Fortunately those occasions are rare but I would not want my kids hanging out in that kind of environment.  There are some basic things that the developers could do to make the environment safer in this respect e.g. insisting they use a private channel and/or banning reported players for not using one.

The Evil Within 2 is a great survival horror, and is released just in time, Friday the 13th! For all the halloween fans out there.
Its story has a very hollywood feel at first, however does grow depth, "I must save my daughter from the horror story" <- The protagonists goal, this is explored much further and...I aint going to spoil it ;).
The game is mostly set in a town called Union, and unlike the first games linear path, you are given a hubworld to explore, and as you progress the story, more areas will be open to you.
Its not better than the first games linear path, but its not in anyway worse, its fresh and different, given how the last survival horror that attempted this type of open exploration was Alone in the Glitch... sorry Dark. Alone in the Dark (2008) <- I liked it despite its setbacks.
Besides the campaign, you can track down side quests, resource drops, and quite a bit to distract you.
Like the first game, you can choose what upgrades to equip, except this time you have more resources, there is ammo crafting, weapon upgrades and the green gel for Sebastion himself, the protagonist whom you play from the first game.
There are many different enemy types, as well very inventive and visually creative bosses throughout the campaign, adding massive variety and replayablity on higher difficulties.
The open environment reflects the weapons you use, giving the player quite a bit of choice in creative puzzles to clear enemies. Most Enemy AI is varied, think 28 days later sprinters, so dont expect Alien Isolation, however there are a few enemies that give the player a challenge later on, as it ends up being one hit kill.
The gunplay is fun and addictive, just like the first game, enemies react to all areas of their body depending on where the player shoots, and is very reminiscent of Resident Evil 4 in almost all ways. The Evil Within 2 takes references in both gameplay and story from a few titles, Silent Hill, Alone in the Dark, Resident Evil, and Alan Wake, all in one way or another the player will come across.
Like the survival horrors mentioned above, There are also light puzzles, which instead of being tedious like in the first game, are fun and rewarding to the players intelligence.
On first glance, the enviroment of Union appears lazy in design compared to the 19th century town of the first game <- which is very typical halloween. And then you explore it, Union, its details, its hidden treasures, and monsters. Its contemporary references might seem uninspired but its done on purpose, to make the player feel uncomfortable in a very famililar but twisted setting. And this is were Silent Hill, Alan Wake, and Resident Evil references come in.
I left out Alone in the dark because the only thing that game has in common is its open world hub exploration, and its a survival horror..kind of, I think.. kidding ;)
Buy it for yourself or someone you care about, either way, someone is getting a great game! :D

This is one of those games that trancends the medium, this is high art. Being a huge fan of the franchise I was astonished to see how every detail from the first film has been carefully implemented into this game. The lighting, fog effects the sense of dread looming over you while creeping in and out of vents. There are multiple enemies such as androids and scavangers that try to kill you along the way. You almost never feel safe and that's exactly on point with the films.
The stealth gameplay is slow but unnerving, you cannot just lunge at enemies out of the blue. Each task must be handled with caution. However, the game isn't gratuitously unforgiving as some reviewers have complained. If you must, start off on the lowest diffuclty. The enemies are still relentless and tough to beat but you have a fighting chance if you get pinned. Just keep in mind if you use a gun, you may alert the alien. So for all intensive purposes sneak your way past as best as you can. If you are caught, run your♥♥♥♥♥off.

*SPOILER ALERT*
Good. ♥♥♥♥ing. God.
Lets get the basics out of the way;
Yes, this is the genesis for more modern Horror-RPG style games (The Bio Shock series, Dead Space etc)
Yes, this game should be considered a classic
Yes, this game has really good story telling
Yes, this game is a cult classic
Yes, this game can be made better through the use of mods from a very dedicated fanbase.
And yes, this game looks pretty decent, considering the thing is almost 20 years old
[b[ HOWEVER [/b]
System Shock 2 is (partly) guilty of setting the standard for RPG sins. The errand style missions with objectives that can only be completed when you complete other quests because of something breaking or being blocked, Doubling back over the map owed to confusing directions. WHO NEEDS THREE SETS OF CARGO BAYS ALL LABELED "A" AND "B"?!
And those aren't even the worst of anything.
The storyline reaches its climax prematurely when one of the scientists (hardcore System Shockers will know her name) just... reveals herself to be SHODAN. It's not even emotionally impacting. It doesn't even feel shocking. It comes at a point in the story where you can only think "well... oh." and move on.
Then there are the Fireball Monkeys. And the Ninjas. And the Spiders. Whoever though that crowding Ninjas, Spiders, Monkeys, Turrets, Flies, and Grenade-Launching zombies all on the same floor was either a genius, or psychopath. Either way, (s)he was a sadist.  Easy enough to put them down, annoying when combined together, and somehow, friendly fire is only a thing when you are in co-op, and someone is trying to hand you something.
Then came the Turrets. Just like so many other things, sometimes they make sense, and other times they ambush you like radical evangelists preaching a religion of lead and "HOLYHELLWHOPUTYOUTHERE!?!?". Some of the placement would only ever make sense to someone who was directly expecting sabotage.
After the fireballs.
After the grenade launching zombies.
After the Invincible-to-All-Except-An-Inventory-Worth-of-Bullets Spiders (unless you have AP or Anti-Personnel)
After the Turrets
After the Ninjas who couldn't ambush you nearly as well as the turrets
The difficulty spikes OUT OF NO WHERE. The first several parts of the game, the biggest threat you face is the giant mechs because they explode (Come on, they didn't even make it onto the rank of "annoying enemies" that was stated above). Everything else is cakewalk. Then, out of NO WHERE you get invisible brain monsters that constantly respawn in the middle of an unintelligible, indistinguishable blob of flesh that calls itself "The Body of the Many."
Life outside of Co-Op is for the brave or the stupid in this game... but it really is too bad that Co-Op is damn near unplayable.
Using all the save files available, you MIGHT be able to strategically save/load your way through the game. But unless your friends live with you and you have a solid internet connection, you will desync, and the game will crash.
The save files sometimes get corrupted (depending on just how hard the ragequit was), causing players to load into the game with no weapons and no map, or the game will freeze all together, meaning you have to start the game back up and do the whole process over again.
The constant start-and-restart that this game has to offer frustrated gamers makes speed-playing this game possible by the time you have completed the game once through. Not because of the advanced equipment, or the ability to start over with a fully upgraded character. This game doesn't offer that.
What this game DOES offer is an endless cycle of potentially corrupted save files, almost worthy of a meme or internet conspiracy that SHODAN really doesn't want you to beat her in the end of the game. As a result, by the time you actually GET to the end of the game you've memorized levels, passcodes, and can be caught up to your previous progresses by  skipping some of the most tedious parts of the game.
Most problems in this game can be solved with the basic pistol. Hacking is nice to have, but it can be worked around. Repair and Maintenance are essential, but one near-waste-of-time is Psi.  To those of you who would tell me I'm wrong, I will respond as such.
There were only 3 places in this game where I found an item only accessible with Psi. Everything else can be solved with enough bullets and parkour. And the only thing that Psi ACTUALLY yields you is Nanites. Nanites are everywhere.  Psi is pointless.
And alas, on to the managerial stuff. I could say something about how the voice talent is based upon whoever they could find in the developing office, or how the enemies arent all that creepy, or how SHODAN's voice probably served as the inspiration for modern Dubstep music, but Id just be saying things that have all been said a thousand different times.
Dont get me wrong, some of the levels did make me uncomfortable. Nothing that would stop me in my tracks and think about what I just saw, but plenty of "oh that's just nasty."
And finally, the moment that Mass Effect so brilliantly cloned. The Anti Climatic Ending. All that work, all the running around, the rage quits because the save files corrupted, the endless respawns because of invisible enemies, or ninja-like-turrets.
One hack and four bullets later, and SHODAN falls.
I stared at my computer for several moments, even through the "surprise ending" wondering what would be next. There had to be more. That couldn't be it. SHODAN could have done far more than begged for her life, then died in a fifth shot that I didn't even have the pleasure of firing.
*takes a deep breath* But.....
This game truely has stood the test of time. 20 years later, and I am still playing it, slightly disappointed there isn't a sequel coming (EA.... separate rant for a separate time).
This game reminds of those days where objectives weren't just met with a hail of bullets, or a stream of swearing and bloodshed. Back to a time when gaming wasn't about the "achievements" to keep us addicted, or the "immersion" to make us feel like we actually were doing something aside from sitting in front of a TV.
Its something of a triumph, something not everyone would want to do, but everyone could do. You hack, slash, blast and treck for hours on end and feel some level of accomplishment in spite of an unreasonably anticlimactic game. (or it might have something to do with the fact that I suck at gaming)
Yes, the ending itself is a steaming pile of garbage, and though I will complain about the horrible balancing, the shoddy voice acting and the impossible-to-truely-master RPG element, it is a journey worth taking.
Ultimately, it's a quaint ride down an otherwise forgotten place, where gaming wasn't about the graphics, or the blood, but rather about the imagination and thought beyond the kill.
Anyone who wants to know where things like Bethesda's "Dishonored" and "Elder Scrolls" came from should play this game. It's a turning point from where RPGs evolved from table tops and board games to a stand-out genre in the gaming industry.
Most of that was nerd rage over/because the ending. It's a good game. You should buy it if you like classics.
P.S. SHODAN isn't nearly as badass as whatever memes you've read.
