If you're a bit skeptical or on the fence like I was before I bought this game then wait till it's on sale and try it out - you can always refund it if you don't like it. A lot of people on here complain saying this game is disappointing, that it isn't a "true Elder Scrolls game". Well I disagree completely!
This game IS a proper Elder Scrolls game. At its core it is everything you would expect from a proper TES game - freedom to explore, freedom to forge your own character and playstyle, freedom of choice and freedom of approach to situations - do you go into a dungeon shouting battlecries and swinging your battleaxe, or do you take the stealthier approach? Both can be done, and are not mutually exclusive at all - you have total freedom in skill choice. It plays very similarly to the older titles in general, and you start off as a prisoner, escape and then go on to explore the world as you see fit. There is no linear progression path like in other MMOs. You could start in Morrowind for example but run around the entire zone in an unrestrained manner, killing monsters and exploring dungeons and ignoring quests if you so choose.
You can do almost everything in this game that you could in the older titles: Sneak around, steal things, murder people, join factions, make choices that affect the world, make your own unique character build, play in FIRST PERSON with the same / similar combat system to the older games with great new features, find hidden dungeons, secret lore, uncover mysteries etc. Even better is that more features will be added as time goes on.
But what this game does also is enhance the experience by adding new features from other MMOs. This makes it feel fresh and new, because it combines the best aspects of the singleplayer TES games and MMOs like WoW - you have an action bar associated with your weapon, with abilities hotkeyed to the number keys, which you use alongside your standard attacks, power attacks, blocking and bashing.
It breathes new life into the MMO genre I think by having a unique combat system that is addictive, intuitive, much more tactical, and above all FUN. It doesn't feel grindy at all either because the quests are all genuinely interesting and fun, the stories are meaningful and touching, as you would expect from an Elder Scrolls game, and the world is one I am deeply fond of and immersed in already from playing the older games for thousands of hours. Plus you can explore areas that haven't been available in a TES game since Arena or Daggerfall, like Summerset Isle and Valenwood - games which you can't exactly call high-tech.
The music is another strongpoint of this game, because even though it's clearly been designed to be as ambient and non-intrusive as possible for the MMO format, you can still hear familiar themes rise up from the pleasant ambience from time to time, like Watchman's Ease from Oblivion and Blessing of Vivec from Morrowind. The theme is also excellent and was composed by none other than Jeremy Soule, adding to the authentic feeling of the game.
Then of course you have the multiplayer. I have yet to experience this, but from what almost everyone else has said it is supposed to be excellent. Time will tell for me, I've only scratched the surface of this beautiful game.
Speaking of beautiful, the GRAPHICS in this game are excellent and miles better than Skyrim's. The colours are vivid and rich, the shadows are excellent and free of striping that plagued the older games, all the animations are wonderful and smooth, the scenery is amazing and the flora / fauna of the world is highly consistent with older games - giant mushrooms, Alits, Netches and more in Morrowind for example.
On top of all this, we get to meet characters that have always been mentioned in books in previous games but whom we never met -  Mannimarco, Molag Bal, Sotha Sil in the upcoming Clockwork City DLC, to name a few. Speaking of DLC, this game is constantly being updated. They frequently add new areas, such as the recently added Orsinium, and factions such as the upcoming Dark Brotherhood. Eventually I hope they will add every last area of Tamriel, especially Vvardenfell!
I think ultimately that the reason someone would dislike this game is not because it's objectively "bad" but simply because it isn't their cup of tea. I however love it - I would go so far as to say that it ranks alongside the older, legendary titles.

Brilliant game.  The core product has beautiful artwork and quests that are engaging.  In fact the storylines are so expertly constructed that it feels as though I'm a character in an online epic.  They've moved me, made me laugh, and made me go "awww" at times.  The quests force you to make decisions that will have consequences later in the game, such as which friends and enemies you will make that might help or block you later on (individual NPCs, not entire factions).  I like the way crafting progression is based around destruction rather than construction.  They've thrown out the rulebook on how different classes must structure their gear and skills and this is really refreshing - it leaves a sense of a limitless and rich structure for defining the characters you want to play.
There are a couple of issues that I've noticed on the periphery of the game.  First is that prices advertised in the in-game Crown Store are not always applied as advertised, resulting in my paying around 30% more than expected in two occasions.  The customer service experience in trying to have this rectified via Steam was not helpful at all.  A friend who had the same problem was sorted with a refund but I was not - so it is "hit and miss" with the service level you can expect.  Second is the erotic Role Players who insist on putting their liaisons out there in public channels, the content of which can be brutal and distasteful.  Fortunately those occasions are rare but I would not want my kids hanging out in that kind of environment.  There are some basic things that the developers could do to make the environment safer in this respect e.g. insisting they use a private channel and/or banning reported players for not using one.

At the time of this writing I'm sitting at around 700 hours played. I've thoroughly enjoyed at least 500 of those. People forget that this is an early access game, and a lot of the hate directed towards the devs is unwarranted. Some of it is justified. I suppose I'll break it down pro/con style.
Pros:
-Love the graphic style. Probably the least important pro for me, but it is nice. Once the game is optimized better I think it will run like a dream.
-PvP is a blast
-Community is better than other survival games I've played (yes you still have ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and plenty of KoS)
-Gameplay is pretty tight and has a small learning curve
-Building is getting really good after this last update
Cons:
-Bugs / unrefined gameplay. This is my biggest issue. Most of the dev-bashing is about lack of content and whining that new bugs pop-up after each patch. Bugs are to be expected. It's EA. HOWEVER, some things have been present since launch and have not been fixed. No-Clipping animals that walk through walls  or get stuck in them while they hit you. The fall damage system is garbage. You can die from 2ft off the ground.
-Bit of scattered direction from the developers. They either completely ignore the community input (They've completely abandoned their subreddit because it was too toxic) or listen to it too much to the point where they struggle to make a clear decision and go with it. They have to learn to compromise, AND not be so softskinned. It's the internets. People are mean. Ignore them and take the good input.
-Endgame is lackluster. Once you have 10 cars, lockers of materials and a nigh-unraidable base, it becomes a bit stale. There's no "unique" items to strive for or prestigious accolades to acquire. This leads to people mindlessly PvPing and even camping the spawn areas.
So, there's a bit of my 2 cents.
Overall I LOVE this game, and will continue to play it and recommend it to others. I do wish the developers would focus on tightening up what they have already before releasing content that isn't polished or thought through. On the other hand of that statement is the fact that without new content the game becomes stale, so I understand the delicate balance necessary for success is a hard one to find.
Keep an eye on this one, if you're not sure, and check back when it releases. Right now, I'd still say you'd get your money's worth. I know I have.

By far the most fun I've had in a game in a while! 9.5/10.
While my review can not be called "thorough" my enthusiasm to report how amazing this game is should say something at the least. What I feel is the best feature of Just Cause 3 is the fact it plays like a game, not like a pseudo movie. The idea of fun was obviously on the creator's mind during the whole development process where as I feel a lot of developers these days are prioritizing graphics or practicing wallet vamprisim over making a fun and memorable experience for their players.
+ The controls are tight and clean. They make me feel when I die it is my fault, not the game's. The gunplay is not only responsive but tie that in with the Spiderman-esque movement and you've got yourself one hell of a good time. The traveling via hook/parachute/wingsuit felt almost perfect if it were not for the delay with being able to quickly deploy then hide the parachute when trying to zip around the battle. All in all this flaw only took the game down about a 0.1 in my books.
+ The new grapnel hook makes for a world of fun. I recall playing Just Cause 2 way back when on my 360 (sorry) and two things really made me feel the game fell short. One, The idea of only having one hook to tether two things together. And  two; The fact the hook immediately broke under pressure. With these small hook adjustments it made the game so much more enjoyable than it's predecessor.
+ It's big. Ok now I know that bigger aint always better (See: Banjo Kazooie: Nuts and Bolts.) but that's only when the huge area to explore is filled with nothing! Thus far I've been able to be a quick 1 minute float away from yet another fun thing to do!
+ Fixed Rico's voice. One of the things I HATED about just Cause 2 was Rico's voice, it was so fake and cringey I couldn't stand any scene where that cardboard box of a man would try to sputter out a thick stream of camel spit coated words.
~ Day one bugs. I've heard a lot of complaints about some people not being able to play the game since launch. While I feel for those people, I REALLY do, there are also a lot of people able to jump straight into the action.
- Lack of direction. There is quite a fine line between "freedom to choose" and "freedom to wander until something comes up" I found myself at the top of a mountain staring, hungrily at the base ahead of me, when I see a message pop up and my screen go white. Turns out, I had to take care of some base defenses. "No problem!" I thought, unknowingly. I searched around the place for a way to shut off the defenses that would bombard where I was standing every 2 seconds but to no avail. (Remember, I have not played this game for long so I could have missed something.) But as I had not been given any form or direction to help me disable the defenses I felt a little thrown int othe deep end.

Slime rancher is a game where you go into the game expecting a cute mediocre game to pass the time, and end up tranced by the interesting yet simplistic gameplay and the wonderfully intriguing world.
The gameplay focus' around farming slimes (obviously). The way your profit from this is that every time you feed a slime food, they give a Plort, which can be sold for money. Each slime has different traits, and special needs you need to know to keep them, although the harder to keep ones have more expensive plorts. There are also different types of food, and most slimes have a favorite that they will give double the plorts if you feed them it.
Then you have the exploring. What i expected to be mostly just a farming game with a small world to gather supplies in, ended up having a wonderfully large but not confusing world, that kept me wanting to know what was around the next corner in anticipation. Not only was the world fun to explore, but its BEAUTIFUL as well. every single area blew me away more than the last one in how it looks, the map design, and the mechanics in them.
Of course, we can't forget about the slimes! Each slime has a unique look so you can tell them apart,  and some interesting mechanic to keep them from being boring, and these mechanics play into the ranching and the exploring.
The music is wonderful, some tracks that stand out for me are the Ruins themes, and the Glass Desert Firestorm theme.
Heres a part that suprised me, the story. I was not even expecting this game to have ANY story at all going in, and i was mistaken. Although it doesn't force you to follow it, the story comes in the way of these notes that Hobson Twillgers left for you before selling the farm to you, and from the Starmail you recieve from people (mostly Casey). the notes generally tell hobsons story, while the emails tell the story of your past live before you were sent to your ranch on the Far Far Range. Casey and Hobbson are both great characters, and really feel like people despite you never actually seeing them (as far as i know).

A lot of the negative reviews here are because of poor performance. I was one of the lucky people who actually had perfect performance from day 1, so just bear that in mind. I do believe, however, that at the time of writing this now there has been a PC patch which has solved the issues for most people.
This game was a very worthy successor to the first, and I played through it twice almost non stop (aside from eating, sleeping and going to work obviously). There were a lot of mechanics that were pulled across from the first game, which gave it that familiar feel and I was able to get going pretty quickly. I played as Corvo the first time through, which was more similar to the first game than Emily's powerset. The powers and mechanics were smooth and effective, providing a large range of ways that each level could be approached.
The world felt alive, and was very well designed. There are nooks and crannies and secrets everywhere, and a whole multitude of different routes you can take to reach your destination, if you are willing to look for them. Both low and high chaos (ie stealth vs brawl-ish) play-throughs were well catered for, which is not something you find verry often.
My first playthrough, as Corvo, took me about 20 hours. I went for full stealth with no kills. I subsequently played through a Emily with high chaos, which took me about 4.5 hours as I already knew the levels inside out thanks to playing stealth first.
I can wholeheartedly recommend this game, and I'd be tempted to say it was my favourite game of 2016!

Fantasic sequel, improves on almost everything from the original.
-Performance is great, never dipping below 60 frames on all Medium-High settings (Shadows and draw distance at Medium). Running on a GTX 970, Intel i5, 16gb RAM.
-Story is very compelling, starting slower in the beginning and ramping up very quickly. You'll explore the main town of Union, which acts as the "hub" town, Underground Catacombs and old hospitals/Sanitariums and many more varied locations.
-Graphically the game impresses, utilizing very pleasing lighting and particle effects. Shadows play a big role and look fantastic. Physics on most destructable items (both enemy and object) look great.
-Gameplay is super fluid and feels much at home other well refined action/horror games. While not genre defining, it uses action/stealth hybrid gameplay, as well as a great crafting system to full immerse the player in the world Tango has created.
-Control is tight, with Sebastian being able to going from quiet sneaking to a full on 180 sprint at the drop of a hat. No horrible mouse acceleration, or any real control issues I found in my 13 hour playthrough.
-Mouse and Keyboard controls are great, doesn't feel as though they were an afterthought. Key bindings are all there, although the base mapping is fine to use.
-UI is clean and never takes up much screen space. Easy on the eyes and shows exactly what you need to know.
-Difficulty is on point, with AI reacting responsively to Sebastians movement and sound generation. Ammo is much more scarce at higher difficulties and gives the tension of the game a very welcome boost. Enemies hit hard, but smart play can circumvent most tough situations.
-Game has a crafting system, and it doesn't have some money grubbing loot box system that seems to be all the rage these days. Automatic plus.
All in all, If you were a fan of the original, enjoy action style horror games, loved RE4/Silent Hill 2/Alan Wake, then this game is right up your alley and well worth the purchase price. Highly recommended to any fan of the genre.
Kudos Tango, you folks nailed this one.
*Completion Edit:*
So far this is my Game of The Year. The story held me until the very end, and the ending left me extremely satisfied. With not many releases coming left for this year (Possibly Wolfenstein), I'm confident this will remain GOTY. Once again Tango deserves mountains of credit for the game they worked so hard on. Phenominal job, looking forward to potential DLC or Sequel.

If you have ever wanted to immerse yourself in the world of the original Alien film (or just the general feeling of being hunted by something that lives only to kill in horrible, penetrative ways), there is very little here that will distract you from that experience.  Stellar world-building with some obvious dedication to and love for the source material more than compensates for the sometimes stale and unnecessary story elements.  I binge-played this game over the course of about a week, which is unusual for me -- especially in a horror game.  I simply couldn't stop and didn't want to.
My one note-worthy gripe would be the endgame... probably due to a combination of my game-fatigue (as a result, in part, of the binge-playing), the overall length of game being a bit long for something so intense (I was very thorough, so it took me 30+ hours), and a few too many narrative climaxes crammed together in the last few chapters (resulting in a shift in tone to the ending gameplay that I didn't entirely need or want).  I also didn't find the concept of Survivor mode interesting enough to pursue/puchase.
In short:  I loved it, despite a few flaws.  My fingers are crossed that the rumors of a follow-up come true.

Although it certainly strays from some of the series mainstays, King's Quest still manages to feel like the classic series while also managing to skillfully update the series for the modern audience.
At the time of this writing, two episodes are available, and I have completed one. I am hoping the remainder will get released soon, but regardless.
The graphics offer a wonderful painted style, and the voice acting is charming and spot on. Hardcore fans of the original series may take issue with the changes made to series canon, but ultimately the new series still maintains those elements while also making a new chapter for the game series. There is lots of puzzles solved by having the right item in your inventory, but fortunately the game is more forgiving and less obtuse and punishing than the original games were.
If you are familiar with the original games, or are at all familiar with Telltale's series of point and click adventure games (The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among us, Back to the Future: The Game, etc.), then you will enjoy this game, as it is ultimately a hybrid of the original series with elements used from Telltale's recent ventures into the genre.

Eternal Senia has a lovely art style, touching storyline and fun gameplay. It isn't groundbreaking or anything but it does have a crafting system and much of the level design includes puzzles which should be solved either for progression or unique pieces of loot.
The story is emotional and compelling. I find myself wanting to venture further and further in order to discover what is really going on and what mysteries are linked to the main characters.
The music in the game most closely reminds me of the midi tunes from early RPG games such as Phantasy Star from the Sega Master System. The music is varied and fits nicely with the game. It never sounded repetative or annoying.
On top of all that, there are weather effects in the game which can be turned on or off. Not sure why anyone would turn them off but, ok. These weather effects add another element of unpredictability to the game which in turn makes the world of Eternal Senia feel somewhat natural and alive.
Again, the manga-style character art is lovely as are the environments and boss designs.
Did I mention that this game is completely free?
Give it a try.

If you take a brief moment to look up the history of “Slimes” then you will find that they have been around for a LONG time. Dating far back, in films such as 1958‘s “The Blob” and then we have the classic 1974’s “Dungeons & Dragons” featuring a multitude of slimey deaths. “Dragon Quest” has its famous slime mascot, that to this day, is still it’s trademark and has been since 1986. Then, in 2017 we got Slime Rancher.
Say what you want about the gelatinous goobers, but geek/gaming culture loves colorful blobs with happy faces on them. My career into games journalism began with a game called “Attack of the Gelatinous Blob”. If it wasn’t for Slime I might not be writing this. Okay, I probably still would be but you get the point. Slimes can do no wrong.
Gaming history lesson aside, I haven't checked out the game since  Monomi Park released the Slime Science update. Since then we have had Ancient ruins added, customization options, Gordo snares, and finally the Glass desert which lead to the final release of Slime Rancher. Then a post patch release came almost right after the games official launch date.(It was hard to keep up while writing this review!) There is plenty to cover here.
Slime Rancher tasks you with capturing slimes, exploring, and maximizing your profits from slime poop. What makes Slime Rancher unique is that it is all done from a first person perspective. The world is a vibrant and colorful place that welcomes you with open arms and makes it hard to leave. I have played Slime Rancher for hours and it felt like minutes. It’s just that fun. There is always something to do or see and usually many goals for you to accomplish.
I know it’s cliche but Slime Rancher is only going to give you as much as you put into it. If you are coming in here expecting Stardew Valley, you are making a mistake. Before, I had compared Slime Rancher to Viva Pinata in the same way Stardew Valley is to Harvest Moon. What I meant by that is that these games have crossing ideas and themes, but at the core are very different from each other. Comparing them is silly, ultimately.
Which brings me to the base features of Slime Rancher. If we boil it down and remove all the fantastic cuteness and sap all the charm and aesthetic. What we have is still a really fun and enjoyable game that gives you quite a bit to do. Capturing ‘livestock’ and mixing them for maximum profit, setting up your Ranch perfectly, exploring and unlocking all of the treasures. Diving into the science crafting system, which albeit is more about fluff then anything.
I have racked up about forty hours, easily, and still haven’t unlocked everything. One thing to keep in mind though is that the late game is more about fluff then anything else. The initial experience of Slime Rancher is by far its biggest highlight. Finding a new slime and sucking it up happily never gets old. Passing my chicken coop and mimicking their squawks never gets old, for me. Discovering a new zone or place always holds a mystery and I loved exploring. Watching my drill and science machines dance is adorable.
Lets get real though, the end of “Adventure mode” isn’t as exciting as I would’ve hoped. However, the game doesn’t necessarily end at that moment. If you are the type who enjoys getting everything in a game or setting up the Ranch exactly how you like it; then there is plenty to sink your teeth into. Still the end is more of a whisper then a bang. There are some things that felt somewhat hollow in this densely rich world. Primarily the story aspect of Slime Rancher I didn’t really care about.
Throughout the game are letters and journal entries that tell two separate stories. The problem is that that they serve no purpose to the game whatsoever. I had a hard time getting involved or caring about the story because it didn’t really have a face. I would say the lack of NPC’s in Slime Rancher is its greatest flaw. It’s just you, slimes and some letters. Why stop and read a letter when I can be off doing something way more fun. If the journal entries had been directly tied somehow to the core gameplay, It might’ve of been different.
Combat at times comes off feeling hollow as well. While I loved that the Tarr existed and I was very careful at all times on the Ranch, out in the wild, combat is pointless and more of nuisance as fear of death is usually zero. I died more from water and falling than anything else. I would’ve loved to have seen some reward from killing Tarr or perhaps a whole area dedicated to them for combat purposes. Bringing in useful science gadgets like the turrets and maybe make fighting slimes?  Using the different attributes of each slime to make them useful in combat? Oh and it would’ve made those health upgrades more useful.
One other gripe I did have was the fact that Slime Rancher didn’t have a map, but one post release patch changed that. So yeah, good job Monomi Park.
Having boiled it down and examined features, lets bring back all the amazing aesthetics, themes and joy which launches Slime Rancher into the stratosphere. I love how Slime Rancher looks if that isn’t clear. Even the Glass desert which is supposed to be a bare, dry and boring area looks amazing. Watching Gordo slimes get fatter and eventually explode is horrific but its adorable!
The music and sounds all enhance Slime Rancher in the visuals department. When The Tarr show up, the music dramatically shifts. Or the humming of my rad slimes. Hearing my slimes play with their toys. There is nothing negative I can’t think to say about the music and sound of Slime Rancher. It delivers exactly what it needs to, but I can’t think of one track that exactly blew my mind. Still pleasant nonetheless.
It’s undeniable that Slime Rancher is cute. The beauty of it being in first person makes it feel like you can reach out and touch the world. This combined with the gameplay makes for an unforgettable experience and one worthy of your attention.
There wasn’t a game like Slime rancher before its release and their hasn’t been after.
From an innovation standpoint, Slime Rancher knocks it out of the park. I can’t think of a single game that works as smoothly in the same fashion, but does things so differently. When you launch Slime Rancher, its helpful guides, tutorials and theme make it very welcoming to new players or to people who have played it since day one.
Just write out the idea of Slime Rancher on paper and it sounds crazy. It’s a FPS game where you farm slimes and their poop with a vacuum gun. My first question would’ve been, “Are you high?!”
I want to see more games like Slime Rancher and I certainly think that it is an Early Access success story. Proving that the system can work if it is treated correctly. The developer seems keen on adding even more content which I will gleefully await. The only thing lacking is probably a replay value. Slime Rancher is very modular in the way it lets you change or remove things. Starting over again is kind of pointless. Perhaps adding different starting ranches might change this.
If you are looking for a game that is relaxing, fun, and doesn’t take itself too seriously then you need to check out Slime Rancher. The game is brilliant, cute and I highly recommend it. Oh and unlike other Early Access games, they didn’t jack up its price on release. Kudos.

- extremely poor engine performance
- visually very so-so
- unexciting gameplay and combat
- weird/uncomfortable mouse panning
- ridiculous load times at the initial screen, followed by unskippable branding videos
- poor NPC AI
- poor 3D sound positioning
- poor, fussy UI design
I could go on but I am starting to feel slightly nauseous even thinking about this game. Its bad parts outweigh whatever good is in this game by such a large margin that I cannot recommend PC version of Dishonored 2 to anyone. I feel I had been cheated by Bethesda/Arcane.

More specific examples include improved optional stealth, safe/save houses with a base of ops (sebastien's office),  a well implemented crafting station mechanic to upgrade weapon stats and produce extra ammunition, the psych chair for upgrading character stats iin diversified fields and responsive gunplay with multiple weapons/gadgets. The general art direction and graphical presentation is breathtaking and deserves special mention with especially great environments (a pseudo open world design working well here too). Theres plenty of psychological thriller moments with great boss battles, interesting NPCs and a generally cliched but very well done story with impressive length (took me 21hours on initial playthrough and im not a completionist by any stretch). I really hope these sort of AAA singleplayer games of such quality continue to be produced.
Topically Its saddening to hear that these type of well made AAA singleplayer games which cost more to produce now than ever before (and yet cost the consumer the same fas 12 years ago) perform poorly in sales when something that can be easily monetised through border line gambling (loot boxes etc) like say a certain blizzard multiplayer game (one among many) seems to be doing so well. (Some light spoilers ahead but I really only "spoil" the early hours of the game)
"Like Alan Wake and Silent Hill had a baby with Resident Evil as the surrogate" - thats how I described The Evil Within 2 to a friend when asked for a brief summary. And after beating the game, I still stand by that description.
The first entry in The Evil Within series was ambitious and a pretty decent game, but it had its problems. The sequel fixes most of these problems but it still has a handful that can really hamper your experience.
A quick recap first though. Three years after the events of the first game, Sebastian is tracked down by his former partner who has been working for the secret organisation Mobius all along. He is told his daughter is actually alive and has been with them inside one of their STEM machines all this time, and they need him to go in and retrieve her.
Not long after setting foot inside the virtual world he encounters the villain of the game, Stefano Valentini, a photographer obsessed with killing people in the name of art, and thus the game sets you free to explore its new partially open world. The open world is somewhat reminiscent of Silent Hill, letting you explore and find various secrets and optional items/areas. Hell, one of the best and scariest encounter I had was entirely optional but the payoff was well worth it.
Before I move on to the issues of the game, I should mention that the PC port is not perfect. Stutters and frame drops galore, I ran it on ultra and while it mostly ran at a smooth 60, some areas would plummet to 30 or below, which was frustrating especially during combat. Despite this though the game looks phenomenal when maxed out and the cutscenes are also much improved, albeit some lip sync issues in one midway through the story.
Considering its a survival horror game where stealth is key to conserving ammo and making it out alive, the stealth in this is truly atrocious at times. You would think that a stealth kill on any enemy (bar bosses of course) would kill them in one hit but no! The masked ones take two stealth kills to be killed and a certain mini-boss towards the end of the game takes three, so what should be a reward for successfully sneaking up on them instead turns into a game of cat and mouse consisting of you doing the stealth attack (that is if they don't magically spot you), then retreating and hiding until they reset to their original path, repeating until they die.
Sure you have the bottles to distract them with and lure into an isolated spot but half the time they don't notice or seem to see you throw it and head towards you. And the crossbow being a silent weapon should kill instantly if you land a headshot, but again it doesn't. It needs to be upgraded to a certain point for that, and thats if the buggers can stop moving around constantly.
Bar the issues with the crossbow that I had, the weapons are overall great, you can feel the power behind them. The pistol is weak at first but can become a powerhouse and is best used for headshots, the shotgun is phenomenal for crowd control, the sniper is great for....well, sniping of course, the assault rifle is perfect for dealing quick amounts of low damage to stagger enemies and the flamethrower is a flamethrower, nothing much to say about it.
Just like the first game, the bosses in this are incredible and pretty goddamn terrifying, especially the first one. Briefly appearing in a mirror as a woman in a red dress, she then appears in the mirror as a multiple headed woman who then smashes through it revealing her grotesque body made of mannequins and then proceeds to stalk you relentlessly. She shows up at certain points outside but these are optional.
In the actual fight with her I downed her in roughly two minutes with my shotgun, only to find out that the arena was packed with traps to use against the monster, which opens up a whole new tactic to fight her for my next playthrough.
The rest of the bosses are best left to be experienced yourself.
A feature that surprised me was the addition of a shooting range just like in my beloved Resident Evil 4. Where that game gave you bottlecaps for getting certain scores on each stage, Evil Within 2 offers different prizes. I highly recommend doing it early on for the extra resources to give you the upper hand.
Whether the game gets DLC at some point in the future or the devs have a third entry planned, all I know is I need more of this series.

This game was a disappointment. I would not recommend this to anyone. Main issues with the game, ignoring the technical problems (which there are a few).
1. Short story, very short story.
2. Very easy game, too easy.
3. Characters feel wooden, story feels boring. I just didn't love or hate the heroes or the villian.
4. Very repetative. All the bases and towns feel the same. It becomes a chore to blow stuff up, does not feel sandbox at all.
5. Big map, mostly empty. Each region has only a handful of actual bases to take, so the content of this game could have been fit into a much smaller map. Don't get me wrong, I LOVE big maps, but you have to fill them with interesting things to do! The only concession to this I will make is that the vistas are truly stunning. It is a very lovely, big empty map.
6. The only "buiildings" you can blow up that are not choas objects (fuel tanks, radars, water towers etc) are the bridges. Don't get me wrong, I loved blowing up bridges. You can only do that so many times though, before you start thinking "why not other things?!?".
So, largely dull game. Weak story, repetative challenges and bases. There is simply not enough to do to justify the £40 price tag, and that sans the DLC. With DLC it is £60, for 15 hours of boredem. It took me a lot to drag the game length even that far.
It does have potential though. Wingsuiting everywhere is pretty cool. So is hijacking helis and tanks, laying ruin to all those around. It falls far short of living up to what it could have been though. I highly advise against buying this game.

I really appreciate the constant updates and improvements over this game, but i'd rather play the original free sourceport. Now, i am not saying this because i like free stuff (but honestly, who doesn't?) but rather the gameplay is really unsatisfying to me.
I like everything about the Steam version of this game, except for the core element: the gameplay.
Let me try to explain what i don't like about the gameplay.
- running and moving in general feels very stiff compared to the sourceport version
- i don't like the updated guns, especially the normal handgun, because it also feels very stiff while firing the gun
compared to the sourceport version. I am aware of the secondary fire in the Steam version but it just feels very
unnatural.
- the autorun function is... weird in this game. I am a regular Half-Life player and as most of you probably know, running
is the default speed in that game. In the sourceport version of the game you can enable that function as well as in the
Steam version, so no problem there for me. What is my problem is that it also feels rather stiff in my opinion. It's not
feeling like in Half-Life where you just constantly move fast, no, in the Steam version it acts as an automatic button
press of the running button. The sourceport version actually feels like Half-Life becuase when you enable the automatic
running it just let's you move fast like in Half-Life.
- one last thing: the part where you jump those crates over the pit, it often happened to me that the jump command
(which is on default) didn't react to my input while running to jump the crates. I checked my keyboard but it is fine and
fuctioning.
These are pretty much my only gripes with the game. I don't mean to be an♥♥♥♥♥and i really like the game still. Everything else is definitely improved and superior over the sourceport version. What i like especially is the jumping! You jump a lot higher in the Steam version which actually improves part of the gameplay compared to the sourceport version. So, no crouch jumping in the Steam version required.
I can recommend the game. I really appreciate all the work and updates put into the game. So kudos to the developers!!

Black Mesa is an excellent remake of the original Half-Life game. I love nearly everything this had to offer. Made in a 10+ year old engine, this game looks gorgeous and I enjoyed playing it. Of course, I'm still waiting for Xen to come out but hopefully it will be worth the weight. The multi-player seems like a nice addition but unfortunately it is a ghost town.

Pro : I can't explain it any better than the game's description. It's Half-life made on the source engine. That enough makes it epic. The gun skins are improved, the gun spread is improved, the AI is improved, but the feeling you get playing it is the same. It's that well-done.
Con : I feel like I held off on buying this for so long, because I wanted it to be finished. I feel like it's been years that people have been saying this game is good, but they're waiting for Xen. Turns out there's not much out there for me at the moment, so I decided to get this. I can't wipe away the good with the bad, but they've been saying they're working on Xen for the longest time. They said they had to revamp a  few things to get Xen exactly how they want it, but there are moments where you see the Xen creep [From lack of a better word] and it looks great, which is mostly what Xen is, so I have trouble figuring that they're being 100% honest with us.
Overall : Full game, for 20$. As it stands right now, I beat everything in 9 hours, and paid 10 bucks when it was on sale. I got my money's worth, sure, but I dread the thought of how long it'll be till the Final Chapter is complete. We'll see.

Its a fun remake, but its not fun. Its quite hard to even express how I feel about this game, because its awesome in multiple ways... but it falls short in so many.
Here are my biggest complaints...
Guns don't seem to do anything, its like if the bullets are made of thin paper. It takes about 20 bullets to kill one npc, less if you try to aim for the head which is good. However, ammo is a consistent issue and it doesn't feel realistic how I have to reload so many times just to kill six dumb npc's, only to run out of ammo much later in game. If this is "realistic", then it should be named ARMA: Black Mesa. Because the issues of gunfight are severe, I don't remember the game playing this bad at the launch of the mod. When it was free, of course... Oh and this was in NORMAL difficulty.
Performance is also mediocre, most scenes look fantastic and show how powerful the source engine can be if used right. Sadly, the game drops fps all the way to 20fps. Even if you have asus strix r9 390 with an eight core processor, there isn't a lot of demanding gameplay happening... yet performance suffers. It seems to be engine based so far, so I suggest them to upgrade towards the better Source 2 if they can. Otherwise, try to make the scenes more optimized.
Multiplayer is braindead, there is no point in playing with the "Community Browser" as Valve states it. Which is god awful, it needs to be redesigned on how broken it is. Don't even try looking for servers, at best you'll find two or three servers with three people. But that's it, nothing more.
The graphics are... dissapointing. "WHAT!?! IT LOOKS FANTASTIC!! HOW COULD YOU!?!?!" - (Probably you right now) While the screenshots don't lie, there is a severe lack of texture quality, most textures have severe degradation. Meaning that there is no uncompressed textures, even at "VERY HIGH" texture setting. Not sure if this is a source engine issue, but even in EA status, it needs to be addressed. I see billboards that have so much detail, only to be ruined by the texture compression. I want to read all the small details, because that would seriously add so much more immersion into this game.
The AI is bs, so many issues with instant-kills with headcrabs taking up to 20 health damage. Soldiers are worse though, their rifles kill you in seconds, while your rifle doesn't do anything to them. I don't know how this is "balanced" but you gonna have to bite the bait for that one. This is on NORMAL difficulty of course, and I presume the HARD difficulty has no ammo / health pickups, because finding ammo is already a hard deed enough.
The PROS!
Well, it does a fantastic job replicating Half-Life, the maps are all recognizable. The effort and love that was added is fantastic, you can truly see they are trying. Graphics are pretty good, and could become better in the future. Gameplay is almost there, but just need the tunning that I've stated before.
VERDICT ===
If you want to help the developers make this better, by all means go grab it and play it for yourself. Constructive criticism and issues pointing is gonna make sure developers to fix these issues before launch. Which is good, but there is many issues if you just want to play the game.
If you want it, which I can't blame you... grab it on sale which is how I did get the copy. Don't pay full price just yet, but if you can't resist, be aware of the current issues. Your i7 might still have some issues or even 8120 fx processors on how odd the game is in performance.

I tried MMOs like WoW and Guild Wars and F2P-stuff and was quickly bored (as single-player). Also disliked the perspective in third person.
In comes ESO, I really dig it. There is a load of content, optional party play, you can still see other players and help them if you like but you don’t have to. The world just feels populated.
There is a massive PvP zone if you like that, there is crafting, exploration, endless quests, Elder Scroll lore and areas, vampires, werewolves, thievery, mounts, achievements, collectables.
It’s not a story/character-RPG, don’t expect “Witcher”-content, just “Elder Scroll baseline”.
It’s an MMO, no overpowered Chrysamere found just lying around in a dungeon also no quicksave scamming.
It's not Skyrim or Oblivion.

Still it’s really nice and I can recommend it esp. when it’s on sale and for ES fans.

Dark Souls' reputation for overwhelming is undeserved. Dark Souls is challenging; there's a learning curve that you need to overcome and if you're not careful you will die no matter how much experience you have. However, I've never been killed without a clear idea of what I did wrong and what I should have done differently.
The good:  Much, much better port than its predecessor. Graphics are beautiful, the 60fps makes everything smooth and fluid, and it runs without a hitch on my laptop, which is a few years old. The game plays much the same as its predecessor, and still has excellent combat mechanics, which are ultimately what you're here for. PVP is competitive and intense, but not inaccessible. Ultimately, I have had tons of fun with this game.
The bad: The world feels a bit less realized than the DS I world. Dark Souls doesn't tell story by exposition and dialogue; 99% of the story is in the environments and they felt a bit more cardboard than the ones in DS I. I think some tweaks are still in order for balance and shoring up some things (those halberd and katana hitboxes, though), but nothing major.

Lets begin my review of Call of Duty Advanced Warfare which is the first game of the new studio Sledgehammer. To start i will break the review in 3 categories campaign , multiplayer and zombies.
The campaign starts really good. You meet the character private Jack Mitchell a former US marine. He gets into a big war against the korean army in the first mission Induction. Something bad happens in this mission and his arm gets cut off and his best friend dies. A few years later Mitchell goes to his friends fineral and there he meets Jonathan Irons the leader of Atlas Corporation. Mitchell unrolls into Atlas and then he meets Gideon and other Atlas members. Then we follow Mitchell as he does really amazing missions with the Atlas Corporation. But something happens with Jonatha Irons because he becomes corupted. Then Mitchell and another Atlas member Ilona join Sentinel Task Force. From there the campign gets really good I dont want to spoil anything so you have to play the game to get the rest of the story. Trust me its really good.
Multiplayer - It has been redefined because of the new exo mechanics. You can double boost jump to the top of a building its just phenomenal. This time arround we get the pick 13 system so basicly its the same thing as Black Ops 2 but you get bonus 3 slots instead of 10. The guns are really good I personally think they are not overpowered maybe the EM1 but thats a diffrent story. Overall the multiplayer is really good and they did a good thing this time except with some crushes and black screens and other things that crash the game sometimes.
Zombies - First of all you get a special zombie round in exo survival once you unlock the Riot map. Which is nice but for people who whant more they can go and purchase the Havoc DLC and other DLC's to come in the future. The Havoc DLC comes with the map Outbreak which follows the adventure of 4 Atlas members who are trap in the Atlas research facility who have to defend against waves of zombies. There is an easter egg on here but the plan to escape dosent go that well. You will find out why. I will update the review once other zombies maps released in the future. This review is updated - The second map is very great it sets you in a burger town like setting and it has some nice challanges along the way. The third map is also very intresting and unique and you get to play with a new character set in a carrier that new character is from the sentinel task force. And for the grand finale you get to enjoy some very twisted unexpected turn out on the final map but no spoilers their. People still play the zombies mode cheers.
I do recommend this game to all my friends and other people. Is it the best Call of Duty experience ? Yes very good one. What is bad now is that is 2016 and nobody plays the game anymore so if you want you can go buy black ops 3 or infinite warfare.

If you are an old time gamer who loved the original King's quest back in the 80's, then this King's Quest may feel a bit of a let down. I liked the open end worlds of the original series. You could make mistakes and get yourself in a corner where you couldn't win. It was a challenge, especially back then because you didn't have the internet to help you cheat through the puzzles. Also in the old games Graham was a bit of a badass. In this one he is a little clumsy dork who has no business being in an adventure game.  The puzzles were too easy and pretty much impossible to screwed up if you click enough buttons. The game play is linear so there are only so many options. It was actually more of a movie than a game. For me this sort of ruined the game and didn't keep true to the orginal series.
If you were never a fan of the original series, you were part of the entitled generation who feels like they should be a king even though they can barely walk without tripping over their own goofy feet, and you like simple puzzles that you can't fail at then maybe this game is for you.
I am on the fence at how to rate this... It would be a pretty good game for little kids, but it isn't a KIng's Quest game.

If you have never played the original Half-Life I'd say get it on sale for one buck as it has aged really well and still is a lot of fun. It also has this cute charm to it that you're playing a game that was made by a (back then) small studio that hoped to gain fame with it. And fame they got.
If you want to play Black Mesa though definitely pick it up on a sale, as ~10 hours of gameplay is not worth $20.
- Good looking level design that is faithful to the original
- Gorgeous soundtrack that captures the spirit of the original composed by Kelly Bailey
- It's nice they have changed some of the weapons back to their original behavior like the Glock and MP5
- Developers ban and lock threads of everyone that states criticism on the forum, so don't bother posting yours
- Weird 3D crossbow scope; the mark is below the actual destination where the bolt will hit and everything you see will be the low-poly version of the distant enviroment (pixelated and half-transparent); I'd prefer a scope à la Half-Life 2 over this
- Horrendous ragdoll physics
- Rebalanced weapons, which I think is weird. Now it takes two Magnum shots on easy difficulty to kill a Vortigaunt instead of one and five Glock shots to kill a Barnacle instead of four.
- Weapons have less overall max ammo
- Stupid AI followers
- Optimization and crashes; they should call it "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Engine"
- Scientists and security guards all look and sound almost the same. While this was the same in the original Half-Life, how much trouble would it have been to just get a few more voice actors with the help of the internet? It's 2017, not 1998 anymore.
- In development since 2005 yet it's still not finished in 2017

I binge-played this game over the course of about a week, which is unusual for me -- especially in a horror game.  I simply couldn't stop and didn't want to.
My one note-worthy gripe would be the endgame... probably due to a combination of my game-fatigue (as a result, in part, of the binge-playing), the overall length of game being a bit long for something so intense (I was very thorough, so it took me 30+ hours), and a few too many narrative climaxes crammed together in the last few chapters (resulting in a shift in tone to the ending gameplay that I didn't entirely need or want).  I also didn't find the concept of Survivor mode interesting enough to pursue/puchase.
In short:  I loved it, despite a few flaws.  My fingers are crossed that the rumors of a follow-up come true.

______________________________________________________________________________
Graphics: Top 5 best looking games of 2015, possibly 1st.
Audio: Unbelievable. The alien's weight is revealed by the thumping, pouding steps it takes. It's size and somewhat clumsiness is revealed by the banging of air ducts. ______________________________________________________________________________
Mechanics and Gameplay: Unpredictable alien. He will search the general area, but he doesn't try TOO hard if he hasn't noticed you yet. However, once he knows you are in the vicinity, he will hunt you down. The flamethrower does make some of the game a breeze, but once it runs out, the panic of realizing you have to actually hide from him again and are utterly defenseless settles in heavily. Humans are also pretty scary in this game, mostly because their gunshots attract the alien, and they kill quickly, too. Working Joes can sometimes be a hassle, but they are overall a positive addition to the game. Originally, raincoat joes♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off, but I realized I didn't need to confront them (this is a stealth game after all). Overall, okay, not as bad as people say they are.

Lasting Impression: I wanted more. Admittedly, now that I think about it, I feel like the Joes stole away some fun sneaking-from-alien time from me. Instead of mashing some robot's head off, I could have been sneaking from the alien. I was sad the game was over, but it was not a dissapointing ending. If you enjoyed the game, you'll enjoy the ending. That's all I'm saying.

This is the best game based on/related to the very first "Alien" movie....the game is so well written they can make a movie out of it. Never heard of this "CA" dev but they built an engine ground up just for this game...and they did an excellent job! This is one of the very few PC games I played that had zero issues on day one and has a rock solid performance.
The game itself is a true survival horror fps. In the main game you play as Amanda Ripley (Ellen's daughter) who must survive using various tools and usual guns...killing the baddies and Aliens or just sneaking around all together. At first the game is really good. Unfortunately as the game progresses there is way too much obvious backtracking which makes the game pretty boring. You'll be like haven't I done this same thing for the last 7/8 missions?
The game is not long at all but it's been superficially made VERY long using this backtracking bs with added do this and do that on each end of the map...while baddies slow you down even more as you try to do it. And in the last missions there's upgraded baddies which take even longer to kill or to sneak around. However there are some variety...very few...I'll not spoil it.
I think the dev knew the main game gets stale pretty quick...so they added the DLC missions based on the first movie...where you play as Ellen Ripley, Dallas and Parker - each with their own mission path. I found them to be way more fun because the Nostromo was done really and it doesn't drag on like the main game. Also a chance explore Nostromo to some degree - very true to source material. I got crew expendable and last survivor for free...and enjoyed them way more. Btw the game looks gorgeous and sound design is perfect.
Overall I would give the dev's an A+ for effort. The main game is like a 7/10 from me but Alien movie related DLC's are 10/10.

Scariest part of this game was constantly wondering if I would regret giving Bethesda $60 for the sequel to one of their poorest rated games of all time.
I was honestly a huge fan of the first game, despite its many flaws (plot holes, atrocious PC optimization, etc.), so I was thrilled to see that The Evil Within was getting another chance at being the great horror game I knew it could be. Shamelessly preordered it and avoided all gameplay videos leading up to release, and my relief was ♥♥♥♥ing palpable when I finished the campaign, because this game really did a great job nailing all the elements it wanted to hit. The Evil Within 2 took the best features from the first game, revamped them, and improved the gameplay significantly. Say goodbye to the archaic controls of the first game and enjoy a control scheme that actually belongs on this side of the turn of the century. Sebastian still controls like an oafish old man, but I'll chalk that up to a design decision since he's supposed to be a raging alcoholic whose body probably isn't functioning at 100%. Standard enemy types are nearly identical to the first game, but there are a few variants now that actually force you to change up your strategy when trying to take them on, which is nice, and the variants are more than just a carbon copy of a regular enemy with an armor mask slapped on thank god. The pseudo open world map is actually very well realized and fun to explore, as well as crucial to explore in order to collect materials to upgrade Sebastian and his weapons. In some respects I'd say that the first game visually looked better than some areas in the new game, as both of them are running on variants of the id Tech5 engine, but the new game is being forced to render a larger open world environment, however the indoor levels in the new game look fantastic and are very immersive. The bosses/mini bosses in this game are all excellently designed from a visual standpoint but all the encounters are a little stale as each boss feels like a bullet sponge. I would have appreciated seeing each boss have a little more variety in terms of how you're supposed to approach fighting them, but at least the final boss fight is redeeming in this category and incredibly memorable. The overall plot is servicable: nothing mind blowingly complex but a pretty engaging story told in a competent way that'll keep you interested through the 14-20 hour runtime.
Overall I'm blown away by how they took one of my favorite games and completely revitalized it and made it into the blockbuster horror game that so many of its fans knew it desrved to be.

I have traditionally hated most MMOs. I started trying them with Ultima Online in 1997. I played for one month before getting bored. Everquest? Hated it. World of Warcraft? Could't catch my interesting. All of this free-to-play nonsense? Too full of whiny children.
But something is different about Elder Scrolls Online. I've played it more than almost any other game in my library, and I doubt I'm going to stop anytime soon. It's very engaging. I almost feel like I'm playing a single-player RPG that just happens to have some other players in it. And that's great!
The amazing amount of content in this game is staggering. At 127 hours played, I have not even finished one-third of the main game yet. The stories are reasonably well written, and the quest structure typically falls outside of the standard MMO faire of "go kill 10 wolves" (though there are a few quests like this). There are various player choices to be made, as well, that have minor effects on the game world.
But it isn't all roses. The built-in UI is woefully inadequate and requires a smattering of add-ons to make it really useable. There are quite a few bugs left in the game (though the support forums show they're fairly quick to address). And some of the choices are very imbalanced (see, for instance, the Mages Guild quest line).
Overall, I highly recommend this game. If you are a fan of RPGs at all, you should find some enjoyment here.

The EW 2 is not, in the true sense of the word, a sequel to Shinji Mikami’s masterpiece.
Trying to be its own thing, namely to be a more “western” type of game, it loses what made the first game great as well as unique and offers a decent yet uninspired game experience.
The level, enemy, environment and encounter designs can’t hold a candle to the EW 1 and rank from good to below average.  Whereas, The EW 1 threw a new combat situation, a new enemy at you every 15 minutes and features some expertly designed game environments, here the combat scenario are quite repetitive and lack creativity. The open world aspect seems a nice addition at first until you realize that not many interesting things are happening in it. Visually, the game looks far worse than the first, bordering sometimes on PS3 level of graphic detail or texture work and locations do not ooze dread and atmosphere as they did in the first game.
However, the worst parts of the game are the story, the voice acting and the script, which are beyond terrible.  Every line, every plot twist sounds like something out of a cheap late night sci fi cable tv sitcom. Everything is underlined, explained, probably in a misguided attempt to not confuse the audience, resulting in a game that sounds absolutely trite  and more often than not plays as a hilarious parody of some bad western drama.
The Evil Within was a masterpiece, a testament to the genius of Shinji Mikami.
The EW2 is its cheap Western knock-off by a well-meaning but far less talented pupil.

It's not easy to find a scary game that disturbs me.  I've seen a lot of horror and I'm not easily freaked out by monsters, gore, or jump scares.  System Shock 2, however, provides a haunting experience that I highly recommend.
There are clunky aspects to the game, however, since the RPG stat-building elements are not well-balanced.  Some paths are far more viable than others, and the game practically begs you to take hacking as a skill.  Even so, it can be fun to make a strange build to provide a greater challenge.
And speaking of challenge, I appreciated what I experienced in System Shock 2.  It's very easy to die in this game, and you need to be conservative if you rely on ammo to kill most enemies because they do respawn.  If you're careful and focus on melee during the early levels you can do well near the end game, but even when I did that the final areas took me a few tries to complete.  When compared to BioShock, which provides most of its challenge at the beginning of the game, this was very refreshing.

This game needs no introduction. It's regarded as one of the best games for PC ever made, as well as one of the best for its genre... and it is wholly deserving of all its praise. System Shock 2 is a game that defies any real review, to do so would to really spoil the experience. It needs to be played to understand why it is so good, and that is what playing it is: an experience.
The game is a rare example of design, gameplay, aesthetic, atmosphere, and presentation all working in near perfect harmony to deliver an engrossing experience that pulls you in and keeps you going until the final hours are passed. The RPG elements are almost completely free form, allowing you to build your character in almost any way you like focusing on what you want as you want it (though in the early game you'll do well to focus on your initial strengths as to not spread yourself too thin), and while initial enemy placement is pre-determined you'll find out that they respawn with alarming frequency in random numbers and placements to constantly keep you on your toes.
The game is not perfect, mind, and has some flaws. Most notable are the level designs for the final areas of the game don't seem quite as well designed as the rest of the game and some other small nitpicks, but these are minor gaffes in System Shock 2's excellent imageand are easily forgiven. If you like science fiction, survival horror, cyberpunk, body or eldritch horror, free form RPGs, first person shooters, adventure games, or any combination thereof of them, then System Shock 2 is well deserving of your attention. And hell, even if you don't like any of that stuff, it may be worth looking into just to try new things! You might just find yourself surprised.

Eternal Senia is like a free sampling of Cake!
A FREE cute, simple, and fun indie turn based strategy RPG where you control one character.  The game took me about 4 or 5 hours to beat to 100% completion, though I did take a sneak peak at some guides near the end to figure out the rest of the treasure hiding places.
Eternal Senia delivers a story about a younger sister searching for her older sister in a mysterious power.  Over the course of the game, the player is taken to several varying landscapes as the background and the characters unfolds through flashbacks.
The game is a turn based strategy style where you control your single character and "bump" into enemies to exchange blows with them.  There are occasions where some strong enemy skills are telegraphed and you have time to avoid them.
There's several pieces of puzzle variety that progress in difficulty, but none get very complex.
There are several large bosses that vary in fighting styles, each with its own types of challenges to overcome.
There are NPCs at the end of each level that help track how much of a completionist you are so you can do the OCD hunting!
Eternal Senia is not the most robust RPG experience, but what it delivers is polished and fun.  For delivering several hours of enjoyment it's definitely worth more than the free price that it's offered at!

A well made script can make it feel like it is not. This is not true with Alien ISO. I really noticed it when I had gotten to a story point in the game and the Alien would not stop hanging around the exit to the area. It would not leave that area no matter what I did. forcing me to die five times or more. By the second death I litterally stood there not moving and let the Alien have its way with me. I had on  a few occations as well used noise makers but they did nothing. What did work were flares. This is an inconsistancey that should have been addressed. In another section it is the same thing. The Alien its self shows up too frequently which then gets rid of the fear of the thing, espeically after you have died and stop giving a♥♥♥♥♥♥about dying to it. The space station is huge, and there was no real reason as to why it is always hanging around ripley (the player). In any of the films specifically the first Alien film, the creature did not just bum around dallas all the time, nor did it chill and have coffee with Parker. NO! It lurked around and you barely saw it. It was the music as well as the sounds that Spooked you, and this should have been what would happen in this game more often. I am 7 hours in and no longer scared, or even full ofsuspence. No I was annoyed at this entry to the Alien series.
The other problem is characters, more specifically Ripley does not cast a shadow. Why spend all this time on the shadows and lighting, if this is not a implamented thing. Why even show the feet and walking animations (which by the way is well done, so kudos to Creative for having competent animators in the gaming industry)? It is the little things that make a game, and while Creative did do a fantastic job of the textures, the lighting, the models, the atmosphere. All of that falls short because of the gameplay with the Alien. The loss of Shadows on Ripley and characters, the Alien being too frequent.
The best part of the game, and most terrifying is the androids. Thier robotic lifeless voices, their brutal treatment of civilians and what happens when you are caught by one. It's sad when secondary enemies take the spot light over the creature you should be fearful of. The Alien is nothing more than a guy in a suit wanting some spotlight and having coffe with you. That friendly neighbour that borrows all your stuff and never gives it back. That thing that is annoying and actually takes away from the game. Dispite the negative points of this game, the over all is vastly better than its predicessor, ACM. But not nearly as good as the marines camp. from AVP2 By monolith.
In closing the game its self is decent, its not worth the full price nor the praise it is getting. espeically when a game from 2000 is superior.

At the time of me posting this review I only have about 4 hours into the game. That said, this review should be taken as a "first impressions" sort of review until I have more time into the game and have experienced much more of it.
All that said:
The feel and look of the game is great. It definitely has an Elder Scrolls feel to the game and it mixes elements from a couple of the previous Elder Scrolls games and puts them into an MMO environment.
The combat is pretty good, it doesn't feel really clunky and its not as much of a press a button, let the invisible dice roll, and watch your character beat up an NPC until it dies while you watch the animations. It is a bit more involved and it isn't overly boring.
Graphically, it doesn't hold up to Skyrim graphics, however it is still a visually pleasing game that gives the Elder Scrolls feel. I have noticed that when I run up to NPCs or load into a new area that there is some texture pop in even though I'm running it with every setting maxed out. It's a minor issue but it is pretty distracting when it happens.
The game can be as bit buggy, that said its not been anything game breaking. It was mainly NPCs kind of quickly changing directions and bouncing back and forth in a small area where they were standing/walking before they stopped as I talked to them. Again, nothing game breaking or serious, but it is quite distracting.
The UI is a bit hit and miss. It's kind of clunky at first but once you get aquainted with where everything is and how to work it it quickly. Over all, not a horrible UI just takes some getting used to. That said, you are able to look at your map, inventory, journal/quest log, and pretty much everything else as you are running across the land so you can look through things as you travel to break up the monotony/get more done as you go.
Overall, my impressions of the game are very good. I did not play ESO when it originally released as the idea of a sub fee and the initial reviews turned me away, at least until the game was improved. They've now made the sub an optional feature and from other reviews they have improved a good bit of what people complained about when the game released.
Overall, defintely worth a shot if you like MMOs and the Elder Scrolls world/series. Do not run into this thinking its Skyrim Online, because you will be disappointed. Instead, walk into it with an open mind and realize you're going into an MMO that's based inside the Elder Scrolls world. You won't have any unrealistic expectations that way.
I bought the game for $24 on sale as I was apprenhensive, even after the Tamriel Unlimited relaunch, to pay a full $60. Whether or not you are willing to wait for another sale or pay the full price is up to you. But considering what I've experienced so far, i like it. Depending on how involved I get with the game I will be considering the optional subscription.
TL:DR: Solid MMO (based on first impressions) that is set in the world of Elder Scrolls. Great looking game and it's quite fun. Worth a shot if you can find it on sale.

As for the game itself... Well given all the options they had a for a sequel after the ending of 1, this must be the worst option they could have come up with. The game lacks any horror and atmosphere or even slasher style atmosphere. It feels like and is literally a clone of RE4 in places, to the extent of a minigame being in it that mirrors RE4. Not only that you then have Seb singing after completing it and if you spend enough time he says "I should get back to that whole saving my daughter thing". The gameplay and story never hits the highs of TEW1 and quite frankly this feels like it should have been a new IP. There is nothing TEW about this game.

* Overall gameplay
cons:
* Totally useless storyline
* Mediocre AI
* Some gameplay issues
I won't write about performance issues, everything has been said about it.
Mild spoilers ahead.
My biggest complaint is about the storyline.
You couldn't make a duller, more boring story if you wanted to.
I found the ending in particular totally frustrating. Quite like the ending of the first installment, actually. Absolutely nothing happens.
Game designers have developped multiple ways of rewarding the player for their implication in the game. This game uses none of them.
I went through the hassle of doing a full nonlethal, undetected playthrough, only to get a few different, short, non animated cutscenes at the end.
Dishonored 1 and 2 are certainly not the only games with this issue.
Several recent AAA games have dull endings. I'm looking at you, CD Projekt!
I think I'm going to get a T-Shirt printed with something like «I spent 200+ hours on The Witcher 3 and all I got was a one minute cutscene.»
I don't know, go check Valve games, goddammit!
Also, you could think that with all thing about lethal vs non-lethal gameplay, there could be some actual reflection about morality.
Well guess what: there is none. Basically, some people are evil, others are not.
At some point in the game, Emily says something like «maybe Delilah's will manage to actually do something good».
Spoiler alert: she doesn't. It could have been a very interesting plot twist, but who cares about plot twists, right?
That's another thing you won't find in this game.
At least the first Dishonored had some.
Also, remember kids: torturing and lobotomizing someone is still better than killing him!
Apart from that, there are other minor issues with the game:
The AI is basic. You learn pretty quick how guards and civilians react. Sometimes it's totally absurd, too.
I was hoping that holding someone in front of you would prevent other enemies form attacking you. It doesn't. They just slash through.
I felt that the detection range was wider than in Dishonored 1, but sometimes I struggled to attract enemies, and sometimes they detected me instantly.
Crafting bonecharms seemed interesting at first, but I found that some effects did not add correctly. I tried stacking the "strong arms" effect (or something like that) four times, and it actully took me much longer to choke enemies.
Movement, which I found nearly perfect in Dishonored 1, now has a few issues. I found myself regularly missing platforms and ledges because Emily didn't cling to it.
I LOVE the atmosphere of this game.  It's like a dark steam punk with assassins and a touch of magic.

You're probably looking in the reviews to see what all the talk is about this game being poorly optimized. You're probably basing your decision on whether the frame rate drop♥♥♥♥♥♥is true for everybody. I'm gonna simplify this so you don't have to read a bunch of♥♥♥♥♥♥
Lowering your settings doesn't do much. If you have a high-end rig, you'll be okay, but it'll still have hiccups. As for low-end or kinda meh setups, I don't recommend you get this. You probably wont be able to run it and you'll waste your time and money.
As for the game itself? Wow. Just wow. I played some of the first dishonered (again) before hopping into this one, and holy ♥♥♥♥ man. INCREDIBLE improvements. The movement is much smoother, the maps are far superior to the last game's, the bone charms crafting system is a godsend, the abilities feel balanced yet powerful, and there is a ♥♥♥♥♥on of creativity you can delve into when approaching each and every mission. There's also a great amount of replayability with picking either Emily or Corvo at the beginning, I'm about to start my Corvo run. The game finally feels like a world rather than a frustratingly small cut of a country. Becoming a shadow monster and sneaking up behind people to put them to "bed" has never felt more comfortable and fluid.
Finally the story. Honestly it was impressive, I'll give it that. There were a few plot twists I didn't expect and a deeper involvement in character development, especially on Emily's part. Each mission built the story up in an incredibly interesting ark that I actually enjoyed, thuroughly. ENDING SPOILER (kinda)
Ultimately the story could've used a little improvement in the right places, I feel like Bethesda kinda got lazy at some parts.
Good game. Bad optimization.
