Just completed my first playthrough, recommend the game wholeheartedly.  It is an immersive world with large intricately crafted levels that allow you to make the most of the skills whether playing stealthy or chaotic.  Most levels after the first few introductory portions introduce interesting twists that keep the gameplay fresh.  I won't go into more detail to avoid spoiling these pleasantly surprising unique mechanics, but it is truly impressive how functional each is within these sprawling stages.  If you enjoyed the first game I believe this sequel preserves the fundamentals and succeeds beyond them.  Considering the varied approaches, powers, secrets, there is high replay potential and you will likely enjoy replaying many sections just to see what is possible.  The AI seems relatively high functioning to me on "hard" but not unfair.  The plot was engaging enough although not the highlight for me, some good cameos on voicework and quite atmospheric.  The graphics are beautifully steampunky.  I am sorry to hear that performance issues have marred the experience for many, I did not encounter any with a geforce 1070, i5-6600 at 3.5GHz, 16gb ram, windows 10 64bit.  If you enjoyed the first game, stealth games, or exploration/action contained within dense urban/fantasy environments then give this one a chance.  It is very well done, one of my favorite games of the year.

TL;DR: Quite possibly my favourite game of the year. It takes everything from the first game and improves upon it.
So It's been over a month since the game has launched and the initial review was that it was a poorly optimized port from console. Now that a series of patches have been launched the game runs beutifully on Ultra settings. That's not to say that the game is perfect and I'll list some issues later on.
What does the game do right? Well it follows a very straight forward story where you seek revenge against everyone involved in the coup that left you in exile. You know what you have to do and the game doesn't force you to hold it's hand. The more tropical location of Karnaca is much nicer than the grey city of Dunwall and I really liked the transition. Re-balancing the Sleep Dart so it wasn't an instant knockout initially was very nice as it made more realistic and slightly harder. There also a very stark difference between the Low Chaos world and the High Chaos world with people generally being more cruel to each other, more guards as well as more blood fly infestations. The implimentation of paintings and other collectables increases the play time of each mission as well as the creation of black market shops. These shops make sure that you don't run out of supplies when you're playing as well as providing a fun mini-game to rob. When choking someone out you move faster and the person's head doesn't wriggle as much making it easier to play. The Clock Soliders that replaced the Tall Boys is an interesting change but ultimately I like them more.
I also enjoyed the change of the Outsider's voice. The magical voice better suits him.
What isn't so great about the game? I have mixed feelings about enviromental kills. Often times they can accidently kill someone when you're trying to achieve the merciful award. The Abbey feels like a joke and they don't use their music boxes against you at all. One major problem is that the missions feel far less memorable or interesting. In the first game you attended the Boyle Party where you had to secretly find out which Boyle was the real one and then assasinate her or give her to some creep on a boat (Yikes) but in this game you don't get that. The closest thing to that party would be finding Aramis Stillton.
Also, why do we have to rebuy our powers when using Corvo? We see him use his Blink power in the intro yet when he boards the ship he doesn't have anypowers. That needs to be explained. Another small issue is that when ally with the Duke of Serkonos and speak into the microphone saying that you are allies the guards still attack you.
Overall, the issues with the game aren't that big. Sure there are some things that I wish the game developers did instead but they probably had a reason to not do it. The game is my choice for the best game of 2016, granted, there weren't a whole lot of amazing games this year.

Meh, this game is okay, but it's not as good as the original Dishonored by any stretch of the imagination.  Powers like Blink (or Far Reach if you're playing as Emily) insist of putting you in the wrong place even when you've made sure to get your aim absolutely perfect.  AI seems almost omniscient sometimes, while being dumb as a brick other times.
The story is good and engaging, but the game is much more buggy than Dishonored 1 was.  I've gotten framerate dips, artifacts, controls not working properly, and even CTDs wtihout any warning at all during combat situations.
Seriously, Arkane Studios made an absolutely awesome game in Dishonored 1.  I was pleasantly surprised when I found out that Bethesda had published an almost totally bug-free gaming experience.  But now I guess Arkane has decided that in order to be more successful, they need to follow Beth's example and make their games really super buggy.
I mean, I like Dishonored. and I do actually like this game, but damnit Arkane, fix it already!
All this said, I do recommend this game.  But be warned: it's buggier by far than its predecessor, and chances are good that you will encounter technical issues and crashes.  But all in all, it is a fun game, and it's a decent continuation of the Dishonored franchise.  Not the best that could ever be done, but it is good enough for a recommendation.

Eternal Senia is a free ARPG that makes you feel two emotions, sadness at the well told story within the game, and rage at the boss who has beat you like a drum for the 8th time in 5 minutes. Do I like the game? Well let's find out!
Story: Eternal Senia stars Senia who is looking for her friend Magaleta. Since the game is rather short I won't spoil anything here, but it's heartbreaking. The writting is great, you get the deep connection these two characters have, and you care. It has a bit of comic relief in there, but overall it's really sad, and it hits you right in the heart.
Graphics: It's an old school rpg, so not much to say when it comes to graphics. Art style is great overall, enemy designs are decent, and the music is solid. Not much to say here
Gameplay: If you don't know, ARPG stands for Auto Role Playing Game, meaning that you have no attack button, when Senia bumps into an enemy they both take damage based on weapons and armor. Senia also has a magic bar that fuels her special attacks, which are activated by the keyboard. Enemies drop items that can be used for crafting, Senia levels up, it's a well done, but fairly standard RPG. Except for one thing...the bosses. So as you progress through the level you get stronger and can take enemies down faster like in most games. Then you get to the boss battle at the end and it's about as easy as knocking down a brick wall with a #2 Pencil. The bosses in this game force you to grind a lot, and even on easy they still hit like a truck. Still, the bosses are a great challenge and I do appreciate the fact they force you to bring your A game.
Length and Replay Value: The game takes about 6 hours to beat (For some reason Steam says I've only played 4) and has hard to find items and multiple endings, so it has a bit of replay value.
It's sad, it's hard, and it's free. I recommend you give it a try.

Well, here I go again making another review. This time for The Elder Scrolls Online.
Well, As freakish fan of the saga I have to say, I was afraid that a MMO experience would ruin a TES game. But fortunately, this is not the case. However, there are a few displeasing details, like some combat physics and such. But they are not really important.
Well, they did it. They actually managed to unite TES and MMO in one single game, with a good result and with a good balance in the components. It feels that way to me
Rewarding exploration, delving dungeons, blacksmithing, enchanting, sneak upon your mobs, block the enemy attacks with your shield, jump over the mountains without following a single road, Public and group instances, Lots and lots of Skill trees, Guilds, PvP, sieges. Main quest and LOTS of side quests. You mention it, ESO has all the ingredients of both TES and MMO games to offer. And you can play it the way you want.
However, there are some dissapointing features such as no horseback combat (Which was avaliable even in TES II: Daggerfall and TES V: Skyrim). I think not allowing PK or PVP other players outside Cyrodiil is a total success for the experience of the game, specially in early game. However, as a newbie I personally wouldn't mind the possibility to challenge or be challenged by other players to a duel (Always voluntarily via request of course.)
The lore has been respected as a whole, more or less. And there are new additions and easter eggs. Sometimes I forget that this is the 2nd era whatsoever. Some of the alliances doesn't make a lot of sense. But is the only way to have 3 solid blocks towards the center of Tamriel. Rather suspicious we can't go to Elsweyr or Alinor (That sure gives a hint to Elder Scrolls VI)
I don't have a very good PC and my Internet connection is not that good either, in fact, I play this on a I3 intel processor laptop and it goes fairly good. They did a good job with that
The crafting system on the other hand is absorbing and very demanding, but also very rewarding both on a personal and ingame scale. It requires a lot of commitment and investment (Skill points you could use to develop your combat skills). Perhaps you'd rather make another character to deal with your crafting issues. Since you can share ALL your objects among them. Also, there ir a e-mail ingame system to send objects to your friends without the needing of make your characters meet and trade.
The soundtrack was created by Jeremy Soule as well, is good and alll. But I guess it lacks that special something to me, it doesn't sound very "TES", it sounds more like a generic MMO, but whatever.
And that's all for now, I'm just a level 12 templar in the Daggerfall covenant, but I'm sure as hell that I want to commit to this game. I totally recommend it.

I mainly liked the 1st half of the game. The graphics and the overall atmosphere made it very promising and the 1st encounters with the alien were terrifying. I liked the fact that the danger was coming both from the alien and the other residents of the station. But towards the end of the game I lost interest. The issue is that the alien became for me a nuisance rather than part of the experience. There's no way it could be popping in and out of the places you are at with such uncanny timing on its part. It felt gimmicky. For example, towards the end, you need to get to a door that looses power (and you need to go back and turn on a generator). Well, as you enter the room with said door, there's another entrance blocked by fire leading to a corridor. The corridor is empty, you can see through the fire. You can also backtrack a bit to the corridor and look at the other side of that door. Empty ! However, the moment you step into that room, the Alien jumps through the fire and challenges you. In other words, it is a trap, not by the alien but by the designers of the game. To me it just became a bit much. So I ended up dying countless times, not really caring anymore about the character just so I could get to the end which I eventually did. And by the way, what's with that ending anyway ? I'm recommending the game anyway because of the 1st half of it and because I know that other people will probably not be as frustrated as I am with the second half.

Finally finished my first playthrough and now here's my review.
Reaction? I absolutely loved it! 9/10 on just about every category.
tl;dr: Whether you are a fan of the Alien series, or just want a well done survival-horror, this game is a must play!
The story was just as well written as the origional Alien movie. Technology, characters, plot development, all were very well drafted and implimented!
I played on Hard mode for my playthrough, and I do not regret it at all. The game was challenging and fun at the same time! The bad guys and alien felt real and you really had to out smart them. You have a pretty decent number of tools in your kit to get around, but you have to be smart or you'll burn though all of it and die anyway!
The level layout was awesome! The game felt linear early on with minimal options for routes, but quickly gave you more and more option for paths! It was a great balance of linear pathing where you needed to get from point A to point B, but increasingly gave you more and more path and combat/non-combat options for how to get there. Also, the game used each zone multiple times with the clever use of "unlockable" doors that couldn't be opened until you got plot required tools. I did not feel this to be tacky at all and kept my sense of exploration high because I wanted to find everthing I could!
There were some glitches here and there in the game and required you to revert back to previous save in order to fix them. Fortunately, the game lets you save pretty often and this was little more than a small bother. I think I encountered 2 total and they were just minor things that prevented forward progression like a door that was supposed to open after doing a plot point, but didn't, then much later, an item drop didn't work because I killed the enemy with the environment, which removes all drop items. Minor things, and honestly, didn't bother me much.
The visuals in the game were consistent and EPIC! Everything was consisten with the first Alien movie technology and visually. The slow revealing of the size of the station, and the views outside the portholes were jawdroppingly epic!
Amazing, one of the best Alien games ever made. Great visuals, sound, story and gameplay. Good length and challenge aswell.

System Shock 2 is one of those milestones in gaming history. It has a deep storyline and the greatest villain of all time. It has a robust class-less level-up system that allows the player to get a different experience on every playthough depending on his choices. It has a great resource management system that really adds to the survival aspect of the game. And lastly it has great atmosphere. The game is truly creepy, and will keep you on your toes as you make your way through a large spaceship infested by all kinds of nasty.
The graphics look dated, but that should be expected from a game form 1999. System Shock 2 has a great modding community that has kept the game alive for over a decade - improving the graphics and fixing the bugs. There's even a mod that completely rebalances the game, making sub-par skills and powers useful again.
If you consider your self more that a casual gamer, or if you're into sci-fi/horror stuff, you owe it to yourself to play this game!

Seriously, Arkane Studios made an absolutely awesome game in Dishonored 1.  I was pleasantly surprised when I found out that Bethesda had published an almost totally bug-free gaming experience.  But now I guess Arkane has decided that in order to be more successful, they need to follow Beth's example and make their games really super buggy.
I mean, I like Dishonored. and I do actually like this game, but damnit Arkane, fix it already!
All this said, I do recommend this game.  But be warned: it's buggier by far than its predecessor, and chances are good that you will encounter technical issues and crashes. Fine. Let's do this!
+ Simple, fun gameplay.
The core gameplay is simple and easy to pick up. Still it feels rewarding and the various skills and their interactions give the game a unique feel.
+ An above average story.
It's a simple story and you've probably seen it before. Still it's handled well and the endings really help it stand out. All the ending felt unique and despite there being a "good" and "bad" ending, all the endings felt like they had their own unique merits.
+ Solid difficulty
Even with maxed out gear the hard mode boss fights were still a solid challenge. Although maxing out your gear will make fighting the normal enemies a joke. Additionally difficulty has no impact on the endings so feel free to grind to the max stats or just set the bosses on easy as you please.
+ Solid Visuals
The pictures above give you a pretty good representation of what the game looks like. Its not a graphical marvel but it's nice to look at. Little things like being able to change the weather in one level and the professionally drawn character art are nice touches as well.
+ A ton of love
Even though it is their first game, the creator really loved the time he spent on this game and its characters and it shows as you play. Each new skill or boss fight feels unique, and even though we dont get to spend much time with the characters they are all easily likable.
+ Free
The game is of a high enough quality that the guy easily could have asked for a few bucks and the game been easily worth it. A game that asks for nothing but your time and is easily worth it.
- Could use a proof reader
The game has some spelling and grammar errors that really stuck out to me. I think they are mostly just due to having only one guy make this and English not being his first language. Honestly, the only reason this was even a problem was that I was enjoying the story enough to care about the exact words a character was saying. Still it does draw from the impact of the story a good bit which is a problem since the story's value ways solely on its emotional impact.
- First game the guy made
This shows from time to time with little glitches and two chests that were a little finicky to get. Still overall the game runs great and although i've heard of others experiencing an occasional error I had none myself.
- It doesn't reinvent the wheel

After the emperor edition Rome 2 is where it should have been on release. The game is now acceptable. Endless bugs, absence of the family tree, taking cities without siege weapons, buttons that magically replenish energy, drunken brawl instead of clever tactics - there's much said about all of this, no need to repeat. From Monomi Park comes Slime Rancher, a first person exploration game. Released only at the start of August, Slime Rancher has ranked extremely high reviews in just twenty odd days. After seeing Jacksepticeye and Markiplier play it and enjoy it so much, and seeing just high reviews all over, I had to give it a try.
In Slime Rancher, you play as Beatrix LeBeau, a slime rancher who has just moved to The Far, Far Range to try her hand at making a living at being a slime rancher.
This is a large world game to explore, with cute little slimes around the place, and it’s a ton of fun. After just eight hours of gameplay, I am totally addicted to this adorable, fun little game. The set up is rather open world, with limitations, but there is absolutely tons to explore throughout the game, with things that will make even the most boring person in the world smile. Collect your slime, put them in a corral and have fun going through different combinations, making different combinations of slimes to make yourself rich.
Of course, once you’ve played for a while, it all becomes pretty much the same repetitive thing, especially if you’re unaware of where to go for other things, such as slime doors and getting slime keys, but it’s fun enough to not become boring. There’s plenty to do and it doesn’t take long to become rather attached to your slimes. Checking in on my ranch once a day has become a daily routine for me already. There’s also plenty to challenge yourself with, with a five day rush to earn as much money as you can in just five days of game play.

I have had this game for quite awhile and it is a lot of fun to play, even for beginners.  The ability to build a base and acquire the necessary tools to do so is relatively easy.  There are some issues I have with the game though.  I prefer unmodded servers because you can get a better feel for the game.  However, you may not make it very far before someone kills and takes all your hard work away from you.  I do realize that this a game that is more PVP than anything, but I would suggest you play on a PVE modded server first before traversing to a server that is mainly PVP or the official servers.
As updates go, the wipes are few and far between which is good and bad at the same time.  Few updates means servers are rarely down, but it can cause a lot of excess clutter on some servers which can cause game issues such as lockups.  The mechanics of the game are pretty straight forward, collect, build, collect some more, build, etc.
The best part of this type of game is the ability to have vehicles.  Most servers only allow one vehicle per player which means you will have to choose between a car with 3-4 seats or a fourwheeler.  The only problem with the vehicles (at least on normal, unmodded servers is the lack of parts.  Most of the time players will receive bullets or paint when a vehicle is broken down or in loot crates.  It takes HOURs to find parts and cars only spawn about every 3 hours.
In closing, I would definitely buy this game now and play the heck out of it!  It is fun despite the few issues it has and the creators are working on updates as quickly as they can.

Oh, well, and it's still dull. And rage-producing. That's my main niggle, by the way: the game which is supposed to channel aggression into innocuous pushing of buttons, in reality does the opposite: it maintains my anger, fuel it, to the point when I'm growling on the people around. I might be able even kick someone, like the trolls who loves pestering around webpages.
What's the fuel of this reaction? Well, for one, it's optimisation. Yes, even now, with all updates of the version 4.2.1, the game engine still crushes, the loading screens still taking more time to proceed than booting of my Windows 10. And the game freezes for about 2-5 seconds on the start of every level, just when you engaging in the first shootout...
Second half of this god-awful feeling the game provides, yes, it's about pointless and mindless killing of dummy people. Which gets repetative just on the first level, and never evolves into anything worthwhile. The AI is still not good, the hitboxes are peculiar and the weaponry is odd.
On the bright side, the game's easy enough (with glitches unlocking the exit before any kills) and fair enough with achievements, so, if you're an achievement hunter, you can play the game just for the badge. On the general score, though... It's not the best pick. I'd vouch for Hotline Miami myself, for the better story, visuals, and challenge. As of mark, 6/10. Dishonored 2 takes the basic gameplay that the first game set up and develops it slightly. It does so by giving the player new powers, each with their own mini skill tree and by allowing you to choose your protagonist. Even though there aren't too many new additions to the gameplay itself, it is still enough to keep the game feeling fresh and to justify the purchase if you've clocked the first game.
Dishonored 2 features some quite nice sound design. Most of the sounds do feel familiar having played the first game, but this is to be expected and is quite welcome. However, I did notice that with Headphone mode disabled enemies sounded as if they were right next to me when they were across the room from me, although this could just be me.
Just like the first game, Dishonored 2 is not the longest of games. However, the replayability of the game is one of its main selling points. The addition of different characters with their own powers and the ability to complete the entire game without even gaining supernatural powers definitely improves the replay value of the game. Though it doesn't have the longest story, it does have multiple endings for you to achieve and each of the missions are filled with collectibles to bring out your inner completionist. Basically, if you're someone who enjoys trying to uncover every secret in a game and is willing to sink a lot of time to 100% a game, this game has quite a lot to offer you.
Without going into Spoiler territory, Dishonored 2's story is basically what you'd expect if you've paid attention to the marketing material up to the game's release. For the most part you could play this game without having played the original, however there are a few references and revelations in there for fans of the original game to enjoy as well.
(As of 21st December 2016) It is no secret that Dishonored 2 isn't the most stable game available on Steam. However, other than a few FPS drops in specific areas I didn't have too many problems with the game myself, however browsing the Community Hub for a while shows that this will differ from person to person so I would advise doing some research before making a purchase.
Apart from the Technical Issues facing the PC version, the game it self is actually quite well executed, minus the odd bug here and there the gameplay is surprisingly smooth and other than a corpse randomly ragdolling for me and my Far Reach glitching out once or twice I didn't really notice any issues in the actual gameplay.
Overall I would say Dishonored 2 is worth the money, if you're someone who is solely put off by the graphical issues, I would say just buy it, see how it runs, then refund it if it doesn't work well on your system. If you are someone who is just looking to experience the story and is not interested in playing a game through multiple times though, I would recommend waiting until this title goes on sale as a single playthrough will not take you too long to achieve. This being said, if you're someone who enjoys replaying a game to try and achieve everything, this game definitely has a lot to offer you at its current price tag.
TL;DR: Solid game with a lot of replayability hindered by a few bugs. Wait for sale if only interested in story.

! A fast, cunning father who's thirst for vengeance knows no bounds. The dark pawn, the antihero, Royal Protector to the throne and star of the prequel to the sequel. He can scale buildings with magic, or his bare hands when he feels like it. Two stories, nine stories, all stories high. It doesn't matter to him. He knows what to do, where to sneak, who to stab...and nobody touches his daughter without getting touched by his knife.
! The faster, sharper daughter of the father with an identical lust for vengeance. She trained in the streets. The hard streets, cold streets--with rats. She knows how to sneak and how to choke. She hasn't choked anyone yet, but she will. Magic is offered to her, but will she take it? Only you can decide.
+ Freedom. Absolute freedom to execute your tasks in any manner you wish. You want to climb that wall? Do it. You want to kill that group of baddies or sneak past them? The question is not if, but how. Guns, stealing, human posession. Dive in.
+ The story? We've all heard this plot before but the wide variety of player choices set this title apart from the rest. Every action has a direct consequence on the physical world. With each drop of blood shed, the streets of the city grow darker. Disease, infestation. At times you will face terrors of the existential kind. Lore-junkies, prepare for mounds of hidden texts around the city. Don't let the bloodflies bite!
+ Visuals are charming. Feels like a painting. A hyper-realistic painting brushed with blood. Upon release, many PC players experienced framerate issues. I did not (using a Quadro card).
+ The game is short, but its length is relative to play style. Murder Simulator is a fun romp, but if you want the full experience, max the difficulty and try to ghost it. Did it. Loved it. Took forever. Replay value is already high. Looking forward to added content in the future.

I have played this game, and I got to say, it's a nice little game. It involves you going to save your friend, who has been possessed by something called the "Inkvil". If you like games like Drawn to Life, this is pretty similar; you get to draw whatever you like. The music has a nice, calming feel, with chiptune laced into the compositions, and you can share your designs. The boss battles are also quite tricky.
BUT there are some complaints, the main one being that it's extremely short, even for a five-dollar game; you can literally complete it in 2-3 hours if you know what you're doing. The other complaint - at least for me - is that the battle system is weird, even for. And also, there's no eraser function. If I want to remove some unnecessary edges, i'd have to undo it and probably make that same mistake again. But these last two are rather minor complaints.
At least it's cute.
Pros;
* THE ART IS SO CUTE
* The story and music is charming
* You get to draw whatever you want. If you want to save Barney the Purple Dinosaur as the Hamburgular, you can do that. If you want to wield a poorly-drawn Master Sword as Mario, you can also do that. Hell, if you wanted to play as a toilet, you can do that as well.
Pretty Minor Cons;
* Story's extremely short. While the pacing's alright, there could have been an extra chapter to make it feel rewarding besides a completion bonus; people who don't like really short stories in video games should keep away.
* Not very accurate point-and-click controls for combat? Not sure.
* No eraser function besides undo.
I rate it a 7/10; nice, but could be improved on for the third game.

To start off I wiould like to mention that I am a 51 yo avid history buff with a not inconsiderable reference library to draw upon. A wargamer for most of my life... until I bought Rome 1 at which point I ditched my wargaming stuff and turned to Total War for my strategy kicks, clocked upo thousands of hours, (gained a wealth of space in my home & a happy wife to boot)  and by & large I have never been disappointed...... until now!
This is without question the worst game I have ever bought - at least at full price ( I have tried and found a few bargain basement mingers, but when you pay pennies - who cares!).
I have always pre-ordered my CA titles on the strength of what they produced previously, a mistake I will NEVER make again!
Rome 2 is ok if you just want a game and you have no inkling of historical fact - that or you just don't care.
It shoiuld be cetegorised under fantasy games as there is hardly a realistic element in there, it is full of Harry Potter nations and Harry Potter units - most, and I mean about 90% of them have no basis in reality and available faction units are in some cases wildly innacurate or non-existant, The nations did exist to be sure, at least on the whole, but not in the way they have been presented.
The playable nations are grossly misrepresented for the time period that TW Rome2 proffesses to cover and the political aspect of the game is almost pathetic, mainly due to the amount of unplayable factions,  as is the political intruige side of the game - there is far too much of it. Hardly a turn seems to go by with out something or other popping up to ruin your day and what comes up has very little historical fact behind it - or relavence.
For all intents CA have already abandonded this game already and moved on to the next money spinner - it seems to be what they are all about these days since SEGA & Steam got involved.
In short; I have just this minute finished reinstalling Rome Total War 1 - Adios CA & thanks for the good times, its unlikely that I will be back.

Alien:Isolation is quite possibly the most fun I've had playing a game in a long while. No longer are you the meathead marine out to blowtorch a nest to the ground and save the day. You're surviving, and trust me when I say you're going to fail to survive, quite a bit, until you start to get the hang of how the alien thinks.
In A:I, you play as Amanda Ripley, the daughter of Ellen Ripley from the original movie, Alien. It takes place about 15 years after the first movie, but around 47 years before the second, so I highly suggest you watch at least the first movie before playing because a lot of familiar ground will be tred. You come aboard a ship, the Sevastopol, in search of the remaining logs from the ship your mother had last been heard from before it was fround destroyed: the Nostromo. But you're not alone.
Quite possibly the strongest element of this game is the gameplay itself. Stealth is favored over going in guns blazing --and in fact, I found myself barely using my weapons because of how strongly being silent is rewarded. You can create traps for yourself, and discover gadgets to help you along the way, but so much of this game defies traditional comparison to other games. You're surviving and exploring, and while the game is somewhat streamlined in where the story will lead you, everything, from the tiny secrets, to the mini-games, to the cut-scenes, will keep you hooked.
Second strongest definitely goes to atmosphere and sound. Play this game with some sort of surround sound, seriously. Hearing a loud 'thunk' as the alien descended behind me and to the right gives me about a second more to dive into a corner and hide than if I wildly start to look around. Couple that with beautiful graphics, (which can be amplified further with mods, which I totally recommend), and an incredible dedication to Ridley Scott's designs for 80's-style technology, and you have an incredibly original experience.
Otherwise, the other elements of the game are really quite solid. Story and voice acting are tremendously well done, level design is decently memorable, and while the enemy and obstacle selection is a little thin, it's forgivable given the other elements. My biggest gripe is the occassional crash with the game, but for the most part it ran smooth like butter.
Buy this game. Even if you aren't a fan of horror, don't worry, the gore isn't horrible. You'll get surprised, but when you tough through it, you'll find an incredibly rewarding experience.

I'm a Skyrim addict, a fan and the collector of ES lore. I've been suspicious and reluctant to ESO ever since it was announced. And I won't lie - the subscription thing was the main obstacle for me, beside the obvious how-can-TES-ever-be-an-MMO? Anyway, it's Unlimited now, there's no subscription so I bought the Imperial edition to give it a try. So here are my thoughts:
1. It looks and feels fresh and new, a bit more like a vastly updated Oblivion than Skyrim. It's missing the Skyrim atmospherics, the mist, depressing Falkareth rain, misty marshes, windy high altitude clouds, snow, etc. But make no mistake - the Tamriel in ESO is truly beautiful! The detail is phenomenal, animation is flawless and the game is so well polished and optimized to run at the same FPS as Skyrim, but with much higher detail with ambient occlusion! The sun setting in the sea, the shores, water, buildings, armours, creatures, distant LODs and horizons, etc. in ESO are the best of any ES game so far and a true eye candy.
2. Crafting, alchemy, cooking, smithing... is SO much more advanced. It's much more complex and sophisticated, with more RPG elements. I won't spoil the fun, you will have to discover yourself. But you will be pleasantly surprised. I'm still happy to be learning!
3. Journal, Skill and menu system, fighting and magic are also much better, more advanced and so much fun. Finally, doing sorcery and magic in an ES game is seriously addicting. I still haven't figured how everything works, it's much more demanding, but rewarding!
4. Guilds. I barely scratched the surface with that one. MMO is really shining here. Players forming their own guilds, recruiting members, trading and such. Sounds exciting. For example, you can dedicate your entire time there to be the best blacksmith (or anything else), to master the craft and buy the special and expensive armor motif styles and then to sell your work to all other players!
5. It's MMO. Be prepared to see the bosses and enemies come alive xyz times if there are other players around or if you're lurking in the dungeons for long. It was a compromise, to follow and experience the story and quests by yourself but also the others at the same time. I think the team behind ESO did this very well. The missions/dungeons aren't always as deep as in Skyrim, but there are many of them, they fork and are all fun! Some NPCs share similar faces, unlike Skyrim where most people had unique and distinct look. It's a minor though. Do know that all your enemies level as you are.
6. Music and sound effects. While Jeremy Soule composed only the main ESO theme (which is absolutely awesome, possessing LOTR epic quality!), the other composers, Brad Derrick and Rik Schaffer did a marvelous job producing grand and very atmospheric music that never annoys and always soothes or brings chills. They are on par with maestro Jeremy here!
You will also be pleasantly surprised to hear many Skyrim voice actors, reprising their roles. People that did Astrid, Vex, Vekel the man, etc. are all here. And - you can even hear John Cleese for free!
7. Everything else I didn't discover yet... and I barely scratched the surface!
All in all - a must buy! Even as a massive Skyrim fan I can say without hesitation that many elements in this game surpass every ES game to date. If you are an RPG/MMO/adventure/action and especially an Elder Scrolls fan, you have to give it a chance. There's SO much to love and praise in this game. It *is* a genuine TES after all, I can feel it everywhere. All my fears were false and I was very, very wrong!
ESO deserves much praise and better marks. The best of all - it is constantly being upgraded, polished and tweaked with lots of DLCs to come. And oh, as with every ES game out there - buy those DLCs! They add tons of more fun and expand the lore even more. You can feel that the team behind TESO do actually care to bring you the best experience possible.

TL; DR: Redux is a superior version of Postal that adds replay value and congruent atmosphere to one of the darkest games available on Steam.
Postal: Redux is a mostly faithful remaster, and it’s differences are highly subjective. On the whole, I would recommend Redux over the original simply because it retains most of what built the original’s atmosphere while adding to the gameplay, making it feel like a more complete package.
Much of the time with older games, their low resolutions and pixelated graphics made all the art meld together cleanly despite their primitive nature. Much of the time when updating graphics to look similar to the original’s low resolution, remasters can end up looking incongruent and “cartoon-ish.” A good example of this not going too well is StarCraft Remastered, which ends up looking less cohesive than its original because of its higher resolution textures, rather than the other way around.
Postal Redux suffers from this but not nearly as bad. As a matter of fact, the art in the game as a whole fits together better than the original. For example, the loading screens of the original Postal were a weird mix of some obvious drawings, some that looked almost like photographs, and some that just looked like weird photoshops, all of which still looks different from the art in the gameplay. Redux on the whole looks more like a cartoon, but instead stays more consistent with it’s art. All the loading screens fit together better, and fit better with the gameplay art.
Similar to the original, Redux’s gameplay is pretty straightforward and can get tedious after a while. However, a first playthrough of Postal should be more about soaking in the dark atmosphere, and should be less focused on the mediocre combat. On a second playthrough, play Rampage mode. It makes the gameplay so much more exciting simply with score attack elements and electric guitars. It truly is the best way to replay this game. Only issue I had was technical, as my mouse kept stuttering about halfway through. The devs are aware of this issue on the community forums though.

It's a good game overall and great for people who like the King's Quest series, but it has seriously horrible saving and loading features. If you want to "save" a game, you have to quit it (and have it revert to the last time it autosaved), copy the file to one of the other 3 save slots, and then go back into the game. To load, quit your current game and change to the other file. Note that if you want your "save" to remain you'll have to copy again. It is very frustrating.
I noticed the issue when I accidentally slept in the bed 2 nights in-a-row in episode 2 and therefore did nothing those days. There was no confirmation that I actually wanted to sleep, and there was no way to go back and undo the action. The autosave made it so that I couldn't just load back to before I slept, so I had to copy the file, restart the entire episode 2, and then figure out that whole "save slots" thing I described in the previous paragraph.
If The Odd Gentlemen fix this issue and allow us to actually save and load games, my review would go from about 3 stars to 4 stars (3.5 stars to 4.5 stars for King's Quest series fans).
UPDATE November 2016:
(original review was in February 2016)
(Note that this update was intended to be a reply to AnD4D's review, but I passed the 1000 character limit, and so I have to write my text here instead. So when I say "your", I'm talking about AnD4D. It's unfortunate that changing my recommendation from Yes to No forces me to clear users' ratings of whether or not this was helpful.... but it seems I got no ratings yet anyway, so it doesn't really matter.)
I mostly agree with your review, except I think Chapter 5 wasn't quite as bad as Chapter 4. They did show the mechanics of Graham not being sure what was where (that he was an unreliable narrator at this point), and so I think the 4th key you mentioned was fair.
The long clue sequence to the frog for one of the numbers for one of the keys was odd, but I followed it anyway - in other words, I chose not to resort to random guessing for that number. And so for that reason I didn't run into quite the same disappointment you did when the clue sequence concluded.
Also, although I personally do like puzzle games, I felt Chapter 4's reliance on them made it less like King's Quest. And the dialogue in Chapter 4? Far worse than Chapter 5 in my opinion. Graham yelling at Alexander for using magic, Graham initially being happy to part ways with Alexander, the ridiculous over-the-top way they were making Gart behave with trashing the King's unopened letter, arguing with Gwendolyn, then picking up the letter later and opening it. Even the opening to the chapter was stupid with having to walk around the toys on the ground while carrying the baby and not making sharp turns was stupid. A worse opener than Final Fantasy XV's car-pushing boredom, which at least had better music and couldn't be failed in the way KQ's baby walking could.
So again.. I agree with you on Chapter 1-3. Now that Chapter 1 is free, I would definitely recommend it to anyone I know who has played King's Quest in the past. But I cannot justify anyone buying the Complete Collection or Season Pass given how bad Chapters 5 and especially 4 are. I suppose if you just have tons of money and don't mind parting with it, sure, buy it.
Actually there is something worth saying about Chapter 2. There's a part in the game where you can easily mess up everything by merely clicking on the bed. Unless they fixed it in a patch since I've played (which seems unlikely, but I'll admit I haven't checked), clicking on the bed will result in you going to sleep immediately - there is no confirmation message asking if that's what you really want to do. So you could by accident end up sleeping your days away while all the characters you would want to save die. And don't think about loading back before you slept, because the game kindly autosaves right after you sleep, and there are no manual saves (aside from copying one save slot to another and then copying back the other save file to your current one (or a third one) when you want to load).
I have no idea what the epilogue entails, as the game itself never even mentions an epilogue. It seems to involve "The Complete Collection", but I am perturbed that by paying for Chapter 1 and the Season Pass in Summer 2015 I wasn't already entitled to that epilogue. I mean Chapter 1 is free now, right? So I think I've actually paid more to them already than someone just buying the Complete Collection now would pay. It's just absurd, and I guess in that sense it makes [the way they handled] the epilogue the worst of all.

Let me start by saying after the Atari, PC gaming was my next step in gaming. My first PC game was the original King's Quest. From there, I was hooked on Sierra's Quest games. Dishonored 2 takes the basic gameplay that the first game set up and develops it slightly. It does so by giving the player new powers, each with their own mini skill tree and by allowing you to choose your protagonist. Even though there aren't too many new additions to the gameplay itself, it is still enough to keep the game feeling fresh and to justify the purchase if you've clocked the first game.
Dishonored 2 features some quite nice sound design. Most of the sounds do feel familiar having played the first game, but this is to be expected and is quite welcome. However, I did notice that with Headphone mode disabled enemies sounded as if they were right next to me when they were across the room from me, although this could just be me.
Just like the first game, Dishonored 2 is not the longest of games. However, the replayability of the game is one of its main selling points. The addition of different characters with their own powers and the ability to complete the entire game without even gaining supernatural powers definitely improves the replay value of the game. Though it doesn't have the longest story, it does have multiple endings for you to achieve and each of the missions are filled with collectibles to bring out your inner completionist. Basically, if you're someone who enjoys trying to uncover every secret in a game and is willing to sink a lot of time to 100% a game, this game has quite a lot to offer you.
Without going into Spoiler territory, Dishonored 2's story is basically what you'd expect if you've paid attention to the marketing material up to the game's release. For the most part you could play this game without having played the original, however there are a few references and revelations in there for fans of the original game to enjoy as well.
(As of 21st December 2016) It is no secret that Dishonored 2 isn't the most stable game available on Steam. However, other than a few FPS drops in specific areas I didn't have too many problems with the game myself, however browsing the Community Hub for a while shows that this will differ from person to person so I would advise doing some research before making a purchase.
Apart from the Technical Issues facing the PC version, the game it self is actually quite well executed, minus the odd bug here and there the gameplay is surprisingly smooth and other than a corpse randomly ragdolling for me and my Far Reach glitching out once or twice I didn't really notice any issues in the actual gameplay.
Overall I would say Dishonored 2 is worth the money, if you're someone who is solely put off by the graphical issues, I would say just buy it, see how it runs, then refund it if it doesn't work well on your system. If you are someone who is just looking to experience the story and is not interested in playing a game through multiple times though, I would recommend waiting until this title goes on sale as a single playthrough will not take you too long to achieve. This being said, if you're someone who enjoys replaying a game to try and achieve everything, this game definitely has a lot to offer you at its current price tag.
TL;DR: Solid game with a lot of replayability hindered by a few bugs. Wait for sale if only interested in story.

Dishonor me twice, prepare to spend $60.
Katy Perry fan or not, odds are you have heard the song with that one line: "
". With an extra dash of sizzle pop and razzle dazzle, Dishonored 2 takes the very same line and sentiment, replaces 'kissed' with 'murdered', and then unleashes a horde of flesh-hungry rats in the street. And I liked it.
Men murdering men, women murdering women. Women murdering men murdering women in front of men. The developers of Dishonored 2 did not hold back. It's all here, and it's all now.
This is a sequel. A bloody sequel about revenge and consequence set in a kingdom where rulers fall left and right, left and down. No place to run, no place to hide. Rulers just can't seem catch a break, especially the empress and her father. As a player, you have two routes before you:
! A fast, cunning father who's thirst for vengeance knows no bounds. The dark pawn, the antihero, Royal Protector to the throne and star of the prequel to the sequel. He can scale buildings with magic, or his bare hands when he feels like it. Two stories, nine stories, all stories high. It doesn't matter to him. He knows what to do, where to sneak, who to stab...and nobody touches his daughter without getting touched by his knife.
! The faster, sharper daughter of the father with an identical lust for vengeance. She trained in the streets. The hard streets, cold streets--with rats. She knows how to sneak and how to choke. She hasn't choked anyone yet, but she will. Magic is offered to her, but will she take it? Only you can decide.
+ Freedom. Absolute freedom to execute your tasks in any manner you wish. You want to climb that wall? Do it. You want to kill that group of baddies or sneak past them? The question is not if, but how. Guns, stealing, human posession. Dive in.
+ The story? We've all heard this plot before but the wide variety of player choices set this title apart from the rest. Every action has a direct consequence on the physical world. With each drop of blood shed, the streets of the city grow darker. Disease, infestation. At times you will face terrors of the existential kind. Lore-junkies, prepare for mounds of hidden texts around the city. Don't let the bloodflies bite!
+ Visuals are charming. Feels like a painting. A hyper-realistic painting brushed with blood. Upon release, many PC players experienced framerate issues. I did not (using a Quadro card).
+ The game is short, but its length is relative to play style. Murder Simulator is a fun romp, but if you want the full experience, max the difficulty and try to ghost it. Did it. Loved it. Took forever. Replay value is already high. Looking forward to added content in the future.

PING!

"Someone tried to shoot me! good thing I was wearing m-"
The guard's life ends shortly after my second bolt reaches its target. I prepare to deal with the second guard, who is just beginning to realize that something went wrong while his back was turned. No More Room in Hell is an amazing Co-Op Survival game with a lot of emphasis on the Co-Op. If you don't work together, you'll fall victim to the hordes. This game has tons of polish, and is very well supported by the developers. It's basically what I describe as a realistic Left 4 Dead. It's the same basic concept, a team of players have to work together to complete objectives while avoiding hordes of zombies. Notice how I said AVOID. More often than not, killing zombies is simply not worth your time unless it's absolutely necessary. Zombies are slow for the most part, except for some runners and the occasional child, but they are also quite resilient. You are not very powerful and tire quickly, so it takes some thought before taking on a horde. You can also take bleeding damage, and even get infected, which makes fighting even more dangerous. Basically, cooperation is the name of the game, and this is an experience not to be missed for zombie fans and co-op fans alike.

System Shock 2 is a game I only looked into because I was such a big fan of the Bioshock series.
This was one of Ken Levine's first big project's, and I almost love it as much as Bioshock. The story and setting are superb, and the semi-linear gameplay is perfectly excecuted. It's only downsides are it's dated graphics, odd controls, some gameplay annoyances, and trash ending.
Additionally, this is more of an RPG than Bioshock is as it has very well thought out skill trees. It is important that you choose what you upgrade carefully, as the game is also suprisingly difficult at times. My main complaints of the game, and also why I personally prefer Bioshock, are the weapon degredation system and the confusing interface.
The weapon degredation system appears to be hastily implemented and is less well thought out than Fallout's own. Also, the tutorial is quite bad, and the enemy AI isn't done too well. Overall, I liked the RPG elements a lot, but I think Bioshock did a good thing by cutting out a lot of the extraneous and tedious gameplay mechanics. However, if Bioshock had a more expansive RPG tree system and maybe some better inventory management, then it would be simply the best.

I have one positive thing to say about Rome II.
It lead me to abandon the Total War series, which I have loved above all others since I bought Medieval I, and let me discover the Paradox series of games.
Paradox doesn't rely on flashy graphics
They don't pimp overpriced DLC
They don't diminish the diplomacy and government simulation at the expense of "epic" battles
I really, REALLY liked every Total War game until this point and was extremely excited to see Rome II in the works, but it would seem as though I'm no longer the demographic they appeal to. I understand that they wanted to try and pull in new players (they have to!). What I can't understand is why a strategy game needs to be played on a super computer. My first and only attempt to play the game, on a computer which can run Shogun 2 pleasantly, was god-awful ugly. Crusader Kings 2 looks so much better because it's simple and runs on a laptop. I can live with simple graphics, the first Medieval was so much fun REGARDLESS of the fact that the campaign map was basically a chessboard.
My opinion, for what it's worth, is that the Total War series should focus on simpler graphics and complex mechanics, rather than the reverse. That way we can all enjoy it. I don't believe that glitter sells as much as gameplay. In the meantime, I'll be happily executing rebellious vassals and heathen captives in CK2 and working my way towards importing said empire into Europa Universalis 4 so I can form a new colonial nation.
I'd also like to thank Steam for letting me save the $60 I would have needed to spend to try this out!!!

気持ち良いだよ！Great atmosphere and direction makes for a real treat for new-commers and veterans to the series alike.  King's Quest: A Knight to Remember is an Adventure game with Action, Puzzle, and Moral choice elements.
The Puzzles are happily varried and are far more straight forward that the traditional King's Quest games, and probably for the better.  You won't be hurting any brain cells figuring them out, but at the same time they are satisfying and enjoyable.  There are also a variety of other puzzle types throughout the game each with their own charms, and well integrated into the games nerrative.
The Action sequences are an Exciting change of form from the previous games.  Senarios such as braving a dragon's lair feel far more epic when you are firing arrows and dodging death traps than in previous incarnations.
The Moral Choice elements are probably the weakest point of this game, but they are still quite good.  Basicallly how you choose to act in the story will leave a strong impression on your Granddaughter.  Your three options are something like Courage, Wit, and Compassion.  All treated as positive traits, and the result being purely superficial, they are mostly harmless and don't detract from the game, but I hope there wasn't too much dev time spent on them.
Overall I highly recommend for people looking for a fun, and enjoyable adventure game, especially if you are a fan of the series.

I haven't played Dishonored 2 for very long yet and I will update my review as I play it more but here are my first impressions.
Gameplay:
From what I have played the gameplay is basically the same as Dishonored but slightly expanded. One example is if you throw a target off ballence with a well timed block you can choke them out instead of having to kill them. All these things make for the same great gameplay that Dishonored acheived.
Audio:
The game sounds fine. The voice acting is pretty good. There isnt much to say about it. Although just so you know the dialogue subtitles are found in the AUDIO section of settings which I found strange but eh.
Visuals/Frames:
While the game isnt amazingly optimized (I play most games on medium graphics and on this I play very low) the frames are fine. I can't say much about the visuals because, again, I play on very low. What I can say though is that I don't know why anyone complains about the frames. I get a solid 60 while I see other people with better specs getting 15. My best guess is that they are doing something like using a second moniter which uses a lot of GPU, and as I stated before the game isn't very well optimized so you have to look out for that.
Story:
As this is a first impression review I can't say much about the story. But what I can say is that so far it seems very promising.
Conclusion:
While the visuals are porly optimized, my frames are fine and the gameplay is amazing. From what i have played the story looks potentialy great and the voice acting, subtitles, sound effects, etc are all very good.
P.S. I always find it funny how you can take a paragraph long review and put it into 2 or 3 scentences that cover pretty much everything you just said over like 14 scentences.

Black Mesa is the best game I've ever played when it comes to a remake. The music was just so perfect and gave it so much emotion and realism, like how it sounds sad when you realise the magnitude of the disaster and then picks up at parts of the game where victory is on the horizon. I absolutely recommend this to anyone who likes the Half Life series, its a game that you wont regret playing.

Even without the Xen chapters, this is an absolutely stunning remake worthy of the highest amount of praise. Nearly all of the great classic moments from the original masterpiece are here and looking better than ever. The shootouts are arguably even better, as the A.I. is ruthless and will stop at nothing to put you into the dirt, requiring an equal amount of reflexes and strategy when they gang up on you in greater numbers, and don't get me started on those black ops assassins. Needless to say, I greatly enjoyed the increased difficulty in the action segments, it made them feel more alive.
On top of that, the tense action and atmospheric environments are aided by a terrific, pulse-pounding soundtrack. Some of my favorites include "Surface Tension", "We've Got Hostiles", and "Questionable Ethics", making the experience feel all the more epic and immersive. Although the head crabs and zombies were scarier in the original, mostly due to the dated visuals, the infamous Ichthyosaur - of which there are three - are more frightening than ever before in their updated form. It took me quite a while to get past a certain section in "Surface Tension" because of them. One even caught me off guard and nearly gave me a fatal heart attack. Spoiler alert: There's two in the water
There really isn't a whole lot to say about Black Mesa that hasn't already been said, and trust me I tried. I bought it when it first came to Steam, and even incomplete, I still feel like I got my money's worth, as you can tell by the amount of hours I spent playing it. The Xen chapters, when eventually finished, will simply be the icing on the cake and a great excuse to revisit the game. I wish the multiplayer was more active, as it's quite fun and the maps I played on were pretty good and could've used more players, but even so, there are better options in that regard. The single player is the meat of Half Life and always will be.
It goes without saying that this really is a must-play, it's by far the best early access game of all time and even surpasses such a label, especially given the bad reputation of it lately. If you've been holding off on buying the game until Xen, have no fear, the game is 100% worth it with or without it. This is the best possible remake of one of the most groundbreaking FPS ever made, so pick up that trusty crowbar and get to whacking.

Hello, i usually don't review the games i play (maybe because i am just that lazy, or simply because i'm not that good :D) , i hope it's helpfull for some of you guys. Here it goes:
By god this brings back so many good memories from the times that i couldn't stop replaying this game.
Was a little dissapointed that the Xen chapters are still not here, but i understand why it's still not here (maybe the most complex part of half-life (in terms of re-texturing,programming and polishing)
We are not talking about "Half-life Re-textured".No no no, Sir, it's much more than that. I mean, yes, you can take a game from 1998 and add new texture above it (i know it's not that easy, but you get the point) and BAM! , you have a good game which looks good. NO . Black Mesa has managed to not only upgrade the graphics to one of the best games of all time, but also to make changes to the placements of objects, to the locations of buttons/valves , to the actual route itself. These changes filled my heart with joy when,for example,  i was running around with my brain acting purely from memory, and suddenly *OMFG* i just fell off and died. A wild hole appeared, it was super effective (and it wasn't in the original Half-Life)
So, to break it down into GOOD and BAD :
GOOD:
-Extraordinary re-texture (it's nostalgic to see all the characters/monsters being made HD)
-Although the route is change here and there, it doesn't affect the storyline at all
-The hat (i laughed my pants off at the ending with the Xen Hat :D )
-Because of the graphical upgrade, the objectives or in other words, the path you have to take are sometimes hard to see.But i consider that a good thing because it makes the player think a little , "hmm, maybe i should do this" (barrel explodes and you load your save )
BAD:  (may be just me, but this is my opinion)
-Movement feel choppy (instead of the precise one i felt in the original Half-Life), you can't really stand on the edge of a building or a handrail because you are always afraid that if you move a centimeter to the wrong direction, you will fall
-The ladders cannot be activated while you are not looking at them (if you run into the ladder while moving backwards). This is especially annoying if you are trying to do the Hat achievement
-The AI sometimes just gives up (with no reason whatsoever)
-Possible bug - When you have the Hat pointing at a headcrab, the headcrab will not see you anymore and will act as though you don't exist
-Needs some fixes on larger maps because for me at least it drops many frames (for example , before entering Lambda Complex)
TL'DR:
Considering it's still in Early Access, i cannot really blame it for having some minor glitches.The good parts of this game overwhelm the other parts of the game.In conclusion, I recommend this game to everyone (New players and Half-Life veterans)

Survival horror games are some of my favorite games, so I was looking forward to The Evil WIthin 2. I like them difficult and where they require a lot of ammo and health conservation. To me, that's the entire point of the genre. In that regard TEW2 is worse than its predecessor. But it does improve on other things, most notable: story.
I played on Nightmare on my first playthrough. Bullets were definitely scarce, and the components to make bullets were rare too. I did find that I had to avoid fighting a lot (well avoid shooting, not fighting, since most enemies could be stealth killed). Health items weren't very rare. Overall, the game was much easier than TEW1. I think the primary reason for this is that most of the game is you versus a room of unsuspecting zombies that you can stealth kill most of the time, and when you do get seen it's easy to just run a few meters away and they forget about you. This may have existed in the first game to a lesser extent, but it wasn't as noticeable, reason being that in the first game you were on the run most of the time, and confronted with a lot more agile enemies than simple zombies.
TEW2 does improve on story. The first game was a lot more mysterious, whereas with this one it's pretty clear what is happening because more is known about TEW2 world. This allowed them to be more straightforward with the storytelling, and you get to learn a lot more about TEW2 world.
The worst part about the game is that I never felt like I was in danger (bad for a survival horror game), and this primarily has to do with the fact that you can run away from just about everything, even if you have no stamina; the stumbling slow run is enough to not be hit by most enemies. Most survival horror games require maneuvering a certain way to escape different enemies, so you have to perfect different movements against different enemies. The stamina bar really serves no purpose in TEW2. I would have liked to see no stamina and had more aggressive enemies that you had to avoid with player skill.
The game is okay. I like the atmosphere and the story a lot. It's a good action game. It isn't a very good survival horror game.

Played through Nightmare mode, clearing as much content and being as efficient with ammo as possible, still spent most of the game severely strained for ammunition. The game was happy to throw a billion weapon upgrade pieces that I didn't want right at me, though. I'd assume that this is because the game is pseudo-open world and has no real way of moderating the amount (or lack of) ammo it gives to you, while the first was mostly linear and gave you a challenging-but-not-unfair amount on all modes. I entered a lot of scenarios where the game assumed that I'd have a good amount of ammo to beat them, having just scoured the map looking for ammo and still having none, and being forced to cheese the encounters in the worst ways possible with like 6 pistol bullets in stock.
I found it really enjoyable up until around 3/5ths through, after you kill the first major boss. After that, the game dumps a tonne of atrocious plot and writing on you while cutting off the supply to ammo so severely that you're best off running around abusing the "Sneak kill from behind cover" ability. And that's what the game became after that, cheesing every encounter by luring low/mid tier enemies towards cover (that was buggy/difficult to use, by the way) and instakilling them.
It's around that point that it also sinks in that most of the game's content is open-world padding (I spent about 8 hours in an area I could've cleared in half an hour just sticking to story objectives) and the game consists of only two major open world zones that aren't very big (a minute to travel across each). Most of the time spent in the game is traversing those zones in the back-and-forth between doing missions, sidequests and searching for ammo/upgrades. ie, a lot of boring filler.
Most of what I liked about the game was what little of the first game carried over: surreal environments, interesting scene transitions and unforgiving challenge in the few instances the game wasn't being straight-up unfair.
The performance that everyone's whining about? It's not great. I've got a Fury x and i7 4770k, hovered around 50-60 in most areas and the game's detail settings didn't do anything to change the performance. On the plus side, when the framerate drops it just drops. It doesn't get stuttering, it doesn't mess with the controls, the game still feels just as responsive while lagging and the engine takes it like a champ. It could be much worse, but it isn't, so I don't have many complaints on that end.

What to say about this game ? I started playing it before it got to steam, from when it still was in beta testing...
I've been looking for something to patch things up, after dota 2 started crumbling down, and i spent so many hours in that game, it was a hard bash... So, what was i looking for precisely? I didn't know either, but wanted to find something similar, yet a change was needed, something to entertain me once again, something different. Smite was that thing, a moba base, with a third person "shooting" implementation ; much more skillshot based and maybe hard to get into after so many hours in an old fashioned moba, but it was interesting, and its mechanics could surely grant satisfying challenges.
So i dived a bit on it, taking it slow, at first it was extremely frustrating , hitting opponents when i had to AIM to get them with my arrows, too used to the old click-over-their-head and shoot automaticly mechanic, it was hell, specially considering they could move and dodge!!
After a while tho, once you get used to it, the real fun begins...
Not too newbie friendly at the very beginning, but if you can hold on long enough , it gets much better, more or less like any moba tbh :)
In my experience , i noticed the community isn't too toxic, maybe for the Macro - text system , allowing even russian to say something that makes sense for everybody in the team, and less keyboard smashing , some very annoying player spamming macros (thank god there is the flood ban which doesn't allow then to do it for too long) but overall the salty players aren't too many.. And sometimes in games like this, we all get a bit salty...
So if you're looking for a moba, where your capability to predict movements and actions from enemies and the ability to move in a very hard to predict way is more important than farm and level (ofc it matters a LOT, but if you can dodge all the hits from a carry, he still won't kill you :D ) SMITE could be the right game for you.
If you're simply looking for something new, and still challenging and where you can cooperate to win a match, you might want to try it.
Enjoy!

+: One of the best games I have ever played, it's up there with Baldur's Gate 2 and Planescape: Torment as one of the best designed Role Playing Games ever. System Shock 2 is an old game that is a horror (Survival Horror on higher difficulties really) first person shooter role playing game and was basically the game that Bioshock and Deus Ex are inspired from.
+: The music is fantastic, the story themes are great and thought provoking, the villain is one of the best villains ever written, the level design is superb, and it creates a great horror atmosphere without relying on jump scares 24/7.
+: While the graphics might not be so good anymore, it does have mod support and you can download a mod pack that improves the graphics greatly without affecting the gameplay what-so-ever over here:
+: Without spoiling really anything I'll just say this game is great and almost every single aspect is damn near perfect except for...
-: The User Interface is terribly designed, it is stuck in 90s UI design and it's just all over the place, sometimes hard to read, doesn't work so well at bigger resolutions, and honestly if they would have completely changed the UI to something reasonable for this Steam upgrade (with an option to go back to the old UI) I think most people would have been thankful. This is my sole complaint with this game and if you can get used to the old school UI design (or are used to far worse from other older games) then you will probably enjoy this game a lot.

It is fair to say that things did not go well for Rome II on release - I played it then, and it was a stodgy turgid mess of a game. Hopefully CA and Sega have learnt from this for forthcoming releases, as where Rome II is now is a good place.
The recent Emperor Edition introduced an overhauled building tree and politics system, making the latter more understandable and the former more strategic (balancing food demands and public order Vs current resources and requirements). Both are simple enough to get on with once you learn how it works. Additionally, there was a swathe of graphical tweaks as well. Colours are now brighter with a wider colour spectrum which makes things easier to review at a glance and the units/maps/buildings look much better than before. The AI has also been tweaked, and will now fight back. It still throws Elephant units away as if they were nothing, but other units will try and outflank, offer up tempting targets, seek out weak points, defend strong points etc etc. It won't ever match a human opponent, but it can give a good account for itself. Sieges aren't all about assaulting a city as soon as the army gets there either, relying on torches to burn the gates down: often the AI will camp outside and build siege equipment to assault with, and/or use ladders effectively.
Rome II has come a long way and is now a very good addition to the Total War stable. If you're an RTS fan, you can do worse than pick this up.

Well, one of the most controversial games ever made, remastered.
Postal, the original killing spree simulator, remade in Unity engine. Looks better, plays more or less the same. The expierence is streamlined, some mechanics rebalanced, but it's the same game - just repackaged.  Is it bad? Not at all. I found it still enjoyable, even after all these years. Nostalgia factor is pretty strong here, so if you're a young gamer, you could be a little underwhelmed. Still, getting it on sale won't hurt your wallet.
So, what is Postal? Simple twin stick shooter with a dark twist. You're a psychotic killer, exterminating everything in your way. Yep, lighting up a parade with a flamthrower will happen here.
Redux version includes all levels (with add ons), new co-op mode and challenge mode. Full package, few hours of stress relieving, mindless slaughter. Sometimes, it's all you need.

I have been playing the King's Quest series since I was a little girl, it was the first PC game I ever played and now that I'm 30 I still play them. It's not just nostalgia for me, I play them at least once a year and have yet to get sick of them. The brilliance of the series can get lost on new gamers, they are an absolute work of art and a game that I have yet to find a match to in modern games. They were visually stunning for their time, the story lines were so thought out and engaging and the game play was magnificent. In saying that lets get to the review on this game.
I think the Odd Gentlemen did an amazing job on this, they kept the old way of game play, finding random things in random places that can solve random puzzles on the other side of the map. I loved how at points I was actually confused on what to do next and spent half an hour wondering aimlessly around (Happily, as the artwork is stunning), it wasn't feed to me, I had to figure it out on my own. Something modern day games lack, intelligence and thought to get to the next part of the game. The characters were lovable and memorable (I really felt for poor Acorn and despised Manny), and the actors were fantastic. The game ran smoothly and I only had one small glitch that quickly fixed itself.
I did have one problem with it, the ability to skip dialog, but it seams they have fixed it in chapter 2. Shows the devs are listening to us. I did miss the ability to move my mouse around the map to look at things, but the ability to move your character to the object does seam more logical.
In all I give this a 9/10, as nothing compares to KQ6... ;)
P.S. THANK YOU for not making it like KQ8 that game was terrible.

Underappreciated and absolutely amazing game. King's Quest is a chapter style visual/puzzle based novel about an old King who tells his grand daughter about his  journey as a young teenager, who goes on a long adventure to become the newest Knight of Daventry.
The game is riddled with puzzles, interesting characters, and amazingly fun storylines. From old chemists who like to lick frogs, to bridge trolls, to heel sharpening royal guards, this game is full of entertainment and truly amazing storytelling(And puns, lots of puns. Don't worry though, you'll warm up to them!)
It's important to understand that nothing in this game is truly important other than the story told. The graphics are simplistic, the sounds are simplistic, the gameplay is simplistic, but it's all good because the only thing you should really be noticing, is the story!
I'll give you some pros and cons all the same:
Pros:
+Very fun, entertaining story that'll keep you going for hours
+Fun chain based puzzles that take you across several places in Daventry to find what you need to progress your adventure.
+Interesting, well-rounded(especially the baker!) characters who have very distinct and unique personalities(Just wait till you meet Kyle and Larry XD I lol'd so hard)
+Well suffice it to say that the developpers are 'pros!' Get it? (I'm saying there are lots of puns in this game...)
+Bridge Troll guilds
+You're a bandicoot, apparently?
+Buta? Affa Nata! c:
+Things are dirt cheap. One shiny gold coin for a 5 feet long starshroom pie? HOW DO I GET TO DAVENTRY!?
+Millions of times better than Undertale.
Cons:
-Simplistic graphics that water down the glorious views you could have of the landscape.
-Each chapter is relatively short(Manny should know), and there are 5 of them, but you need to pay for each chapter to continue.
-Lots of backtracking and retracing steps. The puzzles force you to run hither thither and fro to find the pieces needed to continue. It can get sort of frustrating when you're standing with what looks like a pile of junk and you KNOW it's important, but you have no idea how!
-Scheming fast speaking merchants with goats disguised as unicorns :c
-Buta? Stalama! :c
Overall, the game's absolutely brilliant, and worth the money the developpers want for it. Now I know you guys don't like that you need to pay $10 for each chapter of the game. But honestly, I'm fine with spending that to motivate the developpers into creating bigger, longer, and better future chapters of this game. Can't wait to see what these brilliant minds come up with next!
But please, do me a favor:
It's so much better if you actually figure it out yourself. Cheating, and using the guides, will completely destroy the fun in the game, and provoke negative reviews because, quote 'it was boring and lame, cause I was a 10 year old who wasn't smart enough to figure out the puzzles, boo hoo, rant rant rant'
Seriously. Do us all a favor, and just play the game with no guides. You'll thank me later.
