Let me start off by saying this is a fantastic game. I absolutely loved Demons Souls and Dark Souls, but this one to me shot both out of the water. That being said, it's not without it's flaws, so let me get those out of the way first.
Much like the first one, this game suffers from bad PC controls. While it's not as bad as the first one, I'm beginning to think this style of game simply works better with a controller. If you have no issue with sloppy keyboard controls or just plugging in a controller, buy away.
Frankly, I was rather disappointed by the lack of lighting system that was shown in their tech demo, but there are plenty of other, more proffessional reviewers out there who have beaten this topic into the ground, so go decide for yourself.
The game is a bit more linear than Dark Souls and Demons Souls. I personally don't have an issue with this, and feel that it has created an very fleshed out game, I'm sure some other Souls fans might have an issue with it.
That's really all of the complaints I have about this game. The PC port is incredible by comparison with it's predecessor, and while I've heard complaints, I think the game looks incredible. The areas are fantastic, and the bosses are a delight as usual. The controls on a controller feel tighter than they ever did in Dark Souls or Demons Souls. The beginning of the game definitely feels like it's easier on beginners, which I think is a fair enough design choice.
As I've stated up above, this game is fantastic. There are some cons, but in my opinion, they're far outweighed by all the incredible things this game has to offer.

Hello, i usually don't review the games i play (maybe because i am just that lazy, or simply because i'm not that good :D) , i hope it's helpfull for some of you guys. Here it goes:
By god this brings back so many good memories from the times that i couldn't stop replaying this game.
Was a little dissapointed that the Xen chapters are still not here, but i understand why it's still not here (maybe the most complex part of half-life (in terms of re-texturing,programming and polishing)
We are not talking about "Half-life Re-textured".No no no, Sir, it's much more than that. I mean, yes, you can take a game from 1998 and add new texture above it (i know it's not that easy, but you get the point) and BAM! , you have a good game which looks good. NO . Black Mesa has managed to not only upgrade the graphics to one of the best games of all time, but also to make changes to the placements of objects, to the locations of buttons/valves , to the actual route itself. These changes filled my heart with joy when,for example,  i was running around with my brain acting purely from memory, and suddenly *OMFG* i just fell off and died. A wild hole appeared, it was super effective (and it wasn't in the original Half-Life)
So, to break it down into GOOD and BAD :
GOOD:
-Extraordinary re-texture (it's nostalgic to see all the characters/monsters being made HD)
-Although the route is change here and there, it doesn't affect the storyline at all
-The hat (i laughed my pants off at the ending with the Xen Hat :D )
-Because of the graphical upgrade, the objectives or in other words, the path you have to take are sometimes hard to see.But i consider that a good thing because it makes the player think a little , "hmm, maybe i should do this" (barrel explodes and you load your save )
BAD:  (may be just me, but this is my opinion)
-Movement feel choppy (instead of the precise one i felt in the original Half-Life), you can't really stand on the edge of a building or a handrail because you are always afraid that if you move a centimeter to the wrong direction, you will fall
-The ladders cannot be activated while you are not looking at them (if you run into the ladder while moving backwards). This is especially annoying if you are trying to do the Hat achievement
-The AI sometimes just gives up (with no reason whatsoever)
-Possible bug - When you have the Hat pointing at a headcrab, the headcrab will not see you anymore and will act as though you don't exist
-Needs some fixes on larger maps because for me at least it drops many frames (for example , before entering Lambda Complex)
TL'DR:
Considering it's still in Early Access, i cannot really blame it for having some minor glitches.The good parts of this game overwhelm the other parts of the game.In conclusion, I recommend this game to everyone (New players and Half-Life veterans)

I bought this game a few years back shortly after it was released. At that time, it cost just shy of $60. I didn't mind spending that much, knowing that it was subscription-free with some aesthetics-oriented microtransactions. Lots of games do that these days, which is fine.
I stopped playing since December 2014. This week I decided to get a friend of mine into it, before I decided to try it again myself after basically three years.
What I did not realize at this point is they introduced many DLCs, adventuring packs, experience bonuses, and more microtransactions that HAVE NOTHING TO DO WITH AESTHETICS. I didn't realize this until about 4 days back into the game.
Elder Scrolls Online is a great game on paper. It was originally a big hit with me and my friends. But since they've added DLC's that are just about $15 each, amongst other pay-to-win microtransactions, it's now no longer the "Elder Scrolls MMO Experience" that we hoped for.
ESO is now - unfortunately - another microtransaction-ridden, DLC-plagued, pay-to-win atrocity of a game. It's totally sold out the entire fan base it's been working to create all these years.
Elder Scrolls has a fantastic lore and storyline, but since this release, it's lost all appeal.

Survival horror games are some of my favorite games, so I was looking forward to The Evil WIthin 2. I like them difficult and where they require a lot of ammo and health conservation. To me, that's the entire point of the genre. In that regard TEW2 is worse than its predecessor. But it does improve on other things, most notable: story.
I played on Nightmare on my first playthrough. Bullets were definitely scarce, and the components to make bullets were rare too. I did find that I had to avoid fighting a lot (well avoid shooting, not fighting, since most enemies could be stealth killed). Health items weren't very rare. Overall, the game was much easier than TEW1. I think the primary reason for this is that most of the game is you versus a room of unsuspecting zombies that you can stealth kill most of the time, and when you do get seen it's easy to just run a few meters away and they forget about you. This may have existed in the first game to a lesser extent, but it wasn't as noticeable, reason being that in the first game you were on the run most of the time, and confronted with a lot more agile enemies than simple zombies.
TEW2 does improve on story. The first game was a lot more mysterious, whereas with this one it's pretty clear what is happening because more is known about TEW2 world. This allowed them to be more straightforward with the storytelling, and you get to learn a lot more about TEW2 world.
The worst part about the game is that I never felt like I was in danger (bad for a survival horror game), and this primarily has to do with the fact that you can run away from just about everything, even if you have no stamina; the stumbling slow run is enough to not be hit by most enemies. Most survival horror games require maneuvering a certain way to escape different enemies, so you have to perfect different movements against different enemies. The stamina bar really serves no purpose in TEW2. I would have liked to see no stamina and had more aggressive enemies that you had to avoid with player skill.
The game is okay. I like the atmosphere and the story a lot. It's a good action game. It isn't a very good survival horror game.

Played through Nightmare mode, clearing as much content and being as efficient with ammo as possible, still spent most of the game severely strained for ammunition. The game was happy to throw a billion weapon upgrade pieces that I didn't want right at me, though. I'd assume that this is because the game is pseudo-open world and has no real way of moderating the amount (or lack of) ammo it gives to you, while the first was mostly linear and gave you a challenging-but-not-unfair amount on all modes. I entered a lot of scenarios where the game assumed that I'd have a good amount of ammo to beat them, having just scoured the map looking for ammo and still having none, and being forced to cheese the encounters in the worst ways possible with like 6 pistol bullets in stock.
I found it really enjoyable up until around 3/5ths through, after you kill the first major boss. After that, the game dumps a tonne of atrocious plot and writing on you while cutting off the supply to ammo so severely that you're best off running around abusing the "Sneak kill from behind cover" ability. And that's what the game became after that, cheesing every encounter by luring low/mid tier enemies towards cover (that was buggy/difficult to use, by the way) and instakilling them.
It's around that point that it also sinks in that most of the game's content is open-world padding (I spent about 8 hours in an area I could've cleared in half an hour just sticking to story objectives) and the game consists of only two major open world zones that aren't very big (a minute to travel across each). Most of the time spent in the game is traversing those zones in the back-and-forth between doing missions, sidequests and searching for ammo/upgrades. ie, a lot of boring filler.
Most of what I liked about the game was what little of the first game carried over: surreal environments, interesting scene transitions and unforgiving challenge in the few instances the game wasn't being straight-up unfair.
The performance that everyone's whining about? It's not great. I've got a Fury x and i7 4770k, hovered around 50-60 in most areas and the game's detail settings didn't do anything to change the performance. On the plus side, when the framerate drops it just drops. It doesn't get stuttering, it doesn't mess with the controls, the game still feels just as responsive while lagging and the engine takes it like a champ. It could be much worse, but it isn't, so I don't have many complaints on that end.

The upgrade system has been tweaked and changed with more flexibility for how you wish to approach enemies, whether direct and loud or rushing and sneaking up to smash their skull in.
The boss designs are really fun and interesting, honestly they hit their peak as soon as Chapter 14 rolls around but I'll refrain from spoiling about it.
And the story is a lot more concise and straightforward, characters that are fleshed out and villains you enjoy to see appear or genuinely feel some sort of vengeance against from Sebastian's point of view, Sebastian himself has a lot of character development and a lot of emotional scenes.
Massively more enjoyable than the first game and performs a lot better too.

"Show. Don't tell." That's the first thing you learn in Creative writing 101. I wish I could give the game a thumbs-up, and you should definitely give it a try if third-person shooter (despite a very short first person segment) with some horror and survival elements is your thing, but the sloppy writing and amateurish storytelling along with some pacing issues are something jarring enough in this game that I can't look past.
Unlike its predecessor, where you are thrown right into a phantasmagoric world and spend the entire game trying to figure out what is happening (and you'll still be confused if you don't look hard enough and use some resoning skills to put the pieces together), The Evil Within 2 has a very linear story that is so much easier to understand, but almost too easy. The major plot twists are fine, yet it doesn't make you wow or add much to the experience. In the first game, the mystery is one thing that suits its tone extremely well, and is integral to the whole sort of delirious experience. The story of this game, however, is merely serviceable, and sometimes way too Hollywood-ish and sappy, and even incosistent. It also lacks the grit that sets the first game apart.
The quality of writing is another issue I have with this game. Oftentimes, the writers try to tell you how the characters feel, but apart from the words that come out of their mouths, nothing else indicates that they feel that way. In games such as Life is Strange or The Last of Us, the writing sounds genuine and nuanced because they don't try to spoonfeed you everything; instead, you can tell what is shown. Their dialogues fit right into the environment but I have to say even "jarring" is an understatement for how I feel about this game's conversations and monologues sometimes. To make the matter worse, the voice acting doesn't quite hit the mark either. It seems that there is no voice acting director at all or they couldn't decide where they want to use them. Most characters sound one-dimentional and generally insouciant. They all together make it hard for you to care about the characters even if you want to, and does disservice when the story takes a sappy turn.
Gameplay-wise, the control is much smoother and the crafting comes in handy and makes the game more interesting. Still, I feel the game has some serious pacing issues with regards to the fights. In the first game, the stages are very clearly designed to make sure that you barely make it out alive in every fight (at least in the first playthrough), but with the mightier crafting system and semi-open world in two areas thrown into the mix, The Evil Within 2 has a much tougher job and, unfortunately, sometimes it doesn't deliver. Perhaps for the same reason, very few bosses are as memorable and have the tension that makes the first game extremely satisfying.
Overall, The Evil Within 2 is not a bad game, but it plays too safe and doesn't inherit much of what makes The Evil Within a heart-throbbing and gratifying horror and survival experience.

One of the best RPG/FPS hybrids out there.
In System Shock 2, you'll play as a soldier sent to a derelict spaceship in order to contain an infection, find out what caused it and, hopefully, recover the ship.♥♥♥♥♥♥go down and turns out everything was way worse than expected, and you'll have to traverse dim-lighted corridors, fight monstruous and scary creatures to find out the truth behind the ship's demise. When you finally meet your nemesis, the game will take you through some of the most amazing and iconic scenes in gaming's history.
There are a whole lot of exploring to do, since the ship is huge and you'll have access to every area you have previously unlocked, with some tasks requiring you to go back to places you've already been to. Monsters roam around the ship and areas that you think are clear will be repopulated, making you stand on the edge of your chair at all times. Nowhere is safe, there is no hiding from your nemesis. Conserve your ammo, take good care of your health and plan your character build ahead, otherwise you will not survive the nightmare. The soundtrack will keep you scared and pumped up, while some of the creatures you'll fight will make the most horrendous and disturbing sounds you ever heard on a game. This game is such a blend between survival-horror, RPG and action that it becomes hard to say what exactly you're in for. Expect to be amazed, confused, lost, worried, tense and, most of all, scared. Really scared.
This is a gem, one of those games you have to play at least once in your life if you want to understand what video-games are all about. Go ahead, you won't regret it.

Underappreciated and absolutely amazing game. King's Quest is a chapter style visual/puzzle based novel about an old King who tells his grand daughter about his  journey as a young teenager, who goes on a long adventure to become the newest Knight of Daventry.
The game is riddled with puzzles, interesting characters, and amazingly fun storylines. From old chemists who like to lick frogs, to bridge trolls, to heel sharpening royal guards, this game is full of entertainment and truly amazing storytelling(And puns, lots of puns. Don't worry though, you'll warm up to them!)
It's important to understand that nothing in this game is truly important other than the story told. The graphics are simplistic, the sounds are simplistic, the gameplay is simplistic, but it's all good because the only thing you should really be noticing, is the story!
I'll give you some pros and cons all the same:
Pros:
+Very fun, entertaining story that'll keep you going for hours
+Fun chain based puzzles that take you across several places in Daventry to find what you need to progress your adventure.
+Interesting, well-rounded(especially the baker!) characters who have very distinct and unique personalities(Just wait till you meet Kyle and Larry XD I lol'd so hard)
+Well suffice it to say that the developpers are 'pros!' Get it? (I'm saying there are lots of puns in this game...)
+Bridge Troll guilds
+You're a bandicoot, apparently?
+Buta? Affa Nata! c:
+Things are dirt cheap. One shiny gold coin for a 5 feet long starshroom pie? HOW DO I GET TO DAVENTRY!?
+Millions of times better than Undertale.
Cons:
-Simplistic graphics that water down the glorious views you could have of the landscape.
-Each chapter is relatively short(Manny should know), and there are 5 of them, but you need to pay for each chapter to continue.
-Lots of backtracking and retracing steps. The puzzles force you to run hither thither and fro to find the pieces needed to continue. It can get sort of frustrating when you're standing with what looks like a pile of junk and you KNOW it's important, but you have no idea how!
-Scheming fast speaking merchants with goats disguised as unicorns :c
-Buta? Stalama! :c
Overall, the game's absolutely brilliant, and worth the money the developpers want for it. Now I know you guys don't like that you need to pay $10 for each chapter of the game. But honestly, I'm fine with spending that to motivate the developpers into creating bigger, longer, and better future chapters of this game. Can't wait to see what these brilliant minds come up with next!
But please, do me a favor:
It's so much better if you actually figure it out yourself. Cheating, and using the guides, will completely destroy the fun in the game, and provoke negative reviews because, quote 'it was boring and lame, cause I was a 10 year old who wasn't smart enough to figure out the puzzles, boo hoo, rant rant rant'
Seriously. Do us all a favor, and just play the game with no guides. You'll thank me later.

First impression reminds me much more of Dragon's Lair than the classic KQ series. The game is atmospheric for sure, but it just feels totally "on rails", the QTE interactions are so minimal in parts that it might as well have been done with full motion video. It is annoying that you can't skip the cut-scenes and have to watch them over and over. Once you get into the first "quest", the flow is still very linear, there are only ever one or two things to look at or use in each screen and the puzzles are much more simplistic than the Sierra of old. This game doesn't really seem sure what it wants to be, flicking between QTE, shooting action, dialog trees and semi-interactive cut-scenes, and classic style puzzles, leaving an overall flat impression because it doesn't do any of them particularly well.
One of the great things about the old KQ titles was the openness of the worlds and the lack of sequence in which you had to do the sub-quests, and not every useful object was blindingly obvious. Its a shame that there is not more depth because the graphics are beautifully detailed. I'm trying to like this game, but it just seems very dull and leaves me yearning to play, not the classic point and clicks or text adventures, but a good adventure like Zelda Ocarina of Time where there is an actual world full of things to do and explore.
I'm sure I'd have to get deeper into this game to fully appreciate it, but at the moment, its just not giving enough to keep going and seems too tedious to play. Glad I only paid a dollar on sale as its not worth the retail price.

I got stuck a handful of times, but never for very long. I think this game hits the sweet spot in difficulty compromise. It's not a hard game to complete, but there are achievements for solving puzzles the best way. So, most people will be able to finish the game and the aficionados will still have challenge to get all the secrets. The writing and voice acting are mostly good. I'm now definitely considering getting the full season when the rest of the episodes have been released. The new King's Quest is off to an excellent start.

I am not the biggest fan of the Alien movies however this game really gripped me. It is a single-player survival horror game that excellently captures the feeling of being isolated.
I did not think this game was the scariest game I have ever played. However there are moments that are incredibly tense, like when the Alien walks in front of you while you're in a locker and then turns away just as you think its spotted you. Although running and hiding from the Alien is the pivotal mechanism in this game, it does not become boring as there are many other enemies on the ship and you can deal with them in different ways.
Stealth in this game does not mean hiding behind an object, it means moving outside the enemies line of sight. Sometimes you may have to gamble and hope for the best. This type of stealth makes you fear what is around every corner, especially since the Alien does not have a set path.
Graphics are fantastic and can evoke a sense of astonishment when you look outside the ship and see the vast space that lies around you. These moments can make you forget about the Alien. The Alien is bloody scary though.
Some negatives during my experience with the game. Playing on Hard is more annoying than challenging, I may be playing wrong but sometimes I felt as if the Alien didn't give me a chance to move - I left the locker then got back in the locker and repeated this process for a few minutes. I adjusted it to normal after a few chapters and my enjoyment increased greatly. Also the save system is not the best, I get what they are trying to accomplish but sometimes I found myself focusing too much on getting to a save point rather than exploring the environment around me.
Overall, this game is a great, refreshing and terrifying experience.

I like this game. I really do. I absolutely recommend getting this game when it's on sale (Even at a price of 40-50 dollars, this is still a solid buy for a 15-25 hour long campaign).  However, I have really mixed feelings about this game, similar to the reviewers who rated this game on Gamespot and IGN.  While I think their final verdict is wrong, I feel they had some good constructive criticism about certain aspects of this game that I feel are getting glossed over because of the anger of the scores they gave this game.  Therefore, I'm going to try to write something that will help skeptic buyers eying this game understand the difference between those reviewing this game on Steam and those reviewing this on IGN and Gamespot.
The main crux of this game is that this is simply not a game about closure.  If you are playing this game looking for a payoff, this is not your game.  The plot of the game (while brilliantly paced toward its first four or so hours) begins to deteriorate toward the middle of the game. It simply does not know how to end itself.  It also doesn’t help that the main cast of characters rank from developed but underused to undeveloped but overused. Do *not* play this game expecting Amanda Ripley’s personal journey of finding out what happened to her mother to be front and center in the narrative.  Frankly, by midway in the game, she’s just a shell for the player.  In short, this is not the type of game that is “fun” to play and isn't looking to "reward" to its player upon its completion….which is why the reviewers at sites like IGN and Gamespot ultimately gave negative feedback concerning this game.
What this game is an Alien immersion simulator.  The art and audio teams behind this game did their homework on the Alien lore to perfection.  This is probably the only Alien game in existence to fully capture Ridley Scott’s universe and H.R. Giger’s terrifying vision of the Alien. Everything is there…the lightning, the fog, the retro technology….it’s all perfect.  I’m not going to retread what other reviewers have said about the gameplay.  It’s a great cat-and-mouse game that only gets interrupted by an abnormal difficulty spike in a medical ward and the game’s messy writing calling for an Alien-free section toward midway in the game.  Yes, it is frustrating, but the immersion factor keeps you playing.  If you are anything like me, you’ll be more connected to the complicated history of Sevastopol (told through the computer and audio logs of its residents) than you ever will be with the main characters of the game.
The best way I can summarize this game is that it captures everything about the original Alien movie *except* a cast of great characters and a sense of conclusion.  This is a game that only will ever truly seem to stop until you simply stop playing it.  This game is indeed a triumph for the Alien franchise, but lacks the storytelling and sense of climax and closure the first Alien movie us.  It’s not a game you can replay to get served the same enjoyable meal again; it’s more like to experience the same mental high that will satisfy, but ultimately fade away and leave you burnt out until the next time you are ready to experience the terror of the Alien once more.

How much testing was applied to this game, prior to release?  I can only assume none, because otherwise it would simply not be possible for me to be so utterly unable to proceed after walking down just one corridor and speaking with one character.
I’ve verified that the bugs that I’ve experienced are known issues on the publisher’s web site and have tried all of their suggestions, to no avail, despite at least one of the issues having been formally reported for over two months.  Given that the administrators of that site now appear to be banning new registrations on their forums, it looks like I will not be able to report my experience with any of the errors that I have encounted or any others that I might find in future.

I'm relatively new to the gaming world, but this game transcends everything I've ever seen in the medium.
It has so many different ways to appeal to the players, first off. Amazing story with astounding amounts of lore? Check. First person shooter? Check. RPG Elements that aren't overpowered by gunfire? Check. Incredibly scary atmosphere that could make the most strong minded powerful man curl up into a ball and cry? Check. Enemies that act as more than just bullet sponges? Check.
The graphics are dated, but really, for 1999, the graphics themselves were far ahead of their time. It shouldn't be a problem, because the gameplay is the best you'll find anywhere. I could pick my brain trying to find a flaw in this game, but it's just so...perfect.
The atmosphere. Alone on a spaceship. No one to help you but yourself. Infected crew members. Just...agghhh. The atmosphere is terrifying no matter who you are. It screws with your head on so many different levels, and then, after it reaches the top level of screwing with your head, it keeps tormenting you. The fear flows throughout your whole body and you'll have insane knee-jerk movements and will jump at ANYTHING if you're playing this - whether it be in the game or in real life. This game will scare you in ways you've never been scared before.
The FPS aspects are also more than just "Kill, complete objective, kill." The weapons can become damaged and ammo is scarce, so hoard that stuff like you're trying to get on a bad reality TV show. The RPG elements aren't just there to look pretty, either. They WILL affect your gameplay and you need to do more than just "oh, I'll allocate the cyber modules to this skill because the place to do that is right here next to me." You need to plan out what you improve on and put a lot of thought into it. Cyber Modules, like ammo, are scarce, and if you waste any you're S.O.L.
This game is much more psychological, in case you couldn't tell. It's scary, but it scares you in ways that don't need a lot of violence or blood or anything like that - the fear you feel is genuine fear. It also makes you put thought into the most trivial things and the game can get impossible if you ♥♥♥♥ up too many times with your judgement. First playthrough, I didn't get a single point in my research skill until I *had* to to continue the game, and even after that, I neglected the invaluable skill that I'd find to be a necessity for the survival of all classes. What happened?
I didn't research things, naturally. I didn't know that'd come back to bite me in the♥♥♥♥♥so hard, but it did, and the game got INSANELY difficult because I went the wrong way with my cyber modules. I actually had to backtrack and dig in every nook and cranny in the spaceship to get some to up my research skill, but I was lucky that I found enough to up it to a barely adequate level.
Point in me telling this? If you make poor judgement calls, the game doesn't give you a break.
Hmmm...there's pretty much something for everyone in this game. The only type of person I *wouldn't* rec this game to is someone who doesn't like horror at all, because this game is scary as *♥♥♥♥.* Other than that, buy it. It'd be the best 10 dollars you've ever spent.

It is a much lighter form of fantasy than what we are used to as an audience these days, filled with a lightheartedness that sets the player at ease despite the somtimes dire events transpiring in the story. Filled with multiple paths to success, the game draws replay value from the people you help. How you choose to go about your quests and aiding in their lives will casue them to have different reactions to your progression through the game. Their favor waxing and waning based on how you choose to approach a problem.
When combined with a simple yet effective soundtrack and memorable voice acting the game comes together wonderfully and makes for great relaxing fun. It's art style at once feels like an old style animated adventure movie and a finely polished modern game.
All in all this game is worth buying and playing whenever you have the chance to do so.

So after spending 15 hours of real time, and 89 in game days, I finally reached the FINAL note left for Beatrix in The Glass Desert!
(I'm assuming the end of the game is here, if its not, please correct me)
Honestly, the game is phenomenal, something that seems so childish, yet has such a fantasitc story behind the scenes, you just have to read between the lines.
All the notes, they coalesce into a huge story about H's life out on the Far, Far Range, ranchin' away at what seems like his dedication. But as found from the notes he leaves: He's going on an adventure!
Now I took the story as a story of love; letting your heart make decisions just as much as your head makes them!
The game? Blew me away with that, because I've never known a story to be based on love at the end. This whole story hypes you up near the end, gets you thinking: "Wow, a warp terminal?! This MUST be awesome!" But then the story turns around completely... He didn't go... And by the visible debris of the pillars: It shows that Beatrix isn't going anywhere either!
-Now for the general quick review on the game itself-
Pros:
-The games optimised brilliantly
-Semi-Simplistic graphics, nothing to demanding, so most pc's can run it efficiently
-Fantastic Story/Lore
-Brilliant Soundtrack
-Overall fun for any age group
Cons:
-Repetitive gameplay (eg: grinding for NewBucks)
-Area prices are too high and it means you have to do SO much more to afford them
-Jetpack doesn't feel like a Jetpack, but a OP Pressure Washer... -- ... One that dispenses bubbles
And thats about it... I hope you enjoy my review, I personally LOVE this game!
But.. I'll never play it to the end, ever again! :)

This is one of the best Total War games I've got. It has a lot of nations to play as and they're all very unique in their own way. While I have one problem with the nations, a lot of nations you have to buy in a pack which is pretty dumb because the nations you buy are already in the game, like the Greek States (which I had to buy even though they're in the game already, just not playable) other than the nations you have to buy it comes with a lot of good nations already.
Out of all the Total War games I think this one has the best combat out of them all. The older games had good combat but there was always some pretty big flaws, but in Rome II it's almost perfect.
My biggest problem with this game is how after you take over a city it takes forever for them to even get a little happy. I spoiled a city I took over and they repay me with revolts... all the time. And if you played older Total War games your first tought would be "Why don't you just keep some soldiers there so they don't rebel?" That's the thing... you can't, you have to upgrade your army to have more than abour 4 different armies, and you can't have a lone platoon anymore, they have to be with a general. And that's really my only issues.

One of my favorite things about Bioshock is knowing an area through exploration and audio logs you find along the way. System Shock 2 even with its limited technological resources (which I'm sure was good for 1999) contextualizes every single area both physically with environment and objects and through the story told with great voice acting. Nothing randomly generated or repeated designs or any lame bull like that. Every place you visit and every area you explore seems to have a purpose. Spent a good 30 hours. Well, 22 hours in game. You know how Steam is. All that quality time in the start menu! lol
I got the sense of a real ship. I felt the size and scale just by exploring each deck. Though it has a fine selection of weapons, certain things about combat is of course a little wonky. Melee hits are whatever your weapon hits in 3D space first moving from a left to right swing. There's actually an option for overhead swing so it seems this was intentional. All PSI (space magic) abilities are used through a weapon. Unfortunately there's no quick way of changing or even binding specific abilities and using inventory for selection is real time. That means enemies are chomping on you while you switch from usefull boost to deadly force. These are my only complaints.
A well established community brings you mods which are easy to install. Use the guide on the community page. It does keep faithfully to original design while upgrading to HD visuals in a much needed way.
!!! I will replay this again as an expert in Tech and a Soldier (I want to use those cool weapons!). Excelent game worth every dollar.

Now, it isn't often that I found a game difficult to play but this might be because I'm jumping from newer games to a retro game.
System Shock 2 was fun at first, but it got old quickly. Now, this is by no means a bad game- there is a ton of story to unravel and there is a wide variety of playing style. Now, since I have the binary "Yes or no" options, I'm going to have to say "no" to if I would recommend it or not for these reasons (These are why I personally cannot recommend it I should say):
1- The graphics, although great for their time, are dated and are hard to follow
2- The game requires a great deal of focus and attention to get the most out of it
3- Things aren't really explained, security cameras are bad apparently and it's not discussed why that is until its too late
4- Weapons degrade with use and repairing them is costly, this might be the "survival horror" aspect, but the game feels more like a "stealth shooter" than a horror game.
I wasn't able to play the game as much as I wish I could. I ended up restarting my game multiple times trying to figure out what play style worked for me and really didn't find anything that suited me. Don't let my review stop you from trying it for yourself, but just be prepared that this is an older game and one of the origional "immersive horror" games... it would be like playing the origional Resident Evil game after having played Resident Evil 6- It just has a completely different feel that stands solely on the nastolgia factor.

So far, if you liked the previous game you will enjoy this one.  The story is good enough that I cannot wait to find out what is going to happen.  It also gives you the option to play without powers, while I may never personally do that it is an exciting option to have.  I may update if my thoughts of the story sour but for now I will leave it at that to not spoil much.
As far as performance goes, it tool me a while to get it to run well.  I am running an admitadly underpowered GTX 970 with an i7-4790k @ 4.7GHz so any issues that I face will most likely be graphics based.
Issue #1: Stuttering.  When climbing a wall and seeing a large open space I would get a huge lag spike.  This has seemingly been fixed by (after starting the game) raising its priority from normal to realtime.
Issue #2 Vsync:  Now I had heard that a problem of vsync is that it halves your fps, but I never experienced it, until this game. To fix it you could turn it off but the tearing was terrible. To solve it I went to the Nvidia control panel and overrode the games vsync with "fast" vsync.  So far this seems to work.
As far as settings that I found that worked well are 2560x1440 with everything set to medium except character models, which is set to high, and everything enabled.  I get some dips into the mid 50s but overall a smooth experience.  If you have a 970 and have any questions I will do my best to answer them.
Overall, the game seems to be great from both a gameplay perspective and solid (but not great) from a technical perspective.  While it should not have been released in the state that it was, the post-release support appears to be good enough.

King's Quest is a really fun, light-hearted and beautiful game that is a callback to a genre of gaming that has been lost to time.
Also the man who voiced Gaston plays a rival knight that is exactly Gaston. That's amazing on its own.
Seriously though, the cast of this game is pretty amazing, with Christopher Lloyd (Doc Brown), Zelda Williams (Robin's daughter), Wallace Shawn (Every Pixar movie ever), and even Tom Kenny (Spongebob) lending their expertise to this game, bringing each of the characters to life as well as delivering most of the humor. In a game like this, the characters are half of the experience, so it was important to get them right, and in my opinion, they were excellent. There wasn't a character I didn't enjoy talking to in the game, from the hilarious guards to the eccentric merchants; Graham's voice actors so far lend him a great personality as well, with Lloyd voicing the old Graham telling his story to a granddaughter, and Keaton being young teenaged Graham that you play as.
The gameplay itself is interesting and engaging, with exploration, puzzle-solving, and item-gathering. There's even some brief but fun combat sections with Graham and his bow.
It ditches it's "point and click" roots for a something more along the lines of a Telltale-esque narrative, but I enjoyed this one over the Telltale games that I've played. Yes, there are quick-time events, but I don't ever mind those. If you don't enjoy QTEs, they don't overstay their welcome or not make sense, IMO.
Lastly, the art is fantastic. It's like you're playing a Disney movie. It really shows how focused their vision for the reimagining of the franchise was, with pretty much every aspect of the game benefiting from the cartoony, hand-painted aesthetic. Very pleasing to look at, and the animations are great as well. Some moments in the game made me actually stop and say "That'd be a really nice painting," so I think it's safe to say the visuals only pose to enhance your experience in King's Quest.
I had a few flaws with the game, however. One being I was sometimes unaware as to what I was interacting with, which lead to sometimes re-watching the same cutscene about a sign or entering a door I just left. The environments are rather large as well, so I sometimes forgot which way I needed to go without a map of Daventry included. Some of the puzzles regarding needing certain items to progress to certain places for certain people got a bit confuzing and left me a little stumped, but once you figure them out they are fairly obvious and/or well-hinted at.
Overall I'd recommend King's Quest if you enjoy a game that doesn't take itself seriously and are a fan of the classic-styled adventure genre. I won't buy the season pass they advertise because not all of the episodes are out yet, but I do plan on eventually picking up the full game once it's chapters are available.

TLDR? Buy this game if you like cute things, farming sims, and open-world games.
Disclaimer: I bought this on sale for ~$13.50 several days after 1.0.0, so your opinion may differ if you bought it for full price in Early Access.
Core Mechanics
Slime Rancher is a unique game. It's like a mashup of a farming sim and an open-world game - but it's not entirely either of these. Instead of growing crops, you raise adorable little blobs with different features and colors, and you do unlock areas in a certain order with a format to follow. If you want, it's entirely possible to skip the Indigo Quarry or Moss Blanket, however. And Slime Rancher does actually have a story, though I won't spoil it for you.
In Slime Rancher, the vacpack is the primary way to interact with the world. You use this to catch slimes, suck up food to feed them, and shoot those things out (you can even use it to throw slimes into an incinerator if you're a HORRIBLE MONSTER), among other things. The vacpack has 4 available slots at the start of the game - each slot can hold 20 items of one particular type. Later, you can upgrade this to 60 items and 5 slots, though the last one is reserved for water. You can customize it to be a particular color, which is nice when it's the only part of Beatrix that you see for most of the game, since this is an FPS. Despite being an FPS, though, it's not violent unless you want it to be, and there's never any blood, even when feeding live chickens to slimes -- and the game still manages to maintain its cheerful vibe when doing this!
The game's progression is mainly based around plorts, the crystals that slimes... poop out. They can be exchanged at the Plort Market for cash to buy various upgrades around the ranch and for your vacpack, or you can deposit them in the Refinery in the Lab (once it's unlocked). One upgrade that you can get is high walls for your slime corrals, and these are
useful, even needed once you have enough slimes. If plorts aren't cleaned up and slimes escape, slimes will eat the plorts of another slime of a different type. This isn't just wasteful, it creates "largos," which are huge hybrid slimes that are much harder to corral. For example, a Pink Slime that eats a Phosphor Slime's plort turns into a Pink Phosphor Largo. However, if the slime then eats the plort of ANOTHER type that isn't the same as either of its types, like if our Pink Phosphor Largo eats a Tabby Plort, it turns into the horrible Tarr, which will rampage around your ranch eating all the food it can find and murdering your precious slimes until it despawns or you splash water on it. And every time it eats, it multiplies. This is where the vacpack's water upgrade comes in - you can use it to store 60 splashes of water when fully upgraded, enough to kill 30 tarr at night and 60 tarr in the day.
Personally, I like the vacpack. It does take a while to suck things up and spit things out if you're trying to do so with 40-60 items at once, but it's not that important, as it'll only take 5 seconds max to spit out 60 plorts into the plort market. However, I don't like the way the slots work. If you have 60 of one item but a free slot, you can't suck up more of that item and put it in the extra slot, which makes plort collecting tedious. You can buy plort collector upgrades for corrals, which I have, but when they reach 100 plorts they run out of room. When I'm gone collecting for a while, the corrals where I feed slimes their favorite food (which makes them produce 2 plorts each time they eat rather than 1) are usually full, meaning I have to take two trips to the Plort Market/Lab. When you have enough resources to produce teleporters, that isn't as much of a problem, since you can just set up teleporters there, but they usually need various resources that take a long time to harvest. This is especially annoying because I have Tangle and Puddle Slimes all the way down in the Docks and no teleporters to get back to the market from there.
I enjoy the automation that you can have: auto-feeders and plort collectors, but I wish there was more. I want to be able to automatically harvest crops and hens to feed to my slimes without having to go back to the ranch from exploring every day. At the end of the game, it usually takes me 30 minutes to harvest crops, clean up plorts, stock the auto-feeders, and possibly recharge my water before I can go back out. That's without teleporters, though. I seem to remember the devs stating that there will be drones in some future update, which might do this. If so, I would love it.
I also think it's good that you have to be careful not to make mistakes with Largos, as it gives a bit of conflict and danger to the game. It would be nice if we could have regular slime-sized hybrids, though. I'd really like to keep a bunch of Honey Mosaic Slimes rather than a few Largos. And we need puddle/fire largos. My idea for the implementation of that would be putting plorts in the pond with puddle slimes, which turn them into largos and incinerating plorts for the fire slimes.
Characters
There are not very many characters in the game. Hobson, Thora, Viktor, Ogden, Casey, BOb, Mochi, Casey, and obviously Beatrix are the only characters, and you never see them in person (
BOb hOOmin tRusT meE. chIkkNN). This is where the game falters a bit. Looking at Beatrix, the devs can obviously make a human model that doesn't look creepy (something that older games tend to have trouble with), so why aren't there visible NPCs? It makes the world very lonely, which doesn't seem to fit with the cheerful, colorful terrain and slimes. Portal doesn't have NPCs, but it fits with the game because of the gloomy theme. Maybe we'll be able to meet Mochi and Ogden in the upcoming updates, though Mochi may be the most obnoxious and snotty video game character I've ever seen.
Graphics
The devs did a very good job at making slimes seem realistic in the way they move and bounce, and the textures are often very realistic, such as with the Fire Slime and the Mosaic Slime. The terrain is distinguished in various areas -- I can certainly tell the difference between the Moss Blanket and the Glass Desert (which, by the way, is beautiful after the oases are restored. I'm not sure why people have complained about it on here). I don't have a graphics card -- broke student -- so I play the game on low graphics quality with no antialiasing and on a lower resolution. It still looks pretty good and I only experience minor hitches and framerate drops, usually in areas with a lot of slimes and/or chickens.
Level Design
The level design is generally good and feels free while still blocking off certain areas using Slime Gates, but in some places, you can get over Slime Gates. I first accessed the Moss Blanket by jetpacking over the gate, and I believe I somehow managed to get into the entrance to the Ancient Ruins armed with only a LOT of determination and a grand total of zero slime keys. One other glitch that I experienced also left a sour taste in my mouth: I had just caught a lot of Dervish Slimes and several Fire Slimes, Mosaic Slimes, and Tangle Slimes on my first trip to the Glass Desert. I hadn't fed the Tangle Gordo yet, since I didn't bring enough meat, and I hadn't seen the teleporter near the entrance to the Glass Desert, so I tried to go back through the Ancient Ruins. For some reason, when I started dashing, I fell through the floor. Thankfully, there was another floor beneath it, so I just jetpacked back up through it, but later, I fell through another floor into the Slime Sea because my jetpack wouldn't work to get me out.
There were no gnomes in the walls. Monomi Park lied to me.
Music
I quite enjoyed most of the tracks. I have to say, though, that '1,000 Light Years Away' didn't really appeal to me. I'm just not big on country.

Were I to be reviewing this a few days, or even 6 months after release, this would be a very different review. Plagued by all the problems that indicated an early release the game was a shambles. 15 patches later and it is now worth playing. The recent 'Emperor Edition' update feels like a new game entirely. It isn't quite at the lofty heights of Shogun 2's last expansion pack (our last play of the franchise, and in my opinion the best of it) but it is at least trying to reach those heights rather than sort of rolling around on the ground below throwing up on itself.
The innovations of the title are given time to shine as the bugs recede. It is a graphically beautiful game, with great animations and a real sense of scale. The politics system has been revamped and while not as in depth as I would've liked (I would like them to take cues from Crusader Kings) has slightly more point to it now.
There is huge unit diversity, a massive map, a more interesting end game and an interesting economic system that again has been changed to make more sense.
If you held off til now to play it, lucky you, it is now worth your time.

Just Cause 3 has quite a standard to live up to, seeing as Just Cause 2 was one of the greatest games of all time. Does it succeed? Well, first of all, yes, but it takes a bit of explaining. If Just Cause 2 was a perfect, exact square -here meaning rudimentary, straightforward game mechanics polished to the point of near-perfection- then Just Cause 3 is a perfect circle; really smoothed-out and refined game mechanics that are also really well polished. Think of it this way: Go open Just Cause 2 and do that thing where you save yourself from falling to death by grappling into the ground directly below you. Then do the same thing in Just Cause 3. Notice how in Just Cause 3 it looks and feels really good and believable (almost), but in Just Cause 2 the inherent jolt and speed of the grappling hook bring the joke across better? That's the difference between Just Causes 2 and 3 in a nutshell.
Just Cause 2's biggest issues were problems with difficulty management and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ character animation in cutscenes. Just Cause 3 fixes the animation issue by, well, fixing it, and the difficulty management issue by just drastically lowering the difficulty. That's a fine way to solve the problem, but by no means the best one. As for its own issues, Just Cause 3 is really technically demanding, which has elicited many a complaint from the PC Gaming Master Race. I won't say their claims aren't justified, as slowdown and lag are more the exception than the rule, especially at first, but I used to run and play in a private Minecraft server a lot from an HP laptop that was cheap back in 2010. Try me.
In order to say more things quickly, I'm going to do a Can and Can't list of departures from Just Cause 2.
Unlike Just Cause 2, in Just Cause 3 you can...
...walk around on vehicles
...regenerate health fully, negating the need for health items. I find that regenerating health works best in non-combat games as a sort of slap on the wrist, essentially warning the player to avoid hazards (Portal, for example). Therefore, for Just Cause 3, the regenerating health works well when just screwing around in the world, exploring and blowing things up, but in combat it just does what regenerating health normally does (remove all stakes).
...use the wingsuit. Gameplay element of the f*cking year. It's like flight, but with limitations adding challenge and interest.
...place infinite explosives (yay).
...hack SAMS to be on your side, which I almost never bother to do because it's easier to just shoot them.
...look at the beautiful world, graphics, and aesthetic.
...destroy even more cooler stuff in awesomer ways, which is awesome. I could spend the rest of the review describing all the cool ways to break and explode things and it still wouldn't be enough space. Suffice it to say that my favorite thing to do in the whole game is to try and destroy a bridge as slowly and indirectly as possible, with as many casualties as I can in the process.
...get an airstrike called on your♥♥♥♥♥ which basically is the game telling you to keep moving.
..."Liberate" provinces in the normal sandbox reclaim-the-map kind of way.
...use and contract multiple tethers, which is great but requires the hookshot controls to be overhauled from Just Cause 2, which takes some getting used to.
...buy more than one thing at once, without the need for money.
...do challenges to acquire and improve abilities, which is nice.
...reuse your goddamn parachute.
...hack things and hijack vehicles without doing a pointless minigame.
...do little random encounters.
...play on trains. (Good God, the trains...)
...fire two-handed weapons while grappled to something.
...have an explosive weapon at all times.
..."Re-Oppress" settlements to conquer them again once you've beaten the game, which is great.
Unlike Just Cause 2, in Just Cause 3 you can't...
...do a cute little flip when closing a parachute from high up.
..get into a "skydiving" pose from as low to the ground, or maneuver as well when skydiving (well, that's what the wingsuit is for).
...see your health, or a minimap.
...see nearly as many spectacular atmospheric effects.
...fire a minigun without a lengthy spinup.
...cling to the sides of vehicles.
...spin out cars in cathartic ways.
...die by hitting water (cool).
...airdrop in a new vehicle if you destroy yours mid-race.
...pick up crates to get upgrade points for armor, weapons, and vehicles, or cash.
...do missions for three different factions, two of whom's leaders seem to be flirting with you.
...crouch, roll, or sprint.
...carry two distinct one-handed weapons.
...get in a vehicle without a handheld device; it's purely visual, but it bugs me.
...hold your breath for nearly as long.
...get your hands on a GV-104 Razorback.
...order a vehicle twice within a certain timespan (can upgrade to fix).
...suspend people in the air with bullets.
...get halfway wet.
...lose all momentum when firing hookshot every time.
...pull people by hookshotting them; instead, you do a less convenient but BADASS hookshot kick.
...save, and reload on death; instead, you just do an anomalous respawn, which I never like because it adds to the prevalent feeling that Rico has somehow become less competent since Just Cause 2.
I liked Rico better when he was an insane Hispanic man, not a good-hearted but rough-edged Mediterranean man.
There's less weapon variety, even though there are more weapons because they're all variants on pistols, assault rifles, and SMGs.
There are fewer settlements, but the ones that are there are vastly more visually interesting and cleverly designed than in Just Cause 2. You can spend up to half an hour slowly taking apart just one, flying around and blasting away.
Blood color in any media is often a good indicator of tone; the more seriously death is taken, the darker. In Fallout 3, for instance, it's a very dark shade of red, while in Team Fortress 2 it's practically f*ckin' orange. Just Cause 2 was a bit weird in that the blood color was really dark even though you force people hundreds of feet into the air through the sheer power of sustained minigun fire alone. Just Cause 3 solves this issue with a fairly middle-of-the-road shade.
Terrain variety is less ridiculous, at least at first. When you get to the main island you start to get your snowy mountains right next to deserts and whatnot.
This game takes the Just Cause Idea (massive island nation, lots of mobility and destruction, evil dictator, Rico f*cking Rodriguez) to its logical conclusion. Is that entirely a good thing? It's hard to say. Just Cause 3 is more viscerally fun and replayable than its immediate predecessor, but Just Cause 2 commands this respect and awe that Just Cause 3 (or indeed, any other game) can't quite seem to muster. In the end, I can't decide which is better. However, since Just Cause 2 was and is one of the greatest games ever made, you should get Just Cause 3 as well, preferably as soon as possible. It's fun, it's massive, it has this wonderful sense of freedom, and it's one of those games that's just happy to be alive.
Rico Rodriguez. The man who could fly.

System shock was the second game I ever played on steam and even now I still play this game. (for whatever reason, I still enjoy it.) I recommend playing this game at night, so that it adds more to the eerie feeling of the game. Technically speaking, this is supposed to be a horror game, but at most this would just make you jump a bit from your seat. The game is a bit tricky to play, and sometimes the puzzles require you go to a specific place to do a specific thing, which may sound simple under context, but you are under no instructions to do this -- You are basically put in a hallway and you are forced to understand and to solve the everything thrown your way, (which makes the game a bit up to interpretation) which is great if you are into that sort of thing. The only help you get is a voice that talks to you (under random periods may I add, which may scare you, since it usually happens when you least expect it.)  if you are going into the correct general area, but it's not frequent enough to be a good or very helpful guide, and sometimes if you skip an area of the game, the voice indicates that you should still keep going (so you basically skip a part of the necessary plot, but can still keep going.) On the subject of the plot, the plot has a bit of an outdated feeling (Not as outdated as the look of the graphics though.) but it's still an overall enjoyable experience.
I recommend this game, partially because of the nostalgia, but also because it's just a great concept that still attracts regardless of the age.

Advanced Warfare is more of the same of what you'd expect from a typical COD game. The campaign features the same type of linear mission structures that were present in the first Modern Warfare, and the AIs have not improved much, if at all. As for the storyline, it's rather simplistic; while it certainly isn't the best in the series, it has a much better plot than Modern Warfare 3's campaign, by comparison.
The multiplayer and co-op are pretty forgettable, for the most part. The exoskeleton serves practically no purpose at all to the online component of this game, since most people are usually camping in annoying locations and picking off targets at random (in addition, using the boost ability is a surefire way to get yourself noticed and killed).
So, in summary, if you're looking for an innovative COD game, Advanced Warfare is not the game to get. I also got cursed out by some squeakers who are way to young to be playing M-Rated games - so, there's nothing new there, either.

After two playthroughs, and most of the way through a (no-powers) third, I am still in awe of this game.  The flexibility of approach it allows, and the level design is astounding.  The inevitable "take your powers away" segment is even made enjoyable.
I'd go as far as saying this is the new Deus Ex in terms of how many ways you can approach each situation.
Hint: play as Emily, and make full use of her power set.  Leave the no-kill or full-stealth runs to a later play through.
From a technical perspective, I've been playing the game at a combination of very high/high settings on a i5-4670K and GTX 1070.  Other than an occasional hitch when TXAA is enabled, performance has been smooth.  This has mostly been with Update 1.2 onwards.

Kings quest returns.  Is it worth going back to Daventry?  Hell yes, it is.  This game does have it's problems, but it brings back adventure games in a different form but an equally enchanting vibe.  The story is both funny and often times somber, showing the growth of our great hero, King Graham ans his journey from boy to knight.  It uses inventory puzzles like it's predecessors, but also uses third person controls to make it feel like you are more in control of Graham, along with a few light actions sequences.
Overall, I found the characters to be charming and the world bright, vibrant, and colorful.  The inventory puzzles are clever and true to adventure games past, you can complete the game without all the secrets, but you can also do one better and help everyone.  You can also win a duel using a custard pie.  Because Kings Quest.  The game oozes charm and a unique fairy tale vibe, with some nice musical throwbacks to the original game and an all star cast, featuring Christopher Lloyd and Josh Keaton as King Graham in his old and young personas respectively.  Great stuff.
On the negative side, the game can be a bit slow pacing wise, as you look for the items you need to solve the next inventory puzzle and it can be a bit annoying backtracking all over the place.  The climax is also a bit underwhelming, as it lacks tension, even if it is really fun and funny to playthrough.  They go through the climax of the game pretty early on, unfortunately.
That aside, is the game worth the price?  Certainly, I'd say.  Each episode is worth a playthrough as they give a decent amount of time, but episode 1 is a great re-introduction for old fans or a good start for new fans as well.  Good times.  I'm proud to say, Kings Quest is back and is awesome.

Slime Ranchor is a fun game. But it depends on the person and what type of games you like.

It's adorable, no doubt. It's well made and the mechanics are easy to understand and grasp. Graphically it's nothing great, but the art style makes up for it completely. The game world is large and sectioned, making knowing where you are and how to get there easier with every passing. The game has a day/night cycle that has a moderate gameplay effect. Certain slimes can only be found at night and the evil Tarr seem to only be around at night as well. However, in the end, this is a upgrade grind at it's core. Now that isn't neccessarily a bad thing, if that's your enjoyment. It certainly makes the start at the bottom work to the top formula fun, cute and somewhat interesting. You can mix slimes to create new ones, typically large hybrids of the smaller ones. There is some minor quests under the story/primary quest of becoming the greatest rancher of slimes ever in the galaxy, these minor quests are basically trade requests from NPCs, "Give me X many of this, Y many of that and I'll give you these things". The requests seem to usually be pretty difficult for new players to get and the reward not really worth it.
The game is mostly based on building ranching structures and finding things to populate those structures. You have slime corrals, chicken coops and gardens. Basically your slimes and the two food types. The structures can be upgraded to make ranching easier and growing faster, you can upgrade your character to hold more stuff, run longer and jump higher. Again, this is a upgrade grind. All the 'new' stuff you come across is just a variation of the old stuff. Pink slime, blue slime, rock slime, glowing slime, explosive slime.The more dangerous it is the more valuable it is. Getting these rarer slime are all about upgrading your stuff to explore the more hard to get to areas and earning enough money to buy access to these other place. Everything in the game can be acheived by wash, rinse, repeat gameplay. If you have the patience you will eventually win, even with the cheapest lowest slimes the game has, everything is just a matter of money.
For me the game fell short in that there wasn't much dynamic to the play. The 'night' which at the beginning you are warned to stay in and not go out, is barely more dangerous than the day. Tarrs can be bothersome but they can be sprayed with water OR you can just suck them up and shoot them into the ocean or over a cliff. While there is plenty to explore I felt like a lot wasn't explained, there are locked doors requiring slime keys and these treasure orbs all over the place, but I have no idea how to open them. There are really big giant slimes that don't move, don't eat, can't be picked up either and just kind of ... sleep. I guess in the end, I didn't feel like it was much of a challenge. It was just a matter of having the patience to repeat the motions until victory. I would have been more interested if there was some sort of 'defense' gameplay during the night, build turrets to defend your property from nasty Tarrs that come to raid you in the night. The treasure 'crates' you find randomly also very disappointing, even when they burst with coins you don't get any money from them, they typically have a few carrots (most common food in the game) and maybe a chicken or plort. I guess for me, just because a game LOOKS like a kids game doesn't mean it is a kids game, however this plays very much like a childrens game with some slightly more advanced mechanics. There's nothing wrong with it, it just doesn't provide any real challenge and while I was hoping for something rather diverse, after researching it I found there are only maybe 2 dozen types of slimes in the game world, maybe 3 dozen if you count the largo types and all the mixes you can make with them. In the end, I returned this one. I will probably buy it again someday though, when I'm in a mood to just aimlessly farm some slimes, it certainly is enjoyable if you want something mind numbing to just pass the time and relax with. For the time being though it just isn't what I'm looking for.

I must admit when I first saw images and videos of this game I was very skeptical and thought "this looks childish and empty". Being a fan of farming games like Harvest Moon, Stardew Valley and heck even Animal Crossing which between the three I've probably sunk hundreds if not thousands of hours into I was longing for something new and fresh. (even though Stardew valley is new and fresh) I wanted something a bit different in perspective. After watching a couple reviews I finally decided to jump the gun a try Slime Rancher. Now I must say I LOVE that this game has a demo offer, I feel not enough games offer this anymore, they just want your money upfront and expect full commitment from the consumer. I decided to try the demo annnd the rest is history. I was immediately hooked and spent the next hour chasing slimes, collecting poop and at one point even watched in horror as I accidentally mixed the wrong slimes and within seconds had my entire ranch destroyed by Tar Slimes!!
This games sucks you in from the start, its intuitive, responsive and manages to keep you engaged. This really is one of those "one more day" type of games. If you think you are going to sit down and play this for 10-15 min THINK AGAIN! There's always something new to explore, work towards and experiment with. Creating new slimes (largos) through experimentation can be really rewarding or extremely dangerous (the latter which I experienced). But even after my ranch was wiped clean by the Tar Slimes I didn't feel the need to rage quite, In fact I actually sat there watching in horror and disbelief and was actually somewhat amused by what was taking place in front of me. All my hard work was gone within seconds, I attempted to run around capturing and tossing the Tar Slimes over the edge into the ocean but my attempts were futile as they multiplied faster than a couple of horny hamsters! After all was said and done I chuckled and thought "well...not going to do that again" and quickly researched how to effectively combat the Tar Slimes. I spent the next hour rebuilding my ranch, having just as much if not more fun than the first time and I felt like although I lost everything I was better off for it with the knew knowledge I had.
This game is very much about exploration, experimentation and that light lingering feeling that all hell could break lose at any moment, but it doesn't discourage you or frustrate at any point but gives you something to continue working towards.
I highly recommend this to anyone who enjoys farming or casual games, you have to enjoy grinding a bit and doing the same tasks over and over in order to like this game as it is repetitive in a sense but it does a good job of keeping you engaged. I do wish there was a bit more customization in the layout and overall design features of the ranch, it is currently very "structured" in where you can set up your pens and doesn't give you a lot of freedom in creating your own unique ranch like Stardew Valley does so be aware of that. If you are looking for a game with tons of customization and building this doesn't have it (at least not from what I could see) if I am wrong someone please let me know.
Overall great game with good game play and aesthetics that provides some memorable moments and makes you lose track of time, highly recommend it if you are looking for a new "farming" simulator.

Just Cause 3 has quite a standard to live up to, seeing as Just Cause 2 was one of the greatest games of all time. Does it succeed? Well, first of all, yes, but it takes a bit of explaining. If Just Cause 2 was a perfect, exact square -here meaning rudimentary, straightforward game mechanics polished to the point of near-perfection- then Just Cause 3 is a perfect circle; really smoothed-out and refined game mechanics that are also really well polished. Think of it this way: Go open Just Cause 2 and do that thing where you save yourself from falling to death by grappling into the ground directly below you. Then do the same thing in Just Cause 3. Notice how in Just Cause 3 it looks and feels really good and believable (almost), but in Just Cause 2 the inherent jolt and speed of the grappling hook bring the joke across better? That's the difference between Just Causes 2 and 3 in a nutshell.
Just Cause 2's biggest issues were problems with difficulty management and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ character animation in cutscenes. Just Cause 3 fixes the animation issue by, well, fixing it, and the difficulty management issue by just drastically lowering the difficulty. That's a fine way to solve the problem, but by no means the best one. As for its own issues, Just Cause 3 is really technically demanding, which has elicited many a complaint from the PC Gaming Master Race. I won't say their claims aren't justified, as slowdown and lag are more the exception than the rule, especially at first, but I used to run and play in a private Minecraft server a lot from an HP laptop that was cheap back in 2010. Try me.
In order to say more things quickly, I'm going to do a Can and Can't list of departures from Just Cause 2.
Unlike Just Cause 2, in Just Cause 3 you can...
...walk around on vehicles
...regenerate health fully, negating the need for health items. I find that regenerating health works best in non-combat games as a sort of slap on the wrist, essentially warning the player to avoid hazards (Portal, for example). Therefore, for Just Cause 3, the regenerating health works well when just screwing around in the world, exploring and blowing things up, but in combat it just does what regenerating health normally does (remove all stakes).
...use the wingsuit. Gameplay element of the f*cking year. It's like flight, but with limitations adding challenge and interest.
...place infinite explosives (yay).
...hack SAMS to be on your side, which I almost never bother to do because it's easier to just shoot them.
...look at the beautiful world, graphics, and aesthetic.
...destroy even more cooler stuff in awesomer ways, which is awesome. I could spend the rest of the review describing all the cool ways to break and explode things and it still wouldn't be enough space. Suffice it to say that my favorite thing to do in the whole game is to try and destroy a bridge as slowly and indirectly as possible, with as many casualties as I can in the process.
...get an airstrike called on your♥♥♥♥♥ which basically is the game telling you to keep moving.
..."Liberate" provinces in the normal sandbox reclaim-the-map kind of way.
...use and contract multiple tethers, which is great but requires the hookshot controls to be overhauled from Just Cause 2, which takes some getting used to.
...buy more than one thing at once, without the need for money.
...do challenges to acquire and improve abilities, which is nice.
...reuse your goddamn parachute.
...hack things and hijack vehicles without doing a pointless minigame.
...do little random encounters.
...play on trains. (Good God, the trains...)
...fire two-handed weapons while grappled to something.
...have an explosive weapon at all times.
..."Re-Oppress" settlements to conquer them again once you've beaten the game, which is great.
Unlike Just Cause 2, in Just Cause 3 you can't...
...do a cute little flip when closing a parachute from high up.
..get into a "skydiving" pose from as low to the ground, or maneuver as well when skydiving (well, that's what the wingsuit is for).
...see your health, or a minimap.
...see nearly as many spectacular atmospheric effects.
...fire a minigun without a lengthy spinup.
...cling to the sides of vehicles.
...spin out cars in cathartic ways.
...die by hitting water (cool).
...airdrop in a new vehicle if you destroy yours mid-race.
...pick up crates to get upgrade points for armor, weapons, and vehicles, or cash.
...do missions for three different factions, two of whom's leaders seem to be flirting with you.
...crouch, roll, or sprint.
...carry two distinct one-handed weapons.
...get in a vehicle without a handheld device; it's purely visual, but it bugs me.
...hold your breath for nearly as long.
...get your hands on a GV-104 Razorback.
...order a vehicle twice within a certain timespan (can upgrade to fix).
...suspend people in the air with bullets.
...get halfway wet.
...lose all momentum when firing hookshot every time.
...pull people by hookshotting them; instead, you do a less convenient but BADASS hookshot kick.
...save, and reload on death; instead, you just do an anomalous respawn, which I never like because it adds to the prevalent feeling that Rico has somehow become less competent since Just Cause 2.
I liked Rico better when he was an insane Hispanic man, not a good-hearted but rough-edged Mediterranean man.
There's less weapon variety, even though there are more weapons because they're all variants on pistols, assault rifles, and SMGs.
There are fewer settlements, but the ones that are there are vastly more visually interesting and cleverly designed than in Just Cause 2. You can spend up to half an hour slowly taking apart just one, flying around and blasting away.
Blood color in any media is often a good indicator of tone; the more seriously death is taken, the darker. In Fallout 3, for instance, it's a very dark shade of red, while in Team Fortress 2 it's practically f*ckin' orange. Just Cause 2 was a bit weird in that the blood color was really dark even though you force people hundreds of feet into the air through the sheer power of sustained minigun fire alone. Just Cause 3 solves this issue with a fairly middle-of-the-road shade.
Terrain variety is less ridiculous, at least at first. When you get to the main island you start to get your snowy mountains right next to deserts and whatnot.
This game takes the Just Cause Idea (massive island nation, lots of mobility and destruction, evil dictator, Rico f*cking Rodriguez) to its logical conclusion. Is that entirely a good thing? It's hard to say. Just Cause 3 is more viscerally fun and replayable than its immediate predecessor, but Just Cause 2 commands this respect and awe that Just Cause 3 (or indeed, any other game) can't quite seem to muster. In the end, I can't decide which is better. However, since Just Cause 2 was and is one of the greatest games ever made, you should get Just Cause 3 as well, preferably as soon as possible. It's fun, it's massive, it has this wonderful sense of freedom, and it's one of those games that's just happy to be alive.

I have played many a licensed Alien game from Aliens for the Commodore 64, through the console wars with Alien 3, to the many FPS incarnations that have popped up now and again for PC.  Every time I am excited, and every time I am let down in some way.  However, Alien Isolation seems to have gotten it right this time.  There are some negative reviews out there, mostly from the vocal but meager followers of the FPS’ who are generally not pleased with a game title unless there are large guns to blow up even larger baddies with.
Alien Isolation feels very much like the first Alien movie, as it is geared more towards the survival and suspense that made that film such a success.  Though I found the survival aspect to be tedious at times as your life pool is very small, I feel that the game made up for it with a story that fits well into existing canon, and the general ambiance that you find yourself in as you explore.
For fans of Alien this is a must play.  For fans of Aliens vs Predator, this might be a bit slow for you.
